Rating this game by any objective metric is impossible for anyone that played it when they were young.

Not only that but putting into words what is felt when this game is mentioned is also nigh impossible - if I were put next to someone that never owned a PC for gaming in their entire life and I was tasked to explain why Counter-Strike is a good game, the sheer amount of emotions pouring in would make it literally impossible to properly describe why a video game can have such a huge impact on someone without that other person experiencing the same thing in their childhood.

This game was to kids gaming on a PC in the late 90s and early 2000s what Mario was to NES owners, what Final Fantasy 7 was to PS1 owners, what Pac-Man was to 80s kids, what League of Legends and Minecraft were to people in the 2010s.

This game is also still just as good as it was back then, but times change, of course younger people won't go back and play these games forever, and that's normal. People that grew up on CS surely didn't go back and play games like Wizardry 1 or Doom deathmatching - hell people that grew up on CS didn't even go back to Quake, let alone older games lol.

The simple answer as to what makes CS so good isn't in explaining it, it's in pointing out how its current successor, CS2, is one of the most popular and successful e-sports and in general multiplayer games to ever exist (even with its many, many flaws compared to CSGO that came before it) - and it did that by just lightly evolving the formula this game invented (and which Source and CSGO then evolved again and again). That type of multiplayer purity can never age badly - CS doesn't control badly, CS doesn't look bad, CS doesn't in the slightest have bad audio design, because CS transcends any form of aging game design. It's just perfect.

CS 1.6 is one big time capsule of internet culture - from media outside the game, to mods, to the players and their archaic in game nicks, to the mechanics and aesthetics - it's a time capsule that showcases what peak multiplayer PC gaming was (and by some metrics still is) - it's competitive, it's moddable, it's casual, it's cultural, it's e-sports and it's innovation.

It's not usually mentioned among the discussions of best games ever in the mainstream - those focus more on technological advancements and singleplayer games (mostly console ones even then) - but there's a reason Valve put that "Play the world's number 1 online action game" sentence in the description here on Steam, even though the era of that sentence being literally true passed a long, long time ago.

Counter-Strike 1.6 wasn’t just a game for me — it was a part of my life. I remember skipping classes just to go to the gaming hall, where me and my friends would spend hours playing together. Time didn’t matter — all that mattered were the rounds, the maps, and the fun.

I lost entire nights on LAN parties, playing with people I didn’t even know, who quickly became friends after a few matches. The atmosphere was unforgettable: shouting, laughing, nerves, jokes, and the thrill of every clutch. CS 1.6 had something special, something you rarely find in games today.

I absolutely loved Zombie Mod and Surf. Those mods completely changed the game and made every session different. You’d log in for “just 10 minutes” and hours would pass without you noticing.

Because of CS 1.6, back in 2009, I got my first PC and internet. This game introduced me to the world of gaming, taught me to love competition, and showed me the magic of online communities. Without CS 1.6, I probably wouldn’t have grown to love CS:GO as much as I do now.

CS 1.6 will always remain a legendary classic, a game that shaped a generation and, for me, will never die. It wasn’t just a game — it was the beginning.

Counter-Strike is pure history. This is the game that defined competitive shooters for an entire generation and still feels iconic to this day.

At its core, the gameplay is simple and skill-based, aim, movement, map knowledge, and teamwork. In classic competitive modes there are no built-in abilities or gimmicks, which is why every round feels earned.

That said, the community servers are a whole different world. There are countless mods and modes like COD, Hide and seek, servers with abilities, parachutes, double jumps, and custom mechanics that completely change how the game plays. This variety is a huge reason the game stayed alive for so many years.

This game was addictive, I’ve personally played for three days straight, slept for a few hours, and jumped right back in again. That says everything about how gripping it can be.

The maps are legendary, the sound design is unforgettable, and even with outdated graphics, the gameplay remains timeless.

Whether you played competitive, casual, or spent endless hours on modded servers, Counter-Strike is one of those games everyone should experience at least once.

Counter-Strike 1.6 is one of the most influential and well designed team based shooters in gaming history. At its core the game is simple, one team tries to complete an objective while the other team works to stop them. Despite this simplicity, the game requires skill, strategy and coordination to succeed. I have around 2500 hours in CSGO/CS2 but I have not played CS 1.6 extensively and tried it mainly to experience how the gameplay worked. Even with limited time, the pacing, movement and map design feel different and interesting.

The game emphasizes teamwork and communication. Each player has a role, whether holding a position, providing cover or supporting teammates. Maps encourage strategy and careful movement, and learning the layout is important for success. Small decisions, like timing attacks or choosing when to move, can change the outcome of a round. Players gradually improve by practicing, observing others and understanding both maps and opponents.

Overall, Counter-Strike 1.6 shows how team based gameplay can create a competitive and cooperative experience. Success depends not just on individual skill, but also on communication, timing and planning. Even years after its release, it remains a clear example of classic tactical shooters and helps explain the foundations of modern games like CS GO and CS2.

Team Fortress Classic is a pivotal piece of gaming history whose influence far exceeds its modern playability. As the foundation for the class-based shooter genre, its DNA is visible everywhere today. Yet, returning to it now reveals a game that is equal parts charming, raw, and frustratingly dated.

Strengths: Pure, Archetypal Design
Long before "hero shooters," TFC established the iconic class roster—Scout, Soldier, Heavy, Medic, and others—that remains a blueprint. Each role is distinct and mechanically pure. The exhilaration of the Scout’s speed, the skill-ceiling of rocket jumping, and the mind-games of the Spy still shine. Its simplicity is a virtue: objectives are clear, combat is swift, and there’s a refreshing lack of modern clutter like unlocks or microtransactions. It’s pure, skill-based gameplay.

Weaknesses: Dated and Unforgiving
However, that simplicity feels archaic today. Movement is fast but lacks polish, weapon feedback is weak, and the GoldSrc engine shows its age in blocky visuals and sparse audio. Map design, while iconic, often relies on choke points and narrow corridors, leading to defensive stalemates—especially against stacked Engineer sentries. Balance feels harsh and inconsistent by modern standards, with certain classes (Heavy, Sniper) easily tipping matches depending on context. The game demands coordination, yet public play often devolves into chaotic or stagnant bouts.

Verdict
Team Fortress Classic is an essential historical artifact that genre fans should experience. Its core class design is brilliant and influential. However, as a modern multiplayer experience, it’s held back by dated mechanics, technical limitations, and uneven pacing. The score of 6/10 reflects this divide: immense respect for its legacy, but a clear-eyed acknowledgment that it’s more a museum piece than a living game for most players.

I've been playing Dota 2 for 12 years now, off and on throughout my life it is one of the few constants. In high school, my friends and I spent many nights playing when there was only one courier. In college I played once or twice a year on my rented laptop from school. During the pandemic It was a way for my brothers and I to connect when we couldn't actually visit each other. It holds a great place in my life.

[h3]The Good[/h3]
- Gameplay is dynamic, engaging and rewarding once you get the hang of it. There are so many moving parts that when you make your first big play, there is very little that can match the feeling of satisfaction when played just right. 
- Flourishing Pro Scene: If you want to get better there are countless new and old pro players that stream or release content on Youtube to help you improve, and often times Discord chats to find players to play with.
- Semi Consistent Updates: They just released one of the biggest updates the game has seen since Talents were released in 2016, or neutral items were released in 2019, or when they DOUBLED the size of the map in 2022. Valve isn't afraid to experiment with this game, and while you can get stuck on a single patch for a long time, you can always know that Valve Devs are working on something truly different to add.

[h3]Negatives[/h3]
- Mental Health: This is a team game. I love it for that, but playing with others can be frustrating and demoralizing. You can also find yourself "chain queuing" which after multiple losses can really effect your mood outside the game. My girlfriend and I have a rule that I cant start a game after 10pm because if i lose badly sometimes I will be too angry to fall asleep or talk before bed. You have to find these ways to look inward yourself, and without barriers it can really negatively impact you.
- The Community: I said it a bit above, but if you're new to online games there is so much racism, sexism, anger etc. I've met really great people playing dota, but the brain tends to remember the bad eggs. Remember there is a mute button.
- Communication from Valve: There can be crickets from valve sometimes. They ARE working on stuff, but if you read reddit to much you can get a bit riled for no reason.

Overall, best game I've ever played by a long margin.

[h1]Portal 2 — A puzzle game you’ll never forget[/h1]

I’d heard about the Portal series long before I actually played it. Back in school, people were always talking about how iconic it was, and everyone recommended starting with the second one — they said it’s bigger, more complex, more fun than the first, and it even has co-op. At some point, I just launched Portal 2 without overthinking it, and pretty quickly I understood why it gets so much praise.

Once I started playing, Portal 2 immediately felt different. Every puzzle made me think, try different approaches, and experiment with the portals. At first, it seemed like just physics challenges, but over time I realized how cleverly the game ties together space, story, and humor. Co-op adds another layer of fun: solving puzzles with a friend was hilarious and sometimes chaotic, and every perfectly timed combo gave a real sense of accomplishment.

Portal 2 left an amazing impression on me. It’s smart, engaging, and never makes you feel stupid — everything makes sense, but can still surprise you. The story, the atmosphere, and the puzzles make a playthrough memorable. And the memories of the fun times I had in co-op with a friend will stick with me forever. Personally, I’d recommend picking it up without hesitation — it’s absolutely worth it.

Portal 2 takes everything that worked in the first game and expands it into something bigger, deeper, and more alive. It does not lose the quiet intelligence of Portal. It builds on it.

From the start, the game feels broken in a different way. Aperture is not clean anymore. It is decaying, unstable, and full of history. Every room tells you that time has passed and no one was there to fix anything.

GLaDOS returns, sharper and more dangerous, but also more aware. Her dialogue is funny, cruel, and strangely honest. The humor never breaks immersion. It makes the world feel more real. You laugh, then immediately feel uncomfortable for laughing.

Wheatley is the surprise. He starts as comic relief, but slowly becomes something else. His presence changes the tone of the game in a way that feels natural. Watching that change happen is one of Portal 2 strongest moments.

The puzzles are more complex, but never unfair. New mechanics are introduced slowly and used creatively. The game constantly asks you to think differently without overwhelming you. When you solve a chamber, it feels like understanding the system rather than beating it.

What really sets Portal 2 apart is its sense of scale. Going deeper into Aperture feels like uncovering a buried past. The old testing areas, the recordings, the endless space all make the facility feel massive and tragic.


Portal 2 is not just smarter than most puzzle games.
It is funnier.
It is darker.
And it is more human.

It turns science into comedy, comedy into horror, and horror into something unforgettable.

This is not just a sequel. It is a conclusion that earns its place.

Growing up with cable is a very interesting experience.
With Age, Saturday takes on a different face - obligatory social events, doubling down on chores; if you’re lucky, you sleep in - if you’re very lucky, you have a contract job lined up and work an extra shift.
We fret about more than responsibilities - keeping our concerns filled up with worry about what is right, what is wrong, where we are headed, what the future holds, and what the present means.
Nostalgia, in a sense, is a panacea itself against what we’ve become today. Ruminating on the way things were is medicine enough.

Do you remember the feeling of carpet in the palm of your hand as you lean back and look up at the screen, closer than your parents would suggest? Do you recall whipping those covers off early in the morning and tumbling over to the TV set, changing it to some silly kids shows. Poptarts or waffles in the toaster, feeling a bit rebellious while getting something from the fridge while one of your parents are asleep. Memorizing the channels with the good shows to switch over to during commercial breaks. It was, and continues to be, a small piece of heaven; the adventures were larger than life, the situations were always outrageous, we laughed, we thought, and all of the over-the-top evil bad guys got their cuppa-pence in the end.
It was so simple, so good, and if we went back - we’d have to face a few bumps in the road that we willingly forgot about: The annoying commercials, reruns, lame spots, and your sister taking the channel changer and switching ittosomedumbfriggin’girlyshow ILLNEVERFORGIVEYOULISA

The reason I bring all this up is because, in essence, this is a lot like how it feels to play [b]Portal 2[/b]
It gives a jolt, that particular rush you feel running up to the TV screen and turning it on in the early morning hours. There’s a particular sense of scale, adventure, lightheartedness - and a clear line between friends and villains.
To top it all off, it’s a wicked clever puzzle game that’s full of gaffs, laughs, peril, and progress - you’re a part of a story that has a clear path forward, where there’s [i]always[/i] an escape, and the hero [i]always[/i] emerges victorious. It’s smarter than it gives itself credit for in all the best ways.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3644867072
Now it’s not ALL sunshine, roses, and rainbows.
The big, glaring thing that slaps you in the face are the 2011 loading screens that hit you like a quick ad break every level or so - a leftover of the old [i]Xbox 360[/i] days.
Unlike the original [b]Portal[/b] - this isn’t the kind of game you boot up again to re-experience. The online multiplayer is fun with friends, but the puzzles aren’t as concise and eloquent as the singleplayer experience - it’s a goofy time, but it’s not something you’re going to be coming back for more of. And that’s the real short and long of it.
Some of the puzzles in this game, unlike the original (and especially in the ‘escaped’ segments) are a bit more convoluted than necessary. The developers start truly scratching their heads for ideas towards the end and truly stretch what players can accomplish with 2 (or 4 in multiplayer) different portals and perspectives. It’s just a bit more rushed and janky, but obviously made with love. Even the downsides aren’t so bad.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3644866876
I mean what exactly do you want from a 3D puzzle game - [b]Portal 2[/b] has it.
Great puzzles, well thought out story, interesting characters, laughs, drama, great art direction, multiplayer - the works.
It’s an easy recommendation and a great time - you may not be coming back for seconds, but you certainly appreciate the experience you’ve had.
As a plus, it’s great with friends.

It’s a lot like going back in time and watching those cartoons on that chilled morning carpet. [b]Portal 2[/b] captures that vibe perfectly; it’s so incredibly good that you look back on it fondly, but if you were to go back today - it probably wouldn’t be quite as irresistibly amazing as you’d remember. You listen to the mourning doves for a few hours, and then you start to take it for granted.

It’s enrapturing in a way - it’s simple - and simplicity is all any of us really ever need.

Portal 2 is an amazing sequel to the legendary Portal game. Every aspect about the original Portal has been improved upon, and my critiques about Portal are not present in this game.

The soundtrack in Portal 2 is noticeably improved from its predecessor. The puzzles are harder but more variety and spectacle. The surroundings are varied by far. 

One critique I had about Portal 1 is a few of the achievements are annoying (namely the radio one). This game has no annoying achievements for solo players. (I have not done the CO-OP storyline) The camera achievement from Portal 1 makes and appearance, however this time requires the player to use their brain  in order to find out how to deal with the monitors. 

My one critique of the game is the section that in the underground Aperture section in which I found difficult to know where to go next. This is most likely a fault of my own, however I just wanted to let other aware. (You'll know what I mean) 

All in all, Portal 2 is a perfect sequel to an already great game.

First playthrough review time.

Portal 2 is often called one of the best puzzle games, and it mostly deserves that. Even for players who are not very interested in puzzle games, it can hold attention. The story is much stronger than the first game, with a clearer direction and more background about the world. This makes exploring each level more meaningful and keeps the game interesting.

The gameplay starts simple but becomes more challenging as new ideas are added. Each level builds on what the player has learned before, so it stays engaging without being confusing. I played the first game almost three years ago, and the changes here are clear, especially in level design and how the game flows. The game also has small jokes and funny details hidden in the environment, which make it feel lively. Even after many years, the graphics still look fine, and the game feels unique.

Overall, Portal 2 improves on the first game in almost every way. The cooperative mode adds extra levels and more complicated challenges. The voice work is very well done and helps make the game stand out. Even after all these years, the game still stands out and clearly took a lot of work to make.

I have completed this game a total of 5 times and I think it's become one of my favourite of all time. 

Everything is extremely well polished and optimized and it runs really well even on budget hardware (well duh it's 15 years old but it still feels modern so that's still a nice thing). 

The gameplay is really fun and the difficulty curve is just perfect: the test chambers become more and more dynamic and complex as you explore Aperture's massive facility, but never overwhelmingly difficult, making the whole game feel addicting and encouraging creativity to beat each puzzle. The achievements are pretty fun challenges, some unlocked during the story, others by doing oddly specific series of actions, some just silly and others pretty complex. I'd fix the story completion one sometimes not triggering/unlocking tho.

The "short and sweet" nature of the game allows the player to find details and easter eggs (all really interesting) they missed in their first playthrough without making the final boss battle seem like a distant goal that requires lots of time and dedication when playing multiple times.

The voice acting is excellent, and so are all the lines, both the "serious" ones and the comedic relief ones (gotta love the sarcastic little comments).

The soundtrack is also pretty cool and adds to the already great experience, as some tracks evolve as you make progress in specific chambers.

Portal 2 is similar to Portal, but it features much better pacing, a memorable cast of endearing characters with incredible performances from legendary figures such as Stephen Merchant and J.K. Simmons, a world that adds a significant amount of lore and texture to Aperture Science, and additional puzzle elements like different types of gel and bounce pads that introduce a whole new dimension to solving puzzles with your trusty portal gun. The players must come to grips with velocity, timing, and quick critical thinking skills in order to beat the memorable campaign that stretches 9 acts, with the fun not stopping there as Portal 2 also boasts a co-op campaign and thousands upon thousands of user-created maps that test everything I listed before for as long as the player wants to continue playing.

Are there any negatives to this experience? For my personal liking, the seventh and eighth acts could do with fewer puzzles that rely on you seeing a far-off distant wall to place your portal down, and that's it... Other than that, Portal 2 remains a perfect game even 15 years after its release.

Following up a game as frankly perfect as Portal ought to have been nearly impossible but somehow Valve pulled it off; Portal 2 is absolutely as good as its predecessor. 

Once again we step into the shoes of Chell, a test subject trapped in the endless lab chambers of Aperture Science. Despite defeating Glados in the first game, she wakes to find herself still trapped in the facility, only now it's decaying and crumbling apart. Led by the bumbling Core Sphere Wheatley, she comes across the Portal Gun and tries to escape. This game is far more narratively expansive than the first however, taking an opportunity to dive into Aperture's history and featuring a lot of terribly witty repartee that make its characters live long in the memory. 

The same portal-based physics puzzle platforming from the first game makes a welcome return but with a few new twists to keep the testing fresh. There's a risk that you might find some of these expanded mechanics extraneous, but for what its worth I think the game manages to keep the chapters very tightly designed, making it a worthy successor to one of PC gaming's greats.

Portal 2 is by far an improvement over Portal 1, I love when games in their second installment improve the first one a hundred times over.

First, I’ll talk about the co-op mode. It was an absolutely fun mode and the very first thing I played in Portal 2, totally innovative and very funny thanks to GLaDOS throwing beef at one of us, but above all, fun to play with a friend. I played it with a close friend who DOESN’T HAVE MUCH PATIENCE AND EVEN DROPPED PORTAL 1 IN THE FIRST 15 MINUTES, yes, I’m talking about you David. And honestly, it was amazing to blow his mind with his impatience. If we were a couple, I would have broken up with him. Actually, he’s not my friend anymore thanks to this game. I mean, co-op mode was perfect and many levels were a brain torture, especially one where you have to smash into your teammate. The story is great and it’s kind of a prequel before everything, where these two robots create an almost human friendship to achieve GLaDOS’s objective.

Now I’ll talk about the single-player mode. It was a very versatile experience, every level was different, both the puzzles made by GLaDOS and the exterior facility outside the puzzle chambers. I loved the way we accidentally reanimated GLaDOS, although not so accidentally. Wheatley, the deuteragonist, is incredible, a super funny character with a phenomenal voice actor for the role. I openly admit that every time this guy spoke, I laughed. He says so many stupid things that it’s just brilliant, breaking that lonely essence of the game and making us feel accompanied, at least until a certain moment... The betrayal :( I thought he was going to be good after defeating GLaDOS for the second time, but apparently not. The GLaDOS system makes them corrupt and obsessed with puzzles, and he can’t handle that, since he isn’t as strong-minded as GLaDOS, who is. After a lonely path full of more puzzles, we find GLaDOS again, BUT SHE’S A POTATO NOW. Once again, we have another companion so the game doesn’t feel as lonely as the first one. GLaDOS, during this journey, begins to understand things from a human perspective and, without being connected to that obsession, she gains empathy and starts her redemption arc. The final boss fight with Wheatley is perfect, full of stupid attempts to be smart, which makes perfect sense for his character. We finally defeat him and GLaDOS is back in charge, deciding to forgive our life after we defeated her twice, but also saved her. And that’s how this beautiful game ends. A game eight times better than the first one, with more complex puzzles and variations that make it even richer and more incredible. A perfect puzzle game with a wonderful story that everyone can appreciate, with a very good deuteragonist and antagonist. If you don’t have patience like my friend, play it anyway, I don’t care if you don't want to rip your head off, just play this game please.

Alright, where do we start.

This game is amazing for so many reasons. 
1) Difficulty is perfect. It's not uncommon to get stuck at points, but a little YouTube walkthrough gets you sorted. But even without a skill issue, it's amazing. To me, Portal 1 was cool but it felt more like a tutorial rather than a proper game (hot take). I much preferred the satisfaction of solving a puzzle after 20 mins of trying than the simple fling chambers in Portal 1.

2) Well thought, deep story. Same issue with Portal 1 (Portal 1 is easily one of my top 10 favourite games btw, for me it just doesn't compare to 2), it didn't really have a story. Wake up -> go through chambers -> find messages on the wall -> sentient robot tries to kill you -> blow her up. Whereas Portal 2 has much more depth. You find out about Aperture's history. You learn about the Caroline/GladOS arc. You get to learn more about the portal gun technology, 

3) Perfect length. Portal 1 could be done in less than 2 hours I'd say, Portal 2 is gonna take you at least 5 to properly get through and enjoy it. And you do enjoy it. I've played the game twice, and just loved looking around, taking in the environment, the scenery, and the remarkable graphics for a 15 year old game. (Once again, it sounds like I'm dunking on P1, I'm just comparing it to it's sequel) 

4) Runs really well on mid range hardware. I'm running on my laptop that's got 16GB DDR4 and a Ryzen 7 7730U with integrated graphics and this thing doesn't break a sweat. 

5) When it's on offer, it's a good deal but when it's not on offer, it's also a really good deal. Portal 2 comes in at £8.50, and I picked it up for I think £2.70 and that was a bundle w/ Portal 1. I had already played the game on the 360 wayyyy back in the day tho.

Portal 2 begins after the end, in a place that has been left to rot. You wake not to sterile perfection, but to neglect—cracked walls, flickering lights, test chambers held together by failing machinery and automated routines that no longer understand their purpose. The Aperture Science Enrichment Center is still functioning, but only in the most literal sense. It has survived without anyone truly alive to run it.

GLaDOS returns, rebuilt and resentful, her control over the facility restored but her contempt for you sharper than ever. The tests resume, larger and more complex, layered with new technologies that turn problem-solving into controlled chaos. Hard light bridges, excursion funnels, gels that alter momentum and movement—all elegant systems designed to push you forward whether you want to go or not. The puzzles feel less like experiments and more like infrastructure built to keep something ancient moving.

Then there is Wheatley. Friendly, frantic, and desperately eager to help, he feels like a lifeline in a place that has none. He talks to fill the silence, to reassure himself as much as you. Through him, Aperture becomes less oppressive and more tragic—a monument to arrogance and failure, buried beneath its own ambition. As you fall deeper into the facility, you pass through decades of abandoned innovation, each layer a reminder that progress here never stopped long enough to ask if it should.

The deeper chambers tell a different story. Cavernous testing spheres loom in darkness, held up by rusted supports and blind faith in engineering. Recorded messages from Cave Johnson echo through the void—boisterous, unhinged, and gradually unraveling as the cost of his vision becomes clear. These halls were never about discovery. They were about obsession, and the belief that human cost was an acceptable variable.

Betrayal is inevitable. Power corrupts quickly when desperation replaces purpose, and the system fractures under its own weight. What began as cooperation turns into something personal, something angry and small. The tests become weapons. The facility itself becomes hostile, reshaping to crush anything that defies it.

Yet Portal 2 is not just about escape. It is about consequences. Every system you break was built to replace something human that failed. Every voice you hear is an echo of a choice made long ago. Even victory feels restrained, earned not through dominance but through persistence and refusal to be erased.

In the end, Portal 2 leaves you with a quiet truth. Intelligence does not guarantee wisdom. Control does not equal stability. And progress, when stripped of accountability, buries itself under layers of concrete and steel.

You do not conquer Aperture Science. You survive it—and leave it alone with its own ruins.

[b]Portal 2[/b] is easily one of the best games ever made.  Valve has a philosophy a lot of studios could learn from: release a first game that's already great - shorter, tighter, almost like a brilliant proof-of-concept - then follow it up with a sequel that builds on everything perfectly... and then stop.  No endless milking, no diminishing returns.  The Portal series nails that approach, and I'm completely fine with it.

The single-player campaign moves beyond traditional test chambers and drops you into parts of Aperture you were never meant to see.  You learn new mechanics organically, experimenting with anti-gravity tunnels, propulsion and repulsion gels, and white surfaces that let you paint new portal spots into existence.  The co-op campaign brings back the structured test chamber vibe, with GLaDOS narrating as you and a friend either help each other... or [i]accidentally[/i] sabotage one another.

What continues to amaze me is how [b]Portal 2[/b] tells such a sharp, charming, and witty story without ever interrupting the gameplay.  The first game already proved you could build an entire narrative around one disembodied voice with no cutscenes - but [b]Portal 2[/b] does it with [i]three[/i].  GLaDOS, Wheatley, and Cave Johnson all deliver character, history, and humor entirely through dialogue that plays out while you're solving puzzles.  The pacing is flawless, the writing is unforgettable, and the mechanics are some of the smartest ever put in a game.  It's a masterpiece - a true classic - start to finish!

[h2]Gameplay & Mechanics[/h2]
Portal 2 (2011) retains its unique puzzle solving mechanics from Portal (2007), where the player has control of a “Portal Gun”, a device which allows the player to shoot 2 “portals” on any applicable surface which connect those two places into one, similar to teleportation. The player can see through these portals to what’s on the other side, and momentum is carried through the portals which create some interesting opportunities for speeding through the air, shooting portals as you go, reaching the exit of a level without even having to touch the ground (which at times makes the game feel more like a speedrunning platformer, it’s a brilliant combination). The puzzles themselves have a good balance of difficulty and complexity present in the tools available to solve the problem. There isn’t a single place where you’ll have to make a really awkward jump to get through a small gap to grab an item as the game is designed so the difficulty is in the [i]puzzle[/i] and not the platforming abilities of the player. Any “hints” as to where to shoot portals or get to are discreetly displayed within the setting of the world without giving you a set of instructions as to what to do, which is a tricky feat to achieve in level design.

The gameplay is very well thought out in the sense that, the further you get through the game, the more you understand how the cube needs to go on that button that opens that door that released that laser which redirects to those turrets which destroys them giving you access to the spring plate which propels you to the exit. That might seem horribly complicated, but it all makes perfect sense once you understand each individual puzzle item. The game gives you ample opportunity to understand and play with each individual item in its own introductory test - [b]gradually introducing mechanics so in no way are you overwhelmed[/b]. That said, there are no tutorials or hint pop-ups, you are on your own in those 4 walls. This can create problems with players hitting a metaphorical brick wall if they can’t understand or solve something, which is one of the game’s shortcomings. Having said that, like many older style of games, checking a walkthrough guide to get past a tricky section is only cheating if you personally feel it is.

[h2]Writing, Story & Characters[/h2]
Fundamentally, Portal 2 is a puzzle game. But don't let that fool you into thinking this doesn't have an enticing narrative because oh boy does it. The campaign is not just a vehicle to transport the player from one level to the next, the game [i]is[/i] these mid-puzzle story-driven moments that could so easily be a cutscene but instead you get to experience and live through. The story is interactive, one hell of an adventure, and full of all the twists and turns and unexpected moments that will have any player hooked to do just one more chapter. If you played the original Portal, and thought that most of the narrative heavy-work was done through omnipotent voice-over that struggled to form much of an attachment, Portal 2 does a much better job of letting you build a connection with characters that you journey through the world with together. It's less dry sarcastic comments in your ear (though there's still a delightful chunk of that) and more emotional bonding moments that will make you care a lot more both about what happens to you but what happens to the characters and world you encounter. Having said that, the player is still mute, so you don't get much of a say in what happens. The Rattman mini-comic available online serves to bridge the lore-gap between games.

The game doesn't take itself too seriously, there is a lot of humour to be found. A lot of that is silly robots being silly, with an appreciation for how absurd some of the situations you find yourself in are. But while laughing at one character's utter disdain for your personal safety, you might find yourself for a moment fool yourself into thinking that this place really exists out there, somewhere, at some time. [b]The world-building in this game is simply brilliant[/b], while not at all crucial to the main story or to how quickly you can solve puzzles, the care and attention that's gone into making Aperture Science, the portal technology, the facility etc. feel like a real thing with a real history is fantastic. The game is set many thousands of years in the future, and you truly feel when walking the corridors that many a scientist have walked in your footsteps, you wonder to yourself how things got to the way they are, and you notice all the little human things that make you feel a lot more special and important in a world almost entirely inhabited by robots. To further aid that, the vocal performances by J.K. Simmons, Ellen McClain and Stephen Merchant are fantastic, with a script to match.

[h2]Design, Aesthetic & Music[/h2]
The test chambers (where the puzzles mainly take place) vary from extremely large and open to small and claustrophobic but are always simplistic, in other words no matter how elaborate the setting of a puzzle is – and some parts are pretty breath-taking – there’s only a couple important items that you’ll need. In some sections, this can lead to half the puzzle being just locating the special portal-able wall that you need, which is less fun, but the game does an alright job of leading you down the right path. The visual design goes through several phases as the game progresses, but is mainly centred on futuristic tech and electronics, with clean-cut edges and harsh lighting, minimally painted walls and floors with bare metal scaffolding holding the whole thing up. There is also the sense that the world is "alive" in some way. Test elements animate and buzz, wall panels breathe, equipment is transported in and out of the play area. The whole game world feels dynamic and has a certain beauty if you just stand in a spot and observe for a while, which is good, because you'll be doing a lot of that while wracking your brain for the answer to a puzzle.

The music and sound design is impeccable. Putting cubes on buttons and shooting portals sounds incredibly satisfying, even the exit door opening sounds like a [i]"well done"[/i]. Some of my favourite parts of the game are in the manufacturing areas, where the ambience of machinery working away, conveyer belts moving, robots bleep-blooping, pneumatic tubes rushing sounds very real. Furthermore, all of the decorative items in the world, along with some tools that you actually use in puzzles, seem to sing from the same song sheet. That is to say, clearly a lot of care and attention has gone in to making all of these seemingly unrelated sounds work together to produce some very mechanical but strangely beautiful music. This folds like magic into the soundtrack, produced by Mike Morasky, which sounds robotic and distorted and harsh in parts, melodic, rhythmic and synthesizer heavy in others, and lush and orchestral in more still. It truly takes you for a ride, and does as good a job as I've seen in any game of making the dull parts seem less dull and the impactful, dramatic parts even more so. It's also [b]dynamically responsive to what the player does in-game[/b], producing some fantastic moments where it sounds like the music is being arranged and played live, and is far more than just a neat party trick.

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Portal 2 is well worth your time and money. A captivating core gameplay loop that will make you feel far smarter than you deserve, an expansive alternative world to explore littered with fun and interesting details, characters that are multi-dimensional and genuinely funny, music to bop along to that makes your brain work harder and an adventure story with heartfelt emotion, epic battles and daring escapes. [b]Highly recommend.[/b]

[b]Portal 2[/b] expands on the original with deeper mechanics, cooperative puzzle systems, and more complex environmental interactions, making each test chamber a satisfying exercise in physics, timing, and spatial reasoning.

[b]CORE GAMEPLAY MECHANICS[/b]

[*][b]Portal Gun[/b] - Creates interlinked entry and exit points, enabling creative movement, momentum-based puzzles, and emergent problem-solving.
[*][b]Environmental Puzzles[/b] - Test chambers introduce lasers, gels, excursion funnels, and weighted cubes, all interacting predictably with consistent mechanical rules.
[*][b]Physics & Momentum[/b] - Jumping, falling, and launching through portals obey physics, letting players chain actions for inventive solutions.
[*][b]Timing & Sequencing[/b] - Many puzzles require coordinating actions, moving objects, and triggering events in the correct order.

[b]COOPERATIVE MODE MECHANICS[/b]

[*]Two-player co-op introduces dual portals and complementary movement, forcing coordination and shared problem-solving.
[*]Each player’s actions mechanically impact the other, creating emergent teamwork puzzles.
[*]Communication and timing are critical to successfully navigating co-op chambers.

[b]REPLAYABILITY & ENGAGEMENT[/b]

[*]Emergent solutions from consistent mechanics encourage experimentation.
[*]Complex puzzles scale difficulty while reinforcing understanding of core mechanics.
[*]The combination of single-player and co-op keeps mechanical engagement fresh.

[b]10/10[/b] - clever physics puzzles, mechanically rich co-op systems, and inventive environmental interactions make Portal 2 a timeless puzzle masterpiece.

Luckily only a few levels are affected, but it's really shocking that such an interesting mechanic was so poorly implemented. I even got stuck in an autosave loop after the orange and blue gels propelled me to my death, and the game simply returned to this over and over and over endlessly.

Wheatley is a total moron but he's hilarious, and bouncing around on the blue gel is the most fun you can have with physics. The puzzles are brilliant, but playing co-op with a friend is where the real chaos happens—trapping them in loops never gets old. It’s a flawless masterpiece that makes being smart (or dumb) feel awesome. 10/10

After over 3000 hours in Counter-Strike 2, and playing the series since childhood, starting with Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, I can honestly say CS2 is still one of the most intense and skill-demanding shooters out there. I waited a long time before writing this review because I wanted to actually experience the game properly before coming to any conclusion.

Compared to more arcade-style or cartoony shooters like Valorant, CS2 feels brutally raw and unforgiving in the best way. Every round matters, every mistake gets punished, and those late-round bombsite fights can get absolutely brutal, chaotic, and intense. The tension and adrenaline you get in clutch moments is something I honestly haven’t felt in any other game.

The only serious downside right now is the anti-cheat. Cheaters are still too common and it really hurts the experience for honest players. Valve seriously needs to take this more seriously.

Another thing I’ve noticed is that competitive matchmaking can sometimes take a while, especially during off-peak hours or in certain regions. That’s not really Valve’s fault since it’s just a player-traffic thing, but it can still get a bit annoying when you just want to get into a game.

Even with that issue, CS2 is still a legendary competitive game and easily one of the greatest FPS titles ever made.

Counter-Strike 2: The Game That Killed My Will to Exist

Counter-Strike 2 wants you to feel like a tactical genius, a sharpshooter extraordinaire, a master of bomb defusal. What it actually does is beat your soul into submission while simultaneously insulting your intelligence and sense of fun. This game isn’t a shooter—it’s a grim, lifeless treadmill where every match feels like corporate emails set to gunfire.

The maps are… maps. Grey, generic, and lifeless. You spawn, you run, you die. You respawn, you run, you die. Every bullet fired feels simultaneously pointless and personally offensive. Enemy players move like caffeinated ghosts who somehow know exactly where you are at all times—probably because they do. This is less a test of skill and more a brutal exercise in futility and self-loathing.

Weapons? They exist. Recoil? Sure. But everything feels the same: spray bullets, pray, die, repeat. And the matchmaking? A delightful buffet of “welcome to losing 16-0 in a lobby where everyone is clearly on some kind of performance-enhancing algorithm.” The learning curve isn’t fun—it’s a mountain of despair built on your corpse.

By hour 5, you stop thinking about improving. By hour 10, you stop caring. By hour 15, you realize the game has stolen all your enthusiasm and left your brain a smoking crater. It’s lifeless, soul-crushing, and somehow manages to be both boring and stressful at the same time—a remarkable achievement.

Final Verdict:
Counter-Strike 2 isn’t a game. It’s a public service announcement about why you should never care about rank, aim, or personal dignity. Fun? Dead. Motivation? Dead. Will to continue gaming? Vaporized.

Counter-Strike 2 Prime is a masterclass in how to take a legendary franchise and grind it into a soulless, greedy, corporate money funnel that actively disrespects the people who keep it alive. I genuinely cannot overstate how angry it makes me that Valve has the nerve to advertise “free rewards” while forcing players to pay real money just to access them. That is not a perk. That is not a bonus. That is a scam wrapped in PR language.

Let me spell it out slowly since Valve seems to think players are idiots:
If I have to pay first, it is not free.
Not even a little.
Not spiritually.
Not philosophically.
Not in any universe where words still mean things.

Prime is not an upgrade—it’s a shakedown. You’re not paying for value, you’re paying to remove artificial restrictions that never needed to exist in the first place. Valve created a problem and then sold the solution, all while smiling and pretending they’re doing you a favor. That’s not game design. That’s extortion with extra steps.

And what do you get after paying? Excitement? Satisfaction? Respect?
No.
You get the privilege of grinding your time away for “rewards” that are usually worthless, forgettable, or instantly thrown onto the pile of digital trash. You pay money to unlock the chance to maybe get something someday, as long as you keep playing, keep queuing, keep feeding the machine. It’s manipulative, cynical, and exhausting.

What makes this rage-inducing is that Counter-Strike didn’t need any of this. CS was built on pure gameplay—aim, strategy, teamwork. That’s it. No gimmicks. No psychological monetization tricks. Now it feels like Valve looked at that legacy and said, “Cool, but how do we squeeze more money out of them for doing the same thing?”

And yes, the money matters. When I’m forced to hand over cash just to access features dressed up as “free,” I can’t ignore the bigger picture. Massive corporations don’t just sit on piles of money—they move it, invest it, and interact with governments and political systems around the world. As a player, it’s infuriating to think that money pried out of gamers through deceptive monetization could be feeding into political structures I strongly oppose, including the Israeli government. Even the possibility that my frustration-funded purchase contributes to that makes the entire Prime system feel even more disgusting.

This isn’t about supporting developers. This isn’t about funding innovation. This is about conditioning players to accept that nothing is earned anymore unless you pay first, and even then, you’re expected to be grateful for scraps. Valve doesn’t communicate. They don’t justify. They just normalize it and wait for players to stop complaining.

Prime doesn’t make the game better. It makes it uglier. It divides the player base, cheapens progression, and constantly reminds you that you’re not a valued community member—you’re a revenue stream. Every time the game dangles a “reward,” it feels less like appreciation and more like a leash.

Counter-Strike 2 Prime is not premium. It’s predatory. It’s misleading. It’s corporate arrogance disguised as a feature. Paying money to unlock “free” rewards is one of the most insulting contradictions in modern gaming, and the fact that Valve gets away with it shows just how low the bar has sunk.

I didn’t buy Prime because I wanted to.
I bought it because the game punished me for not having it.
And that’s the part that makes me angry enough to write this in the first place.

Timeless Gameplay and Constant Evolution
I’ve been playing Counter-Strike for years, and one of the things that keeps me coming back is how consistently the game evolves. Developers have done a solid job of updating mechanics to maintain balance between the two opposing forces—Terrorists vs. Counter-Terrorists. This constant fine-tuning ensures matches remain fair and competitive, a sentiment echoed by many players who describe CS as “the purest FPS experience out there”.
Weapons, Customization, and Fairness
The arsenal of weapons and customization options is vast, offering variety without tipping into a pay-to-win scheme. Skins and cosmetics are purely aesthetic, which makes the game appealing without compromising fairness. As one Steam review notes, “No predatory cosmetic system, no fancy and distracting graphics… this game is simply the purest FPS experience”. That’s exactly how it feels—your skill matters more than your wallet.
Community Challenges: Hacking and Mods
Like any competitive online game, hacking exists—walling, aim assists, and similar exploits—but Valve’s anti-cheat efforts keep them to a minimum. While not perfect, the developer team actively works to preserve integrity. On the content side, CS doesn’t chase trends like battle royale or tower defense modes. Personally, I don’t miss them, but it’s worth noting for players who crave those experiences.
Maps: Quality Over Quantity
If there’s one area I’d love to see expanded, it’s map variety. New maps take time to arrive, and understandably so—balancing them for competitive play is no easy task. Still, more options would add freshness to the rotation. Many players agree that while the core maps are iconic, expanding the pool would enhance replayability.

Counter-Strike 2 feels like a confident evolution of one of the most iconic competitive shooters ever made. It doesn’t try to reinvent Counter-Strike—and that’s exactly why it works so well.
The first thing you notice is the upgrade to the Source 2 engine. Maps look cleaner, lighting is more realistic, and animations feel smoother without losing the sharp clarity that competitive players rely on. Classic maps like Dust II and Mirage still feel familiar, but they’re more readable and alive than ever.
Gameplay-wise, CS2 stays true to the high-skill, low-margin formula that made CS legendary. Gunplay is still unforgiving and deeply rewarding, where precision, timing, and positioning matter more than flashy mechanics. The updated tick system and improved responsiveness make gunfights feel more consistent, which is crucial in a game where milliseconds decide rounds.
One of the biggest improvements is the smoke grenade rework. Smokes are now dynamic—bullets and grenades can temporarily clear them, and they interact naturally with the environment. This adds a fresh layer of strategy without overcomplicating the core gameplay, keeping matches tactical and exciting.
Sound design is another strong point. Audio cues are clearer and more directional, making it easier to track enemy movement and react intelligently. This enhances both casual play and high-level competitive matches.
CS2 isn’t perfect—some players may miss certain legacy features or feel the changes are subtle—but overall, it succeeds at modernizing Counter-Strike while respecting its roots. It’s a polished, competitive-focused shooter that rewards dedication, teamwork, and skill.
If you enjoy intense, tactical FPS games where improvement comes from mastery rather than upgrades, Counter-Strike 2 is absolutely worth your time.

Counter-Strike 2 feels like a confident evolution of one of the most iconic competitive shooters ever made. It doesn’t try to reinvent Counter-Strike—and that’s exactly why it works so well.
The first thing you notice is the upgrade to the Source 2 engine. Maps look cleaner, lighting is more realistic, and animations feel smoother without losing the sharp clarity that competitive players rely on. Classic maps like Dust II and Mirage still feel familiar, but they’re more readable and alive than ever.
Gameplay-wise, CS2 stays true to the high-skill, low-margin formula that made CS legendary. Gunplay is still unforgiving and deeply rewarding, where precision, timing, and positioning matter more than flashy mechanics. The updated tick system and improved responsiveness make gunfights feel more consistent, which is crucial in a game where milliseconds decide rounds.
One of the biggest improvements is the smoke grenade rework. Smokes are now dynamic—bullets and grenades can temporarily clear them, and they interact naturally with the environment. This adds a fresh layer of strategy without overcomplicating the core gameplay, keeping matches tactical and exciting.
Sound design is another strong point. Audio cues are clearer and more directional, making it easier to track enemy movement and react intelligently. This enhances both casual play and high-level competitive matches.
CS2 isn’t perfect—some players may miss certain legacy features or feel the changes are subtle—but overall, it succeeds at modernizing Counter-Strike while respecting its roots. It’s a polished, competitive-focused shooter that rewards dedication, teamwork, and skill.
If you enjoy intense, tactical FPS games where improvement comes from mastery rather than upgrades, Counter-Strike 2 is absolutely worth your time.

I really wanted to like CS2. I gave it so many chances, played for hours, telling myself “okay, maybe this time it’ll be better,” but honestly, the more I played, the more tired I got. Throughout all the time I’ve spent in the game, there are just way too many cheaters, and it’s become seriously frustrating. After a while, you just lose all motivation.

You join a match and at first everything feels normal. Then a few rounds in, something feels off. Someone keeps one-tapping you through walls, never misses, always knows exactly where you are. You tell yourself, “Maybe they’re just really good,” but by the end of the match, you realize it’s not about skill at all.

What annoys me the most is this: you actually put in effort. You practice your aim, you try to improve your game sense, but someone else can wipe out all that effort with a single cheat. It really kills your enthusiasm. Even when you win, it doesn’t feel satisfying anymore.

CS2 isn’t a bad game. It has a lot of potential. The graphics, the gunplay, the overall feel of the game are actually good. But if the cheating problem keeps going like this, no matter how good the game is, it just pushes people away. At some point, you start asking yourself, “Why am I playing a game just to get angry?”

In short, I want to love CS2, but the game isn’t giving me the same energy back. I don’t want to leave matches feeling stressed and annoyed instead of having fun. :(

I really wanted to like CS2. I gave it so many chances, played for hours, telling myself “okay, maybe this time it’ll be better,” but honestly, the more I played, the more tired I got. Throughout all the time I’ve spent in the game, there are just way too many cheaters, and it’s become seriously frustrating. After a while, you just lose all motivation.

You join a match and at first everything feels normal. Then a few rounds in, something feels off. Someone keeps one-tapping you through walls, never misses, always knows exactly where you are. You tell yourself, “Maybe they’re just really good,” but by the end of the match, you realize it’s not about skill at all.

What annoys me the most is this: you actually put in effort. You practice your aim, you try to improve your game sense, but someone else can wipe out all that effort with a single cheat. It really kills your enthusiasm. Even when you win, it doesn’t feel satisfying anymore.

CS2 isn’t a bad game. It has a lot of potential. The graphics, the gunplay, the overall feel of the game are actually good. But if the cheating problem keeps going like this, no matter how good the game is, it just pushes people away. At some point, you start asking yourself, “Why am I playing a game just to get angry?”

In short, I want to love CS2, but the game isn’t giving me the same energy back. I don’t want to leave matches feeling stressed and annoyed instead of having fun. :(

The Source 2 engine brings a stunning visual overhaul that makes every map feel alive, yet it keeps the core DNA that I’ve known for over a decade. Whether I’m playing a quick round to de-stress or staying up late to relive the glory days, CS2 bridges the gap between those childhood memories and the present. It’s a polished, modern tribute to the game that defined a generation of gamers like me.

Each serving provides 256 kcal, 7g protein, 35g carbohydrates (of which 9g sugars), 9.5g fat (of which 5.5g saturates), 1.5g fibre and 1.2g salt.

## Ingredients
- 135g/4¾oz plain flour
- 1 tsp baking powder
- ½ tsp salt
- 2 tbsp caster sugar
- 130ml/4½fl oz milk
- 1 large egg, lightly beaten
- 2 tbsp melted butter (allowed to cool slightly), plus extra for cooking

To serve
- maple syrup
- butter

## --- Method ---

1. Sift the flour, baking powder, salt and caster sugar into a large bowl. In a separate bowl or jug, lightly whisk together the milk and egg, then whisk in the melted butter.

2. Pour the milk mixture into the flour mixture and, using a fork, beat until you have a smooth batter. Any lumps will soon disappear with a little mixing. Let the batter stand for a few minutes.

3. Heat a non-stick frying pan over a medium heat and add a knob of butter. When it's melted, add a ladle of batter (or two if your frying pan is big enough to cook two pancakes at the same time). It will seem very thick but this is how it should be. 

4. Wait for about 3 minutes until the top of the pancake begins to bubble, and the edges begin to set.  Flip it over and cook for another two minutes until both sides are golden brown and the pancake has risen to about 1cm/½in thick. If the pancake is too dark, reduce the heat slightly for the next round. 

5. Repeat until all the batter is used up. You can keep the pancakes warm in a low oven, but they taste best fresh out the pan.

6. Serve with lashings of real maple syrup and extra butter, if you like.

The Source 2 engine brings a stunning visual overhaul that makes every map feel alive, yet it keeps the core DNA that I’ve known for over a decade. Whether I’m playing a quick round to de-stress or staying up late to relive the glory days, CS2 bridges the gap between those childhood memories and the present. It’s a polished, modern tribute to the game that defined a generation of gamers like me.

Maybe it’s time to seriously consider stricter age restrictions or some kind of verified age system for competitive matchmaking. In theory, that could reduce the amount of immature behavior in ranked games.

But honestly, I’m not even sure that would fix anything. These days, kids from 8 to 16 can swear and flame harder than most adults. Sometimes it genuinely feels like half the lobby just came straight from Dota, bringing all that chaotic energy with them.

At the same time, I have to admit — CS2 is probably at the peak of its pace and dynamics in the entire history of the game. The speed, the aggression, and the mechanical skill ceiling are higher than ever. The core gameplay feels intense and competitive in the best way possible.

And on a more nostalgic note — I’d honestly love to hear the old knife sounds again. Those classic hits had a special feeling to them. But I also understand that this is probably just nostalgia and a bit of fantasy at this point.

This is just my personal opinion, and I completely understand that others might disagree) But until moderation improves or matchmaking becomes smarter, it’s hard for me to truly enjoy playing with random teammates.

Counter-Strike 2 is, without a doubt, a legendary shooter. The franchise has defined competitive FPS gaming for decades, and the core gameplay is still incredibly satisfying. The gunplay feels sharp, the movement is responsive, and the tactical depth is what makes this game timeless. When everything works as it should, CS2 is one of the best competitive experiences you can have.

However, there is a serious issue that’s hurting the game right now — cheaters.

It’s extremely difficult to play more than 2–3 matches in a row without running into someone who is clearly cheating. Wallhacks, aimbots, suspicious behavior — it happens far too often. This completely ruins the competitive integrity of the game and makes grinding Premier or matchmaking feel pointless.

Another problem is Deathmatch mode. Instead of being a solid warm-up environment, it’s filled with AI bots and questionable accounts. It doesn’t feel like a proper practice mode anymore, which is disappointing for players who want to improve.

If someone truly wants to play CS2 seriously, the only real option right now is Faceit. Third-party platforms offer much better anti-cheat systems and a more competitive environment. That alone says a lot about the current state of official matchmaking.

CS2 has legendary potential — the gameplay foundation is amazing. But without strong anti-cheat improvements, many players will continue to feel frustrated.

I really hope the developers take the cheating problem seriously and prioritize fixing it. This game deserves better.

After almost 12,000 hours in DayZ, this is not a review I expected to write.

DayZ, at its best, is still a uniquely powerful experience. The emergent gameplay, tension, paranoia, and long-term survival stakes created by the community — especially through mods and custom servers — are unmatched. The modding ecosystem is not a bonus feature; it is the game’s longevity.

Unfortunately, this is also where the problem lies.

Over time, it has become increasingly clear that the relationship between the platform holder and the modding/server community is unstable, opaque, and at times openly hostile. Decisions with massive impact on creators and server owners are enforced abruptly, communicated inconsistently, and often without clear, institutional explanations.

When enforcement appears personal, absolute, or indifferent to remediation or transparency, it undermines trust — not just in individual cases, but in the ecosystem as a whole. The result is burnout among experienced server owners, fragmentation of the community, and a chilling effect on high-effort mod development.

This is not about defending mistakes or bad decisions by mod authors. Those should be addressed.
It is about proportionality, process, and respect for the community that has carried this game for over a decade.

At this point, I cannot recommend DayZ to new players — not because the core game lacks potential, but because investing time, creativity, or community-building effort feels increasingly precarious.

DayZ remains irreplaceable.
That is precisely why this is so disappointing.

But here’s the twist: DayZ is still one of the greatest, most unforgettable games I’ve ever played. I’ve met some of the coolest people imaginable and had adventures so ridiculous I wish they were recorded — they’d probably go viral for all the wrong reasons.

Interesting game and a lot of fun but quickly grows old and boring. The loot system is geared towards trying to get people to fight one another but for low population servers and some of the DLC, the loot system doesn't do any favors. I purchased a private server to learn the game without having the fear of a other players causing issues for me. This allowed me to see just how ridiculous the loot system is. As if it wasn't hard enough for people to find things, they allow for you on the official servers to jump across official servers with whatever you have on you. You'll find that low population servers throughout the day has at least 1 or 2 people on them and they tend to be people collecting things to go back to their higher population server with. I ran into one of them when I was still on the official server. He was kind enough to break it all down for me and told me it was a common practice. Even more common with people gathering things for Sakhal since the loot is worse there and you risk dying of lack food, water, and warmth. Others generally will just jump servers to grab military gear, weaponry, and ammo to go back to the high population servers for the battles they have between the large groups that have formed teams/militia groups or just to restock their bases because their server is picked bare.

Some of the loot is spawned into the ground or inside of items where you can't retrieve them.

The contaminated zones offered if you were lucky 1 or 2 good things the rest was all stuff you could find at military roadblocks or police stations. Given all the work that goes into securing an NBC Suit and gas mask filters, the reward is nil. The filters don't last long at all and you can find yourself blowing through 6 or 7 giving just one portion of the contaminated zone a thorough run through. 

The inventory system is nice but also kind of dumb. Some things you can stack, but you can't stack pieces of paper. Some items being ridiculously oversized taking up a lot of space in the inventory.

The crafting, I had to use a wiki to learn how to craft and what was available to be crafted for DayZ. First game I ever played where there wasn't a button to open a ui for crafting. There is so much wrong with this that they clearly don't care about. They have skillets and cooking pots, but there is nothing to keep your food preserved in. The only logical course of action is to smoke all of your food. Great nutrients, also somehow increases your hydration, and I have kept smoked meat in my backpack and car for days and they are still kicking. There are vegetables you can grow which makes you think you could possibly add it to the rice, and add some potatoes and meat and make yourself a good stew. Nope. Everything you would expect to be in vanilla based on what is provided to you in vanilla, you can only get by installing mods. I don't do mods. I pay for a complete game, a game that has been out long enough that these small QOL things should have been fixed. There has been no problem collecting money from people for DLC, so why are we not getting the stuff that should have been corrected or fixed years ago?

The building mechanics in the game are trash as well. So much effort to build small sections of walls and people can demolish them in a short amount of time with a sledgehammer. You can build walls, flagpoles, gates, and the palace of your dreams........... wait............ what is that?.............. You can only build a lean-to with a storage locker that has a capacity of 20 slots? That is right, this amazing, and it truly is an amazing game, offers so many possibilities but they don't allow for you to build building to live in, or storage sheds. You can build a storage container but the capacity is not much. The best storage is with the tents. I have a village of tents on my private server all just holding what little I can scavenge. But good luck with building a wall around your compound. Just google the requirements for what is needed for one panel of wall.

That is when I started thinking about all the issues and such and how a lot of it seemed unfinished, like the cooking. This game has been out long enough, and the devs have collected enough money, that the code in the core part of the game should be completed and the partial features completed or removed. It is a slap in the face to push out 1 soon to be 2 DLC without completing the game everyone paid for. It is great that there are mods out there for the things I would like to see in the game, but I didn't pay for their mods. I didn't pay for a game in beta. I paid for a complete game. DayZ is a game for people that have an actual attention span, a desire to solve problems, and ones that don't give up on the first fxck up. If you fit into these catagories, and you enjoy survival games, this will be a blast for you. Most people quit on the first couple deaths, because "They can't find food.". I won't give advice on how to find food, but finding food is the last of your concerns playing this, I assure you, there are more ways of getting food, than finding it in a house in the spawn area where everyone has already looted. So please, before you uninstall and leave a review about how its hard to live in this game, think of other ways to survive.

DayZ has no end goal, no lore that really matters (unless you really want to know), and nothing to tell you what to do. All of that is made up from you, you decide what your goal is, and that one life you had when you somehow got food, a weapon, and starting going in-land, thats your lore. In DayZ, everything is up to you on how you want your character to be. A bandit robbing other players? Someone geared driving around helping fresh-spawns? A farmer simply trying to survive? It's all up to you, you can roleplay, you can just get geared for pvp, or you can make friends, again, all up to you.

If it's your first time playing the game, like any other game, play the vanilla version first, might be boring, but understanding the basics before getting into a modded server with tons of different add-ons that make it a QoL sim, would help.

With trusting players: Just try and think about what they might be thinking, if they kill you, that COULD mean they just want to kill other players, but it could also mean that they just don't trust you, and killed you because they want to live a bit longer. So, here's some tips on interacting with players. If they have a weapon in hand, don't approach, if they have a biker helmet, or anything that would muffle their voice, dont approach, that could mean they don't want to talk, and would kill on sight; understand this even with the possibility of them not knowing that it muffles their voice, or they don't know that having a helmet like that on means they don't want to talk.

But to conclude, this game is amazing. After understanding the map, items, and guns, you will create memories here. Here's a memory I had.

I had spawn in Светлоярск, and I went to the gas station after finding farming equipment, and I wanted to create a base at the gas station. During the construction, many players passed by, most of them stayed and helped me create the base, and we had this one guy we called santa, he didnt talk at all, but he had a white beard and a santa hat. We had the farm going, had a great supply of food for the 7 people we gathered. An IRL friend and I went uphill from the gas station, finding a locked, player created base inside of a warehouse, we went back to the group of people and my friend and I decided that I'll be the leader (Didnt really say that but I was the one telling everyone what to do.). Once we were back, I explained there was a base we could raid, and we made a plan: We didnt have the explosives, so we will bring the supply of axes, hammers, and others things of the sort up there, then we will break in slowly. After talking, another player showed up wanting to join, so we let him, I told them not to give him a gun yet, and wait till he was here for a bit, but someone did anyways. I told everyone to meet up at the raid, and we started hacking at the wall, but during it, we were getting shot at, I looked behind me and the new guy was shooting at us, and everyone at the raid site was killed, including me, and there was only one guy left, and it was santa, he was defending the base while we were gone. After spawning back in, we came back, the garden we made was destroyed, and the new guys body was on the floor, and so was santas hat, santa killed him and went off on his own. he avenged us and went off on his own journey.

And that was just one of the cool stories I made in this game, that story has more to it, but it would be way too much text, this game is worth it if you play it right.

I’ve spent 10,000+ hours in DayZ. That’s over two actual years of my life crouching in bushes, dying of dysentery, talking to myself in Russian accents, and staring at cans of baked beans like they’re made of gold.

This isn’t just a game.
It’s a lifestyle.
It’s a psychological experiment.
It’s therapy.
It’s trauma.

🧄 A normal DayZ experience:

Spawn on the coast, half-naked and starving.

Eat raw chicken because "how bad could it be?"

Die.

Respawn.

Trust a stranger.

Die.

Become the villain.

Get sniped from 400 meters by a guy named xXx_PvP_Monkey420_xXx

Respawn.

Find a can of food. No can opener.

Die.

✅ Pros:

The most immersive survival experience out there

No match is ever the same – pure chaos

Random encounters can be hilarious, terrifying, or deeply emotional

Community servers keep things fresh

It’s the best game you’ll ever hate

❌ Cons:

– You will lose hours, days, years of your life
– Still buggy after all these years (but hey, charm?)
– UI is about as user-friendly as a Soviet toaster
– Your friends will leave you for dead. Repeatedly.

Final Thoughts:

If you’re looking for a polished, hand-holding, battle-pass filled, dopamine-drenched modern game…
Run.
But if you want something raw, unpredictable, frustrating, and completely unforgettable –
Welcome to DayZ. Your life is pain now.

DayZ is one of the best hardcore survival games ever made — when it works. No hand-holding, real consequences, and unmatched tension. Every life becomes a story, every player encounter feels dangerous, and the survival mechanics (hunger, sickness, weather, medical system, gunplay) are deep and incredibly immersive.

The game truly shines on community Vanilla / Vanilla+ servers with active admins. That’s where DayZ feels fair, intense, and close to its original vision. Official servers, unfortunately, still struggle — cheating on higher-pop servers is a known issue and actively hurts the experience.

There are also long-standing frustrations the community keeps calling out: inconsistent zombie AI and pathing, desync, hit registration issues, clunky character actions (especially throwing items and vaulting), vehicles behaving unpredictably, and general jank that breaks immersion in critical moments.

Despite all of this, DayZ remains special. No other game creates this level of tension, paranoia, and player-driven storytelling. The foundation is incredible — it just desperately needs polish, bug fixes, and stronger anti-cheat support to reach its full potential.

If you want a true survival experience that doesn’t care about your comfort, DayZ is absolutely worth playing. Just know: the game is amazing — and it could be so much better.
