If you're a fan of MMO's, but not a fan of the generic fantasy setting and monotonous fetch and kill quests (I'm looking at you WoW) then Warframe might be your game.

You have to be a major fan of the grind in order to truly enjoy this game. No matter how hard the grind gets though, you're always having fun and feeling like a badass because at its core, the gameplay is just fun. Warframe will have you feeling like a true space ninja right off the bat, with its fast paced third person shoot-em-up and hack-n-slash action.

Warframe is Digital Extremes' swan song. This is the game that has been in their dreams since as far back as 2005, and it shows. There's just so much love and support put into this game from the developers and they truly are devoted to making this game the best that it can be. There were so many times playing this game where I [i] THOUGHT [/i] I had experienced everything the game had to offer and then all of a sudden there would be this new level, gametype, enemy, feature, or whatever and it would blow my mind that there was just this much content in the game for free.

Pros:
[list]
    [*] Free to play, and you never have to pay a cent to progress, as long as you're patient.
    [*] TONS of depth and content
    [*] Really fun gameplay that not even your ADD can resist.
    [*] Super fun with friends
    [*] The game is pretty much never frustrating, but there's definitely tons of challenge for those seeking it.
    [*] PvE is the main focus.
    [*] Interesting and fresh form of progression system and gearing.
    [*] The newer quests are extremely fun and exciting, breathing more life into an already vibrant gameplay experience.
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
    [*] A lot of waiting around for items to finish building. If you don't pay money for platnium, you'll have to wait several days for larger items to finish building, as well as adding rooms onto your clan Dojo.
    [*] The story and lore really take a backseat and aren't that interesting to me.
    [*] PvP and other game modes just don't have a lot of effect on the main game so there's not many reasons to venture into the other game modes. This is unfortunate because those modes are actually all fun, but underpopulated it seems.
    [*] Pretty steep learning curve when you are starting out. It's good to get help from a more experienced player and have them show you the ropes. There's a lot to learn in this complex game.
[/list]

I got into playing warframe a bit later than all the cool kids but It quickly became my favourite free to play game of all time. There is no denying the value you are getting in this package without having to pay a thing upfront. The game does however have a few minor issues which, however insignificant, should still be mentioned.

Pros:
The game has a intricate and interesting lore which is just ripe for exploring. Whether thats done via scanning different things in mission or completeing the various quests there is always more to learn about this world. That said you won't be running out of content any time soon. The variety when it comes to weapons, warframes and equipment is truly amazing and they keed adding to it constantly. Furthermore the extensive customization and upgradability of different items provides even more depth,
My personal reccomendation for anyone is to play with a group of friends because that's when this game really shines. The public matchmaking isn't too bad either however you may encounter lag as well as AFK playes which are to be expected.

Cons:
Playing this game alone can sometimes be extremely boring and on higher tier mission it is directly discoraged as the game can get pretty difficult and going solo will just be a pain. The higher level equipment often requires a fair bit of farming which can quickly get repetitive and what doesn't help is that the rng sometimes seems utterly broken. And don't get surprised if it actually is broken as the game does suffer from its share of bugs and connectivity issues. Oh yeah and everytime you launch the game prepare yourself for 15 minutes of downloading new content....but maybe that's just me.

Overall I think warframe is a stellar example of how ftp games should be done. Whilst having microtransactions most of the high tier equipment isn't actually purchasable so forget about the ''pay to win'' strategy. There is no denying the ammount of content, lore and hours of fun you can have with your friends without paying a dollar.

In my opinion, EU4 is probably the best grand strategy game ever created. I've spent way too much of my life playing this game. Even after 10 years, I still can't put it down.

You'll see a lot of negative comments, and most of them are true, but most of them don't matter all that much:

Yes, it's got a lot of DLC and can be expensive to buy them all at once, but don't buy them all out of the gate. Sign up for a monthly subscription for a month and if you fall in love then buy the game and buy the DLC when they're on sale; most of the bundles and DLC go on 40-50% off sales every couple of months. Also, do your research on DLC, you don't need them all, many features of older DLCs have been pulled into the base game so there's fewer DLC packs that are really important.

Yes, EU5 has been released and is way more modern than EU4, but do yourself a favor and try EU4 instead. EU5 is a mess right now, they'll make a good game out of EU5 eventually (meaning in a year or two) but EU4 is a great game now. Plus, EU5's mechanics are way more complex so if you're getting into GSGs for the first time this is a much easier place to start.

Yes, this game is over 10 years old and its a bit dated, but it's a map painter, how spectacular of graphics do you really need for that? Besides, EU4 is still the standard by which other GSG's are measured. Don't let it's age hold you back.

All in all, this game is a 9/10 and that's only because every game has things you wish were a little different.

My favorite game of all time, from my favorite game studio of all time (Paradox).

Don't get fooled by the 1k hours count, I don't play videogames that much. EU4 captured the majority of my gaming time for almost 10 years, thanks to an addictive gameplay and virtually infinite replayability.

Each playthrough (i.e. each country you pick) is unique and presents different challenges to overcome. Learning curve is very steep but once you get it it becomes really straight forward (war, trade, economy, policy and tech research). I also found that regardless of how many games I played, starting a new gameplay never felt a "deja-vu" of an old game.

The presence of a clear time window (all games end in year 1821) ensures end-game doesn't become too boring or repetitive (a rarity for strategy games), although early and mid-game are definitely the most enjoyable part of the game as you try to establish your nation as a leading power.

The only downside from my perspective is the over-reliance on DLC which feels predatory. I purchased a couple of them, and more recently opted for the monthly pass to unlock them all for a specific gameplay.

This is my love letter to my favourite game of all time.

I’m well over 3,500 hours in, with no intention of stopping anytime soon. EU4 is one of those rare games that genuinely grows with you. The mechanics are deep without being inaccessible. Easy enough to learn the basics, brutally hard to actually master. Even after thousands of hours, I’m still learning new interactions, optimisations, and edge cases.

I’ll probably move to EU5 eventually, once it’s properly polished, but for now I’m more than happy staying here. Modern EU4 feels mature, dense, and rewarding in a way very few strategy games manage.

Mods help enormously when you want a break from vanilla. They keep the game feeling fresh and experimental. Third Odyssey deserves a special mention. It’s exceptional and feels like an alternate-history love letter layered on top of an already complex sandbox.

That said, I’m not going to pretend it’s perfect.

Paradox’s pricing model is predatory. There’s no real way around that. There are far too many DLCs, many of which add marginal value, and the sheer weight of years of expansions and updates has made the codebase creaky. Load times can be slow. Bugs and small glitches still crop up. New players should absolutely stick to the core gameplay DLCs and ignore unit packs and cosmetic fluff. You’re not missing anything meaningful.

What’s undeniable, though, is how much the game has evolved. Release EU4 and today’s EU4 barely resemble each other. Mechanics have been introduced, removed, reworked, and rebuilt over the years. Some changes landed better than others, but the end result is a staggeringly rich grand strategy game that rewards patience, planning, and long-term thinking.

If you like deep systems, historical sandboxes, and games that respect your intelligence, EU4 is still one of the best ever made. Even with its flaws, nothing else quite replaces it.

EU4 is an RNG based grand strategy sandbox game from 2013 that allows you to play as any country from every continent (except Antarctica) from 1444-1821. Your goal is to become the most powerful nation on Earth by conquering as much as you can before 1821. You have three types of powers that you spend on a multitude of things to strengthen your country, administrative, diplomatic, and military power. Admin is spent primarily on stability and administrative tech, diplo is spent on reducing war exhaustion, admirals, and diplomatic tech, and military is spent on generals and military tech.

Every country has one currency called ducats. Ducats can be attained from subsidies from other countries, through base trade, base tax, base production, war reparations in peace deals, and through demanding ducats in peace deals. Ducats are extremely important for buying a lot of things and if you run out of ducats and take too many loans you can go into bankruptcy for 10 years which plunges your country into -3 stability, wipes out all three powers to leave you at -100 for each one, gives your armies and navies -50% morale (basically hp modifier), and wipes out all of your loans. Bankruptcy is one of the worst things that can happen in EU4 besides stackwipes (your entire army getting destroyed after one battle) but is usually easily avoidable if you're skilled/experienced at the game. 

I could go on about all the mechanics but I just wanted to go over the big basic core parts of the game. The ONLY negative is the ridiculous amount of DLCs over the span of 12 years, much of it having a big impact on core mechanics of the game like developing provinces. 

Overall this game deserves a 9.5/10, if on sale I highly recommend buying and paying the monthly subscription to see if you want to buy any of the DLCs or not.

As I write this review, the next title (EU5) is slated to release tomorrow and I felt compelled to write a review and pay homage to the greatest strategy game of all time before I must say goodbye. 

This game is so much more than just a map painter, it's a an escape to a different world, a glimpse from a time long gone, a strategy sandbox where you can write history in so many different ways. For many of us, the year 1444 has become as familiar as our own birthdays, the borders and rulers of that frozen moment etched into memory like a second language. This game has taught me more about history and geography than any college class or textbook ever could. 

There’s such a simple joy in choosing a nation and immersing yourself in its story, roleplaying its triumphs and disasters, navigating diplomacy, warfare, and economics in a living, reactive world. 

Sure, it has a significant learning curve, but it incorporates the best systems and ideas about economics, warfare, and diplomacy from similar games into one massive sandbox. Even after 4000+ hours, every campaign is different, a unique story told through the lens of ambition, power, and chance.  A single decision can ripple through centuries. Truly a game with a unlimited replayability. 

The multiplayer is another aspect entirely. I could write pages more on that, but to keep brief, they were the fondest gaming memories I'll have. 

No other game has continued to captivate me 10 years later.

It's truly a masterpiece in its genre.

As Europa Universalis V is on the horizon, I want to leave a review for a game that I have enjoyed for almost a decade at this point. What can I say about EUIV? I can say it is by far my favorite game of all time, at least that I have ever played. I started playing this game when I was 15 years old, I am now 25. It has sparked my love for the early modern era of history and provided thousands of hours of entertainment. 

In regards to game play, I feel I am not the best to cover the learning curve, I have learned this game over the span of a decade, very slowly. I can say, it is outdated, naturally. It has no regard for population growth other than mana-based development. The military is easy to control but does have a learning curve in regards to combat engagement modifiers. The trade system I have heard from others is difficult to grasp, however I found it rather easy to understand.

As time has gone on, updates have made nations outside of Europe viable and even stronger than the European powers if you play "correctly" (Mughals and Mamluks especially) which is great because Europe, despite being the center focus of this title, can get very boring. 

I would absolutely recommend this game, however I dont know that I recommend playing it without the DLC, which I have bought gradually as they came out since 2017. As an up front cost, I would probably never touch it. I think it is worth it, but I am incredibly biased and recognize that not everyone will have the same affinity to this title as I do!

EU4 is the real Europa Universalis experience.
If you love war, conquest, and rewriting history from the Renaissance to Napoleon, this is the grand strategy game. Years of polish, systems that actually work together, and campaigns that stay fun for hundreds (or thousands) of hours.

EU4 might be an old veteran now, but it’s aged like fine wine. Tight pacing, satisfying campaigns, and warfare that feels rewarding instead of exhausting. It’s the grand strategy war game I’ve enjoyed the most, period.

EU5, on the other hand, feels like a chore disguised as a sequel.
I tried to like it. I really did. But it’s slow, clunky, and weirdly lifeless. The pacing is miserable, the UI/gamefeel is heavy, and so much of the time you’re not making bold strategic decisions, you’re fighting the interface and babysitting boring mechanics. It doesn’t feel “deeper,” it feels bloated.

Worst part? It loses what made EU4 addictive: momentum. In EU4, you’re planning wars, reacting to crises, building power, making moves. In EU5, you’re watching bars crawl, clicking through menus, and wondering when the game will finally let you play. It’s like they took a war-focused grand strategy classic and turned it into a sluggish resource-management simulator with extra steps.

And the playerbase (go to steam charts) tells the story better than any review: EU4 is still thriving because it’s simply more fun. EU5 being newer doesn’t matter if it’s less enjoyable.

If you’re choosing in 2026: play EU4.
EU5 can wait until it becomes a real game instead of a slow, frustrating prototype.

Rust is not a game — it’s a social experiment designed to answer one question: How fast will a grown adult scream when a naked man with a rock ruins their day?

You spawn in with nothing but shame, a rock, and the unsettling realization that every other player has thousands of hours and unresolved anger issues. Within 30 seconds, you’re either being hunted by a wolf, a scientist, or a 12-year-old screaming slurs through a $5 microphone. Sometimes all three. At once.

The crafting system is incredible. You can turn a tree into a gun, a gun into confidence, and that confidence into immediate death because you trusted a guy named “xX_RaiderGod69_Xx.” Building a base feels amazing — right up until someone offline raids it at 4 a.m. using explosives they somehow made out of your own door.

Rust PvP is peak comedy. Gunfights last two seconds, involve zero accuracy, and end with you yelling “HE’S ONE HP” before watching your corpse ragdoll down a hill. The proximity chat is pure art: one minute it’s diplomacy, the next it’s screaming, barking, or someone playing the recorder while looting your body.

The best part? You’ll swear you hate this game. You’ll uninstall it. You’ll write a thinkpiece about toxic communities.
Then 20 minutes later you’ll reinstall because this wipe is gonna be different.

Rating: 10/10

Verdict: A brutal survival game where player interaction—not systems alone—defines the experience.

Rust’s mechanics are deliberately unforgiving. Progression, base-building, and combat are tightly intertwined with social dynamics, making every encounter meaningful. Trust, deception, and power structures emerge organically rather than through scripted systems.

The game excels at emergent storytelling. No two wipes play out the same, and player-driven conflict creates moments that feel more intense than most scripted experiences. However, this same freedom can be overwhelming or frustrating, especially for solo players.

What Works Well

Emergent, player-driven gameplay

Deep base-building systems

High tension and stakes

Strong long-term replayability

What Needs Improvement

Extremely punishing for new players

Time investment can be excessive

Community behavior varies WILDLY

Final Thoughts:
Rust is not a comfortable game—but for players willing to embrace its harsh design philosophy, it offers unforgettable experiences and unattainable fantasies.

Rust markets itself as a “survival game.” That’s a lie. Rust is a full-time job where your salary is trauma and your boss is a 14-year-old with a shotgun and a racial slur ready to deploy at 3am.

You spawn naked on a beach, optimistic. Ten minutes later you’re dead, looted, and questioning your self-worth because someone named xXCLANLEADER69Xx beat you to death with a rock while screaming into a £300 mic. This cycle repeats until optimism is fully removed from your personality.

Progress in Rust is measured not in fun, but in hours lost to paranoia. You will wake up in the night to “check the base.” You will cancel plans because “the wipe just started.” You will defend this decision to loved ones who are already planning interventions.

Every base you build is temporary. Every friendship is fake. Every door code will be betrayed. Rust teaches powerful life lessons like:
• Trust no one
• Sleep is optional
• Your time means nothing

The game excels at giving you hope just long enough to hurt you more. You farm for six hours, log off for ten minutes, and come back to ashes. No note. No mercy. Just silence and the distant sound of someone recycling your stuff.

And yet… you’ll reinstall it. Every time. Because once in a while, you win a fight. Once in a while, the sun hits your base just right. Once in a while, you feel something again.

Rust doesn’t respect you. It doesn’t care about balance. It doesn’t care about your life.
But you’ll keep playing. Because Rust isn’t entertainment.

It’s Stockholm Syndrome with crafting.

Would I recommend it?
Absolutely not.

See you after wipe.

Rust is one of the most exciting and unpredictable survival games I’ve played. The core gameplay—gathering resources, crafting gear, building a base, and defending what’s yours—always keeps you on your toes. The sense of progression feels great: you start with almost nothing, and before you know it you’ve built a fortified compound and are running around with high-end weapons. The PvP is intense and nerve-racking in the best way, and even when you lose everything it’s strangely fun to scramble back and life begins again.

What really makes Rust fun for me is the player interactions—whether it’s teaming up, ambushing someone, trading goods, or forming alliances, every play session creates its own stories and memories. The building system is versatile, and although the graphics aren’t flashy, they fit the gritty atmosphere perfectly.

Sure, it can be tough and sometimes frustrating (especially when raided), but that’s part of what makes it memorable. If you’re into open-ended survival where anything can happen, Rust is a blast.

Wild, emergent gameplay with real player drama

Deep crafting and base building

Great sense of achievement and progression

Tons of replay value

Rust markets itself as a “survival game.” That’s a lie. Rust is a full-time job where your salary is trauma and your boss is a 14-year-old with a shotgun and a racial slur ready to deploy at 3am.

Progress in Rust is measured not in fun, but in hours lost to paranoia. You will wake up in the night to “check the base.” You will cancel plans because “the wipe just started.” You will defend this decision to loved ones who are already planning interventions.

Every base you build is temporary. Every friendship is fake. Every door code will be betrayed. Rust teaches powerful life lessons like:
• Trust no one
• Sleep is optional
• Your time means nothing

The game excels at giving you hope just long enough to hurt you more. You farm for six hours, log off for ten minutes, and come back to ashes. No note. No mercy. Just silence and the distant sound of someone recycling your stuff.

And yet… you’ll reinstall it. Every time. Because once in a while, you win a fight. Once in a while, the sun hits your base just right. Once in a while, you feel something again.

Rust doesn’t respect you. It doesn’t care about balance. It doesn’t care about your life.
But you’ll keep playing. Because Rust isn’t entertainment.

It’s Stockholm Syndrome with crafting.

Would I recommend it?
Absolutely not.

See you after wipe.

I bought Rust thinking it would just be another survival game I’d mess around in for a weekend. I’d seen clips of raids, roof camping, and funny naked players running around with rocks, and I figured: “Yeah, I’ll try it out. Looks chaotic but fun.”

That was one of the worst decisions I’ve ever made.

At first, Rust felt amazing. The tension of hearing footsteps outside your base, the fear when a helicopter flies overhead, the rush of finding your first gun — it was all addictive in a way I didn’t fully understand yet. I told myself I’d just play a couple hours… then suddenly it was 3 AM. Then 5 AM. Then the sun was coming up and I hadn’t slept.

Fast forward to 70+ hours, and I realized something terrifying: Rust didn’t just become a game I played — it became my entire life.

I stopped caring about other games. I stopped caring about my normal routine. I’d sit at my PC thinking about Rust even when I wasn’t playing. “Should I move my base?” “Did my doors decay?” “What if someone is raiding me right now?” I’d be lying in bed stressing about pixels in a video game like it was real life.

The thing about Rust is that it messes with your brain. You don’t just play it — you live in it. Every scrap matters. Every minute matters. Every decision feels high stakes. If you log off for too long, you might wake up to your base completely wiped and everything gone. That fear alone keeps you glued to your screen longer than any game ever should.

Socially, Rust also destroyed me for a bit. I stopped talking to friends as much. I skipped calls. I ignored messages because I was “busy defending base.” I’d tell people, “Yeah, I’ll hop off soon,” and then not log off for another four hours. My sleep schedule got absolutely cooked. I started staying up way too late, grinding for loot that would probably just get raided anyway.

And that’s the cruel joke of Rust — no matter how hard you work, you can lose everything overnight. You can spend 10 hours building a base, farming, crafting guns, grinding components… and then some sweaty clan comes along at 3 AM and blows it all up while you’re offline. All that effort? Gone. For nothing.

But here’s the worst part: even after all that, I still wanted to keep playing. Rust is rage-inducing, stressful, and sometimes downright miserable… yet it’s also insanely compelling. The highs are ridiculously high. Winning a big raid, surviving a crazy fight, or outsmarting other players feels better than almost any other game I’ve played.

So did Rust ruin my life? In a way… yeah. At least for a while. It turned me into a sleep-deprived grinder who cared way too much about a virtual base. It made me angry, paranoid, and obsessed. I lost track of time constantly.

But was it also one of the most memorable gaming experiences I’ve ever had? Also yes.

Rust isn’t just a game — it’s a psychological experiment disguised as a survival sandbox. If you value your time, your sleep, or your sanity… do not buy this game. But if you’re curious, reckless, and want to experience pure chaos, betrayal, adrenaline, and stress in digital form… welcome to Rust. You’ve been warned.

I went outside for the first time in years. It was winter. I wore sunglasses. Not for style — my eyes weren’t calibrated for daylight anymore. I flinched at footsteps. I checked corners. Rust followed me home.

Every kill felt illegal.
Every death felt personal.
Every wipe felt like a chance to finally be happy (it wasn’t).

I bought Rust thinking it would just be another survival game I’d mess around in for a weekend. I’d seen clips of raids, roof camping, and funny naked players running around with rocks, and I figured: “Yeah, I’ll try it out. Looks chaotic but fun.”

That was one of the worst decisions I’ve ever made.

At first, Rust felt amazing. The tension of hearing footsteps outside your base, the fear when a helicopter flies overhead, the rush of finding your first gun — it was all addictive in a way I didn’t fully understand yet. I told myself I’d just play a couple hours… then suddenly it was 3 AM. Then 5 AM. Then the sun was coming up and I hadn’t slept.

Fast forward to 70+ hours, and I realized something terrifying: Rust didn’t just become a game I played — it became my entire life.

I stopped caring about other games. I stopped caring about my normal routine. I’d sit at my PC thinking about Rust even when I wasn’t playing. “Should I move my base?” “Did my doors decay?” “What if someone is raiding me right now?” I’d be lying in bed stressing about pixels in a video game like it was real life.

The thing about Rust is that it messes with your brain. You don’t just play it — you live in it. Every scrap matters. Every minute matters. Every decision feels high stakes. If you log off for too long, you might wake up to your base completely wiped and everything gone. That fear alone keeps you glued to your screen longer than any game ever should.

Socially, Rust also destroyed me for a bit. I stopped talking to friends as much. I skipped calls. I ignored messages because I was “busy defending base.” I’d tell people, “Yeah, I’ll hop off soon,” and then not log off for another four hours. My sleep schedule got absolutely cooked. I started staying up way too late, grinding for loot that would probably just get raided anyway.

And that’s the cruel joke of Rust — no matter how hard you work, you can lose everything overnight. You can spend 10 hours building a base, farming, crafting guns, grinding components… and then some sweaty clan comes along at 3 AM and blows it all up while you’re offline. All that effort? Gone. For nothing.

But here’s the worst part: even after all that, I still wanted to keep playing. Rust is rage-inducing, stressful, and sometimes downright miserable… yet it’s also insanely compelling. The highs are ridiculously high. Winning a big raid, surviving a crazy fight, or outsmarting other players feels better than almost any other game I’ve played.

So did Rust ruin my life? In a way… yeah. At least for a while. It turned me into a sleep-deprived grinder who cared way too much about a virtual base. It made me angry, paranoid, and obsessed. I lost track of time constantly.

But was it also one of the most memorable gaming experiences I’ve ever had? Also yes.

Rust isn’t just a game — it’s a psychological experiment disguised as a survival sandbox. If you value your time, your sleep, or your sanity… do not buy this game. But if you’re curious, reckless, and want to experience pure chaos, betrayal, adrenaline, and stress in digital form… welcome to Rust. You’ve been warned.

I like the building site of the game and the PVP and I love the update they do every couple months.

Rust is not a game. It’s a long-term psychological condition. You don’t start playing Rust — you slowly disappear from real life and nobody notices because you’re “just busy this wipe.”

You spawn naked, afraid, and hopeful. This is the last time you’ll feel hope. Within minutes, a man who hasn’t seen the sun since Obama was president kills you with military-grade hardware and screams something illegal into voice chat. This becomes normal.

I skipped three Christmases with my family. Not because I was busy. Because there was a wipe. While normal people ate dinner and exchanged gifts, I was sitting in a dark room, listening for footsteps, heart rate at 140, guarding virtual doors that no longer exist.

I played 19 hours a day. Sleep was a suggestion. Food was optional. Hydration was replaced with Mountain Dew until my body started sending error messages. Rust didn’t just simulate survival — it tried to kill me in real life. Immersion 10/10.

The progression system is genius. You farm for days so someone else can take everything in 10 minutes while you’re offline experiencing something meaningless like “human connection.” Base building isn’t content — it’s charity.

The community is the final boss. Children screaming. Adults roleplaying war crimes. “Friendly” players betraying you before your crafting menu closes. Voice chat feels like a leaked audio file from a court case.

Eventually, my graphics card burned out. Literally died. The only thing that saved me.
I went outside for the first time in years. It was winter. I wore sunglasses. Not for style — my eyes weren’t calibrated for daylight anymore. I flinched at footsteps. I checked corners. Rust followed me home.

And yet… I miss it.
Every kill felt illegal.
Every death felt personal.
Every wipe felt like a chance to finally be happy (it wasn’t).

Recommended
For players who:

don’t need a social life

think trauma builds character

hear footsteps in silence

10/10 — lost time, sanity, relationships, a GPU, and part of my soul.

O Geometry Dash, thou trial of flashing light and cruel design,
Where cubes do leap and spires do bite with merciless delight.
Each beat a heartbeat of the soul, each spike a sharpened doubt,
Yet still the player presses on, though failure shouts aloud.

For in thy realm, no victory comes to those who fear the fall.
A thousand deaths must school the hand before one stands up tall.
Mistakes are writ in crimson sparks, but lessons burn in gold,
And patience turns the trembling novice into spirits bold.

What art thou, Dash, but life made pure
A single path, no turning back?
The rhythm guides, the eyes must trust,
The mind must hold where hands may crack.

Press on, brave heart, when progress seems a lie,
When one more spike denies the dream you seek.
For triumph lives not in the flawless try,
But in the will that rises, weak yet speaks:

“Once more.”

And so thou jump’st again, refined by every loss,
Till chaos bends to mastery and fear is but a ghost.
At last the final portal fades, the level stands complete
Not just the game is conquered then, but doubt beneath thy feet.

Remember this, when worlds beyond the screen feel just as steep:
No spike eternal stands before a soul that dares to leap.

Geometry Dash is a rhythm-based platformer that has captivated players with its challenging levels and vibrant aesthetics since its release. The game is not just about jumping and flying through danger in a geometrical world; it’s also about timing, precision, and patience. Players can progress through the levels in the main game, but there's also a vast array of user-generated content thanks to the level editor, which has created a thriving community around the game. Apart from the gameplay, Geometry Dash allows players to customize their cube with different colors and skins obtained through achievements or purchased in the shop. These customization options add a personal touch to the gameplay, giving players a sense of ownership over their progress and style.

Jump again.

And still the cube moves.

Not because it will win.
But because stopping was never an option.

10/10 The Rhythm Game That Carried Me Through High School

Geometry Dash was legitimately my lifeline back in high school. Whenever the stress of exams, assignments, or just teenage nonsense got too heavy, I’d plug in my headphones, fire up the game, and lose myself for hours. It’s not just a game—it’s therapy with sick beats.

The soundtrack is straight-up phenomenal. Every level has its own personality because of the music—those perfectly synced drops, the build-ups, the moments where the beat just hits right as you nail a tricky section. The immersion is unreal; you stop thinking about everything else and become one with the cube/fly/ship/whatever you’re controlling.

And yeah—it’s brutally tricky. You’re going to die. A lot. But that’s the magic. Every failure teaches you something. You learn the patterns, you memorize timings, you train your fingers and your brain until suddenly that impossible section clicks and you’re screaming “LET’S GOOO” at 2 a.m. It forces you to actually get better through repetition, muscle memory, and pure stubbornness. There’s no hand-holding here—just you vs. the level vs. your own limits.

If you want a game that’s equal parts frustrating and insanely rewarding, with a soundtrack that still slaps years later, Geometry Dash is worth every single rage-quit and every perfect run. Still boot it up to this day. Still top-tier.

Buy it. Suffer. Improve. Vibe. Repeat.

10/10 The Rhythm Game That Carried Me Through High School

Geometry Dash was legitimately my lifeline back in high school. Whenever the stress of exams, assignments, or just teenage nonsense got too heavy, I’d plug in my headphones, fire up the game, and lose myself for hours. It’s not just a game—it’s therapy with sick beats.

The soundtrack is straight-up phenomenal. Every level has its own personality because of the music—those perfectly synced drops, the build-ups, the moments where the beat just hits right as you nail a tricky section. The immersion is unreal; you stop thinking about everything else and become one with the cube/fly/ship/whatever you’re controlling.

And yeah—it’s brutally tricky. You’re going to die. A lot. But that’s the magic. Every failure teaches you something. You learn the patterns, you memorize timings, you train your fingers and your brain until suddenly that impossible section clicks and you’re screaming “LET’S GOOO” at 2 a.m. It forces you to actually get better through repetition, muscle memory, and pure stubbornness. There’s no hand-holding here—just you vs. the level vs. your own limits.

If you want a game that’s equal parts frustrating and insanely rewarding, with a soundtrack that still slaps years later, Geometry Dash is worth every single rage-quit and every perfect run. Still boot it up to this day. Still top-tier.

Buy it. Suffer. Improve. Vibe. Repeat.

The Hundred Years' War (French: Guerre de Cent Ans; 1337–1453) was a conflict between the kingdoms of England and France and a civil war in France during the Late Middle Ages. It emerged from feudal disputes over the Duchy of Aquitaine and was triggered by a claim to the French throne made by Edward III of England. The war grew into a broader military, economic, and political struggle involving factions from across Western Europe, fuelled by emerging nationalism on both sides. The periodisation of the war typically charts it as taking place over 116 years. However, it was an intermittent conflict which was frequently interrupted by external factors, such as the Black Death, and several years of truces.

The Hundred Years' War was a significant conflict in the Middle Ages. During the war, five generations of kings from two rival dynasties fought for the throne of France, then the wealthiest and most populous kingdom in Western Europe. The war had a lasting effect on European history: both sides produced innovations in military technology and tactics, including professional standing armies and artillery, that permanently changed European warfare. Chivalry reached its height during the conflict and subsequently declined. Stronger national identities took root in both kingdoms, which became more centralized and gradually emerged as global powers.[2]

The term "Hundred Years' War" was adopted by later historians as a historiographical periodisation to encompass dynastically related conflicts, constructing the longest military conflict in European history.[3][4] The war is commonly divided into three phases, separated by truces: the Edwardian War (1337–1360), the Caroline War (1369–1389), and the Lancastrian War (1415–1453). Each side drew many allies into the conflict, with English forces initially prevailing; however, the French forces under the House of Valois ultimately retained control over the Kingdom of France. The French and English monarchies thereafter remained separate, despite the monarchs of England and Great Britain styling themselves as sovereigns of France until 1802.

Origins
The root causes of the conflict can be traced to the crisis of 14th-century Europe. The outbreak of war was motivated by a gradual rise in tension between the kings of France and England over territory; the official pretext was the interruption of the direct male line of the Capetian dynasty.

Tensions between the French and English crowns had gone back centuries, since the Norman Conquest of 1066 had put a king of (Norman) French origins, William, duke of Normandy, on the throne of England. Since that time, English monarchs had held titles and lands within France, which made them vassals to the kings of France. The status of the English king's French fiefs was a significant source of conflict between the two monarchies throughout the Middle Ages.[citation needed] According to military historian and author Michael Livingston, the conflict began in 1337, when Philippe VI of France claimed that France controlled English holdings in France.[5]

In 1328, Charles IV of France died without any sons or brothers, initiating a succession crisis. A similar crisis in 1316 had resulted in the Estates-General in 1317 deciding that "Women do not succeed in the kingdom of France". Charles's closest male relative was his nephew Edward III of England, whose mother Isabella was Charles's sister. Isabella claimed the throne of France for her son by the rule of proximity of blood, but the French nobility rejected this on the basis of the 1317 decision, declaring that Isabella could not transmit a right she did not possess. An assembly of French barons decided that a native Frenchman should receive the crown rather than Edward.[6]

The throne passed to Charles's patrilineal cousin instead, Philip, Count of Valois who had been made regent on the death of Charles IV. Edward protested but ultimately submitted and did homage for Gascony. Further French disagreements with Edward induced Philip during May 1337 to meet with his Great Council in Paris. It was agreed that Gascony should be taken back into Philip's hands, which prompted Edward to renew his claim for the French throne, this time by force of arms.[7]

Edwardian phase
In the early years of the war, the English, led by King Edward III and his son Edward the Black Prince, saw resounding successes, notably at the battles of Crécy (1346) and Poitiers (1356), where King John II of France, having succeeded his father Philip from 1350, was taken prisoner.

Caroline phase and Black Death
By 1378, under King Charles V the Wise and the leadership of Bertrand du Guesclin, the French had reconquered most of the lands ceded to King Edward in the Treaty of Brétigny (signed in 1360), notably reducing English control on the continent, leaving them with few cities.

However, both countries faced challenges and problems. The Black Death, a deadly plague that spread through Europe between 1347 and 1351 caused catastrophic widespread damage. In France, 6 to 12 million people died, 30% to 60% of the population,[8] resulting in major labour shortages, economic collapse, and widespread social dislocation. England also suffered from the Black Death, but to a lesser extent, with roughly 2–3 million deaths. Economic consequences of the plague and the war led to major unrest in both kingdoms, widespread poverty, and a weakening of royal authority.[9][10] These crises were resolved in England earlier than in France.

The gameplay loop for survivor or killer is very addictive. As killer you can dominate and control the match as you try prevent other players from escaping alive and this is a feeling of power/immersion as the monster/killer you can rarely experience in any other game. Survivor is the opposite side of the spectrum where you must work together with 3 other players to repair 5 generators to escape alive all whilst hiding or evading the killer and the mechanics and strategy is suprisingly complex at high level which makes replayability very fun. The only other game I have played similar that was also addicting was a game that died called evolve which was also 1v4 or Friday the 13th which was like a 1v10. This game is by far the most polished Asymmetric multiplayer game I have seen and the community has made many attempts to balance gameplay for both sides. Flaws I have noticed is that playing as killer I feel confident I can win 80-90% of the time with certain killers like nurse or singularity which tells me that maybe a slight nerf might be in order (nurse has gotten nerfed so its a little bit better) the oppressive nature of killers needs to balance with not having any effective counter play for the other side. The other flaw is if you are playing survivor alone with 3 random people its doable but not as effective as having a 4 man team I would suggest the developers add some sort of proximity chat or a way for people to communicate in the game. Prox chat would be so funny and bring in more players for sure I believe

At the end of a long workday, once I’m home and settled, my first instinct is to boot up Dead by Daylight and run a few matches. That’s how deeply this game has worked its way into my routine—and honestly, I’m perfectly fine with that. Dead by Daylight, this game was a unique breath of fresh air with its dark game of tag that had me interested since starting in 2019 as primarily a solo queue player. It has been several years since and this game has had ups and downs since that time, but I did what I could to enjoy the time on it whenever I did play.

This review is a warning to anyone who is thinking about playing this game alone. If you have depression, rage issues, or lacking self worth, then completely ignore everything and buy the game immediately because this could really scratch that itch if you have that addictive tendency to games like that.

Perks, are you a theory crafter? That's good, this game has a ton of perks in it to try new things for you. However, more than half of them will be unusable for you due to various gameplay/teamplay aspects that will rut your build useless in most cases.

Gameplay, I'll speak for survivors only here, sorry fresh killer mains. Once you load in, your match is going to be decided by a few factors. The first is the map you spawn into, the second is the RNG MMR you were given, is it a baby Pig player learning the game like you are? Or is it going to be a Ghoul/Krasue player who has every unenjoyable perk and addon equipped with 8,000 hours and a deep desire to see you uninstall by force tunneling you out of the game? Ohh goodie, surprises! You can tell the priority for quality gameplay matches isn't there because match lobbies pop in under 5 seconds these days. Nobody is the same skill level and it is all variable.

Do you like the cosmetics? Good, you will be spending years to obtain a handful of them unless you pay up front. Earning your cosmetics, DLC and other things in this game is a massive time sink. You can easily complete tons of other game series, MMOs and other content before you collect all the perks and DLC in here at the rate that they come out currently, be wary as this would require over 1,000+ hours of gameplay to get through.

Surely, the community buffers any of this does it? Yes and no, there are some good eggs in here still I'm sure, but the ratio of negative and otherwise bad experiences of people throwing a fit has gone from what felt like 20% of matches before 2020 all the way up to 70-80% of matches in the current day. This translates to about 4 of your 5 matches being matched with people who do an assortment of [Sweat, DC, Troll, Flame, Act entitled] among several other things. There came a point where Dead by Daylight wasn't as popular as it is now and with that popularity I'm sure Behavior has had one hell of a time trying to contain the kind of people this genre will attract.

As for the company themselves, I cannot add much of a comment here as I'm sure they take enough heat as is. I do genuinely believe that this game is very overdue for a competitor in order to push the company to proactively fix a large plethora of in game bugs, issues and overall community concerns.

Wrapping this up, Dead by Daylight is simply not a good experience in these recent years if you are a solo player who can see themselves going more than 100 hours deep into the game, I can only advise you take a look at the game's health in a few years and make your decision then. I will personally still be playing out of sunk cost fallacy alone, but if I could reverse the hours down to 500 or less, I would.

Extra Info for insight: I gave this game a break, I even play it casually, I do my dailies at times, and attempts have been made to "keep things fresh". It is still a miserable experience the moment killers/survivors misbehave over the dumbest things. League of Legends solo queue ranked has harbored less toxicity than what I witness here these days. Plenty of people I've met in Dead by Daylight also have mentioned it being terrible, they just get by and tolerate it. I didn't outgrow this game, the core gameplay loop itself is still there, but it is plagued by too many negatives to continue to give it the time of day anymore.

Anyways, hope this adds another stroke of paint to the picture this experience might be like if you decide to give it a go now or not. Best of luck to any journey you decide on regardless, take care.

My review as a survivor main:
I kinda love and hate this game at the same time. It is sometimes so unfair and hard, so you think about uninstalling it for good. But then you get a few matches, where you have so much fun and do so good, you will play again the next day. It's always luring in the back of your head, manipulating you to come back.

But honestly the fun starts (as survivor), when you really understand the perks of both sides, the killer powers and how to outplay them, to loop the different tiles and how to mindgame them, the management inside the team what to prioritise, do flashlight saves and so on. It's even more fun to play it with friends cause playing alone can get really frustrating. I really like the variety of different playstyles the game gives you with the 280 different perks. You can focus on the generators, on looping, on healing, or do a meme build, and so on. You can play how you want and test what build fits you best or you have the most fun with. It keeps the game interesting for me.

There are for sure some bad sides of it. For example a lot of bugs, broken game mechanics, bad mmr (you get queued with a surv with 10 hours and a killer with 5000 hours) which makes it really hard and frustating to play the game. The community is very mixed but mostly negative minded I would say. When you play really good and clean as a surv, the killer gets hella mad and camps you, or humps or insults you in post game chat. Even though you play the game as intended. A lot of people don't realise it is still to some part skill based and you can't blame everything on the game itself. Sometimes you're just bad.

Even with all the controversy, I would still recommend it cause It's just such a fun game. You need to invest a lot of time. But the real fun starts with some game knowledge.

[h2][i]Dead by Daylight[/i] remains a genre-defining asymmetrical horror game, but years of accumulated systems and design debt have left the experience feeling uneven and increasingly unfocused.[/h2]

[h2]Highlights[/h2]
✅ Unique asymmetrical horror gameplay
✅ Iconic killers with strong visual & audio identity
✅ Consistent updates & new characters
✅ Strong skill expression and long-term player improvement

[h2]Flaws[/h2]
⛔ Lackluster MMR system
⛔ Severe perk bloat
⛔ Poor optimization & limited settings
⛔ Outdated visuals & lighting
⛔ Grind-heavy progression

[i]Dead by Daylight[/i] excels in its moment-to-moment gameplay. The asymmetrical horror formula remains largely unmatched, with iconic killers and strong visual and audio identity. There’s genuine depth in learning how to loop, mastering maps, understanding matchups, and countering different builds, which creates a strong sense of player improvement over time. Regular updates and new characters help keep the experience feeling fresh.

However, long-term issues hold it back. The MMR system often produces one-sided matches, perk bloat has led to stale metas and an overwhelming learning curve, and poor optimization paired with limited settings gives unfair advantages to players using configs or filters. The visuals feel dated, with weak lighting, inconsistent textures, stiff models and physics, and many low-quality cosmetics. Combined with an increasingly grind-heavy progression system that discourages experimentation, the experience becomes more frustrating the longer you play.

Overall, Dead by Daylight is still a one-of-a-kind horror experience that keeps me coming back. The tension, mind games, and thrill of learning new strategies make every match feel fresh, and no other game captures that mix of fear and skill quite like it. That said, without meaningful refinement to its core systems, balance, and progression, the experience can feel held back by its own design baggage rather than fully elevated.

[h2]Grade: B+[/h2]
Dead by Daylight is fun, unique, and deeply rewarding, but systemic flaws and aging design prevent it from fully realizing its potential.

It was fascinating to watch and last summer I caught the game on 75% sale and gave it 80hours of my life as a survivor, since that was the only way to get a match going in a minute or two.
Over the following 80h alongside some video guides an the 2v8 event event, I came to the following conclusion.
There are 3 groups of players: the newbies who just bought the game and will spend the following dozens of hours not truly sure of what are they doing
                                                      the middle class, that has in a hundred or few hours in and have some vaque idea of what everything does and what they should do
                                                      the old guard, they have 1000 and more hours in the game and view the game like Neo does matrix
I bought it mostly for that hihihi feeling when you are chased by the monster, something which I would get alongside a lot of frustration.
There are obvious meta killers/builds and I learned early on to recognize when I will not have much fun, anytime Wesker,Blight or the Tyrant showed up my urge to just close the game went rapidly up, but I stayed and unsurprisingly got absolutely wrecked.
Then some poor soul would attempt to have fun by trying a niche killer and spend the entire much trying to catch a glimpse of a single survivor.
The game is horribly unbalanced by design, since the only way to play some kind of tourney everyone has to stab themselves by issuing severe restrictions on each side in order to provide a modicum of fairness.
How wonderful that in order to have things fair you have to throw away vasts swats of the gameplay mechanics that game offers.
Behaviour Interactive lives far above their players in an ivroy tower that is still getting flooded by money, they poach in new players by dangling a popular horror character in front of them and squeeze the rest by offering them overpriced skins while blatantly ignoring any atempt to fix their game.
The longtime players have their share of the blame, since the veterans on both sides will abuse any unintended mechanic to win which helped achieving the games current status.
Once upon a time when the game just released the game was what it was meant to be, a horror experience that offered both sides of the baricade, now it turned into an unintended competetive mess both because of the players and the developers.
Its impossible to recommend this game to anyone in good will, the only way to enjoy it somewhat is to hope that the matchmaking will spare you and group you together with someone who is as clueless as you, while the 1000h players will stay grouped up together so they may screw each other over in peace.

Let me start off by saying, between Steam and my Nintendo Switch, I have over 2000 hours invested in this game and have been in this community for quite a while.

I'll start off with some of the positives by saying that this game can be fun, when you get lucky enough to get in a good lobby. The crossovers are cool and their original characters are pretty neat, too, so you have a variety of characters to choose from and you can dress them up all cool and stuff, too. The game has relatively consistent updates and quite a few events throughout the year, including some limited-time game modes to spice things up, which are pretty fun. Some of them are even more fun than the default game mode.

Now onto the bad stuff... Killer queue times are absolute ass. You will be sitting in lobbies for AGES just to get into a single match. Survivor queue times aren't as bad, thankfully. Secondly, this game is not beginner friendly at all in terms of it's players and basically everything about how THE GAME ITSELF is. I'll start off with the players; the player base has a HUGE aggression problem and is generally unwelcoming towards new players, so if you're trying to figure out how the game works in a public lobby, then prepare for hostility from other players. Hell, even if you aren't a new player, lobbies have issues with griefing and, best of all, harassment in endgame chat. Lovely. As for the game itself not being beginner friendly, it is a CONSTANT learning curve because of how much there is in the game. There are 48 survivors, each with three perks they come with, and there are 38 killers, also with three unique perks they come with AND the killers come with special built-in abilities. There are also general killer/survivor perks. You can probably do some of the math on that. I bring this up to say that there is so much stuff to keep tabs on what it does that any newcomer would be overwhelmed by it. This isn't to say the variety is a BAD thing, but it's just reasonably confusing to anyone trying to start the game. This is made worse by the SUPER out of date tutorial. The tutorial teaches you very basic shit, but there is NOTHING to tell you about perks and items in said tutorial. 

Now, onto the bigger and way more disappointing issue... The devs themselves are incompetent. There is a lack of proper care taken when it comes to listening to the community... And by that I mean they hardly seem to listen to community issues at all, unless it has to do with cosmetic contests and what crossovers people may want, and even then, they often fuck those up, too. There has been such a MASSIVE amount of bugs over the years that have affected the quality of the game. Sure, bugs are bound to happen, but when you do public test build runs before chapter releases and have the community make you aware of massive issues, only to ignore them and release the new update without doing a proper bug fix anyways, it's not just a "bugs happen" type of issue, it's a "the developers do not care enough about their product" sort of issue. Speaking of developers not caring and bugs, it has become a habit of the devs not fixing game breaking stuff until MONTHS down the line, and I feel that it's important to bring up that these bugs have been so drastic that one of the instances includes a strobing bug that caused quite a few players to have SEIZURES. What was the dev teams response? Not giving a fuck. There's so many instances of the developers not listening to community feedback  and neglecting to properly care for the state of their game, that, if I keep going off about them, I will have a full college essay for my review. It's that bad.

I will leave off on a final note that I wish the developers would treat this game with the care that it deserves. I feel they forget this has been their only successful project, and if this game goes down, then BHVR themselves are done for. It would be a shame, considering it's one of the only games of this kind that have actually lasted a decade and have an active player base.

How does a game live on? Originally starting out as a serious co-op horror experience, Dead by Daylight has morphed into an arcade game rife with pop culture characters and needless tweaks. A question posed by many players is, "Does it work?" And the answer is: sometimes.
    If one were to look back on Dead by Daylight's humble origins, they could see a game brimming with potential. A limited array of characters and a highly addictive game-loop gave DbD a leg-up in comparison to its multiplayer competition--even trumping the asymmetrical-horror competition that would later follow as a result. The game ran on atmosphere and depended on you (the player) being terrified or being terrifying. Many would say this was the 'golden-age' of the game (and it was good), but to say that is to disregard the improvements made by the modern DbD.
    Dead by Daylight might not be terrifying anymore--or at the least, not in the intended way--but still it survives. But how? The 'game-ification' of DbD has vastly improved (or made engaging) the previously barebones gameplay loop. What was once a cast of a measly three killers has now expanded far into the double digits.  Both the survivors and killers have benefitted from licenses concerning some of the biggest names in horror and each game is now a true surprise in terms of what killer you'll face. Additionally, the game's weakened focus on horror but instead on engagement creates matches that feel more fun to play in succession. Balancing issues aside, games are usually a tense toss-up of abilities. However, these aforementioned balancing issues and the lack of focus on horror (among other aspects of the game) fail to connect with many players, and rightfully so. Newly added killers are usually nerfed into oblivion following their release and following dominance in matches, and new survivors are usually only justified by their licensing and expensive skins, hardly ever having decent or fun perks. Such is the consequence of bloating the game's perk pool and character slots beyond what was once thought possible in the early epochs of the game's existence. Yet, DbD has survived even when many other games of its kind have died. And that's because it refuses to stay still. The game is constantly evolving: both to its benefit and detriment.
   So, again: how does a game live? In the case of DbD, the answer is momentum. Pure inertia. There have been multiple moments when the game has almost faltered and faded into obscurity, but whether Behavior Interactive actually balances the game's prominent issues or just piles on another broken DLC, people still tune in to see how it's holding up: which is by a shoestring. But still, it holds. All in all, DbD is certainly adequate, but only time will tell if it stays that way.

I’ve spent over two thousand hours in Dead by Daylight, and this is one of those cases where the number isn’t there to flex, but to make one thing clear: I know what I’m talking about. I started playing in 2017, and even before that, back in 2016, I was already following the game closely — watching streams, reading forums, trying to understand where it was heading. Back then, it was genuinely a unique project. Dead by Daylight was a horror game, not an attraction. Tension was constant, every sound mattered, every mistake was punished, but every correct decision gave you a real sense of control and satisfaction.

A killer could wipe the entire lobby if they played well, if they thought ahead, if they knew how to read the map and the players. At the same time, a single truly skilled survivor could loop the killer long enough for the team to calmly finish three, four, sometimes even five generators. Not because the killer was weak, but because the survivor understood timings, positioning, how to run loops properly, and didn’t panic. It wasn’t chaotic running — it was deliberate gameplay, where your individual skill genuinely mattered. That honest exchange of skill is what kept the game alive.

Very little of that remains today. Dead by Daylight has stopped being a horror game and has turned into a mass-market live service. Behaviour deliberately chose the path of simplification and monetization. Instead of atmosphere and fear, we get skins. Instead of tension, we get endless killers and survivors from movies and TV shows. Instead of proper balance, we get constant buffs designed to make new content sell better. From a business perspective, this might be a success, but from a gameplay perspective, it’s a slow and steady killing of the original idea.

Playing killer today is laughably easy. You can be an average player, you don’t even have to think that much, and you’ll still consistently get 4Ks. The game forgives mistakes, the mechanics actively push you toward winning, and most killers don’t require serious mindgames or planning anymore. And yet there are still people who somehow struggle to win as killer, and honestly, I don’t understand what you have to do wrong to lose under the current conditions.

On the other side, survivor gameplay has become a parody of itself. It’s no longer survival or horror — it’s endless running in circles with constant downs. Even if you’re a skilled survivor, your individual skill barely matters anymore. Maps feel like they were deliberately designed without proper safe structures, and you go down every thirty to forty seconds simply because there’s nowhere left to play. Add killers’ bloodlust, their constantly buffed abilities, and what you end up with isn’t gameplay, but a mess where skill isn’t rewarded — it’s devalued. Skill checks stopped being a challenge a long time ago; they’re just a mechanical rhythm-game action that does nothing to compensate for the overall imbalance.

The worst part of all this is the lack of real competition. Dead by Daylight is effectively a monopoly in its genre, and Behaviour knows it. When there are no real alternatives, developers don’t have to listen to their players. They can keep adding more paid content, dozens of DLCs, hundreds of skins, and call it “development.” Paid characters often come with strong perks, and even if this isn’t pay-to-win on paper, in practice you’re either paying with money or paying with your time and nerves.

The latest Stranger Things Chapter 2 update was the final confirmation of where this game is heading for me. They released an extremely overpowered killer, completely unbalanced, against whom survivors can do almost nothing. And the funniest part is that the studio had several weeks for testing and polishing, but instead they chose the familiar strategy: release a broken character, cash in on sales because people will buy it after getting destroyed in a few matches, and only then — maybe, someday — nerf it. It feels cynical and kills any remaining trust.

Dead by Daylight was my favorite game for many years. I defended it, recommended it to friends, and justified the developers’ decisions. But over the past few years, Behaviour has been systematically turning it into a soulless monetized product. This isn’t evolution or growth — it’s degradation. That’s why I can’t recommend this game for purchase. If you still decide to get into it, be aware that you’re signing up for dozens of DLCs, hundreds of skins, and a constant feeling that the game is deliberately pushing you to spend more money and more time. It’s a sad example of how a company, chasing profit, is willing to completely kill an idea that was once truly unique.

Let me start off by saying, between Steam and my Nintendo Switch, I have over 2000 hours invested in this game and have been in this community for quite a while.

I'll start off with some of the positives by saying that this game can be fun, when you get lucky enough to get in a good lobby. The crossovers are cool and their original characters are pretty neat, too, so you have a variety of characters to choose from and you can dress them up all cool and stuff, too. The game has relatively consistent updates and quite a few events throughout the year, including some limited-time game modes to spice things up, which are pretty fun. Some of them are even more fun than the default game mode.

Now onto the bad stuff... Killer queue times are absolute ass. You will be sitting in lobbies for AGES just to get into a single match. Survivor queue times aren't as bad, thankfully. Secondly, this game is not beginner friendly at all in terms of it's players and basically everything about how THE GAME ITSELF is. I'll start off with the players; the player base has a HUGE aggression problem and is generally unwelcoming towards new players, so if you're trying to figure out how the game works in a public lobby, then prepare for hostility from other players. Hell, even if you aren't a new player, lobbies have issues with griefing and, best of all, harassment in endgame chat. Lovely. As for the game itself not being beginner friendly, it is a CONSTANT learning curve because of how much there is in the game. There are 48 survivors, each with three perks they come with, and there are 38 killers, also with three unique perks they come with AND the killers come with special built-in abilities. There are also general killer/survivor perks. You can probably do some of the math on that. I bring this up to say that there is so much stuff to keep tabs on what it does that any newcomer would be overwhelmed by it. This isn't to say the variety is a BAD thing, but it's just reasonably confusing to anyone trying to start the game. This is made worse by the SUPER out of date tutorial. The tutorial teaches you very basic shit, but there is NOTHING to tell you about perks and items in said tutorial. 

Now, onto the bigger and way more disappointing issue... The devs themselves are incompetent. There is a lack of proper care taken when it comes to listening to the community... And by that I mean they hardly seem to listen to community issues at all, unless it has to do with cosmetic contests and what crossovers people may want, and even then, they often fuck those up, too. How does a game live on? Originally starting out as a serious co-op horror experience, Dead by Daylight has morphed into an arcade game rife with pop culture characters and needless tweaks. A question posed by many players is, "Does it work?" And the answer is: sometimes.
    If one were to look back on Dead by Daylight's humble origins, they could see a game brimming with potential. A limited array of characters and a highly addictive game-loop gave DbD a leg-up in comparison to its multiplayer competition--even trumping the asymmetrical-horror competition that would later follow as a result. The game ran on atmosphere and depended on you (the player) being terrified or being terrifying. Many would say this was the 'golden-age' of the game (and it was good), but to say that is to disregard the improvements made by the modern DbD.
    Dead by Daylight might not be terrifying anymore--or at the least, not in the intended way--but still it survives. But how? The 'game-ification' of DbD has vastly improved (or made engaging) the previously barebones gameplay loop. What was once a cast of a measly three killers has now expanded far into the double digits.  Both the survivors and killers have benefitted from licenses concerning some of the biggest names in horror and each game is now a true surprise in terms of what killer you'll face. Additionally, the game's weakened focus on horror but instead on engagement creates matches that feel more fun to play in succession. Balancing issues aside, games are usually a tense toss-up of abilities. However, these aforementioned balancing issues and the lack of focus on horror (among other aspects of the game) fail to connect with many players, and rightfully so. Newly added killers are usually nerfed into oblivion following their release and following dominance in matches, and new survivors are usually only justified by their licensing and expensive skins, hardly ever having decent or fun perks. Such is the consequence of bloating the game's perk pool and character slots beyond what was once thought possible in the early epochs of the game's existence. Yet, DbD has survived even when many other games of its kind have died. And that's because it refuses to stay still. The game is constantly evolving: both to its benefit and detriment.
   So, again: how does a game live? In the case of DbD, the answer is momentum. Pure inertia. There have been multiple moments when the game has almost faltered and faded into obscurity, but whether Behavior Interactive actually balances the game's prominent issues or just piles on another broken DLC, people still tune in to see how it's holding up: which is by a shoestring. But still, it holds. All in all, DbD is certainly adequate, but only time will tell if it stays that way.

I’ve spent over two thousand hours in Dead by Daylight, and this is one of those cases where the number isn’t there to flex, but to make one thing clear: I know what I’m talking about. I started playing in 2017, and even before that, back in 2016, I was already following the game closely — watching streams, reading forums, trying to understand where it was heading. Back then, it was genuinely a unique project. Dead by Daylight was a horror game, not an attraction. Tension was constant, every sound mattered, every mistake was punished, but every correct decision gave you a real sense of control and satisfaction.

A killer could wipe the entire lobby if they played well, if they thought ahead, if they knew how to read the map and the players. At the same time, a single truly skilled survivor could loop the killer long enough for the team to calmly finish three, four, sometimes even five generators. Not because the killer was weak, but because the survivor understood timings, positioning, how to run loops properly, and didn’t panic. It wasn’t chaotic running — it was deliberate gameplay, where your individual skill genuinely mattered. That honest exchange of skill is what kept the game alive.

Very little of that remains today. Dead by Daylight has stopped being a horror game and has turned into a mass-market live service. Behaviour deliberately chose the path of simplification and monetization. Instead of atmosphere and fear, we get skins. Instead of tension, we get endless killers and survivors from movies and TV shows. Instead of proper balance, we get constant buffs designed to make new content sell better. From a business perspective, this might be a success, but from a gameplay perspective, it’s a slow and steady killing of the original idea.

Playing killer today is laughably easy. You can be an average player, you don’t even have to think that much, and you’ll still consistently get 4Ks. The game forgives mistakes, the mechanics actively push you toward winning, and most killers don’t require serious mindgames or planning anymore. And yet there are still people who somehow struggle to win as killer, and honestly, I don’t understand what you have to do wrong to lose under the current conditions.

On the other side, survivor gameplay has become a parody of itself. It’s no longer survival or horror — it’s endless running in circles with constant downs. Even if you’re a skilled survivor, your individual skill barely matters anymore. Maps feel like they were deliberately designed without proper safe structures, and you go down every thirty to forty seconds simply because there’s nowhere left to play. Add killers’ bloodlust, their constantly buffed abilities, and what you end up with isn’t gameplay, but a mess where skill isn’t rewarded — it’s devalued. Skill checks stopped being a challenge a long time ago; they’re just a mechanical rhythm-game action that does nothing to compensate for the overall imbalance.

The worst part of all this is the lack of real competition. Dead by Daylight is effectively a monopoly in its genre, and Behaviour knows it. When there are no real alternatives, developers don’t have to listen to their players. They can keep adding more paid content, dozens of DLCs, hundreds of skins, and call it “development.” Paid characters often come with strong perks, and even if this isn’t pay-to-win on paper, in practice you’re either paying with money or paying with your time and nerves.

The latest Stranger Things Chapter 2 update was the final confirmation of where this game is heading for me. They released an extremely overpowered killer, completely unbalanced, against whom survivors can do almost nothing. And the funniest part is that the studio had several weeks for testing and polishing, but instead they chose the familiar strategy: release a broken character, cash in on sales because people will buy it after getting destroyed in a few matches, and only then — maybe, someday — nerf it. It feels cynical and kills any remaining trust.

Dead by Daylight was my favorite game for many years. I defended it, recommended it to friends, and justified the developers’ decisions. But over the past few years, Behaviour has been systematically turning it into a soulless monetized product. This isn’t evolution or growth — it’s degradation. That’s why I can’t recommend this game for purchase. If you still decide to get into it, be aware that you’re signing up for dozens of DLCs, hundreds of skins, and a constant feeling that the game is deliberately pushing you to spend more money and more time. It’s a sad example of how a company, chasing profit, is willing to completely kill an idea that was once truly unique.

They've also taken away the ability to use 90% of those event offerings so that we can't get even the smallest bit extra BP without using a letter, flowers, or the party streamers. The devs bow down to suck off the people who whine and complain, disregard actual feedback that makes sense, and have ultimately killed their own game. 2025 was supposed to be a health year, and instead, it turned into the year of it's death.

Update after update, the devs have proven that they do not care about the players. Let's not even talk about the walking dead update, and how they were incredibly obscene with their approach to it all. As well as just how far downhill it started to go after that. All of last year, they basically shoved into our faces just how little they care. Might I add, their blissful ignorance toward the cheat users. Goddess kay still plays this game every single day without being banned, and all of their patrons who make the game unplayable for everyone else.

Sometimes one decent player on a team saves not only the game but also the mood.
The only thing that really ruins the fun is the ping in Kazakhstan. I almost always have a minimum of around 95, and because of this, there are times when you seem to have pressed the right button, dodged or reached a pallet or a window but the game seems to "miss the mark," and you still get caught. It's especially frustrating when the game is super intense, you're trying your best, and then you realize some of the mistakes weren't even yours, it was just the internet letting you down. But I've gotten used to it: before a match, I mentally prepare myself for the possibility of lag:D
  In short, it's my only favorite game, the one I always come back to, even if it sometimes annoys me. Because no other game gives me the same emotions as DBD❤️

Dead by Daylight is a horror game, but not because of the killers—because of the emotional damage it inflicts on anyone stupid enough (hi, it’s me) to rack up 20,000 hours in it. At this point I don’t even play DBD, I merely inhabit it, like a ghost trapped in the Entity’s realm because I clicked “ready” one too many times in 2017. Every match is a fresh new nightmare: teammates who treat generators like they’re optional side quests, killers who tunnel like they’re late for a dentist appointment, and matchmaking that confidently puts a baby Meg with 12 minutes played against a 9k-hour Nurse who hasn’t felt joy since the Obama administration. The balance changes are a recurring prank—perks get nerfed into museum exhibits, broken mechanics survive for years out of pure spite, and every patch note reads like a threat. Maps are either a pallet-filled jungle gym Disneyland or a dead zone where hope goes to die, and somehow I still queue again, telling myself “just one more match” like an addict scratching at the fog. And the worst part? When the game actually works—when the chase is clean, the mind games are spicy, and nobody DCs at five gens—it’s incredible, which is how it keeps you hostage. Dead by Daylight isn’t just a game after 20k hours, it’s a legally binding contract I signed with my soul, and every time I boot it up I know I’m about to be mad, disappointed, and weirdly excited all at once, which honestly might be the most terrifying design choice Behavior ever made.

They've also taken away the ability to use 90% of those event offerings so that we can't get even the smallest bit extra BP without using a letter, flowers, or the party streamers. The devs bow down to suck off the people who whine and complain, disregard actual feedback that makes sense, and have ultimately killed their own game. 2025 was supposed to be a health year, and instead, it turned into the year of it's death.

Let's not even talk about the walking dead update, and how they were incredibly obscene with their approach to it all. As well as just how far downhill it started to go after that. All of last year, they basically shoved into our faces just how little they care. Might I add, their blissful ignorance toward the cheat users.
