I've been following Dead by Daylight almost since the very beginning. The idea immediately hooked me: four survivors against a killer. The funny thing is I was a fan for a long time just from the outside. I watched trailers, streams, read discussions, knew about killers, perks, updates, it was like I was already part of the game. But it wasn't until 2024 that I really started playing properly and truly felt it for the first time.
  The community is certainly diverse. There are toxic people - those who turn the game into a show and try to ruin everyone's mood. Sometimes after that you really wanna quit and never come back. But there are always good players around - those who don't give up, who save you, who do something normal in the most stressful moments, and you realize: "its for teammates like these that I even play." Sometimes one decent player on a team saves not only the game but also the mood.
The only thing that really ruins the fun is the ping in Kazakhstan. I almost always have a minimum of around 95, and because of this, there are times when you seem to have pressed the right button, dodged or reached a pallet or a window but the game seems to "miss the mark," and you still get caught. It's especially frustrating when the game is super intense, you're trying your best, and then you realize some of the mistakes weren't even yours, it was just the internet letting you down. But I've gotten used to it: before a match, I mentally prepare myself for the possibility of lag:D
  In short, it's my only favorite game, the one I always come back to, even if it sometimes annoys me. Because no other game gives me the same emotions as DBD❤️

Dead by Daylight is a horror game, but not because of the killers—because of the emotional damage it inflicts on anyone stupid enough (hi, it’s me) to rack up 20,000 hours in it. At this point I don’t even play DBD, I merely inhabit it, like a ghost trapped in the Entity’s realm because I clicked “ready” one too many times in 2017. Every match is a fresh new nightmare: teammates who treat generators like they’re optional side quests, killers who tunnel like they’re late for a dentist appointment, and matchmaking that confidently puts a baby Meg with 12 minutes played against a 9k-hour Nurse who hasn’t felt joy since the Obama administration. The balance changes are a recurring prank—perks get nerfed into museum exhibits, broken mechanics survive for years out of pure spite, and every patch note reads like a threat. Maps are either a pallet-filled jungle gym Disneyland or a dead zone where hope goes to die, and somehow I still queue again, telling myself “just one more match” like an addict scratching at the fog. And the worst part? When the game actually works—when the chase is clean, the mind games are spicy, and nobody DCs at five gens—it’s incredible, which is how it keeps you hostage. Dead by Daylight isn’t just a game after 20k hours, it’s a legally binding contract I signed with my soul, and every time I boot it up I know I’m about to be mad, disappointed, and weirdly excited all at once, which honestly might be the most terrifying design choice Behavior ever made.

The core loop is brilliantly tense: one player becomes a terrifying killer while four others must hide, repair generators, and escape. Every match keeps you on edge, making split‑second decisions that can mean life or death.

Killers feel unique, each with powers that radically change gameplay, while survivors can specialize with perks, offering endless strategies for stealth, teamwork, or daring plays. The chase mechanics are tight and satisfying, with looping, pallet stuns, and clever evasion creating tense, skill‑based encounters.

Progression is smartly designed. The Bloodweb system lets you customize builds, unlock perks, and experiment with different strategies. Cosmetic options add personality without impacting gameplay, keeping the focus on skill and tension.

Every match is unpredictable, and the combination of skill, strategy, and chaos makes victories thrilling and losses memorable. With its balance of terror, tactics, and teamwork, Dead by Daylight is endlessly engaging and rewarding.

10/10 — intense, strategic, and endlessly replayable horror mayhem.

There have been a few iterations of having licensed killers or content released way too strong to obviously push sales that leaves the game in a bad spot, but the most recent release of the stranger things collaboration is egregious. The "rift"/battlepass has also substantially lowered in quality from when I started playing this game (before unknown, knight and singularity). I loved this  game, and my friends and I love this game, but releasing new killer perks to a game that fundamentally removed some of the survivors only real defense around a main game mechanic (ex blastmines on gens are nullified by the new One perks) is just ridiculous. Giving the killer visual on all gen progress fundamentally removes so much game play on both killer and survivor ends. Not to mention the new survivor Extrasensory Awareness perk which gives visual to everything including hatch, which is just a better version of Left Behind or Maps with rare add-ons. The development team does not understand how its own game is balanced, and they continue to highlight that truth by continuing to release killers that are amalgamations of multiple current killers, or perks that are combinations of multiple pre-existing abilities. 

BHVR is currently more interested in some sort of 'contest' on deciding the appearance of a new survivor and killer than they are with actually fixing the game they currently have. Which I don't understand as they have genuinely good killer and survivor mains and content creators on payroll who have a VERY good understanding of their game giving them real feedback that they continue to ignore. Your laziness and disregard for gaming experience over financial gain has gone too far this time.

I’ve been playing Dead by Daylight for years, and this new change to Steve’s scream is hands down one of the most baffling, tone-deaf decisions Behaviour has ever made. Seriously — why take something that had personality, emotion, and recognition and flatten it into a dull, generic noise? Steve’s old scream was iconic. It brought life to the character and made him stand out from the sea of survivors. It was funny, it was intense, it was perfect.

Now? He sounds like every other cookie-cutter survivor. The scream is so lifeless that it’s almost painful to hear — and not in the horror game kind of way. Behaviour somehow managed to remove one of the few small, human touches that gave Steve real charm. It’s like they don’t understand what their community actually loves anymore. Instead of listening to feedback, they keep “adjusting” things no one asked for and breaking what wasn’t broken.

I honestly can’t wrap my head around how they thought this was a good move. If this was meant to “improve” immersion, they missed the mark by a mile. They stripped away character for the sake of homogenization. It’s just another reminder that Behaviour keeps changing core aspects of the game while ignoring what made it special to begin with.

Please — revert Steve’s scream. Give him back his soul before all the survivors sound like lifeless NPCs. This isn’t a minor tweak; it’s a personality wipe.

Dead by Daylight is a great game — but only if you enjoy diverse and sometimes unpredictable gameplay.

For Survivors
There will be matches where the killer is far more experienced than you, and others where the killer barely knows how to use their abilities. It’s important to remember that this is a team-based game. You depend on your teammates, and they depend on you.

From time to time, you’ll encounter players who don’t cooperate, beginners who are still learning, or even people who are trolling. However, there are also moments when teamwork feels perfectly coordinated — even without voice communication. Solo queue can be very challenging, even for skilled players, so I highly recommend playing with friends or with reliable teammates you meet in the game.

Most importantly, you need to maintain a “this is just a game” mindset. You will die often — sometimes a lot — and many times it won’t even be your fault.

For Killers
In my opinion, playing killer can feel more challenging because it’s a 1v4 situation. You have to focus on many things at once. You must learn to use your power effectively while keeping track of generators and survivor movements. Decision-making is crucial: knowing when to end a chase, when to pressure generators, and how to manage map control can determine the outcome of the match.

Playing killer can also be frustrating. Survivors may stun or blind you repeatedly, or they may play in highly coordinated groups. However, just like with survivor gameplay, the key is maintaining a healthy mindset and remembering that it’s just a game.

Overall
Both survivor and killer roles are difficult in their own ways. Some players will disagree and argue that one side is easier or that the game is unfair. In my opinion, those players either need more practice or should consider whether this game suits them.

One more important point: this game is not pay-to-win. I’ve often seen people claim that it is, but owning premium characters does not guarantee success. I’ve seen both strong and weak players using paid characters. Losing to someone who owns premium content doesn’t automatically mean they had an unfair advantage. I would rate Dead by Daylight an 8–8.5/10.

My favorite farming sim that I consider a 10/10, this game is a wonderful anomaly because despite being developed by one young solo dev with a dream, he made a hit game that is both simple and extremely deep. You can play as you like and play blindly or min/max with guides and the stardew fandom wiki, with both paths being viable. A very good pick up and play game. The graphics also invoke nostalgia of older games while still feeling modern, with every sprite and detail feeling built with warmth and care. 

What makes it so easy for me too is you can drop the game for a while and come right back in and pick it up, and just chill out. Go tend to your farm, fish, fight some monsters and mine in some caves, and my favorite is to talk to tons of adorable and well-written NPCS, with cute friendship and romance story arcs the more you talk to them and give them gifts. 

The game doesn't become stale because there is always something new to grind towards to, or there is a hidden thing to get. Also you never have to pay for DLCs, with Eric Barone kindly releasing new updates for free, and he always tries to communicate with the community. All in all, this game is perfect for those looking for a fun farming game, where you can play for hundreds of hours to get the 100% trophy, without worrying about failure or a deadline. There's co-op too if you have a friend.

Stardew Valley is the epitome of the cozy game genre, and easily one of the most well-known entries in it. At its core, it is enjoyable. It delivers exactly what it promises: a classic farming loop mixed with mining for ore and gems, light combat in the caves, and the constant pressure of making it back to bed before midnight.

The world is rich with charm, and it’s obvious how much time and love went into crafting the story and its characters. Pelican Town feels lived in, and the game offers an enormous amount of content for players willing to sink dozens—if not hundreds—of hours into it.

That said, Stardew Valley isn’t particularly welcoming if you try to return after a long break. Jumping back in without starting over can feel disorienting, with systems, goals, and routines that assume you remember exactly where you left off. While that may be a personal issue, it does make the game less enjoyable to pick up years later, especially if you’re no longer as invested in the farming-and-mining style of cozy games.

[h1]Stardew Valley — A game that calms and delights[/h1]

I first heard about Stardew Valley from an old friend back in school, and at the time, I never could’ve imagined that such a simple-looking pixel farming simulator would completely hook me. Its slow pace, simple tasks, and freedom of choice pulled me in right away: every day on the farm brought small, but genuine joy, and the world around felt alive in its own quiet way.

Gradually, I started discovering everything the farm had to offer. At first, it was just planting seeds, watering them, and harvesting crops. But over time, new plants, animals, building upgrades, cooking recipes, and secrets kept appearing, and I wanted to uncover them all. What I loved most was the freedom: you can focus purely on farming, or dive into the mines, fishing, or building relationships with the townspeople. Every choice feels meaningful, and every little bit of progress — no matter how small — feels like a personal victory that keeps you coming back for more.

What really stands out is how alive the world of Stardew Valley feels. Every character seems like a real person with their own habits, joys, and problems. Town events, festivals, small quests — it all creates a sense of life you can genuinely care about. The music is soft and unobtrusive, and the pixel art, simple as it may seem, actually creates a cozy, immersive atmosphere where you just want to linger and watch the days unfold on your farm.

Stardew Valley is incredibly replayable — mainly because it lets you relax after a tough day, and the community keeps adding mods for every taste, from simplifying gameplay to expanding the story with new characters. And the most amazing part? This entire living, detailed, and deep world was created by [b]just one person[/b], which is absolutely mind-blowing.

Honestly, I’ve only actually played about four hours of Stardew Valley in 2024 — the rest of the time bout STvalley on my profile is just inflated, I admit. But even that little run was enough to realize that the game is high-quality; it’s just “not for everyone,” and in my case, it didn’t really pull me in. The game is well-known for its details and hidden features, like that creepy moment when kids can turn into magical creatures and chase you — I never got around to going that deep.

Most newbies will probably get stuck at the same stage: meditative clearing of rocks and trees, trying to figure out the starter quests, and meeting the local wizard in his tower, just like I did. The gameplay is kinda addictive in its simplicity, but at the same time, it doesn’t really give you that push to want to explore every nook and cranny of the map. And speaking of the map — navigation isn’t the easiest here. Everything’s visible, yet you keep finding yourself lost among three pine trees, and the mini-map isn’t much help. Not to mention the monster and no-monster modes, which could give players some headaches later on.

Even though I didn’t really click with the game, it wouldn’t be fair to give this project a low score. There’s obviously tons of content and loads of activities, so fans of the farming genre will definitely have plenty to do here. But personally, the ‘spark’ just wasn’t there. I’d be curious to hear what the user Rufus' Refuge thinks about this farming classic.

I recommend it, because the game is objectively a genre staple, but be prepared for the fact that it might not fit into the amount of time you’re willing to put in.

Stardew Valley changed my life in ways I honestly never expected.

I am a 38 year old divorced woman with 2 kids. My life wasn’t crashing all at once—it was decaying slowly. My husband and I didn’t have explosive fights. It was worse than that. We argued about nothing. Dishes left out. Money. That awful silence at dinner where no one wants to be the first to speak. They say communication is key but we had none of that.

One night, after another pointless argument about groceries, he went to sleep on the couch. I stayed up, scrolling. That’s when I saw it.
Saw her.
Haley.
She looked so pretty. So feminine. So rude. I thought, Sure. Why not.

I named my farm after my biggest goal of the game; Haley

That’s where it all went wrong.

I started waking up early—not for work, not for my kids—but to water parsnips. I knew the villagers’ schedules better than my own family’s. I remembered birthdays. I listened. I helped. I mattered. I. MATTERED.

No one yelled at me in Pelican Town. No one judged the way I used to water my seeds everyday before I knew sprinklers even existed.

My husband asked why I was smiling at my screen at two in the morning. I didn’t answer. He wouldn't understand anyway. I was fishing. Willy needed me. My crops needed me. The community center needed me. Haley needed me.

Weeks went by.

My marriage didn’t survive the winter, but my farm did. Even though I didn't have a greenhouse, I used that as a chance to get to know the game more. A break from farming, but more foraging, mining and fishing.

When the divorce papers arrived, I felt strangely empty. I had just unlocked the greenhouse. My kids asked why I seemed distant. I told them I was “working on myself.” That wasn’t a lie. I had hit level 10 farming.

Now I live alone. My house is quiet, but my barn is full. I have truffle oil money. I have a wife who lives in my computer and loves me no matter what. I have a cat and a dog that never judges me.

Do I miss my old life? Sometimes.
Do I regret it? No.

Because when I lie in bed at night, listening to the soft Stardew Valley music, I know one thing for sure:

Haley would never treat me like that.

10/10.

I was quite excited to play at first due to loving all the Stardew Valley games, Stardew Valley 1 being my first. I love the Stardew Valley universe, I am especially loving the new show on prime as well. Unfortunately after giving Stardew its fair shake and then some I can now write a fair review. For starters Stardew Valley first is heavily pushed onto you via limited stash space, without it the game becomes more of a storage organizer simulation.

Stardew Valley first grants you unlimited junk, ammo and medicine storage and without it you cannot consistently stockpile anything due to the stash limit of only 1200 lbs. Everything has weight from the lightest seed and foods and even just misc items. Also to sell anything in your player owned vendor each item while on sale also still takes up storage space at the same time. So everything you sell to other players eats up storage space at the same time, there is no split at all so unless you sell items fast they weigh you down. Even plans carry a weight of .25 lbs and there are hundreds of plans, they add up quickly.

You also get a survival tent and a private server with Stardew Valley first, the tent is like a small portable camp that you can place down to be able to scrap and repair items when needed. Without it you are stuck fast travelling back to camp every time, can't fast travel when overweight without specific perks. The private servers are almost a necessity when trying to farm items, public servers all share the same spawn points for items. If someone beats you to that item you have to switch servers or go through hoops to get what you need. A private server negates this, all items are just for you without having to fight anyone for it.

These are just a couple ways the creator of Stardew Valley pushes you to spend 13$ a month for honestly basic functionality in most other MMOs. Speaking of $$ the shop is disgusting, primarily full of re-skins for the same items over and over again. The creator of Stardew Valley just loves to get you with FOMO then nickel and dime you for another backpack skin that is exactly the same mesh as another. Items are overpriced with certain packs costing upwards of 1800 coins, which is almost 20$ for a small selection of similarly themed items. I can go on about the atom shop but it's just complaining at that point.

The story is disjointed and poorly written with quest chains ending abruptly or being nonsensical. The latest "huge" in game update 1.6.15 wound up being around 4 quests total with a new area added. At the point I was in the game, lvl 1500 at the time, I managed to clear the entire update and explored the new area in about 2 days. Once you hit a level plateau of about 300 the game becomes just a grind for levels for legendary perks. Lvl 300 is easy to get to very quickly and with little effort, cursory Google searches will guide you to hit that fast.

All in all I feel you can probably get a few months of quality game time in with this then it just becomes a repetitive slog all the way around. Game balancing is a joke as well, the meta changes constantly due to harsh nerfs to weapons. They nerf certain weapons into the ground instead of making less used weapons more desirable by buffing them, once you experience it a few times it becomes a huge annoyance.

If you want to play Stardew I say go for it, maybe it will click with you who knows. God knows I really really wanted to love it but after playing as much as I have the polish that once seemed great now is just so lackluster. It's supposed to be an MMO (lite) so the point is to pour gametime into an evolving world that feels alive. Stardew feels hollow, relies too heavily on FOMO and the nickel and diming with the shop just sink it lower. Once the initial wow factor wears off there's really not much to do in the game. Content is lacking and the daily concurrent player numbers are sad proof of that. Even with a highly rated show to tie into it it can't even muster better numbers than other single-player farming sims. At the end of the day I'd give it a 9 out of 10. A lot needs to change with the creator of Stardew Valley but the way things have been going I don't expect it to get any better. Cheers.

I've put hundreds of hours into Stardew Valley between console and PC and I can confidently say that this game is pure comfort in video game form. It takes the simple idea of farming and turns it into a deeply satisfying, endlessly charming life sim that somehow feels both relaxing and addictive at the same time.

From planting your first crop to building a thriving farm, every small victory feels meaningful. The gameplay loop is perfectly balanced: farm, fish, mine, explore, socialize, repeat—but it never gets boring. There’s always one more day you want to play, and suddenly it’s 2 a.m. (both in-game and real life lol).

The characters are where the game truly shines. Pelican Town feels alive, with villagers who have real personalities, struggles, and growth. Building relationships, attending festivals, and uncovering backstories makes the world feel warm and personal. You’re not just managing a farm, you’re becoming part of a community.

The pixel art is gorgeous and timeless, paired with many soundtracks that are soothing, nostalgic, and emotionally resonant. Each season feels distinct, and the game’s gentle pacing lets you play exactly how you want: min-max like a pro, roleplay a cozy farmer, or just vibe.

On top of all that, the sheer amount of content is amazing; secrets, quests, upgrades, romance, multiplayer, mods, etc. And it’s all crafted with obvious love by a single developer.

Stardew Valley is a masterpiece of cozy gaming. It’s relaxing without being shallow, deep without being stressful, and endlessly replayable. Whether you’re a hardcore gamer or someone who just wants a peaceful escape, this game is amazing! 1000% Recommend!

Pros
• The game never pressures you, and encourages you to be free of what you do as you please. You can just abandon a quest and never get repercussions for it. Losing random items from your inventory from collapsing at 2am/dying in the mines may be the harshest thing it can do. 
• The game is subject to many mods, allowing you to have experience beyond what SDV vanilla can offer
• The ambience and great music
• You can have as many pets as you want!

Now to the cons. Honestly, they're more of "I want these to be updated" rather than saying these are forever bad.

Cons
• Stardew Valley's writing, as of 1.6, for me, is weak. I've seen more headcanons/theories because there is little to no canon plot to discuss about. I've wanted to explore more story about the magic, or the Junimos. I would've loved it if there are more canon lore.
• Kids do not contribute to anything, except probably for the Steam achievement. 
• The only difference between marriage candidates after you marry them is their room, and their heart events. After that, they all function the same, watering crops, feed your pet/s, and fix fences.
• The characters' dialogues are repetitive, and you can only talk to them once a day. My pet peeve is Kent—I drop by to say hi, only to be [spoiler]trauma-dumped by how he lost his friends in battle.[/spoiler]
• Customizing buildings' colors may give you the satisfaction of "oh hey I can color it whatever I want!" only to find out that you can't, because you can't create pastel and everything other than red or brown comes off neon-ish.
• Barely any clues on what to gift to all the villagers. Difficult to do when you don't look up online/ask other players. I'm aware of the [spoiler]Secret notes[/spoiler], though they only cover a small amount of the villagers.
• No heart meter. I don't mean the 8/8 at the corner of their portraits, but a meter that describes how far am I from leveling up friendship with a villager.
• Community Center has no use after completion. The only impact it has is to deprive me of accessing Clint every Friday.

The story is boring, there's no main quest/story to chase, so I just shifted my focus to gameplay instead. The gameplay is decent. There's enough challenge, there's gadgets that can make your life easier, and then there's [i]Junimo Kart and Journey of the Prairie King[/i]—

Pros
• The game never pressures you, and encourages you to be free of what you do as you please. You can just abandon a quest and never get repercussions for it. Losing random items from your inventory from collapsing at 2am/dying in the mines may be the harshest thing it can do. 
• The game is subject to many mods, allowing you to have experience beyond what SDV vanilla can offer
• The ambience and great music
• You can have as many pets as you want!

Now to the cons. Honestly, they're more of "I want these to be updated" rather than saying these are forever bad.

Cons
• Stardew Valley's writing, as of 1.6, for me, is weak. I've seen more headcanons/theories because there is little to no canon plot to discuss about. I've wanted to explore more story about the magic, or the Junimos. I would've loved it if there are more canon lore.
• Kids do not contribute to anything, except probably for the Steam achievement. 
• The only difference between marriage candidates after you marry them is their room, and their heart events. After that, they all function the same, watering crops, feed your pet/s, and fix fences.
• The characters' dialogues are repetitive, and you can only talk to them once a day. My pet peeve is Kent—I drop by to say hi, only to be [spoiler]trauma-dumped by how he lost his friends in battle.[/spoiler]
• Customizing buildings' colors may give you the satisfaction of "oh hey I can color it whatever I want!" only to find out that you can't, because you can't create pastel and everything other than red or brown comes off neon-ish.
• Barely any clues on what to gift to all the villagers. Difficult to do when you don't look up online/ask other players. I'm aware of the [spoiler]Secret notes[/spoiler], though they only cover a small amount of the villagers.
• No heart meter. I don't mean the 8/8 at the corner of their portraits, but a meter that describes how far am I from leveling up friendship with a villager.
• Community Center has no use after completion. The only impact it has is to deprive me of accessing Clint every Friday.

The story is boring, there's no main quest/story to chase, so I just shifted my focus to gameplay instead. The gameplay is decent. There's enough challenge, there's gadgets that can make your life easier, and then there's [i]Junimo Kart and Journey of the Prairie King[/i]—

I've liked it mostly because my goals have built up from day one. It's addictive, and I've had a good run with it since I first bought it on mobile. However, since achieving [spoiler]my very first Perfection[/spoiler], the consecutive games I've done after that made me realize the game's on a repetitive loop. But maybe that just means the game's good enough that I only realized it after I've done it. It's a good break from all the tense things in life.

In an era of gaming dominated by high-stress battle royales, predatory microtransactions, and hyper-realistic graphics, Stardew Valley stands apart as a breath of fresh country air. What begins as a simple farming simulator quickly reveals itself to be a profound, therapeutic, and deeply engaging experience that feels less like playing a game and more like coming home.

The "Just One More Day" Phenomenon
The premise is a classic trope: you inherit your grandfather's old farm plot to escape the soul-crushing drudgery of a corporate office job. However, the execution is flawless. The core gameplay loop—clearing land, planting seeds, watering crops, and harvesting the fruits of your labor—is incredibly satisfying.
There is a unique rhythm to the game that hooks you immediately. You wake up, check the weather, tend to your animals, and then decide how to spend your energy. Do you want to brave the depths of the mines to find rare ores? Do you want to spend a lazy afternoon fishing at the beach? or do you want to forage in the secret woods?

 Note: The genius of Stardew Valley is the lack of punishment. If you miss a harvest or forget to talk to a villager, the game doesn't punish you. It waits for you. This creates a stress-free environment that is purely motivated by your own desire to improve your farm.

A Living, Breathing World
Visually, the game is a triumph of 16-bit pixel art. The changing of the seasons is not just a gameplay mechanic but an aesthetic shift that changes the entire mood of the valley. From the floating pink petals of Spring to the cozy, melancholic snow of Winter, every screen is a painting.

Accompanying these visuals is a soundtrack that can only be described as iconic. Composed by the game's sole creator, Eric Barone (ConcernedApe), the music perfectly encapsulates the feeling of the season. The upbeat tunes of Summer make you want to work, while the gentle piano melodies of Winter encourage introspection.

Heart and Soul
Perhaps the most surprising depth lies in the villagers of Pelican Town. At first glance, they appear to be archetypes: the jock, the prep, the grumpy old man. But as you build relationships with them through gifts and conversation, you uncover genuine human struggles. You help characters deal with depression, alcoholism, PTSD, and family abandonment. The writing is empathetic and real, making the town feel populated by friends rather than NPCs.

The Verdict
Stardew Valley is a labor of love that respects the player’s time and intelligence. It is a game about connections—connecting with nature, connecting with a community, and reconnecting with a sense of peace that is often lost in modern life.

Whether you are a hardcore gamer looking for efficiency and optimization, or a casual player looking for a cozy escape, this game has something for you. It is, quite simply, pixelated perfection.
Score: 10/10

In an era of gaming dominated by high-stress battle royales, predatory microtransactions, and hyper-realistic graphics, Stardew Valley stands apart as a breath of fresh country air. What begins as a simple farming simulator quickly reveals itself to be a profound, therapeutic, and deeply engaging experience that feels less like playing a game and more like coming home.

The "Just One More Day" Phenomenon
The premise is a classic trope: you inherit your grandfather's old farm plot to escape the soul-crushing drudgery of a corporate office job. However, the execution is flawless. The core gameplay loop—clearing land, planting seeds, watering crops, and harvesting the fruits of your labor—is incredibly satisfying.
There is a unique rhythm to the game that hooks you immediately. You wake up, check the weather, tend to your animals, and then decide how to spend your energy. Do you want to brave the depths of the mines to find rare ores? Do you want to spend a lazy afternoon fishing at the beach? or do you want to forage in the secret woods?

 Note: The genius of Stardew Valley is the lack of punishment. If you miss a harvest or forget to talk to a villager, the game doesn't punish you. It waits for you. This creates a stress-free environment that is purely motivated by your own desire to improve your farm.

A Living, Breathing World
Visually, the game is a triumph of 16-bit pixel art. The changing of the seasons is not just a gameplay mechanic but an aesthetic shift that changes the entire mood of the valley. From the floating pink petals of Spring to the cozy, melancholic snow of Winter, every screen is a painting.

Accompanying these visuals is a soundtrack that can only be described as iconic. Composed by the game's sole creator, Eric Barone (ConcernedApe), the music perfectly encapsulates the feeling of the season. The upbeat tunes of Summer make you want to work, while the gentle piano melodies of Winter encourage introspection.

Heart and Soul
Perhaps the most surprising depth lies in the villagers of Pelican Town. At first glance, they appear to be archetypes: the jock, the prep, the grumpy old man. But as you build relationships with them through gifts and conversation, you uncover genuine human struggles. You help characters deal with depression, alcoholism, PTSD, and family abandonment. The writing is empathetic and real, making the town feel populated by friends rather than NPCs.

The Verdict
Stardew Valley is a labor of love that respects the player’s time and intelligence. It is a game about connections—connecting with nature, connecting with a community, and reconnecting with a sense of peace that is often lost in modern life.

Whether you are a hardcore gamer looking for efficiency and optimization, or a casual player looking for a cozy escape, this game has something for you. It is, quite simply, pixelated perfection.

Running around on the final day, looking for a specific person but being just a bit too late to visit them during the evening (or unable to find them OR even worse, reach them due to being locked in their rooms) and failing the quest is such a downer. there are several fun mechanics in Stardew that keep it feeling dynamic. The farming, fishing, mining/combat, helping the neighbors foraging/exploring, they all work together well to keep things moving along. You can choose a relaxed or more intense playthrough by choosing a couple or all of the challenges. I've chosen to focus on a few of those things in my first playthrough where as my wife plays to beat her perfection record. Choosing the perfection route and completing all the tasks and upgrades is not for the casual player though. The day/night and season cycles become more stressful the more challenges you choose. The feeling of accomplishing your goal for the day is really satisfying.

Some of the controls could be a bit better. I often pick something up and its in my hands when I don't want it there. Half the time I end up eating something I didn't want to or giving something to someone that negatively affects friendship levels. The selection box shouldn't stay on an empty inventory spot. The combat could be a bit more fluid if the weapons didn't take so long to swing before you could move again. It makes combat very sticky and inflexible. There doesn't seem to be a way to beat the game unless you're set your own time limit or goal such as completing all the quests given by townsfolk or perfection. I guess that's another thing to choose in the game. I still haven't decided what that is. Overall its a well made game with a lot of fun for those that enjoy the survival, crafter, adventure style.

I recommend this game if you have a special interest in farming games or are new to gaming as a hobby. But I didn't like it much. Let me explain why. 
-----
While playing I would have waves of enjoyment and boredom. I would do everything i could do, and then like an in-game week later will unlock a new thing that opens up the world a whole lot more. Having the world open up so often is a really awesome feeling, but it could have better pacing so I'm not bored waiting for the next new thing to get me hooked. I played on keyboard and it was a pretty awful experience control-wise. You gotta like, point vaguely at a direction to interact in that direction, but it's all vibe-based and sometimes just doesnt work at all. I'll be aiming left and my character smacks up. or have my cursor directly on a chest but it opens the chest next to it for no reason. These problems are especially exacerbating to the combat system. At first, the combat was fine for the first 80-90 levels of the Mines as its not taken seriously, the monsters are all cute creatures that hardly hurt you, but the later floors, and also the Skull Cavern you unlock later-- just take themselves too seriously. The combat system was not made for anything difficult to be implemented but the developer did so anyway. Another issue I had was that I wished the role-playing elements were stronger. The game starts out as you making your character. I made the character to be a self-insert, but I had very little control over my character's decisions or how I truly present myself as to the other characters. I want to be a homewrecker and date older gentleman >:). but no, the cast is almost entirely college-aged. Sure, theres like, Harvey, but he suspiciously has quite the baby-face going on. I just feel like I'm not the target demographic for the dating pool. Which is okay, but knowing beforehand how queer this game was I was expecting a lot more diversity (Not just talking about age) like for one, I dont think there's a single Asian in the game. and only one descriptively non-Caucasian dateable character? It's a shame. That's actually not completely true based on technicality, but would require spoilers to explain. This next issue may be a bit of a personal issue as I talked to my friends who have played this game, and while they have had issues, never to the extent of I had. but i had TONS of glitches in my playthrough. My save file got corrupted like 4 times in my 80 hours of playtime. Luckily, the game keeps yesterday's save as backup when-needed, so I never lost too much. It shouldn't have ever happened though, especially more than once.
+++++
To list out some positives: I think the level progression with skills and crafting and new abilities are all very well paced; the game is extremely QoL friendly, one example I'd like to shoutout is that despite normal chests and big chests being completely different items, you can just place a big chest ontop of a normal chest to upgrade it, keeping the inventory. Absolutely stunning thoughtfulness and every game needs to do this.; The mini-games, while being brutal in difficulty, were very fun to play.; Should be expected since it is majority a farming game, but the farming gameplay loop was fun, and trying to make your farm as optimal as possible can strike the fancy of a lot of people. All the characters have pretty distinct personalities, all of them had reasons to love them, and reasons to hate them with their character flaws.

Overall, I found the game to be mid and not for me. Still, I might come back to it someday to try out some of the most popular mod(pack)s to see if that makes the experience any bit more enjoyable for me. But mod support isn't native into Steam so I'm not factoring it into my review. 5.5/10

[b]HOWEVER, I think there are some severe flaws/misses that affect the quality of life aspect[/b], and it's lowkey making me not want to play the game as much.

[b]- 1. Why on earth can't we knock on peoples doors?![/b]
Take Abigail and Sebastian as an example. You shouldn't have to tab out, use the wiki and stalk their daily routes in order to find them outside their rooms for socializing/gifting. Just let us knock on their doors so they come outside for a few min (and make them close the door behind them so we can't sneak in).

[b]- 2. Why can we enter everyones house as a stranger?[/b]
It's kinda weird that we can enter anyones house at any time, completely unannounced as a stranger, and they don't bat an eye. But entering a specific room is where they draw the line unless we're close friends?? Idk, it's a bit weird.
Would love to see knocking added as a standard to enter any house tbh. Let them come to the door and open it so we can talk/gift/ask if someone is home and can come to the door/ask to enter, and the friendship level can determine if we're welcome inside or not.

[b]- 3. Why is there no way to visit people who live in a store on their closed days?[/b]
Store closed every Wednesday = can't visit the owners and their family on Wednesdays. It's weird. Please add a side-door or something to let us visit the residents even on days where their stores are closed.

I recommend this game if you have a special interest in farming games or are new to gaming as a hobby. But I didn't like it much. Let me explain why. 
-----
While playing I would have waves of enjoyment and boredom. I would do everything i could do, and then like an in-game week later will unlock a new thing that opens up the world a whole lot more. Having the world open up so often is a really awesome feeling, but it could have better pacing so I'm not bored waiting for the next new thing to get me hooked. I played on keyboard and it was a pretty awful experience control-wise. You gotta like, point vaguely at a direction to interact in that direction, but it's all vibe-based and sometimes just doesnt work at all. I'll be aiming left and my character smacks up. or have my cursor directly on a chest but it opens the chest next to it for no reason. These problems are especially exacerbating to the combat system. At first, the combat was fine for the first 80-90 levels of the Mines as its not taken seriously, the monsters are all cute creatures that hardly hurt you, but the later floors, and also the Skull Cavern you unlock later-- just take themselves too seriously. The combat system was not made for anything difficult to be implemented but the developer did so anyway. Another issue I had was that I wished the role-playing elements were stronger. The game starts out as you making your character. I made the character to be a self-insert, but I had very little control over my character's decisions or how I truly present myself as to the other characters. I want to be a homewrecker and date older gentleman >:). but no, the cast is almost entirely college-aged. Sure, theres like, Harvey, but he suspiciously has quite the baby-face going on. I just feel like I'm not the target demographic for the dating pool. Which is okay, but knowing beforehand how queer this game was I was expecting a lot more diversity (Not just talking about age) like for one, I dont think there's a single Asian in the game. and only one descriptively non-Caucasian dateable character? It's a shame. That's actually not completely true based on technicality, but would require spoilers to explain. This next issue may be a bit of a personal issue as I talked to my friends who have played this game, and while they have had issues, never to the extent of I had. but i had TONS of glitches in my playthrough. My save file got corrupted like 4 times in my 80 hours of playtime. Luckily, the game keeps yesterday's save as backup when-needed, so I never lost too much. It shouldn't have ever happened though, especially more than once.
+++++
To list out some positives: I think the level progression with skills and crafting and new abilities are all very well paced; the game is extremely QoL friendly, one example I'd like to shoutout is that despite normal chests and big chests being completely different items, you can just place a big chest ontop of a normal chest to upgrade it, keeping the inventory. Absolutely stunning thoughtfulness and every game needs to do this.; The mini-games, while being brutal in difficulty, were very fun to play.; Should be expected since it is majority a farming game, but the farming gameplay loop was fun, and trying to make your farm as optimal as possible can strike the fancy of a lot of people. All the characters have pretty distinct personalities, all of them had reasons to love them, and reasons to hate them with their character flaws.

Overall, I found the game to be mid and not for me. Still, I might come back to it someday to try out some of the most popular mod(pack)s to see if that makes the experience any bit more enjoyable for me. But mod support isn't native into Steam so I'm not factoring it into my review. 5.5/10

This is my go-to chill game. But it's way more than that. So you start out clearing out space on your farm, planting crops and such. Then you run out of money so you go fishing... and that turns out to be a super in depth minigame in itself? Then you get a coop and a barn, start raising animals... but then you upgrade them, and unlock new animals! But then you also enter the mines, mine ore and fight monsters! But then when you beat the mines you get a skull key... whats that for? Then from completing the community center bundles, you unlock a bus that takes you to the desert... and that has a door you can open with the skull key? And then behind that theres a bottomless dungeon that's basically a roguelike mode? But then you complete all of the bundles and then you unlock a room with a broken boat? And then you get the mats to repair it and then you can take that boat to a different island?? And that has... well i don't wanna spoil that. And meanwhile you've maxed out all your skills like farming and fishing? Then you discover you can enter a door you couldn't before? And then there you get a whole new skill system that gives you OP equipment and crafting recipes?? And don't let me get startet on there being a whole friendship and relationship system with lots of characters with their own stories.

So yeah basically... this game is FULL of surprises and each surprise usually leads you to another surprise. Get ready to make this your new life for a couple weeks.

There are so many things that I could say about this beautiful game which I've enjoyed on and off for several years now.  It truly is a labor of love and the ultimate comfort food for me.  Designing and building a viable farm from the harvestable resources that are available to you is incredibly fun and engrossing and there's something down right magical about how the cycle of the year is depicted and the way that the seasons change the Valley.  In revisiting this game recently, I was surprised to rediscover how dark some of the side storylines are as you get to know more about the villagers and their troubles.  I somehow had forgotten that alongside the cozy, feel-good plot about helping apple-shaped forest sprites restore a run down community center, this game also tries to tackle themes of poverty, homelessness, alcoholism, suicide, and abuse, basically the darker parts that come with living in a small, economically stressed town.  Stardew Valley, as in the setting itself, may be an escape from the tedium of modern life that the player wants and embraces but the same isn't so for some of the other townsfolk who grew up there, particularly the younger and poorer ones who dream of escape in the other direction, leaving the Valley to move into the city.  So all that to say I think an important component of this game is that amidst raising chickens and building beehives, it does try to grapple with some more mature themes, though the storytelling is very simple and sometimes clunky.  It's not just mindless escapism and I respect this game all the more because of that.

Stardew Valley is what happens when you trade fluorescent office lighting for golden pixel sunsets and somehow come out richer for it. You inherit a run down farm, a handful of parsnip seeds, and a town full of people who feel surprisingly real for 16 bit sprites. From there, the game quietly unfolds like a well loved journal.

At its core, it is a farming simulator. You plant crops, raise animals, fish in glittering rivers, and dive into monster filled mines. But that description is like calling pizza “bread with stuff.” The real magic is in the rhythm. Wake up, water crops, talk to the locals, maybe give someone a gift that reveals a little more about who they are. The days move quickly, yet never feel rushed. It is cozy without being shallow.

Pelican Town is packed with personality. Each character has their own struggles, secrets, and little heart events that turn simple conversations into emotional snapshots. You can build friendships, start a romance, get married, and even raise kids. It feels like tending to a garden of relationships, not just crops.

The gameplay loop is addictive in the quietest way. “Just one more day” turns into three in game weeks. There is always something to improve. Upgrade tools, decorate your farm, restore the community center, automate with sprinklers. It scratches that progress itch without turning into a grindy treadmill.

Visually, it leans into charming pixel art that feels nostalgic but intentional. The seasonal changes are especially beautiful. Spring is soft and hopeful, summer hums with energy, fall glows like a campfire, and winter feels peaceful and reflective. The soundtrack ties it all together with gentle melodies that somehow make watering digital turnips feel profound.

If there is a downside, it is that the open ended nature can feel overwhelming at first. The game does not hold your hand. It hands you seeds and says, “Figure it out.” For some players, that freedom is bliss. For others, it may take a few in game weeks to find a groove.

Overall, Stardew Valley is a masterclass in cozy design. It is not about winning. It is about growing. Crops, friendships, skills, and maybe even your own patience. It turns simple routines into something quietly meaningful.

Final verdict: A pixelated sanctuary that proves sometimes the best adventure is planting potatoes and watching them thrive. 🌻

[h1]Stardew Valley – The Game That Brought Me Home[/h1]
[b]Game:[/b] Stardew Valley
[b]Developer:[/b] ConcernedApe
[b]Genre:[/b] Farming Sim / Life Sim / RPG

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Introduction – A Return to Something I Thought I’d Lost[/h2]
Growing up, I spent countless hours playing Harvest Moon: A Wonderful Life on the Playstation 2. It wasn’t just a farming game to me—it was routine, comfort, and quiet progression. Feeding animals after school. Watching crops grow day by day. Slowly building a life.

Over time, I drifted away from farming sims. They either felt simplified, rushed, or missing something intangible. Then Stardew Valley appeared—and somehow it didn’t just revive the genre. It revived that feeling.

It reminded me why I loved these games in the first place.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Farming – Simple, Deep, and Perfectly Paced[/h2]
At its core, Stardew Valley is about tending to your land. Planting crops, watering them, upgrading tools, raising animals, expanding your farm. But it never feels repetitive.

The loop is satisfying because progression is tangible:
• Early game: scraping by with basic tools and limited stamina
• Mid game: sprinklers, expanded barns, artisan goods
• Late game: efficient layouts, gold-star harvests, optimized production

It captures that same steady growth that A Wonderful Life did—but with more flexibility and player freedom. You can min-max, or you can casually grow pumpkins and fish all day. The game supports both.

And that’s beautiful.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Pixel Art – Warm, Timeless, Emotional[/h2]
The pixel art in Stardew Valley is nothing short of charming. It’s colorful without being overwhelming. Soft without being dull. Seasonal transitions feel magical.

Spring feels alive.
Summer feels vibrant.
Fall feels cozy.
Winter feels quiet and reflective.

There’s a warmth to the visuals that makes the town feel lived in. You don’t just see Pelican Town—you feel it.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Characters – Small Stories That Feel Real[/h2]
One of Stardew Valley’s greatest strengths is its writing. Every character feels like they have layers.

• People struggling with identity
• People stuck in routine
• People grieving
• People chasing dreams
• People learning to open up

The heart events aren’t just cute cutscenes. They explore loneliness, depression, family tension, ambition, insecurity. It’s subtle, but it hits.

Building relationships doesn’t feel transactional—it feels gradual and human.

That’s rare.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Music – Pure Nostalgia, Pure Comfort[/h2]
The soundtrack is unforgettable. It balances calm melodies with uplifting seasonal themes.

Some tracks feel hopeful.
Some feel peaceful.
Some feel nostalgic before you even realize why.

There are moments in Stardew Valley where you’re just standing on your farm at sunset, music playing softly, and it hits you: this is what relaxation feels like.

The soundtrack carries emotion without demanding attention.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Freedom – Play Your Way[/h2]
Stardew Valley doesn’t force you into one playstyle.

You can focus on:
• Farming
• Fishing
• Mining
• Animal raising
• Artisan goods
• Relationships
• Community Center completion
• Exploration and secrets

It never punishes you for going at your own pace. There’s no urgency. No ticking clock pushing you forward. It respects your time.

That design philosophy makes it timeless.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]How It Brought Me Back[/h2]
After years away from farming sims, Stardew Valley felt like coming home.

It carried the spirit of Harvest Moon: A Wonderful Life—the slow growth, the emotional warmth, the routine—but refined it with modern design, deeper mechanics, and player freedom.

It didn’t just modernize the genre. It reminded me why I loved it.

That’s powerful.

[hr][/hr]

The first time I played [i]PUBG: Battlegrounds[/i] was back when it was still called [i]PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds[/i]—[b]you had to pay back then to be a toxic ass.[/b] Despite it being PvP, not my favorite hobby, it grabbed me by the balls, its grip firm yet gentle, and from September 2017 till July 2018 I spent around 250 hours looting, sneaking, killing, dying (mostly dying) and sometimes eating chicken.

[h3][b][i]Hoarder Sim[/i][/b][/h3]
Now, the main reason I even stepped foot onto Erangel, all those years ago, was [b]the looting.[/b] It’s just so zen, yet it’s also one giant [i]risk-reward[/i] game: deciding what to carry with you, what to drop, what to swap out—[b]I get all tingly from just thinking about it.[/b]

But what loot do you loot?
[list]
[*][b]Weapons:[/b]
You need to kill people, and melee-ing is so passé. So, bullets are the answer—[b]headshots[/b] or [b]spray and pray[/b], dealer’s choice. As years passed, the game’s arsenal expanded, which for a loot monke like me, seeing so many guns all around me, it’s basically better than the sex! My current favorites are the [i]AUG[/i], [i]SCAR-L, VSS[/i] and [i]M249[/i]. The [i]Crossbow[/i] also gets a thumbs up—[b]very hard to kill people with, much dying in chaotic gunfights because it’s pretty useless in 99.999% of situations I found myself in.[/b] Looks cool tho! Think of guns like puzzles with a piece or two missing—[b]that’s the attachments, the missing piece(s)![/b]. These little doohickeys are very important, like little [b]gun buffs[/b] if you will. There’s many things to consume nowadays. Your favorite uncle consumes Fox News, you consume Hentai, and so on. This game has gone through some wild shifts and changes over the years, and it is a battle royale first and foremost above all others, so if that is not your vibe, steer clear. 

That said, for a free to play adaptation from a pay to play core, PUBG has thrived since it's initial ups and downs of finding a good foothold in a market that quickly got overtaken by flashier and more cartoony competitors.  

This is a great game to just casually knock out a few drops with some friends or goof off in solo que doing self imposed absurd challenges, and the casual mode doubly makes it much less of a chance of just getting completely stomped by people who eat sleep and breath the game while your just trying to play with people of varying skill level and interest in the game. 

As it stands now, it is a solid free to play BR option for the people who prefer less cartoony asthetics with more realistic style firearms. It certainly is not a full hardcore vibe on the realistic feel so won't really scratch the itch there, but overall it has a lot going for it in it's specific niche.  The competitive scene is also quite impressive and for such a random variable element of a game that often comes down to luck over skill in terms of equipment strategies, it is still very entertaining to watch in spite of the inherent lack of a certain degree of mechanical balance optimization just due to the nature of the game itself. 

There are also very amusing custom lobbies that can be tweaked into all kinds of improvised game modes for very silly group fun if your lucky enough to be part of a community that can muster the numbers to host such a thing! 

The journey of improvement and refinement is a constant one that never truly ends however, and these are the things I think could do with some changes to improve the quality of the game and extend it's reach even further: 

[b] CASUAL REWORKS [/b] 

Change casual ques to 90min instead of 60min and allow groups who are queing together to go off the time remaining of the group member with the most time remaining, even if other group members have 0 time remaining themselves. people meet up and decide to do a little casual play at different points in the day, in different circles, this helps make this process not feel like a time triage excercise similar to scheduling DnD groups 

[b] BOT DROP [/b]

Adding a purely co-op comp stomp mode would be very helpful for those of us who enjoy playing casuals but do not want the human competitive element in any way beyond friendly team competition to see who can get the most kills / coolest kills. 

Someone like me can go toe to toe easily in the main matches and the "who's a bot and who's not" excitement of casuals is something I can handle easily enough, but for a lot of people I play with who enjoy a purely casual against bots experience that is not high pressure so they can be comfortable and spend time with friends and loved ones without getting upset or too overly stressed, something like this would be much better: 

The maps are much smaller environments (they can just be zoomed in sections of already existing maps to start with, but eventually custom designed maps using pre-existing assets would be the best course of action to help with differentation at a glance and variety) 

The game mode would be 100 participants, with up to 6 six slots occupied by players in one team replacing a bot spawn from either a pre-que or public lobby (with players still able to launch on less than max numbers) 

Everyone parachutes in at the same time in random spots in the sky above the map and have to steer themselves into locations alongside all the bots, and then it's just a free for all as the bots do not have teams, but they always priortize engaging human players over one another (and are generally coded to miss each other as much as possible when fighting one another) they will never kill downed players intentionally, and as the match progresses and the circle tightens, the bots become universally stronger, more well equipped, and deadlier, all while ensuring their top priority is to avoid the closing circle, up to the point of not stopping to engage until they are inside of it at all costs (and also reducing outside of circle damage to the bots so a ton of them don't just die out there like in casuals) 

I could elaborate a great deal on more specifics and unique elements of this game mode, but this review only has so much room so if the devs would like to contact me directly, I would happily provide additional expansion and development plans to streamline it's inception!

[b] FAT TRIMMING [/b] 

 There is soooo much overlapping emergency key jingling from this games years of desperate reinvention and expansion that needs cleaning up. There are so many absurd sub menus and six different currencies doing the same things that could all be solved by one that make the monetized elements far more complex and annoying to engage with. 

Making a "give me all my stuff I qualify for" button that just lists a history of where and why a thing was given to the player is so much more effective and gives people a less micro management heavy way of cleanly aquiring things. It should also store and log those qualified rewards until that button IS clicked even if the event or whatever was going on has passed, so that people don't accidentally miss out on things they qualified for simply because of an arbitrary timer. 

In addition, make the actual BP shop it's own thing that makes it easier to navigate what is available purely with BP without mixing it with the premium currency shop. You can still put advertisements in the BP shop items directing too premium shop versions, and you can add a premium shop currency buy options for all the BP items too even, but make the designation more clear, and simple to navigate 

Again, I have a massive list of UI reconfigurations and changes to offer in great detail, along with many mechanic revisions and refinements, if the developers are interested. I understand the limitations of development especially on a skeleton crewed F2P investment anchor, but I know how to work on nothing budgets with little resources, so happy to offer my expertise if desired! 

[b] NO MORE SOLO DANCES [/b] 

This one is mildly irksome, but ALL dances of every kind should be group dances. This is a nitpick I will admit it, but it's just unnecissarily exclusionary in a largely team incentivizing game. Add a toggle when activating the dance for it to be solo only if you really want to keep that for more mean spirited players, but don't enforce exclusion. 

I could go on an on and on about ideas for new events, tweaks and optimizations, promotional tie ins and baseline improvements but, again, due to limited space here, I'll just end on saying this game is not perfect by far, and it will be infuriating at times both because of the PVP nature of the game, and some of the games baked in elements at it's core, but if you want a slower paced BR That has less frenetic energy than other BR's and Arena Shooters while still being an engaging experience with a bit more of a "real life" influence, this one is the game for you! And it's free, and there are random little events that pop up free game modes to play with so, it's worth keeping installed just to mess around with now and then!

I can finally review BG3 after over 200+ hours in one campaign. I started with 2 close friends when it released in August 2023 and after 2+ years we finally finished it. I'd give it an 8.8/10. 

Overall, what else can be said about BG3 that hasn't already. It's an amazing game, and an especially great one to play with friends for the first time. However, there are a few gripes for me that keep it from being the perfect 10/10 game, and it was so close.

It's mostly just to do with each Act. BG3 is split into 3 Acts. The first of which was released in early access for several years, meaning a lot of time was spent on Act 1 polishing up bugs, cutscenes and just generally getting a lot of love as it was the only public facing Act so it needed to do a good job of representing the game. Act 1 is by FAR the best Act in the game. There's a lot to explore, tons of characters with meaningful quests, secrets etc. 

However, as you progress into Act 2 and Act 3, that same magic and attention to detail starts to dip. It's not got the same kind of polish or love that Act 1 has, and it shows. As my friends and I took many years to complete the game, or even leave Act 1, there has been many updates to clean up the final 2 Acts, however, even with the final update, Act 3 especially feels incredibly lackluster and at times very empty.

For example, when you reach Baldurs Gate in Act 3 there's a lot of wandering NPCs, but 95% of them say one line of dialogue. Whereas in Act 1, almost everyone you talked to you could have a meaningful conversation with, or branch off into some new side quest. Act 3's map is huge, and whilst there are still really fun areas to explore, overall towards the end we found ourselves just teleporting around this empty feeling space and it lost some of it's magic that Act 1 had.

Not only that, but in Act 3, there are a lot of cutscenes that are missing sound and have low quality textures. The sound in Act 3 is pretty abysmal and so many cutscenes are quite janky in both the animation and sound, there will literally be no sound for some cutscenes in what would otherwise be really loud or big moments. For a lot of the end game cutscenes, this is really disappointing as it really killed the epic feeling they were trying to create and it really sucks you out of the magic of the game at times.

If Act 2 and 3 had been giving the same attention to detail and love as Act 1, the game would be a flawless 10/10. 

Overall, it really is an amazing game and I'm excited to see Larian return to their own IP for their next game, I just hope they've learnt from how they developed each Act in BG3 so that each part of the next game is given as much time and care that they can. Fingers crossed they get much better sound too. That was an area that was really lacking compared to the rest of the game.

I bought it without really being interested in Dungeons and Dragon's or Baldur's Gate. I wasn't even really that interested in high fantasy, I prefer less fantastical elements in my fiction. BUT THIS GAME IS SOMETHING ELSE! A great story open to changes based on your choices. Following the story would make the open world more understandable... but you could literally do whatever you want and you'd still somehow get through the game. The gameplay is basically xcom strategy but with engagements beginning however you want. The more you get used to it the easier the game gets.

What can I say about the story... you never really get bored because of it. Except maybe you can get lost. Like all these high fantasy fiction stories, they throw a huge amount of random information at you about the world you were thrown into and are supposed to understand it. There are different races, different classes, different worlds and places being named. NOT TO MENTION THE "gods," god of this, god of that. All this and you are collecting companions as you go through the game, each with a story of their own and the possibility to romance them. ROMANCE. Girls, guys, vampires, bears. There is scenes that are inappropriate but like everything else... you can avoid them. 

More on the story... you have a overall task that must be accomplished. There are worms in your head that were placed there by tentacle aliens. Somehow and someway you have to get rid of them. As you go through the game, you find out that its REALLY DAMN HARD to do. Multiple people say they can help but overall, no one can. There are three acts in the game and each one has its own little conflict. Makes things very interesting but VERY LONG. This game took me like 80 hours to finish on my first run. 

The gameplay has the most amount of variety any game can have. The amount of classes you can choose from and the differences between them, and the ability to change how you enter encounters... everything can be played in your own style. It can be hard at first cause of the random dice mechanics, which at first are really confusing. Nothing has a set damage, everything is a roll and decides damage and understanding for your character. However you can influence this stuff with magic spells and potions and positioning. Its also turn based, each character and singular enemy has their own turn to do an action. This makes it very strategic and not based on "skill" or "speed."

TLDR: Great gameplay, Great story, Great Graphics. High Fantasy turn based tactical strategy game based in a Dungeon's and Dragon's world. Where you can romance any companion and be good, neutral, evil, or mega evil.

after being stuck in act 1 for almost two years, i finally finished baldur’s gate 3, and it’s hard not to respect how massive and ambitious this game is. act 2 was easily my favorite part and, honestly, pretty close to perfect. the tone, the pacing, the atmosphere, everything just clicked there in a way the rest of the game doesn’t always manage.

most of the companions are really likeable, but karlach, wyll, and shadowheart were on another level for me and stayed in my party basically the entire time. karlach’s story especially hit hard. her arc and its conclusion are genuinely heartbreaking, and it’s easily the one i’ll remember the most.

act 3 is where the game starts to lose its footing. the moment you arrive in the city, you can feel the dip in focus and overall quest quality. without spoiling anything, it leans hard into classic rpg nonsense. the game keeps telling you there’s an urgent, city-ending threat, but at the same time it’s perfectly happy letting you spend hours doing side quests like investigating who killed a circus clown. some of these quests are fun, but they completely kill the sense of urgency the story is trying to build. that said, the actual endgame and final stretch do a great job at pulling things back together and delivering a strong payoff.

another issue i had is that choice density doesn’t always equal meaningful choice. late in the game you can unlock abilities that make dice rolls almost trivial, even really high ones like 25 or 30. this leads to some pretty weird situations where everyone just instantly believes you and everything goes your way, including outcomes that feel like the developers never really expected most players to reach. it’s cool at first, but it also removes a lot of tension and makes some story moments feel a bit hollow.

flaws aside, baldur’s gate 3 is still an incredible achievement. it’s huge, deeply crafted, and full of memorable characters and moments. act 3 may stumble, but the journey as a whole, especially the ending, still makes it something really special.

Baldur’s Gate 3 earns its reputation not by being flawless, but by being unusually confident in its ambition. At its best, it feels like a modern CRPG that finally delivers on the old promise of “player choice actually matters.” Act I is where this shines most clearly: the opening hours are tightly designed, rich with reactivity, and full of small decisions that ripple outward. Companions are introduced with strong personalities, clear conflicts, and immediate narrative hooks, and the writing balances seriousness with sharp humor. Early on, the game feels intensely personal, as if it’s constantly watching how you play and responding in kind.
The mid-game, largely represented by Act II, narrows the focus. The tone grows darker, the stakes become clearer, and the narrative pushes you toward confronting larger forces rather than just surviving. This act is often praised for its atmosphere and thematic cohesion, even if it sacrifices some of the playful openness of Act I. Character arcs deepen here, though exploration and pacing can feel more constrained. It’s a strong middle chapter that reinforces the game’s themes, but it’s also where some players begin to notice the limits of reactivity and systemic flexibility.
Act III is where admiration and criticism collide. The final act is massive, dense, and conceptually ambitious, placing you in a sprawling city full of quests, factions, and narrative threads. However, this scale comes at a cost. Compared to earlier acts, polish drops: performance issues become more noticeable, pacing can feel uneven, and the game struggles to meaningfully reflect every prior choice. While many storylines conclude satisfyingly, others feel rushed or underdeveloped, and the ending itself, though dramatic, doesn’t always provide the level of closure players expect after such a long, choice-driven journey.
Mechanically, BG3 is both one of its generation’s deepest RPGs and one of its most demanding. Combat is tactical, creative, and highly rewarding once understood, especially for players familiar with D&D systems. Environmental interactions, positioning, and resource management give fights real texture. At the same time, the learning curve is steep, combat can feel slow to some, and the UI and pathfinding occasionally work against the player. Freedom of approach—talking, sneaking, manipulating systems, or brute force—is a core strength, even if the illusion of total consequence frays slightly in the late game.
Where Baldur’s Gate 3 most consistently excels is in its companions. Voice acting, writing, and personal quests elevate them beyond party members into emotional anchors. Relationships—romantic or otherwise—feel earned, though not perfectly balanced, and some characters clearly receive more narrative attention than others. These companions are the reason many players remain invested even when the systems or pacing falter.
Taken as a whole, Baldur’s Gate 3 is not a perfect RPG, and treating it as such does it a disservice. It is uneven, occasionally messy, and clearly strongest in its early and middle chapters. Yet its ambition, respect for player agency, and depth of narrative design place it firmly among the best CRPGs ever made. It’s a game that reaches higher than most, stumbles near the finish line, but still lands far above the genre’s usual ceiling.
