Pros

Extremely well written. The characters are highly compelling with nuanced story arcs and mocap use bringing the acting to life, with hundreds of hours worth of dialogue and lots of freedom of choice in dialogue, action and character customisation, where you have special options on offer depending on your race and class as well as 7 pre-made “Origin” playable characters with their own story variations. It's also easy to get to grips with the setting even if you have no experience with D&D or the Forgotten Realms setting the game uses.
Extensive freedom. 12 classes branching out into 58 subclasses, a huge array of spells, abilities and items, combined with the vast dialogue options and choices, although the general journey you go on is fixed, who you bring with you, what they make of you and what you do in between the key story beats is highly open ended, making for one of the most open feeling games I’ve ever played.
Variety. As well as the game’s 3 Acts feeling visually and thematically unique, near enough every combat encounter feels original with unique enemy types that have their own sets of abilities, so no matter how many fights you get into there’s no real sense of repetition.
Longevity. Each act has a huge array of content on offer, minus time lost to failed attempts at combat encounters my playthrough clocked in at just over 50 hours, and that was after leaving sizeable parts of each of the 3 Act’s maps unexplored, if you’re the completionist type a single playthrough can easily run to hundreds of hours, and even after that you’ll only ever see one version of the story, with lots of replay value on offer from making different choices and playing as different characters.
Quality presentation. Across the board the game has excellent graphics and a fitting soundtrack, with strong performance including a consistent high framerate and crash freedom.
In-built modding. The in-game mod manager is available right from the title screen with 1 click downloads for approved mods that can vastly change and improve the experience, with thousands of mods to choose from, making for much more simple modding access than most games.

Cons

Slow levelling. If you don't really extensively do side quests you can be badly underlevelled as you progress through the game, which can be crippling as there are huge gaps in stats like health and ability between levels and encounters have no level scaling at all. On any difficulty above the game's lowest, Explorer, being a level, 2 levels or more below what's expected for an encounter can be extremely punishing. Sometimes the game will warn you if you're underlevelled before you enter a new area, other times it doesn't, it can lead to intense difficulty spikes and it was really annoying ending up with that problem just because I didn't side quest as much as the devs expected me to, feeling like something that undermined the “player agency” and freedom rooted in the design.
Performance issues. Though in general the game was technically very well running, many times there would be lengthy delays between an NPC getting their turn and actually taking an action, rarely this could sometimes happen to player characters too where there would be a long delay between taking an action and it actually happening, which can massively slow down combat, texture pop in and slow loading in of areas was also sometimes an issue, especially in Act 3.
4 party limit. You're strictly limited to only 4 party members at any time, this usually being your main protagonist and 3 companions, you can still recruit far more than this but they have to stay in your camp, only being able to join you if you swap them out of yourself. This means you have to either constantly faff about with party swapping or neglect most of your potential members, not having a character travelling with you can lead to you losing out on large amounts of their dialogue and missing opportunities to influence their opinion of your protag, as (except for some very rare instances) their approval will only change as a result of choices you make while they're in the party, it's a totally arbitrary restriction that can leave you losing out on a lot of character development.
Unintuitive quest design. In general quest design is excellent and clear, but sometimes the quests, including major story quests, can have really irrational outcomes for your choices or lack clarity, for example giving you no idea where to go or what to do to start a quest if you didn’t follow certain specific lines of choices.
Highly inconsistent urgency. Some quest events are time sensitive, but their mechanics are wildly inconsistent, sometimes “running out of time” is caused by waiting too long in real time, sometimes it's caused by ending the day via a long rest, sometimes it's by leaving a region, other times the game will heavily imply an event is time sensitive when it actually isn't.
Class building. Levelling up often requires you to make major choices like subclasses, picking from vast lists of abilities like Spells and Feats, with no real idea of their use cases, and you can’t accept the stat boosts of level ups (like flat health increases) without also making these ability choices, making it easy to end up bumbling your way into less useful or ideal builds, although Respeccing is cheap and easy to do if you make choices you’re unhappy with later, it can be easy to be overwhelmed or lost by the build choices.
Extensive RNG reliance. This is more a personal preference thing than an objective con, but since the game mechanics are imported from tabletop D&D, unchanged at their core, the game is highly reliant on dice rolls for nearly every aspect of the gameplay, whether your attacks hit, how much damage they do, the effectiveness of your abilities, whether enemies can resist them through saving throws, the turn order of combat, the results of skill checks, it would probably be quicker to list the mechanics that *aren’t* impacted by the dice, and you can shift the odds but never totally control them. You can have a 70% chance to hit an attack and still miss 4 times in a row, in a boss fight one attempt might see you placed in a long dragged out encounter, another might see you killing them in the first few turns, not because of skill or strategy, but the dice, that can make for some real frustrating unfair feeling moments. The ability to quicksave at any time means no dice roll can truly sabotage you long term, but the extensive monopoly RNG has on the gameplay, which can make or break the experience as much as your own choices, can be hard to stomach.

Having finally finished BG3 I can really see why it has its reputation as one of the greatest games of all time, it’s a real favourite for me, the story is one of the best I’ve ever experienced, the gameplay is incredibly open ended and reactive and the presentation is excellent.

I formed a real love hate relationship with it through most of the first Act thanks to the balancing issues, turning to pure love in the second Act when they basically vanished as I was properly levelled for all encounters, until the Act 2 finale which had a massive untelegraphed difficulty spike with me not being at the right level, which finally snapped me and had me turn the combat difficulty down to the easiest, Explorer, these combat encounters were some of the most frustrating experiences I had with the game and my enthusiasm for all its other aspects kept me motivated up to that point, but by then I got exhausted and kicked it down, I would recommend considering Explorer for a first run to avoid potentially stumbling into intense frustration.

The clunky quest design at times makes it really hard to play blind and some of the design feels off, partly due to the vast changes made to the game in Early Access and the last minute nature of some additions, but overall BG3 is definitely great value for money and a real work of passion that really deserves the love it gets.

The characters and story are great — genuinely interesting, and I really want to keep playing to see what happens next.

But the gameplay feels like it assumes you already know D&D rules. The game barely teaches its own mechanics, so if you’re new to this system everything becomes trial-and-error guessing: who is strong vs weak, which items are rare vs just cheap consumables, what you should save, and what you can freely spend.

Wizard leveling is especially confusing: you’re asked to pick spells without really understanding what they actually do in real combat. On top of that, healing spells suddenly run out — and at that point your whole party can just wipe in a “normal” fight.

And the worst part: it constantly feels like the game is punishing you for everything. For not knowing mechanics, for making “wrong” choices you couldn’t realistically understand, for exploring, for fighting, for leveling — for basically playing the game as a newcomer. There’s no satisfaction in that, only frustration.

It honestly feels like a card game where everyone knows the rules except you. As a newcomer, it’s painful and stressful even to fight on the first map.

The world, the story and your ability to change the outcomes are first rate.  The game allows plenty of player creativity and the world is both curated and expansive.

But this game requires a lot of the players:

The inventory management is a disaster, like just a total mess, you pick up so much shit with no clue of when/how/if you'll use it.  I finished my first run with sacks of potions and scrolls I kept holding for a rainy day and just wound up carrying around forever.  The alchemy supplies just piled up and I crafted them into things I never used.  You don't know what armor to bother holding onto until Act 3 at which point you just start cleaning house.  In short it's just a big pain in the ass that detracts from the experience.

The DnD ruleset introduces SO many spells and abilities that are useless clutter that just make building characters more cumbersome than it needs to be.  Also there is zero attempt to balance difference class builds whatsoever.  I didn't get into multi-classing and just did what felt right on my playthrough and Lae'zel was basically more powerful than any other 3 guys I had in the party combined.  She basically solo'd half the game while everyone else stood around doing f-all.  

The combat system is clunky and slow and at times frustrating.  It's the kind of game you can basically glitch with knowledge of what you're doing.  Or maybe you'll luck into it, like I got Raphael pinned down with GodQueen Lae'zel, Hope and a Pole and he just stood there and let me pound his ass until he died, El Pole being the 3rd strongest member of my party that fight.  If you have 4 optimal builds and good positioning you'll destroy everything.  And again there's just too many abilities.  And I could excuse all the bloat if the combat system was really good because then you would want to dig into the finer details but it isn't.

The game is functional with a controller, there are times it is annoying and you will need to take time to clean up all the radials at least a bit.  I'd say its an odd split where fights would be better with KB/M and exploration with a controller, which is kind of annoying.

So in short, it's a memorable game but it's also a chore, I was happy to hit the ending credits and just be done.  Maybe in 5 years I'll be staring at my library and have the itch, but I kind of hope not lol.

I don’t need to say much about this game, it’s already known far and wide as one of the best in its genre. Instead, here are a few things that stood out to me during my playthrough that might help new players.

1. A near‑perfect CRPG with a few natural limits
The game delivers everything people praise it for: incredible storytelling, phenomenal voice acting, a rich world, and a style that feels as close as you can get to a living D&D campaign.
But it is still a computer game. Dialogue options can feel limited, romances can swing between all‑or‑nothing, and companions, as amazing as they are, sometimes don’t react as often or as deeply as you’d expect.

2. Huge, but not open‑world
The game is massive, but it isn’t an open‑world sandbox. Each area is carefully designed and fairly contained. Exploration is rewarding, but it often feels guided or scripted rather than freeform.

3. Choices matter, sometimes more than your sanity
The game’s commitment to consequences is impressive, but it can be tough on completionists or min‑maxers. With branching storylines and mutually exclusive paths, you’re constantly leaving things behind. You’ll miss conversations, companion reactions, and entire story beats simply because you chose one direction over another.

This makes the game highly replayable but not so replayable that everyone has the time to run multiple full playthroughs.

Final Thoughts
Despite all that, the game is absolutely worth playing, even for people like me who struggle to “just sit back and enjoy the ride.” The challenge isn’t a flaw in the game, it’s a unique difficulty for players who want to see everything.
You’ll constantly wonder who to bring, who will approve, and what you might have missed. It’s a testament to the game’s quality that these choices feel meaningful, even when they drive you a little crazy. In the end, I did my best to enjoy the story that unfolded for me without obsessing over the one I didn’t see, and it was still unforgettable.

baldur's gate 3 is of course an astonishing achievement in role playing games, a wildly intricate experience that pushes the genre both forward into modernity but also backward in that it recaptures the magic of some of the old CRPGs from the 90s while removing rough edges and dull production values. they seemingly motion captured ALL dialogue in the entire game rather than relying on canned animations - that alone is awe-inspiring. it makes the whole thing feel so much more alive than any other rpg out there.

my biggest beef with this game, though, is that conversations are, for whatever reason, locked to one person at a time. if any party NPCs or other multiplayer players are engaged in conversations, they can't interact. they can't butt in or interject in any meaningful way other than the NPCs expressing their emotions/stances, or try to sway the vibe of the conversation or save a tense situation from erupting. they can passively cast spells like guidance, but that's it. they wrote so many different dialogue options for every character, to the point that any one person starting the same conversation can see it go in tons of different ways, but each conversation is locked into that one specific person, the others just stand behind, passively observing and judging you for what you say.

i would have loved it if, say, i had lae'zel selected and she was being a dick, but then i could swoop in as my bard character and save the situation from going bad with a persuasion check. or vice versa - sabotage a healthy conversation that then leads to battle. the modular way these conversations seems to be designed, a group-speech dynamic would have been great. as it stands, you largely want to go into every conversation with whoever your most charismatic party member is, which can make multiplayer characters who aren't charismatic feel bored)

I spent over a year completing my first playthrough, 157 hours in one playthrough on a game that has endless replayability. I got this on sale but I'd say it's worth the full price. The characters are interesting and dynamic, the mod options are so fun, and as someone who's not played strategy rpg's before the combat was really interesting. There was a challenging learning curve to the game for me too which will make me a better DnD player. As soon as I finished my first playthrough I started my second.

I will never tire of this game. 
Even after 550 hours I am still getting new lines and interactions from companions by playing differently. The other day I discovered a hidden chest in an area I've looted completely at least five times before. I haven't seen all the different outcomes for companion questlines yet.

Not only does this game have a truly wild amount of content, it does a good job of balancing it. As a player you get to decide your focus; strategic battles fighting enemies head on, or use tricks & strategies to minimise time spent fighting? Talk to npc's and be immersed in story, or focus on quests & goals? 
On top of that, there's room to play with morals & ethics. Or to just spend hours customising your character (as I have definitely done lol).

And I haven't even gotten started on the amount of mods... I personally prefer to play the game pretty vanilla, only with mods for customisation and some quality of life things. But I know people who loooove mods that add extra classes, encounters, higher levels, etc. There's something for everyone, and the devs embrace the community & fan-made mods. 

All in all; absolutely my favorite game of all time. Great immersive storytelling, amazing visuals, never ending ways of playing and a lovely community. If I could buy it again, I would. Without question.

Greetings,

Thank you for your attention. I’ll summarize the good and bad aspects of the game according to my own experience, and hope it helps you out somehow. Please feel free to play the game by yourself in case you disagree with the following review.


Positive Aspects

1 – Narrative Depth & Archetypal Storytelling; BG3 doesn’t just tell a story; it embodies one. The dialogues, companions, and branching choices feel like stepping into an Arthurian myth, where you can be king, knight, sage, or peasant. The game role‑plays back at you, validating the archetype you choose. This is where the artistry shines: you stop seeing pixels and start seeing eternal archetypes.

2 – Atmosphere & Music; the environments, bard songs, and ambient scores elevate the experience into something unforgettable. A simple moment, like a girl singing with her lute in the druid camp — becomes a piece of art. The music and atmosphere don’t decorate the game; they carry its soul.

3 – Role Customization & Party Synergy; your character isn’t just a set of stats. Whether you build a noble commander, a sage, or a brute, the party responds fluidly. Companions feel alive, reacting to your choices and shaping the narrative. This synergy makes every role meaningful, even if you’re not the highest damage dealer.

4 – A Living World; exploration feels like inhabiting a myth. Every corner of the map holds stories, secrets, and lore that respond to your presence. Unlike older RPGs, BG3 doesn’t just let you project a role, it mirrors it back, making you feel part of a living legend.


Negative Aspects

1 – Graphics Modesty; for a game marketed as “next gen,” the visuals aren’t revolutionary. They’re beautiful, with god rays and atmospheric effects, but not groundbreaking. Yet this modesty is almost thematic — like a princess in a simple gown, hiding the enchantment in her voice and soul.

2 – Performance & Bugs; as with many expansive RPGs, technical hiccups exist. Occasional glitches, long load times, or odd AI behavior can break immersion. These don’t ruin the experience, but they remind you of the limits of the medium.

3 – Complexity for Newcomers; the depth of systems, dialogue checks, spell preparation, tactical combat — can overwhelm players expecting something simpler, like KOTOR. BG3 demands patience and learning, which may discourage casual players.

4 – Party Management; while synergy is fluid, managing inventories, equipment, and spell preparation across multiple companions can feel cumbersome. It’s part of the richness, but also part of the burden.


Important Mentions

1 – Spell Preparation & Roleplay; paladins, Wizards, Clerics, each class embodies its archetype through spell preparation. Choosing Bless or Moonbeam isn’t just mechanics; it’s storytelling. Your build reflects your role in the myth.

2 – Companions as Archetypes; each companion embodies a timeless role: the knight, the trickster, the sage, the bard. Interacting with them feels like living inside a modern NeverEnding Story or Labyrinth.

3 – Emotional Resonance; few games make you cry not from sadness, but from artistry itself. BG3 overwhelms you like entering an MMA arena and being struck from all sides, narrative, music, dialogue, atmosphere, until you fall humbled by its beauty.

4 – Excessive Combat and Traps: even though your choices change the outcome, you're almost always led into a fight. The game insists on ambushes, forced encounters, and traps that create a sense of a straight line full of obstacles. This can lead to fatigue, as the narrative and exploration are often interrupted by constant battles, leaving the player stuck in dense and repetitive maps.


Conclusion

Honestly, one of the most unforgettable RPGs ever made. BG3 doesn’t just entertain; it humbles. It’s a modern Gesamtkunstwerk, a total work of art where music, narrative, visuals, and roleplay converge. If you’re into storytelling, roleplay, and immersion, this game will stay with you long after you finish it.

The key factor that makes BG3 stand apart is simple: it doesn’t just let you play a character, it lets you become one, and then reflects that archetype back at you through a living, breathing world, so If you’ve ever dreamed of inhabiting a myth of being the knight, the king, the sage, or the peasant, BG3 is not just a game. It’s art.

I know that many people absolutely love this game. However, there are quite a few things I personally didn’t enjoy, and it often feels like most players prefer to focus only on the positive side of game.

Let’s start with the pros: a huge world, a wide variety of game mechanics, strong replay value, and good optimization. Larian has clearly put a lot of effort into this game, and it will probably be remembered for many years. Players will keep replaying it and finding new things every time.

Now for the cons. Everything written below is purely my personal opinion, and you may disagree with it. Maybe this is part of Larian’s signature style, but Baldur’s Gate 3 constantly puts the player in front of difficult and often dumb choices. Sometimes these choices feel so absurd that I just want to make no decision at all and close the game. Very often, you’re forced to choose between two dumb outcomes - for example, between your own death or letting someone else die in a much worse way, while knowing that you might get testicular cancer.
Sometimes during dialogues, you have to pass several skill checks, and since this is a DnD-based game, you can easily fail them even if your skill level is high. This isn’t exactly a downside. It’s actually one of the game’s strengths. But if you’re on a second playthrough and want to get a different outcome from a quest, this can make things quite frustrating.

Throughout the game, you meet characters with their own personal motives. From the start, some of them clearly show that they want to use you or might even harm you. At the same time, you can’t really do much about it, because they are important to the main story. You’re basically forced to go along with it and let these characters act however they want.

The same problem applies to companions. If you choose not to help a companion with their personal quest, or if you solve it in a way they don’t like, they can get offended, leave your party, or even attack you. In some cases, characters may become hostile or distance themselves from you even if you genuinely try to help. This isn’t really about gratitude or morality. The game has many deep and well-designed systems, and NPCs can react differently depending on your actions and the situation. Still, there are moments when their reactions feel incredibly stupid or completely unpredictable, especially when you expect something more logical.

I didn't feel like writing a whole essay for my original review but I already made this response and I think a game like this deserves some elaboration. I appreciate anyone willing to put up with my opinion, I know this is alot of people's favorite game, and if someone made a review like this about Clair Obscur I would be mad too. Don't forget that you are ABSOLUTELY NOT allowed to criticize art in any way, ESPECIALLY not popular art that everyone likes, or that makes you a bad gamer and that's an irredeemable sin. I've actually never liked any video game ever, in fact I hate all of them and wish my hobby would just die already. With that in mind, here's what I dislike about the game:

Every character is written with MCU dialogue. Everyone is witty and funny and "we're all going on an adventure team!" and it's so boring. I remember specifically Shadowheart saying "I guess that's what I like about you, you're different." Like seriously? My silent protagonist that has done nothing but stare and pick dialogue option number one the entire time is special? Why? Why am I different, literally tell me what I did, all we've done is battle and talk to people. It's just cringe all around, all the characters are cringe. That one annoying devil that just showed up and kidnapped me, then started speaking in poems as he tried to convince me he "totally didn't want my soul for bad things, only good things." Can you try at all? Or Gale who makes no attempt to come as someone you would even want in your party? Astarion didn't even join me until I needed a fourth member. Look at Ifan from Divinity Orginal Sin 2, he's immediately interesting. When you meet on the boat he's personable but still kinda mean, you can see there's more beneath the surface instantly. He's always meeting mysterious people doing very hush hush things, you want to know what the big secret is. I don't care about any of the companions or their secrets in BG3. Why should I? I can't interact with them like they interact with me, and most of them are really annoying anyway. I didn't meet a single character during my gameplay that I thought "Oh wow, you're really cool, whether you're a companion or not I like your voice acting, story, and design so much that you're gonna be one of my favorite characters." It just isn't there, it's like they made caricatures based off D&D and some MCU Collab Clorox they found in a shed. 

Every single dialogue is awkward because of the silent protagonist. Why are people just talking at me, and I'm just reacting? I can't give a little "uh-huh" whenever I nod or something? Combined with the seven different dialogue choices that all do nothing except progress the dialogue, why should I care about the dialogue at all? Yeah the voice acting is cool, but if I know they'll just say the same thing anyway, I'll just pick number one, read, and skip. It's like Larian looked at all the bad rpg dialogue trees and said "Ok, so if we give them seven dialogue choices instead of five or three, then the illusion of choice will actually matter to the player." No it doesn't. I ordered RPG with my CRPG, like it comes with the order. I shouldn't have to sit here and beg on my hands and knees to play a different game than other people are playing. "Oh I've replayed Act 1 so many times, it's so reactive." Literally how, show me the reactivity. I played for almost 11 hours and the world didn't acknowledge my existence at all, and it was made all the more obvious by the fact that everyone else was acknowledged because they had a voice! It's all fake, you know what a fugazi is? I hate this illusion of choice bs, it's the quickest way to turn me off a game.

Also notice how nobody cared that I picked a Tiefling in the first quest? Here I am thinking "Maybe the Tieflings will be different to me because I'm a Tiefling, and I can cast Tiefling specific spells and help them more than I would in say, a dark elf playthrough." Lmao, why would I think there would be RPG elements in this game? Here's a couple random dialogue choices, they won't do anything different but maybe the character will mention tieflings in that response, then carry on with their original monologue. And they are monologues btw, I keep referring to them as dialogues but my party members were extremely silent the whole time.

And your character just stares. Everyone else is having a grand old time but me? I'm just there to react. Grandpa died? Sad face. Grandpa came back from the dead? Happy face. Tell me more in great detail about how your grandpa came back to life, I'd love to sit and react to your story while I click different buttons to make you say things. 

Can we talk about the build variety I've been dying to talk about the build variety.
What build variety? You get spellllllls, god I love spells. There's a scroll for this and a scroll for that, a spell for this and a spell for that. And you WILL be using the same party composition as everyone else is, because Astarion HAS to be a vampire rogue, and Lae'zel HAS to be a melee swordfighter. Which means your main character HAS to be viable or it throws the balance off, which means you get NO build variety. "Oh boy I levelled up, what do I get?" A stat increase, now clap. Maybe you got a spell or two. What am I even supposed to do with that, why should I care that my party members are levelling when they just get "more powerful +1".

Oh and Act 3 is still unfinished apparently? Why didn't they patch it later, or was it all that motion capture that was getting in the way? 

The reality is whenever Larian got a license from Wizards of the Coast it was going to be terrible from the start. Of course WoTC is going to make them charge $60 constantly because it's Wizards of The Coast. Of course the ingame mod loader will disable achievements but downloading them from Nexus won't, it's WoTC and they're anti-competitive, and of course you will have Larian defenders blindly parrot "every other game does it with mods." Of course the game would be as dumbed down as possible, it's WoTC, they need to make it "palatable for modern audinces". Speaking of which, really crazy how they went with 5e and not 3.5e right? Such a little coinky-dink. Of course they have to make their money back for their really expensive motion capture and voice acting work. And, of course, there will be people that shut off their brain, plug their ears, and say "lah lah lah, I can't hear you." because they don't want to admit they didn't know what a CRPG even was before this took home every game of the year award in an objectively really mid year for video games. 

If you care about voice acting, and motion capture, and beautiful graphics, and shallow hot characters, that's fine! But be honest about it, don't go touting your game around as God's gift to the earth because it has all those things. The constant $60 implies quality, and in those things I can find quality in. Baldur’s Gate 3 genuinely surprised me in a very positive way. As someone who had no prior experience with the series, I wasn’t entirely sure what to expect going in. Now I can say one thing with confidence: there is a reason this game won Game of the Year. Even though the title itself does not always mean much these days, Baldur’s Gate 3 truly deserves it.

First and foremost, this is a game made in the old-school, best possible way. It is clearly made for players. You can feel that the developers put real heart into this project and genuinely respected the audience, knowing that players ultimately decide whether a game succeeds or fails. That level of care is visible throughout the entire experience.

The developers anticipated an incredible range of player behavior, including chaotic, stupid, and completely unexpected choices. This often leads to hilariously memorable situations. At the same time, when the game needs to be serious, it fully commits to that tone. It knows when to be lighthearted and when to be heavy, and that balance works extremely well.

The characters are one of the game’s strongest elements. Many of them are well-written, memorable, and emotionally engaging. Each companion feels distinct and meaningful, with clear motivations and personal stories. Two of my favorite companions are Minthara and Shadowheart, both of whom stand out thanks to their depth and strong narrative presence.

The locations are beautifully designed, and the audio work including voice acting and soundtrack is outstanding. The storytelling is consistently strong and keeps you invested in the world and its conflicts. Even the turn-based combat, which I was initially skeptical about, becomes genuinely enjoyable over time. The creative use of elements and the environment is excellent. In some fights, you can completely change the outcome simply by using your surroundings properly, such as igniting alcohol that enemies are standing in.

At its core, Baldur’s Gate 3 is a true sandbox RPG. You are thrown into the world, given tools, and allowed to play exactly the way you want. This is how role-playing games should be designed. The ambition behind the game is especially visible in the massive number of dialogue options and hidden interactions. There are many conversations and outcomes that most players will never see, simply because they did not make a certain unexpected choice.

I can confidently recommend Baldur’s Gate 3. This game sets a strong standard for modern RPGs and clearly shows what can be achieved when developers truly respect their players.

Final rating: 9.1/10

As someone who’s put over 1000 hours into Baldur’s Gate 3, I can confidently say that this game has something special. From the moment I started playing, it was clear that Larian Studios had crafted a world that was as deep as it was expansive. And the craziest part? I’m still having a blast, even after over 1000 hours of gameplay.

First off, the game’s story is an absolute triumph. The writing, the characters, and the plot twists never fail to impress, no matter how many times I revisit the game. Whether it’s exploring the vast and varied environments or navigating the morally complex decisions, Baldur's Gate 3 always offers something fresh. You can genuinely feel like your choices matter in a world that reacts to them in ways I haven’t seen in many RPGs before.

The combat is just as engaging. The tactical, turn-based system is a joy to master, and I find myself continually coming up with new strategies to tackle the challenges the game throws at me. It's the kind of combat where no two battles ever feel quite the same, and even after 1000 hours, I still get that rush from nailing a perfectly executed strategy or surviving a brutal fight.

But it’s not just the solo experience that’s kept me coming back; the co-op play in Baldur's Gate 3 is phenomenal. Being able to team up with friends (or even strangers) for epic runs is one of the best multiplayer experiences I’ve had in years. The depth of interaction and cooperation needed between players really makes the game shine. There’s always something to discuss, plan, and react to, and playing together with friends just enhances the already amazing experience. Whether it’s working together in Honor Mode for that extra challenge or simply enjoying the chaos of a well-coordinated party, the game is endlessly replayable.

Honor Mode, in particular, adds an insane level of challenge and tension to every decision, and the satisfaction of completing a run with friends in this mode is one of the most rewarding experiences I’ve had in gaming. There's no "easy" way out; it's all about thinking on your feet, reacting in real-time, and making sure every move counts.

What makes Baldur’s Gate 3 truly exceptional is that even after over 1000 hours, I still discover new things. Whether it's a hidden quest, a character interaction I missed, or a strategy I haven't tried yet, the game continues to surprise me in ways that most titles just don’t. It has so much depth that it feels like I’m only scratching the surface every time I jump back in.

In short, Baldur's Gate 3 is an absolute masterpiece. If you're into immersive RPGs, tactical combat, and epic storytelling, there's no reason not to dive in. With its ever-expanding world and endless replayability, it’s the kind of game that will keep you hooked for years. For me, it’s been over 1000 hours, and I can confidently say I’ll be coming back for hundreds more.

I bought Baldur’s Gate 3 thinking, “Cool, I’ll play a bit after work.”
That was a lie I told myself.
This game didn’t just consume my free time it respectfully asked for it, then took it anyway while rolling a natural 20 on charm.

The writing is absurdly good. Every companion feels like a real person with depth, trauma, questionable morals, and the ability to emotionally ruin you with a single line of dialogue. I came for the turn-based combat and stayed because I accidentally started caring deeply about fictional people who now live rent-free in my head.
Your choices actually matter. Not slightly different dialogue matter entire questlines, relationships, and outcomes change based on what you do or say. I have never saved so often while also refusing to reload because “no, this is my canon now.” The game respects your agency and then quietly judges you for it.

Combat is tactical, creative, and wildly flexible. You can win fights by planning like a genius… or by shoving enemies off cliffs, setting the floor on fire, and accidentally blowing yourself up. Both approaches feel valid. Both are fun.
The production value is insane. Fully voiced characters, cinematic cutscenes, gorgeous environments, and a soundtrack that makes even walking through a forest feel epic. It feels like a passion project with a blockbuster budget.

Downsides?
You will lose sleep.
You will start a second playthrough before finishing the first.
You will say “just one more quest” and look up to see the sun rising.

If you like RPGs, storytelling, meaningful choices, or games that respect your intelligence: buy this.
If you don’t like those things: honestly, still buy it. It might change your mind.

The best game I couldn't recommend to someone. This is a spoiler free review because I don't believe you should have to be spoiled about content of the game to decide whether you want to buy it or not. It will contain references to how many species there are and how many Companions of said species there are to highlight the lack of diversity in companions, however.

Before we go any further, it is worth mentioning that Larian Studios, the developers and publishers of BG3, have announced that they will be using Generative AI in their future products. So far it is, allegedly, only for Concept Art but if this fact bothers you, you have the right to know. As far as I know, no Gen-AI was utilised in the making of BG3.

Baldur's Gate 3 is a game divided into Three Acts, Two of which, the first two, are amazing in their own ways with about 60+ hours worth of content between them.

 I started playing this game before it even came out, I was one of the first people who played it during Early Access and I was there every step of the way until release, I was so incredibly excited when the game came out and I enjoyed it for a long time, I even bought it for a friend of mine, but the more I look at it the more glaring the problems become.

Character Creation - Great but limited

Baldur's Gate 3 is, unsurprisingly to most, based on the incredibly popular TTRPG Dungeons and Dragons, and with that one expects a certain degree of customisability over their characters. Depending on the species you select, you may have more or less customizability, with said customisability options decreasing the farther away you get from Humans and "Humanesque" species. You lose a lot of customisation in the face, you choose a pre-made one and can only alter your skin, add vitiligo (which, don't get me wrong, is a great addition), change your eye color and so on. Things like your nose, lips, or further customisation of your facial structure are not present. Body customisation is, otherwise, even more limited, you choose between 1-4 body types, 1-2 if you're less human-like (height-wise), which represent the traditional male and female bodies, you get some customisation in deciding whether you'd like to have body hair, if it applies to your species, and you get to choose your genitals which, as far as I know, doesn't affect the gameplay or story in any way shape or form, and lastly you choose a gender identity between male, female and non-binary and have a limited array of voices that you get to assign to your character, regardless of body type or genital choice. 

Overall it's a very decent character creator with some unique options but it lacks in deep customisability of your characters and, if the character you want to play wasn't a core species in 2014, you're unable to play it without mods (with the exception of Githyanki). Additional mods allow you to further customise your hair options and add custom faces, expanding the range you have for creating a character's "look". Additionally, due to limited body customisation, your character can't be anything BUT fit, there are no chubby or even fat custom characters.

This all might sound like a nit-pick but from a videogame that fully came out after 2023 that's based on a TTRPG where you can be almost anyone or anything, the character creation ends up being a let-down, even if it is EXTREMELY enhanced by mods.

The Story - Great until the final act

This section will not include Companions, the people whom you may choose to travel with. Additionally, although this is a numbered title, you needn't play Baldur's Gate or Baldur's Gate 2 to play this one, there are many references to the old games but the story can very much be stand-alone.

The main story is great until the final act, with the first and second acts having a multitude of interesting quests, many of which do have some sort of effect or continuation after they're completed in the later acts, however, as you get to Act 3, you are bombarded with an innumerable amount of quests, many of which end up falling flat in continuity and even the main quest itself seemingly culminating in a disappointment after so many expectations were set up. The experience of Act 3 is now more palatable than it was when the game was release, with the game receiving a multitude of Hotfixes to improve its quality, at launch, Act 3 was extremely buggy and borderline unplayable and to some people on lower end PCs, it still is. Since the update, additional endings have been added as well as an epilogue, which seeks to add more soul into an otherwise careless ending.

Companions - The fun guys and gals that travel with you!

If you're ready to travel with a diverse cast of characters, I'm sorry to disappoint you but you won't get much. Most companions are great, and have interesting stories that you can get invested in throughout your playthrough. Most companions are also humans, or some brand of elf, with exclusion of one Tiefling and one Githyanki.

Companions are divided into two sections, Origin and Non-Origin companions.

Origin Companions are characters you'll meet early on during Act 1 and you are also able to play as them if you decide not to make a custom character.

Non-Origin Companions are people you meet later during Act 1 or 2 and can be recruited to your party depending on your actions throughout the story, they are, understandably, less fleshed out than Origin Characters and don't feel very relevant story-wise after their questline is done.

Companion Species, as previously mentioned are limited, out of the 11 Species, not counting Sub-Species, the Main Cast represents 5 of them, with some Companions being of the same species. If you'd like to travel with a Half-Orc, a Dwarf, a Gnome, a Halfling or a Dragonborn and see unique insights they might have into the story as someone with their background, you'll unfortunately need to be content with NPCs.

Each Companion has their own story-line, with most being connected in some way to the narrative. Baldur’s Gate 3 is a masterclass in how deep, systems-driven RPGs should be made. From the moment you step into its world, it’s clear that this game is built around player choice, creativity, and meaningful consequences. It doesn’t rush you, it doesn’t hold your hand, and it fully trusts you to engage with its mechanics—and that trust pays off in a huge way.

The combat is easily one of the strongest aspects of the game. Every encounter feels deliberate and tactical, where positioning, elevation, action economy, spell synergy, and environmental interactions all matter. You’re constantly encouraged to think outside the box: shove enemies off ledges, ignite surfaces, combine spells in unexpected ways, or completely change the flow of a fight with a well-timed control ability. It captures the spirit of tabletop D&D perfectly, making each battle feel less like a routine grind and more like a dynamic problem to solve. Even after dozens of hours, fights stay engaging because the systems are flexible enough to support endless approaches.

On the RPG side, Baldur’s Gate 3 truly shines. Character creation and builds feel deep and impactful, with your class, race, background, and choices all influencing how you interact with the world. Dialogue isn’t just flavor—it’s a core mechanic. Conversations can open new paths, avoid combat entirely, or lead to unexpected consequences later on. The companions are especially well done, each with their own beliefs, flaws, and personal arcs that evolve based on your decisions. They feel like real characters rather than quest dispensers, and building relationships with them adds emotional weight to the journey.

What really sets BG3 apart is how reactive the world is. The game consistently acknowledges your actions, remembers your choices, and adapts accordingly. There’s a genuine sense of agency here—you’re not just following a story, you’re shaping it. Whether you’re role-playing a noble hero, a morally conflicted adventurer, or a chaotic force of nature, the game supports it without judgment or restriction.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is demanding, deep, and incredibly rewarding. It’s a game that invites you to slow down, think, and immerse yourself fully in its systems and story. If you love tactical combat, rich role-playing, and games that respect your freedom as a player, this is an absolute must-play and one of the best RPG experiences in years.

Baldur’s Gate 3 — одна из лучших игр, которые я проходил с искренним удовольствием от начала и до конца. Сразу отмечу: я не являюсь поклонником данного жанра. Divinity: Original Sin мне не зашла, а в предыдущие части Baldur’s Gate я не играл, поэтому оцениваю игру без сравнений и предвзятости.
Перед нами максимально проработанная пошаговая RPG по правилам D&D. Игра даёт редкое для жанра ощущение настоящей свободы. Вариативность решений поражает: ты можешь действовать как угодно — через диалоги, скрытность, силу, магию или нестандартные подходы — и в большинстве случаев игра это учитывает. Практически каждое решение имеет последствия и отражается на диалогах, квестах, отношениях с персонажами и развитии сюжета.

Отдельно стоит отметить персонажей и диалоги — они живые, хорошо написанные и озвученные. Спутники запоминаются, у каждого есть характер, мотивация и своя история, за развитием которых действительно интересно следить.
Боевая система поначалу может показаться сложной, особенно для тех, кто не знаком с D&D, но со временем она раскрывается и начинает приносить удовольствие за счёт тактической глубины и разнообразия возможностей.
Романтическая система реализована немного странно и местами спорно, но в целом она не портит впечатление и воспринимается нормально — сильного разочарования не вызвала.
Игра явно рассчитана на повторные прохождения: разные классы, пути развития персонажа, альтернативные решения и сюжетные развилки делают каждый новый забег потенциально уникальным. Планирую пройти её ещё раз, уже принимая совсем другие решения. Рекомендую к покупке

If I have any criticisms, it would be the occasional bugs and performance issues, but these are minor compared to the overall experience. Larian's commitment to post-launch support and patches gives me confidence that these will be resolved.  

In short, Baldur's Gate 3 is not just a game-it's an immersive, emotional journey through one of the most beloved settings in fantasy. If you're a fan of CRPGs, storytelling, or just great games in general, do yourself a favor and dive in. You won't regret it.

Baldur’s Gate 3 ist nicht einfach nur ein Spiel – es ist ein monumentales Rollenspiel-Erlebnis, das so gut ist, dass man sich danach fragt, warum man jemals etwas anderes gespielt hat. Wenn das hier nicht das beste Rollenspiel aller Zeiten ist, dann zumindest der Maßstab, an dem sich alle zukünftigen messen lassen müssen.

Die Freiheit ist absurd groß: Jede Entscheidung zählt, jede Dialogoption kann dein Schicksal verändern, und selbst scheinbar harmlose Aktionen können komplette Questlinien explodieren lassen – manchmal wortwörtlich. Die Charaktere sind so gut geschrieben, dass ich mich dabei ertappt habe, fiktiven Gefährten emotional näher zu stehen als manchen Menschen im echten Leben (sorry an dieser Stelle).

Das Kampfsystem ist taktisch, fordernd und gleichzeitig unglaublich befriedigend. Wer denkt, Rundenkämpfe seien langweilig, wurde hier eines Besseren belehrt – vor allem, wenn man Gegner mit Kreativität, Magie und gelegentlich auch purer Gemeinheit austrickst. Und ja, man kann Dinge tun, die man besser nicht tun sollte. Genau das macht es großartig.

Technisch, erzählerisch und spielerisch ist Baldur’s Gate 3 ein Meisterwerk. Humor, Drama, Tragik, epische Momente – alles ist da. Dieses Spiel respektiert die Intelligenz der Spieler und belohnt Neugier wie kaum ein anderes.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is one of those rare games where the journey truly matters more than the ending — and I say that after 240 hours played and still not finished.

That’s not because the game is long for the sake of it, but because it constantly invites you to slow down: explore every corner, investigate every dialogue option, follow side quests that feel as meaningful as main ones, and experiment with choices just to see how the world reacts. Almost every time I thought “this is probably nothing,” it turned into a fully fleshed-out story, character moment, or consequence hours later.

The amount of freedom is honestly insane. You’re not just choosing dialogue options — you’re shaping outcomes through actions, timing, class abilities, party composition, and sometimes pure curiosity. The game rewards exploration and experimentation in a way very few RPGs ever have.

The characters are another massive highlight. Your companions feel alive, layered, and reactive. Their personal stories evolve naturally over time, and your relationship with them actually feels earned, not scripted. Voice acting, writing, and facial animations are all top-tier and elevate everything.

Combat deserves special mention too. Turn-based battles are deep, tactical, and endlessly flexible. Whether you’re playing “by the rules” or doing something completely unhinged, the game usually says “yes, that works” — and that’s part of the magic.

Even after hundreds of hours, it still feels like I’ve only scratched the surface. Different choices, different classes, different paths — it’s the kind of game that makes you already plan your next playthrough before finishing the current one.

In short: this is not a game you rush. It’s a game you live in.

I genuinely have no words. Baldur’s Gate 3 reminded me why I fell in love with gaming in the first place.

I went in expecting “one more run” and ended up living an entire story where choices actually matter. Not in a “different dialogue line” way — in a consequences that stick way. Relationships shift, allies become enemies, companions react like real people, and the world doesn’t forget what you did. The roleplay isn’t a side feature here — it’s the core of the experience.

Gameplay-wise, the combat is brilliant: tactical, creative, and endlessly replayable. It starts simple and then turns into high-IQ chess with positioning, spell synergy, items, environmental plays, and those “I can’t believe that worked” moments. Every class and party setup can become powerful, but it never feels like mindless button-pressing. When you win, you earned it.

The writing and voice acting are on another level. Companions aren’t NPCs — they’re characters you get attached to, distrust, admire, or fear… sometimes all at once. And the late-game intensity? Absolutely relentless in the best way.

If you want an RPG that rewards creativity, punishes arrogance, and makes you think about your decisions even after you log off, this is it.

I went into this game with some hesitation. I’d never played a turn-based D&D game before, and coming from games like Skyrim, I thought immersion meant real-time combat and full freedom of movement. BG3 completely changed how I see that.

I’ve spent over ten hours barely leaving the starting area—not because the game is slow, but because there’s so much happening everywhere. Every conversation feels worth having, every place feels like it has a story, and the game actually trusts you to figure things out instead of holding your hand. Curiosity constantly pays off in ways I didn’t expect.

What really surprised me is how heavy the choices feel. For the first time in an RPG, the main threat doesn’t feel like something you can just ignore while doing side quests. It’s always in the back of your mind, and it made me genuinely anxious about what I should do next. I even felt tempted to look things up, before realising that the uncertainty is part of the experience.

This isn’t a game where the world bends around you. Your actions matter, your approach matters, and things don’t always work out the way you expect. Baldur’s Gate 3 doesn’t just let you play a role—it makes you live with it.

[h1]There’s not much to say here: BG3 hits hard. [/h1]

The replayability is basically [b]infinite[/b], because everything changes based on how you play. I wanted my save to line up with how I played Baldur’s Gate 1 and 2, so my first playthrough was absolutely packed with mods—purely to accommodate personal details and role-play choices.

And this is where Larian deserves massive credit. The level of support they give to the modding community is insane. Mods help smooth out small issues, improve quality of life, and massively boost immersion. Whether you’re a long-time fan doing deep roleplay (me) or a newcomer trying to survive your first D&D dice roll, the options are there.

You can feel the care Larian has, not just for the game, but for the community around it. I absolutely recommend playing and exploring everything it has to offer—and yes, I do recommend the modded experience.

That said, since this game is deeply rooted in tabletop D&D, some mechanics can feel rough if you’re new. Vanilla is totally viable, but if you go that route, just know: it will not be easy.

I’ll probably do a no-mod run later for achievements, but honestly? Even without a single achievement, being able to live this story the way it was envisioned and expanded by the community is incredible enough to me.

I was excited to play this game, considering all the hype and praise. Unfortunatley, while very expansive, the game is limited by the very strict DnD ruleset, that ends up making the game combat dull, and too much of the game progress reliant on chance rolls of the dice (skill checks).

Combat makes up alot of the game, but due to the strict adherence to the DnD ruleset, you end up being very limited in the choice of spells available for magic casters. The most powerful spells require "concentration", which means throughout the game your spell casters will cast just one powerful spell, and then hide from enemies so as to not have their "concentration" broken.

The abundance of locks that block the progress of the game means that in every playthrough, the player is forced to include a thief character in their party. Such characters are very weak combat-wise and do not pull their weight.

One of the joys of adventure games is supposed to be the upgrade in armour and weapons as one progresses. The game provides very little scope in that regard. My characters all had the same gear from level 7 up until the level cap of 12.

The crafting mechanic is so simple and primitive, it could have been left out of the game entirely without affecting the quality of gameplay.

The maps are poorly designed. 40% of the areas of the maps displayed in each act are impossible to explore or access. In act 2 it is very easy to complete one sequence of quests earlier than the developers intended, and by doing so, the game will eliminate a major hub and quest lines from the game entirely. This is very poor design.

This will be the last time I purchase a game based on the DnD ruleset.

You are REWARDED for thinking outside the box. They've designed and voiced so many random things that very few people will ever see in their run. The sheer amount of choice you have and how much it impacts your story is just amazing. And you're not burdened with silly weight or inventory limits because they're incredibly generous with carry weight, quantity is infinite AND you can send things right to camp (infinite storage) if you can't carry it. Basically everything I've ever wanted. 

You can place items inside of containers while they're in your inventory - say, a body inside a barrel - then throw that barrel and it will break open and the body and everything else will spill out. Fill it to the brim with explosives and throw it on some fire (or throw fire on it) and BOOOOOM! Make a nuke with your entire stash if you feel like it. There's just no reason to do that and yet they did it. You can push and throw people off cliffs, into lava, etc. You can make people drop their weapons, steal them, enchant them with spells, throw them away or at someone else and so on. You can shut doors on people and put magical locks on them to divide and conquer groups of enemies. Instead of drinking them, you can throw potions AT people or at the ground and run through them to get the effect. You have SO MANY COOL OPTIONS and you'd be surprised how useful they are in a pinch.

This game has secrets within secrets and you may never find them and that's GOOD because it has insane replayability. The fact that you can freely kill off important characters that have extensive roles in this game is just mind-boggling. And you'd never know how extensive. You're tasked with killing someone but you choose to knock them out instead? They might just come back later. No hand-holding here either. You must REMEMBER that you can do these things. It's all your intuition. It truly is your choice that matters. 

Visually, the game is absolutely stunning and detailed. No aliasing whatsoever either. Beautiful, crisp and clear in 4K with FSR 4 via OptiScaler. Far clearer than when it originally released. Shadows dance on the walls when you light your torches and they will POP in HDR. Gorgeous, colorful fantasy environments you can tell they put a ton of thought into designing. The smallest items are often detailed and intricate. And you can display them at camp if you wish, placing them wherever you want (just be careful, it will all go into your stash once you change Acts!). Speaking of camp, camp often if for no other reason than to see how many camp environments they designed! That attention to detail is what separates Larian from the rest.

The voice acting is incredible, the NPC models are awesome looking and facial expressions/motion capture is fantastic. The sound design and music are both amazing and epic. Great photo mode as well with lots of options.

Gear is unique and interesting and it's actually useful to keep gear in your bag so you can buff up and swap it out for different situations or when you run out of charges to use on the item. It makes finding new items exciting and cool. 

Fast travel times are insane. 3 seconds to go from one area to another within the same Act and 10 to 15 seconds between Acts.

I've only just finished Act 1 at the time of this review, 127 hours in. You may not spend this much time in Act 1 but I've spent entire afternoons replaying a single situation just to see how many ways I could do it and how creative I could get in my attempt to break the game. I scoured every corner in this game to find everything I could. And when I'm finished, I'll probably do it all over again with different followers and a different class, making different choices.

I know people say that Act 1 is the best and most fleshed out Act but I've already gotten my money's worth. It'd be a shame if the quality dropped off a cliff but either way, given enough time and passion for a project, Larian has already proven that they are in the business of making MASTERPIECES.

As far as I'm concerned, they are the new GOAT in the RPG game and I will be there will bells on when Divinity releases.

The actual gameplay, at its core, is good. The story is entertaining, and the ability to make choices and see different reactions from characters is genuinely well done. That said, all of that good content is viciously undermined by the sheer volume of bugs.

Again and again I find what excited me about playing a D&D game had been limited or removed entirely and replaced with systems that felt better suited for a different game license.

- Often, the choices are illusory and lead to either a fight or someone's dissatisfaction with the party and/or an additional task.

For example, you meet a goblin who wants to heal you, and either there's a fight followed by a puzzle, or you use intimidation, but you still have to promise her something; otherwise, there's a fight. Another example is meeting Laezel the second time. You can fight alongside her against her people, but it's going to be tough, or you can roll three times correctly on persuasion and avoid battle, but she'll be unhappy.
- The fights are too long.  I know DnD fans won't agree, but you control four characters, the enemy has, say, seven, and it all drags on and on. Someone blocks your actions or summons something, or other reinforcements suddenly appear from the darkness, and it just goes on and on. I miss the option to automatically move companions and not waste time planning their moves, or some form of autobattle.

An example is the witch who creates illusions – you either waste moves searching for the real one or you load, unless you prepare a detection spell beforehand, but this constant optimization is boring.

Another example is two dwarves in the underdark by a ship. In the first turn, one raises corpses, another blocks your actions, and two appear out of nowhere. The fight is easy but too long; everyone has to move, etc.

Unnecessarily dragging; you feel like you've been playing for three hours, but all you've done is complete one quest and explore a bit.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is easily one of the best RPGs I’ve ever played. If you enjoy turn-based combat and anything Dungeons & Dragons–based, this game is an absolute must.

The turn-based system feels incredibly rewarding and strategic without being overwhelming. Every fight feels like a puzzle, and your choices—both in combat and dialogue—actually matter. It genuinely feels like playing a D&D campaign where the dice are always rolling behind the scenes.

The story is rich, emotional, and deeply immersive. Your decisions shape the world, your companions, and even who you become by the end of the game. Speaking of companions—each one is well-written, complex, and memorable. They don’t feel like NPCs; they feel like real party members with their own motives, flaws, and growth.

What really sets Baldur’s Gate 3 apart is the freedom. There’s no single “right” way to play. You can solve problems creatively, fail forward, embrace chaos, or play things safe—and the game adapts to you. It rewards curiosity and experimentation in a way very few games do.

I would highly recommend Baldur’s Gate 3 to anyone who:
- Loves turn-based combat
- Enjoys D&D or tabletop-style storytelling
- Wants a game where choices truly matter
- Likes deep character development and branching narratives

Baldur’s Gate 3 is easily one of the best RPGs I’ve ever played. If you enjoy turn-based combat and anything Dungeons & Dragons–based, this game is an absolute must.

The turn-based system feels incredibly rewarding and strategic without being overwhelming. Every fight feels like a puzzle, and your choices—both in combat and dialogue—actually matter. It genuinely feels like playing a D&D campaign where the dice are always rolling behind the scenes.

The story is rich, emotional, and deeply immersive. Your decisions shape the world, your companions, and even who you become by the end of the game. Speaking of companions—each one is well-written, complex, and memorable. They don’t feel like NPCs; they feel like real party members with their own motives, flaws, and growth.

What really sets Baldur’s Gate 3 apart is the freedom. There’s no single “right” way to play. You can solve problems creatively, fail forward, embrace chaos, or play things safe—and the game adapts to you. It rewards curiosity and experimentation in a way very few games do.

I would highly recommend Baldur’s Gate 3 to anyone who:
- Loves turn-based combat
- Enjoys D&D or tabletop-style storytelling
- Wants a game where choices truly matter
- Likes deep character development and branching narratives

TL;DR: Incredible combat and environments. Please stop zooming into my face and asking me to emotionally commit.

Incredible production value, great combat pacing, and beautiful environments, but the game leans too heavily on cinematic storytelling and guided interactions. Exploration feels segmented into Acts rather than discovered organically. Dice rolls lose tension due to constant rerolls, and companions feel more like a curated cast than people in a living world. I respect the ambition, but I miss the systems-first design and emergent gameplay of classic CRPGs.

Pros:
Outstanding production value (voice acting, visuals, environmental detail)
Combat pacing feels tight and satisfying
Encounter design is generally strong

It is the kind of experience that will be referenced years from now when people talk about what the genre is capable of at its best. Every system, from storytelling to combat, feels intentional rather than filler.

What truly sets BG3 apart is the sheer freedom in its dialogue and decision making. Your choices do not just tweak minor outcomes. They shape relationships, alter entire story paths, and can fundamentally change how the world reacts to you. It genuinely feels like your story, not one you are passively moving through. The characters feel alive, the conversations feel natural, and more often than not, you find yourself pausing just to think about what you would actually say or do in that moment.

For anyone wondering whether Baldur’s Gate 3 is still worth playing in 2026, the answer is an easy yes. Skipping it would mean missing out on a once in a generation work of art. This is the kind of RPG that reminds you why the genre exists in the first place. Deep role playing, meaningful consequences, and a world that respects your intelligence as a player. I would absolutely recommend it to anyone searching for a truly one of a kind RPG experience.

It is the kind of experience that will be referenced years from now when people talk about what the genre is capable of at its best. They shape relationships, alter entire story paths, and can fundamentally change how the world reacts to you. It genuinely feels like your story, not one you are passively moving through. The characters feel alive, the conversations feel natural, and more often than not, you find yourself pausing just to think about what you would actually say or do in that moment.

For anyone wondering whether Baldur’s Gate 3 is still worth playing in 2026, the answer is an easy yes. Skipping it would mean missing out on a once in a generation work of art. This is the kind of RPG that reminds you why the genre exists in the first place. Deep role playing, meaningful consequences, and a world that respects your intelligence as a player. I would absolutely recommend it to anyone searching for a truly one of a kind RPG experience.

Let's get this out of the way, like a lot of people, I thought Baldur's Gate 3 was an absolute masterpiece! Not perfect; no game is, but entertaining and engaging to the highest degree for me. It has an unbelievably great story with so many different paths and events you can experience in a single playthrough, loveable characters with intricate backstories and personal quests augmented by the excellent character animation, beautiful graphics, a moving soundtrack, and gameplay that gives you the freedom to tackle things in so many ways. A lot of this has been talked about to death over the past year, and despite being someone who initially resists the hype train, I still found myself head over heels for this game by its conclusion.

For me, this game felt a lot like playing Mass Effect 2 for the first time, but with everything cranked up to 11. The characters are just as deep if not deeper, and their personal quests lead to some harrowing decisions and twists that flesh them out even more. There is so much more freedom on where you can go and what you can do. Not to mention, roleplaying and decisions here are far more nuanced. I really enjoyed bringing over an existing D&D 5e character I've been playing for years and roleplaying as that character in this new setting. It's not nearly as open as the tabletop game of course, but it still gives you a ton of options. By the end, I was hitting multiple conclusions to sidequests and companion quests that had me in tears, and the romance I pursued for this playthrough, Gale, was immensely satisfying as it tied really well into the main narrative while also being a good romance subplot on its own merits. I also feel like I got a really good conclusion overall due to my choices, so that was immensely satisfying. The whole ending also felt like the Suicide Mission from ME2, though again, cranked up to 11 as you also get squads of AI-controlled ally units to call in based on who you helped throughout the campaign. It all coalesces into a masterful narrative experience by the end.

Where it stumbles here though is that not every Act is made equal. I'm not going to spend too much time criticizing a game I'm giving a perfect score to, but it's worth mentioning some things. Act 2, while I still immensely enjoyed it due to the strong gameplay foundation the game has, is just way too linear. It felt so condensed narratively compared to Act 1. Thankfully, Act 3 opens things back up in a huge way that made it my favorite act.

Getting into the combat, this is definitely the part of the game I had to grow to love the most. I've generally had a hard time connecting with CRPG's and their combat in the past. I liked Wasteland 2 Remastered, but struggled with the combat at times and ended up being really sick of the game overall by the end. I barely got through Divinity: Original Sin II before abandoning it as I was just bored, lost, and frustrated. What helped this time though, is I'm very familiar with the system Baldur's Gate 3 is largely based on: Dungeons & Dragons 5th edition. Now, the game does tweak some things to make it work better as a video game as well as to improve balance and enjoyability overall (5e like most systems is far from perfect as much as I've come to love it), but it still mostly aligns with that system. That familiarity helped get me through the door a lot quicker than in the other CRPG's I've played, but I stilled bounced off some of the difficulty spikes for a bit. There are fights, especially in Act 2, that I felt were overtuned, especially with the amount of crazy spells enemy mages can spam at you at times. It was very frustrating, but as I got through and beat these fights finally (not without some cheesing), I finally started to learn more about how to better strategize to win. By the end, I was blazing through very similar fights in Act 3 without too much issue, so it definitely was just an experience thing from me more than a design issue with the game. This has me more excited than ever for a second playthrough, as I feel I'll be able to handle some of these same fights even better now. 

And finally, I did unfortunately run into some technical issues. Don't get me wrong, the game overall is extremely polished and runs great, but with such a huge game, there are going to be issues that slip through the cracks. Most for me were very minor: dialogue audio wouldn't play at some points, enemies would get stuck or just not do anything during their turn in combat (honestly not going to complain too much about that one hehe), and in Act 3 especially I had some nasty issues where my controller kept de-syncing during combat. It's definitely something to note, though I will say compared to other large RPG's from recent years, these issues are far rarer and far less impactful than its peers.

Overall, Baldur's Gate 3 is easily one of my favorite games I've ever played. It may even be my new favorite. The freedom in how you can tackle almost everything (looking at you Act 2), the narrative and its emotional impact on me, and the satisfying combat (once I got gud) all combined to make this a special game. If you have any interest at all in this game and have one of the many platforms you can play it on, whether you're a D&D or CRPG veteran or someone who hasn't played or enjoyed the genre before, you owe it to yourself to give Baldur's Gate 3 a go. In my experience, it really is as special as everyone has been saying this past year.

Some games ask you to save the world.
Baldur’s Gate 3 politely hands you a tadpole, ruins your mental stability, and then says, “Good luck, champ.”

This game doesn’t just have characters. It has personalities. The kind that make you forget you’re holding a controller and not just binge-watching the greatest fantasy drama never aired on HBO. The voice acting? Absolutely criminal. It’s so good it makes other RPGs sound like they were recorded in a bathroom with a potato. Every conversation feels cinematic. Every line delivery hits.

And then there’s Lae'zel — possibly my favorite personality in the game. She’s rude. She’s intense. She treats kindness like it’s a contagious disease. And her inability to understand sarcasm is pure gold. After a fight with Shadowheart, Shadowheart asks, “Have we buried the hatchet?” and Lae’zel, with the confidence of someone who has never encountered a metaphor in her life, responds: “No. Why should it be buried? Is it broken?”

That moment alone deserves an award.

You can feel the developers poured passion and love into this game. Every quest, every tiny interaction, every weirdly specific dialogue option screams: “Yes, we thought about that too.”

Now let’s talk about the Dark Urge origin. Playing as the Dark Urge is like letting intrusive thoughts win — but narratively. It twists the entire story in ways that are both hilarious and horrifying. I laughed. I gasped. I questioned my fictional sanity. It’s like the game looks at you and says, “You wanted choices? Oh, I’ll give you choices.”

The combat system is chef’s kiss. Turn-based, yes — but so flexible and creative that you can basically weaponize the environment itself. Push enemies off cliffs. Set the ground on fire. Throw random objects because you can. It’s tactical, chaotic, and deeply satisfying. You’re not just fighting — you’re improvising.

Playing with friends? Absolute chaos in the best way. It genuinely feels like playing tabletop Dungeons & Dragons, except the dungeon master has a massive budget and motion capture. The random decisions people make mid-conversation are comedy gold. Someone’s trying to negotiate peace, someone else steals a fork, and suddenly you’re in combat with half the town. Beautiful.

The story and lore are ridiculously well made. Even if you’re new to turn-based games, this is a must-try. The world pulls you in and refuses to let go — politely at first, then violently if you pick the wrong dialogue option.

The in-game modding menu makes it effortless. You don’t like something? Fix it. Add to it. Break it responsibly. On top of that, third-party support has exploded past 16.000 mods and counting. This game isn’t just alive — it’s evolving.

Don’t like the UI? There’s a mod.
Want new subclasses? There’s twenty.
Think the game needs more hairstyles, dice skins, armor sets, or completely unbalanced spells? Done.

And then there are the mods I would absolutely never install… but respect deeply.

Like turning every character into a goblin.
Or replacing dragons with Thomas the Tank Engine.
Or adding a romanceable mind flayer with voice lines that whisper aggressively supportive affirmations.
Or the mod that makes everyone absurdly muscular for no narrative reason.
Or the one that gives Withers a disco outfit and a permanent dance animation.

Would I use them? No.
Am I glad they exist? Absolutely.

That’s the beauty of it. If something bothers you — difficulty spikes, inventory clutter, camera angles — you can just download a mod and move on. The game bends without breaking. That kind of longevity means Baldur’s Gate 3 isn’t going anywhere. It’s going to age like fine wine… or like a cursed artifact that only grows stronger over time.

The bad?

Honestly… not much. The dice can be a little annoying. Nothing humbles you faster than failing a 90% chance roll in front of your companions. But even that becomes part of the charm. You’re writing your own story — whether you accept your fate like a hero or shamelessly save scum like the rest of us.

10/10. I genuinely wish more developers cared about crafting games like this. Baldur’s Gate 3 isn’t just a great RPG — it’s a love letter to storytelling, player choice, and the beautiful chaos of rolling dice when your life depends on it.
