[h1] A game set apart. [/h1]

Where do I even begin with a game like this? It's praises have been sung from the highest of mountain peaks. Not to mention, it's already been almost 3 years since its release (at the time of writing this review). I probably have nothing to add that you haven't heard before, but I just can't shake the compulsion of an almost duty-like pull to honor this game still. In an age of money hungry corporations taking over our beloved medium, Baldur's Gate 3 stands out for delivering a top quality game at a fair price, and not asking for anything further than the price on the box (or steam page). [b] The short of it, buy this game and support this studio. [/b]

[h3] The long(ish) of it [/h3]

This game is a masterclass in many fronts. From detailed and consistent worldbuilding and lore, to loveable characters with real depth and meaning. There is almost no area in this game where you can say [i] "I wish they thought of this as an option" [/i] because chances are, they did. There is so much attention to detail, and love for gaming and gamers on display in this title. I'd argue that it's impossible to play this game and not feel that the people who made it were having a blast doing so. It's funny, sophisticated, raunchy, emotional, strategic, and so much more.

I had never played an RPG of this style of gameplay, with the more top-down(ish) view and turn based combat, and I will admit, it took a brief period of getting used to. But once I got it, I was hooked. The gameplay is engaging and presents so many ways of handling various situations, that there is always a way out of trouble if you have a bit of imagination. The various classes and multi-classing that the game has allows you to make your playstyle unique and cater to how you want to play. You can approach various encounters with different ways of weapon combat, magic, spells, stealth, wordcraft, deception, and so many more.

The story weaves many narrative threads across three acts and while some resolve in earlier acts, the late game tales are astounding. I was engrossed and always eager to explore every in of a new area to see that I could find, and how it pushed me along the quests of the game. 

Characters were always interesting and compelled me to learn what makes them who they are, and how I can help (or hinder) them from achieving their goals in this world. None of the main cast were 'one-dimensional' or 'typical archetypes' once you got to their core. How invested you become in a character can be up to you, and how you decide to approach their individual quest lines.

There is no shortage of secrets to find, loot to collect, characters to befriend (or foe), stories to unravel, skills to master, and memories to make that will last for a long time to come. Baldur's Gate 3 is a very special game, and I can wholeheartedly encourage anyone interested to take the plunge and dive head first into this wonderful world.

Honestly, I’ve played a lot of games and a lot of RPGs, but when it came to Baldur’s Gate… after a while I realized I was standing against something I had never encountered before. A challenge. A very complex challenge. And since I like challenges, I definitely didn’t back down. Let’s be honest — nowadays you don’t really have to use your brain much when playing games. Developers practically make idiot-proof experiences… but not Larian Studios.

Warning: spoilers and potential mind-blow.

The story itself is a bit more complicated, so I’ll try to explain it briefly. You are a person who has been abducted by so-called Mind Flayers, who implanted a tadpole inside you. That tadpole will eventually transform you into one of them — all in the name of the Absolute… well, in the name of a higher power. Along your journey, you meet other poor souls who also carry a tadpole inside them, and you all share the same goal… well… not exactly. Some of them have their own “personal goals” they want to achieve as well. Whether you like it or not, allies will be extremely useful at the end of the game. But to keep them from leaving you, you need to make sure they feel good around you, follow their personal questlines, and help them complete their own stories. Sometimes it’s not easy. Sometimes it’s frustrating. But trust me — it pays off. Unless you make a mistake. Your companions won’t be fighting in their underwear either. Just like you, they need proper gear — specific armor and weapons suited to them. Obviously, you wouldn’t give a wizard a sword… well… you could, but then I’d love to see those spells.

But seriously, your companions should wear armor appropriate for their class. I still haven’t found a companion who can wear Heavy Armor without locking themselves out of their spells — and that’s important. Whenever you equip a companion with a new piece of armor, check its description carefully. If there’s a small exclamation mark in the tooltip, take that armor off. Otherwise, they won’t be able to use their spells and abilities.

Every character should have a proper weapon, the right armor (or modded gear — that’s up to you), and also a crossbow or a bow. Some can use a shield as well, but that depends on how you want to build them.

Your main goal is to reach Baldur’s Gate… well… what a surprise, right? You want to remove the tadpole and live normally again. Honestly, the story is massive, but Steam doesn’t have a large enough character limit for me to explain it all, so let’s move on.

If you’ve played The Witcher or Life is Strange (that LiS mention is a joke, okay?) then you know that your decisions matter… but here, the game slaps you in the face in a way you’ve probably never experienced before. Your decisions matter a lot. Like… you make one choice, walk into a town, and suddenly you’re in combat because you insulted an NPC who has a friend, and that friend has an army, and that army kicks your ass and you have to reload your save. So yes — remember F5 for Quick Save and F8 for Quick Load. You’ll thank me later.

Seriously, be careful what you say and how you behave. It can help you — or hurt you badly and keep you stuck somewhere much longer than you’d like. I have to admit, I’ve never seen such a well-crafted decision system. At the same time, it can be frustrating when you either have to agree to something you don’t want to… or technically have a choice, but none of the options end well for you.

Your decisions also affect how your companions see you. And if you want to romance one of them, you’d better watch your words and actions. Most people probably fall in love with Shadowheart immediately — the best character I’ve ever met (sorry, Yennefer…). Also… under no circumstances let any of your companions leave. Again — you’ll thank me at the end.

This game also has combat… well, you’re not playing cards for life and death here, are you?

The combat system is… okay, I’ll say it — similar to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Yes, you can whip me now. The reason I compare it is because it’s turn-based. Each character has limited movement and actions per turn. You can move a certain distance and usually attack once per turn. And this triggers a beautiful thing called thinking. Yes, exactly. Combat isn’t about waiting until all enemies are dead — you actually have to consider every move and decide who to focus on. And you should save before every fight. Personal experience.

And honestly… I’ll say it for the last time, okay? I finished Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on New Game+, where enemies are more aggressive and faster and you really have to think or you’ll repeat the whole fight. But I’ve never experienced a combat system as difficult as this one. This is the hardest combat I’ve seen so far. Or maybe it’s just my brain pulling the “Gone fishing” card every time a fight starts and I insist on doing things my way. Still, every fight feels rewarding. Or at least most of them.

I don’t personally think games like this should release too often — it might actually fry my brain because I don’t think I have the mental capacity for RPGs this advanced. But it’s a very welcome change.

There’s also alchemy. If you played the first Witcher, it’s almost the same interface and a similar system — nothing too complicated. However, alchemy is mostly pointless. Most potions you can craft can also be bought from regular merchants for a few gold coins, which makes the whole feature feel unnecessary. Honestly, it kind of is. The only time I used it was to craft healing potions. You can also find scrolls with various spells, which is great and very useful. They can help you through tough sections or even entire fights, and I really appreciated that.

What’s truly key in this game is exploration. The game assumes you’re not stupid and that you can find clues on your own. Many quests don’t even have quest markers telling you where to go or what to do. You have to explore — and most importantly, READ BOOKS. A lot of information is hidden in texts and environmental storytelling. If you expect everything to be served on a silver platter, this probably isn’t the game for you. Personally, I had to get used to this. But after some time, it becomes natural and even meaningful.

Baldur’s Gate excels in many areas. For me, it feels like a combination of The Witcher, Clair Obscur, and Sekiro — Sekiro mainly because some enemies caused me the same kind of pain. Overall, this is a truly impressive game that every RPG fan should try. Its elegance lies in how simple it seems at first — only to surprise you with mechanics that leave you speechless. And it’s definitely not a one-time experience.

If the game really hooks you — like it did with a certain unnamed person — you’ll gladly replay it with a different approach, try new paths, or behave completely differently. Overall, I think this game had enormous potential and squeezed every last drop out of it. Nothing went to waste.

(No wonder it deserved the Game of the Year award.)

Larian Studios has created something that feels less like a video game and more like a living, breathing world that actually reacts to your presence.

Total Player Freedom
The sheer volume of choices is staggering. I’ll be honest: it’s overwhelming at times, but in the best way possible. Every time I think I’ve found the "right" way to solve a problem, I discover three other paths I could have taken. Your decisions don't just change the ending; they ripple through every conversation and combat encounter.

Characters You Actually Care About
The writing here is on another level. Every companion is:

Well-written: They have distinct voices, complex moralities, and deep backstories.

Engaging: I found myself genuinely invested in their approval and their personal growth. They aren't just stat blocks for combat; they feel like a real party.

Unmatched Depth
The fact that I’ve put 60 hours into the opening act and still feel like I’m just scratching the surface is a testament to the content density. There is no "filler" here—just secrets, stories, and surprises tucked into every corner of the map.

Hear ye', hear ye', Baldur's Gate 3 review for thee, from RPG enjoyer of me.

When I said I want to play RPG games, it's not just about having varied builds, class, or a lot of perks tree skills, but what I want is a roleplaying immersion from gameplay and dialogue. Definitely the latter, I've played Kingdom Come and Witcher for that solely reason, to have my own approach dialogue, given as many options I can do to resolve a conflict, respecting me either it's a "bad" decisions or "good". I love that this game fulfilled the desire of playing a good RPG game.

To have so many dialogue options that unlocks different path from the first solution is just so fun! Many games will just give you "yes" or "no", but this game give you "5 W + 1 H" and "yes" or "no"  options. Because many conflicts need to be dug down more and I need to observe more, I can't be too judgy at the start. And in gameplay manner, there are many approach like books or items and different NPCs POV (even pets!) you can interact with that will be added to dialogue perspective, reveal more options and having the best solution. And I love that sooooo much. The choices can be harsh and filled with dilemma, but let's be real, the game is generous enough for me to save before progressing with the dialogue, leaving with safer outcome where, If I messed up or don't like the solution, I gotta go back. Many quests are like that, where I believe, having silver tongue is better than solving things in combat. Well, because the combat is so hard to understand.

Don't get me wrong, I really am not familiar with the combat mechanic. When the game says turn-based-combat, my brain will think something like final fantasy 7 or recent game like Expedition 33, where combat and exploration are in different section. Well, jokes on me, the combat is in real-time, WHAT?! I didn't know that. I'm just saying that early gameplay curve was really was high where the game overwhelmes me, both gameplay and mechanic. I don't know how to play, I don't know what to press, which skills I have to press, what is concentration, uhh spell slots, 1, 2, 3? More worse, I don't even know what my character role. Even I was in despair time and googling on internet like, "how to beat these, it's too hard". One of the solution that open my eyes is, "use the environment". After that, I forgot that this game give me so many freedoms to approach everything in combat such as high ground, stealth, surprised, and one of my favorite thing to do, push them out to cliff (best solution). I realized that after mid-game, this freedom is really fun. Unlike other game that force you to fight your way through, I don't like that, I want to stealth, and the game respect me to it. One time the boss fight swarmed with many enemies and traps before the main room and I just went stealth bypassing everything maximazing the gameplay mechanic like flying, teleporting, stealth, and even I became a gas once to positioning, my God this game is really fun!

Better yet, this combat gameplay are actually contemplating with dialogue approach where, at first I didn't know, but I can spare them somehow, having more dialogue and better solution for them, WHAT! There are many conflicts where, I don't want to fight them but it can't be avoided, somehow I just spared them and can let them go. "This is the best game ever!" took the word out of my mouth. To be fair, it's not every encounter does this, even there's many bosses where it feels anticlimatic because they can't be spared even though, yes, I know they're just pure evil, but having more dialogue or finisher would be much more fun.

This game is beautiful, beautiful places, beautiful city, beautiful design, but let's be real, 80% of the time I'm just looking at the ground and that's what I kind of hate in this game. I swear everytime I navigate the characters I want to cry because it's so difficult to navigate, and I have to navigate 4 people. Especially in the cities. It's really hard to navigate to each floor and sometimes I missclicked and starting the dialogue with my teammates like, "Okay Gale, move out of the way". And yes, you can make it horizontal angle, like a third person angle, but now it's harder to click. The dissapoinment is that when I tried to adjust it on options or googled it, they want me to instal mods and I really don't like that solution. So having more optimization on settings would be really great. I can't even do the third person angle in exploration because things like "ambushed" or "traps" are everywhere. That's why the dialogue are more fun to watch because they're in horizontal angle where I can see the skies or see the background, but not the floor.

I do love the characters in the game. I played as Wyll because he's giving a main character energy and I didn't customize my character, because and because, I thought he will talk in dialogue. These dialogues are so awkward because my character doesn't say the word I chose, making it more bland. Even worse on romance options, Shadowheart the love of my life, my character just smiling awkwardly not saying the love words and it feels one-way.  I do believe having more playable teammates are not a good approach especially in "companion quest". I love Jaheira, Astorion, Minsc, and Halsin quest, but they're not even in my main team. The worst part is I used them for that specific quest but not having gear on because I'm not even aware of their gameplay. I bet the quests are bland if they're not in the team, I was even in awe in Astorion performance and I don't even like his gameplay. It would be great if these characters are scattered in the whole map and meeting them as I explore the place or better yet, fighting alongside as NPC in the big fight, but they're just ended up in the camp talking like, "Yes we defeat them together", no you don't...

I had so much fun in my playthrough because the class and teammates roles are diverse enough where I made my teammates like Lae'zel, Shadowheart, and Gale being the most broken character ever wearing the most drippy gears meanwhile my Wyll are focusing on charisma, learning music (I go with the flute), and having all the essential skills. That is like peak roleplaying immersion gameplay wise. It does get a bit dissapointing where I maxed level so early in the late game and can't be overleveled, but I just have to go through the harder difficulty I guess.

Honestly, the game is really fun in terms of roleplaying, immersive world, fun and quality-over-quantity side-quest, loveable and memorable characters, varied builds, freedom of gameplay, but things like frustating navigation, okay main-story conclusion, looking at the ground gameplay, "solve things by downloading this mods", held me back to loving it more. 8,5/10

You already know this is a great game. I just want to nuance it a bit by highlighting a couple of things which annoyed me:
One is the "all doors should be open" approach to game design. You can romance pretty much every adult humanoid you spend time with (non-exclusive), and you can completely respec your character mid-adventure for a nominal fee. I get that some will see these as positives, but to me, it just cheapens it a bit, and dimishes the immersion.

Another issue is that there is a bit of fatigue towards the end. I found the earlier quests and stories more compelling than what's in the last third, where the game keeps throwing even more side quests at you, at the same time as the main story heads towards the standard "save the world" kind of end. Perhaps it's just that I've seen this so many times, the stakes always have to be raised to cataclysmic levels. Perhaps it's in part because this is a very large game, and they feel the stakes have to keep increasing throughout. Still, fact remains that I care more about what I did in the first two acts than the last.

Despite these complaints though, I absolutely recommend BG3. It's a fantastic game in most ways. It's deep and detailed, vast in content and possibilities, impressive in presentation.

Larian Studios has once again proven their mastery, taking it to new heights with Baldur’s Gate 3. The game delivers an excellent story, carefully structured across three acts, with Act 3 standing out as the clear highlight.

For explorers, this is a content-rich adventure—a true fun fest that can easily last 150+ hours if played comprehensively. The world is brimming with secrets, quests, and branching paths that reward curiosity at every turn.

Boss encounters are particularly impressive. Many are optional yet fully fleshed out, with proper leveling and unique story elements that add layers of depth to the narrative. This design choice makes every confrontation feel meaningful rather than filler.

Companions are another strength. Larian has crafted optional companions with strong story integration, ensuring that each one feels like a natural part of the journey rather than an afterthought. Their arcs intertwine beautifully with the main plot, enhancing immersion.

One of the most striking improvements over Divinity: Original Sin 2 is the use of cutscenes. They are a genuine game-changer, elevating the storytelling.

Overall, Baldur’s Gate 3 is a monumental achievement in role-playing games. With its rich narrative, expansive content, and groundbreaking presentation, it earns nothing less than a 10/10.

For me, Baldur’s Gate 3 has become a personal outlet – a space for emotional release, creativity, and escape. It’s an elaborate world with a life of its own that invites you in, lets you shape your own story, and makes you feel like part of something both warm and terrifying at the same time. There are no right or wrong choices, you do what you think is right, how you want to direct the story, adapting to the random, sometimes unfavorable, dice values.

What makes Baldur’s Gate 3 so powerful and so personal is the sheer freedom it gives you. Built on the Dungeons & Dragons Fifth Edition system, the game offers a level of creativity in both combat and exploration that few RPGs even attempt. It’s not just about stats and turns – it’s about improvisation. Lose your weapon? Improvise with a nearby object or even toss a party member! Can’t reach that annoying archer? Drench them in magical darkness and force them out. Angered a genie? No problem – turn yourself into a delicious wheel of cheese and hope no one takes a bite. This kind of playful chaos makes the world feel truly alive and makes every decision, however absurd or heartfelt, yours.

I also want to highlight the amazing community and the genuine support from the developers. The game inspired an incredible amount of creativity from videos and fan art to cosplays and memes. The six years of titanic effort poured into making this game paid off not just financially, but in the deep love people feel for Larian Studios. Throughout development, they actively listened to player feedback, adjusted mechanics, fixed bugs, and reworked entire systems based on what the community needed. Even after release, they didn’t stop adding features like multiplayer and official mod support, which lets players enhance the game with everything from subtle cosmetic tweaks to brand-new locations you can explore with your companions or real-life friends. They’ve also continued to release major patches, expand origin character content, improve endings, and polish narrative details based on fan input. Their dedication didn’t end on launch day; they treated the game as a living world, and the players as part of its ongoing evolution.

When it comes to mechanics, Baldur’s Gate 3 excels in every aspect, from combat to dialogue and puzzles. Built on the foundation of D&D Fifth Edition, the game implements the famous d20 dice rolls, bringing that classic sense of uncertainty and excitement to every action – whether it’s attacking in combat, convincing someone in a tense conversation, or searching for hidden chests. The puzzles in the game are another highlight, often requiring you to think creatively or use your surroundings to your advantage. It’s not all about brute force. Sometimes it’s about using your wits, whether you're figuring out ancient riddles in Shar’s Temple, cracking open secret doors in an old vampire castle, or navigating moral dilemmas in Druid Grove. This balance of tactics, cleverness, and roleplay makes the world feel immersive and dynamic.

You'll want to play Baldur's Gate 3 over and over again, as each new playthrough reveals unexpected aspects of the story and characters. Thanks to a huge number of options for how events unfold, a choice of classes, races, and decisions, as well as different endings. Each time, the story unfolds in a new way, and your actions affect the world and the fate of your companions. Even after hundreds of hours, you will still find new quests, dialogues, and unexpected consequences of your actions, making replay not only possible, but exciting.

Baldur's Gate 3 lore and locations are breathtaking in their scope and depth, as the game is set in the legendary Forgotten Realms, one of the most elaborate worlds in D&D. The story leads the player through the most diverse corners of the Sword Coast: from the Emerald grove of druids and the magical darkness of Moonrise Towers to the gloomy dungeons of the Underworld and the majestic city of Baldur's Gate, one of the largest and most influential cities of Faerûn. Apex Legends used to be an incredible game—especially around 2020 and the years that followed. The movement, the gunplay, the characters, the pacing… it all came together in a way that made it one of the most exciting battle royales out there. It was even the game that kicked off my streaming journey, so I’ll always have a soft spot for it.

But somewhere along the way, the magic faded. Instead of focusing on long‑standing bugs or quality‑of‑life fixes, the developers kept pumping out new content, reworking characters that didn’t need to be touched, and releasing new legends that felt overpowered right out of the gate. The balance issues piled up, and the game slowly shifted from fun and competitive to sweaty and exhausting.

These days, the lobbies feel dominated by players who treat every match like a tournament, and that casual, chaotic fun the game used to have just isn’t there anymore. The core of what made Apex special is buried under layers of imbalance and design choices that never quite landed.

I’ll always appreciate what the game meant to me, but it doesn’t feel the same—and at this point, it probably never will.

Preface: I do recommend this game - Only for short lengths of time. Maybe an hour or two TOPS. Any more than that and you run the risk of rage quitting and uninstalling due to one or more of the issues I list below. You have been warned.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

This game has now been around for over 2 years. PLENTY of time for the developers to establish a trusting relationship with their players/users. Typically, that is what a decent developer does: A swath of players will complain about a certain aspect of the game and the developers will actually listen and at least make attempts at fixing the problems.

NOT. IN. THIS. CASE. EVER.

I understand that a portion of what a game developing company does is supposed to generate revenue for the company - And they do! A separate, and equally important, aspect is that the company is also supposed to improve the game by listening to their users and addressing issues in a timely manner - hopefully, before their users get angry enough to drop the game altogether.

This is precisely where EA/Respawn have failed. And I will break it down for you, precisely HOW they have failed.

1. Cheaters:
This game has an inordinate amount of cheaters. There really is no easy way to say it. And it is OBVIOUS and BLATANT. EA relies upon the absolutely defunct Easy Anti-Cheat system. Please, hold your laughter... In their defense, however, they have made sure to spread rumors of a revamped anti-cheat system, designed specifically for Apex. The real issue is how LONG they have been spreading this rumor. I can only assume that it was a PR stunt to quiet those complaints of cheaters. How can I make that assumption? Mainly because they seem to focus on things of little or no consequence - Like adding badges to shield batteries and medkits... I mean, what?! Why would you focus on cosmetics when you have a huge cheater problem?!

2. Match-Making (MM):
Very rarely have I seen an MM quite as laughable as the one being used in Apex. I understand that there it a lot of complexity involved, what with ranked splits resetting every month (for the most part) and making everyone, essentially, noobs. But, there is a SUPER easy way to fix it (which I will detail later). I understand why they do the ranked split as well: they want to force players to play more often to keep their ranking high - DUH! The more players there are, the more likely it is that they make money and that those players will spread the word so that even more players will play and give them even more opportunity to make more money. But an MM based solely on your current in-game rank is absolutely asinine. And that is just ranked. What if you don't play ranked? Good luck! You could be paired against ANYONE, professional players and noobs alike.

3. Maps:
Currently, there are a total of five maps in Apex (for BR). Every season they have two maps in rotation for pub games. TWO. And those two maps rotate every hour or so. For ranked matches, they use ONE. Over and over, on and on... Maps should be randomized except in tournaments. Going into a game, you should not know where you are going to land, what characters you should be playing, etc. It should be a friggin' BATTLE ROYALE! Formulate your plan based on who is on your team and what the map is, ad-hoc, just like everyone else. No one should know what map your're landing on until the drop ship starts its flight across it. Add some aspect mystery to the game.

4. Weapons:
There is a good selection of weapons in the game, but the real issue is with practicality. Take, for instance, the so-called top sniper rifle in the game - the Kraber. It's supposed to be a .50-cal sniper rifle. It LOOKS great, but that's where the good news ends. If you hop into the firing range and test out all of the sniper rifles available to you, you will catch the glaring issues. The Sentinel, the Longbow, and the Charge Rifle all use sniper rounds (NOT a .50; Something smaller like a .308). All three can reach WAY out and touch your enemy. The Charge Rifle can literally reach all the way across an area of the map - over 800m. The Sentinel and Longbow can shoot pretty accurately to 400+m (depends on optics in use, graphics, screen size, FOV, etc). With the Kraber, the bullet starts dropping wildly at just 200m. Yeah...the highest-powered weapon in the game, using the highest-caliber bullet can BARELY eke out a 400m hit with accuracy. Let's add to this the 30-30 Repeater and the G7 Scout - A heavy ammo, medium range pew-pew and light ammo medium range pew-pew, respectively. Both of these rifles can out-shoot the Kraber with accuracy. WHY? And the Charge Rifle - Why does this not use energy ammo? I mean...CHARGE Rifle...it shoots a beam of light!...sigh...

5. Legends:
Don't get me wrong, there is a use for every single legend in the game. Whether it be for hiding, sniping, guarding, tracking...it's useful stuff. It is also getting really out of hand. First, how many freaking legends does a game like this need? At some point in the near future, you could probably have a pub match where every single player in the game is a different legend. I'm not even joking though I wish I were. Second, when EA unveils a new legend, they typically add it to the game and then they forget its existence. No re-balancing of legends, no fixing bugs, etc. And if they DO fix something with a legend, it is usually a heavy-handed nerf beyond what anyone that actually PLAYS the game was expecting. The abilities of the legends are pretty unique, but the overall effect of those abilities is copied across other legends. The exception to this is both Loba and Lifeline. Loba has her black market (so you don't have to hunt around an area if you know what you are looking for) and Lifeline has her health drone - The only legend that can heal your flesh-wounds. Other than those two, you can pretty much classify all other legends into categories like defense, offense, or recon and their abilities, while varied, have ultimately the same effect on the game. Offense legends can quickly get up in your face and kill you, defense legends can slow your entry into an area while sapping your health, and recon legends can track you and your team down. Simple. And boring too. Meh.

On to my ideas on how we can fix BOTH the cheater AND MM issues in Apex:

1. New DB table - Player AVG DMG (>10) Last 10 Games (PAD).

2. New DB table - Player AVG DMG Rating (PADR); 11-300: Rating 0; 301-700: Rating 1; 701-1200: Rating 2; 1201-2000: Rating 3; 2001-3200: Rating 4; 3201-4200: Rating 5 (AND account marked for review); 4200+: Rating 6 (Insta-banned - If the pros can't do it, pubs can't either without cheating).

*NOTE - Keep in mind that these are averaged over the last TEN games where damage done was greater than 10.

3. Players can only be matched with other players of the same PADR -/+1.

4. Teams have an AVG DMG Rating (TADR) of ((PADR1+PADR2+PADR3)/3)-1 (always rounded UP) for BR Trios. 1 player with R2, 2 players with R3 would be ((R2+R3+R3)/3)-1=R2. Teams can only be matched with other teams of the same TADR.

THREE birds, one stone. Fix MM, catch a boatload of cheaters, AND the games are more fun because you are playing with players very close to your own skill level instead of non-stop sweats OR non-stop noobs.

*I'm not saying it is not possible to play a 4K+ DMG game. I AM saying it IS impossible to play 10 *consecutive* 4K+ DMG games without cheating. Again, if the pros can't do it, neither can the pubs without programmatic assistance (cheating).

Bugs, more bugs, in the lobby bugs, in-game bugs, garbage servers, more and more cheaters (aimbots...wallhacks...you name it), questionable design/game mechanics...the usual BR scene after X amount of time. Apex could be great - there are aspects to it that are fantastic such as the movement, the variety of legends and weapons to choose from, even the colour palette and map design (for the most part)...but the bugs, the poor servers and the cheaters are going to be its eventual downfall if Respawn doesn't get its act together soon, especially with new FPS games on the horizon. Personally, I could never get over the bizarre choice to have punches deal absurd damage (at least early game with white/blue armour) while 10-20 rounds of light/heavy ammo more or less hits for the same amount. It's a weird, one-step-too-far case of 'jumping the shark' or 'nuking the fridge' that's been in the game since day 1.

The fundamental mechanics of the game is also clearly conducive to 3rd party opportunism from the get-go and, once past the mid-game stage, serves up Gold/Red shield bullet-sponge fiestas ad nauseam. More often than not I have more fun in the early stages of a game when white/blue and maybe the odd purple armour is mostly all you see. I'm inclined to think that the game would be less tedious if Respawn had stopped at Purple or Gold armour (the latter being very rare). 

Ultimately though, for all of its good qualities, Apex just isn't hitting the mark for me anymore. The bugs, the bad servers and the bypassed Easy anti-cheat just makes for a BR that could be great, but often serves up a disappointing experience that is more of a miss than a hit. As always though, your mileage may vary.

[h3] An okay Sci-fi adventure [/h3] 
[b] Overall Vote: 6.5/10 [/b] 

[b] Brief Review [/b] 
Andromeda is a memorable, but sadly not amazing space RPG experience capable of scratching that Sci-fi adventure itch. 
Whilst having the best combat system and character progression of the series, it unfortunately falls behind in the story, characters, writing and quest design that are unable to engage as much as its predecessor.

[b] In more details [/b]
The story is not incredibly captivating, but it keeps you going and delivers a somewhat satisfying ending.
Characters often fall flat and are not extremely memorable (or can be straight up annoying) with a few rare exceptions that save the day.
The writing was at time frustrating and cliche, and at others was able to steal a smile or a chuckle.

What makes Andromeda stand out is its very dynamic and creative combat system that improves on its predecessors without losing its main identity and still feeling very "Mass Effect".
The direction is different, focusing on a more action approach and abandoning some of the more strategical roots of previous games (such as being able to control often your allies' skills), but I felt it served the experience well and created its own identity.
The on-foot movement can be sometimes clunky both during exploration and combat, but when mastered it feels good as dashing, jumping, weaving skills and shooting becomes an organic second nature.

Environments look interesting and are aesthetically pleasing, whilst characters tend to have this uncanny valley effect that makes them feel weird for the first few hours of the experience.

[b] Final Thoughts [/b] 
If you want to experience a space Sci-fi adventure similar to the Mass Effect trilogy because you haven't had enough of it, Andromeda is a worth game to pick up.

Mass Effect: Andromeda is the gaming equivalent of being the younger sibling of a straight-A student. You’re trying your best, but everyone keeps asking why you aren't more like Commander Shepard. You play as Ryder, a "Pathfinder" whose job is to find a new home for humanity because Earth got a bit too crowded and "Reaper-y." You wake up after a 600-year nap only to find that the new neighborhood is full of grumpy aliens, ancient killer robots, and a giant space-cloud that eats ships for breakfast.

The combat is actually the overachieving part of the family. It’s fast, frantic, and lets you hop around with a jetpack like a caffeinated kangaroo. You can swap "Profiles" on the fly, meaning one minute you’re a biotic god throwing people into orbit with your mind, and the next you’re a tech-wizard summoning a turret to do your chores for you. I found the Nomad—your planetary rover—to be a massive upgrade over the original trilogy’s Mako, mostly because it can actually drive up a hill without having a physical breakdown. It’s the closest you’ll get to an interstellar off-road rally, just with more blue aliens shooting at you.

Now, let's address the elephant in the room: the faces. At launch, the characters looked like they’d been hit with a shovel and then asked to act out a Shakespearean tragedy. It’s been patched since then, so people actually have human-adjacent expressions now, but the dialogue still ranges from "genuinely touching" to "written by a robot trying to understand sarcasm." The story feels a bit like a "Greatest Hits" album of the original games, but the sense of exploration is real. You’re literally landing on golden worlds and trying to figure out why the local flora wants to dissolve your boots.

7/10. It’s a solid sci-fi adventure that suffered from being the follow-up to one of the greatest trilogies ever made. It’s like going to a tribute band—they’re hitting all the notes, but you can tell they aren't the real thing. Still, if you like jetpacks, romanceable aliens, and scanning every rock in the galaxy, it’s a fun ride.

Brother, let me lay it out for you like we’re talking on the sidewalk after a long day. Mass Effect: Andromeda is that friend who shows up to the party wearing a sharp suit, big smile, full of confidence — but everyone keeps whispering about the legend who used to run the place.

When I started to play the Mass Effect franchise, everyone I knew and played it told me to avoid ME: Andromeda like the plague. Other reviews too. That it was a disgrace to the franchise and should be completely ignored. So naturally, my desire to play it has multiplied exponentially.

There are indeed, problems, but let's start with what I liked:

It starts off differently, in a huge spaceship full of people in cryogenics. After 600 years of travel, we do not know what happened in the Milky Way, but the Salarians, Turians, Krogans, and Asari prove that it is, in fact, Mass Effect. Habitat 7 starts off strong with beautiful landscapes, strange plants, floating rocks, lightning, strange formations, a different race attacking, and the story starts for real. The story is fine, it's entertaining, but it is not really exceptional, which is obviously a huge blow, considering the name in the title, but it keeps you engaged for its long duration. While the story's stake is high, it feels way too light. You don't really feel the urges or the despair, it lacks grit. The choices are there but are not nearly as impactful as other MEs. It's overall a lighter tone, with a few dark parts. I don't want to get into details, but your objective is to make hostile planets hospitable.

Characters start off really weak and annoying, but the cast gets way better as you progress. The Tempest crew is interesting, some of them deep, and some could even say are even on the same level as the Normandy crew characters. Naturally you will have affinity with a few and dislike a few and not care for others. It's BioWare, their characters and most of the writing still kick ass here. My favorites are Drack and Jaal, but Vetra and Peebee were also nice. Suvi and Kallo are obscenely cute, and Lexi is a massive upgrade over Dr. Chakwas, a medic that actually interacts with the crew? Hell yea.

Ryder, on the other hand, I liked mine, but that's cause I played with a more Paragon character. The "Renegade" options are not nearly as mean as Shepard's, and it heavily impacts the replayability (that I honestly don't care about), it seems Ryder is good by nature with a few sarcastic traits, but that's it. 

The dialogues on the Nomad are also so much fun to listen to, sometimes funny, sometimes philosophical, sometimes even mean, very good stuff and one of the highest qualities of the game. Ah yes, the Nomad. Mako on roids, it's much more fun to explore the planets here, there are actually good things to do and places to be.

Graphically, it is a genuinely beautiful game. I counted: 52 screenshots over my 74 hours of gameplay. That's more than all the other games I've played so far. Planets are very varied and fun to explore, the game's illumination system is great and feels super nice to look at, textures are good stuff and animation-wise, it's well made (not touching facial animations yet).

For gameplay, this is probably the most developed gameplay I've played from a BioWare game, and that's by a long shot. It's super responsive, fast, weapon variety is tremendous, including biotics, techs, and even synergies. Headshots are "gory," and the enemies ragdoll in the funniest imaginable ways with a dozen different enemies, from different races, and even fauna. Calling it varied is an understatement, you will spend hours and not find similar enemies.

It also has a multiplayer component, but I didn't even touch it. Sending teams to complete missions and reap some rewards was fun, tho :>

Baaad:

Seeing all this I just wrote, I realized that the failing point for Andromeda was exactly this. "Too much", too many quests, too many characters, too many planets, too many everything. They tried too hard, and in the end, ME:A could've been an enticing 40-hour RPG instead of an exhausting 75-hour one. I know back there, people were all about the "bang for your buck" craze, but I would rather have a compelling experience short than a tiresome long one.

The result is this:

You go to complete a fetch quest in a remote place, and this place has 6 other fetch quests, and it's this interminable loop of going to Tempest, facing a loading screen, selecting a planet, loading screen, fast traveling to the location, loading screen, completing the mission in 15 seconds, and nothing but complete emptiness just to go back to Tempest and loading screens again. Rinse and repeat. And no, we are not talking about Starfield.  It does not respect your time. Why can't I just fast travel directly to the planet I want from the map screen? Come on.

This is the Assassin's Creed Odyssey of BioWare. This negatively impacts the story's pacing, it could have been great and concise, but sorry, now you have to scan 15 different rocks just to scan 20 different animals later on 8 different planets for some whatever scientist and get some XP and credits you don't even need. Fuck off.

MAKE INTERESTING QUESTS, OR NOTHING AT ALL. We never had this amount of filler in Mass Effect, and this is incredibly detrimental to the experience. First off, it is very gorgeous and it really nails its key aspect: exploration. You get a couple of planets that you need to "fix up" as your role as Pathfinder, and each of them are wonderfully crafted and beautiful to see. The open world, while sometimes sparse, feels adequate, as these are uncharted worlds mostly, with fledgling colonies. The combat has been greatly improved over the original (which to be fair was a bit stiff at times), and I would go as far as say that it is one of the greatest strengths of the game. 

The crew of the Tempest are also nice (honorary mentions to Drack and Jaal) and while they do not have the color or spark of the original trilogy crew, they are fun in their own right.  I also quite liked to see the OT races interacting with new environments and exploring. 

The bad? Many missions and interactions feel very bare bones, and most side quests are endless fetch quests from system to system (which can get tedious since there is an unskippable cutscene when entering or exiting any planet). The main antagonists (the Kett) are also bland and boring for the most part, and I quickly grew tired of the lack of variety when fighting them. A massive downgrade from the fearsome Reapers from the OT.

Overall however, the game is a lot of fun. I imagine it would be even better if you played it standalone and didnt have the original trilogy to compare it to. A solid 7/10 I would say.

[h2] All a Matter of Expectations [/h2] 

Mass Effect Andromeda depends heavily on what you expect from it. If you go in looking for a true continuation of the legendary Shepard trilogy, you will inevitably be disappointed. That series was a once-in-a-generation epic—and Andromeda neither can nor tries to replicate it.

However, if you approach the game the way we approached Mass Effect 1 back in the day—expecting a new sci-fi title with Bioware’s signature strengths—you’ll find that Andromeda is far from a bad game. In fact, it offers a strong blend of familiar elements and new ideas, set in a distant galaxy full of danger, mystery, and possibility.

[h2] Bioware at Its Core [/h2] 

It is unmistakably a Bioware game. That means:
- emotional interactions,
- lively crew dynamics,
- characters who grow on you.

And here, Andromeda achieves something impressive: the cast has only a single game to forge those bonds—not three. Yet it works. The Codex entry [i] A Crew Like No Other [/i] even documents the evolving relationships among the team. The ongoing setup and eventual payoff of the [i] Movie Night [/i] event is another charming example of solid team storytelling.

[h2] Narrative Weaknesses [/h2] 

Unfortunately, the choices you make throughout the game have very little impact on the actual story path. The narrative is essentially set, which stands in stark contrast to how impactful decisions felt in the original trilogy.

Many side missions also could have been more tightly connected to the main story. As they stand, several feel more like chores than meaningful content—busywork the game doesn’t really need.

[h2] Conclusion [/h2] 

In a direct comparison with the trilogy, Andromeda doesn’t hold up. As a “Part 4”, it simply isn’t an epic.
But as a standalone sci-fi action RPG by Bioware, it’s a solid game—one with strong character moments, an intriguing new galaxy, and the emotional touches fans have come to expect.

[h1]Mass Effect Andromeda Review[/h1]

[hr]
[h1]Overview[/h1]
Pretty solid. I picked it up because I love Mass Effect 1, 2, and 3 and wanted more of that universe. Andromeda kind of gives you that feeling in the gameplay side, but it falls short in story and a few other areas. If you want more shooting, powers, planets, and exploration in the same universe vibe, this delivers. If you want OG trilogy level story and choices, temper expectations.

[hr]
[h1]What It Is[/h1]
New galaxy, new crew, new lead. You play as Pathfinder Ryder, exploring the Andromeda galaxy to find new homes for the Initiative. Think Mass Effect combat and planetary exploration with bigger spaces to roam, a beefed up movement kit, and a loadout system that lets you mix biotics, tech, and combat the way you like.

[hr]
[h1]Story Overview[/h1]
Spoiler light. The Andromeda Initiative arrives in a new galaxy and things immediately go sideways. As Ryder you inherit the Pathfinder role, scout worlds, deal with a hostile new species, and try to bring scattered arcs and colonies together. It is an adventure about exploration and settling rather than saving an old war. The pace is uneven and it never hits the emotional highs of Shepard, but it keeps you moving across the cluster.

[hr]
[h1]Combat and Abilities[/h1]
Feels like Mass Effect, just faster. Shooting is clean, the ability variety is there, and you can run wild with biotics, tech, or guns. The jump jet and quick dash make fights more mobile than the OG trilogy. Profiles replace fixed classes, so you can swap playstyles on the fly. Weapons support mods and augmentations so you can tune them how you like. On the gameplay side, I had fun.

[hr]
[h1]Exploration and Planets[/h1]
Planets scratch that Mass Effect itch. Open zones with points of interest, side quests, vaults, and hazards. Driving the Nomad and scanning stuff feels familiar if you liked roaming in the older games. Visuals are stunning and the art across biomes is on point. It is the same loop as before and it works.

[hr]
[h1]Choices and RPG Systems[/h1]
Choices matter less than in ME2 or ME3. Dialogue tones exist, loyalty missions return, and there are consequences here and there, but do not expect trilogy scale branching. Crafting, research, and development let you build gear, apply mods, and drop augments, which helps the build variety even if the narrative agency is lighter.

[hr]
[h1]Ryder, Crew, and Relationships[/h1]
Ryder clicked for me. Not as iconic as Shepard, but a decent lead. Companions rotate with you and romances are here if you want them. Writing is okay, a bit uneven, but the squad banter helps. It felt like more Mass Effect, just not the highest quality Mass Effect.

[hr]
[h1]Movement and Vehicles[/h1]
Jump jet plus dash is a clear upgrade over the older games. The Nomad handles better than the Mako and makes crossing big spaces less of a chore. Platforming bits are fine once you get the timing down.

[hr]
[h1]Performance and Visuals[/h1]
Visually, the game looks amazing. Environments and lighting carry a lot. Animations and faces were rough at launch, but later patches improved them. On modern hardware it runs fine, with the usual open zone hiccups.

[hr]
[h1]Multiplayer (Optional)[/h1]
Co op horde mode exists if you want more combat and loot grinding. It ties loosely into single player rewards but is fully optional.

[hr]
[h1]What Works[/h1]
[list]
[*] Gameplay loop feels like classic Mass Effect
[*] Abilities, mods, and augments give real build variety
[*] Planets look great and are fun to roam with the Nomad
[*] Jump jet and dash make combat and traversal feel good
[*] Ryder and crew are serviceable with some nice banter
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]What Falls Short[/h1]
[list]
[*] Story and choice weight do not match the OG trilogy
[*] Pacing drags toward the end
[*] Side content can feel checklist heavy
[*] Writing quality is uneven across quests
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Recommended if you want more Mass Effect gameplay and exploration and can accept a weaker story. Not recommended if you are chasing the emotional hits and branching choices of 1, 2, and 3. For me it was pretty solid, gave me that universe feeling, and the combat and mobility were genuinely nice.

I've been thinking a long time about playing this game. I'm a big Mass Effect fan. I've played the whole trilogy, read all the books, and even been part of some non-official forums. I was afraid to play Andromeda because I thought it wouldn't be the same experience and wouldn't be up to par with the OG trilogy. You know what? This is a kind of amazing game.

 I need to clarify one thing before I go into details about my journey. I was playing this game and not expecting it to be like the OG trilogy. It really helped me, because the story itself is nice. Mass Effect, for me, was always about epic fights, heroic actions, and lines like "We have to save the world!" Mass Effect: Andromeda has this. I had the same feelings when I started my journey in Andromeda as when I started Mass Effect 1 - joy and the desire to explore. I wanted to check out this world and get to know these amazing characters. I really liked that Andromeda was focused on exploring; I felt like a Pathfinder looking for resources and a place to stay and checking if the planet is in good condition to settle.

 I must say that movement in this game is great. Ryder with his jump-jet made exploring smooth. I saw some people complaining about Nomad. I don't know why, because Nomad was really responsive, and I never really had a problem with driving this vehicle, but to be fair, I also liked Mako in ME1, so maybe you should take my opinion with a grain of salt. I love exploring these planets, and I think that the number of planets was satisfying. I was happy when I scanned new flora and fauna (even though some planets have the same stuff in this category, and I think it was a bit disappointing in that regard). The only issue I had with doing my tasks on certain planets was side missions. Side missions are the thing that I have mixed feelings about, because some of them were well written and some of them were either bland or boring (collect x amount of stuff, scan x amount of stuff, get x amount of parts, etc.). I will be honest - I didn't really finish every side mission type "do x amount of stuff" because I didn't really feel like it does anything, and to be fair, I think it's a bit of an unnecessary grind, and I don't like wasting time on those kinds of objectives. 

 Let us talk about combat and companions. Combat is fun, and I like that you aren't really restricted to a class and you can change your powers and mix them. I have lots of fun resetting my character's points and trying other builds. I also love that you can make combos yourself or with your allies. I had a wonderful time meeting and getting to know more about my companions. I won't try to compare them to the OG's Trilogy companions, because I think that the Andromeda Team can stand on its own legs, and I'm not a fan of shortening a whole character's story to "Female Garrus" or "Wrex wannabe." Loyalty missions were cool, but there were some hits and misses. Some of them had repeating themes and objectives, but the interactions with your comrades after their missions were heartwarming and made me feel that it was worth it.

 Story. I will probably say something controversial for some ME fans... I liked the story. Now listen, I know, I know, it's not up to par with Normandy's Crew Story, but in my opinion, Andromeda has some good foundations for continuation. The main villain was quite interesting, and I believed in his motives. The Tempest Crew was likable, and I never doubted that they believed in the Initiative mission. The only thing I feel that this game had a bit of a hiccup with was pacing. It was kind of weird, because at the beginning the pacing was fine, and it was slowly creating the foundations of our character's idea and goal, but when we got to the point where we had a clear objective of what to do, suddenly the game rushed the story, and I think that it went a bit too fast. I was a bit disoriented because it went so fast to the final stages, and I was wondering why. I think this game should've given the player more time to understand the situation, and some characters didn't have much screen time. I thought that some of the characters would evolve into something bigger, that some event would lead to some sick plot twists or moments where I'd be reacting like, "Holy sh*t, it's happening. Everybody stay calm!" But I was a bit disappointed that BioWare didn't really go nuts with some events and characters. As I wrote before, the story was amazing, but I would probably sacrifice those side jobs for more hours of story and better implementation of introducing Ryder into the world, politics, and relations between certain characters. I mean, how can you introduce me to a character and try to make me care about them in 5 minutes when I don't understand who that person is and how they got here? How can you put in some lines like "there's a fight between members of Initiative" and never really go back to it? It feels like there was a seed planted, and I waited for something to happen, and I realized that the game was sometimes like, "What? I said that? Weird."

Now we are at the final question of this review. Do I recommend this game? Yes, but on sale. If you're a Mass Effect fan, I think you should try this game, but if you're a hardcore Normandy's crew story fan, this game is not for you. I went into this game, not expecting the same stuff that I saw and felt with OG's Trilogy. So if you want to try it, I recommend playing with an open mind and not expecting another Shepard and Normandy.

“Mass Effect: Andromeda” Deluxe Edition is a large-scale action RPG built around exploration, party customization, and third-person combat. The premise shifts the series into the Andromeda galaxy, where you lead the Pathfinder initiative to locate viable homes for humanity. Narrative structure focuses on frontier settlement rather than political intrigue. The tone leans toward optimistic discovery.

Combat is one of the game’s strongest elements. Mobility is high thanks to jump jets and quick dashes. Powers combine into biotic and tech detonations that reward timing and positioning. Weapon variety supports different playstyles. Enemy encounters escalate with shield types, armor layers, and mobility units. Feedback is clear, and combat flow stays brisk.

Progression systems feature flexible skill allocation across biotic, tech, and combat trees. Instead of class-locking, you mix abilities freely. This encourages experimentation but dilutes distinct class identity. Squadmates gain fewer custom options, limiting tactical depth. Loot variety and crafting offer long-term optimization, though menus can feel dense.

Exploration spans multiple open planets. Each world offers side quests, collectible routes, and environmental hazards. The vehicle traversal feels smoother than past entries. However, many objectives repeat familiar patterns: scan, clear outposts, gather items. Terrain variety helps, but quest design can become routine across long sessions. The sense of scale remains impressive.

Story pacing is uneven. Some loyalty missions deliver strong character moments, while main arcs can feel underdeveloped. Dialogue relies on lighter tones compared to earlier entries. Emotional stakes land inconsistently. Character personalities are earnest but less layered. The narrative rewards players who invest time into companion arcs rather than the central plot.

Presentation quality varies. Planet vistas are impressive, with strong lighting and skyboxes. Character animations range from serviceable to awkward, reducing emotional impact. Combat effects read cleanly. Technical issues appeared at launch, but later patches mitigated many problems. Performance remains stable on modern hardware.

Overall, “Mass Effect: Andromeda” Deluxe Edition delivers energetic combat, broad customization, and wide exploration. Its weaknesses are repetitive quest structures, inconsistent writing, and uneven presentation. Players who enjoy open-world scanning loops and flexible builds will find value. Fans seeking the political depth and character nuance of the original trilogy may feel underwhelmed.

This game is what God of War (2018) is to the original trilogy--an odd one out in the franchise shunned by the original fans. A Mustang Mach-E to the great 5.0. Performance is great even with vast amounts of foliage on some planets. Combat is expressive and fully encapsulates that mid-late 2010's "next-gen" feel. The Angara look fine, but there was no comparison to be made there with the original trilogy. One of the primary Krogan characters has what look like teeth growing out of his chin; WHY?! The human NPCs are similarly weird; many of the background humans have absurdly dyed hair that doesn't fit the story and breaks immersion. For instance, a guard at an outcast colony had neon blue hair; you're telling me that either (a) humanity suddenly evolved the ability to grow neon blue hair, or (b) despite being more-or-less stranded in space and cut of from most supplies (these people were supposed to be banished from the main explorers) were still unconcerned enough with the events unfolding around them (like getting attacked by an unknown alien force and their ships disappearing) to bother dying their hair. Bring back the OG trilogy character design; it looked good and it was far less offensive than whatever this was.

Right off the bat, I can advise very quickly that if you set your expectations much lower than your experience with the original trilogy, I strongly feel you'll have a rather decent time with Andromeda. I bought this game on a Steam sale in 2025, so I don't know the past knowledge on its performance and all the patches that have come since, but at this stage I don't run into too many glitches or loading issues that are game breaking.

If you've already played Dragon Age Veilguard like myself, then you would notice a pattern of rather bland and generic voice lines from the protagonist and other key companions who accompany you on your journey. It doesn't really get any better the further you progress, however there's some really nice moments that other companions have within their own storylines. In particular, the Krogan's are always represented so consistently that I've found throughout the whole Mass Effect series. 

The open-world structure, however, is a double-edged sword. Certain planets are vast and beautiful, but are also bloated with repetitive fetch quests and scanning objectives that limit the sense of discovery. It’s easy to lose momentum in the sea of “busywork,” even as the graphical upgrade over the trilogy is fantastic. The combat as well in particular is a welcome change and offers plenty more fights which are faster, more vertical, and more fluid than ever before. Swapping between biotics, tech, and weapons mid-battle feels very smooth.

The general arching storyline is a mixed bag, as some standout with great personality whilst others don't really feel worth your time and feels like it was added to make up the numbers, which is very similar to the companion storylines too. Many of these quests lack the drive and passion that you experienced with previous entries. Still, Andromeda shines in smaller moments: quiet conversations aboard the Tempest, exploring alien ruins, it's all there but scattered unevenly. 

Overall, I feel that if you have an opportunity to get this game on sale, then it's well worth seeing how you like it, seeing that it goes on sale often and the discount is immense! It's a solid entry to the series, and even with the uneven writing moments, there's still a fun RPG experience here to be had!

Mass Effect Andromeda is like that one friend who constantly trips over their own shoelaces but still manages to nail karaoke every single time. Yes, it stumbles. Yes, it has some questionable design choices. But it also made me laugh, cry, and care in ways I didn't expect, and will cherish as a part of this franchise. 

First off, the companion banter is awesome. Driving around in the Nomad while PB and Jaal trade one liners had me grinning like an idiot. Liams end quest banter? 'Hold me Liam' will forever live rent free in my head. Drack starting a bar fight is peak space grandpa energy. It’s the kind of character writing that makes you want to take the long way around the planet just to hear what ridiculous thing comes next. And i did.

Speaking of the Nomad, it drives like a dream. IDGAF if yall don't like that part of this game. I did. Smooth, weighty, and the upgrades feel like actual upgrades instead of fancy labels. Exploring the planets feels rewarding too since each world looks and plays so differently. Jungle, desert, ice, everywhere I went was stupidly gorgeous. Sometimes I would just stop and spin the camera around like a tourist.

Combat is also excellent. Gunplay feels sharp, biotics feel devastating, and pulling off combos is endlessly satisfying. Playing as a biotic made me feel like an intergalactic wrecking ball. I even appreciated how I did not have to deal with outfitting companions. Just set their skills and go. It made swapping party members easier so I could enjoy different interactions without worrying about whether their guns were good enough.

Romance kept me coming back. When the planets got long and i got bored i kept fighting to see where the story went. I went with Jaal because big purple soft heart boy is my angel, but Reyes almost pulled me away a few times.  I thought I would dislike the non companion love interests, but the truth is they often had more to say over time which made them feel real. Those storylines had weight and the payoffs hit hard. By the last missions I was crying.

Now for the messy parts. The monolith puzzles drag on and glyph hunting feels like someone’s idea of padding. The quest journal is a mess of tabs and markers that sometimes lie to you outright. Not being able to save during missions is pure pain. Exclamation point, Exclamation point, Exclamation point.

Ryder also does not get enough credit. I cleared kett outposts, I solved monoliths, I kept whole colonies alive, and people still talked to me like I was useless. I am not asking for fireworks and fanfare, but a little gratitude would have been nice. Towards the end this changes but its a slog to get there. I think that comes down to how some interactions felt lacking, like they didn't say anything about terraforming a literal freaking planet, a little thank you would be nice. 

And while I adore the banter, sometimes it feels like I am just the driver while everyone else has fun. They will sit there talking about biotics right next to me even though I am a biotic. My love interest even flirted with other people in the car. I about kicked his ass out. The audacity. Someone should have been walking home from the next ice planet.

Traveling between planets is better than the probing minigame of the old trilogy but it still takes too long. It feels less like exploring space and more like sitting through an animated loading screen. I also wish companions had more to say when I checked in with them on the Nexus or the ship. They will not shut up in the Nomad, but when I visit their quarters they suddenly have nothing going on.

Andromeda nails the big picture. It looks stunning, the characters are memorable, and the story made me feel like I was carving out something new in the galaxy. At the same time, it misses a lot of small details and quality of life improvements that could have made it truly great. It is a flawed game, but the kind of flawed game I still loved every second of.

50+ hours into the game I saw a "Vega Bull Jr." joke, which felt apt as Andromeda is very Mass Effect: Inquisition in its (non-combat) gameplay. Not to make this about Dragon Age but it's my favourite series ever and I vastly prefer it to ME (which I still love) in terms of everything, so I can't believe Veilguard is that much worse than this. All I had heard for years is how bad MEA is, but DAV - my most anticipated thing ever besides TWOW and a new Joanna Newsom album - was worse. My essential point with this comparison is that Andromeda doesn't feel like a huge step backwards for ME as a series and the hatred is pretty overblown. 

The undeniable tonal shift isn't bad in itself. I wouldn't want Shepard 2.0, in fact most of the OT references were just corny. Mass Effect's world is our theoretical future and these games will always play like a fast-paced sci-fi action movie that's also homey, conventional. They're sentimental in their Earth patriotism. In this way, the series hasn't changed. Aliens have human reactions and qualities: you can kiss their carapaces, have relatively normal sex with them, and despite past differences everyone other than the big baddies ultimately want to get along or are fairly open to it (save the Batarians and nvm this is the most unrealistic part). It's nice to have this world expanded on and Andromeda's only major problem is that it's too cringey. The story works quite well and is just as interesting as the OT, whose plotlines, for me, were serviceable but secondary to the worldbuilding and interspecies conflict. The essence is clearly there if you put up with numerous bad jokes and over-sentimentality, it's Citadel DLC flippancy. 

That DLC has a lot to answer for. You don't necessarily want to see companions cozying up together and planning movie night by the end of Game #1, especially since there hasn't been any antagonism between them that would make this development worthwhile. It's great for Ryder, not for us. Companions aren't as likeable overall compared to the OT, granted I'm comparing 3 games vs. 1, otherwise I wouldn't call it a huge step down. Peebee (yes), Drack, and especially Jaal with his earnestness are good and have great banter. If I compare it to the first game, I think Andromeda's companions are tightly written and have more depth because of the quantity of conversations, whereas ME1's characters are a lot more entertaining on average. Probably cause they're bigger assholes. But the original companions also served as representatives for their species which helped establish them as real and serious characters through facts and history. Only Jaal has the same role and he's the standout. 

Generally I want silent protags in RPGs, though I don't expect that in ME and Ryder is actually distinct as a character. Whether you like Ryder's personality or not is up to you, of course. They're not as cool or competent as Shepard, pretty lame really, but they do feel fully realized in their dweebiness and inexperience. Ryder is a part of the world and involved in the initiative - you feel like you're pathfinding and doing your job. Rook is like a rehash of this without all the positives. I dislike open world exploration and I'm glad they're moving away from it, but I know many people enjoyed exploring planets in ME1 and I'm surprised more aren't appreciative of this aspect. You don't have to do every mindless side quest, I think most are available after the final story mission as well. The... galaxy recognizes the central conflict has been resolved, which helps with immersion if you continue playing. I was satisfied with how reactive the game is.

Before DAV even came out I had a feeling most of Bioware's reassurances about it were in response to MEA's failings, and I was proven correct in more ways than anticipated. The bugs, meaningless side quests, etc. But while I didn't particularly like most of MEA's side quests, even the more inconsequential ones felt fitting for a very humble Pathfinder who's in over their head. I won't defend the bugs, I ran into a few where I had to reload due to unreachable enemies or the game thinking I was in combat when I wasn't. However the game isn't even close to unplayable anymore, and I'd rather put up with a buggy game than one that shits all over its established world. Andromeda is fine. Silly. Rarely but occasionally funny. A good time when I'm not driving around with a massive headache.
Still view this as one of the best scifi series of all time.

[h1]The biggest issue with having so much cringe aboard an exploratory space craft is that the jokes never land[/h1]

Mass Effect Andromeda had all the hallmarks of a hilarious disaster upon release back in 2017. It was a buggy, disjointed, ugly mess of a game, a production hell behind the scenes, and an amphitheatre of pointing and laughing from its audience. Even before this, it faced a weird legacy challenge; the original trilogy was (and still is) widely adored, meaning it had very large shoes to fill. At the same time, Andromeda needed to rally against the exceptionally poor reception garnered by the lacklustre ending to Mass Effect 3 that had finished the series on a sour note. To combat this, EA gathered the celebrated creative team behind the previous three games and put them right to work. On new IP, Anthem. History has not judged this to have been a good idea. Instead, Andromeda was to be built by an entirely new team. On an entirely new engine. With the scope and direction being changed completely every time someone in a position of leadership was cycled away from the title. Which was shockingly often.

The new engine meant that none of the assets from the previous games could be reused. Everything from entire galaxies, character animations and muzzle flashes needed to be created anew by an unfamiliar team with revolving door management. So, it's of little surprise that what day one buyers got was a game populated by murderous-looking mannequins with lizard lips and legs constructed entirely of kneecaps. Walls became suggestion rather than reality. Stairs were a softly whispered rumour, unascendable monstrosities of broken dreams, the possessive guardians of slightly raised platforms. But the faces, dear reader, the faces have gone down in derpy meme legend. Many were bad, but the truest victim was that of the female default protagonist, who seemed to have been expertly sculpted to scientific imperfection. The unsettling facial tics, the disturbing smoothness and expansive reach of the cheeks and forehead. Eyes that can't help but wander, as if trying to escape the hellscape in which they were trapped. But it was mainly that smile, equal parts predatory and gormless. It haunts my dreams.

Fortunately, the walking nightmare that was Sarah Ryder has since been patched to the point where she's merely just horrific to look at. Structural integrity has been enforced so most walls are no longer constructed of mist. Cut scenes no longer feature suicidal characters holding their guns backwards. It's better, but not perfect. For example! During my playthrough, one member of the crew was so intent on avoiding a conversation that his pathfinding took him into and through a computer embankment, where they stayed until the next time we docked the ship. Another time, upon completing a side mission, an in-game cut scene triggered where the team gathered around their won objective and discussed the next step. Only, the world around them remained active and a pack of ravenous space dogs spawned in and killed everyone while they calmly stood around chatting. I wasn't even mad; ignoring a horrific mauling while casually discussing the mundane transportation of glowy space rocks was pretty funny.

As of right now, the game is as solid as it's ever going to be, its oft-mocked technical flaws relegated to frustrating rather than game breaking. For people like me (Gary Hartley, noted Mass Effect enjoyer) who avoided the game at launch to join in with the pointing and laughing from afar, that reason for abstention isn't nearly as valid. It was brave of me, I know, to wade in to see if there was something hiding there behind the bug wall. In my 100 or so hour odyssey through Andromeda, I still found plenty of things to be disappointed by. But more than my fair share of pleasant surprises.

Let's start on a high. The main idea and mission behind Andromeda are great. Trilogy hero, Shepard, was a Spectre agent who, by design, had all their universe's political weight and resources at their disposal. In contrast, Team Ryder has been bundled aboard an ark ship, frozen for 600 years and transported an entire galaxy away. There's no safety net; there's no resources or help at all, and anything they need they're going to have to scourge up themselves from a collection of unexplored systems. The only upshot is that before they left the Milky Way behind, they'd managed to earmark several golden planets, ripe for habitation. That was a lie. Instead, they find inhospitable death worlds filled with unbreathable air, intolerable atmospheres and homicidal local wildlife. The first plant you visit is a disaster; crash landings, scattered crewmates, heavy background radiation and rock-faced xenophobic aliens trying to gun everyone down. It's far from the shiny new home the expedition promised. There was also supposed to be a huge hub ship constructed by the time you arrived, something akin to a smaller scale citadel from the original trilogy. It exists, but it's bare bones. Half constructed, low on power and short staffed. Many people died during the construction, many more abandoned the project, exiling themselves, gambling on having better luck on the scattershot planets that are only nearly inhabitable. More still stay cytogenetically frozen; the way things are, there's not enough resources available to justify thawing them.

Your first real mission is supposed to change that. There's a nearby planet that would merely be a horrific place to live if not for the absence of water and sweltering non-stop desert heat. There's been two previous attempts to establish a settlement, both of which have led to the death of many prospectors. The few survivors returned so damaged and shell-shocked, they were placed back on ice. It's a suicide mission by any optic, but it's also the best part of the game. Failure means everyone dies, so you need to brute force yourself through the endless obstacles your would-be hellfire home presents. At this point, all that really awaits you is various shades of failure. You're under levelled; you're under equipped and if you stray outside the heatproof barrier set up inside the now dead settlements, you'll fry on the spot. Also, those barriers, the only thing keeping you alive, are all failing. There are scavengers picking the bones of the sites; To Shepard, this would be a minor inconvenience, one easily bullied, manipulated or shot into compliance. Ryder can do none of these things; they can only appeal to the scavenger's humanity and shared interest in the newest expedition's success. But this does net new resources. A small victory, but one that gives you more options, the ability to push a little further into the planet. It's the Wild West out there; unexplored desert plains filled with unforeseeable dangers. Lost alien artifacts, acid-spitting sand bugs, rolling metal-melting heatwaves and rock-faced alien arseholes with laser rifles.

You can't do much, but you can do something. So, you scrape. And you scramble. You find little pockets of progression and each small win makes the world of difference. As the planet is slowly tamed, as your foothold in this new galaxy becomes firmer, things change in your favour. You find ways to make the planet more hospitable; you find ways to drive hostile forces out; you find the means to establish a new settlement. With the means to support more life, more people are defrosted at the hub; new areas on the ship are opened and become explorable. Old departments are expanded, looking into newly discovered life and flora and geography. And you've done this. You've explored the unknown and you've been directly responsible for every advancement. You've seen it grow in real time. It's as exhilarating as it is short lived; none of it is present for the remaining five planets.
