I've played through the original trilogy at least six times now... And after recently playing through it again I figured I should give Andromeda another chance. I've seen many people say that it has gotten much better since launch and while the story isn't so great compared to the trilogy, the combat supposedly is the best...

I disagree, vehemently. 

My main gripe is, it's just not a mass effect game imho. The combat is very different and I guess people that say it's better just prefer a different style of game. The biggest change is that the power wheel is gone. You can't pause combat anymore to look around, command your teammates and choose your powers. Instead it's all real-time and you can only have three powers on your bumpers (one of which by hitting them together). As far as I've been able to see you can't command your teammates to use powers... Actually in the time I've played I don't think I've seen anything to indicate that they have any at all, it's just that I've seen there is an achievement to combo with them so they must. But there is no more tactical looking around and combining powers. 

The shooting seems pretty good, but not really anything special. One other thing that annoys... They still have the weight system to hurt your cooldowns if you carry too many weapons. I started as an infiltrator (it's called differently now, operative maybe)... But if I take a sniper with me my cooldowns immediately are shot. So I end up bringing an assault rifle because with the sniper I can't use my cloak very often. This can be fixed later with skill points, but it kind of kills the class at the start. 

Graphics are pretty cool, as long as you don't look too closely at the faces (especially the Rider men look like they got a skin condition).

Controls are a bit weird and coming from ME LE it's annoying they changed everything and you can't customise the controls (not on a controller anyway). One thing that really frustrated me is that x is reload, but holding x is swap weapons and that seems to be glitchy where it triggers a lot even though I was not holding the button down. I have had so many times where I was suddenly shooting the damn pistol instead of my AR... Also pressing B is dodge, which is pretty cool... But you can't manually go into cover anymore, you just have to kind of walk into cover while having your weapon out. And if you press B you just blink forward, which has made me jump off a cliff several times. Maybe it's partly me but even after playing for 6 hours I still find the controls overly complicated and unintuitive. 

The story so far is pretty uninteresting, but this was expected, no-one praises Andromeda for its story. 

The worst part though, coming back to that this is not a Mass Effect game... They could have dropped Mass Effect from the name, changed the names of some skills and weapons, changed the models of some aliens to humans and you wouldn't have been able to tell it was supposed to be a mass effect game. Yes there are Asari, Krogan, Salarian and Turian, but they act just like humans. There is no difference, the only thing they took from Mass Effect is how they look. 

So in the end this is just a generic scifi shooter with rpg elements... It's not bad per se, but there are so many much better games, that I just can't recommend anyone wastes their time on this.

It’s honestly hard for me to review this game because I started playing it right after finishing the Mass Effect trilogy. I was still emotionally attached to the characters and the whole universe and didn’t want it to end, like an addict taking a weaker drug just to slowly come off the stronger one.

The graphics are beautiful, and the gameplay is solid. There are multiple class/playstyle variations again, but system is more flexible, you’re not locked into one class and can switch profiles depending on your skills.
I do have to say the game felt a bit bloated in terms of exploration and missions. There’s a lot of filler content. Personally, I didn’t mind it too much and ended up completing everything, but I know other people found it repetitive. The game also has several easter eggs connecting it to the original trilogy, references to the Milky Way, mentions of Shepard as a legendary figure, audio logs hinting at Liara work as an information broker, Krogan settling on a New Tuchanka, and familiar N7 gear.

As for the story… I’ll be honest, the new Angara race didn’t fully click with me. Something about them felt a bit off, and the whole plot sometimes came across more like a side story rather than a strong main narrative driving the universe forward. The dialogue also lacked the weight and emotional punch of the original Mass Effect games. It felt a bit flat at times. And don't get me started on Liam... he’s the one character I genuinely avoided talking to whenever possible. I don’t think I’ve seen a more poorly written character in the series. It almost felt like a self insert by a developer or something because of how annoying he was. The storyline involving the Jardaan, the Remnant, and the Kett felt somewhat unfinished, becuase they teased a sequel, but since that clearly not happening, the overall narrative ends up feeling a bit underwhelming.

The game isn’t bad by any means. If you enjoyed the Mass Effect trilogy or sci-fi exploration games in general, you’ll probably have a good time here too. Just don’t expect the same level of storytelling, character depth, and emotional impact as the original trilogy.

Half constructed, low on power and short staffed. Many people died during the construction, many more abandoned the project, exiling themselves, gambling on having better luck on the scattershot planets that are only nearly inhabitable. More still stay cytogenetically frozen; the way things are, there's not enough resources available to justify thawing them.

Your first real mission is supposed to change that. There's a nearby planet that would merely be a horrific place to live if not for the absence of water and sweltering non-stop desert heat. There's been two previous attempts to establish a settlement, both of which have led to the death of many prospectors. The few survivors returned so damaged and shell-shocked, they were placed back on ice. It's a suicide mission by any optic, but it's also the best part of the game. Failure means everyone dies, so you need to brute force yourself through the endless obstacles your would-be hellfire home presents. At this point, all that really awaits you is various shades of failure. You're under levelled; you're under equipped and if you stray outside the heatproof barrier set up inside the now dead settlements, you'll fry on the spot. Also, those barriers, the only thing keeping you alive, are all failing. There are scavengers picking the bones of the sites; To Shepard, this would be a minor inconvenience, one easily bullied, manipulated or shot into compliance. Ryder can do none of these things; they can only appeal to the scavenger's humanity and shared interest in the newest expedition's success. But this does net new resources. A small victory, but one that gives you more options, the ability to push a little further into the planet. It's the Wild West out there; unexplored desert plains filled with unforeseeable dangers. Lost alien artifacts, acid-spitting sand bugs, rolling metal-melting heatwaves and rock-faced alien arseholes with laser rifles.

You can't do much, but you can do something. So, you scrape. And you scramble. You find little pockets of progression and each small win makes the world of difference. As the planet is slowly tamed, as your foothold in this new galaxy becomes firmer, things change in your favour. You find ways to make the planet more hospitable; you find ways to drive hostile forces out; you find the means to establish a new settlement. With the means to support more life, more people are defrosted at the hub; new areas on the ship are opened and become explorable. Old departments are expanded, looking into newly discovered life and flora and geography. And you've done this. You've explored the unknown and you've been directly responsible for every advancement. You've seen it grow in real time. It's as exhilarating as it is short lived; none of it is present for the remaining five planets.

I've played through the original trilogy at least six times now... And after recently playing through it again I figured I should give Andromeda another chance. I've seen many people say that it has gotten much better since launch and while the story isn't so great compared to the trilogy, the combat supposedly is the best...

I disagree, vehemently. 

My main gripe is, it's just not a mass effect game imho. The combat is very different and I guess people that say it's better just prefer a different style of game. The biggest change is that the power wheel is gone. You can't pause combat anymore to look around, command your teammates and choose your powers. Instead it's all real-time and you can only have three powers on your bumpers (one of which by hitting them together). As far as I've been able to see you can't command your teammates to use powers... Actually in the time I've played I don't think I've seen anything to indicate that they have any at all, it's just that I've seen there is an achievement to combo with them so they must. But there is no more tactical looking around and combining powers. 

The shooting seems pretty good, but not really anything special. One other thing that annoys... They still have the weight system to hurt your cooldowns if you carry too many weapons. I started as an infiltrator (it's called differently now, operative maybe)... But if I take a sniper with me my cooldowns immediately are shot. So I end up bringing an assault rifle because with the sniper I can't use my cloak very often. This can be fixed later with skill points, but it kind of kills the class at the start. 

Graphics are pretty cool, as long as you don't look too closely at the faces (especially the Rider men look like they got a skin condition).

Controls are a bit weird and coming from ME LE it's annoying they changed everything and you can't customise the controls (not on a controller anyway). One thing that really frustrated me is that x is reload, but holding x is swap weapons and that seems to be glitchy where it triggers a lot even though I was not holding the button down. I have had so many times where I was suddenly shooting the damn pistol instead of my AR... Also pressing B is dodge, which is pretty cool... But you can't manually go into cover anymore, you just have to kind of walk into cover while having your weapon out. And if you press B you just blink forward, which has made me jump off a cliff several times. Maybe it's partly me but even after playing for 6 hours I still find the controls overly complicated and unintuitive. 

The story so far is pretty uninteresting, but this was expected, no-one praises Andromeda for its story. 

The worst part though, coming back to that this is not a Mass Effect game... They could have dropped Mass Effect from the name, changed the names of some skills and weapons, changed the models of some aliens to humans and you wouldn't have been able to tell it was supposed to be a mass effect game. Yes there are Asari, Krogan, Salarian and Turian, but they act just like humans. There is no difference, the only thing they took from Mass Effect is how they look. 

So in the end this is just a generic scifi shooter with rpg elements... It's not bad per se, but there are so many much better games, that I just can't recommend anyone wastes their time on this.

It’s honestly hard for me to review this game because I started playing it right after finishing the Mass Effect trilogy. Personally, I didn’t mind it too much and ended up completing everything, but I know other people found it repetitive. The game also has several easter eggs connecting it to the original trilogy, references to the Milky Way, mentions of Shepard as a legendary figure, audio logs hinting at Liara work as an information broker, Krogan settling on a New Tuchanka, and familiar N7 gear.

As for the story… I’ll be honest, the new Angara race didn’t fully click with me. The game isn’t bad by any means. If you enjoyed the Mass Effect trilogy or sci-fi exploration games in general, you’ll probably have a good time here too. Just don’t expect the same level of storytelling, character depth, and emotional impact as the original trilogy.

This is another one of those games where I wish Steam had a "Neutral" option. To preface, I played Andromeda immediately after finishing my first playthrough of the Mass Effect series (Legendary Edition), so this review is coming from someone that can be considered "relatively new" to the series.

That being said, if you're expecting a continuation of the main Mass Effect trilogy in Andromeda, you might want to reconsider playing Andromeda. It is WILDLY apparent that Andromeda was made by a different team compared to the OG Mass Effect trilogy. The best way I can describe it is "Walmart Mass Effect". Pretty much the only thing Andromeda has in common with its predecessor are the aliens, and even then, the aliens are cheap knockoff versions of the originals. The Asari ALL have the same face, the Turians are all pale as hell for some reason and look like they're constantly trying to sit in a chair, and the Salarians all look like they're wearing cheap lipstick. It's very uncanny. The story also has almost no ties to the original trilogy except from a few passing comments here and there during side quests that are easily missable. You will not be seeing Shepard or any other characters from the original trilogy, and the closest thing you will get to a cameo are some audio recordings from Liara. Even the villains of Andromeda are just Walmart versions of Mass Effect 2's Collectors - oh no, evil space aliens want to abduct people and steal their DNA! Now where have I seen that before?

However, if you go into Andromeda without any of these expectations, then you're probably going to have a good time. The combat is undeniably the best in the entire franchise. You can literally become a space ninja dashing around and teleporting everywhere with the right build. There is no rigid "class" system, so you can build your character however you like with whatever skills and traits you like - they're really generous with skill points, so don't worry about running out. You can also respec anytime on your ship if you feel like your build is getting stale or underperforming. The closest comparisons I can draw are Warframe and Borderlands, so if you enjoy those games, you'll probably enjoy Andromeda.

The second thing Andromeda does right is exploration. Andromeda really nails the feeling of being "strangers in an entirely new galaxy". Map completion and making worlds habitable by completing quests and tasks is very satisfying. Speaking of quests, there are A LOT of quests. You will probably be overwhelmed the first time you play because Andromeda has a bad habit of just immediately dumping 15-20 side quests on you whenever you land on a new planet. Some side quests are also hidden behind ambient NPC dialogue or just talking to NPCs, so if you're a completionist you might find yourself worrying about whether or not you missed something (don't worry, you WILL miss stuff just because of the sheer amount of content). This is not inherently a bad thing because it just means more content, but some people might find this offputting.

Now onto the objective negatives. The game is buggy as hell. You WILL get stuck in terrain and have to reload saves. Enemies WILL spawn inside walls or out of bounds, making you unable to complete quests where you have to kill every enemy. If you don't stop what you are doing and take your hands off the keyboard/controller whenever someone starts talking (and they talk A LOT), you risk interrupting the dialogue. Sometimes it doesn't even matter - NPCs will walk into you and interrupt dialogue even if you're standing still. SAM (the AI in your head) is infuriating and will NOT SHUT UP. This is especially bad on planets with environmental hazards such as cold or heat. Expect a nonstop barrage of "LIFE SUPPORT IS FAILING" "TEMPERATURE IS DROPPING" "LIFE SUPPORT IS IN RANGE" "TEMPERATURE IS RISING" from SAM every 3 seconds on those planets. And yes, SAM can ALSO interrupt dialogue. Entering and leaving planets also prompts a 30 second unskippable cutscene for some reason (and you're going to be doing that A LOT).

Luckily, there are certain mods that rectify the issues I mentioned, and yes, they're pretty much mandatory in order to make the game playable (in my opinion). MEA Bugfixes, Shut Up SAM, Faster Mining, and Shorter Landing and Departure Cinematics are the ones I absolutely recommend installing before playing. 

All in all, you can have quite a bit of fun with Mass Effect: Andromeda if you completely ignore the fact that they were trying (and failed) to be a Mass Effect game. Just pretend it's like open world Warframe, install the requisite mods, laugh at how bad the Asari and Turian models are, and you'll probably have a great time. 6/10.

Mass Effect Andromeda was a fun foray into the Sci-fi Open World RPG genre. It has a nice little mix of everything, from third person shooter combat, to very basic space exploration, to exploring strange planets. However, reader beware, this is NOT like the Mass Effect Trilogy. There are a lot of similarities, and mechanics that are identical, and a lot that this game took from the trilogy and changed. However, because this game took the open world approach, the story telling is not as linear. It's padded with tons of extra side missions, and tasks (which are basically side side missions). It's to the point where it becomes too much, as most are fetch quests having you running from point a to b, sometimes planet to planet, with nothing more than some minor dialogue (aka no real world building). This isn't too much a of a problem as a lot can be  ignored (Specifically anything labeled "task". Still, it can be overwhelming. 

Overall, the game was still very much enjoyable, and a little sad that there is not and potentially will not be a sequel, but aside from the lingering questions, the main thing that really felt disjointed to me, was the lack of control over squad mates. As the main character you can spec yourself out to play any role from the previous games, and mix it up. Your squadmates, tend to be quite similar in functionality, but you can no longer command them to use their special abilities. It is up the AI to use them, and frankly, the squadmates AI is really rather poor. If you play on Insanity, they practically commit suicide.

That aside, gameplay wise I have no major complaints. It wasn't as smooth as say Mass Effect 3, but it wasn't quite poor either. I don't think it's worth the full price, personally, but I got it on sale for under $10. If you like Mass Effect, like open world games, and like third person shooters, then this is a great game to sink 40-50 hrs (for full achievements, closer to 65-70 hrs).

Thoughts: This is my favorite BGS game so far no question, despite the online forces telling me not to get this game or all the noise in general. I enjoy this, I love space, and I love the type of games this studio makes. This isn’t to say the game is without issues, but it is to say the internet doesn’t guide my tastes. Game is immersive, people can dislike it all they want that’s fine. But conversely I’m allowed to enjoy the game. No one rules my compass except me.

Dislikes: Steam Deck performance could definitely use a lot more work, I’m not sure what they could do to optimize this further but I would enjoy it if they could. 

Settings Used On My Deck: Within Steam itself, go to Starfields Game Profile settings and set the max resolution to 800x600, I then within the Decks built-in Performance Settings locked the framerate to 35fps, I also set the scaling to fit the screen so it eliminates the black bars associated with lower resolutions. I also set the sharpness to max. Then within the game I set all the visual settings as absolutely low as possible, set the resolution scale to MAX, chose XeSS for the in-game image scaling, and I set it to Quality. The results are pretty impressive, it looks pretty good on my 4k OLED TV, a lot better than it has any right to. Also, while the framerate tanks in busy areas, for the most part this is a locked 35fps which is perfectly playable as a docked TV experience. Hopefully someone else can experiment more than me. In handheld I’m getting anywhere from 50-70 frames indoors thanks to these tweaks. Outdoors it’s fluctuating from 35-40.

Recommendation: I caution any Deck User to know that you’re gonna have to tweak A LOT of settings to get the game running. This isn’t a simple “buy, download, and play” so be prepared to have to put in the work. 

As for non Handheld-PC users, I fully recommend this game at full price or on sale, it’s worth it. If you like NASA, Star Trek, Star Wars, and just space in general there’s a high chance the game will at least spark some curiosity in you. The lore alone is fascinating enough if you’re someone who grew up watching Carl Sagan. Don’t let the people online who are anti-science dissuade your curiosity.

Second the quests are all basically the same: Fly here, go there, put this there, grab that, fly back, talk to a bunch of Lobotomites, fly to planet, fight pirates, fly back. While there are a bunch of unique things that happen, none of them are significant enough to pull me back in. I still don't event really know what the storyline is about. Third, Landing on a planet doesn't really mean anything because its randomly generated and always the same square cell with 5 points of interest (dungeons). Fourth, combat is extremely weak. It makes Fallout 4 look like a tactical shooter. The enemies have no sense of direction and only seem to do lots of damage at super close range. To preface this, when I was younger I played Oblivion, Skyrim, and Fallout 4 on console and loved them. After moving to PC, I played them all again with mods, often spending more time building and testing mod lists than actually playing. I didn’t follow much of the controversy around Starfield before launch, but I knew it had a long development cycle and a somewhat rocky reception.

When Starfield released, I watched a friend play and decided to hold off. Despite being excited for a new Bethesda IP, what I saw felt undercooked, possibly rushed. Reviews mentioned frequent and lengthy loading screens, limited procedural generation for planetary POIs (with a very small pool leading to repetition), and no proper ground transport, meaning long walks across fairly bland terrain. All of this put me off initially.

I finally picked up Starfield four days ago and have already put around 30 hours into it. Since launch, the game has clearly seen some much-needed updates, most notably the addition of land vehicles, which massively improves planetary exploration. I also jumped straight onto Nexus and installed the Odyssey – True RPG modpack, which expands space encounters and increases the procedural POI pool to around 65, alongside numerous fixes and tweaks. On top of that, I picked up a few Creation mods that add new missions, quests, factions, and locations such as The Watchtower, The Veil, and Everbright. The game is installed on an SSD, so my load times are usually only 1–4 seconds.

With all of this in place, I’ve been really enjoying the game. I’m currently playing through the UC Vanguard questline and it’s been a great experience. You can fully embrace being a loot goblin, collecting not just weapons and armour but also decorative items like statues and plushies to personalise your ship or outposts for role-play. Bethesda’s trademark environmental storytelling is present, and in my opinion the updated graphics look genuinely good.

Overall, I’m having a lot of fun, but I’m glad I waited until the modding scene had time to mature. You can clearly see the missed potential on Bethesda’s part, and I can only hope they don’t somehow undermine what’s been built going forward. I’d recommend Starfield if you’re willing to use mods to address or enhance its weaker areas and you have the hardware to keep load times short. If you didn’t enjoy Skyrim or Fallout 4, or didn’t enjoy modding them, this probably isn’t the game for you.

If you’re willing to spend $70 on what amounts to a watered-down, space-themed version of Skyrim—without truly feeling like the main character—then this game may be for you. Dialogue often feels antagonistic, with NPC interactions that lack warmth or meaningful engagement.

One of the few genuinely compelling features is shipbuilding. The customization system allows for impressive creativity, including recreations inspired by other sci-fi franchises. Unfortunately, this strength is not enough to carry the overall experience.

Much of the gameplay feels like a re-skin of mechanics from Fallout and The Elder Scrolls. While that familiarity could have been a positive, it instead highlights how little innovation there is. The game evokes comparisons to DayZ in space, but without the benefit of unique or memorable environments.

The New Game Plus mechanic is an interesting concept, but its execution is disappointing. After completing the main story and side quests, there is little incentive to replay when progress, equipment, and even meticulously built ships are lost—with no option to save or preserve custom designs. Rebuilding everything from scratch quickly becomes tedious rather than rewarding.

I’ve been playing Bethesda games since Morrowind. Back in the good ol' days where installing mods required only having WinZip installed. Now look at mods like the mod that adds hair and cape physics to Skyrim SE. It’s dependency nightmare and mod manager shenanigans.

I’ve played Arena and Daggerfall as well, unlike most TES fans. I’ve played Fallout 1 and 2, unlike most Fallout fans.

I like Bethesda games. A lot. I enjoy the gameplay loop. I enjoy modding the heck out of them. So, once Starfield finally went on a sale that I found acceptable, and after being disappointed with New Vegas, the game the community overhypes as the best Fallout (it’s Fallout 3 that’s the true best, in my opinion), I figured it was time to try it out.

Ohh boy.

This is a brand new universe, IP, franchise for Bethesda. Elder Scrolls games start you off slow and easy and if you’re interested in the world, there’s tons of lore books scattered around. Fallout games usually start with the “War… War Never Changes” guy giving you a brief recap of how the world got the way it is. Starfield has none of these things. I had no clue about the history of this universe until I stumbled upon the UC Vanguard faction questline, which briefly recaps how Earth lost its atmosphere and the subsequent events that followed. Why wouldn’t the game open up with this?

Then you are given a ship just because and you end up joining Constellation; a faction of explorers looking for artifacts. This faction also has the four most annoying and insufferable companions of all Bethesda games. Granted, most companions in Bethesda games are either just there (Oblivion, Skyrim) or approach Bioware-level greatness yet don’t fully live up to that potential (FO3, FONV, FO4). Here, all the companions share the same morals and ethics. Every time you do something in a questline that they don’t like, the game will interrupt you as these companions lecture you about your choice. In a game where you’re encouraged to be and do whatever you like. Bethesda thought it was great that companions will berate you and chastise you whenever you don’t play the way they prefer.

Then there’s the outpost building mechanic. In FO4, the Settlement system worked well enough, but it was too clunky to use for extended periods. Installing Sim Settlements is basically a mandatory step to fix this, because as the tradition goes, you gotta install mods to fix stuff Bethesda just left there. Here, there’s no such mods, instead, there’s a few helpful ones like the Universal Stash mod that are, in my opinion, mandatory to enjoy this game. The problem with outposts is that you’re encouraged to have many of them in order to have them grind materials you’ll need for research projects and weapon/spacesuit mods. Well, getting all the materials transported from 8 outposts to the one you want is a logistical nightmare. Why couldn’t they all just share the same inventory? No, you have to “ship” a limited number of materials to the outpost you select, eventually setting up an overly complex supply chain. Dude, this is a western RPG, not Victoria 3 or Anno 1800. It needs to be simpler than this.

All this aside, you install mods to fix the game and make it more bearable, and what’s this? Why does my character look like the Michelin mascot? Because, Bethesda, when given the chance to work on a brand new IP, they choose “NASA punk” as the aesthetic. I could not deal with this at all. So, I waited until there were mods to fix this. Do yourself a favor and install KZ Tachyonic Core Arsenal and KZ Aggregation of Scraps for some actual attractive Mass Effect-like space suits.

Then, as you play, you’ll find an Astra, a rare material that if you have three, you can exchange it to get a random Legendary item. Kind of like a gacha game except you get the currency as you play. Not bad. I amassed around 13 Astra and let’s get some loot…. oh, the loot table is broken because I started the Freestar Rangers questline. How does this even happen? Apparently this bug has been here since before Shattered Space came out, and it still hasn’t been fixed. So instead of the loot table having everything, it only has Loredo branded weapons and a few spacesuit types. So, Astra are now worthless… until installed the McClarens Outfitters mod that lets me remove Legendary effects from armor and apply it on the armor of my choice. With 1 Astra, it lets you duplicate items and even upgrades them to the next tier. It’d be nice if I could do it for weapons too… oh you can! But you have to do a gigantic grind to get to modify your weapons too with this mod. So, not even modders can get this game design right. I don’t get what’s so hard about this.

“Dude, stop ranting, hows the story?” Warning, spoilers ahead! [spoiler] Well… it’s barely a story. I don’t tend to like stories in most Western RPGs, I’ve realized. I seem to have the most fun with JRPG and VN storylines. That said, it’s an okay sci-fi story about exploration and space anomaly shenanigans. The plot twist would have been decent, if I didn’t see it coming from miles away. It’s entirely too predictable and the way they choose which party member gets to die is ridiculously stupid. Bethesda chose the top 2 party members you always use and put them into a dangerous situation where you must pick who to save. If I knew this beforehand, I would have used Sam and Barret exclusively since I don’t like them. Heck, I don’t like Sarah or Adreja either. This whole sequence just felt bland and empty to me.

Then there’s the whole “Unity” thing. You lose all your gear and items, and you essentially start a new game+ with your level, perks and abilities intact. New things happen during this mode as well. The reason I bring it up is because during this sequence, you get to hear your character talk, and it reminds me of the best feature of Fallout 4; the voiced protagonist. It seems people vastly prefer playing as a mute. I don’t understand how that aids in roleplaying in anyway. To think, a universe where Starfield has a voiced protagonist. Now that’s a universe I’d make a Unity Jump for. [/spoiler]

The combat is pretty much Fallout 4 without VATS and with Dragon Shouts. That pretty much sums it up. It’s a lot of fun, and I love fighting legendary enemies to get that loot. The loot system is improved from Fallout 4. It’s closer to Diablo now. Blue tier items are rare and have one special effect. Purple tier items are Epic and have two special effects. Yellow tier items are Legendary and have three special effects. It’s satisfying. 

My favorite companion was the Adoring Fan. I think that says it all. 

I liked this game, and I will play more of it in the future. I still haven’t finished the UC Vanguard, Freestar Rangers and Shattered Space questlines yet. But, it seems like loop I have for this game is excitement and then disappointment and then fix with mods. And, after 105 hours, I feel exhausted. I want to play a game that “just works” out of the box, Todd. Right Todd?

I have mixed feelings on this game. I love space, so that gives it most of its pull for me. Plus, Bethesda is a pretty good studio for the most part, though I do have some thoughts on how lazily some aspects of their games are put together because they know people will write it off as 'Bethesda Jank' or let the modders fix it.

That being said, if you're going into this thinking it'll scratch your space exploration itch - Don't. It's not worth it. Exploration is repetitious and dull, finding the same POIs in the same proc-gen landscapes. While the occasional POI is interesting, it simply is not enough to save the game. Space flight is a glorified loading screen, too. Piloting the ships feels fine, but actual ship combat is quite dull. Aside from the fact that there simply isn't much to do in space, you'll mostly spend time accessing your map to move to a different system, where you can then access your map to land on a planet. Space exploration is as wide as an ocean, but as deep as a puddle. If you want actually interesting gameplay in space, I advise playing No Man's Sky or Elite Dangerous. Even EVE has more fascinating space gameplay, and that game is just Microsoft Excel.

So, how are the quests? Well... They're okay. For the most part, storylines of side quests are serviceable. There are some highlights that have stuck with me from the occasional quest, but it's mostly forgettable. Beyond that, even the quests that ARE good will often feature a choice in quest design that either confuses or angers you. Take for example the quest where you have to choose to release an experimental bio-weapon with a chance of mutating and attacking humans or bringing a creature back from extinction that would serve the same purpose as the bio-weapon, but over a longer scale. So, if you're like me, you'd assume that gambling on a bio-weapon isn't the ideal outcome. That's not what your companions think. At worst, they chide you for not being forward-thinking enough, and at best they hand-wring about how 'it doesn't seem like the right choice'.

The main story itself is utterly dull, which isn't necessarily new for Bethesda. But for a game that espoused its 'awesome New Game+', you think there would be more motivation to actually finish the main quest. Speaking of the New Game+ mechanic, it's similarly shallow. There are a wide variety of changes that can occur, but hardly anything that will keep you interested enough to complete another playthrough.

The gunplay is fun, but it's dragged down by the classic Bethesda artificial difficulty of bullet sponges. Of course, guns aren't your only weapon. You're also given access to a variety of powers that your character 'shouts' to activate--

Yeah, everybody knows about the Dragonborn in space shit. It's egregious, barely justified by the plot and genuinely laughable. I think Skyrim's success broke Todd Howard's brain. The powers themselves are fine. They can be fun, but never quite as interesting or enjoyable as Skyrim's shouts. Partly because you've played this exact game before, just in a medieval high-fantasy setting instead.

Companions are basically cardboard cut-outs. They do have quests, but they're rarely interesting. I found Sam to be the most enjoyable one, and that was only because he was supplemented by his daughter, Cora. Together, they make about 2/3rds of an interesting character (though that itself might be a generous figure).

So, I've been pretty harsh, but is Starfield worth it? Short answer - No. It's not worth £59.99. 

At most, I'd recommend spending around ~£30 on the game, and that's only if you REALLY enjoy Bethesda's formula and are into space games enough to keep you chugging to the finish line. Even if that was the game's asking price, my review would still be negative. Bethesda released a below-standard game at their usual asking price, talking it up as an 'exciting new IP' but there's little worth here. I was willing to give it a chance, and dumped a not-insignificant amount of hours into the game. From my 126 hours, I came to realise Starfield's biggest crime. 

You constantly think the game is on the verge of getting good.

Each main quest, each side quest, each new system - There are just enough good ideas and concepts there to present something interesting and worth exploring. But time and time again, Starfield will show a flashy intro and then promptly fall on its face, breaking its nose and chipping its teeth. Yet, it'll stand back up and perform an impressive flourish, just enough to make you think, 'Oh, okay. We're getting into it for REAL this time!' And then Starfield falls again. 

The main quest always feels like you're on the verge of something interesting happening, but it never does. The side quests will occasionally have fascinating set-pieces, introductions or concepts, but they never land the execution. 

Ultimately, there is nothing to be gleamed from Starfield. It'll only make you look at Bethesda with a more bitter outlook on their formula and the games that came before. I have little hope in TES6 or Fallout 5, or any other game Bethesda chooses to work on (god forbid they make Starfield 2).

This game is not really worth 70 euro/70 dollars BUT for anyone who loves Bethesda or bethesda-esque games this is a great pick up ON SALE(!!!).I never jumped on the Starfield hype bandwagon so im basically judging this solely on my experience with it. Honestly,this game's main story is a bit lackluster.I immediately found myself doing a bunch of stuff other than the  main quest that seemed immensely more interesting to me. Some of the sidequests did a much better job at worldbuilding and player immersion than the main story line, that seemed more as a backdrop to the whole setting than anything else.The UC main quest for example felt more like a New Vegas faction questline(and believe me i say this is a compliment).There are a tonne of things that this game does right or does better in comparison to other Bethesda titles only to fall short because of bad implementation into the whole premise,or not really giving you any incentive to partake in said activities,for example settlement building.Theres literally no reason to build settlements or outposts as this game calls them other than make money through producing drugs or other items or as a player home,of which there are plenty in the game,so why build in the first place?
That said mechanics like character traits and shipbuilding are really interesting,and can really alter the way you play; You're an empath and your companion doesnt approve of the shit you do?  The shipbuilding system is easy to familiarise with and i have to say really fun,also there's a lot of variation which gives you a lot of leeway to create your own fleet of ships.I could literally go on for hours about the things this game tries albeit sometimes falls short of doing and i think this all is commendable for Bethesda to try.

I understand why many Bethesda fans hate this game so much. People who grew up playing Skyrim or Fallout 4 may find this game uninspiring and boring compared to those titles. However, as someone who only discovered Bethesda in the past few years and enjoyed playing Fallout 4, but is not really into the medieval fantasy theme of Skyrim, I can say that I enjoy Starfield.

As a No Man’s Sky player, I think Starfield is trying to combine the NMS formula with Bethesda’s storytelling-driven RPG approach. They implement procedurally generated maps, surveying flora and fauna, and material farming. Many people think that surveying planets and farming materials are boring, but for me, they can be fun and even mindful.

There are also spaceship battles, which make it feel similar to No Man’s Sky. However, due to engine limitations, Starfield cannot offer seamless interplanetary travel, so it relies on loading screens—far too many loading screens. This is why it feels inferior in terms of space travel compared to No Man’s Sky.

That said, there are several things that make this game interesting for me. First, the environments are more realistic and less colorful compared to NMS. Second, Starfield offers deep character customization, allowing players to create the character they want. As a fan of character customization, I see this as a major positive point. Overall, I do enjoy Starfield as it is, without comparing it to Fallout 4. So yes, by my standards, Starfield already offers an enjoyable experience.

The game about exploring outer space, does not actually have any aspect that lets you travel and explore through space. Almost all of the traversal through "space" is loading screens and maps. It is completely avoidable and I felt practically incentivized to do so. Planets are empty gigantic open areas of seemingly random mishmash. City Environments feel baren and empty, New Atlantis is basically just a handful of stores placed across a giant empty floor. Starfield is like a comfort food game to me - familiar, but fresh and endearing. Perhaps this is because I grew up playing Bethesda RPGs. Or perhaps its because of the atmosphere the game itself produces.

Does it have its flaws? Oh definitely, Bethesda had gotten complacent and this game came out in the wake of the disastrous Fallout 76 launch, so it was already going to be viewed with heightened scrutiny. But it got an unfair, unbalanced hate mob mobilized by social media influencers needing to pay their bills, rather than a fair, balanced critique and analysis it deserved - praise for both its vision and creativity, and criticism for its repetitiveness.

The world of Starfield, not the procedurally generated planets, but the WORLD of Starfield itself is crafted with intriguing lore and attention to detail and love for science-fiction. It feels simultaneously utopian and dystopian, post-apocalyptic and ascendant, lived-in and empty, busy and quiet. This is a game that is contemplative, meditative, with a central question asking what it means to explore the unknown and if we are willing to accept that there might be no satisfying answers (or even answers we can comprehend). It dares to ask what it means to find one's purpose in a universe that appears to be utterly purposeless, and what that means for us as a species. The game's lore is appropriately esoteric and purposely conflicting, no surprise from the studio that brought us The Elder Scrolls, but the reveals at the end (and how they integrated the way of doing NG+ into the game world and lore itself) are absolutely incredible the first time through. This game is well worth your attention, especially on a sale, and if it's not for you then that's okay.

I've seen enough. Here's my opinion:

This game has a very solid base, and a lot went into the world building and design. But all of that falls short with the technical aspects. I don't know how to explain it, but this game feels like something from 15 years ago. Controls feels dated, ai feels incredibly dumb, gunplay feels boring and also dated. Leveling is way too simple and straight forward for this type of rpg. Followers are forced at the beginning and they are annoying as hell. They get in your way, get stuck on tables, take a seat in mid air and engage in the classic Fallout/Skyrim clunky combat. You are bombarded with info dumps from all sides, and it is quite overwhelming.

And then there is the story and quest system. Again, it feels old, uninspired and at the same time convoluted. Go talk to this person, join this group, go grab some random item from a pirate infested ship, etc. A lot is thrown at you, while you're still trying to get a grasp of the game. I got no less than 10 random non-related quests added to my journal by me just walking around the city, while my companion is talking to me constantly, and others try to do the same. All of the sudden I am loved and I'm surrounded by people that want me in their guild. I don't want that. I don't feel like I have a reason to do those things, and the dialog options always force you into a certain path. "Oh yeah, random miner, have my ship for no reason. You're amazing, go here and join this group of space explorers and become their favorite guy." "Oh, hi! Welcome to the Companions. Have a 4 star suite and join in our conversation!" "I think you should have the honor of placing this chunk of metal on our floaty hologram doohickey. You've done so much for us" (said the lady that I just met 10 minutes ago)

Then there is the massive amount of systems and mechanics that you're trying to learn, as the story forces you to keep going forward. Like, let me breathe! I don't want to travel to that planet/moon, etc. Not yet. I arrive at Mars, and not even 5 minutes later, that lady whose name I forgot, already wants me to jump in the ship and go to a different system, then to a random station, and then to some derelict ship. I don't even know what 90% of the ship's systems do, or how they should be handled, because a mini tutorial was thrown at me in the middle of a battle and some lady trying to talk to me about some group I don't care about.

Why do I need a spacesuit, if I can walk naked out in a planet with no oxygen and not die? Why do I have fuel if it never runs out, and I can travel wherever I want to? Why do I have a carry weight limit if I never get encumbered? Have I ran into a bug? Why do I have an option to sell items from my ship, but I get zero items listed, when I know they are in my ship's locker?

But anyway, another thing that really bothers me: This is a soft sci-fi/fantasy world, so why the hell am I stuck being a human, and there's only humans all around the universe? Where's the aliens? There should be different races, with different abilities, perks, etc. Speaking of which, the character design is horrendous. There aren't many CC options that even let you be however you want to look. Everyone looks blocky and... ugly.

Performance wise, this game runs great on my end. Experiences might vary. The game looks okay, but it doesn't hold to modern standards. It looks like Fallout 3 with texture and lighting enhancements. As mentioned before, the game looks and feels old.

Sound is terrible. While the music is great, sound effects are incredibly weak. Gunshots are very silent.

Controls are stiff, yet too snappy at the same time. You are either too slow or too fast.

Enemies are bullet sponges. And I get it that it is an rpg, but this is why I hate guns in rpg's. It makes for very unrealistic gunplay, when I have to unload two magazines into an enemy's face so they die.

Flying in space is pointless. I get what they were going for, but it doesn't work for a game. There is nothing out there. The scale is realistic, but it serves no purpose. You can't directly land in a planet either. They are a gigantic low poly balls with no collisions, and it will; literally take you real life days to get from one to the other without fast travelling.

I can go on, but I think I've mentioned everything that there is to be mentioned. I'll mod this game to hell, and see if that improves the experience. Vanilla = Not worth it.

Other reviewers say “wide as an ocean, deep as a puddle.” I completely agree with this statement. I especially hate the shallow exploration mechanic exploring the same ten “randomly” generated abandoned outposts occupied by the same infinitely respawning pirates and spacers, with no differences between the outposts except the terrain. Seriously, can’t there at least be slight differences inside and around the outposts?

I also hate the fact that a few of those outposts we are supposed to explore are clearly meant for a planet with an atmosphere, like the tall science outpost, but you can still find it on planets or moons with no atmosphere. This really breaks immersion when the massive open entrance area, which is also supposed to be the airlock, takes seconds to open and doesn’t even let the outside door fully close before opening the inside door.

The planets and moons all feel empty and bland, with no real settlements except the few created by Bethesda. Even those are quite bland and boring, except for New Atlantis, which is just okay on a surface level. Also, why doesn’t this game have the space equivalent of frontier towns? Since this is mostly a procedurally generated game when it comes to exploration, it really makes the planets feel empty, and unbeliveable that all of these outposts don't have any accociated local settlement that the workers commute from that isn't just 1 building or 4 habitats.

Are you seriously telling me people on a planet like Jemison only has one city/town? Does everyone there just commute to their outpost job on the other side of the planet? That could have been a fantastic way for Bethesda to explain why their main cities have such a low population, by explaining that the majority of the population lives in frontier towns and that large settlements don’t really exist anymore like they did in the old world.

The main story is really bland and unreplayable, except for the part of the main story involving the science outpost with the dimension shifting. Most of the side quests are quite shallow and boring, with no variation depending on your decisions, except for the Crimson Fleet infiltration story, which is still shallow in the end.

For some reason, you can join opposing factions the UC and the Freestar Collective and there is no real sense of progression in anything. Even when you supposedly cripple the pirate faction, they are still just as bountiful as before.

The lore of the starfield universe is uninspired, bland, and boring. For example, the reason that we can't visit the earth could have been more simply explained, that the earth is simply unopen to most of the people of the settled systems do to a settlement policy do to massive overpopulation and pollution with the earth goverment wanting to restore a more natural ecology to the earth and only their settlements in sol and in other systems that haven't become independent, being open to outsiders.

It would also be a much better explanation why the settled systems are so homogeneous compared to the real word, if the people of earth would have to evacuate in a few decades in a panic from the earth, they would be alot less homogeneous then the game portrays, with separate goverments choosing diffrent colonies for their populations. But instead they leave a gaping plot hole in the logic of the jump drives that they are all ticking time bombs from one bad part or bad refurbishment away from stripping away the atmosphere of an entire planet.

I despise the filler NPCs, which are somehow worse than other filler NPCs from a game that came out the same year as Bethesda’s last release fallout 4 before this one, The Witcher 3. This is mainly because they look ridiculous and don’t seem to be doing or going anywhere. In The Witcher 3, I can fully immerse myself in the fact that the filler NPCs in Novigrad are going somewhere for some reason, like going to the market or going to work to churn some butter, but here they are just awful, And the regular NPCs are no better, with them seemingly having no life, working 24/7 and requiring no sleep.

I honestly do not understand why Starfield gets so much hate. It is a genuinely impressive game with strong visuals and many beautiful, memorable locations, each with its own unique atmosphere and style. The scale of the game is massive, offering hundreds of quests, side stories, and hidden secrets to discover. Ship building and customization are deep and flexible, allowing you to create something truly personal and adapt it to your playstyle. Space combat is intense, satisfying, and requires real strategy rather than just button mashing. Exploration on planets is rewarding, with varied environments, interesting landmarks, and occasional surprises that make every trip feel worthwhile. The crafting, economy, and resource management systems are detailed and meaningful, giving purpose to gathering and upgrading. The main weakness is the characters, who feel flat and cardboard-like compared to the richness of the world, but this hardly diminishes the overall enjoyment. There are bugs, yes, but they are relatively minor and do not break the experience. Overall, Starfield is an ambitious, polished, and extremely engaging game that delivers far more than it is often credited for, and it’s easy to lose dozens of hours just exploring and experimenting.

Starfield, Bethesda Game Studios' ambitious space exploration role-playing game released in 2023 and enhanced by subsequent updates including the 2024 Shattered Space expansion, offers a richly detailed interstellar universe within the Settled Systems, where players uncover ancient artifacts amid faction conflicts and philosophical narratives. Its core strengths lie in unparalleled ship-building and outpost customization, fostering deep immersion and ownership, alongside engaging main and faction quests with moral depth, atmospheric horror elements in the expansion, and vast exploration across over 1,000 procedurally generated planets enriched by modding support and performance improvements. Nevertheless, the experience is tempered by notable repetitiveness and grind, particularly in planetary surveying, resource collection, and formulaic side missions involving similar outposts and combat encounters, which can diminish novelty during prolonged sessions despite serviceable mechanics and frequent loading transitions. Overall, Starfield remains a compelling recommendation for enthusiasts of open-world RPGs in a science-fiction setting, with its immersive triumphs and creative freedoms outweighing the repetitive elements, delivering hundreds of hours of discovery for dedicated players. Rating: 8.5/10.

I'm gonna start with the cons since they kinda overshadow the good.

Cons:

- The writing for the most part is god awful, at least for the main story. Literally "Uh, he's right behind me isn't he?" levels of writing. Feels like a PG-13 marvel movie set in space, yet somehow feels like you're being talked down to the entire time. I can't stand pretty much every single one of the main companions you get in the game, with the exception of Vasco. (I love Vasco so much and if you hurt him great harm will befall you.) So I tend to avoid the main quest, because the dialogue is just really bad and not a fun way. The concept is cool, but that's about it.

- The amount of loading screens and screen transitions for everything from leaving buildings to leaving a planet to traveling between planets and systems is insane. I feel like a large portion of my gameplay so far has been navigating menus, probably close to 50% of my game time. I've heard they're fixing this early 2026 so I'll edit this review when that's done.

- Settlements are as of this review (Jan 2026) pretty barebones. Coming from Fallout 4 it feels like they took a significant amount of steps back.

- The cities still feel pretty lifeless and incredibly small. Neon is the size of a small shopping mall. Like, I'm pretty sure I've seen interior locations in Fallout bigger than Neon. Akila City and New Atlantis are slightly bigger than Neon but they're maybe the size of a medium-sized hold from Skyrim at most. I know a lot of humanity was wiped out by the Colony Wars and leaving earth but come on dude the capital city of the UC shouldn't be the size of a suburb.

- I enjoy exploring planets, I just think the walkable area needs to be much larger and the POIs much further apart. No reason I should land on some random remote part of an uninhabited PLANET and see a bunch of factories and bases not even 1km apart, especially outside of settled space. Unfortunately that requires making planets more interesting in general, and I have no ideas on how to do that other than making it seem less like a randomly generated terrain box with little to nothing in the distance and more like you're actually exploring an entire planet. Maybe upgrade the fauna AI so you can do some more in-depth Xenobiology? Random interesting weather events you can document? Strange anomalies?

Pros:

- Customization is really good, still wish we had the option to mix and match bottoms and tops. Still not a thing in Bethesda games I guess lol.

- The aesthetic of the game is great, love the NASA-punk theme and the graphics (with some HDR tweaks) are absolutely beautiful. But I just have to say, please do something about the characters having completely dead eyes even when they smile. It's a little uncanny-valley.

- The ship building is really fun, I wish there were a little more options available to really make your ship yours (decals, hab shape variants, etc.) but it's still fun. I love making my ship cozy and just chilling in there out in the middle of space.

- Gunplay is really great in my opinion, better than Fallout 4 even. I could spend hours and hours getting into shootouts with pirates and spacers and it's fun every time. Fast paced but with room to be as tactical as you want, especially in higher difficulty settings.

- People tend to be really mixed on this, but I like the ship combat personally. It's a little simple but it gets the job done and feels responsive enough. Actually feels like you're flying a giant space boat, and you can really feel when you fire your guns, especially the cannons. Sound effects are great too, though I think if Bethesda is aiming for realism with the NASA-punk aesthetic they could make space truly silent unless you're in the cockpit, with maybe just some reverberation of the hull or deep rumbles or something. Also, we all want space walks. NMS has it now, Starfield still doesn't.

- This game captures the loneliness of what I imagine space travel to be like really well about 75% of the time. I love wandering around a planet after a couple shweezies of the beezy and getting lost imagining what it must be like to watch a different sun set on a different world. The strange nature sounds on lush planets, the muffled sounds on planets with low atmospheres, the strange and almost uncanny silence on a moon orbiting a massive gas giant. Makes you feel really small in a good way, but again I hope they expand upon terrain generation. It's pretty much all the same as of right now, I want to be able to wander into different biomes.

- The modding community is going strong and there are plenty of great mods out there to improve upon what Bethesda's done with the base game.

- There are genuinely plenty of different ways to play the game and make it YOUR space story, which in my opinion is what makes it a great RPG. As I've mentioned before, I hate the writing in the main questline so I've started doing anything from Xenobiology on one character to being a bounty hunter on another, to being a space trucker, to a chem dealer on Neon. It does allow for plenty of play styles, and I'm hoping Bethesda expands upon this even more.

Overall, wait for a sale. It's a fun game you can put hundreds of hours into but it's not the best Bethesda game by any means. The issues are frustrating and strange, but what the game gets right it really gets right. The potential is there though, and I'm really hoping this eventually becomes THE space RPG. Also please hire better writers, Bethesda. Where'd your Fallout and Skyrim team go?

Starfield is a wonderfully large game that fits in perfectly with every other Bethesda game that has been released. If you are looking for Fallout 4 in space, well, this is about as close as you are going to get! The game has several things it does better than Fallout 4, and several things it does worse. Here are a few bullet points if you don't feel like reading all of my thoughts.

The Good:
* Dialogue actually matches what you want your character to say
* Tons of planets, with some relatively diverse wildlife
* Picturesque views
* Satisfying gunplay
* Maneuvering on planet surface is easy
* Relative lack of bugs for a Bethesda title (only had one major bug and I have since fixed it myself)

The Bad:
* Ship combat in outer space is needlessly complicated and unfun.
* Ship travel from planet to planet is boring and done poorly
* Story is pretty forgettable so far (side content though isn't bad).

Ultimately, I have played 88 hours, and fully explored 3 of the roughly hundred solar systems in the game. So large is this game that if I continue my current rate of exploration it will take me 3000 hours to give a comprehensive review of every planet the game has to offer. The reality is that there will be many planets I don't touch to this level, because I cannot imagine the random generation gets more varied later in the game, and once I hit max level and have the highest level gear, the reward for exploration will just be the exploration itself.

For a gamer like me, this is fine. I love games that are built for explorers, even when the content itself is procedurally generated, because you can find some unintentional beauty in procedural generation sometimes. The human generated content that was done by hand is done well, and the worlds do feel lived in, although given the vastness of space, this is understandably few and far in between. If I have any complaint with this, it is that sometimes the game feels a little too large, and could do with some condensing to make the content that does exist shine more.

The gunplay is the most satisfying of any Bethesda game I have played, and it keeps me coming, even when I'm being swarmed by 10 Terrormorphs on a planet that the navy tells me I absolutely should not land on. I do fear later sections of the game being a bit repetitive, but that is why they allow you to edit reviews. I will edit this review if I need to in another 1000 hours.

The game follows the classic Bethesda formula, but seems dated in terms of how the quests and stories are structured. The gun play and combat is similar to Fallout 4 and skyrim and doesn't seem to be up to date with other similar titles.

The graphics looks amazing and they have stuck with a more "realistic" sci fi aesthetic rather than futuristic. 

I have played through the majority of the story and done a lot of ship building, colony building and quests  thoughout the known galaxy.

I have always enjoyed Bethesda games and have been a big fan of both the Fallout and Elder Scrolls franchises. I love Sci fi and have played all the major titles across multiple genres such as Mass Effect, Halo, Stellaris, Dead Space, Outer Worlds and X4, so I have experienced a lot of the aspects that Bethesda tries to cover in this game.

Overall it is a very traditional Bethesda game, but doesn't really live up to todays standards. The quests are slow, generic and repetitive. The characters arent that memoriable and unique and the lack of alien races doesn't seem to improve this issue. We have the classic stereotypes with Sarah as a Soldier and Sam as a Cowboy. The most memoriable character seems to be Vasco who is a robot with no story at all.

The colony building seems more limited than in Fallout 4 and you are stuck with the same modules even though you max out your skills - except for some upgrades to mining and some additional decorations.

Shipbuilding doesn't seem that exciting as the basic modules usually makes you end out with a sort of rocket shaped ship and in general the ship designs nudge you towards either a block or a rectangle due to the way the builder forces you to build the ship - the number of modules also seems very limited even though you mix and match between different manufacturers.

Ship combat is somewhat exciting, but you easily get ganged up on by pirates and the game lacks the finesse and flexibility in how you maneuver your craft such as in elite dangerous or X4. This means that space combat very easily becomes a slug fest. where you either target specific parts or have to use specific parts.

Enemy variety is a big issue as well as you have spacers, pirates, cultists and aliens. each have the same behavior and tactics as fallout 4 and are very easy to cheese. The gun play feel sluggish compared to other titles and the guns lack customizability in terms of how they look and feel in combat. For example the old earth rifle looks really weird compared to a normal springfield rifle which seems to be their inspiration. The varuun Starshard seems to be one of the best guns in the game, but it is limited what you can actually do to customize it.

Shipbuilding, colony building and weapon/suit crafting seems to be really important aspects of the game and they have designated quite the number of skills to these elements, but they seem lackluster compared to their importance.

Weapon and Suit variety is also an issue as most suits look the same, laser weapons are limited to orion, solstice and equinox while ballastic weapons have a lot of variety. The rarity system doesn't really make this better as you are constantly looking for the right mix of traits as normal weapons are kind of useless when playing on higher difficulties. the same for the suits.

Capacity is also a big issue in this game. The game wants you to pick up every ressource you find so you can upgrade, research and build, but you have very limited capacity. This leaves you with two options - either go back and forth between your spaceship/base or increase your capacity through the settings (if you have that as an option in your game you know it is bad!). suits, skills and food doesn't really solve this unless you change the setting, so you will spend a lot of time on traveling or constantly having low health.

Mods solve a lot of these issues and a lot of the story mods seems to be better structured and more engaging than the actual in game story - for example the cryomancer or farseer stories. mods that augments shipbuilding and add parts also makes up for this and mods that add different traits or upgrades to weapons and armor has also improved my game.

The only issue being that Bethesda is now taking money for these through their creations shop.

Overall i wouldn't recommend this game unless you want a fallout 4 in space, but with all the down sides of fallout turned up to the max as the game it self hasn't improved any mechanics beyond the graphics.

[h1]Skyrim vibes with added space travel![/h1]
This game is [u]a lot[/u] better than I would have given it credit for, and I'm honestly enjoying myself quite a bit. Now, don't get me wrong here: I'll be the first to state that this definitely isn't a perfect game or such. Heck, I've already experienced a few glitches myself.

Thing is... games don't have to be perfect in order to be perceived as such.

[b]Maybe too high expectations?[/b]

Each to their own (!) but I think that one of the issues with people not enjoying this game is setting your expectations too high. See, this [i]isn't[/i] "Skyrim in space"; space travel is simply an added game mechanic which exists within the way you normally play most Bethesda games.

So... no, you can't use your spaceship to sour over the surface of a planet in order to map out the location of most structures. Nor can you decide where you're going to land your ship. All of that is a bit static. However... the game does compensate for all that, because once you discovered a location on a planet you can tell the game to go there after which you won't have to go through the whole routine of landing and walking again.

And honestly?  I like it this way. Despite the fact that I already discovered quite a few locations I still more than often just refuse to fast travel and instead get into my spaceship, close the door(s), take a seat in the cockpit and then I take off. Only to do the test of the navigation once I'm in orbit. I even perform a (semi-) manual jump into the next system.

No, I'm [i]not[/i] "wasting my time", I'm roleplaying. Ever heard of it?

[h2]This game is [u]massive[/u][/h2]
There are a lot of NPC's for you to meet and missions for you to complete, and I really love it. Sometimes small, sometimes silly and sometimes you also need to make a bit of your own fun. And what I love the most here is that not everything gets presented to you or is made obvious.

For example...  early on in the game you'll discover the city of New Atlantis and [u]a lot[/u] of of the game will be done here or from here. Plenty of missions for you to pick up. And it seems like the perfect playing map... huge city, citizens everywhere and plenty of NPC's to talk with. Dare I say that the layout even gives me "Kotor" and "Mass Effect" vibes?

So [i[then[/i] I wondered... ey... the game also talks about vegetation, fauna and minerals ("resources").  Is there more to all this than the game is showing me?  So I decided to hop over a fence, slide my way down and... oh dear: all of a sudden I'm in a whole new (dangerous!) part of the world. And I'm [b]loving[/b] every moment of it. I even met other NPC's which got me laughing quite a bit: "[spoiler]I'm sorry, can't you see I'm busy dying?  ugh... [/spoiler]", and sure enough; that's exactly what happened (not by my doing btw!).

Experiences like these make me convinced that sometimes... it's also what you make of things. And this game puts plenty of attention into detail.

[b]Destructive tools are also weapons![/b]

I've seen this so many times: you have this powerful tool which is strong enough to tear through rocks, but as soon as you point it to some hostile creature then... "of course" it doesn't work, why would it? This isn't a weapon you silly player!

Starfield does that "a little" different and I was quite surprised when I discovered it. To me it simply adds up to the complexity and vastness of this game.

No, like I said before it isn't perfect...  but I'm sure am having a lot of fun so far!

[b]Get the editor too![/b]

Starfield, just like Skyrim before it, is a game that runs on its own so called "game engine". Studios often rely on such 'engines' to help them separate between the process of game design and actual game development. For example.... say I want to add a new datapack ("note")... thanks to the engine I don't have to worry about adding the right textures or having to make my own opening effects: all of that is something the engine can handle for me. [i]So..[/i] I just tell it that I want to add a new datapack ("Book" / "DataSlate") and the engine will handle all the details like the way it looks, how it'll sound when I pick it up, whether I can actually pick it up or not, etc. All I have to do is select what I want to use, add the text I want to add and eventually I also need to place this new item somewhere in the world.

No coding, no making new graphics, just design.  And that's what [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/2722710/Starfield_Creation_Kit/]the Starfield creation kit[/url] can help you with. If you're going to play Starfield then I highly suggest that you also pick up the editor. Heck... if you're stuck in a mission... you [i]could[/i] consider to check it out in the editor to see what you might be missing. 

[h1]In conclusion...[/h1]
Look, if you were expecting a whole new game with lots of different new mechanics and such.. maybe even secretly hoping for an actual spacesim (?) then sorry to say but you may end up disappointed. But if you can enjoy the idea of being able to travel through space and visit all sorts of strange planets and explore weird locations, meet new NPC's and such then you might be in for a treat.

The world is pretty big, and there's [u]a lot[/u] of stuff to discover & do, plenty to keep you busy for dozens of hours to come. The voice acting is very well done I think and although some characters look a bit weird... look, didn't we say the exact same thing for those in Tamriel?  Here I was thinking that elves would be the most beautiful beings in the world, not some bizarre looking hags.

Yes, there are loading screens and yes: your spaceship only gets used when you're actually out in space (so: in orbit), as soon as you're on a planet it basically becomes your (static) base of operations. Extra storage space to take with you wherever you go! ;)

But the vibes of old are all here...  exploring a planet, using your scanner and seeing "unknown" somewhere in the distance?  Let's go check it out!  Oh wait, there's another one!  Being able to find new loot, upgrade and customize your stuff, meet up with new friends (and enemies) ...

Each to their own, but I'm having a great time with this game, and can definitely recommend it because of that.

I have often given Bethesda games my silent approval, a simple thumbs‑up without the need for words, because their worlds spoke for themselves. My journey began with Fallout 3, sometime around 2012, and I was captivated by its strange brilliance: the absurd humor, the weight of a single choice, the way pressing one button could ripple through a mission and alter its fate. Exploration was not just movement across a map—it was immersion into loneliness, a haunting silence broken only by the fragile persistence of a fractured society clinging to life.

New Vegas deepened that spell. There, I was nobody, and in being nobody I was free to become anyone. The narrative did not bind me with a backstory; it invited me to carve my own. Fallout 4 enriched the formula further, and I lost myself in the endless creation of settlements, aided by mods, shaping entire communities from ruins. Skyrim, too, was a marvel, though its construction was more modest, its magic lying elsewhere.
And then came Starfield. What should have been the vast solitude of space instead feels like a hollow echo. Exploration yields not wonder but desolation, not because of the stars themselves but because the narrative is empty. Characters—companions, NPCs—stand scattered across worlds like seeds dropped from a careless hand, growing without roots, without ties to the soil of social, economic, or political reality. Even the companions falter: Sarah, for instance, is written as a commander of the United Colonies Navy and president of Constellation, yet her youth undermines the believability of such roles. The story becomes accessory, a backdrop without depth, leaving the player unable to truly empathize with its universe.

Gameplay repeats familiar notes: combat and ground exploration echo Fallout, while ship handling is reduced to a decorative gesture, a transition masked by loading screens—Planet → Orbit → Planet. Encounters with pirates or NPC vessels exist, but they feel like distractions, attempts to break monotony rather than meaningful engagements.

Construction, however, is where my disappointment crystallizes. Outposts and ships should be canvases for expression, yet here they are shackled. Other, older games—cheaper even—offered richer systems of creation. In Starfield, the player’s intent is overridden by the game’s logic. Build a ship, connect corridors and habitats, and the system responds by weaving a labyrinth of doors and stairs that defies human sense. What should be architecture becomes absurdity.

So, to you, READER WHO HAS NOT YET PURCHASED THIS GAME: watch gameplay footage before you decide. See for yourself the mechanics, the exploration, the construction. Do not rely on promises of vastness alone.

Edit (after playing 50+ more hours):  
My initial impression was negative, but after diving deeper I’ve completely changed my perspective. Two things stood out:

1. New Game Plus – Unlike other titles where NG+ is just a menu option after the credits, here it’s fully integrated into the narrative. Each cycle feels justified and meaningful, turning replayability into part of the story itself. This design choice deserves recognition.

2. The modding community – Creators have expanded the universe in incredible ways. One standout is WatchTower, which makes the galaxy far more dangerous with brutal battles, fleet management, and even air support. It’s a fantastic addition that feels worth every cent.

I also hope the developers continue creating more expansions that incorporate new functionalities. It’s not always about having a good story, but also about offering more options to build, create, and explore.

Together, these elements transformed my experience. What started as disappointment has become admiration for a game that grows richer with time and community creativity.
