Usually, I start my reviews with some sort of a backstory. Just because it's always interesting to know how did things happened the way they did, in my opinion. This time, though? There is nothing really interesting to tell. It's Todd Howard. End of the story. Todd was always a big fan of video games. One of the reasons why he wanted to join Bethesda. Todd used to love a game called SunDog: Frozen Legacy and always wanted to make such an epic space game himself. Bethesda wanted to explore a space theme too. They actually had that a game called The 10th Planet, which was ultimately canceled back in the '90s. So... yeah. Todd wanted something like that to happen, Bethesda wanted something like that to happen and, well, it happened. And since it's Todd we are talking about...

OK, OK, let's just admit it, we all knew it was going to be Skyrim in space. Everything Todd touches, he turns into Skyrim. Like I said, nothing really interesting to talk about. So, let's ask ourselves a question instead. What makes a good game? Personally, I believe it's two things. Said game should be interesting and addictive. You should always want to know what will happen next and the process of getting there should be as satisfying as possible. Ideally, those two things should co-exist, but honestly, even one of them is more than enough. Now, the problem with Starfield? The problem with Starfield is that it has neither.

First of all, I must say I really don't dig the “NASApunk” design (and yes, they actually called it NASApunk). I mean, it sounds cool, but it looks... boring. The Elder Scrolls IV had those stylish gates and impressive armor and weapons. Skyrim had that thing about dragons. Here? it's just some metal and space. And I get it, they wanted things to look realistic. Nice idea, actually. They actually tried to make visiting a moon for the first time a big thing (they really wanted you to feel like you're getting there for real), there are ruins of the old Earth, etc. The problem is—this game is anything but realistic. It was [i]planned[/i] to be realistic (more akin to Kingdom Come: Deliverance in a way, with tons of survival elements), but Todd thought something like that would be a “fun killer” and, as usual, decided to stick with his formula for success—to keep things as simple as possible. The result was a shockingly colorless game, in which most of the locations look exactly the same.

But OK, we can live with that. Unfortunately, the story is like that too. We are a random miner who found some boring-looking artifact and is now collecting more of those. The end. I mean, I do like it how the writing touches on lots of topics I am interested in—the quantum physics, the religion, stuff like that. The problem is—it does a terrible, terrible job with all that. Remember Star Trek: Discovery? A show, in which we had those giant tardigrades as a nod to the real-life creature of the same name that became the very first living being to become quantum entangled. We had a character named after mycologist Paul Stamets; we had that thing called the mycelial network... It was a brilliant thing. Lots of people disliked that show because it looks like they weren't ready for the a new way of thinking and just wanted more of the old-school “green men from outer space,” but still, it was rather brilliant fiction. Starfield? It just makes you chase artifacts and then tells you “a big truth,” which is extremely disappointing. And again, boring. So, the “interesting” part? Big fail. Now, what about the addictiveness? Well... about that.

See, Starfield is a pretty big game. It has lots of planets; you will be able to explore them (I like it how the map screen reminds me of SunDog), learn about their flora and fauna, you'll be able to build outposts (which are, like, an evolved version of settlements from Fallout 4), etc. Sounds cool. The problem is—there is neither reason nor real motivation to do that. The problem with Starfield is that it offers you lots of things to do, but somehow fails to make you [i]want[/i] to do them. Just think about it. You just wasted hours scanning planets for life and resources. What is your reward? Well, you can make some money from it and get a rather unimpressive amount of experience. That's pretty much it. Sounds like a lot of fun, huh? I mean, remember, there are lots of planets. 1,692 to be precise. It's a game you, most likely, will never complete, at least not for real. Just because you will get bored. Yet they failed to come up with an interesting mechanics for exploration and just gave us... this. Sure, there is also crafting, but, surprise-surprise, it's boring too. To craft something, you need to do the corresponding research first and it will require a hell of a lot of gathering, so... yeah. “Screw that, I am not going to waste my time on that” is the most likely outcome here. Joy.

And yes, before you say anything, it's still the Creation Engine. Creation Engine 2, sure, and it's, like, the biggest upgrade ever (technically, Todd did not lie when he said that planets would revolve around each other, at least not completely), but the infamous clunkiness is still there. And so are loading screens. Lots and lots of loading screens... And it's a bigger problem than usual, since while in, say, Skyrim all we needed to do to visit a certain NPC was to, well, go and visit them, here we are supposed to go to our ship, to take off from the planet, set a course to the right planet (the UI is incredibly uncomfortable, BTW), and only then will we be able to find our guy. In other words, we have got lots and lots of extra actions and loading screens between A and B. It's just... annoying. And it won't get any better.

Does that mean there is nothing good here? Well, I did like some features. Like, in Starfield we can disable enemy ships and then board them to take control. In other words, we can steal enemy vessels. And it's not a bad thing to have, but hey. Let's admit it. It has been a thing since the '80s (Starflight, Sentinel Worlds I: Future Past, etc.). Cannot call something like that an advanced feature in 2023. Same goes for hiring your own crew. Especially thanks to how basic that feature is. And again, it's something you probably won't bother with.

And it's not like this game is perfectly made either. I mean, of course it's not. it's from Bethesda after all. Still, it's rather shocking to see that after eight years in development this game gives you trouble... changing the resolution. Personally, I didn't even find the way to properly switch to 4K through the menus. Manually editing the .ini file was the only thing that helped. With the game being good it would be an easy thing to forgive, but like I said, Starfield is anything but good.

Is it bad? Well... not really, no. If you 'll find yourself on an uninhabited island with only this game installed on your laptop? It would totally be possible to have some fun with it. I mean, it's a game. It feels a lot like Skyrim in space (yes, it even has powers), there are ships to fly, guns to shoot, quests to finish, factions to join, etc. It's not like there is something especially terrible about it or something. And it's not like it's a complete mess. There are bugs, sure, but those are not overwhelming. Not at the moment I am writing this, at least. The problem is—at the moment I write this, there are more than 120,000 other games available on Steam. And lots and lots of those are [i]extremely[/i] good. Much better than Starfield. So, let me act like Mr. Spock and say that wasting your time (and as I said, Starfield wants, like, [i]all[/i] of your time) on this game? It sounds is illogical. There's literally nothing in this game that it does better than others. As sad as it's, Starfield is a boring routine, not an entertainment. Go pick up something else to play instead of it. Dixi.

Starfield is a first and third person, roleplaying game, set in it's own sci-fi setting and pursuing what the developers call a "NASA punk" aesthetic.  As someone who played hundreds of hours of Bethesda's previous titles and a big sci-fi fan I was really looking forward to Starfield, bought it on day one. 

The space cowboys, pirates and Starborn powers in Starfield don't really mesh well with NASA realistic aesthetic (not that any of them are badly done, they just don't fit).

Graphics are higher resolution than Fallout 4, but not as good as Cyberpunk 2077.  Starfield doesn't have Fallout 4's classic music either.
Starfield suffers from frequent loading screens, feeling like far more often than necissary (this has been improved a bit since launch). 

Starship piloting and driving (which was added after lunch to get around the foot slogging across Starfield's many desolate planets and moons) are both new to Bethesda and janky.

Base building and crafting are crippled by the bewildering variety of resource types in Starfield.  I never seem to have the right combination of resources to do what I was trying with these systems or any one stop shops to get the resources I needed.

The user interface around moving inventory items from the player to and from containers, NPCs and ships is also janky.  Bethesda have been doing this for decades, I can't believe they messed up this very common part of CPRGs this badly.

I achieved the game's goal of reaching the Unity before writing this review, in the hope this would unlock some saving grace, but no... just more of the same jank.

In conclusion I do not recommend Starfield, it is a total disappointment.

Easily the most over-hated and underrated game of the modern era. By no means a masterpiece, but the game's pros easily outweigh its cons. The world that Starfield immerses you in is absolutely beautiful. The planets are gorgeous and varied, the outposts are intricate with thoughtful details, the cities feel lived-in and bustling in their own way, the faction quests weave beautiful and engaging tales, and the characters are all incredibly interesting, each with their own backstories and motivations that draw you in.

I found the game's story to be very good overall. The Constellation quests are great, offering a true sense of uniqueness and exploration, with the concept of the Starborn and the multiverse being very well- executed and thought-provoking. The faction quests are all phenomenal - the Freestar Collective's frontier vibe, the United Colonies' political intrigue, and the Crimson Fleet's adventures stand out as highlights. The only story criticism I have is the Ryujin Industries questline - just no. It was trying to emulate Cyberpunk 2077, but it's clear Bethesda has no idea how to capture that essence properly. Again, just no - it SUCKED and felt extremely out of place. 

The way the New Game+ concept is implemented in this game has to be the best in any game ever, period- it's insane how it ties into the narrative and encourages replayability. Very creative. 

Gameplay-wise, I found space combat, regular combat, movement, the engine, and the overall gameplay loop to be all very interesting and engaging. It's very Bethesda in style, with clear elements reminiscent of Skyrim, but also upgraded and enhanced - you really feel the evolution in mechanics like zero-gravity fights or ship dogfights. The skill points system, customization options, traits, and all related features are also very, very, very well done, allowing for deep personalization and strategic builds that keep things fresh.

So one might think the game is a masterpiece... but it isn't. Starfield still has glaring issues - issues that have been exaggerated by the community, for sure, but issues that definitely exist nonetheless.: 

- Small cities
This is the number one thing that kills immersion for me. It's hard to believe that the cities of New Atlantis, Neon, and Akila are the biggest in the Settled Systems - especially New Atlantis, which feels way too small for an interstellar capital hub. The lack of crowd density only makes this issue even worse, as streets can feel empty and lifeless. Bethesda should've expanded the cities heavily, even if the new areas were inaccessible or just for visual scale. It would've made the world much more believable and immersive.

- Poor space travel and lack of things to do in space
While ship building and space combat are phenomenal and deeply satisfying, space travel itself is lackluster. I don't mind the orbit system, but we need a) hidden loading screens during grav drives, landings, and takeoffs to smoothen the experience, b) a cruise mode for interplanetary travel like the AstroGate mod for more fluid navigation, and c) more random space encounters, plus additional activities in space such as spacewalking. These would make the game much better, and I believe they're all coming in future updates, which I love - the potential for post-launch improvements is exciting.

- Creation Engine 2 issues
I find the Creation Engine to be beautiful visually, and it plays amazingly well in terms of performance. But there's one clear problem: rendering and loading screens. It's almost embarrassing that you have to experience a loading screen for entering a simple room in the game or an elevator - it kills immersion completely. Something like the RED Engine puts this one to shame in that regard. Starfield also has issues with rendering long distances. I think Bethesda should move to Unreal Engine if they cannot fix the loading screens and rendering issues, because they'll unfortunately get a lot of flak for it with The Elder Scrolls VI - fans expect better nowadays. 

- Outpost building is too surface-level
While ship building is phenomenal and detailed, allowing for creative and functional designs, outpost building is a bit lame in comparison. You can build a decent bit, but it doesn't have enough to do or depth. I'd like for it to evolve into towns with a population level, complete with a proper simulation experience where NPCs interact and grow. That would be even better, but it might be unrealistic for the engine's scope. It's cute as a small feature, but it needs fleshing out to feel like a core mechanic.

- Lack of interesting POIs
Unlike most people, the procedural generation system does not affect me negatively because it doesn't come at a decrease in handcrafted content - there's plenty of hand-made locations and quests. People act like nothing in the game was handcrafted, but that's not true at all; major hubs and story elements are meticulously designed. The problem is that there aren't enough possible POIs to spawn in when you randomly explore planets, which causes repetition after extended play. Nobody would complain about this issue if there were at least 50+ more POI possibilities to discover, with a deep algorithmic system embedded in the game to avoid repetition until you've seen all of them. Boom - problem solved with smarter variety.

I also have several suggestions to elevate the game further: an animal and plant life compendium for cataloging discoveries, a blood and gore overhaul for more visceral combat, pets (how do we not have dogs, cats, and alien pets!?!?! - huge blunder!), more properties to buy, businesses to purchase and manage for economic depth, the introduction of a limited banking system, more vehicles beyond ships for traversal, a better UI for smoother navigation, and an improved inventory system to handle loot without frustration. Most of these exist as mods already, but it would be better to include them in the vanilla game for accessibility.

I also have to commend the modding scene of the game. I particularly recommend StarUI for inventory and UI improvements, New Atlantis Awaits for expanding the city, Neon: Vertigo for enhancing Neon's cyberpunk feel, At Hell's Gate for an amazing quest, and Watchtower for better outpost management and a brilliant story. These mods show the community's passion and how Starfield's foundation is solid enough to build upon endlessly - people who say the modding scene is dead have NO IDEA what they're talking about. 

All in all, Starfield is a phenomenal game with some clear issues. Many of these have already been addressed post-launch, and while it seems like some more issues will be addressed in the coming months, many others are simply unfixable - which makes me sad. Regardless, this is a game I KNOW i'll be playing for years, and I can't wait until I get my hands on Starfield 2.. whenever it comes.

This game has many of the positive aspects of a Bethesda game.  Immersive first-person view, good voice-overs, and NPCs that have reactions based on choices you've made and things you've accomplished.

Sadly, it also has numerous negatives that take away from that immersion and make it feel like too much of a grind to maintain enjoyment.  Those negatives include:

👎 Inventory management:  I swear I spend more time encumbered or trying to figure out which resources to keep and which resources to sell.  Fallout 4's unlimited storage in a settlement's workbench was much better.

👎 Item interaction:  Per past Bethesda games, picking up anything and everything and finding a use for it is encouraged.  In this game, the Miscellaneous items are either decorations or vendor fodder.  These items are *EVERYWHERE* and in a game where you can manufacture all sorts of stuff, you cannot break these items down into components.

👎 Crafting:  Gated by skill points AND limited resources, crafting is uninteresting and yet another grind.  You can replace mods on items, but the prior mod is lost.

👎 Space suits, Helmets, Packs, Outfits, and hazards:  My end goal would be to have a set of equipment that lets me safely visit any or all destinations without having to constantly swap equipment to match the destination.  Firstly, the current implementation contributes to the inventory management and crafting issues.  Second, it means I can never just stick with the gear that has the visual aesthetic I want.

👎 Outpost linking:  Instead of having one landing pad per outpost that handles traffic for incoming and outgoing resources, you have to have a pair of landing pads per link (one at each end) and they're dedicated to that one link.  Once again, Fallout 4 had a better idea by allowing you to assign a settler to establish a link between settlements.  This should have been easily converted to Starfield with ships, crew, or a combination thereof.  In fact, it would encourage collecting ships and hiring more crew.  If things needed to be more complex, defining a ship's routes to different outposts would have been a possibility.

👎 Container linking bugs:  A cursory search online will show that there's a well-known bug involving linking storage containers and those links breaking if a player manually places any items in one.  The "fix" is to delete and re-establish the link, which when you have rows and columns of containers that are snapped together, is nigh impossible.

👎 Outpost object placement:  Specifically, rotation.  It's horrid!  The recommendation I've read is to use a controller for finer control, but I'm a keyboard and mouse player so that's not acceptable.  Object snapping is very limited and it's so difficult to place things neatly aligned.

All these negatives make the game feel like a complete and utter GRIND.  I have hundreds of hours in Fallout 4, largely because I enjoyed building out each and every settlement.  I have hundreds of hours in Satisfactory because I enjoyed building out sensible logistics.  Neither felt like a grind the way that Starfield does.

Starfield a great space exploration game in the action RPG genre by Bethesda Game Studios of the legendary Elder Scrolls and Fallout series. I can recommend it to players that like decent first or 3rd person shooter combat and like progressing their character with skill trees. 

Pros:
- pretty tight shooter combat
- lots to explore, many side missions
- new game plus extends play time on one character, unlocking more Starborn powers and slightly increasing the challenge each time
- overall good graphics and smooth performance
- has base and ship building
- has space dog fights
- an excellent modding scene to change all sorts of aspects of the game and add new content, and if you're on PC, you can use Nexus Mods that has the largest number of mods

Cons:
- minigame to get Starborn powers gets old after a while
- random points of interest are well done, but there aren't that many, so you'll see the same ones over and over - they only vary by level of the system and which faction occupies the POI
- space travel is not seamless; there is a series of load screens when not fast traveling
- paid mods - Creations - vary a lot in quality and value for their price
- points of interest can be kind of far from where your ship lands

Note that there have been some improvements since launch, such as adding land vehicles and the company has promised more content.

This is ... legitimately a below average game for being a "big studio triple-A" title. This doesn't even qualify as a "Bethesda game". Now, don't get me wrong, I enjoy some of their games, such as Skyrim, despite its flaws it's one of my all time favourites. The major problem is that everything that made Skyrim enjoyable for me is ... gone, in Starfield:

- World building is non-existing, and exploration is completely axed by a lazy map system with loading screens. Now I understand it's space and everything, but was it too hard to just ... make less planets and fill them with proper stuff to do? For example, Borderlands 3 did the planets system much better. You actually have things to do and explore, they're not just background, and they did not go over their heads with "space exploration in your ship". You CANNOT just pick a direction, walk, explore and find cool things. You look at a map, click planet, click destination, watch animation, wait for loading, you're there. Now you can MAYBE explore and just find the random spot 20 kilometers apart, conveniently shown already in your map.

- "Dungeons" (if you can even call them that...) are 99% just empty caves and abandoned facilities filled with Raiders. There's nothing. NOTHING. You just kill, pick the "rewards chest" and done. That's your dungeon. Now piss off. Rinse, and repeat. All the time. It's not even made interesting because of locations, everything is copy and paste. It all looks the same. And I thought Oblivion's dungeons were samey, this one takes the cake.

- Writing has been laughable since Skyrim, honestly, so I was not expecting anything. Writing is not something to play Skyrim for, but there are tidbits of something good here and there, it COULD be worse. And Starfield is that: worse. In everything. The characters are boring, the writing is so predictable and low effort, a children's book has more depth than this. I didn't expect it to be the greatest ever writing, but AT LEAST something good considering the time this game has been in development. But I guess until Emil Pagliarulo will be the lead writer, things can only get worse. Shame.

The only redeeming qualities of Starfield is the shooting (which is still far from great, but a good jump in quality from FO4), and to an extent the graphical presentation. I can't say anything, the game does thankfully look good, the art style is nice, and they seem to have done proper graphic updates to the engine, I can't deny that. 

But everything else both reeks of old and incompetent. Fallout 4 was already quite the dip in many aspects, but AT LEAST the gameplay loop kept it fresh, and the world building\design is actually fun, making Boston fun to explore and look at its many secrets.

Here? There's nothing like that. Just a mess of radiant quests, no real world building and design, boring "writing", uninspired everything.

I should have waited instead of pre-ordering it. This was my wake up call.

Starfield a great space exploration game in the action RPG genre by Bethesda Game Studios of the legendary Elder Scrolls and Fallout series. I can recommend it to players that like decent first or 3rd person shooter combat and like progressing their character with skill trees. 

Pros:
- pretty tight shooter combat
- lots to explore, many side missions
- new game plus extends play time on one character, unlocking more Starborn powers and slightly increasing the challenge each time
- overall good graphics and smooth performance
- has base and ship building
- has space dog fights
- an excellent modding scene to change all sorts of aspects of the game and add new content, and if you're on PC, you can use Nexus Mods that has the largest number of mods

Cons:
- minigame to get Starborn powers gets old after a while
- random points of interest are well done, but there aren't that many, so you'll see the same ones over and over - they only vary by level of the system and which faction occupies the POI
- space travel is not seamless; there is a series of load screens when not fast traveling
- paid mods - Creations - vary a lot in quality and value for their price
- points of interest can be kind of far from where your ship lands

Note that there have been some improvements since launch, such as adding land vehicles and the company has promised more content.

This is ... legitimately a below average game for being a "big studio triple-A" title. This doesn't even qualify as a "Bethesda game". Now, don't get me wrong, I enjoy some of their games, such as Skyrim, despite its flaws it's one of my all time favourites. The major problem is that everything that made Skyrim enjoyable for me is ... gone, in Starfield:

- World building is non-existing, and exploration is completely axed by a lazy map system with loading screens. Now I understand it's space and everything, but was it too hard to just ... make less planets and fill them with proper stuff to do? For example, Borderlands 3 did the planets system much better. You actually have things to do and explore, they're not just background, and they did not go over their heads with "space exploration in your ship". You CANNOT just pick a direction, walk, explore and find cool things. You look at a map, click planet, click destination, watch animation, wait for loading, you're there. Now you can MAYBE explore and just find the random spot 20 kilometers apart, conveniently shown already in your map.

- "Dungeons" (if you can even call them that...) are 99% just empty caves and abandoned facilities filled with Raiders. There's nothing. NOTHING. You just kill, pick the "rewards chest" and done. That's your dungeon. Now piss off. Rinse, and repeat. All the time. It's not even made interesting because of locations, everything is copy and paste. It all looks the same. And I thought Oblivion's dungeons were samey, this one takes the cake.

- Writing has been laughable since Skyrim, honestly, so I was not expecting anything. Writing is not something to play Skyrim for, but there are tidbits of something good here and there, it COULD be worse. And Starfield is that: worse. In everything. The characters are boring, the writing is so predictable and low effort, a children's book has more depth than this. I didn't expect it to be the greatest ever writing, but AT LEAST something good considering the time this game has been in development. But I guess until Emil Pagliarulo will be the lead writer, things can only get worse. Shame.

The only redeeming qualities of Starfield is the shooting (which is still far from great, but a good jump in quality from FO4), and to an extent the graphical presentation. I can't say anything, the game does thankfully look good, the art style is nice, and they seem to have done proper graphic updates to the engine, I can't deny that. 

But everything else both reeks of old and incompetent. Fallout 4 was already quite the dip in many aspects, but AT LEAST the gameplay loop kept it fresh, and the world building\design is actually fun, making Boston fun to explore and look at its many secrets.

Here? There's nothing like that. Just a mess of radiant quests, no real world building and design, boring "writing", uninspired everything.

I should have waited instead of pre-ordering it. This was my wake up call.

TL:DR; Bethesda questing game set in space; if you enjoy that sort of thing, wait for a sale. 

You know, I'm having a great time with this. 

If you play Starfield looking for a spaceflight sim, or a sci-fi shoot-em-up, or Bethesda-Jedi, you will be disappointed; but if you play Starfield as a questing game set in space, you'll probably enjoy it!

Honestly, I think the 'mixed' reviews are partly because of people overhyping themselves on what to expect; it does quite a few different things reasonably well - as a game it's gone for a selection of options to keep you engaged, rather than deep-diving on one particular aspect. 

It plays quite similarly to Fallout 4 in regards to combat, somewhat Skyrim++, but without VATS. I vibe pretty well with that style of combat, but it's not for everyone. That, and you will have to be more proactive to discover quests, tasks, and what-have-yous; space is big, it's easy to miss things. 
My biggest praise is for the worldbuilding and setting. It's a really novel near-future world (worlds?) with some excellent attention to setting detail and history. I'm having a great time learning about the history from 2025 to 2305. 

My biggest disappointment is actually the music and soundscape; whilst most of the music is great (Bethesda usually are ppretty good with their soundtracks), there are a few tracks that are extremely irritating to listen to: discordant, inconsistent in intensity, and enormous ear-worms that refuse to leave my brain. 
So much so I've turned off the music and replaced it with ambient tracks on winamp... which then highlights the noticeable lack of good ambient / environmental sound in busy areas. It seem the music was doing the heavy lifting there. 

The thing they could improve the most? More variety in radiant missions - the ones you get from random little settlements. 

I don't think this game is worth £59.99; don't buy it at that price. £29.99? Sure. Anything less than that, give it a go!

Took about thirty hours for the game to click with me, and once it did I was able to really get into it. The game unfortunately feels like the core systems for three different games were cut out and glued together, which can occasionally lead to really fun gameplay, but more often than not results in tedium. 

Despite this, I really appreciate how the game innovates upon the loop from Fallouts 4 and 76. Where those two games slowly pushed for more survival-lite mechanics, Starfield introduces optional systems for hunger and status effects that can enhance gameplay pressures, and lead players to engage with the cooking and pharmaceutical crafting systems that were previously easy to overlook. 

The weapon customization sees a handful of improvements over previous titles, with the recon scope being much more useful, and its effect being available on scopeless weapons via a new laser sight. The only real setback in the weapon customization department comes from weapon tiering, which while keeping loot engaging into the later hours of the game, prevents many unique weapons (Fiscal Quarter comes to mind as an obvious example) from being useful at all, especially upon entering New Game+.

New Game+ is a first for a Bethesda RPG, and it adds a compelling source of replayability, allowing players to keep their skills while also being able to solve problems in different ways. Unfortunately, this isn't as compelling as it could be. The main story features little variance, and outside of a single choice at the end of the story, the only place where a choice actually felt significant was during the Crimson Fleet faction questline. 

Stealth gameplay saw a handful of improvements over previous Bethesda RPGs. The Ryujin Industries questline is entirely based around stealth and espionage, and even killing enemies is frowned upon. To enable more effective stealth, non-lethal options are available for many energy weapons, allowing enemies to be incapacitated instead of outright killed. Additionally, limited invisibility effects and stealth chems are featured, alongside a number of skills that enhance stealth capabilities. Level design for stealth-specific quests is also regularly very good, featuring security cameras to avoid or destroy and occasional disguises.

Dialog is fun, but only sometimes. Skills, traits, and your character's background can open additional dialog, which allows for certain persuasion challenges to be skipped, or for additional resources or information to be provided. The persuasion challenges have been expanded to full minigames, where you need to select the right options to win over your target, each of which will slowly chip away at convincing them.

Smuggling is technically a feature of the video game, and that's all I have to say about it.

Ship customization is fun, though cargo capacity can be a bit annoying early on. My final ship ended up being a behemoth with automatic particle turrets, 4500 cargo capacity, and ten entire landing legs. Money becomes no obstacle as the story progresses, allowing the ship customization to truly open itself to you, and I truly believe that in a different game this system would be really good. Alas, it isn't, and so it feels mostly like a novelty.

Basebuilding is back, and this time you don't have to spend like thirty dollars for all of the building items. It's fine. There's an achievement for connecting five bases with cargo links, and it made me want to pull out my hair, but otherwise it's an interesting enough system.

The story is decent, but it takes a while to get good. Took about thirty hours for the game to click with me, and once it did I was able to really get into it. The game unfortunately feels like the core systems for three different games were cut out and glued together, which can occasionally lead to really fun gameplay, but more often than not results in tedium. 

Despite this, I really appreciate how the game innovates upon the loop from Fallouts 4 and 76. Where those two games slowly pushed for more survival-lite mechanics, Starfield introduces optional systems for hunger and status effects that can enhance gameplay pressures, and lead players to engage with the cooking and pharmaceutical crafting systems that were previously easy to overlook. 

The weapon customization sees a handful of improvements over previous titles, with the recon scope being much more useful, and its effect being available on scopeless weapons via a new laser sight. The only real setback in the weapon customization department comes from weapon tiering, which while keeping loot engaging into the later hours of the game, prevents many unique weapons (Fiscal Quarter comes to mind as an obvious example) from being useful at all, especially upon entering New Game+.

New Game+ is a first for a Bethesda RPG, and it adds a compelling source of replayability, allowing players to keep their skills while also being able to solve problems in different ways. Unfortunately, this isn't as compelling as it could be. The main story features little variance, and outside of a single choice at the end of the story, the only place where a choice actually felt significant was during the Crimson Fleet faction questline. 

Stealth gameplay saw a handful of improvements over previous Bethesda RPGs. The Ryujin Industries questline is entirely based around stealth and espionage, and even killing enemies is frowned upon. To enable more effective stealth, non-lethal options are available for many energy weapons, allowing enemies to be incapacitated instead of outright killed. Additionally, limited invisibility effects and stealth chems are featured, alongside a number of skills that enhance stealth capabilities. Level design for stealth-specific quests is also regularly very good, featuring security cameras to avoid or destroy and occasional disguises.

Dialog is fun, but only sometimes. Skills, traits, and your character's background can open additional dialog, which allows for certain persuasion challenges to be skipped, or for additional resources or information to be provided. The persuasion challenges have been expanded to full minigames, where you need to select the right options to win over your target, each of which will slowly chip away at convincing them.

Smuggling is technically a feature of the video game, and that's all I have to say about it.

Ship customization is fun, though cargo capacity can be a bit annoying early on. My final ship ended up being a behemoth with automatic particle turrets, 4500 cargo capacity, and ten entire landing legs. Money becomes no obstacle as the story progresses, allowing the ship customization to truly open itself to you, and I truly believe that in a different game this system would be really good. I don't have much to add that hasn't already been said. It definitely feels like a Bethesda game, except that there's very little to explore that isn't throwaway procedural content. All the Bethesda jank is still present with the positively ancient game engine they stubbornly continue to use, tons of bugs and glitches that won't ever be officially fixed, and awful balancing with the skills and weapons. This is sadly normal for a Bethsoft game, but the redeeming virtue was a handbuilt world full of interesting places to explore. Take that away and you end up with Starfield.

I'm not going to say it's the worst game ever because it's not and it can be fun to play (some mods are practically essential though), but it's definitely a massive disappointment. There's so many missed opportunities in the game and so little interesting content outside the story missions. I kind of see what Todd Howard was going for, but the game missed the mark pretty badly. There's not really an easy fix, what this game needed was a lot more direction and time to flesh things out and there's not much for modders to really work with to properly fix the base game.

If I had to pick some feasible (i.e. not needing to build a completely new engine/game from scratch but still probably a lot of work) things to do to fix the game, here's what I would do:
- Add a LOT more points of interest that can be found (hundreds, see Empyrion Galactic Survival) with multiple variations (different factions/state of repair for a standard outpost layout for example)
- Give earth it's own unique POIs and biomes to actually look like an abandoned planet with the ruins of civilization and have a whole scavenger faction/questline that searches for hidden treasures in the ruins
- Add a lot more hand built locations to make the systems actually feel lived in
- Vastly increase ship cargo hold capacity, especially in the early game
- Rebalance skills to make everything useful in some way even in the end game
- Rebalance resource and crafting, especially weight (crafting magically creates mass out of thin air in way too many recipes)
- Bring back something like VATS, this is a RPG and it was really nice in Fallout to be able to RP a super sniper/gunslinger without personally having the crazy shooting skills
- Rebalance combat so all guns are viable in the end game and have appropriate variants (bonus points for a full combat system overhaul with more realistic gunplay and not the magic damage increases from skill points and pitifully low damage per bullet with full auto, make most guns select fire and make skills affect accuracy, recoil mitigation, reload speed, aim speed, etc, and have weapon damage be calculated primarily from the ammo plus use the barrel length as a lesser modifier).
- Add mechs and small aircraft that can be used on planets

Just like the general vibe of the average reviewer, I have mixed feelings about my experience playing this game.

Overall I find it to be satisfying and engaging. I have certainly gotten many hours of gameplay out of it and that's a difficult bar to clear for any game these days. I enjoy the story, the characters and voice acting even if some of it does seem like generic filler (hey, it's a big game with lots of content). There are a good variety of things to do to keep me busy with like questing, combat, character building, base building, ship building, storytelling etc. You can get sucked into any one of these things and waste endless hours of your life before even noticing, which is what games are for, however...I completely understand why people complain endlessly about it.

Personally, my biggest gripe is the perplexing absence of quality of life features. Things as simple as having a scroll bar enlarge when you hover over it so that you can ACTUALLY target it to move it up and down the screen. I don't know how many times I have made a proper fool of myself trying to click a scroll bar in the inventory just to have it not activate because it's tiny and doesn't automatically enlarge when hovering over it with the cursor. Most primitive websites have figured this out in the 90s yet BS didn't find it prudent to include as a feature. Also, every time you fast travel with a companion following you, they spawn directly in front of you so that you always have to run around them to go in the direction you're intentionally travelling. Did they not play their own game? Did they not have time to fix this obvious persistently annoying issue? Are they purposefully antagonizing me? It boggles the mind. These are just a few of the dozens of amateur-rank QoL features overlooked which makes you wonder how much pressure is put on the devs to wrap up their slice of the pie, and how little regard is allocated to fixing these issues post-launch. 

I also loathe Bethesda's approach to carryweight, inventory management and a cruel penchant for cluttering up the game with completely useless items that can be picked up for no discernable reason. I feel like I'm being mocked by every junk item laying on the ground. It completely takes me out of the game when I have to stop and look up every item to see if it has any use at all, especially when you taunt me with your ridiculous inventory management system. I suppose I'll never have to worry about Alzheimer's trying to memorize all that crap, but that should be my choice, not yours.

Once you figure out how to get around all that annoying rubbish, it can be a pretty fun game worth many hours of play, especially if you like sci fi and spacefaring.

[h2]Likes:[/h2]
- It is a fun and casual extraction/shooter

- PvP can be fast paced, but you can also have fun & wholesome interactions with friendly players

[h2]Dislikes:[/h2]
[u] Inventory Management [/u]. It can be bothersome without knowing what to keep or get rid of until you've got some time in the game, and sometimes you can unknowingly sell off a hard-to-find item that you'll need to turn in a couple missions later (only to spend hours trying to find later on). 

I wish that most items, aside from the 5 basic building blocks (i.e., cloth, metal scraps, plastic, chems, rubber pieces) could stack a bit more. This could be mitigated if we could turn in workshop upgrade items  as we obtain them, instead of needing to hoard everything until we have 100% of the necessary items.  

[h2] Overall Takeaway [/h2]
I've enjoyed playing Arc Raiders as a solo player trying out various methods of play, be it as a friendly medic or as a stealthy guy trying to stay off other people's radar. I've also thoroughly enjoyed going in as a team of of 2 and 3 people actively looking for fights. This game is definitely what you make of it, so if you like extraction style shooters, then I'd suggest you give it a try. Voice comms, in my humble opinion, make this game much more enjoyable, but it will vary depending once again on how much you put into it.

I have multiple friends who have never played extraction shooter games or any real punishing games in general who are absolutely hooked on this game less than 10 hours in. As someone with 300 hours and 130 topside, this game just gets even more fun the more you play and learn. The game is much more straightforward than your typical extraction shooter at the surface, but as you play more, you realize the depth of some of the mechanics and the variety of ways you can play. There's rats, opportunists, betrayers, PvE players, PvP players and everything inbetween. Most low level solo lobbies are filled with peaceful players which often leads to low level players working together to learn the game and start completing their early game objectives. I originally picked up ARC raiders hoping it would replace the gap left by The Cycle Frontier. It didn't do that. Rather, it gave me something else: it gave me ARC Raiders. And ARC raiders is awesome.

This game doesn’t scream at you—it watches you, waits, and then punishes your mistakes.

ARC Raiders absolutely nails atmosphere and tension. The world feels hostile and lived-in, like you’re scavenging through the aftermath of something big and unknowable. The ARC machines aren’t just enemies—they’re part of the lore, and every encounter reinforces that.

PvP is where it really shines. Fights feel earned, unpredictable, and brutal without being spammy. No constant chaos, no gimmicks—just positioning, sound, timing, and nerve. Every player encounter gets your heart rate up because the stakes actually matter.

This isn’t a game that holds your hand. It respects your intelligence and rewards patience and awareness.

If you like extraction shooters with real tension, strong worldbuilding, and meaningful PvP, this one’s a no-brainer.

For many new players, it may be difficult to start ARC Raiders at this stage, whether they are primarily interested in PvE or PvP. In practice, beginners can be repeatedly killed by experienced players roaming the starting area, losing whatever basic loot they have gained from early PvE encounters.

The game appears to offer limited early-game protection or onboarding space where new players can learn core mechanics and build a minimal gear baseline. As a result, new entrants are being forced into unfair PvP engagements against players with substantially more time in the game.

This is a known challenge in extraction-style and open PvPvE games, and other titles often address it through measures such as starter-zone protections, matchmaking bands, opt-in PvP, grace periods, or other guardrails. In ARC Raiders, the current setup can create a persistent imbalance: some experienced players enjoy preying on new players in early areas, new players churn, and the environment continues to favor established players, which in turn discourages new-player retention.

If you enjoy the struggle and challenge of trying to survive a very hostile, and sometimes toxic player environment, while trying to enjoy the beauty of the game - give it a shot.
If you are like me who think a game should provide ample opportunities to actually experience the game you payed good money for, stay away.

The reverse of that coin is creeping in silence or waiting to target unaware raiders is evidently the safest way to play. This, unfortunately, becomes the most profitable way to play which ultimately overshadows the excellent PvE content. Fighting Arc is at it's core, simple and fun. Even after learning weaknesses and patterns I felt that adding my own challenge by working to keep as many raiders alive and well looted made the matches refreshing. It became less about loot and more about laughs. Great map layouts [Buried City might be the best multiplayer map ever] and increased pressence on environmental conditions also help rotate you through new encounters. The focus of the PvE content becomes about goofing around or becoming more daring for the sake of your fellow raiders enjoyment. The focus of PvP content becomes all about isolating yourself or sticking with your party with little raider interaction. The difference between the two play styles is so polarizing that I don't really feel that playing without aggression is viable anymore.
Overall I loved the time I have put into it and the experiences that were generated from other raiders but no matter how hard I have tried, these last few days have been filled with raiders no longer interested in cooperation. I love Arc raiders, its my cozy game now! "Cozy??? How is Arc Raiders Cozy?!?!" I hear you saying, scarred from 99 matches of pvp in a row, but Hear me out... 

A Non PvP-er's review

Going into this I did NOT expect it to hit so hard but this??? This?? this is a game! Game of the year? Game of the decade! 

I've been adulting for some time and not been fully enraptured into a game for quite some time, since games like skyrim, Left4Dead, and Black ops 2, a lot of stuff just feels like fillers these days, but holy moly does this game shake up the scene!

It takes me back to Early Gmod days, where Proximity chat + fun games  was a great time, for whatever reason games went silent. You really didn't see anything quite like this, team v team games usually let you talk to your team, and battle royale games let you talk to your friends, this game lets you talk to everyone. It really feels like a social experience first, before its a shooter. The game really feels cozy, I've seen girls come to this game from Animal Crossing of all games, and heres why:

The aggression based match making is the perfect solution, to satisfy many playstyles. Where my friends have said they had to drop this game because the PvP is too toxic its every match for them, and I have to look at them a little dumbfounded. As I've been able to just hop in, find easy-going gamers and have a good time =) It's such a wonderful time helping and working together. I love the vision of a robot army uprising, us VS them gameplay game with uneasy alliance. 

Sure sometimes you get exploded fifteen billion times by a guy using ten different trip mines and eating cheetos loudly, but that happens so rarely. A player could misfire shooting right past us, Where some of my friends spring up like a cat spooked by a cucumber, thinking maybe this person turned on us, I just think maybe the friendly misclicked.

I love going on Combat-Medic runs, where I go agile and try and heal / revive as many players as I can, and support team fights against big arcs, something about it feels like a new kind of fun. Being helpful as a treat, contributing to the total joy in the lobby as much as possible lol. Sometimes PvPers find their way into my lobbies (which is insane hahaha, my lobbies are usually 100% chill.) 

And a lot of the time, it works out =). The stories, decisions, moment-to-moment, and the general feel of this game all feel so riddled with stakes, and consequence, mixed in with a narrative that is bitingly real. I think it was about time for a game like this. One where sure you're free to do whatever, but the core concept? The core heart of this game?

That would be the teams of strangers helping out one another, gifting the newbie things, risking their biscuit to revive others, people they'll likely never see again, whole squads of randomly assembled troops taking down a common enemy and not ruining eachother's fun even though the incentives are there?! That creates such a chaotic and fulfilling experience, that can strengthen a friendship and even lead to new ones! That, in my opinion, is what Arc Raiders is about. Humanity's capacity to come together and rise up against a task that is greater than yourself! 

So with all that said, You can't do it alone raider! Happy raiding, and maybe bring a defib... Maybe... For any unfortunate Cozy gamer that gets caught in the crossfire.

I really tried to like this game. The core gameplay is fun: avoiding or destroying the ARC, looting, and extracting. However, there will always be players who abuse the matchmaking system.

The main appeal of an extraction shooter is the uncertainty: What will happen? Can I trust this person? You never really know. In this game, we have Aggression-Based Matchmaking, which works on paper, but human nature is unpredictable. There will always be players who find ways to exploit the system.

For weeks, I didn’t have to worry about getting shot in the back. Now, in almost every match, someone betrays me, and I end up losing weeks of loot. Just like that, gone.

The game is marketed as a PvE experience with PvP elements, but almost every mechanic fails when PvP is involved, especially for solo players.

Want to grab a Queen Reactor? Just drop with nothing, use the free safe pocket, loot the first breakable part, and die. No effort, no risk.

Want to complete Trial Challenges? Pray you don’t load into a lobby with sweaty tryhards. They will show no mercy if you attempt trials in the same match.

It’s a great concept with huge PvE potential, but all of it is wasted because of PvP.

This game is an absolute blast. Some of the most intense and sweaty multiplayer shootouts I've ever had while simultaneously being one of the coolest naturally social games I've played. The PvPvE gameplay is fresh and fun, and going topside to scrounge up materials while fighting for your life is a joy. Totally worth the price.

All that being said I have some major concerns with the state of the game and its future. I have full confidence in the devs to find a strong equilibrium with the mechanics of the game and continue to take new risks while continuously releasing updates, but I also can't remember a time I've been so torn between salivating to boot up a game while also completely dreading it.

Currently the community is divided between purely PvP and purely PvE in a game that offers clear ways to enjoy both. Just go to any tiktok, twitch clip or reddit thread and you'll see in every single comment section PvP players calling PvE players whiners and dilusional for not expecting to be shot in the back in a game that might as well be called "shot in the back simulator 2026" And conversly you'll see PvE players blaming the games toxcity and lobbing personal attacks at anyone who dares camp the extraction point in a game that totally encourages you to do that.

Thanks to these opposing camps, it creates an edge to every round where you don't know who's friend and who's foe which is really the game's secret sauce for infinite hours of fun/fear. While I personally enjoy both aspects of the game, the severely underwhelming endgame content (a hefty prestige system and I guess raid bosses?) and the rapid speed at which players obsessively consume it's content as quickly as possible, has lead to a growing majority of players chosing PvP as the only real end goal. Because for as inteligent as the enemies are, nothing beats the rush of getting into a life or death firefight with a real person. I do believe PvP has a place in the current landscape of the game, but unfortunately ARC Raiders is starting to lose the unique interactions that made it so speacial in favour of a pure extraction battle royale.

To prove my point, there has been some bizarre gamer psychology bent around the game's matchmaking. Large swaths of players have been trying to "cheat" the system to get back into "PvE friendly lobbies" which don't actually exist. They don't exist because for as much as people would like to believe if you're a "good gamer" you'll be specially selected to join a group of like minded "good gamers" who want to loot peacefully and dance around in a circle holding hands, HOWEVER there will always be players in EVERY lobby with GOOD and BAD intentions. The fact that players despise the PvP part of the game so much they'd rather spend their time fighting the matchmaking system than other players, illustrates its biggest problem. The game's systems have created a negative feedback loop either intentionally or unintentionally. 

As an example, "friendlies" try not to shoot first and die to PvP players who are ecstatic to smoke someone who gives away their position and hesitates before pulling the trigger. Which then leads to once friendly players tired of dying and losing all their shit, choosing to shoot first, completing a cycle of turning friendly players into PvP players, effectively decimating their own population and growing a bloodthirsty one.

So while I do enjoy hopping on and playing with friends in duos or trios, getting into intense fire fights and barely making it out with my well earned loot, playing the game solo has become an incredibly taxing and miserable experience. Where paranoia wins out over trying to cooperate with strangers, leading to those cool ermergent social experiences, quickly dying off.

I don't know what the solution is and I don't think Embark does either. Its the natural progression and growth of a game community happening right before our eyes, for better or worse. While the game is still very fun and totally worth a try, at this time, I can't find myself playing much more of it. The game has begun its rapid slide into the battle royale category. A genre that doesn't really entice me as much as it might other players. While I'm very much looking forward to more updates and shake ups, I'm also incredibly weary of a community that has started to turn a super unique multiplayer experience into a run of the mill PvP looter shooter.

Arc Raiders is a competent third person shooter only bogged down by the genre in which it presents itself and the story.

In the game, you begin as a nomad wandering down a road waiting to be given a tutorial on basic shooter and looting mechanics. Afterwards, you find a home with an indeterminant group of people who wander around a partially sunken city at all hours. These people send you and other players in pneumatic bank tubes to five areas so as to kill each other and find parts for expresso machines. The world has been destroyed, likely by the cliche evil AI that plagues the imagination of many science fiction writers. There isn't much more to the story than that there may be humans and robots in space.

The gameplay consists of inventory management, point selection in three skill trees which offer minute enhancement to the player's character, and spawning onto five maps to collect materials to make the next spawn in easier. The movement in the game is about as good as Eldin Ring. The player does not get a yak to ride, but must sprint around a map and sometimes roll. The shooting mechanic consists of pointing at weak points on drones, some drones have yellow colored weak spots, and others have propellers to shoot off, and shooting a leaving player in the back at the end of the match after indicating oneself to be friendly. Weapons do use projectiles and must be aligned accordingly to strike distant targets.

 Speaking of weapons, the weapons offered are rather strange in that there are colored tiers of weapons, but the higher tier is not usually better. The most perplexing to me is that there are legendary weapons which are markedly inferior to an easier to acquire lower tier. Other than the three legendary weapons, weapons have the ability to be upgraded four times and to have added attachments as to increase their ability.

There are some quests, but they are somewhat tedious or silly. The story presents itself poorly, although the story isn't good. I've seen rude people in any game that is multiplayer and this game is no exception. However, if you conduct yourself courteously and utilize voice chat, you will be spared the virtual back shooting 99% of the time.

I've played much longer than I realized. I have had very memorable instances of meeting a stranger or two and taking on the two largest bosses in the game. I have stored up the most coveted items. I have been shot in the back by people I have revived or otherwise aided. My pvp experience has only ever been to defend myself or another at the extraction elevator or extraction train. Generally, I have had fun with the game, but there comes a point when the maps have been explored, the guns have all been collected, and there is nothing to do. This isn't unique to Arc Raiders, but the five maps and no end game content do detract from the game's value, in my opinion.

I will add that you may erase your character and begin again. This is a prestige mode which grants the new character a permanent five extra skill points if the player collected five million in currency and items previously, along with twelve extra home base inventory slots. I have also read that there will be multiple new maps added this year of 2026. There are even supposed to be new enemy types added.

As I've gotten older, I've struggled to stick with games for awhile. But occasionally a game comes along that grabs my attention, and Arc Raiders is one of them.

[h2] General Gameplay [/h2]
It's a super fun and addicting gameplay loop where you drop into a raid, loot what you can, kill some ARC enemies, maybe kill some other players, and then extract. Whatever you managed to extract with, you get to keep. You can take it into the next raid, or you can put it in your ever-growing stash for later.

If you're struggling with managing your stash, I'd say recycle cheap guns you don't need at the moment, especially the easy to craft ones. I was holding onto everything for awhile and it was taking up a ton of space. Same with other items that are easily craftable once you level up your workbenches. It's worth hanging onto things like Springs, Wires, Duct Tape, etc. that you can only find topside or buy in limited quantities from Celeste.

[h2] PVP [/h2]
I'm not sure if it's officially been stated by Embark, but aggression-based matchmaking does seem to be real to some extent. As I was learning the game and leveling up, I mainly was focused on getting loot and killing ARC for quests and to level up my workbench. Most other raiders were friendly and doing the same thing. I only got shot at a handful of times in the first 20 hours or so. Eventually I wanted to try out some PvP, so I started killing people I came across. This definitely put me into lobbies where everyone was shooting on sight.

This has held true for the most part in the 100 hours I've played so far. That's not to say if you're a passive player, someone won't decide to kill you and take your loot, but it's definitely not as sweaty as the hardcore PvP lobbies.

Generally though, people have been very friendly in this game. I've had people drop me blueprints and other items, and I've teamed up with people to take out some of the bigger ARC enemies. Only twice have I had someone say they were friendly, and then shoot me while I was looting. It sucks, but it has been very rare in the whole time I've been playing. Most PvP players will just shoot on sight in my experience.

[h2] Stability [/h2]
I have run into some stuttering mid-game (usually seems to be a connection thing, as I see the icons flashing on the right side of the screen), and a few times it's just totally frozen for a couple of seconds, but generally the game runs pretty smooth on my computer, and I haven't adjusted any settings. It's only crashed once for me in 100 hours.

[h2] Suggestions [/h2]

[h3] Saved Loadouts [/h3]
When you inevitably end up dying and losing your whole loadout, it can be a pain to craft everything you need again. The free loadout option is nice to quickly jump back in with the bare minimum, but there's no safe slot, which is a bummer if you come across something valuable. The ability to specify a loadout would be amazing. Ideally you could specify all of the guns and items you want, and if you have them in your stash, it would just pull them all into your inventory. If you're missing some of them, there could be an option to craft what you're missing if you have the materials -- or you could just let it pull in whatever you do have and go from there.

[h3] Not loading into games super late [/h3]
It feels pretty bad to load into a game at 18 minutes, run to the nearest POI, and find that every container has been looted. I've heard that this is supposed to then encourage you to kill other players who have already looted, but many times, those players have already extracted after 12 minutes. I've had several games where I run around to a few areas, find that everything is looted, and I can't even find another player. So I just extract with some basic materials. I get that they want to keep the lobby populated even when people extract early, but I wish the cutoff for when you can spawn in was a bit earlier. I've loaded in at like 25 minutes (I think?), and it wasn't QUITE as bad.

[h3] More stash size increases [/h3]
I maxed out my stash size pretty quickly, but I still spend a good amount of time figuring out what to sell or recycle, as I'm usually pretty full. I wish there was a way to increase it more. I've seen that Expedition gives you an increase, but I'm not entirely sure if it will be permanent. Even then it's a small increase, and you have to reset all of your Skills and lose all of your stash and learned BPs, which kind of sucks. Even if they upped the cost of the stash size increase by a lot, and gave us a few more increases, I'd be happy.

[h3] PvE Option for boss events [/h3]
This is sort of a polarizing topic, but I do think it could be nice to have the events like the Matriarch and the Queen have the option for PvE. These are FAR more fun to partake in when everyone is working together to take them down and helping each other out. Believe me, I love the PvP aspect of this game, but it feels really shitty to be working with 10+ people to take down the Matriarch, and then someone shoots you in the back. Obviously it's good to be aware and just stay in a big group, as people will generally help you out if there's a solo that's ratting and taking people out, but it definitely happens in the duo and trio lobbies more. Having people work together for the boss events feels way better in my opinion, but I know others will disagree.

This game is amazing, I've been having so much fun on it with some of my friends and especially running through all the quests with my main man. The maps are nice, the lotting and extraction aspect is fun, everything to do with upgrading everything at your room in Speranza. And to top it all off, fighting all the ARC is the best experience, there is a perfect amount of small ones sprinkled around the map and enough big ones that you have to watch where you're going unless you're prepared for a fight.
In saying all this, you probably knew I was gonna get to this point... the PvP has been nothing but a bad experience every single time. And that's not me carrying on and whining, that's just my truth. It sucks, it pulls me out of the experience and brings the vibe down 100% of the time. And the worst part is, majority of the time, you don't really get a chance to fight back, if someone that has no chill spots you they shoot and you're down in seconds with no hope of running away OR fighting back. Now, you might be thinking, why not just shoot first? That's not why I play the game, just because there is PvP in the game doesn't mean it's the main point. I know how it feels to die to other raiders and lose my stuff, I will never willing inflict that on people that wouldn't do it to me. But the people that are like that don't talk. They just shoot you. Kill you. And ruin your experience because they don't care.
The best part of this game is when people can come together to accomplish something that you couldn't do otherwise. I just fought AND killed a Queen with my friend, and before I could even loot a single thing I was shot, downed and knocked out by players who very clearly wouldn't be able to keep everything for themselves. That's gotta be the worst thing that's happened to me by far and it is so incredibly discouraging.
I don't wanna winge and not try and solve the problem though, so on the of chance this sparks some sort of uproar in the community or catches Embarks eye, I'll leave my ideas as well.

1. The obvious one is turn off PvP completely, but that would upset the people who enjoy it, and as much as I don't care for those people and their play style, they don't deserve to have it ruined for them.
2. Provide the option when loading into a match to toggle PvP, this way all the nice people who wanna do their own thing or even team up or interact with other friendly people are welcome to do so. And the ruthless players that are out for blood can simply do the same and keep to themselves. This way everyone gets what they want without spoiling it for other people.
3. The devs could put in more work than is probably worth it to pretty much overhall the armor system and provide different types that prevent more damage from players OR Arc, other similar stuff of that vein.
But option 2 seems like the common sense solution and a win win for all.

Seeing as this is a review however and not an angry email straight to the dev team I'll leave you with this.
Buy the game, I guarantee the good majority of your time playing SHOULD be enjoyable, whether it be from fighting arc, looting peacefully or mucking around with an entire lobby of friendly people for no reason (true story) you will have fun. Just please be wary and keep in mind that you ARE going to have games where you get completely dunked on by not so friendly players before you even know what's happening. Good luck and be careful.

Verdict: A promising extraction shooter with a strong identity that prioritizes tension and cooperation over pure twitch reflexes.

ARC Raiders immediately stands out through its atmosphere. The world feels hostile and oppressive in a way that supports its core loop—every decision carries risk, and survival is never guaranteed. The sound design plays a huge role here; distant machine noises and environmental audio constantly keep players on edge.

Gameplay leans more toward deliberate pacing than frantic action. Combat rewards positioning, awareness, and team coordination rather than reckless aggression. Encounters with AI enemies feel purposeful, and resource management creates real tension during longer runs.

Visually, the game establishes a clear aesthetic without overcomplicating the presentation. Environments are readable, enemy silhouettes are distinct, and performance during testing felt stable given the scale of encounters.

As with most playtest builds, content depth is currently limited. Progression systems show potential, but it’s too early to judge long-term retention. Some mechanics would benefit from clearer feedback, especially during high-pressure situations.

What Works Well

Strong atmosphere and audio design

Tension-driven extraction gameplay

Encourages teamwork and planning

Clear visual readability

What Needs Improvement

Long-term progression depth remains uncertain

Some systems need clearer player feedback

Balance tuning will be critical as content expands

Final Thoughts:
ARC Raiders has a solid foundation and a distinct voice within the extraction shooter space. If progression, balance, and content variety continue to evolve, this could become a standout title rather than just another genre entry.

It's a great game at it's core, and I get the tension, suspense, risk and reward, but sadly what ruins the experience is the other side of humanity. The gamers that shoot on sight, the extract campers, the ones that scream "dont shoot!" then the minute they get close, mow you down, those who play solely for the purpose of ruining the experience for others. We call these players, RATs.

It changes you, it's a toxic cycle.
You start off friendly and enjoy interactions with other raiders, working together to keep each other safe from Arc, a super helpful community who even drop items at your feet, then after a while you get mowed down by one of the aforemented rats, and again, and then again, and again, and again. Then you start playing cautiously, you're suspicious, you no longer trust human intent, and when players don't respond to your greetings, you default to concluding they're hostile, and so YOU engage first, you mow them down, you slowly become, the RAT.

Then every interaction from there on out, you become what you hated, and you become responsible for ruining everyone elses experience.

Embark have done their best with aggression-based-matchmaking, but the key flaw is that it does not decipher player intent - and how could it without reading your thoughts? If you attack someone in self defense, the system still considers that you engaged in PvP and then matches you with more lobbys of players inclined towards PvP - the opposite of your intent.  I don't know what the answer is, but after a while it gets tiring, and the fun, stops.

That's just the solo cycle. Duo's and Trio's are almost 100% PvP. If you want to chill with friends and take down some Arc - forget it, Arc Raiders with friends does not accomodate for that.

Then there's the streamers, 100% PvP gameplay, influencing others into adopting the same play style.  I'm not sure what's worse, the streamers who influence players, or the sheep who are so easily influenced because they don't have a single thought for themselves.

Yes, PvP can be fun, but if Arc raiders is to have any longevity, it must accomodate all audiences - it needs to be a choice.

The Ugly: PvP is a mess in this game. On paper the idea is solid: scavanging in a post-apocalypse world, not knowing who to trust, possibly having to defend yourself in the event a player migtht be hostile. It adds a layer of anxiety and tension to every player encounter and that aspect I do like.

[h2]ARC Raiders understands what makes extraction games compelling—then removes the uncertainty that gives it meaning.[/h2]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]TL;DR – Core Claims[/h2]

- Extraction games are at their best when [b]player behavior is unpredictable[/b], driven by mixed goals, playstyles, and risk tolerance.
- ARC Raiders has strong foundations for this: [b]PvE creates objectives and exposure[/b], [b]PvP creates unknown threat[/b], and extraction choices and loot value create tension.
- [b]Aggression-based matchmaking undermines that tension[/b] by sorting players, by and large, into predictable PvE or PvP-only lobbies.
- This removes a core pillar of extraction gameplay: uncertainty about other players—their presence, their intent, and the consequences of being noticed.
- PvE lobbies become safe, repetitive loot-farming with little risk or long-term meaning.
- PvP lobbies strip away PvE objectives and context, leaving mechanically weak PvP compared to dedicated alternatives.
- The optimal way to progress on reset is to avoid PvP entirely, incentivizing [b]hoarding instead of meaningful risk-taking[/b].
- Over time, both PvE-focused and PvP-focused players are likely to leave for games that do those experiences better.
- What’s lost is the mixed highs and lows that only unpredictable triumph and failure can create.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Long Version (for "Better Than a Game Journalist" Magazine)[/h2]

Extraction games live and die by uncertainty. They work best when players enter a map with different goals, levels of investment, and tolerances for risk. PvE objectives pull players into vulnerable situations, while the possibility of other players—hostile, neutral, or unseen—creates tension. Preparation is mandatory; you’re rarely reacting to what is happening so much as what [i]might[/i] happen, and that tension is what makes both success and failure meaningful.

ARC Raiders understands this mechanically. PvE enemies aren’t meant to be lethal on their own; they create objectives, noise, and risk. Even tougher encounters become manageable with the right tools. The real danger is time, positioning, and whether another raider notices. Extraction choices—limited exits, timed extracts, night maps—reinforce this by making loot matter only if you escape.

[b]Aggression-based matchmaking undermines that loop.[/b]

By sorting players into mostly PvE- or PvP-focused lobbies, the game removes the uncertainty that gives these systems meaning. In PvE lobbies, player interference is akin to a cryptid sighting. In PvP lobbies, it’s constant and expected—fire a few shots, set off some flares, and you’ll have sharks circling in minutes. In both cases, the unknowns that drive tension are flattened.

The result is two diminished experiences. PvE lobbies become safe, repetitive loot runs against simple AI. PvP lobbies lose PvE context and objectives, leaving constant combat that struggles to compete with dedicated PvP games. Each half is outclassed by alternatives that fully commit to those roles.

This also encourages players to optimize the fun out of the game. On reset, the most efficient path is to avoid PvP entirely—complete quests, farm loot, and build wealth with minimal risk. Progression is faster, loss is rare, and hoarding replaces meaningful risk.

Over time, this predictability erodes replayability. PvE-focused players will seek richer, intentionally designed cooperative experiences—looter shooters, Monster Hunter–style games, and other PvE titles built around depth and variety. PvP-focused players will gravitate toward tighter, more rewarding combat elsewhere, whether that’s battle royales or PvP-first extraction games like Hunt: Showdown. What’s lost is the mixed space in between—the tense highs and lows that come from not knowing whether a decision ends in triumph or failure.

ARC Raiders has the foundations of a compelling extraction game, but aggression-based matchmaking cuts against the very uncertainty that gives the genre its edge.

ARC Raiders Review – Incredible PvE, Ruined by Rats

ARC Raiders has serious potential. The PvE is actually the best part of the game — fighting ARCs, planning routes, deciding when to engage or extract — it’s tense in all the right ways. When you get to experience it, it’s great.

The problem is you almost never get the chance.

I can’t load into a match without being instantly killed by rat players camping spawns. Solo, duo, or trio — it doesn’t matter. The matchmaking is fair on paper (1v1, 2v2, 3v3), but that doesn’t help when the other side’s entire strategy is to sit on spawn points and farm kills before anyone can move.

This isn’t about getting outplayed in PvP. PvP is expected. The issue is that the PvE — which is clearly the heart of the game — is completely overshadowed by players who refuse to engage with it at all. I can’t raid, loot, knock down a big ARC, or even touch the Matriarch because most runs end in seconds.

The gameplay loop quickly becomes:
Spawn → die → reload → repeat → question life choices.

When the most efficient strategy is ignoring the game’s best content and griefing fresh spawns, something is broken. The game needs better spawn protection, smarter spawn placement, or a short grace period — anything that lets players actually play the PvE they queued for.

I really want ARC Raiders to succeed. The foundation is strong, and the PvE proves it. But if rat gameplay continues to dominate, it’s going to drive away players fast.

Verdict:
Excellent PvE. Solid PvP foundation.
