A Masterpiece Left to Rot in a Den of Thieves

My Total Playtime: 500+ hours 

The Tragedy of Wasted Potential
It breaks my heart to write this. From a technical and creative standpoint, ARC Raiders is a triumph. Embark Studios has crafted something truly special here:

Atmosphere & Visuals: The world-building is hauntingly beautiful, and the graphical fidelity is industry-leading.

Mechanics: The gunplay is tight, the movement is fluid, and the player interactions—ranging from tense standoffs to desperate alliances—provide a unique adrenaline rush.

On paper, this is a 10/10 game. In practice, it is a 0/10 experience.

The Cheat-to-Player Ratio is Absurd
After over 500 hours of dedication, I can no longer ignore the elephant in the room: the integrity of the game has completely collapsed. The competitive landscape is not defined by skill, but by who has the better cheat software.

The "Fresh Account" Epidemic: Nine out of ten times I am killed in PvP, it is by a Steam Level 1–3 account with zero profile history, or worse, an account with multiple existing VAC bans. These are disposable burner accounts used specifically to grief legitimate players.

Widespread ESP/Wallhacks: My own testing confirms that at least one-third of any given PvP lobby is using some form of Wallhack/ESP. I have performed "patience tests" where I sit motionless in obscure, illogical locations for several minutes; without fail, a cheater will eventually track me down and pre-fire my exact position.

Final Verdict: Do Not Enter
To anyone who values fair play and competitive integrity: Stay away. It doesn't matter how good the looting feels or how immersive the atmosphere is when the outcome of every engagement is predetermined by a script. The current state of the game is fundamentally broken.

Message to Embark Studios: You have built a masterpiece, but you are currently letting it be dismantled by bad actors. Until you implement aggressive, effective anti-cheat measures and hardware-level bans, this game is nothing more than a playground for cheaters. You are losing your most loyal players. Fix it, or watch your hard work vanish.

After the most recent update, ARC Raiders’ matchmaking feels fundamentally misaligned with how a big chunk of the player base actually plays the game. I’m someone who leans PvE-first—my ideal run is about scavenging, planning routes, managing noise, and making smart disengagement decisions. But right now the system keeps funneling players like me into lobbies that play like full-on PvP hunting grounds, and it’s creating a miserable (and honestly avoidable) experience.

The core issue isn’t “PvP exists.” PvP belongs in an extraction game. The issue is matchmaking no longer seems to separate intent or behavior, so PvE-leaning players are repeatedly loaded into matches where coordinated squads or high-aggression players dominate the pacing. The result is that the match stops being a tense extraction loop and turns into a constant forced duel—often before you’ve even had a chance to engage with the map, objectives, or the risk/reward decisions that make PvE fun.

What makes this feel worse is how predictable it has become: spawn, move, fight a little AI, and suddenly you’re being tracked like a bounty. It feels like the system is either overweighting combat performance, underweighting survival/extraction behavior, or just widening the skill/party-size brackets to speed up queues. Whatever the cause, the outcome is the same: players who don’t queue to “wipe the server” are treated as free loot piñatas for players who do.

And that’s not just frustrating—it’s damaging. PvE-focused players are the ones who keep the ecosystem healthy: they explore, they craft, they create the moments that make an extraction shooter feel alive. If the matchmaking keeps pushing them into lobbies where the dominant strategy is to ignore PvE entirely and hunt spawns/extract paths, you don’t get “exciting risk.” You get one-dimensional play. People either start ratting in the worst way (not smart stealth—just hiding because the system punishes movement), or they log off.

If this is intentional design—if the goal is “everyone must be PvP-ready every match”—then it needs to be communicated clearly, because right now it feels like a bug or a tuning mistake. But if it’s not intentional, then the fix is straightforward in concept: matchmake around behavior and intent, not just MMR-ish combat metrics. Track extraction rate, time spent engaging AI/objectives, distance traveled, damage dealt to players vs. AI, solo vs. squad survival curves—then use that data to stop mixing extremes. At minimum, tighten the party-size rules so solos aren’t constantly fed into squads that are clearly running PvP routes.

I want PvP to be there as a threat, not as the entire match identity. Right now, the matchmaking is turning “PvE with PvP risk” into “PvP with occasional AI speed bumps,” and it’s pushing a huge group of players into a mode they didn’t opt into. If ARC Raiders wants long-term retention, it can’t afford to make PvE-leaning players feel like they’re only in the lobby to populate someone else’s highlight reel.

Except, YouTube was filling up with awesome Role-play clips happening in the game. I held off at first as I figured it was just a honeymoon phase phenomenon and the game would quickly devolve into non-stop Kill-on-Sight PvP. Except it didn't. The clips kept coming. Why?

Aggression-based Matchmaking.

I have:
- Protected a flautist with my life for no other reason than obviously that's what you do.
- Sang someone a lullaby in exchange for a rare weapon blueprint.
- Gotten free rare loot from veteran Raiders just because.
- Unlocked rare loot rooms for other players just because (this requires a key that is consumed).
- Been killed at extract by a camper
- Camped an extract
- Shotgunned someone as they opened a door
- Been shotgunned while rounding a corner
- Worked together with strangers to take down a large PvE enemy
- Been saved by strangers who willingly used themselves as a decoy so I could extract
- Been shot in the back after killing a large PvE enemy after using items that took me hours to acquire
- Shot someone in the back because something felt off about them
- Shot someone in the back just because

...and every single one of those things was awesome fun because thanks to ABMM, I had a rough idea every round how much danger I was going to be in. I just killed 1 or 2 raiders? Next lobby is gonna be hot. I've been pacifist for 2-3 raids? Next lobby is probably going to be chill. Now that's not to say it's an absolute. They mix in killers in every match to keep you on your toes, it's just a question of how many you're likely to encounter.

Add to that loot that feels worth farming and crafting that feels good to interact with and you have a genre defining experience. Because that's what ARC Raiders is: an experience.

I highly recommend anyone who wants some chill PvE type experience in extraction shooter game. I really like the aggression based match making, where If I dont shoot other players and then i am matched against calm and friendly players who are busy with doing missions, fighting arc and grinding and not engaging in any PvP nonsense. This is my first extraction shooter game and I am having a total blast.

This game really is a blast. I think that, while the core gameplay itself is quite solid, the real standout stuff is the social aspect of raiding. Having little "Mexican standoffs" each time you encounter another player or team is always a tense, exciting experience. Whether it ends in actual combat or not, it never fails to at least get my heart beating a bit faster. In the case that it DOESN'T end in a fight (which is most of the time in my experience) there is always the possibility of gaining a new friend and helping each-other to complete objectives or extract together, which also creates a dynamic and fun player experience.

in terms of the gameplay loop, Arc Raiders is a game of high highs and moderately low lows. Gear fear still exists, as it does in any extraction game. But the losses are mitigated significantly by how generous the looting/quest rewards can be - and there's always a free loadout to basically eliminate gear fear entirely. Losing a loadout (even a very expensive one) doesn't feel as crushing as it does in Tarkov or similar games because there are enough systems in place to make it fairly easy to catch back up to where you were. 

In short, this is a very fun game that can generally be as sweaty or as friendly as you want. I think people who say that everyone is now kill-on-sight are either very unlucky or are probably very aggressive themselves and are thus being put into aggressive lobbies. I think this has solidly one of the most friendly and welcoming communities of any extraction game, and maybe even most PVP games in general.

I’ve been playing ARC Raiders mostly through solo raids, with some duos and trios mixed in here and there. I started about a week after launch due to being on vacation, but ever since then I’ve been having a genuinely great time with the game.

What really stands out to me is the PvE-first design. PvP is absolutely there, and when it happens it can be intense and exciting, but it feels more like a choice than something you’re constantly forced into. I enjoy PvP encounters, but I’m not a fan of games where the only objective is shooting other players over and over. ARC Raiders does a great job of giving you meaningful objectives beyond just PvP, which keeps the gameplay from feeling repetitive.

I know there’s a lot of discussion around how fast new content should be released. As someone who also creates content around ARC Raiders, I understand why people want more things to do. That said, I appreciate the pace Embark is taking. Rushing content just to satisfy short-term demand or content cycles can hurt a game long-term. It’s clear the developers care about making ARC Raiders something that lasts, not just another game that burns hot and fades fast.

I recently switched over to PC, and in the last month or so I haven’t really run into many issues with cheating. That might be because I don’t live in the most PvP-heavy lobbies, but overall my experience has been clean. I trust that Embark will continue doing their due diligence when it comes to handling cheating concerns.

Visually, the game looks great on PS5, but on PC it looks immaculate. Even as someone who isn’t super deep into PC graphics settings, the upgrade was immediately noticeable.

Overall, ARC Raiders has been a very enjoyable experience for me. I’ve loved playing it, I’ve loved creating content around it, and I’m genuinely excited to see where the game goes next. If you enjoy PvE-focused gameplay with optional PvP and meaningful progression, this game is absolutely worth your time.

This game is fantastic at its core, but I cannot recommend it in its current state.

This game was marketed as both a PVP and PVE experience, yet the reality is that the PVE side has been almost completely erased by the way the community and loadout system function. The overwhelming majority of players have adopted the kill-on-sight or worse, the befriend and betray mentality, which wouldn't necessarily be a problem if the risk and reward were balanced.

Right now, there is little to no incentive to bring high-tier gear into a raid. Any player can load into a game with a free loadout and still reliably kill someone who is risking valuable gear. This creates a situation where hoarding gear isn't just encouraged, but required, because bringing anything good almost guarantees you'll lose it to someone with nothing to lose.

As a result, the PVE content suffers immensely. ARCS are actively avoided because engaging them requires gear that is too risky to bring. This problem is even worse for new or casual players, because they cannot acquire and retain the gear needed to take down bigger ARCS. This means a lot of quests cannot be fulfilled unless you are blessed with a kind lobby, or you simply join the rats and steal from others. The PVE aspect essentially becomes useless then, and you are left in a frustrating loop where ignoring half of the advertised experience is the only way to progress.

The longer this continues, the worse this problem will become. As the weeks go by and the player base becomes more established, new and casual players will have an increasingly difficult time acquiring the materials needed to upgrade their workstations. Without upgraded workstations, they cannot craft better gear, meaning they cannot engage with PVE content, which is required for the majority of quests. This leaves them effectively stuck at the start of the game.

The aggression-based matchmaking does little to alleviate the loadout problem, because in most matches, there are still multiple highly aggressive players who camp the spawn and extraction zones and kill Raiders, again risking little on their part. Some of these spawn camp deaths also occur while the players load in, as mid-game spawns are enabled and poorly protected from trolls.

If this game were marketed as a PVP extraction shooter or a PVE co-op game, there would be no problem with either playstyle. However, the current blend of both creates an unfun, toxic and exhausting loop full of childish people who cannot work cooperatively and who believe that shooting people in the back while risking none of their own gear is the only way to enjoy the game. And any attempt to raise these concerns is routinely dismissed as a skill issue on the new player's part, despite the fact that the game actively rewards low-risk griefing over meaningful cooperation or PVE battles.

TLDR - ARC Raiders is supposed to be a blend of PVP and PVE, but its current systems reward zero-risk PVP with free loadouts while punishing anyone engaging with PVE. This makes progression nearly impossible for new and casual players, and any criticism is brushed off by the community as a 'skill issue', despite the issue being rooted in the poor balance and design.

First few games:
Community says, “Hey Raider, don’t shoot.”
Wow. A friendly community? In this economy?
We loot together. We vibe. We emote. We believe in humanity.

Then it hits me.

Friendly lobbies are actually the worst thing ever invented.

Why? Because we’re sharing loot spawns. That shiny, delicious, good good goop is now split between us like a sad pizza. Progress slows. Frustration rises. Monkey brain activates.

So I hit a guy with my stick (Raider tool) because it is not my loot anymore, it is OUR loot. 

Suddenly I’m in a whole new world.

“Don’t shoot” now translates to:
“I will wait for you to loot this container so I can shoot you in the ass.”

Now I can’t PvP (Because I suck).
I can’t loot.
I get 0 items and 100 emotional damage.

Do I stay friendly?
Do I betray first?
Do I want loot or inner peace?

This game is not an extraction shooter — it’s a philosophical experiment.

And let’s talk about the Arc robots.
Because apparently ARC robots — especially Rocketeers — are esports professionals.
They never miss.
They predict my movement.
They predict my misclicks.
I panic, run the wrong direction, and the Rocketeer already knew I would do that before I was born.

It kills me, then hovers there…
watching me…
menacingly…
after destroying both my character and my ego.

After 200 hours, here’s my verdict:

Arc Raiders is a good game.
It is fun.
It is unique.
It is absolutely worth the mental torture.

ARC Raiders can be best described as the shopping-cart litmus test of multiplayer shooters. Your objective is simple: go in, get loot, and leave alive. How you go about doing this exactly is up to you.

To say that you see a target, a full magazine in your hand, and make the assumption that you should shoot at it is incredibly reductive. Everything is a choice. What you decide to take home, what people or ARC you choose to engage, whom to drop some loot for, and which person to side with in a fight you walked into. You are the judge, jury, and in some cases, executioner. You don't even have to go into a raid with a gun. This game will bring the best of the good and the worst of the bad. There will be rats cosplaying as high-tier players with the ill-gotten gains of the slain. There will be raiders that simply pass you by, guns at the ready but not yet pointed at you. If you're lucky, you might be saved by an angel on the grounds, coming to revive a complete stranger in the nick of time. You will get to see the entire moral spectrum on display, and I think that is actually the best quality of this game. Everything else is just a setup that enables the wide variety of experiences you will encounter. 

The game, however, is not apathetic in its matchmaking. This allows a certain degree of control in getting the sort of rounds one would like to partake in. The more hostile one remains, the more hostile the type of servers one will be placed in, and vice versa. This prevents the game from devolving into a race to the bottom that reinforces aggression and a first-strike mentality at all times. This also extends to the solo, duo, and trio queues, the latter of which increase drastically in hostility and with solos being generally non-hostile.

ARC Raiders is not an extraction shooter. It's a psychological thriller that looks like an extraction shooter.

As an avid FPS player I tend to avoid extraction shooters because often times they are just a blood bath that throw you from your highest highs to your lowest low in the time it takes to just play a few matches. Arc Raiders managed to break that cycle and make nearly every match a fun time. Well...that is until you've ran Stella 30 times in a row looking for a Magnetron that doesn't seem to exist and you gaslight yourself into thinking it's a conspiracy cooked up by Big Arc to torment you and only you specifically.

In the 20 hours I've played, I've had so many differing experiences on this game, and nearly every time I walk away saying "That was fun/hilarious/unexpected" - even if I died and lost my entire kit, I still had fun doing it. Solo's are full of really great people who are often down to help one another. I can't tell you how many times I've been downed in solo's only for another player to defib me while expecting nothing in return cause the fact that they saved someone that they didn't have to save is enough to make you feel like a hero. Trios can be a bloodbath, but sometimes you'll have 1 guy playing a flute with 3 full teams following him around dancing before everyone extracts together in harmony while cracking jokes in proximity chat.

Sometimes someone will ask you to team up, then kill you once you're looting. Sometimes you make a friend, only to never see them again, yet you'll remember that experience with them because it was a moment you and a stranger came together to do something cool, hectic, or crazy. Sometimes someone will kill you, only to say sorry and get you back up once they realized you weren't much of a threat.

What I love is that this game makes you think. It makes you consider human nature and puts you in a place to be able to come together, or realize you can't trust someone else as much as you thought, and it feels real.

The game does have some flaws, but overall, it's a really fun experience. Arc enemies are challenging, and even the weakest, smallest robots can easily overwhelm you if you're not careful. The larger Arc robots can be terrifying, especially if encountered alone. I don't think there is a single moment in my gaming lifetime that made me sh*t my pants the way I did the first time a Leaper jumped 200m right onto my face.

The aggression-based matchmaking is great because it pairs people up who have similar playstyles, which overall creates a better experience for those who like active PvP, and those who want to PvP situationally based on the potential gain or loss from it. From what I can tell, the only people who hate it are the people who want to be bullies and get satisfaction from shutting someone else's good time down. These people tend to be aggressive PvP'ers wishing they could go against people who won't fight back so they can get free loot, and that doesn't sound fun to me. People who go out of their way to kill people get their comeuppance from others looking to do the same. This is truly a game of karma, where you get back what you put out into the world, and honestly I think that's beautiful.

3. Quests have no map markers, and when you get to an area you have to search around for *something* to interact with, usually without a description of what that thing is.

My favorite 3 things about this game:
1. The community - it's honestly so good. I've had so many good experiences with random people that I'll probably never see again.
2. The movement and combat feels great.

Lastly, please for the love of god fix the bug that doesn't show you your teammates health bars/location. It can be fixed by taking damage and which refreshes the HUD state on that teammate, but it's annoying to have to encounter at all in the first place.

This isn’t an extraction shooter – it’s just a shooter. Why? The current matchmaking splits players into two camps: "carebears" and PvP "sweats." The first group is basically a Teletubby-style trash-collecting simulator. Players run around, wave at each other, and have dance parties in the extraction elevator, while the ARC machines pose zero threat. There’s no risk, no tension – which is the polar opposite of what this genre is supposed to be.

In the second group, you’re just playing a deathmatch. Players couldn’t care less about loot, progression, or extraction – it’s a pure slugfest to see who can rack up the most kills. There’s absolutely zero "extraction shooter" DNA in that experience.

What’s missing is the middle ground – mixed lobbies where you never know what to expect. There’s no tension because you never have those emergent moments: one minute getting shot in the back by a traitor for your loot, and the next finding a random ally to help you take down a tough ARC. That unpredictability is exactly what should be driving the excitement, but in the current state of the game, it’s non-existent.

I really hope Embark is actually playing their own game and realizes that, in its current state, Arc Raiders isn't what they intended it to be. Then again, after selling 12 million copies, they could just as easily stop caring about development, pack their bags, and move to Hawaii.

The game is still young and new content is on the way – we’ll see if they can actually make something out of this.

This game is fantastic at its core, but I cannot recommend it in its current state.

This game was marketed as both a PVP and PVE experience, yet the reality is that the PVE side has been almost completely erased by the way the community and loadout system function. The overwhelming majority of players have adopted the kill-on-sight or worse, the befriend and betray mentality, which wouldn't necessarily be a problem if the risk and reward were balanced.

Right now, there is little to no incentive to bring high-tier gear into a raid. Any player can load into a game with a free loadout and still reliably kill someone who is risking valuable gear. This creates a situation where hoarding gear isn't just encouraged, but required, because bringing anything good almost guarantees you'll lose it to someone with nothing to lose.

As a result, the PVE content suffers immensely. ARCS are actively avoided because engaging them requires gear that is too risky to bring. This problem is even worse for new or casual players, because they cannot acquire and retain the gear needed to take down bigger ARCS. This means a lot of quests cannot be fulfilled unless you are blessed with a kind lobby, or you simply join the rats and steal from others. The PVE aspect essentially becomes useless then, and you are left in a frustrating loop where ignoring half of the advertised experience is the only way to progress.

The longer this continues, the worse this problem will become. As the weeks go by and the player base becomes more established, new and casual players will have an increasingly difficult time acquiring the materials needed to upgrade their workstations. Without upgraded workstations, they cannot craft better gear, meaning they cannot engage with PVE content, which is required for the majority of quests. This leaves them effectively stuck at the start of the game.

The aggression-based matchmaking does little to alleviate the loadout problem, because in most matches, there are still multiple highly aggressive players who camp the spawn and extraction zones and kill Raiders, again risking little on their part. Some of these spawn camp deaths also occur while the players load in, as mid-game spawns are enabled and poorly protected from trolls.

If this game were marketed as a PVP extraction shooter or a PVE co-op game, there would be no problem with either playstyle. However, the current blend of both creates an unfun, toxic and exhausting loop full of childish people who cannot work cooperatively and who believe that shooting people in the back while risking none of their own gear is the only way to enjoy the game. And any attempt to raise these concerns is routinely dismissed as a skill issue on the new player's part, despite the fact that the game actively rewards low-risk griefing over meaningful cooperation or PVE battles.

TLDR - ARC Raiders is supposed to be a blend of PVP and PVE, but its current systems reward zero-risk PVP with free loadouts while punishing anyone engaging with PVE. This makes progression nearly impossible for new and casual players, and any criticism is brushed off by the community as a 'skill issue', despite the issue being rooted in the poor balance and design.

I went in thinking:
“Oh cool, another battle royale.”
Buys game. Loads in.
Wait… this is definitely not that.
(Poor research was done on my behalf.)

Turns out it’s an AI-robots-taking-over-the-world extraction shooter, with loot decided by RNGesus himself. And honestly? I liked it. Loved it, even. Butterflies. Real ones. The kind that steal your lunch money later.

First few games:
Community says, “Hey Raider, don’t shoot.”
Wow. A friendly community? In this economy?
We loot together. We vibe. We emote. We believe in humanity.

Then it hits me.

Friendly lobbies are actually the worst thing ever invented.

Why? Because we’re sharing loot spawns. That shiny, delicious, good good goop is now split between us like a sad pizza. Progress slows. Frustration rises. Monkey brain activates.

So I hit a guy with my stick (Raider tool) because it is not my loot anymore, it is OUR loot. 

Suddenly I’m in a whole new world.

“Don’t shoot” now translates to:
“I will wait for you to loot this container so I can shoot you in the ass.”

Now I can’t PvP (Because I suck).
I can’t loot.
I get 0 items and 100 emotional damage.

Do I stay friendly?
Do I betray first?
Do I want loot or inner peace?

This game is not an extraction shooter — it’s a philosophical experiment.

And let’s talk about the Arc robots.
Because apparently ARC robots — especially Rocketeers — are esports professionals.
They never miss.
They predict my movement.
They predict my misclicks.
I panic, run the wrong direction, and the Rocketeer already knew I would do that before I was born.

It kills me, then hovers there…
watching me…
menacingly…
after destroying both my character and my ego.

After 200 hours, here’s my verdict:

Arc Raiders is a good game.
It is fun.
It is unique.
It is absolutely worth the mental torture.

10/10 — would trust strangers again and get shot in the ass.

Absolutely nailed the environment and atmosphere. Can easily play solo or with a squad and still enjoy it the same. Feels like something we could have got from the last of us 2 multiplayer in terms of atmosphere. Graphics are pristine, performance has been smooth for me since day  1.

Personally this was my game of the year for 2025. Gunplay and PVP feels good if that is your thing, teaming up and doing PVE feels good if you prefer. I think it's really cool that you get more casual friendly lobbies depending on how you play, and I'll often oscillate between these lobbies and the more PVP focused queues depending on how I feel that night.

The only real complaints I've heard is about some of the gun balancing, but pretty much everything feels viable if you play around what you have, however I concede that some of the higher rarity weapons don't feel as rewarding to use when the cost to build and repair them is taken into consideration.

The graphics and overall aesthetic of the game are what pulled me in, and hundreds of hours later I still constantly stop while moving around topside to take in the scenery, it truly is a beautiful game. The two things that kept me around were the high intensity and rewarding social environments the game creates as well the feeling you get when you get out of a successful raid and contribute to whatever goal you were working towards at that point.

The only bad thing I can personally say about the game is that if you sink ungodly amounts of hours into it you will get to a point where there isn't many goals the game puts in front of you anymore. However, that's not really the game's fault, most people won't play that much and, and even if you do, I can appreciate the almost sandbox-like feeling you can get from loading into raids just for the love of the game, after you've already done all the quests, upgraded all of your benches, and fully funded your expedition.

I've already made some great memories in the game, and I'm eager to continue to do so as Embark rolls out more content.

ARC Raiders can be best described as the shopping-cart litmus test of multiplayer shooters. Your objective is simple: go in, get loot, and leave alive. How you go about doing this exactly is up to you.

To say that you see a target, a full magazine in your hand, and make the assumption that you should shoot at it is incredibly reductive. Everything is a choice. What you decide to take home, what people or ARC you choose to engage, whom to drop some loot for, and which person to side with in a fight you walked into. You are the judge, jury, and in some cases, executioner. You don't even have to go into a raid with a gun. This game will bring the best of the good and the worst of the bad. There will be rats cosplaying as high-tier players with the ill-gotten gains of the slain. There will be raiders that simply pass you by, guns at the ready but not yet pointed at you. If you're lucky, you might be saved by an angel on the grounds, coming to revive a complete stranger in the nick of time. You will get to see the entire moral spectrum on display, and I think that is actually the best quality of this game. Everything else is just a setup that enables the wide variety of experiences you will encounter. 

The game, however, is not apathetic in its matchmaking. This allows a certain degree of control in getting the sort of rounds one would like to partake in. The more hostile one remains, the more hostile the type of servers one will be placed in, and vice versa. This prevents the game from devolving into a race to the bottom that reinforces aggression and a first-strike mentality at all times. This also extends to the solo, duo, and trio queues, the latter of which increase drastically in hostility and with solos being generally non-hostile.

ARC Raiders is not an extraction shooter. It's a psychological thriller that looks like an extraction shooter.

Filters. For long long before we had AI humans have been changing how their voice sounds digitally and to extreme variation. No, I'm not saying everyone should sound like Daft Punk (that'd be funny though) but think of it like this, the input is a regular voice and some filters and modulation they are able to make their voices sound like. That which means every sound from a regular voice to those voices and ones past it are all doable without AI. Picture a world where instead of giving us an AI voice that sounds robotic and X pitches, you got a bunch of sliders that could change how your voice sounded. As an avid FPS player I tend to avoid extraction shooters because often times they are just a blood bath that throw you from your highest highs to your lowest low in the time it takes to just play a few matches. Arc Raiders managed to break that cycle and make nearly every match a fun time. Well...that is until you've ran Stella 30 times in a row looking for a Magnetron that doesn't seem to exist and you gaslight yourself into thinking it's a conspiracy cooked up by Big Arc to torment you and only you specifically.

In the 20 hours I've played, I've had so many differing experiences on this game, and nearly every time I walk away saying "That was fun/hilarious/unexpected" - even if I died and lost my entire kit, I still had fun doing it. Solo's are full of really great people who are often down to help one another. I can't tell you how many times I've been downed in solo's only for another player to defib me while expecting nothing in return cause the fact that they saved someone that they didn't have to save is enough to make you feel like a hero. Trios can be a bloodbath, but sometimes you'll have 1 guy playing a flute with 3 full teams following him around dancing before everyone extracts together in harmony while cracking jokes in proximity chat.

Sometimes someone will ask you to team up, then kill you once you're looting. Sometimes you make a friend, only to never see them again, yet you'll remember that experience with them because it was a moment you and a stranger came together to do something cool, hectic, or crazy. Sometimes someone will kill you, only to say sorry and get you back up once they realized you weren't much of a threat.

What I love is that this game makes you think. It makes you consider human nature and puts you in a place to be able to come together, or realize you can't trust someone else as much as you thought, and it feels real.

The game does have some flaws, but overall, it's a really fun experience. Arc enemies are challenging, and even the weakest, smallest robots can easily overwhelm you if you're not careful. The larger Arc robots can be terrifying, especially if encountered alone. I don't think there is a single moment in my gaming lifetime that made me sh*t my pants the way I did the first time a Leaper jumped 200m right onto my face.

The aggression-based matchmaking is great because it pairs people up who have similar playstyles, which overall creates a better experience for those who like active PvP, and those who want to PvP situationally based on the potential gain or loss from it. From what I can tell, the only people who hate it are the people who want to be bullies and get satisfaction from shutting someone else's good time down. These people tend to be aggressive PvP'ers wishing they could go against people who won't fight back so they can get free loot, and that doesn't sound fun to me. People who go out of their way to kill people get their comeuppance from others looking to do the same. This is truly a game of karma, where you get back what you put out into the world, and honestly I think that's beautiful.

My biggest 3 issues with this game are:
1. Lack of teaming options - why do I have to queue solo or trio? Why can I not queue for duos with a random stranger?
2. Stash size limitations are extremely frustrating as a new player, especially when you don't know what items to keep, recycle, or sell. 
3. Quests have no map markers, and when you get to an area you have to search around for *something* to interact with, usually without a description of what that thing is.

My favorite 3 things about this game:
1. The community - it's honestly so good. I've had so many good experiences with random people that I'll probably never see again.
2. The movement and combat feels great.
3. The PvE elements are challenging and fun. They hit a homerun on the PvE side of things.

Lastly, please for the love of god fix the bug that doesn't show you your teammates health bars/location. It can be fixed by taking damage and which refreshes the HUD state on that teammate, but it's annoying to have to encounter at all in the first place.

If you are looking for a fun social FPS experience, this game is it.

This isn’t an extraction shooter – it’s just a shooter. Why? The current matchmaking splits players into two camps: "carebears" and PvP "sweats." The first group is basically a Teletubby-style trash-collecting simulator. Players run around, wave at each other, and have dance parties in the extraction elevator, while the ARC machines pose zero threat. There’s no risk, no tension – which is the polar opposite of what this genre is supposed to be.

In the second group, you’re just playing a deathmatch. Players couldn’t care less about loot, progression, or extraction – it’s a pure slugfest to see who can rack up the most kills. There’s absolutely zero "extraction shooter" DNA in that experience.

What’s missing is the middle ground – mixed lobbies where you never know what to expect. There’s no tension because you never have those emergent moments: one minute getting shot in the back by a traitor for your loot, and the next finding a random ally to help you take down a tough ARC. That unpredictability is exactly what should be driving the excitement, but in the current state of the game, it’s non-existent.

I really hope Embark is actually playing their own game and realizes that, in its current state, Arc Raiders isn't what they intended it to be. Then again, after selling 12 million copies, they could just as easily stop caring about development, pack their bags, and move to Hawaii.

The game is still young and new content is on the way – we’ll see if they can actually make something out of this.

while i know that extraction shooters are not for everyone, even me, this game has brought back my love for gaming. Even had moments in being able to be a hero for a raider that was backstabbed or knocked by arc. I don't get to play as often as I'd like to but this game is rent free in my mind. There is constant debate about what the true purpose of this game is, PVP? PVE? but the reality is this game is truly PVEVP. it is what you make of it. at first I hated being killed by an extraction camper or being backstabbed and it still can upset me, but honestly its forced me to be better. check my surroundings better, be more cautious of other players. the tension of the game is real and the ai enemies are actually a threat. listen you will be killed and lose good gear, legendary gear even. times where you die to the AI. times you team up with a random player. times you play instruments and vibe out on the topside. This is Arc Raiders. I'm a gamer at heart and always have been. This is the first game i ever left a review on. Arc Raiders is game that brings me mixed feelings, but in its current state, I can't honestly recommend playing it. But let's start with the good.

The Pros:

Arc Raiders premise is excellent, if not original. Earth was razed by war and the surface has become a barren land, hostile to life itself. The story arch of Arc Raiders focuses on an underground settlement known as Speranza, where survivors scramble through and gather hoping to survive as they prepare to resurface. However, they found that the surface is not quiet either, a variety of automatons, machines called "ARC", patrol the ruins of what remains topside, and they are hostile, it seems their mission and endeavor to eliminate any remaining humans. With this in mind, groups of "Raiders",one of which is you, the player, organise to raid the surface and scrunge up any supplies, intel and tech they can get their hands on, to both survive, learn more about the enemy and their motivations, and prepare to fight back. 

This is pretty great - and even moreso when the gameplay itself, is great as well. Technical issues with server connectivity aside, the controls are responsive, the weapons are varied and have each their own identity, strengths and weaknesses, and the combat feels fluid and action packed. Arc Raiders is a beautiful extraction shooter, with clean, responsive controls, and an interesting premise to back it all.


The cons:

While the game was originally devised as PvE game, probably similar to Helldivers (in fact, the reward system seems to be a shameless copy from Helldivers) at one point they made the decision to add PvP to it, but unfortunately, that must have also skewed their development direction too, because the game has no content whatsoever. It does have several maps, but there are no progression systems. No difficulties, tiers, nothing. The first time you load the first map you ever play, as a level 1 greenhorn with a default pistol will be exactly the same map wiith the same enemy dificulty, density, and rewards as the map 2.500 you enter 1000 hours into the game.  

The gameplay loop is setup much like a  mobile gacha game, and its designed to fire off your dopamine receptors and create artifcial addiction at every turn. Every container you open gives off lively slot machine sounds, with increasingly higher pitched gratifying jackpot sounds when you get higher rarity items, that in truth are not that rare. Every run you'll end up with more purple (epic) + blue (rare) items in your inventory than gray (common)+ green (uncommon), but that will keep you chasing those slot machine sounds, to create the artificial addiction that may even fool you for some time before you stop to think if you're actually having fun, or just hoarding things of the colors the game makes chirpier slot machine sounds for.  Case in point, the best weapons of the game are the starting ones, white and green (common and uncommon) both for PvP and PvE, while the epic (purple) are widely known to be some of the worst weapons in the game. But the purple ones give out a jackpot slot machine sound when you find them, and you'll see people getting super hyped about getting one, just to stash it and never use it because a starting Stitcher gun is better anyway.

 When your dopamine receptors are about to blow, you will realize there is nothing to play for. There's no PvE progression, difficulty, or systems that incentivize getting better at the game, that reward player skill or dediucation. And then you'll find yourself basically playing a glorified fetch simulator, just hoarding your 7th "Hyperconductor tape" item your stash, just incase one day one NPC gives you a fetch quest about getting one, and saves you the trouble of having to go get it then.  

I haven't spoken of the PvP side of things, because I don't even consider this game to be PvP. A hundred percent of the player kills happen because someone gets the jump on someone else and kills them before they can fight back, or they're so bad at pointing their crosshair that the person being shot turns around and kills them back. There's no tactical gameplay, no nuance, no player skill expression, and none of it is supported by any ranking systems, matchmaking, ladders or anything of the kind. It's mostly if you';re cool with trying to kill someone to get their loot instead of trying to find your own loot, go for it. Nothing stops you, and nothing supports you. In the end, it doesn't matter, whatever they had, you could have gotten yourself, and they won't miss it either, since loot is abundant, and there's very very little you can do with it. 



Conclusion: 

This is a game to keep in the radar, if it survives this phase where it's more of a server performance stress test than anything else and they make a game out of it. I realise people can think differently about what is fun or what is not, to me, right now, Arc Raiders is a shell of game that offers nothing beyond being popular due to streamers promoting it, and creating a "monkey see monkey do" effect that will die sooner or later, unless it gets turned into a real game. They need to add content, in all fronts. Tiers, difficulties, meaningful rewards, progression, ladders, systems, proper matchmaking; both in PvP and PvE, make it feel like you're playing for something more than looting items that make slot machine sounds when you pick them up just to fire up your dopamine receptors in the cheapest possible way. 

If they don't, at least I played 80 hours of this game so you don't have to. Consider using your hard earned money and your limited time in a better way, good chance you won't regret.

After 540+ hours, it’s safe to say ARC Raiders hasn’t just hooked me-it’s lived rent-free in my head. The game absolutely nails that high-stakes extraction loop where every decision matters and every run feels like it could turn legendary or disastrous in seconds. Gunplay is tight and satisfying, movement is smooth and responsive, and the constant PvE/PvP tension keeps your heart rate up from drop-in to extraction.

The world is gritty, atmospheric, and full of quiet dread, pulling you in without ever holding your hand. ARC enemies feel genuinely dangerous, not like filler content, and player encounters are unpredictable in the best way -sometimes it’s a tense standoff, other times it’s pure chaos. Progression feels rewarding, skill-based, and earned, and the deeper your map knowledge and game sense get, the more the game opens up.

Where ARC Raiders truly shines is in its moment-to-moment choices: push your luck or play it safe, take the fight or disappear into the environment, extract now or risk it all for better loot. It creates unforgettable highs, painful losses, and endless “one more run” moments. It’s intense, addictive, and incredibly rewarding-and clearly, it worked on me.

[h1]Not Recommended[/h1]

[b]I hate that I’m writing this.[/b] I loved Arc Raiders. I still do, in a messed-up way. That’s what makes this so painful.

After [b]160+ hours[/b], I finally uninstalled.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Matchmaking That Punishes You for Playing[/h2]

The matchmaking design is [b]genuinely awful[/b]. The game actively punishes you for [i]defending yourself[/i].

You get a few calm, friendly raids:
[list]
[*]People coexist
[*]You loot
[*]You progress
[/list]

Then a rat camps an extract. You shoot back because you need the loot for a quest.

[b]Congratulations.[/b]
The game now decides:
[i]“YOU SHOT BACK, SO YOU MUST WANT PVP.”[/i]

From here on out:
[list]
[*]Kill the rat → sweatlord PvP hell
[*]Don’t kill the rat → lose loot, time, and progress
[*]Either way → you’re punished
[/list]

There’s zero nuance. Zero context. Zero care.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Bugs That Literally Kill You[/h2]

Not funny bugs.
Not “haha early access jank” bugs.

[b]Run-ending. Loot-deleting. Time-wasting bugs.[/b]

Add in constant server instability and it genuinely feels like the game is fighting you at every step.

[h3]Spawns Are TERRIBLE[/h3]

Enemy spawns are a disaster:
[list]
[*]Awful early-game spawns
[*]Even worse mid-game spawning
[*]Enemies popping in where they absolutely shouldn’t
[/list]

It kills immersion. It kills fairness. Sometimes it just straight-up kills [i]you[/i].

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Loot System: Clunky, Dishonest, and Insulting[/h2]

The game tells you:
[i]“Go to red areas for higher-tier loot.”[/i]

Reality:
[list]
[*]Same Burletta
[*]Again
[*]And again
[*]And again
[/list]

Every. Single. Time.

That gun is so useless you’d do more damage [b]sneezing[/b] on a Raider than actually shooting them. High risk, zero reward. The loot doesn’t feel connected to the map info or progression at all.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Worst Part? It Could Be Amazing[/h2]

When this game is good, it’s [b]beautiful[/b]:
[list]
[*]Atmosphere
[*]Tension
[*]Concept
[/list]

When everything lines up, it [i]hits hard[/i].

But when it’s bad—and that’s more often than not—it [b]SUUUUCKS[/b].

Bugs, bad spawns, broken matchmaking logic, ignored community feedback, and systems that punish you for playing naturally.

This game has [b]insane potential[/b]. Watching it fail to reach it hurts more than if it were just bad from the start.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Verdict[/h2]

[b]I LOVE this game.[/b] Don’t get it twisted.

If they:
[list]
[*]Fix the bugs
[*]Stabilize the servers
[*]Rethink matchmaking
[*]Make loot and spawns actually make sense
[/list]

I would [b]GLADLY[/b] come back.

But as it stands?

[b]Don’t waste your time.[/b]
[b]Don’t waste your money.[/b]

This work feels completely derivative compared to The Finals. The fact that Arc Raiders is far more popular than The Finals (another game by the same company) blows my mind. The gameplay of Arc Raiders is basically a steam punk copy-paste of the extraction shooter genre.

It's nothing special -- aside from one key feature: aggression based MMR. This is the only reason that I continue to play this game. It is quite fascinating to see how different shooters are when they make matches based on whether or not you like to PvP. When I play solo, I do not fight humans. And I get into the most chill multiplayer lobbies I've ever seen, where there is little to no PvP violence, and it is common for people to talk to strangers and help one another find the loot that we're looking for. When I play with my friends (I come from a fairly hard-core competitive shooter background) the experience is entirely different, and nothing special -- it's shoot on sight (with strategy and coordination), just like any other extraction shooter.

Originality 1/10, story 1/10, weapons 0.5/10, the fact that it's TPP instead of FPP -5/10, having to wait for a fake loading screen to see loot even though computers are fast these days -10/10, decent default mouse sensitivity 7/10, aggression based MMR 9/10.

In my opinion, this game is terrible compared to The Finals, which is one of the most innovative and interesting shooters of the past decade. However, the unique MMR system makes this game worth experiencing if you enjoy PVE gameplay. I hope to see this MMR system adopted into other games, which will make this game a cool piece of OG gaming history worth playing to know, but not worth playing on repeat.

ARC Raiders delivers a strong first impression through its atmosphere and core concept. The world feels heavy and hostile, and the constant threat of the ARC machines creates real tension during gameplay. Unlike many shooters that focus purely on fast action, ARC Raiders emphasizes caution, teamwork, and survival, which makes every encounter feel meaningful. The sound design and visuals do a great job of selling the idea that humanity is no longer in control, especially when exploring the surface and hearing distant mechanical movements.

The cooperative aspect is one of the game’s biggest strengths. Working with teammates to scavenge resources and decide when to fight or retreat adds depth and encourages communication. However, this reliance on teamwork may feel punishing for solo players, as mistakes can be costly and progress can feel slow without coordination. At times, combat can feel unforgiving, especially when resources are limited, which may discourage new players.

Overall, ARC Raiders stands out for its immersive sci-fi setting and tense survival mechanics. With some balancing improvements and clearer onboarding for beginners, it has the potential to become a memorable and rewarding cooperative experience for players who enjoy strategic, high-risk gameplay.

ARC Raiders wants you to believe it’s a tactical extraction shooter about teamwork, strategy, and survival. What it actually is: a beautifully rendered anxiety simulator where giant murder-robots exist solely to ruin your day and humble you in front of strangers.

You drop in feeling confident. Slick gunplay. Clean UI. “This feels good,” you think. That’s mistake number one. Within minutes, a mech the size of a small office block notices you breathing and deletes your entire squad with military-grade disinterest. No cutscene. No warning. Just instant obliteration and a loading screen that quietly asks why you bothered.

The PvE enemies are relentless, the PvP players are worse, and both are united by a shared goal: making sure you extract with absolutely nothing. ARC Raiders has perfected the art of letting you almost succeed. You’ll be one corridor from extraction, pockets full, heart racing... then a third party shows up like a tax audit with legs.

Every run teaches valuable life lessons such as:
• Never get attached to loot
• Trust no teammate named “SoloKing”
• Hope is a resource you should not invest in

The maps are gorgeous, which is ironic because you’ll spend most of your time face-down on them. The sound design is so good you can hear your impending death approaching from three zip codes away. The tension is real. So is the disappointment.

And yet… you queue again. Because when it clicks—when the squad syncs, the shots land, and you extract clean... you feel unstoppable. Briefly. Until the next run reminds you who’s actually in charge.

ARC Raiders doesn’t just punish mistakes. It punishes confidence.
It doesn’t hate you.
It just doesn’t care if you survive.

Would I recommend it?
Yes, if you enjoy stress, teamwork arguments, and the slow erosion of joy.

Arc Raiders is a highly social extraction shooter with adaptive matchmaking, and these features are probably what makes it stand out the most within its own extraction shooter genre. 

Unlike Tarkov or Hunt:showdown this game isn't trying to be stressful, competetive, none of that. The experience here started as PvE where players would need to work together to overcome machines that were stat-padded beyond belief to force teamwork. With the right preperation/loadout you can still solo whatever problems you run into. The game definitely allows for work smarter not harder solutions to almost any problem.

The game has a matchmaking system that puts like-minded players together. If you join lobbies and always shoot first, other players in your lobbies will also always shoot you first. If you never PvP and avoid combat at all costs you'll see tons of CoOp players and empty lobbies. 
This feeds into the PvE side of the game. Some people do want PvP but a lot of players just want to create experiences. This is similar to Sea Of Thieves in how the game can play. The PvP exists so any player can play "their part" but it's not like the game uses this as a foundation for your decisions. There really isn't much reason to kill other players unless you outright enjoy the PvP or enraging casual players who don't want to deal with it. (Most common complaint about this game I've seen is Non Pvpers being forced to PvP. I can't relate because the matchmaking actually seems to work REALLY WELL. Are these "friendlies" killing other people in their spare time then complaining about the consequences maybe?)

Anyway first glance the game seems like another third person extraction shooter. The difference is how hard the devs are promoting players to work together or finding ways to keep the ones who will apart from the ones who won't. I don't know if trying to cater to two communities can work long-term but we'll see how that goes. 

Gun balance can be pretty bad but small team. There's one particularly bad purple weapon that uses expensive ammo, fire fast, and deals real low damage. The cost on firing in excessive for no reason and isn't even backed by good damage. I'll just run any other rifle or handcannon thanks.
Bad balance relates to PvP, not PvE. I do not think balance can be bad enough to matter in PvE here. You're likely going to be running explosives/tools anyway. 

The weakest part of the game is the lame-ass quests. It's basically just Tarkov, Find objective, hold E to interact, extract. One of the weakest part of almost all extraction shooters are these boring time wasting objectives that exist to make you feel a sesne of progression so you hopefully won't just quit if the gameplay loop gets stale/boring. 
These quests are never the reason I keep playing, and I have my doubts I'll even complete them if 100%ing achievements doesn't require it.

When Ark Ascends the Extraction shooter genre and adds RPG elements (The right kind, like from Witchfire) so we can take unique items found in-raid to another raid and use it at a specific map location to summon a 1-time boss or similar mechanics then I'll start crediting them for interesting quests/objectives. For now the replay value comes down to you and the community though.

Man, I actually hate Arc Raiders. I'm trying to remember another game where my interest was as flatlined as that game. It's kinda like with movies, where the worst thing a movie can be is completely middle-of-the-road boring, almost like horseshoe theory, where the worse it gets the more interesting it gets.

I think Ark: Survival and Dying Light come close though... and both have really shoe-horned in loot-finding, crafting, and skill trees, "hold button to fill circle to *then* be displayed a list of literal trash you've found to then click through" search mechanics. Busy work for the sake of """being addicting""" to keep you playing because the game's main focus is real-time mass multiplayer, where if the player base dies, then the game dies. In 5-10 years, no one will remember this game, no one will talk about it.

Also they all have the "menu hell" that every modern game has. Reminds me of the worst aspects of Ni-Oh, or Quake Champions, or  ANY battle royale game, but with none of the good aspects. I feel like a lot of people view gaming as "just something to do to fill the void", so they love all this kind of sh*t. Which, to be clear, is why modern gaming is the way it is. Because something like what a bunch of more esoteric indie games (UFO 50, for example) go for is too... "jagged", polarizing, experimental. People like the familiar & generic, they don't want to be challenged.

You might say you could just ignore the looting & menu hell altogether, and just roll a free load out, sure, but the core gameplay is still uninspired run-of-the-mill 3rd person shooting action with cut-and-paste exploration. Regardless, you most certainly will need to engage with the loot autism on a long enough time line. You can buy weapons & gear from the store, but you'd need to get money from selling the loot. You'd save time by memorizing/looking up what you can craft from that loot or upgrade from that loot (or break down to recyclable sub-trash) to save money, since you're already hunting that same loot to get money anyway. So you'd need to memorize/look-up what to keep, sell, and recycle. Then use your extra money to shortcut where it makes sense. And you need to do all this since when you inevitably run into aggressive players, the upgraded, better guns are just flat out better. You lose your good stuff if you die, so you then will need to do brain-dead busy work loot runs. In addition to all this, you get EXP from looting. You need the EXP to climb the skill tree to get basic "More stamina" "run faster" "suck ass-hole less" "take less damage from explosions" BS that all the people who are aggressive and have already sank hundreds of hours into the game already have, along with their better guns.

The circular logic here is crazy. If anyone likes this, that's fine. I just struggle to think of a game I'd rather play less, which is **not** and exaggeration. It's the gaming equivalent of making license plates in a prison work line, or turning big rocks into little rocks.

Arc Raiders is an extraction shooter. It says exactly what it is on the box and you get exactly what you buy from it. 

The issue is the fundamental flaw with extraction shooter genre, and whether you can over come this flaw and still enjoy it.

Gear Inequity. Due to how the game is structured you have to win to get good gear. Die? You lose everything, Even if you have 2 other players in your squad win, dying means you lose. Have a good gun? Die and it's gone, make a new one. Made a new gun? Die and it's gone. Now you are down 2. If you don't win you continue to lose and continue to lose gear to actually run with. 

Then the game gets to a point where the only people left playing are people with better guns. And since guns in this game are Statistically better when upgraded, and will kill you FASTER than your weaker guns, you are now ALWAYS playing with a disadvantage. Ope you just died to a guy with a gun that killed you in 2 hits. He has 6x times your shields and was holding a corner you could never push. Now you have no gear. 

The game attempts to allieviate this by giving you free loadouts, but this doesn't actually stop the problem. Free loadouts will almost never beat upgraded guns. 

You are now in an endless cycle of attempting to get enough garbage crafting materials out just to make a gun, or a kit, or something. 

Allow me to showcase an event that happened in game.

A Masterpiece Smothered by PvP Extraction Tropes

​Current Status: Mixed / Thumbs Down (Pending Improvements)

​I want to love this game. I’ve spent hundreds of hours in this world, and the core of what Embark has built is genuinely special. However, the recent shift in direction—leaning heavily into a "Tarkov-lite" PvP mindset—is systematically dismantling the atmosphere and camaraderie that made the game unique.

​The Good: Atmosphere, Design, and Moments of Humanity
​Visual & World Direction: The art style and visual fidelity are top-tier. The "unknowing" challenges and the way the world presents itself keep the gameplay loop fresh.
​The ARC AI: The mechanical threat feels imposing and intelligent, making every encounter with the machines a true challenge.
​Organic Camaraderie: There is nothing like the feeling of saving an overwhelmed player with a defib or building trust with a stranger. My real-world hunting skills actually feel applicable here—tracking, sneaking, and picking the right moment to move.
​The Critical Issues: The "Tarkov" Shadow
​Inventory Chaos: The inventory system feels like it was designed by a team that doesn’t communicate. Stash space is far too limited, and the lack of proper stacking for basic materials makes maintenance a chore rather than a mechanic. Putting a "value" on a loadout feels meaningless when the gear balance is this skewed.
​PvP Toxicity: Shifting the focus to hard PvP has invited a "heartless" community. The sense of mystery is being replaced by "ratting"—players just waiting at doors or extracts to kill you in the back for loot they didn't work for. It’s unbalanced, cheap, and kills the PvE design.
​The Gear Disconnect: High-tier gear is too costly to maintain and often underperforms compared to "cheap" meta weapons. It feels like high-tier gear is a letdown, while low-tier gear allows PvP players to "stat-check" everyone without risk.
​Mechanical Imbalance & Augment Design
​The Shield Problem: There is a massive lack of balance between Augments and Shields. Seems like only combat and tactical augments will be giving medium shields. All MK3 aug should allow for Medium Shields. Being punished for using a looting mk3 that doesnt have a med shield makes me feel like im just goop for pvp players. 
It makes no sense that a high-tier looting mk3 augment build forces you into a weak defense, making you a walking target for PvP "chops."
​Augment Logic: The new augments feel like "band-aids" for base game issues. One lets you put a gun in a safe pocket—which should have been a base feature—while the unlimited defib has such a long cooldown (4 mins) that it’s useless in late-match entries.
​The "Late Entry" Trap: The CEO has suggested that entering a match late (15–20 mins in) leads to "better loot," but in reality, you just find empty boxes and plastic because everything has been picked clean. It feels like a nudge to stop looting and start killing other players for their bags—a total pivot from the "pioneer" PvE roots.

​Proposed Solutions for Embark
​Separate Servers: Stop treating us as data points. Give us a choice: PvE-only servers for those who want to immerse in the world and the machine threat, and PvPvE servers for those who want the sweat.
​Standardize Extracts: Get rid of the randomized hatch times. Make all extracts consistent so "rats" can't just camp the only open exit.
​Self-Revive: Give players a single self-revive chance. In a world where even "friendly" players are being pushed to loot your body, we need a way to get back up once without relying on a toxic community.
​Balance the MK3s: Give the MK3 Augments all a Medium Shield. If it’s meant to be a high-tier survivability build, let us actually survive.
​Final Word
​Embark is currently leaning into a crowd that tells PvE players to "go play Minecraft." If the devs continue to ignore the community that fell in love with the original PvE vision in favor of chasing a rude, PvP-focused meta, they will lose the heart of their player base. I have the passion to stay, but not if my opinion as a dedicated player doesn't matter.

A game I have been waiting years to play, when it was still supposed to be PVE. 

The world is beatiful and breathtaking, from lush swamps to concreate and desert, I cought myself many times just enjoying the view. The scale and monumentality of the loacations topside seems intimidating at first but quickly makes you feel at home. Reminds me a bit of Denis Villeneuve portreyal of Dune, looking at you Spaceport. You can even find some cinematographers directing short scenes in the game, that's how you know it's great. The game offers 5 unique maps, each with different environments, challenges and threats, what works on one may fail you on others, that makes things interesting and rewards those who adapt. Add seasonal and permanent events like electromagnetic storm or night raids and double the variety.

The Arc are a threat that command respect and fear, they are no joke and evolve their tactics alongside the Raiders who balance betweeen prey and hunter. When possible you pick your fights, sometimes taking cover and hiding is the only way out when alarmed Arc call for backup with their terrifing electronic howls and circle around you like wolves. You can hide but you can't run, they will get you and the next thing you see is Speranza.

As last humans under mechine terror we are not defenceless, the world provides us with diffferent kinds of weapons to fight the Arc, from simple firearms like handguns, SMGs, shotguns and bolt or lever action rifles to granade launchers and energy weapons. The arsenal of gadgets, mines and grenades deserves a whole different chapter as their use cases are fueled by human creativity alone, even the devs were impressed - flying deadline :0 

We are not alone. More often then not you will encounter other riders who like you want to survive and get back home with what they managed fill their backpacks with, maybe you will help each other fighting the Arc, share supplies, extract together and be friends, maybe. 

Maybe they will betray you when you type in the security codes in the elevator just before your return to speranza, laughting at how gullible and naive you are and they are right. There are many ways to protect yourself from Arc but what saves you from other riders are your instincts, raiders will lie to you, they will gain your trust and hit you when you least expect it, you will learn how and who to trust the hard way and the lessons are punishing. You get to know yourself a lot in situations like that, will you preemptively kill a "friendly" just because they feel off? Will you kill another to save yourself? What if there is a witness? Will you kill them too? Will you kill out of fear? Or will you die becase you are brave enough to trust?

That was what the good part, now the bad and ugly.
The core of the game has not yet crystallized so it's a gamble, it has potential to become a great game over the years but right now Embark Studios is not sure what their game is supposed to be. After few hundred hours it's safe to say the endgame is nonexistent, play loop becomes either boring or frustrating, excietment wears off, novelty fizzles down and all that's left is stash full weapons that are prohibitively expansive to repair. Freeloadaout was initially good idea that was implemented in a way that serves only cheaters, who by the way just recived 3 strikes before permanently banned. 

Close to no content updates, too much focus on skin microtransactions, timegated events, lackluster projects, dozens of tabs and menus just to gear up for a game where a freeloadout kills you.
Want to kill a Bastion or Bombardier in an epic fight? Forget it, after first agro nearby raiders will make sure you are not getting out alive and even if you do a rat will kill you at extraction.

If you like PVE this is not a game for you.
If you like PVP this is not a game for you.

Arc Raiders is a great game – it really is.

I decided to pick the game up because I heard good things from people I trust.  I was worried because I don't typically play extraction shooters due to literally the core mechanic of getting killed and losing everything in your inventory.

My first round, I was absolutely terrified. I hid in a bush for 25 minutes and then sprinted into a elevator under duress.

My second round, I completed a mission, hid in a building for 10 minutes, then died because a Wasp found me and called a second Wasp, which I was completely unprepared for. I really should have looked up gameplay before I bought this game.

After several more rounds, I started encountering other players, which was also initially terrifying. I didn't really know the communication meta and expected people to just walk up and blast me.  However, I quickly got the hang of things and begun the early game resources grind to upgrade your crafting stations and get better gear. Player interaction was never quite co-operative, but people would run by, flash their light or use a greeting emote, and be on their way.  I was finally getting confident in the gameplay, especially in knowing where things were on the Dam level. I could get into a round, fill up my inventory with goodies, and hit an escape elevator whenever it suited me.

Then, one game, someone just walked up and shot me in the face. Oh yeah, this is a PvP game. I stared long and hard at my empty inventory. Why did I do this to myself? Hours of progress gone in an instant of blind trust. Anyway, I queued up again and got all my stuff back quicker the next time around.

Overall I think it's a good game because I stepped outside my comfort zone and was rewarded. I think the  artwork and environment design are great and best of all, it's enjoyable to use your weapon. There are some minor issues here and there but that's how it goes. I think crafting could be designed a little better, I found myself having to click in a lot of different places to get what I wanted. Also, unless there's something I missed about the Blueprint mechanic, it seems like I am waiting on random chance to get the Blueprints I need to reliably create and maintain my gear. After forty hours of Arc Raiders with my squad, I can confidently say this game feels like someone took Starship Troopers, mixed it with Destiny, sprinkled in a little chaos, and then handed it to a group of sleep‑deprived soldiers who think “tactical” means “run at it until it stops moving.”

Gameplay Vibes

• 	The firefights hit that sweet spot between “cinematic” and “why is everything exploding again.”
• 	Every encounter turns into a full‑blown platoon operation except with more screaming and fewer safety briefs.
• 	The physics engine deserves a medal for how many times it launched one of us into low orbit.

Team Dynamics

Playing with an Army team adds a special flavor:
• 	Someone is always trying to flank… even when flanking is physically impossible.
• 	Someone else is hoarding ammo “for later,” then panicking when the ARC drop a titan on us.
• 	And there’s always that one guy who insists he’s “just testing the fall damage.”
Honestly, the game should give bonus XP for “maintaining unit cohesion despite questionable decision‑making.”

The ARC

The ARC enemies feel like they were designed by someone who asked, “What if robots were angry about everything?”
They swarm, they snipe, they drop from the sky like they’re late for formation.
We respect them.
We hate them.
We keep fighting them anyway.

Highlights from 40 Hours

• 	Accidentally discovering that teamwork does matter when we actually try it.
• 	Perfectly timed revives that felt more heroic than anything we’ve done in real life.
• 	That one mission where everything went wrong but we somehow pulled it off and acted like it was intentional.

 Final Verdict

Arc Raiders with the squad is chaotic, hilarious, and surprisingly tactical.
It’s the closest thing to a field exercise without the heat, the sand, or someone yelling about accountability formation.

If the next 40 hours are anything like the first, the ARC don’t stand a chance though our comms discipline probably does.

I’m about 15 hours in, and I’m still kind of mixed. The PvE + PvP setup keeps every run tense — you never really know how it’s going to play out, and that unpredictability is what makes it fun. When it works, it really works. The game looks and sounds great, the guns feel good, and the atmosphere does a lot of the heavy lifting. There are moments where everything clicks and it pulls you in hard.

The best parts are easily the unplanned player interactions. I’ve been trash-talked and wiped, had clean extractions, and even been saved at the last second by random squads just doing their thing. Extraction camping shows up a lot, and on top of that, load-in times can be rough — sometimes we spawn late with only around 15 minutes left, which is a huge disatvantage when it comes to looting the spots you need to farm.

The game also leans pretty hard on AI, and that’s where PvP starts to feel off. Drones jump in forcing loud engagements that burn your ammo, give away your position, and leave you weak before the player fight even gets going. When it finally wraps up, it’s less about aim or movement and more about who still has resources left. By the time you reach extraction, you’re usually worn down — which is exactly when players who’ve been camping the extract all raid step in and clean up with their full loadouts. It makes surviving the run feel less rewarding. If drones are meant to create chaos, it’d make way more sense for them to pressure extraction zones so campers actually have to play the game.

Cosmetics are also insanely overpriced, and while the core loop can be fun, it starts to feel repetitive faster than it should — loot, craft, repeat.

Overall, it’s not a bad game, but it’s also not quite hitting what I expected yet. It’s already given me some genuinely memorable moments, and if you’re into tense extraction games with strong atmosphere and player-driven chaos, there’s definitely something here — just go in knowing there’s a lot of camping and heavier AI pressure than you might want right now.

[h1]100 hours in a casual game is exceptional, for me[/h1]

Arc Raiders is an extraction shooter, that gives you the opportunity to decide if you shoot other players. You can play alone, or with up to three friends. The rules are simple, [b]just survive.[/b] At the end, it only matters that you are safe with your loot at home.

[h2]Why I like this game[/h2]
[b]It is nearly perfect. I mean, nothing can be perfect, but Arc Raiders is unique.[/b]

The thing that makes this game so good for me is because it gives me a special feeling that I can´t describe. I mean that feeling when I randomly find an Aphelion blueprint, or I meet other Raiders. The emotions and actions that happen during a game are the things that make me play this game. I really enjoyed when I had to laugh, or even if I raged, just everything. I can´t rate the graphics because I don´t play enough games to really understand them.

[h3]Game experience[/h3]

You queue in a game and you always have a different mood. Just imagine you have 10 Wolfpacks with you, and you hope that nobody shoots you. Maybe you are chill and run a free loadout. Or you take your Tempest with you, that you have found last round. Your mood already changes before the round starts. That is literally amazing, I think it is an unnoticed detail that many people don´t see.
You search for good stuff and then another player appears. This is the moment when you need to make a decision. You either shoot him or you don´t. Trust me, thats not as that easy as it sounds. Many players are friendly, but be aware there are a few that pretend to be are friendly and then shoot you in the back. Of course, if you are in PVP lobbies, this is something different but in most lobbies a few will shoot and a few won´t. And really you will feel bad, if you eliminate a friendly player. This makes you think twice before shooting at someone. But if you think to long and the player is hostile. Well then it is over for you. Keep that in mind.

[i]"Arc Raiders it lets you play how you want and not how the the game wants you to play"[/i]
Random Raider that I meet.

Summary: You search for loot and need to make decidions that change the end of the match.

I really don´t want to spoiler to much. Thats why I end here.[b] I can really recommend this game to every type of gamer. It doesn´t matter if you are a casual or a competitive player.[/b]

Thanks you for reading this review. I hope you found it helpful.
