I expected this game to be a little bit like Warframe, where you walk around a safe hub, craft gear, experiment with your build by mixing and matching the various components, and cooperate with teammates to finish quests and get out alive. In reality, this game has a narrow-minded poorly thought out philosophy of gameplay. Here are the main gripes I have with ARC Raiders:

- There is no way to test loadouts and weapons safely. You cannot experiment with loadouts or specific weapons to see how they handle unless you are ok with running the risk of losing them. We are therefore disincentivized from building a skill set and crafting an identity.

- There is no obvious way to use text chat. On top of being a valuable fallback option for team communication, text chat could also offer a way to log information to the squad without having to repeat oneself over voice chat. Unfortunately, the narrow-minded design philosophy of the developer renders them incapable of even conceiving that text chat might offer valuable and meaningful utility. The fact that the game has existed for several months without a staple like text chat should make it clear that this developer is not worth wasting time on.

- Controls do not automatically remap to accommodate for alternative keyboard layouts. This is not a very serious problem since all controls can be remapped manually, albeit with no way to tell what bindings controls had before they were overwritten. Still, auto remapping is an industry standard. Refusal to follow this standard could potentially be a sign of sloppiness under the hood, so I thought I would include this gripe here.

- There is no way to sync up quests. How many more of an item does my teammate need to complete a quest? How do I show my teammates how many more items I need? I was unable to find a way to relay this information. This just compounds the profound frustration around being unable to communicate basic information. This is another problem that no competent developer would ever allow to see the light of day. It also segues into my final gripe...

- There is no way to divvy up the loot in a safe environment. Say you have just returned from a bountiful journey with squad mates. Surely there must be a way to swap the loot you each found while on your journey, all from the safety of the local bar or an apartment? Does my teammate need one last of a certain item that I found in surplus during our journey? Astonishingly, there is no way whatsoever to do any post-game loot swapping.  This is yet another industry standard that somehow managed to slip the mind of the developer. You actually have to bring the loot back up to the surface just to exchange it. That's like having to go to the international space station just to split some chicken nuggets from McDonald's.

If I were the developer, I would be way too embarrassed even to provide the canned response that they probably use to answer reviews like this, let alone provide an actually thought-out defense, which would be borderline impossible. It's a damn shame too. This game could have been great if it hadn't been dragged down by what I can only assume is developer complacency.

Arc Raiders is a rare breed of game. A common theme following the looter/extraction genre and yet it brings to the table a few things that most developers currently cannot. Above average quality across the board from the launch. Legit. 

The graphics are solid and the production design on the levels is fantastic. The AI intelligence is dangerous, hard and annoying, presenting some real challenge to initially get used to and still fully capable of ending a good run real fast if you don't respect the threat. 

The game has its own style of future that fits well and looks good. Character creation is limited, There are real money outfits but also a whole host of free and obtainable options too so you can find some style you like. 

There are bugs in the game but they are constantly trying to be ironed out, as is the whole package. We have seen a few dire bugs (wall glitches mostly) that have been rectified and a couple of balance changes here and there, so I expect a couple more to come.

Now my biggest fear for this game was the 3rd person shooting (yes there are corner peeks, the camping is hard and pushing takes a little getting used to) but the fighting across different maps can still be tactful, strategic and a lot of fun. They have a decent selection of weaponry which can be very slightly improved with levelling up using materials and a basic selection of attachments.

There is a basic base to build up, some workbenches to construct and level and then blue prints that must be found and extracted in raid for pretty much all the gear, explosives and weapons in the game. There is a seasonal reset that you have to choose to go for and complete some pretty annoying tasks to achieve it. One of my biggest gripes currently is the inventory management, with limited storage space and so much crap and goop to hold, despite the numerous upgrades, you run out quick.

The funniest part of the game for me has been the interactions with other players along my Arc Raiders career and I can only express my thanks and gratitude to the players I randomly met and shared some crazy games with. There are a LOT of people that think this is a friendly game, and to a large extent, it can be thanks to the basic voice lines your player can shout as well as using your mic to talk out loud, but if you play the passive role, you will die many times to the more aggressive and greedy players.
I cannot express this more clearly:
The game is PvPvE. 
Solo's play with solo's, duo's play with duos and trio's play with trios, but the 2's and 3's are non stop gun fights 99% of the time.

Arc Raiders is a rare breed of game. A common theme following the looter/extraction genre and yet it brings to the table a few things that most developers currently cannot. Above average quality across the board from the launch. Legit. 

The graphics are solid and the production design on the levels is fantastic. The AI intelligence is dangerous, hard and annoying, presenting some real challenge to initially get used to and still fully capable of ending a good run real fast if you don't respect the threat. 

The game has its own style of future that fits well and looks good. Character creation is limited, There are real money outfits but also a whole host of free and obtainable options too so you can find some style you like. 

There are bugs in the game but they are constantly trying to be ironed out, as is the whole package. We have seen a few dire bugs (wall glitches mostly) that have been rectified and a couple of balance changes here and there, so I expect a couple more to come.

Now my biggest fear for this game was the 3rd person shooting (yes there are corner peeks, the camping is hard and pushing takes a little getting used to) but the fighting across different maps can still be tactful, strategic and a lot of fun. They have a decent selection of weaponry which can be very slightly improved with levelling up using materials and a basic selection of attachments.

There is a basic base to build up, some workbenches to construct and level and then blue prints that must be found and extracted in raid for pretty much all the gear, explosives and weapons in the game. There is a seasonal reset that you have to choose to go for and complete some pretty annoying tasks to achieve it. One of my biggest gripes currently is the inventory management, with limited storage space and so much crap and goop to hold, despite the numerous upgrades, you run out quick.

The funniest part of the game for me has been the interactions with other players along my Arc Raiders career and I can only express my thanks and gratitude to the players I randomly met and shared some crazy games with. There are a LOT of people that think this is a friendly game, and to a large extent, it can be thanks to the basic voice lines your player can shout as well as using your mic to talk out loud, but if you play the passive role, you will die many times to the more aggressive and greedy players.
I cannot express this more clearly:
The game is PvPvE. 
Solo's play with solo's, duo's play with duos and trio's play with trios, but the 2's and 3's are non stop gun fights 99% of the time. 
Solo's is... very mixed bag. Some days the whole server will come together to bring down the biggest machines in the game to achieve victory together, then other days you will be non stop camped, betrayed, or simply lose fights to other people or the AI. If you are not prepared to let go of what you have, don't bother playing, it will only sour your soul.

TLDR: Fucking good quality all around game. Props for actually putting something out that really felt crafted and cared for. Also way more fun than I expected from a 3rd person looter/shooter. I hope to see you top side Raider.

Arc raiders is truly a great looking and feeling game, from the audio design to the animations and parkour system, it all feels crafted with care for the purpose of providing a near cinematic experience.

This, however, is just skin deep. Below the beautiful graphics, quirky arc ai and fun gunplay lays a broken core system. Matchmaking is divisive and extreme, audio is as broken as it is beautiful and can't be relied upon in almost any circumstances for a plethora of reasons, spawns and spawn times are not at all thought out or balanced, and the devs seem to be trying to take the game two different directions at once and have strayed far from the original idea and intent of the game. To say nothing of the server issues.

 No longer is it a game of unknown risks. No longer is it a game where you have to think about the people around you and their intentions. It no longer truly plays like PvPvE game it was at the start, but more like two very different games. On one hand you have a pve game who's players don't hurt others for fear of being banished to the shadow realm, and on the other you have said shadow realm: the pvp game. On paper it's not a terrible thing, but in effect it's effectively gutted the entire feel of the game.

 Pve lobbies are boring and full of players who will just ignore you 90% of the time, but you can fill your stash for free. Pvp lobbies are basically just call of duty but with more steps. The issues this creates are many. They are two incredibly different gameplay loops that use the same core balancing and systems.

 I'm not often in pve servers so I can't elaborate too much on any problems they see frequently, but the pvp side of things is in fairly poor state. Since every game is full of players who just chase shots/flares 3rd partying is absolutely insane. You can regularly get 4th, 5th, and even 6th partied on big open maps. With consistency. Spawns being so close together at times means you can literally spend more time crafting your loadout (I'm not even going to get into the frustration that is this games crafting system/ui) than being in a game with it. Add things like player audio not even existing at times and server instability and it can feel borderline unplayable at times. This not even including absolutely game breaking bugs/the leniency shown to cheaters and exploiters.


TL;DR: The gunplay/visuals/audio/movement all feel fantastic and immersive. The gameplay experience/audio is deeply broken and this is not a game I'd recommend for anyone looking for a consistent or balanced pvp experience. However, if you're looking for a pve game or just don't care about anything that's deeper than just the gunplay/movement then this IS a game for you.

Oh it’s overhyped. Painfully so. Glitchy like it shipped with a shrug and a prayer. A background that constantly asks you the same existential question you are asking yourself WTF am I doing with my time. A reward and ranking system that actively celebrates bad play and punishes competence because accountability is apparently toxic now. Welcome to the game that looks like Fallout 4 and Call of Duty hooked up at a family reunion and nobody stopped them.

Graphically it’s shiny. Distractingly shiny. Gameplay though is reheated leftovers. Two missions in you will have the horrifying clarity that the entire experience is about six maps on a sad little rotation, sprinkled with NPC bots who outnumber you, outgun you, and apparently trained at a private military academy you never got the invite to.

Then come the kids. Endless waves of twelve year old spawn campers whose only known coping mechanism is griefing strangers. They camp entry points, exit points, and anything resembling fun, all while teetering on the edge of an emotional collapse because someone somewhere reminded them that the universe does not care about their feelings.

As a delightful cherry on top, the developers offer cosmetic items. You know, the important stuff. For credits. Which you buy. In exchange you get dance moves and clothing that looks like a chicken lost a knife fight with a blender and was reassembled by someone who actively hates color theory. Congratulations. You now look like a rejected mascot from a gas station energy drink.

So yes, by all means, get swept up in the hype. Spend your money, or your parents money, on this experience instead of literally anything else. A different game. A movie. A book. Staring at a wall. Putting the cash on a table and setting it on fire. At least the fire would provide warmth, light, and a brief moment of honest entertainment. Unlike this game, which mostly offers regret, wasted time, and the creeping realization that you paid for it.

[i]ARC Raiders[/i] is pretty unique when compared to the other games in the Extraction Shooter Genre. This game really is fun, the AI is challenging and the experience with other raiders in VOIP keeps you on your toes. There were some issues that started to appear during what I call "[i]The Honeymoon Stage[/i]", however they seemed more as minor annoyances that you would learn to shake off rather than something that deterred you from playing. However, the past month or two has begun to change the momentum of the game in a [b]negative[/b] way.

[h2]Gameplay Loop[/h2]
This game is way more casual and laid back compared to other games within the genre. Despite that, many people, especially streamers have played the game with the same commitment and intensity that they had on other games. Even people who do not create content but enjoy the grind run into the same wall. There is not much to go through, the endgame is extremely weak. The quests do very little to reward those who spend time doing them (especially re-doing). I am not suggesting to just copy [i]Escape From Tarkov[/i]'s mechanics but adding an extra benefit to completing quests such as lowered prices, higher item purchase caps, exclusive trades/offers, or being able to purchase upgraded weapons would be a great addition in my eyes. It would also give people an incentive to complete quests, I know several people who grind out the Expedition Project and then put the game down until "wipe". That won't retain the player base's attention and eventually people will get out of the news loop and will miss the Expedition window being open. Now I find the whole Expedition to be unique and a really inventive idea, I just believe it should be slightly more tasking to obtain. To be clear, I do not mean in the way of gathering more materials to construct your vessel. Either certain questlines should be required or a feat system could be interesting, killing a number of ARC or Raiders, bringing out a target total value, or possibly having multiple options and you pick which ones you are going to complete. I believe there should be more to do, not necessarily more difficult, just more.

[h2]Content & Earnable Cosmetics[/h2]
While the shop is updated with a new outfit every week, there should be something else that is going to engage people other than the [b]Wallet Warriors[/b]. This goes without saying but the [i]Raider Decks[/i] need to be more frequent at the very least, assuming the amount of content within the decks remains the same. Additionally, to reward people who quest and/or repeatedly complete quests after each expedition, there should be some permanent cosmetic rewards. There could be multiple ways I see it going, one is to keep the outfits & charms you get from completing chapters and add permanent ones alongside it. On top of that, make the permanent rewards change for each expedition the player has gone on. Going a step further, you can give players cosmetics for completing an achievement or an event (preferably having the cosmetic match the theme of the event). I am a big fan of obtainable cosmetics to show off and be proud of.

[h2]Bugs & Exploits[/h2]
In my experience, spanning from late November(2025) to early January(2026) the game seemed extremely odd. The Flying ARC seemed to have forgotten how to navigate the maps, getting stuck & being able to be cheesed with little effort. During December is when it seemed to really fall apart and people started abusing bugs. From players sitting in ratholes within walls & getting into places you shouldn’t be able to, to duplicating and exploiting, things seemed to have gotten out of control quickly. While I find it incredible how fundamentally broken the foundation of this game must be if there are such a vast amount of ways to exploit geometry, physics, and gear, there is a much bigger problem. [b]The Anti-Cheat System[/b], it is definitely one of the most discussed aspects of this game, and for good reason. The 3 strikes to a permaban is outrageous. [b]Cheating has battered and bullied the gaming industry for what seems like a long time now[/b]. People are not going to stop cheating because you suspend their account for 60 days. They most likely have already created a system for this atrocious method. One account gets suspended, then you play on another and fill in the gaps of time just to return 2 months later. It is not the deterrent the developers think it is. Using an external software and unfairly overcoming other raiders is not something that is accidental and will be fixed with a slap on the wrist. There is a reason this method is not popular or utilized by any other game, at least to my knowledge. 

[h2]Mechanics, 3PP, & HUD[/h2]
Originally I absolutely hated this game, playing for possibly 60 minutes during the Technical Demo before launch. My biggest complaints were it being third person, and the HUD having absolutely no feedback. Granted the latter was a bit of a nitpick however I do believe there should be a little to make it more immersive. You are protected by an ARC-adjacent shield system, there should be some feedback besides the auditorial & visual effects on your character. However, with it being 3PP I can understand the argument for not needing it. That is one thing I have yet to shake, I can’t help but imagine this game in First Person. The environments and enemies would be so much more intimidating, and it would undoubtedly affect the PvP encounters. My biggest issue with 3rd person PvP games is the peeking around corners coupled with sitting & waiting for them to get into your ideal spot before ambushing. The first person combat is just superior, you have to expose yourself to get visual, otherwise you are going by ear. The weapons feel closer and heavier, the damage hurts more, it simply would’ve been so much more intense. Looking from another angle, I’m sure the rolling & dodging mechanic is more pleasing to think about in a third person perspective like [i]Star Wars Battlefront[/i], although I do believe it would be just as good in FPP. I love the ability to roll, sometimes I do think it is a little whacky. A good example would be with players using the Toro coupled with shooting a shot and then rolling. It seems a bit too fast & accurate, while it is fun to do, being on the other side of it seems very difficult to track (especially for controller players I would imagine). Now that could just be my disdain for using shotguns in PvP games though, but it does need balancing. 

[h2]Why I gave it a Thumbs Up[/h2]
This game is great and has a lot of room for growth if the developers take control of the current issues. The PvP encounters are addicting, and the PvPvE encounters (running into players but not fighting each other) can range from vibey & wholesome to awkward & goofy. This game is great for casual & collaborative play, and for the most part works for intense & grindy play, just don’t go through it too fast because you will run out of stuff to do.

I really wanted to like Arc Raiders.
Seriously. The world design is cool, the gunplay feels solid, the scavenging loop has that tense “one more run” energy, and the whole PvPvE thing should be a perfect mix of risk and reward.

Should be.

Instead, most matches feel like daycare for feral raccoons with keyboards.

The biggest threat in Arc Raiders isn’t the ARC machines.
It isn’t the storm.
It isn’t resource scarcity.

It’s other players acting like complete jackasses for no reason.

Not tactical ambushes. Not smart PvP. Not “we fought over loot and only one team walks away.”

No.

I’m talking:

Camping extraction for 20 minutes just to delete someone who did all the work

Chasing fresh spawns across the map like it’s a personal vendetta

Ignoring objectives entirely just to grief

Third-partying fights purely to ruin both sides and not even looting

Teabagging like it’s 2009 Xbox Live

There’s zero strategy behind it. Zero survival logic. Just pure “how can I waste someone else’s time today?”

It’s not tense PvP — it’s toddler behavior with rifles.

And that’s what kills the experience.

Because the game wants you to scavenge, explore, plan routes, manage risk.
But you can’t do any of that when every lobby has at least one squad whose only goal is to make sure nobody else gets to play.

There’s a difference between “dangerous players” and “pointless griefing.”

Dangerous players make the game exciting.
Griefers make it exhausting.

Half my runs end not with “wow that was intense,” but with:

“Cool. Wasted 30 minutes because some dude with nothing to gain decided to sit in a bush like a fungus.”

And after enough of that, you just stop caring.

Which sucks, because underneath all the nonsense is a genuinely fun game trying really hard to exist.

But right now?

It feels less like a tactical extraction shooter and more like a social experiment proving that if you give people proximity chat and guns, they immediately become goblins.

If the devs don’t add better incentives, smarter matchmaking, or something to discourage brain-dead griefing, this game is going to eat itself alive.

I didn't expect much from Arc Raiders. I admit that I bought it just to see what my shiny new PC could do.

Wow, this game!

PvE and PvP and all cleverly stitched together so that you can largely opt into and out of either organically, based on your good or... less than well-meaning behavior.

The ARC? Fairly clever bastards. Well, some of them anyway. A few are as dumb as rocks. That is, if you get them to box *YOU* in, you can take pot shots at them, while ducking and covering, until you win.  The AI is fun to play against.

The terrain. The movement. The gear. It all *feels* solid. Embark tuned the hell out of this game.

What I love most about the game is its emergent properties. Each round can play out drastically differently based on where you begin, your loadout, the raiders (players) you encounter, and where the ARC spawn and which ones. All to say, sometimes dying is just dumb luck. But squeaking out a return home while skirting the edge of the blade? What a f***ing rush!

You have to think do to well in this game. Sure, casuals can enjoy it too. But it takes prudence to succeed.

ARC Raiders is a wonderful extraction game, especially if you enjoy learning valuable life lessons like “never trust anyone.”

There’s nothing more fun than running into other players during a match screaming “don’t shoot.” That’s usually when you make the rookie mistake of believing them. Your new “friend” follows you around the map, helps you destroy ARCs, lets you loot in peace, and really sells the whole teamwork fantasy.

Then, at the most important moment — right before returning to Speranza — their true nature reveals itself. You get shot in the back, your character dies in complete confusion, and you’re left staring at the screen wondering when exactly you lost all faith in humanity.

Naturally, in the very next match, you evolve. Anyone yelling “don’t shoot” gets shot immediately. No questions asked. Character development at its finest.

ARC Raiders isn’t just a game; it’s a social experiment about betrayal, paranoia, and how fast a player can go from friendly explorer to emotionally damaged war criminal.

Highly recommended if you enjoy extraction games, emotional scars, and shooting first — just to be safe.

This game is great. It is the most social game I have played, as you need to interact over voice chat or character emotes to discern whether other players are hostile or friendly. This is the only way to determine whether someone will be friendly or hostile, team up with you or if there is some other exchange to be made between you. The game forces you to interact with others, which is a great mechanic.

Now that there's aggression based match making, I recommend starting the game with not engaging other hostile players and playing in PvE lobbies until you no longer fear losing valuable weapons.

This approach makes the game a social event where you meet other solo players and raid together, make online friends and get some nice high value loot from more experienced players (there's a very generous community in the non-aggressive lobbies).

Even as you level up you're never very powerful in this game. If you are out in the open, the easiest enemies are still a big threat to you if they come in number above two or three. If you don't stay focused and calm you will perform much worse and with the countdown ticking, this is a great challenge at some times. So you are always on your guard in open terrain, and engage enemies from different covers. There is this continous feeling of being exposed and vulnerable because you are essentially weaker than the ARCs.

After you get a bit higher level and maybe aren't in it for the loot and craft bench upgrades anymore there's the trials. Getting higher scores in them is a puzzle in and of itself that is a lot of fun to figure out. Seeing my rank rise on the leaderboards after a succesful trial run feels great.  I just did one, exceeding my high score and I was shaking afterwards because the final minutes before extracting were so intense and I was so so close to not making it. I don't remember playing another game that affected me so much.

The bullet physics are rewarding as they make it difficult to perform at a distance and so when you do, it is satisfying. Figuring out the timing of different enemies and when they're easiest to take down (which is usually when they're the biggest threat to you) is a lot of fun. Embark has struck a great balance between skill and reward. Perhaps my favorite thing about this game is how disadvantaged you feel against the ARCs.

I haven't had too many PvP encounters yet but the ones I have had turns the game into something completely different. This is basically two games in one. I think this will be my game of the year 44 hours into playing it. But let's see how my interest for it develops.

it looks amazing. The art style, world design and atmosphere are top-tier and the PvE gameplay is genuinely fun. Exploring, fighting AI enemies feels great. With a stronger PvE focus, this could've been a really solid MMO-like experience.

Sadly, the PvP kills it for me. It's some of the worst PvP I've ever played. Hit feedback is awful and inconsistent, gunfights feel random. I'm also not a fan of  third-person PvP in general, and here it just makes ancounters feel clunky and frustrating. Other players can sit safely in cover, move their camera around corners and see me long before i can see them. From my perspective, they're completly invisible.  This leads to cheap ambusches where the fight is basicly decided before i even get visual contact.

From a story and immersion perspective, the PvP also makes very little sense. We all come from the same city - a city thats barely surviving. Raiders are supposed to risk their lives to gather resources and help the city endure, so why are we killing each other out there? Instead of feeling like survivors working toward a common goal, we're forced into PvP that feels disconnected from the wolrd and its narrative.

Forcing PvE and PvP together is a huge mistake in my opinion. Dedicated PvP zones or aPvP flag system would massively improve the experience and let different player types enjoy the game their own way.

So this is my kinde mixed review. Love the Worldbuilding but cant stand the PvP. Its still worth checking it out, its not a bad game.

Arc raiders is truly a great looking and feeling game, from the audio design to the animations and parkour system, it all feels crafted with care for the purpose of providing a near cinematic experience.

This, however, is just skin deep. Below the beautiful graphics, quirky arc ai and fun gunplay lays a broken core system. Matchmaking is divisive and extreme, audio is as broken as it is beautiful and can't be relied upon in almost any circumstances for a plethora of reasons, spawns and spawn times are not at all thought out or balanced, and the devs seem to be trying to take the game two different directions at once and have strayed far from the original idea and intent of the game. To say nothing of the server issues.

 No longer is it a game of unknown risks. No longer is it a game where you have to think about the people around you and their intentions. It no longer truly plays like PvPvE game it was at the start, but more like two very different games. On one hand you have a pve game who's players don't hurt others for fear of being banished to the shadow realm, and on the other you have said shadow realm: the pvp game. On paper it's not a terrible thing, but in effect it's effectively gutted the entire feel of the game.

 Pve lobbies are boring and full of players who will just ignore you 90% of the time, but you can fill your stash for free. Pvp lobbies are basically just call of duty but with more steps. The issues this creates are many. They are two incredibly different gameplay loops that use the same core balancing and systems.

 I'm not often in pve servers so I can't elaborate too much on any problems they see frequently, but the pvp side of things is in fairly poor state. Since every game is full of players who just chase shots/flares 3rd partying is absolutely insane. You can regularly get 4th, 5th, and even 6th partied on big open maps. With consistency. Spawns being so close together at times means you can literally spend more time crafting your loadout (I'm not even going to get into the frustration that is this games crafting system/ui) than being in a game with it. Add things like player audio not even existing at times and server instability and it can feel borderline unplayable at times. This not even including absolutely game breaking bugs/the leniency shown to cheaters and exploiters.


TL;DR: The gunplay/visuals/audio/movement all feel fantastic and immersive. The gameplay experience/audio is deeply broken and this is not a game I'd recommend for anyone looking for a consistent or balanced pvp experience. However, if you're looking for a pve game or just don't care about anything that's deeper than just the gunplay/movement then this IS a game for you.

Oh it’s overhyped. Painfully so. Glitchy like it shipped with a shrug and a prayer. A background that constantly asks you the same existential question you are asking yourself WTF am I doing with my time. A reward and ranking system that actively celebrates bad play and punishes competence because accountability is apparently toxic now. Welcome to the game that looks like Fallout 4 and Call of Duty hooked up at a family reunion and nobody stopped them.

Graphically it’s shiny. Distractingly shiny. Gameplay though is reheated leftovers. Two missions in you will have the horrifying clarity that the entire experience is about six maps on a sad little rotation, sprinkled with NPC bots who outnumber you, outgun you, and apparently trained at a private military academy you never got the invite to.

Then come the kids. Endless waves of twelve year old spawn campers whose only known coping mechanism is griefing strangers. They camp entry points, exit points, and anything resembling fun, all while teetering on the edge of an emotional collapse because someone somewhere reminded them that the universe does not care about their feelings.

As a delightful cherry on top, the developers offer cosmetic items. You know, the important stuff. For credits. Which you buy. In exchange you get dance moves and clothing that looks like a chicken lost a knife fight with a blender and was reassembled by someone who actively hates color theory. Congratulations. You now look like a rejected mascot from a gas station energy drink.

So yes, by all means, get swept up in the hype. Spend your money, or your parents money, on this experience instead of literally anything else. A different game. A movie. A book. Staring at a wall. Putting the cash on a table and setting it on fire. At least the fire would provide warmth, light, and a brief moment of honest entertainment. Unlike this game, which mostly offers regret, wasted time, and the creeping realization that you paid for it.

[i]ARC Raiders[/i] is pretty unique when compared to the other games in the Extraction Shooter Genre. This game really is fun, the AI is challenging and the experience with other raiders in VOIP keeps you on your toes. There were some issues that started to appear during what I call "[i]The Honeymoon Stage[/i]", however they seemed more as minor annoyances that you would learn to shake off rather than something that deterred you from playing. However, the past month or two has begun to change the momentum of the game in a [b]negative[/b] way.

[h2]Gameplay Loop[/h2]
This game is way more casual and laid back compared to other games within the genre. Despite that, many people, especially streamers have played the game with the same commitment and intensity that they had on other games. Even people who do not create content but enjoy the grind run into the same wall. There is not much to go through, the endgame is extremely weak. The quests do very little to reward those who spend time doing them (especially re-doing). I am not suggesting to just copy [i]Escape From Tarkov[/i]'s mechanics but adding an extra benefit to completing quests such as lowered prices, higher item purchase caps, exclusive trades/offers, or being able to purchase upgraded weapons would be a great addition in my eyes. It would also give people an incentive to complete quests, I know several people who grind out the Expedition Project and then put the game down until "wipe". That won't retain the player base's attention and eventually people will get out of the news loop and will miss the Expedition window being open. Now I find the whole Expedition to be unique and a really inventive idea, I just believe it should be slightly more tasking to obtain. To be clear, I do not mean in the way of gathering more materials to construct your vessel. Either certain questlines should be required or a feat system could be interesting, killing a number of ARC or Raiders, bringing out a target total value, or possibly having multiple options and you pick which ones you are going to complete. I believe there should be more to do, not necessarily more difficult, just more.

[h2]Content & Earnable Cosmetics[/h2]
While the shop is updated with a new outfit every week, there should be something else that is going to engage people other than the [b]Wallet Warriors[/b]. This goes without saying but the [i]Raider Decks[/i] need to be more frequent at the very least, assuming the amount of content within the decks remains the same. Additionally, to reward people who quest and/or repeatedly complete quests after each expedition, there should be some permanent cosmetic rewards. There could be multiple ways I see it going, one is to keep the outfits & charms you get from completing chapters and add permanent ones alongside it. On top of that, make the permanent rewards change for each expedition the player has gone on. Going a step further, you can give players cosmetics for completing an achievement or an event (preferably having the cosmetic match the theme of the event). I am a big fan of obtainable cosmetics to show off and be proud of.

[h2]Bugs & Exploits[/h2]
In my experience, spanning from late November(2025) to early January(2026) the game seemed extremely odd. The Flying ARC seemed to have forgotten how to navigate the maps, getting stuck & being able to be cheesed with little effort. During December is when it seemed to really fall apart and people started abusing bugs. From players sitting in ratholes within walls & getting into places you shouldn’t be able to, to duplicating and exploiting, things seemed to have gotten out of control quickly. While I find it incredible how fundamentally broken the foundation of this game must be if there are such a vast amount of ways to exploit geometry, physics, and gear, there is a much bigger problem. [b]The Anti-Cheat System[/b], it is definitely one of the most discussed aspects of this game, and for good reason. The 3 strikes to a permaban is outrageous. [b]Cheating has battered and bullied the gaming industry for what seems like a long time now[/b]. People are not going to stop cheating because you suspend their account for 60 days. They most likely have already created a system for this atrocious method. One account gets suspended, then you play on another and fill in the gaps of time just to return 2 months later. It is not the deterrent the developers think it is. Using an external software and unfairly overcoming other raiders is not something that is accidental and will be fixed with a slap on the wrist. There is a reason this method is not popular or utilized by any other game, at least to my knowledge. 

[h2]Mechanics, 3PP, & HUD[/h2]
Originally I absolutely hated this game, playing for possibly 60 minutes during the Technical Demo before launch. My biggest complaints were it being third person, and the HUD having absolutely no feedback. Granted the latter was a bit of a nitpick however I do believe there should be a little to make it more immersive. You are protected by an ARC-adjacent shield system, there should be some feedback besides the auditorial & visual effects on your character. However, with it being 3PP I can understand the argument for not needing it. That is one thing I have yet to shake, I can’t help but imagine this game in First Person. The environments and enemies would be so much more intimidating, and it would undoubtedly affect the PvP encounters. My biggest issue with 3rd person PvP games is the peeking around corners coupled with sitting & waiting for them to get into your ideal spot before ambushing. The first person combat is just superior, you have to expose yourself to get visual, otherwise you are going by ear. The weapons feel closer and heavier, the damage hurts more, it simply would’ve been so much more intense. Looking from another angle, I’m sure the rolling & dodging mechanic is more pleasing to think about in a third person perspective like [i]Star Wars Battlefront[/i], although I do believe it would be just as good in FPP. I love the ability to roll, sometimes I do think it is a little whacky. A good example would be with players using the Toro coupled with shooting a shot and then rolling. It seems a bit too fast & accurate, while it is fun to do, being on the other side of it seems very difficult to track (especially for controller players I would imagine). Now that could just be my disdain for using shotguns in PvP games though, but it does need balancing. 

[h2]Why I gave it a Thumbs Up[/h2]
This game is great and has a lot of room for growth if the developers take control of the current issues. The PvP encounters are addicting, and the PvPvE encounters (running into players but not fighting each other) can range from vibey & wholesome to awkward & goofy. This game is great for casual & collaborative play, and for the most part works for intense & grindy play, just don’t go through it too fast because you will run out of stuff to do.

I really wanted to like Arc Raiders.
Seriously. The world design is cool, the gunplay feels solid, the scavenging loop has that tense “one more run” energy, and the whole PvPvE thing should be a perfect mix of risk and reward.

Should be.

Instead, most matches feel like daycare for feral raccoons with keyboards.

The biggest threat in Arc Raiders isn’t the ARC machines.
It isn’t the storm.
It isn’t resource scarcity.

It’s other players acting like complete jackasses for no reason.

Not tactical ambushes. Not smart PvP. Not “we fought over loot and only one team walks away.”

No.

I’m talking:

Camping extraction for 20 minutes just to delete someone who did all the work

Chasing fresh spawns across the map like it’s a personal vendetta

Ignoring objectives entirely just to grief

Third-partying fights purely to ruin both sides and not even looting

Teabagging like it’s 2009 Xbox Live

There’s zero strategy behind it. Zero survival logic. Just pure “how can I waste someone else’s time today?”

It’s not tense PvP — it’s toddler behavior with rifles.

And that’s what kills the experience.

Because the game wants you to scavenge, explore, plan routes, manage risk.
But you can’t do any of that when every lobby has at least one squad whose only goal is to make sure nobody else gets to play.

There’s a difference between “dangerous players” and “pointless griefing.”

Dangerous players make the game exciting.
Griefers make it exhausting.

Half my runs end not with “wow that was intense,” but with:

“Cool. Wasted 30 minutes because some dude with nothing to gain decided to sit in a bush like a fungus.”

And after enough of that, you just stop caring.

Which sucks, because underneath all the nonsense is a genuinely fun game trying really hard to exist.

But right now?

It feels less like a tactical extraction shooter and more like a social experiment proving that if you give people proximity chat and guns, they immediately become goblins.

If the devs don’t add better incentives, smarter matchmaking, or something to discourage brain-dead griefing, this game is going to eat itself alive.

I didn't expect much from Arc Raiders. I admit that I bought it just to see what my shiny new PC could do.

Wow, this game!

PvE and PvP and all cleverly stitched together so that you can largely opt into and out of either organically, based on your good or... less than well-meaning behavior.

The ARC? Fairly clever bastards. Well, some of them anyway. A few are as dumb as rocks. That is, if you get them to box *YOU* in, you can take pot shots at them, while ducking and covering, until you win.  The AI is fun to play against.

The terrain. The movement. The gear. It all *feels* solid. Embark tuned the hell out of this game.

What I love most about the game is its emergent properties. Each round can play out drastically differently based on where you begin, your loadout, the raiders (players) you encounter, and where the ARC spawn and which ones. All to say, sometimes dying is just dumb luck. But squeaking out a return home while skirting the edge of the blade? What a f***ing rush!

You have to think do to well in this game. Sure, casuals can enjoy it too. But it takes prudence to succeed.

ARC Raiders is a wonderful extraction game, especially if you enjoy learning valuable life lessons like “never trust anyone.”

There’s nothing more fun than running into other players during a match screaming “don’t shoot.” That’s usually when you make the rookie mistake of believing them. Your new “friend” follows you around the map, helps you destroy ARCs, lets you loot in peace, and really sells the whole teamwork fantasy.

Then, at the most important moment — right before returning to Speranza — their true nature reveals itself. You get shot in the back, your character dies in complete confusion, and you’re left staring at the screen wondering when exactly you lost all faith in humanity.

Naturally, in the very next match, you evolve. Anyone yelling “don’t shoot” gets shot immediately. No questions asked. Character development at its finest.

ARC Raiders isn’t just a game; it’s a social experiment about betrayal, paranoia, and how fast a player can go from friendly explorer to emotionally damaged war criminal.

Highly recommended if you enjoy extraction games, emotional scars, and shooting first — just to be safe.

This game is great. It is the most social game I have played, as you need to interact over voice chat or character emotes to discern whether other players are hostile or friendly. This is the only way to determine whether someone will be friendly or hostile, team up with you or if there is some other exchange to be made between you. The game forces you to interact with others, which is a great mechanic.

Now that there's aggression based match making, I recommend starting the game with not engaging other hostile players and playing in PvE lobbies until you no longer fear losing valuable weapons.

This approach makes the game a social event where you meet other solo players and raid together, make online friends and get some nice high value loot from more experienced players (there's a very generous community in the non-aggressive lobbies).

Even as you level up you're never very powerful in this game. If you are out in the open, the easiest enemies are still a big threat to you if they come in number above two or three. If you don't stay focused and calm you will perform much worse and with the countdown ticking, this is a great challenge at some times. So you are always on your guard in open terrain, and engage enemies from different covers. There is this continous feeling of being exposed and vulnerable because you are essentially weaker than the ARCs.

After you get a bit higher level and maybe aren't in it for the loot and craft bench upgrades anymore there's the trials. Getting higher scores in them is a puzzle in and of itself that is a lot of fun to figure out. Seeing my rank rise on the leaderboards after a succesful trial run feels great.  I just did one, exceeding my high score and I was shaking afterwards because the final minutes before extracting were so intense and I was so so close to not making it. I don't remember playing another game that affected me so much.

The bullet physics are rewarding as they make it difficult to perform at a distance and so when you do, it is satisfying. Figuring out the timing of different enemies and when they're easiest to take down (which is usually when they're the biggest threat to you) is a lot of fun. Embark has struck a great balance between skill and reward. Perhaps my favorite thing about this game is how disadvantaged you feel against the ARCs.

I haven't had too many PvP encounters yet but the ones I have had turns the game into something completely different. This is basically two games in one. I think this will be my game of the year 44 hours into playing it. But let's see how my interest for it develops.

it looks amazing. The art style, world design and atmosphere are top-tier and the PvE gameplay is genuinely fun. Exploring, fighting AI enemies feels great. With a stronger PvE focus, this could've been a really solid MMO-like experience.

Sadly, the PvP kills it for me. It's some of the worst PvP I've ever played. Hit feedback is awful and inconsistent, gunfights feel random. I'm also not a fan of  third-person PvP in general, and here it just makes ancounters feel clunky and frustrating. Other players can sit safely in cover, move their camera around corners and see me long before i can see them. From my perspective, they're completly invisible.  This leads to cheap ambusches where the fight is basicly decided before i even get visual contact.

From a story and immersion perspective, the PvP also makes very little sense. We all come from the same city - a city thats barely surviving. Raiders are supposed to risk their lives to gather resources and help the city endure, so why are we killing each other out there? Instead of feeling like survivors working toward a common goal, we're forced into PvP that feels disconnected from the wolrd and its narrative.

Forcing PvE and PvP together is a huge mistake in my opinion. Dedicated PvP zones or aPvP flag system would massively improve the experience and let different player types enjoy the game their own way.

So this is my kinde mixed review. Love the Worldbuilding but cant stand the PvP. Its still worth checking it out, its not a bad game.

Started out extremely fun, but the endgame is lacking atm. I do nothing but PvP, so keep that in mind with this review. 

1. If you're descent at the game and bring a great loadout you will be put in skilled PvP lobbies where the loadout is Venator IV + Toro IV. If you're not running Toro you're at a massive disadvantage, it's just too strong. 

2. Every single fight in said lobbies is started or ended with 6 trigger nades. 

3. If you don't run snap hook you are at a massive disadvantage. You should NOT be able to put the snap hook in your safe pocket nor should you be able to swap to a weapon by the time you land. That would immediately balance this. 

3. There are toooooooo many bugs and exploits for an extraction shooter. If you're gear is on the line you shouldn't have to deal with the broken flavor of the week. When something gets fixed after being completely broken for weeks something else is immediately exploited or broken. 

4. The de-sync is out of control on some servers. I solved this mostly by turning cross-play off when I'm ready to sweat. Console timmys seem to be most of the problem here for me, at least. 

5. The PvE side of this game is completely non-existent if you're half descent at video games and kill each enemy type a few times. I honestly don't understand what these people who are pure PvE do for hours in this game. You can only kill a matriarch or a bastion with the same exact strat so many times before you want to gouge your eyes out. 

6. Most importantly, there are almost no quality of life improvements or innovations happening. Rebuilding gear sets and crafting things over and over again is tedious. There are dozens of great ideas online to streamline this, but Embark can barely get ahead of all the bugs in the game so I expect nothing here. 

TLDR: The hype is real and the game was disgustingly fun, but the depth is gone if you don't enjoy playing in the absolute meta and farming the exact same locations every single round. Even with the fun, the bugs and exploits shit on the experience way too hard. Get it on sale when they add a few more maps and weapons and clear out bugs.

3) Gameplay and matchmaking was fun - until January 2026.

3) Hackers aren't banned instantly. Instead, they're given three strikes.

6) They really need to lower the amount of ARC in this game in certain game modes/maps. It's just becoming annoying, especially when the lobbies are PvP, given that you have 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th party enemies to deal with.

I truly do not understand the hate for ARC Raiders. This game rules. And yes, you might get absolutely obliterated in the beginning. That’s part of the process. Here’s the secret sauce nobody wants to admit. Let yourself get killed. Over and over. Don’t shoot back. Don’t resist. Just accept death like a raider monk. After about ten deaths, the game basically says “okay, you’re chill” and drops you into the friendliest lobbies known to mankind.

Everyone loves to scream about PvP, but you’re only in PvP if you’re acting like a menace and hunting other players. If you’re not doing that, the vibe completely changes. The friendly lobbies are insane. People are just vibing, looting in peace, handing out blueprints, dropping weapons like it’s a garage sale. No stress. No sweat. Just good raider energy. It feels more co-op than PvP, and it’s honestly hilarious how different the experience is compared to what the angry reviews describe.

If you’re wondering if you can play this game without constantly getting dunked on by PvP tryhards, yes. Absolutely yes. I’ve been doing this for around 100 hours and it’s been amazing the whole time. So don’t let the negative reviews gaslight you into skipping this game. Give it a little time, die with purpose, and you’ll see why ARC Raiders is actually something special.

I’m honestly starting to hate this game.

Every single time I finally secure high-value loot, I get wiped by rats and free-loadout players camping in corners like that’s the entire meta. It’s not skill. It’s not smart play. It’s low-risk behavior that the game actively rewards.

What’s the point of grinding for gear, planning routes, winning fights, and taking real risks if someone with nothing to lose can sit in a dark spot for 20 minutes and delete you in two seconds? That’s not “hardcore.” That’s broken design.

The risk-reward system feels completely backwards. Players who bring real gear and actually engage are punished the hardest. Meanwhile, people running free or disposable kits have zero fear and zero consequence. If they lose, nothing happens. If they win, they walk away stacked. That imbalance ruins the competitive integrity.

Instead of rewarding mechanical skill, smart rotations, and tactical decision-making, the game rewards patience-abusing campers who avoid interaction until the easiest possible moment. It turns intense raids into coin flips. You can do everything right and still lose to someone who contributed nothing to the match except hiding.

That’s not tension — it’s frustration.

A hardcore game should reward risk, skill, and confidence. Right now, it rewards passivity and cheese tactics. The balance feels off, the flow feels stale, and the overall experience feels more unfair than challenging.

If this is the intended gameplay loop, then it’s a serious design problem. Because at this point, it doesn’t feel competitive — it feels punishing for anyone who actually tries to play the game properly.

Fix the risk-reward balance. Stop incentivizing rats. Reward actual engagement.

Until then, this just feels bad.

Toxic PvP players are ruining this game, both with the nastiness they bring to the community and with their "playing style," which mostly consists of waiting in some dark corner and shooting a distracted or wounded player in the back, often right at the point of extract. It's profoundly unbalanced. It allows players who have put in little to no time or effort to take advantage of others who have, with no investment, little to no risk, and no meaningful consequences. It also requires no skill, which is why it's so appealing to a certain type of player.

A game based around the premise of an underground city full of resistance fighters has serious immersion-breaking and narrative defying problems when murderers and thieves are welcomed back with open arms. There should be some sort of "rat faction" for those who wish to play that way.

They can live in unfurnished holes in the ground, deprived of the amenities of Speranza civilization, with no access to traders. They should have limited extraction point options, they should be denied access to certain skins so they're more easily identified, and they should be seen as what they are: the sworn enemies of those who are trying to liberate what's left of civilization from whatever force is sending these killer robots from orbit.

I love 90% of this game. I hate that final 10%--it's just game breaking--and it's why I'm not playing this game in its current state. As it stands now, I'm hoping the developers address the toxicity issues as soon as possible. Toxic player bases kill games. Embark has to know this.

The duplication glitches, the hacking, the cheating has to be addressed, but that's going to happen in any MMO that becomes this popular, and it's only fair to give the developers time to respond and adjust.

But the PvP is incredibly unbalanced, takes no skill, and the vast majority of PvP consists of getting shot in the back and instantly killed without the opportunity to defend yourself. If you do manage to pull a gun before a coward manages to knock you, you'll be sent to PvP lobbies just for defending yourself.

PvP was added very late in the development cycle, it wasn't adequately implemented, and it just doesn't stack up against the rest of the game.

Unfortunately, I couldn't recommend this game in its current state, and I wish I had known about these far reaching problems before purchase. I hope to be able to come back and change this review. We'll see how that goes.

This game is the "perverse incentives" simulator.

For the uninitiated, a perverse incentive in economics is "when the rules, structures, or practices of any system reward bad behavior or sociopathic outcomes (Brownstone Institute)."  As you can probably guess, in this case it involves pvp vs. pve players.

The developers have acknowledged an aggression-based matchmaking (ABMM) system that learns who shoots first at other players, and who doesn't.  It "tends" (emphasis on "tends") to put players with higher aggression scores into matches with the ganker-aligned by raising their aggro score.  Alternatively, players who do not attack other players will eventually end up in "care bear" matches with other players who don't kill on sight and want to, oh I don't know, take down major enemies together or cooperate on objectives.  While theoretically gankers will end up in lobbies where everyone kills everyone all the time and nothing get accomplished.

Herein lies the rub, due to a spectacularly bad design philosophy even defending yourself against PVPers and gankers AFTER THEY HAVE SHOT YOU FIRST gives you aggro score.  So players who get attacked DON'T FIGHT BACK for fear of spending the next 10 matches getting shot on sight, killed by spawn campers, or being attacked as soon as they take down a major enemy (and therefore are low on health or ammunition).  They either submit or run for the exits.  Even if you run, the PVP damage is so high that the person who shoots first can usually down a player in 2-3 shots max.

Scientists in a lab could not design a better perverse incentive.

This ABMM sorting doesn't always happen, and it's easy to game by doing what are called naked runs of doing a free loadout, entering a match, then exiting a handful of times to reset your aggro score.  PVP players know they can attack other players and know the players are unlikely to fight back.

For a lot of gankers, randomly ruining someone else's game is psychotic fun (the boards are full of people writing Nietzschean Cosplay fanfic about how it reveals a truer state of the human condition to spawn camp people who won't fight back).  For a lot of other players, who've maybe worked a long day and don't want to grind the resources necessary to rebuild their kit, it's pure aggravation.  When you die, you lose everything that's on you except for what's stored in the safe pocket (aka the prison purse).  Once you are downed but before you are out of the match, you cannot access your inventory to secure valuables or look at the map to attempt to crawl toward an exit.

Bottom Line: unless and until this game makes it so defending yourself isn't counted as aggression, it's broken.

In my experience in many, many shooters over the years, Arc Raiders managed to find some uncharted territories. The movement and combat style is rugged, but realistic. Firefights have a very intense feel. This applies to both arc and other raiders...

The constant presence of arc makes you play into the PvE element of the game, one way or another. With deadly consequences for ignoring them and valuable loot within, each game is preloaded with a set of "bosses" that provide replayable content and can play a huge part (wanted or not), in PvP fights.

Of course the biggest component of the game is its looter extraction style. For the most part, all of the valuables you can find in game are at stake until the final seconds of an extract. With the value of life so high, Embark incorporated a slew of utility items to help keep you off your hands and knees...each one highlighting a different style of gameplay. Traps can create defensive strongholds while ziplines can make for a great escape. Some grenades can clear a room, while others can strategically block passage.

Every game makes you feel like you're fighting for your life in both a battle of wits and will. And more importantly, you're fighting for that sweet sweet goop.

First things first, throughly make sure you find a build that you enjoy visually before devoting anytime into this game, don't just look up the most meta broken high dmg build! I spent a lot of time on POE1 struggling to grasp the concept of making a build and wish i could have it back lol. Now on POE2 i have found a flame twister amazon which has a very unique play style but fills the entire screen with fire tornados (thanks POB Builds).

I want to preface this review by saying I consider myself a casual/weekend warrior on this game (someone who works a lot during the week and can only play 2ish hrs a day when i work but dedicate as much time as i can on my days off). After 463hrs on Poe1 i was left with a sour taste in my mouth, mainly because i invested all that time and never really made it past getting a build to barely lvl90 and never really having enough currency to truly have a broken or strong build. This game much like POE1 will throughly chew you up and spit you out if you dont have proper direction from either a reliable/well made guide or a very experienced player in your ear. With that being said this is the best game ive ever played, i can say that because even when most games would frustrate me from the learning curve (good luck) i look forward to setting time aside to run maps and farm currency and make use of it to make my build stronger and looking forward to that feeling of the steady grind with the occasional high currency drop. 

Now that im 238hrs into POE2 after having played during 0.1 (about 80hrs) then and the other 160 ish hrs during 0.4 i have finally “broken through” to understanding the basics  and full understanding of making a strong build. Mind you, i still follow a build guide religiously so that i can focus on having fun and progressively improving my build day by day (i look forward to being confident enough to make my own visually appealing yet strong build eventually). Im Finally able to grasp the concept of farming an end game mechanic thats rewarding enough to buy good gear/experiment as well which if you dont spend some time learning one you will not farm efficiently enough to keep you motivated. 

I know this review is all over the place, but the main takeaway should be if you want a challenge and want to play a game that tests you like no other game before, then play this game. There are many things to learn between the itemization, crafting, mapping, end game mechanics, using currency efficiently (more important for casuals players with limited amounts), what mechanics your specific build farms best etc. but even myself with 700hrs between POE 1&2 learn something new almost every session. So buckle down and get ready for the best ARPG experience.

Path of Exile 2 suffers from the same problems that plagued Path of Exile 1: Endless convolution, a horrendous new-user experience, and a toxic playerbase.

The game is explicitly designed for veteran players that know the mechanics inside and out and can min-max from the start. For example, "Fire", "Burning", "Ignite", and "Detonate" are all DIFFERENT effects in the game, so you might invest in a skill that says it creates a poison cloud that can be ignited to cause an explosion, but when you try to set it off with fire skills, nothing happens. You don't realize "fire" and "burning" don't "ignite" things until you spend several minutes reading tooltips and hovering over key words.

Imagine this happening not just dozens of times, but HUNDREDS of times. The game is just layer upon layer upon layer of very similar effects with near-identical descriptions interacting in niche ways. And this is NOT a game where you can even just play it once for the story and be satisfied, because by Act 2 you must start stacking these niche, obscure effects to make your builds work. You will end up kiting mobs around in circles, whittling them down slowly, unless you learn exactly what effects to stack and grind out some gear that boosts those effects.

Which means you don't get to experiment or try new skills. In every other game in this genre, when you first unlock a new ability, you can equip it and test it out and see how you like it. Not so in PoE2. In this game, if you try to do that, none of your bonuses will affect the new skill 99% of the time, so trying a new skill out will be a harsh downgrade. You'll go from easily killing groups of enemies to taking over a minute to kill a handful of them.

The game also doesn't communicate to you that you must rely on the market for equipment to make your builds work. If you don't know to use the market, or if you play Solo Self Found, you will have to grind all your gear on your own, and the odds of ever getting the gear you need for your build that way are astronomically low.

Worst of all, if you seek help for this, you're extremely likely to get mocked and derided by the toxic players in chat. Again: The game caters exclusively to people that are diehard veterans. So the chat is full of people that tolerate no hint of criticism of the game, and who assume everyone else must know as much about the game as they do. Even if you tell them, "Hey, I'm new, do these two skills not interact? The wording is confusing to me." You will likely get half a dozen people calling you a "noob" and telling you to, "Go back to Diablo 4."

So, if you're looking for a game that you can no-life and sink 1,000 hours in to learn all the niche details and make broken characters while feeling smug and trash talking anyone that knows less than you, then Path of Exile 2 is the game for you.

But if you're someone looking for a more balanced experience, and you're hoping to play through the campaign and enjoy the story and see if you like the game before investing hundreds of hours into it, Path of Exile 2 is NOT for you, and you should go play literally any other game in this genre instead.

Side note: Most other games in the genre can be played offline. Path of Exile 2 seems to be online-only. Meaning you can get disconnected mid-fight if your internet is unsteady, or if the game servers hiccup.

On top of all that, Path of Exile 2 already offers a huge amount of content at launch, and yet it still feels like only a drop in the ocean compared to what the game can become in the next 5–8 years. The foundations are incredibly strong, and the long-term vision is clearly there.

The game has enormous potential to become a true lifetime ARPG, one that players can return to for years or even decades. Its systems are deep enough to support constant expansion without losing identity.

What really stands out is the fully procedural nature of the gameplay loop. Each run, each map, and each progression path feels dynamic rather than scripted, which keeps the experience fresh and replayable.

Things That Could Use Improvement
Endgame Structure

At the current 0.4 stage, the endgame is not bad, but after some time the endgame map becomes hard to read and overly chaotic. I would personally prefer a clearer structure — for example, a regional system where players close off regions one by one, then move into citadels. After completing a region, unnecessary paths and nodes could disappear, improving readability and making progression feel more intentional and strategic.

Boss Access & Progression

Instead of simple boss tickets, I believe endgame progression would benefit from a region-closing system, similar to citadels, where completing regions grants fragments or keys that lead to major encounters. This would make boss access feel more earned and narratively consistent.

Player Direction in Endgame

Overall, the endgame currently lacks strong player direction, especially at the beginning of a league. There should be a clearer initial choice or branching path that helps players decide early on what kind of content they want to grind and how they plan to generate currency. A meaningful early decision would give the endgame more identity and purpose right from the start.

Experimental Loot

I would also love to see more experimental loot in the endgame — items that introduce unexpected twists to builds, encourage experimentation, and potentially redefine how a character plays instead of just being raw numerical upgrades.

Build Variety Through Weapons

Most importantly, rather than adding more classes or ascendancies, the game currently needs more weapon types. New weapons would naturally diversify builds and playstyles far more than additional class layers, and they feel like the missing piece in truly expanding build creativity.

Final Thoughts

Overall, everything is moving in the right direction. I really enjoy the Vaal temple system — it requires some time investment, but the payoff feels meaningful and satisfying.

I also truly appreciate that crafting is finally accessible to regular players during normal gameplay. Currency drops at a healthy rate, allowing players to experiment and engage with crafting systems instead of hoarding early Exalted Orbs just to buy upgrades because it’s faster or more efficient. This makes the game far more fun, interactive, and rewarding.

Path of Exile 2 already stands on very solid ground, and with further refinement — especially in the endgame — it has the potential to define the ARPG genre for many years to come.

Economy Perspective

In terms of the economy, I think a lot of players are approaching Path of Exile 2 exactly like Path of Exile 1, and to me that is completely misguided — almost a joke.

First of all, at the moment PoE 2 contains maybe 20% of the total content PoE 1 has built over years. With the current scope, a player can realistically experience all available mechanics within 50–100 hours and, with a bit of luck, assemble most of the items needed for their chosen build. At this stage of the game, a heavy trade-driven economy should not even make much sense.

The game should provide enough currency drops so that every player investing those 100 hours can genuinely enjoy crafting. Trading should be something you look at occasionally, not a mandatory shortcut where you hoard early currency just to buy power because it’s more efficient than playing the game. In this regard, PoE 2 is actually doing a lot of things right.

Currency exchange works very well. If you don’t roll citadels naturally, you still have the option to buy fragments and keep progressing. That’s a healthy, functional system.

The Vaal Temple “Drama”

The whole drama around the Vaal temple was honestly embarrassing. Many players simply didn’t understand the mechanic and reacted like children in a sandbox, throwing tantrums because some players discovered a method that paid off well and was temporarily disabled.

What makes this even more ironic is that the very same people were recently arguing that GGG shouldn’t introduce permanent mechanics at all, but instead release frequent patches and slowly iterate toward 1.0. That’s exactly what is happening now.

The fact that GGG introduces fast nerfs, then partially reverts or adjusts them a few days later, doesn’t indicate incompetence — it shows that they are actively observing the game, collecting data, and learning decision-making during Early Access. That’s literally the point of EA.

Long-Term Economy Reality

I sincerely hope the developers don’t take community outrage too seriously and instead continue working calmly and methodically.

The harsh truth is that 90% of players don’t understand that a real economy only starts to make sense when, after 200+ hours, a player still cannot fully “solve” the endgame, unlike in PoE 1. Once the game reaches that point — which I believe will happen after 2–3 more years of development at the current pace — players will naturally split into different farming paths, specializations, and progression branches. That is when the economy will truly come alive.

Right now, hearing all this crying about the economy and the Vaal temple drama honestly just makes me laugh.

The sheer amount of wonderful ways to brutally wade through enemies is so satisfying, with crossbow bolts that kill an enemy mid air as its jumping at you, and instead of like with blizzard and diablo where the enemy dies in place with a small blood spatter and generic death animation (dont want to be too violent, gotta appease those grandmas out there), the enemy continues on its trajectory, hits the ground and rolls several times before coming to a stop, dead. You blow limbs off, cleave heads, defeat an enormous naked woman who is bathing in a pool of literal sh*t. It's wonderful. The spells are cinematic and powerful, the damage states, like being frozen, are intricate and awesome looking. The weapons are as varied as their freaking swing patterns and you get orange tier items at least once every five minutes, each of which is completely unique and completely accurately shown on your character the same as the items looks in your inventory. The game was clearly made by people that loved diablo 2, and saw with horror what blizzard was heading for, so they decided to step in. I mean, its right down to having four acts, the first in some moors and farmers fields, the second in the desert, the third act is in the jungle, and the fourth is actually different than diablo 2 so I wont spoil it. This game is EVERYTHING diablo 3 could and should have been. I've never played a game like this that was this satisfying; swinging a battle maul and crushing through ribs while sending swathes of enemies flying away with different trajectories and different animations. Just buy it, basically, if you dont like the way blizzard toned down and mobile-ized diablo,. We owe it to these guys for picking up blizzards slack and actually doing something great. Besides, if you dont buy this you're essentially saying that blizzard was right. This was my favorite rogue-like game up until the endgame (I played a self-founded ranger on hard). 

Before the endgame I appreciated the creative enemy designs and difficult but learnable boss mechanics. I didn't find anything super challenging besides the act ending bosses, and it was fun revisiting them later and learning how I improved.

The intermission was a red flag when it was practically an asset flip of prior encounters. Finished it and was initially excited when the endgame map popped up, but now it's just a cycle of repetitive mechanics/encounters, awkward scaling, and poor game design. The waystone system is strange, the home base is sad, and the characters stop caring about the story alongside you (barely anyone talks to your character unless it's an instance of you saving them). 

Examples would be losing xp when you die, not being guaranteed a higher tier waystone after beating a boss at a lower waystone level, and progression stopping if you can't make areas you explore high enough level to drop higher level waystone (I got an appropriate level waystone by doing a dijini trial, doesn't seem intended).

I'm not sure why they went this route rather then simply making another act. I would point people to play the first four acts solo and then maybe replay it with friends, but definitely not worth the money right now. I will probably pick the game back up in the future at some point, but I feel discouraged with the direction the game is going.
