As someone that has played each league since early access began, I simply cannot recommend this game at this time.  The latest league introduced the Vaal Temple, and that mechanic is the extreme end of everything that's currently wrong with the game.

The Vaal Temple mechanic is the most illogical unintuitive thing I have ever encountered in a game.  It provides you with no real way to discern for yourself how to optimally use it or progress it.  And in fact, it completely contradicts itself in several ways.  On the surface, it looks as though you are supposed to place rooms wherever you can until you can eventually reach a boss called the Architect that, if defeated, "drops" more rooms that you can place in the temple that give various rewards once you are able to path to them on subsequent runs.  One of those rooms is the Royal Key chamber that, if placed and pathed to and cleared will allow access to the ultimate boss of the temple - Atziri.  This is the first major breakdown of the mechanic.

The game does not indicate to you that you must path to and reach the Key chamber AND the boss chamber on the same run.  On top of this, after reach run, many of your paths and rooms that you placed will be destroyed randomly.  Meaning if you have bad rng, you could go many runs and never actually reach the boss.  I am level 93 and have reached the boss exactly 2 times.  I only defeated her 1 time because the first time I reached her I had to learn her mechanics and what she does.  I ultimately died and of course, the game being as unforgiving as it is, you are locked out until you can place enough rooms and paths to unlock and reach her on a future run.  Some rooms have tooltips that tell you they "destabilize" which means they will be destroyed after you run them.  But other rooms that don't say this ALSO are destroyed at temple end with no way of knowing which ones will.  

The problems don't end there.  As it turns out, the most optimal way to do the temple isn't to try to reach the boss at all.  It's to try to endlessly connect certain rooms together and buff them in a way where they aren't destroyed after your runs, creating a "snake" that, if you want the best loot from, requires you to block access to the boss altogether.  Oh, and the way to prevent them from being destroyed relies on a randomly dropped medallion that allows you to "lock" the appropriate room so that they aren't destroyed.  I've seen exactly 3 of those medallions the entire league.  

Furthermore, there's no rhyme or reason to which rooms can be connected or chained together.  There's nothing that indicates what the optimal paths or ways to proceed are.  In fact, the best temples don't even use the "reward" rooms that you would get from defeating the aforementioned Architect.  None of the temple mechanics can be figured out by the average player who instead must depend on elaborate hard to understand guides made by streamers that have spent hundreds of hours in this league alone running the temple over and over and in which most of them actually exploited during that time to accelerate the number of temples they were able to run.  GGG left this exploit in the game for 2 weeks only to finally fix it without resolving the gigantic gap between hardcore and causal player loot that this caused.  

If you are one of the lucky players (or one of the players who can play for 12 hours a day), then you might have finally created a temple that provides more loot in a single run than someone like me has earned in the entire league.  The consequence of this is that for a regular player like myself that has barely gotten anything worthwhile to drop and sell or trade, the cost of items due to the absurd amount of drops in a bloated temple mechanic has skyrocketed to an unaffordable point preventing the acquisition of any substantial upgrades. 

On top of all this, with no optimal temple to run, the drops I have received from tier 15 mapping this league have been abysmal.  Juiced Abyss, rituals, expeditions, none of it has provided anything worthwhile that would help me catch up and afford an upgrade for my character.  I've done hundreds of maps and not seen a single Citadel.  Without citadel fragments, I can't do the Arbiter boss which allows you to upgrade tablets further to make your maps more lucrative.  

In conclusion, the temple highlights a huge flaw with the game.  It has way way too many layers of RNG that can make you either the luckiest player alive or you can have such bad RNG that you're fighting for scraps for an entire league.  And the game offers no insight into how you could fix this.

I have been playing this game since season 1 in December 2024 when it came out in early access. I expected a lot from it and for the first season, I thought at the time that it somewhat delivered. The current league, at the time of me writing this is Fate of the Vaal and I don't believe that anymore and I would urge you to rethink before buying this game at its current state. Maybe in the future GGG will rethink their actions but currently this game is not fun if you have a job or a life outside of gaming.

I will start simple with the pros and cons.

[b]Pros:[/b]
* Great visuals.
* Great monster design.
* Most skills feel good to use.
* Interesting campaign.
* A nice variety of builds.
* Rewarding crafting system.

[b]Cons:[/b]
* Although the campaign is interesting the first time, you need to complete it for every character in the season and its abysmally long, near 20 hour, runtime kills any motivation to create a character.
* The maps can get huge and there are nearly no movement skills so movement in maps feels janky af. On top of that if you don't have %MS boots you are essentially a turtle. They tried adding a sprint mechanic to alleviate this but everyone hates it because it takes monsters 1 hit to hard stun you while sprinting and if you are hard stunned you are pretty much dead.
* Performance issues persist 1 year after release.
* No QA testing going into any league mechanic or any new addition at all.
* No variety in farming strategies. There is almost always one way of making currency each league and if you aren't doing it you are choosing to stay poor while prices skyrocket.
* The top farmers always inflate the prices so if you're not constantly playing, building a decent character gets more and more difficult over time as prices increase.


The cons list goes on and on but I believe I covered some specific points that really bugged me. GGG cannot get this game straight for over a year now and they just go 2 steps forward and 3 steps backwards. Wherever there is fun to be had, GGG refuses to look at the player statistics and ignores public opinion and does whatever it feels like doing by either nerfing the relevant mechanic to hell or removing it completely. I have been in every league, I just wanted to play the game the way it was intended: by farming maps as quickly as I could. In no league was this ever viable if you didn't farm for a ludicrous amount of time. There were times were I literally had to resort to buying currency with real money to continue playing because I was stuck with level 40 gear with a level 82 character. I don't want to get into arbitrage trading or crafting and selling or finding a niche mechanic to exploit or providing leveling services to get currency. I just want to play the game normally. Without having to hunt for rarity on every piece of my gear or exploiting a mechanic that will be 100% fixed in the next 48 hours. GGG could not deliver something so simple. And it is shocking because they did deliver with POE1 or so I've heard. I have been patient with POE2 and it was not worth it. I won't be playing the next season unless it is groundbreakingly different and good.

Anyways TLDR; the game is grindy as hell and if you have a life or a job get ready to pay for currency on third party platforms because ground loot will never be enough to get you even the most basic gear. Even if you forget your life and quit your job, the content is repetitive and the ultra end-game content is non-existent so you'll be disappointed either way.

Best is to wait until GGG either flops completely or makes and amazing comeback.

[h2]PoE2 review, it's a tough one.[/h2]

The only reason I could recommend PoE2 is because it's still in the EA and after playing last season I'm still having fun.

Considering game is still in Early Access I think there's a high probability, that GGG will work on this for a longer while. I'm almost certain we're going to see a final release in some shape of form. There's probably a long way ahead though.

To provide a bit of a context, I've played PoE 1 from beta and just after the release, so about a decade ago. I would profile myself as more of an experienced casual with irregular play time. I'm absolutely taking my time with PoE2, slowly progressing on my own pace, learning the game and playing solo. I have zero FOMO or pressure to complete something, reach a ladder or some seasonal goal. I also put ARPGs highly on my favourite genre list. I imagine that perspective from a HC ARPG gamer familiar with the series, might be completely different. Please keep it in mind.

[h3]Let's start with the cons:[/h3]
[li]
[*]The Inventory micromanaging and all the BS involved with it can be quite annoying. It really does feel like playing Diablo 2 at times. I really wish there would be some UI functions to cut down on this micromanagement. Maybe a 
 list view of backpack, sorting, filtering and mass moving of items. Locking and highlighting items? Removal of inventory tetris? Do games really have to waste our time? Identification scrolls, really? Please modernise PoE.
[*]I imagine that if you want to get serious with the game, you'll want to expand your stash, which is an extra expense out of your wallet.
[*]Loot boxes, I'm not touching this crap, so don't even care what's inside them. It's presence upsets me.
[*]Bugs, personally haven't experienced anything game breaking, rather smaller annoyances, but if you dig deeper people encounter some nasty stuff sometimes. Not surprised to see those as we're in EA, kind of beta version.
[/li]

[h3]And the pros:[/h3]
[li]
[*]The audio visual side of the game. The style and graphics feel good, look good, provides feedback and immersion. I really like what I see and hear. Could compare the style to Grim Dawn, but it's an older game now, so PoE2 just looks better.
[*]Combat, I really liked Lost Ark's combat, and coming to PoE2 I seem to see some similarities. I like addition of dodge, It seems to add a bit of depth. Also ability to move with WASD is an interesting twist, personally I play with Rzr Naga and mostly melee, so aren't using this option much. Combat isn't getting boring easily and simply speaking, for me, it's fun. Although there are some one button builds.
[*]Passive skill tree and ability to customise your build. PoE1 blew my mind back in time with the amount of freedom and customisation, and so did PoE2. If you like crafting your build and tinkering around it, you'll have a good puzzle. There's an option to redo your passive tree with ingame gold, but it's rather expensive, at least early on. You probably will mess up your build to a point where you can't progress further, so if you want to save yourself some time, I would recommend a tried and tested build found online.
[*]Souls like encounters with bosses. I really liked those, challenging but not too challenging (unless your build's broken). Going in blind progressing boss fights wasn't lengthy and felt satisfying. Personally really enjoyed this aspect of the game.
[*]Campaign is good. Maybe it's not as good as D4's, but it's good. Despite myself loosing trust with Blizz I think they're still excellent at providing story. PoE2 has decent story too, however it can get boring quicker and doesn't have as much depth as main competitor in this regard.
[*]Level design, I just liked all those grim and dark corridors filled with monsters. I like the whole look and style of the levels, the variety of looks and monsters. Also once again boss fights. GGG did well there.
[/li]

[h3]In the end...[/h3] 
I would say the game is worth a try especially if you like ARPGs. Although it's Early Access I already had a fair share of fun for the money. I hope GGG will keep polishing this title long after it's release. From a rather casualish perspective, it's pretty fun.

The base gameplay can be very fun when played single player. It's very satisfying to stack gear and get that damage up. However, there are a lot of issues with this game, so I don't recommend playing it in its current state.

Multiplayer design is abysmal. Quests are not synced between players, meaning if even one person didn't talk to an NPC during a questline, they cannot progress whatsoever. I could understand that the developers want people to experience the story and don't want people rushing each other through, but that doesn't excuse neglecting such an important feature for multiplayer. Also, here's the thing: the story is garbage. It doesn't compel me, and I don't think it will compel many other people. Do not force players to engage with one of the worst aspects of this game.

Here's a big problem with the story: There's a boss kill stealing issue. You are not allowed to kill any of the act bosses. They either become passive towards you, or get killed by another character. This completely kills the enjoyment of going through the effort of killing one of the dogshit bosses from this game. If my character is the only person who can fight the boss, let me kill the boss god damn it. Don't let some badly written and stupid NPC come in at the end and steal that satisfaction.

On the topic of bosses: They're not fun. The developers have gotten lazy with the boss design and added a bunch of bullshit AOE explosions and other quick large attacks that instant kill the player. My armor is high, my resistance is high, but if I get nicked by one stupid attack, I die. 90% of these bosses attacks do nothing to the me, but suddenly, the boss gets a burst of damage and kills me. I would rather have fewer higher quality bosses that are fair than a lot of bullshit. I would rather die because I chugged heals and ran out like an idiot, rather than get instant killed with some badly telegraphed attack.

One last thing: This game's challenge modes are not fun. The Sekema Trials and Chaos Trials are annoying grindy bullshit where the game forces you to take masochistic modifiers to make the game more difficult. This would be fine, if it wasn't imperative for your build to do these trials. Your ascendency progress is directly tied to these modes. Trial of Sekemas specifically is bullshit since you have to prioritize not getting hit, but the stupid developers decided to make all the bosses do AOE explosions and have large health pools. This is a nightmare for melee players. 

I hope these things are changed. They make what would a great game an annoying slog.

As someone who isn’t a hardcore ARPG player, I’ll admit the endgame can feel tough. It demands more planning, better gear knowledge, and tighter execution than the early and mid game. That said, it never feels unfair—just challenging. Even when I hit a wall, the depth of the systems makes me want to learn more and try again rather than quit.

What really stands out is how engaging the experience remains overall. The combat feels impactful, progression is meaningful, and the sheer build variety gives the game incredible longevity. Even if I take breaks, I always find myself coming back with a new idea or build in mind.

Path of Exile 2 strikes a great balance: deep enough to reward dedicated players, but still enjoyable for someone like me who plays at their own pace. Challenging, customizable, and endlessly replayable—it’s a game that sticks with you.

Excellent fundamentals but flawed in some finer details.  Path of Exile 2 is an absolutely fantastic ARPG, following in the footsteps of its first incarnation and delivering complexity, stunnign visuals and of course that ever so frustrating excess loot decisions making we all love of these games.

That being said, this game is not for everyone, and I really do mean this.  PoE2 is not an easy game, you aren't going to one-shot bosses and sail through content.  You aren't going to be able to collect all those shiny items that drop (at least not easily).  But by far and away the most frustrating things are:

a) Lack of resources - as a new player, you will struggle with gold, you will struggle for items, you will struggle for upgrades and customisation options.  That adds a little to the joy of actually getting somethign cool, but it can be a massive grind at times, leaving you feel rather underpowered and worried about actually spendign anythign you DO get given its rarity.

and

b) Boss fights that just aren't fun.  The boss fights go on, for a while.  More so than most other ARPGs I've played.  This in and of itself isn't a bad thing... if it was a case of gearing up, learning the fight mechanics etc, but sadly there is often just too much health, too many random things shooting all over the screen and no real easy way around it.  It doesn't make for compelling gameplay, just frustration.

The builds can feel overwhelming, they've tried to give you maximum flexibility, and I like that but do yourself a favour... make sure you find a good one for that first run through or you will probably quit with a smashed keyboard.  

Well worth a go, but infinitely frustrating that I feel a lot of players won't appreciate the difficulty and frustration as a good thing.  This isn't a dark-souls game, the creators need to find a way to balance difficulty with progression... and quicker than they are right now.  A stunning game let down by a huge learnign curve and outright gear level caps far too often in just the campaign does not make for an exciting or appealing game for the masses.  Keep the difficult progression to end-game and you will have a far happier playbase.

A fine game, but not what I'm looking for.  I'm hoping it grows to become that, and I look forward to revisiting in the future.  For now it's too slow, the drops are crap, and the skill forest is too unfocused.  Some people love these things so this could be a great game... for not-me.  

The art is detailed and well-crafted ("beautiful" is not really an apt term for many of the environments, but I won't disagree with those who claim it is that).  The voice acting is above par if occasionally overwrought.  The animations are solid.  This is a well-crafted game.

But: I haven't had anything useful drop in forever.  I understand that crafting is the name of the game, but currency is precious enough that it sucks to blow through your stash to end up with an item that basically sucks.  I've read that I should probably be perusing the vendor more often.  That's boring.  And if I want to spend all my time looking at the marketplace I might as well play Eve.

The passive tree is intimidating.  I often find myself frustrated when I level up - the exact opposite of what a new level should bring!  Instead I have this skill point I can put towards one of dozens of dubious goals, but with no clear path towards a powerful build.  No, I'm not following a guide.  If I wanted to run a cookie-cutter build I would follow a guide and I'm sure I could have the exact same build as everyone else and it would perform the same as everyone else's build.

The skill tree would be less problematic if it were easier to respec, but it's tedious and potentially expensive.  Not to mention the shuffling of skill gems and support gems that is needed.  If I could easily save a couple builds (including everything socketed), and switch between them, that would greatly increase the freedom to experiment. 

I was hoping to play with the end-game content.  In Diablos 3 and 4 I enjoyed being able to just jump on, go run a dungeon by whatever name, and collect one or two drops that might enhance my character before logging off.  But here I have to slog through the campaign twice (or so I read) before I get to something that might approximate that experience.  

Give me more access to the Temple (don't make me find six Vaal shrines, or whatever, before I can go back).  Let me jump straight to maps.  Don't make me go through the campaign.  The story is, frankly, superfluous (as nearly all video game stories are).  If I want a good story I can read any number of fine novels that don't force the tedium of sorting through gear and agonizing over which skill path to follow.  Just let me run a dungeon, make sure I get some interesting loot drops (or enough currency to craft something), and let me play around.  

Oh, and for the level 2 act boss, for the love of consistency have the companion say "Stay close and I'll keep us safe from the storm!"  I died 10 times before I realized that's how I could survive, meanwhile half the other bosses have your character shouting "Watch out for the tail!" when it's obvious you're getting whacked with a tail, or "Look out for what falls!" when it's obvious shit is dropping on you.

TL;DR:
Unoriginal, exhausting, and frustrating by design. Path of Exile 2 mistakes annoyance for difficulty. Stay away.

Long version:

Path of Exile 2 desperately wants to be “Isometric Dark Souls,” but it completely misses the most important ingredient: rhythm.

Boss fights are a nonstop barrage of AoE spam and overtuned movesets. There are no clever mechanics, no memorable patterns to learn—just more overlapping AoEs, smaller arenas, and bigger damage numbers. Every encounter feels the same, only louder and more punishing. Add to that bosses with absurdly inflated HP pools, and fights turn into tedious endurance tests rather than engaging challenges.

Get ready to spend 10–15 minutes dodging and weaving, landing a single attack whenever the game allows it… only to die in less than one second because you made one mistake or the screen filled with effects. It’s not tense. It’s not satisfying. It’s exhausting.

Progression is nearly nonexistent. Leveling up feels pointless when your reward is “3% something” or “5% something else.” In the later stages, it can take days of grinding just to gain a single level. Maybe you’ll get a useful skill gem along the way—if you’re lucky. More often than not, you won’t.

The lore doesn’t help either. Who is the Beast? Why should I care? Why does every character feel like a variation of the same warlock fantasy? Ascendancy classes aren’t earned through mastery or meaningful challenges, but through poorly designed “Djinn” trials that feel more like punishment than progression.

Those trials deserve special mention. First, you grind a token just to attempt them. Then you’re thrown into a gauntlet of misery where your build barely matters. Tank? Maxed shields? Doesn’t matter. A new mechanic drains a special currency every time you get hit, regardless of whether you actually take damage. Lose it all and it’s over. Back to grinding another token. Dodge 30 times, attack once, repeat. Fun is not part of the equation.

On a technical level, the game is riddled with bugs and performance issues. Frame drops, stutters, visual clutter—you name it. But somehow, the microtransaction shop works flawlessly. It even has its own shortcut key. Priorities, I guess.

After just one hour of playing, I don’t feel excited or challenged. I feel tired.

Path of Exile 2 has a “right” way to play, and that way is abandoning your own idea of fun, grinding endlessly, and eventually copying a popular build from the internet. If that sounds appealing to you, maybe this game is for you. If not, do yourself a favor and stay far away.

Path of Exile 2 – A Masterclass in How to Waste Your Time

Path of Exile 2 is a stunning reminder that no matter how good your trailers look, you can still ship a complete mess. This game feels less like a sequel and more like a public beta duct-taped to a marketing campaign.

Let’s start with the exploit disaster. Watching the whole Fubgun situation unfold was embarrassing. An exploit runs wild, certain players benefit massively, the economy gets warped, and the response feels slow, inconsistent, and half-hearted. Whether you exploited or not, the damage was already done. Nothing screams “competitive integrity” like letting broken mechanics exist long enough for people to get rich off them before quietly sweeping it under the rug.

Now onto the servers, which are somehow worse than the balance. Constant disconnects. Infinite loading screens. “Failed to connect to server” over and over again like it’s a core gameplay mechanic. Nothing kills hype faster than sitting at a loading screen wondering if you’re about to play the game or just get booted back to the login screen—for the fifth time in ten minutes.

And when you do connect? Enjoy rubber-banding, instance failures, and random desync like it’s 2013. For a modern ARPG that’s supposed to compete at the top of the genre, this is straight up unacceptable.

The worst part is that PoE 2 could be great. The bones are there. But instead of feeling polished, it feels rushed, unstable, and disrespectful of players’ time. Between exploit scandals, server instability, and endless connection issues, the game constantly fights you instead of letting you have fun.

Right now, PoE 2 isn’t a next-gen ARPG.
It’s a stress test with loot.

Final verdict:
Amazing potential buried under bad decisions, broken systems, and servers held together by hopes and prayers. Come back in 5 years—maybe it’ll be finished by then.

Path of Exile 2 – A Masterclass in How to Waste Your Time

Path of Exile 2 is a stunning reminder that no matter how good your trailers look, you can still ship a complete mess. This game feels less like a sequel and more like a public beta duct-taped to a marketing campaign.

Let’s start with the exploit disaster. Watching the whole Fubgun situation unfold was embarrassing. An exploit runs wild, certain players benefit massively, the economy gets warped, and the response feels slow, inconsistent, and half-hearted. Whether you exploited or not, the damage was already done. Nothing screams “competitive integrity” like letting broken mechanics exist long enough for people to get rich off them before quietly sweeping it under the rug.

Now onto the servers, which are somehow worse than the balance. Constant disconnects. Infinite loading screens. “Failed to connect to server” over and over again like it’s a core gameplay mechanic. Nothing kills hype faster than sitting at a loading screen wondering if you’re about to play the game or just get booted back to the login screen—for the fifth time in ten minutes.

And when you do connect? Enjoy rubber-banding, instance failures, and random desync like it’s 2013. For a modern ARPG that’s supposed to compete at the top of the genre, this is straight up unacceptable.

The worst part is that PoE 2 could be great. The bones are there. But instead of feeling polished, it feels rushed, unstable, and disrespectful of players’ time. Between exploit scandals, server instability, and endless connection issues, the game constantly fights you instead of letting you have fun.

Right now, PoE 2 isn’t a next-gen ARPG.
It’s a stress test with loot.

Final verdict:
Amazing potential buried under bad decisions, broken systems, and servers held together by hopes and prayers. Come back in 5 years—maybe it’ll be finished by then.

If you have really bad frame dips on really good hardware this is probably why. Go to your documents -> My game -> POE2 -> poe2_production_Config. In there change network mode from auto to predictive.
 
The game uses a lockstep networking model, meaning your client waits for server confirmation before advancing frames—so high or unstable latency creates visible stuttering or freezing, especially during movement or combat. 

This should be available from in the client. We should not have to trouble shoot the game to find out about secret settings.

If you have really bad frame dips on really good hardware this is probably why. Go to your documents -> My game -> POE2 -> poe2_production_Config. In there change network mode from auto to predictive.
 
The game uses a lockstep networking model, meaning your client waits for server confirmation before advancing frames—so high or unstable latency creates visible stuttering or freezing, especially during movement or combat. 

This should be available from in the client. We should not have to trouble shoot the game to find out about secret settings.

First off: I haven’t played POE1, I have no baseline for how easy or hard POE2 is in comparison.
The only thing I do know is, that the game feels fun for most of the leveling/campaign experience. Notice how I wrote „most of“. Here’s a few points that bother me so much that they in my opinion value a negative review:
- the game sometimes feels unfair. Not talking about getting killed because of stupid mistakes, no, the game flat out kills you because you don’t have any more health or mana potions left.
- some bosses are a joke with some builds, close to unbeatable on others.
- loot feels rewarding, but the lack of tooltip explanations for what’s permanent, what removes something, how something interacts feels bad when you figure that out by „accident“
- isn’t POE2 supposed to be for a broader audience? I felt like this really didn’t hit the mark at some points. It feels intuitive from time to time, tutorials are nice and all, but some key mechanics, some interactions won’t be explained to you
- figuring stuff out on your own is impossible with the relatively high respec cost, the time investment and the expensive currency costs to get a build rolling
- there‘s not really any build variety and the game (as stated above) doesn’t encourage you to try stuff. It’s just way to punishing to do so.
- it’s kinda mandatory to at least invest into some stash tabs (which is fine). This is more of an information than it is a critique about the game. Every game needs to make money, they chose this route and I’m good with that. Just keep this in mind, when you decide to start playing.

Path of Exile 2 is a game that tries to give you a lot of gratification from optimizing your build, but in the end it is always the same early-game experience, using the same stuff for every class, you always end up with either lightning, fire, or some other boring element applied to four attacks which are the only skills worth using from the whole skill tree until the end, the only thing that changes is the weapon you use which is separate for every class.

You can look at those numbers going up and stuff and this is [b]cool[/b] on paper but at some point your weapon becomes useless and you can't find anything better without a grind yet before reaching endgame and trust me - the "campaign" mode is as boring as you can imagine - this is actually typical for every game with any predefined campaign mode.

You don't feel that a certain "optimization" you've made was worth it because changes are so minimal, you oneshot cannon fodder and struggle with bosses anyways because they are all simply damage sponges. 

Bosses have some unique attacks that are supposed to be challenging but in the end they are annoying at most, stat-checking you with no actual skill expression.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

That being said, if you want cool bosses and skill go play Dark Souls. If you want stats that actually matter and you can see the outcome while using your brain go play Europa Universalis 4 since Path of Midxile 2 shucks aaashh periodddd

The game is fun. It has really awesome mechanics and the setting is such an atmospheric masterpiece. It has a TON of flaws in its current state though. The major glaring issue that aggravates me the most is the unfair damage spikes that occur.
 I have a character that is "near" invincible. I consistently run juiced t16 way stones fully corrupted with ZERO issues. However, you will begin to consistently experience a wonderful thing. You get one shotted by a monster from off screen or something exploding that you literally cannot see. No way to avoid, no way to prepare. You're just running happily, full health full shield, and BOOM, dead. And upon that, their xp loss penalty for dying is completely ridiculous. Good luck getting past lvl 90. You die unfairly on a map, you loose 10% of your total xp needed to get the next level. Why GGG thought this was a good idea is beyond me. 
Also, if you die on a certain map, even playing it was pointless because you cannot repeat the map with the same benefits again, or even use your modifiers as a punishment for dying. I get that GGG wants to have a difficult experience but this is just brutal and honestly, not fun when it happens constantly.

Path of Exile 2 refines and expands its predecessor’s deep systems into a more cohesive, responsive, and mechanically expressive ARPG, blending familiar loot-driven progression with ambitious combat, skill, and scaling mechanics.

⚔️ Combat & Skill System — Fluid At Its Core

Combat in PoE2 feels sharper and more impactful than before. Hits connect with a satisfying weight, movement is snappy, and evasion/dodge feels like an active choice rather than a passive stat. The combat loop — move, position, attack, react — has more rhythmic responsiveness, making both clearing hordes and fighting bosses feel mechanical rather than random.

Skill customization remains a defining system, but in PoE2 it’s been streamlined without losing depth. Skills aren’t tied to a simple gem-socket system; they are now part of a hybrid action framework that blends traditional ARPG inputs with modular modifiers. Each ability has:

Clear roles (burst, sustain, crowd control),

Scalable augmentations (AoE radius, cast speed, additional effects),

And modifiers you slot in that behave predictably instead of randomly.

This makes builds feel like intentional constructions of mechanics, not just collections of numbers.

🌳 Passive & Specialization Trees — Strategic Expression

The passive tree has been reworked to be more meaningful and less sprawling, focusing on distinct paths of mechanical identity rather than just raw stat increases. You still invest progression points, but choices now yield clear gameplay changes — whether that’s stronger elemental conversion, improved dodge windows, or enhanced life leech synergy. There’s less “grind for incremental numbers” and more decisions that change how your build plays.

Each class’s specialization isn’t a dead end — rather, it unlocks unique mechanical layers that shape combat rhythm and role:

Frontliners gain better positioning and threat management tools,

Spellcasters get stronger charge and area mechanics,

Rangers enhance mobility and reactive systems.

Classes feel mechanically distinct, not just cosmetically.

🪙 Loot & Crafting — Predictable Power Growth

PoE2 keeps its signature loot depth but retools item crafting to be less opaque and more strategic. Currency items are tied to specific upgrade outcomes rather than random rerolls, giving players clearer control over gear growth. This turns crafting into a tactical system rather than a gamble:

Want more sockets? You know which currency to use.

Want to tailor resistances or utility mods? You can focus your resources mechanically.

This removes a lot of the old uncertainty and elevates player intention in gear progression.

🧠 Difficulty Scaling & Encounter Design

Difficulty ramps through predictable but challenging encounters — enemy behaviors telegraph more clearly, and mechanics reward observation and reaction rather than blind DPS stacking. Boss fights especially feel like mechanical puzzles in motion: pattern recognition, positioning, and resource timing matter just as much as stats.

Encounters aren’t random spawns — they are designed with mechanical intent, meaning teamwork (in co-op) and build synergy feel meaningful rather than incidental.

🗺️ Endgame & World Systems

The endgame here is no longer “reach a level cap and hope for better RNG” — the Atlas and region progression systems are player-driven loops. You choose how to scale challenges, manipulate map modifiers, and decide which mechanics you want to emphasize:

Higher risk for higher reward?

Targeted boss tracking?

Layered modifiers that dramatically change combat?

These decisions shape how the world responds to you, and that adaptive mechanical feedback is the backbone of long-term engagement.

10/10 — refined combat systems, intentional gear mechanics, and strategic progression loops that reward both tactical play and build creativity.

Path of Exile 2 has been a really pleasant surprise for me. The biggest selling point was native local co-op with shared screen on PC. Unlike Diablo IV, Grim Dawn, Titan Quest, Torchlight and even the first Path of Exile, which only offer online co-op and/or couch co-op on consoles, this lets me play on the same PC with my wife. That's a huge selling point for us, and I honestly think the store page should clearly mention it with the appropriate tag.

I barely played the original PoE, so I cannot really comment on lore or continuity. I have just reached Act 3, so I have no feedback on the endgame content yet, which seems to be the focus of many controversial reviews. So far I am just enjoying the strong Diablo 2 vibes. I played that game nonstop back in the day and loved its atmosphere, and the environments here feel very close in spirit.

The graphics are good, with a strong art style, and performance has been solid for an Early Access title. I do not have deep experience with classes, but the three I tried felt balanced and different enough to support distinct gameplay flows.

Some quality of life improvements are needed, especially for the gamepad interface. I would love easier access to certain features across menus, like being able to socket support gems directly from the skill menu, and generally making some interactions less convoluted. That said, it is still Early Access, so this feels understandable.

I did run into some server instability, heavy lag, and a few cases where the game froze with a "Game Paused" message. From what I read around this may be tied to ping going over 100 ms. That could be a problem if you live far from the available servers, so it might be smart to check the server list before buying the Early Access support pack. I also had long freezes after several hours of play that eventually turned into a loading screen and put me back exactly where I left off, with no progress loss. I am not sure if that is a local memory issue or a server desync.

Overall, my experience has been positive. As a Diablo 2 LoD veteran playing alongside my partner, who is still fairly new to isometric ARPGs, we are both having a great time.

This is my reflection on what I have played, nothing more nothing less.

Path of Exile 2 Early Access. Overall, I like the game — it has strong ideas and is genuinely addictive. Progression feels satisfying, and if you can invest the time, the endgame is reachable for normal players.

Campaign: Being able to skip the campaign would be a welcome quality of life option. Running it repeatedly gets boring no matter how fast you are.

Classes: The Druid is a great addition. There are some rough edges, but overall, it’s fun and well designed.

Temple: I don’t enjoy the Temple runs. The RNG required to create a viable run is frustrating, and I don’t find it fun to repeat it many times until I get the setup I want. And in that, atlas mechanics work better and faster, so temples do not make sense for a player like me.

Technical: The game is not very stable on PC. I experience a lot of rubber banding, and the Nvidia driver issue should have been resolved ASAP. Stability and server reliability need to be top priorities; I have died dozens of times because the server is not performing.

Mid season balance changes: As a casual player, mid season nerfs are a dealbreaker. If I invest limited time into a build to reach endgame and it gets hit with a 25% damage penalty, I’m unlikely to come back. I understand rebalancing between seasons but changing a build mid season after players have committed to it is extremely frustrating.

Verdict: An okay Early Access overall, with good core design and addictive progression, but stability, server issues, and mid season nerfs are the main problems for me.

Closing
This isn’t a bad game, it’s an Early Access with the wrong priorities right now. If you’re a casual player who values your time, wait for launch or for the devs to fix stability and rethink mid season balance decisions.

Honestly, I don't get the hype for this game. I'm coming from 200+ hours in Diablo Immortal and Diablo 4 Season 3, so I know what I'm talking about when it comes to quality ARPGs. Path of Exile 2 feels like a massive step backward for the genre.

Here are the negatives (because I couldn't find any positives):

Way too slow and Clunky: The character moves like they have constant lag. In Diablo 4, combat is fluid and visceral; here, you're locked into animations forever. They tried to copy Elden Ring with the dodge roll but failed miserably. If I wanted to play a Souls-like, I'd play one, not this.

The Passive Tree is a JOKE: Who has time to read all that? It's just artificial complexity to make "tryhards" feel smart. They should simplify it like D4 where you have a clear path. Having to use an external guide just to play is bad game design, period.

No Auto-Pathing? It's 2026, where is the button to auto-walk to the quest objective? I got lost in the first map for like 10 minutes. Mobile games solved this years ago.

Dark and generic graphics: Everything is just gray and brown. It lacks the art direction and polish of Blizzard games. You can tell it's an ancient engine with some HD textures slapped on top.

Archaic Flask System: Why do I have to kill monsters to refill potions? They should just have a cooldown or be infinite. Outdated mechanic from the 90s.

Conclusion: A pretentious game made for people with no jobs and no social life who enjoy suffering. If you want a real ARPG, just buy the Diablo expansion. [b]Path of Exile 2 has the potential to become one of the best action RPGs ever — but right now, in early access, I do not recommend buying it.[/b]

I’ve played PoE 2 for over [b]1,000 hours[/b] in its first year of early access, and I don’t regret the time — but the experience has been increasingly frustrating, and in its current state I don’t think it’s a fair or stable experience for new players.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Economy Is Not Optional[/h2]

PoE 2 is a game that — in my experience — can only be enjoyed properly if you meaningfully participate in the in-game economy. To do that effectively you need premium stash tabs and especially AFK shop tabs. Without them, trading efficiently is difficult, risky, prone to scam attempts, and time-consuming.

Community creator GhazzyTV once described Path of Exile as:

[quote]
“Free to try, not free to play.”
[/quote]

That still applies to PoE 2.  
Meaningful economy participation costs additional money.
Plus, PoE 2 early access costs money straight away! It will only be [i]"free to play"[/i] on full release.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Fate of the Vaal – Economy Collapse[/h2]

The most recent Fate of the Vaal league exposed how fragile the economy can be. A new league mechanic — the Temple — was poorly balanced at release, and an abrupt rewards increase just before a holiday break caused massive inflation. By the time GGG returned and patched the situation, many players were so far behind they could no longer participate meaningfully. A league intended to last ~4 months became effectively unplayable after about [b]1 month[/b] for a large portion of the player base.

GGG did not:

[list]
[*] Roll out a patch quickly  
[*] Reset the economy  
[*] Roll back progress  
[*] Punish exploiters  
[/list]

The situation was justified with “it’s early access.”

Technically true. Practically devastating.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Community Response Says Everything[/h2]

The community organized and crowdfunded a private league called:

[b]Second Wind: Fate of the Vaal[/b]

[list]
[*] ~51,000 total slots  
[*] ~48,000 registered players  
[*] One of the largest private leagues in PoE history  
[/list]

Tens of thousands of players voluntarily paid to join a community-run reset league because they wanted:

[list]
[*] A fresh economy  
[*] A fair start  
[*] A playable league  
[/list]

That level of participation speaks louder than any forum post.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]There Are Good Things[/h2]

To be clear:

[list]
[*] Combat feels good and challenging  
[*] Build depth is promising  
[*] Core systems have real potential  
[/list]

But none of that matters when:

[list]
[*] The economy can collapse without proper measures taken by GGG
[*] Exploiters go unpunished and are incentivized to always look for new opportunities to break the game for everyone
[*] Progress becomes meaningless due to developer negligence  
[*] Player time investment isn’t protected  
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Verdict[/h2]

I believe PoE 2 can become something special, maybe even the best action RPG so far.

[b]But right now: I do not recommend buying Path of Exile 2 during early access.[/b]

Wait for later development stages when economy handling, balance processes, and player-time protection are clearly more mature.

I expect — and hope — to change this review in the future.

I booked no more than 10 hours in Path of Exile across a couple season attempts.  The biggest issue isn't even that I found it daunting or intimidating - I just thought it didn't feel good to play.  The camera hanged unimaginably close to your character's head.  Click-to-move didn't bring me joy in the accessibility age.  Very few tooltips and progression recommendations made for a confusing experience where I could not determine if I was effective, or how to become such.  

I'm 286 hours into PoE 2 at time of writing, most of this time spanning across 3 characters in both Solo Self Found and Trade leagues.  The SINGLE criticism I can drum up across nigh 300 hours would be aimed specifically at the league structures:  SSF can feel a little slow and sometimes punishing since loot and currencies drop slower as one person without an economy; conversely, trade league felt almost too "easy" for me as you could acquire high-grade gear and currency with very little effort or luck.  I still haven't decided if I will main a specific league, or which one I would main.  

To be at almost 300 hours into the game and still feel like I'm in the "experimentation" phase of feeling out a character, the progression and gear systems, the league's nuances and interactivity...just feels like such a joy and a blessing.  By this much time I'm usually done and dusted with most of my library picks, and I'm staring at this title (still in Early Access for probably another 3 quarters, BTW) and just cannot imagine when I will stop having fun.  There's SO MANY characters I want to build on my own and take through the campaign and try endgame progression with.

As a player who likes very minimal engagement with guides and meta playstyles, I have not felt ineffective with the exception of brief slumps where the build or my gear need an adjustment.  At my own humble devices, I devised a build that took me to the 90s in SSF and it still has room to become much stronger.  I have reached a point where I can see the benefit of trade league - knowing it might take several hours to grind some currencies or loot when I could just start hawking my own items and quickly buy upgrades.  The crazy part is that if you don't like SSF, you can just switch - for the most part mitigating half of my grievances.  

Bringing it all around, if you don't want to play the economy, you don't have to.  If you don't want to play alone, you don't have to.  If you don't want you use a guide, you don't have to.  

IF YOU DON'T WANT TO PLAY THIS GAME BECAUSE YOU DIDN'T LIKE POE 1, PLEASE RECONSIDER!

I wouldn’t call myself a Battlefield veteran in the gatekeeping sense, but I’ve spent thousands of hours with this franchise. I started with Battlefield 2 and experienced what Battlefield used to feel like. Battlefield 3 and 4 were the peak for me. Even with controversial decisions like Premium and paid DLCs, the core gameplay was strong, cohesive, and rewarding.

Battlefield 6 initially felt promising. A bit too fast, but still directionally right. Gunplay felt okay, movement was energetic, and for a short moment it felt like Battlefield again.

That didn’t last.

Right now, the game simply feels bad to play. And that’s the most frustrating part. Not broken in a spectacular way, not outrageously buggy. Just… bad. Weightless movement, inconsistent gunplay, unclear feedback, and a general sense that nothing quite clicks together. The Battlefield DNA is technically present, but it feels diluted, unfocused, and cheap.

The closest comparison I can make is Battlefield Heroes or Battlefield Play4Free. And that hurts to even say. Those were free-to-play side projects, and Battlefield 6 somehow manages to evoke the same shallow, unsatisfying feeling while being a full-priced title.

What makes this worse is that this isn’t anger. It’s disappointment. I wanted this to be good. I wanted to enjoy it. I gave it time because Battlefield mattered to me. Seeing it end up like this genuinely feels heartbreaking.

At this point, this is easily the weakest Battlefield experience I’ve had. Worse than the spin-offs, worse than the experiments. It doesn’t feel like Battlefield anymore. It feels like a franchise that forgot why people fell in love with it in the first place.

BF6 is a complicated game to review. A lot of negative discourse around this game comes from a die-hard core of players who want to see this game succeed. However, this die hard player base is one of BF6 greatest strengths and proves what EA has here - BF6 is an immensely fun FPS with something for everyone with a player base who will stick around for it to become the best it can be. 

As of Jan 20th, BF6 has gone through a content drought that will end theoretically on Feb 17th. The drought is complicated, and might explain some negative reviews. Justifiably, it was a bad decision to release 3 'major' content updates in the first months and then go contentless for 2.5 months after that. Developers went on holiday, Vince Zampella tragically passed, and a mountain of regular players who want their voice to be heard continued playing... There are a lot of weeds there. 

BUT, the future this game offers is among the series' best - and when youre playing with a good group, or just have TOOL cranked up while driving a tank, these issues fade quickly into the great experience this game offers. The history of the Battlefield franchise points to the fact that every title receives support to get it to a place where fans are happy, and I have no doubt starting in Feb BF6 will round this corner. 

To prospective buyers in Jan 26', as a weekly player I'd recommend completely. What BF6 offers to new players is massive and very fun, and as more content begins to arrive in February, it is the perfect time to hop in and enjoy this title as things start ramping up.

Squad play shines, rewarding teamwork with memorable moments like clutch revives, coordinated pushes, and heroic last stands. Battlefield 6 doesn’t try to slow things down or overcomplicate the formula, it leans into spectacle, scale, and fun. Firstly, this is a review for Battlefield 6, not any other Battlefield title. The launch was the best Battlefield launch in history. There are some netcode issues here and there, but they are literally nothing in comparison to the Battlefield 4 launch—unless everyone forgot that the game was almost unplayable for the first three months due to insane rubber-banding.

The gunplay is excellent overall. The maps are on the smaller side, so there is always action; there is no need to run for three minutes to a dead-zone objective only to die from a random jet bomb. If a running simulator is what you are looking for, then this game is not for you. If you want nonstop action, explosions, and chaos, this is the game for you.

Unfortunately, unlocking weapons is very slow, but this is easily fixable with a future patch—just keep that in mind. I do not care for Redsec, so no comments there other than it being a waste of development resources. Portal mode is cheeks.

Overall, the core Battlefield experience is fun and chaotic, which makes for a great time. Finding friends to play with is also easy using the official Discord. This was written at 600 hours of gameplay, and I have no intention of stopping there.

Do not believe the hype. This is not a grand return to form for Battlefield fans, but rather a blatant shift to capitalize on Call of Duty's recent failures and FPS fatigue in order to attract CoD players. It has all the elements of a Battlefield game but plays more like Call of Duty Modern Warfare 2019's ground war mode. By itself, it isn't a bad game, but compared to BFBC2 through Battlefield 1 it sucks. 

Other reviews cover the fundamental problems of this game pretty well, but from my personal experience:
1. Classes: all the classes lack variety in equipment and playstyle (mostly due to unlocked weapons), the perks are a mess (the XP requirement is wildly inconsistent), and overall it feels likes I'm fighting the same dude instead of a diversified squad.
2. Weapons: all guns feel extremely similar in their respective classes with a few exceptions but not enough for $70. Also placing unlockable guns near the end of a battle pass sector is egregious.
3. XP gain: it feels like for any single gun in the game I have to grind as much as I did to get class ranked 10 in Battlefield 1 which discourages using a diverse arsenal and is obviously just trying to make players play longer for that $$$$.
4. Netcode/Weapon ADS Bloom/CoD movement/Balance issues/etc: makes TTK and gunfights wildly random. Sometimes you can kill a guy in 1 second, but sometimes it takes 10 seconds for the same gunfight. Sometimes the same dude can be a superhero and dive 6 feet out of the way and kill you using his YouTube clickbait gun build that has zero recoil, fast ADS, and a huge magazine.
5. Maps: too small and very generic. Not nearly enough to justify the price tag. 
6. FOMO: if you don't do x, y, z in this amount of time you might miss out :0. Again another trick to boost player retention that hurts the casual player that can't play for 8 hours every week.
7. AI generated assets that players PAY for: I can understand the use of AI in game development to some extent, but a $5 sticker pack containing something I can generate for free (and at better quality)? Might as well be the pink Darth Vader skin from Battlefront 2 because it is just as lazy and greedy.

The goal of this review is to give my honest opinion about the game in its current state. My first Battlefield game was BF3 and I've been playing every title since (except for 2042), so I think my opinion can be valuable to some people. 

The core gameplay is good but there are many things holding the game back from being what it's supposed to be. First, the netcode is horrible, you constantly die around corners and hit reg is a mess. Second, most maps are mediocre at best. There is no variety in gameplay across the maps, they may look different but they all feel the same. Besides Siege of Cairo, there is no map that feels memorable. Third, progression is a slug fest. The amount of work you need to put into this game to unlock attachments or progress for the battlepass is ridiculous. Fourth, legacy features like a server browser or persistent servers are missing. Honestly, I don't understand why these things aren't present in the game. Finally, squad balance is also a mess, support has way to much utility while recon and assault feel practically useless. 

There's a lot more things I can list (e.g. Stale vehicle combat, use of AI for cosmetics, lack of content, skins and bundles appearing to be the main focus of the devs, ...), but the ones I listed are the most important imo.

It's fine if you like the game (I like it too at times) or disagree with some of my statements, but you have to acknowledge that BF6 has some glaring issues that need to be addressed urgently. I really want this game to succeed but it's becoming increasingly more difficult to be optimistic about its future. After all, the player count doesn't lie.

If you're looking to buy this game, I would advise to wait a couple of weeks until season 2 drops. Hopefully, the most important issues will be fixed and the game will be in a much better state.

I stuck around only to finish the free version of the battle pass in season one. Now I'm 200 hours in and look forward to putting the game down for the foreseeable future. I would not recommend this game to anyone until new maps are added and the net code is fixed. BF6 had the easiest path to overtaking Call of Duty we've ever seen. Veteran Battlefield player review

I’ve been playing Battlefield since Bad Company 2 on PS3 back in 2010, and I’ve played pretty much every entry since then except Hardline. I know Battlefield has always had quirks, but Battlefield 6 feels like the least Battlefield-like game in the series. It almost feels like a Battlefield clone that understands the pieces but never quite puts them together right.

On paper, it has what Battlefield should have. Big maps. Vehicle combat. Weapon variety. Classes with different roles. But in practice, it just does not feel right.

The class and gadget design is a mess. Recon is basically just spotting and sniping. Assault feels borderline useless now that Support does both ammo and healing. Assault’s only standout features are a spawn beacon and a secondary weapon as a gadget, which honestly feels like something every class should have, not a class identity. Most classes end up with one gadget you want and one filler gadget you never touch.

Engineer should be my favorite class, but it is crippled. You only get one launcher, and launchers are awful. Tanks take way too many rockets to kill, so every spawn turns into dumping half your ammo just to finish one vehicle. Lock-on launchers are even worse. Helicopters can break locks by hiding behind tiny debris or hovering a few feet off the ground. Even when you successfully bait flares and relock, rockets will sometimes just fly off in a random direction like they are still tracking flares that no longer exist.

Gunplay feels bad. Everything feels like a marshmallow shooter. Even heavy sniper rifles often take two hits to kill. Most weapons are four or five shots to kill, and headshots barely matter because the multiplier is so low. Attachments make this worse. Many of them don’t explain what they do, so you have to look up YouTube videos, and a lot of them come with dumb tradeoffs like recoil reduction only while standing still. That’s not an upgrade, that’s a restriction.

Explosives are especially frustrating. RPGs and grenade launchers feel like weak grenades. A direct RPG hit should not be survivable. If explosives are limited and balanced, fine, but they should actually do damage. Right now they just tickle people, which makes entire gadget slots feel wasted.

Custom games are another missed opportunity. The idea is good, but half the modes are locked down. There is no clear XP on or off system, and even when XP is off, there is no option to just unlock everything and have fun. It feels like fake freedom. I understand not wanting people to farm bots (even though they couldn't care less in 2042), but if challenges feel like chores that I want to rush through instead of something I naturally progress while playing, the challenge design is bad.

They also renamed everything. Long-time Battlefield players know Conquest, Domination, Rush. Now modes are renamed and don’t always play how their names suggest, which just adds unnecessary confusion.

Hit registration is one of the biggest problems. Even with low ping servers, fights feel unfair. I’ll shoot someone who is looking the other direction, land a hit, and suddenly their model snaps to me and I’m dead instantly. It feels like the game is correcting itself after the fact instead of showing what is actually happening. On top of that, ADS still has an accuracy cone that is poorly explained, making it feel like shots just don’t go where you aim.

The battle pass is the icing on the cake. I already hate battle passes, but this one feels especially pointless. You pay money, grind like it’s a job before the timer runs out, and unlock cosmetics that all look nearly identical. I appreciate that the game stays military themed, but if everything looks the same, why am I paying extra at all? The deluxe edition price is honestly insulting for what you get.

In the end, this isn’t a terrible game. It’s still Battlefield at its core. But it has too many small problems that stack into one big frustrating experience. Every issue by itself might be tolerable, but together they push me away. I’d rather boot up Battlefield 1 or even 2042 with bots and just have fun.

I’ll probably keep playing and I hope it improves, but this is not worth full price right now, and the deluxe edition is absolutely not worth it. I really hope the devs start listening to the community. Let us make fun game modes. Let guns kill people. Let gadgets actually matter. Stop telling players how they’re allowed to have fun.

I grew up on Battlefield 3 and Battlefield 4, and compared to them, Battlefield 6 feels like a downgrade in almost every way that actually matters.
One of the biggest problems is weapon balance. Out of ~20 weapons, people realistically use 4 meta guns, because everything else is objectively worse. There’s no experimentation, no personality, no reason to master different weapons. In BF3/BF4, almost every gun was viable if you learned its recoil and role. In BF6, if you’re not running the meta, you’re throwing.
The TTK and TTE are awful. You die almost instantly, but enemies somehow still feel inconsistent to kill. Time to engage is basically zero — you’re shot from five angles the moment you move. There’s no room to react, reposition, or outplay someone. BF3/BF4 had slower, more readable engagements where gunfights felt fair and skill-based.
Map design is one of the biggest failures. BF6 maps are small as hell, extremely compressed, and overloaded with cover. Instead of large-scale Battlefield flow, you get constant third-party deaths, spawn traps, and chaotic meat grinders. There’s no breathing room, no frontlines, no sense of scale — just nonstop cluttered fights.
Vehicles suffer because of this too. Tanks and aircraft feel restricted and disposable instead of powerful battlefield tools like in BF3/BF4. Maps aren’t built around combined arms anymore.
Gunplay lacks weight, recoil barely matters, and fights feel dictated by stats and meta rather than positioning and aim.
The class system being diluted kills teamwork. Everyone can do everything, so no one plays a real role. Battlefield used to reward coordination — now it rewards solo play.
The UI and presentation are soulless and arcade-like. BF3/BF4 were immersive and grounded. BF6 looks and feels like a generic live-service shooter.
BF4 launched rough but became legendary because its core design was strong. BF6 feels like it learned nothing from that history.
BF3 and BF4 are still better Battlefield games more than a decade later.
Verdict: Not Recommended. Battlefield lost its identity.

At it's core, the game is a Battlefield title, a decent one. Good gunplay, good audio and art design, not too fast TTK and a good amount of guns for you to choose, but man does it have some huge problems as well. Let's start from the most talked one, the maps. 

The maps are either a hard miss or barely decent at best, with one single map being actually very good no matter how many times I play it. They're either too small or they have huge spaces of nothing. To give an example, Siege of Cairo is probably the best map in the game, which is funny since it's probably one of the smaller one where infantry fight is most common. But somehow they managed to make the map feel good to play, even for the vehicles. Then, on the complete opposite of the spectrum, we have New Sobek City and Blackwell Fields, where they're just terrible. One is just people fighting above rooftops in a very small rat house (it's an easy fix really, just add the pyramides that you see in the background), while the other one is just a big open field of nothing. And right in the middle we have maps like Mirak Valley and Manhattan Bridge, where they're not terrible, but I wish they had something more going on for them (Manhattan Bridge man, it's in the name, allow the players to fight on the big ass bridge instead of just being there as scenery). 

Then we have the obvious problem of having way too many gamemodes, which are either very similiar to one another or have no reason to exist. I'm looking at you King of the Hill. Plus we also have REDSEC with the Battle Royale (WHICH NO ONE ASKED FOR, STOP LISTENING TO THE STREAMERS THEY DON'T KNOW WHAT THEY'RE TALKING ABOUT) or Gauntlet, which spreads the community even further.  

The classes are cool, with the idea of subclasses which is just wasted potential. Sub-Classes are supposed to make the class you're playing focus on something, but so far the only one that has actual real changes it's the Engineer, with the Combat Engineer for driving vehicles and the other one (forgot the name) for playing purely infantry and going for enemy vehicles on foot. The other classes either have a slight change given to them (which is either useless or a straight upgrade) and that's it. Which is sad, because the idea of sub-classes sounds really interesting , allowing you to specialize in something out of necessity or because you want to play in a specific way.

Then there's probably the worst part of the game, the bugs. God I have seen so many bugs in this game, and half of them were in the menu, which baffles me. How the hell is the game this messy after months of it's release? Sometimes I forget I paid 60 euros for this game, thinking I got this for 19,99 and made by an indie dev studio. Some bugs are slightly annoying, even funny at times. Some instead forces you to restart the game entirely (literally a black screen after exiting a match and going back to the main menu, how did this happen). 

Also, since we're on the topic of main menu, God it's just AWFUL to use,  have to click so many things if I want to just start a match, or find a gamemode I want to play (again, it wouldn't be a problem if we didn't have so many). 

In short, the game is fun, but if it continues to go on like this I don't see it going far. 5/10

Review after 200-ish hours:

In summary: It's okay game, but there are plenty of flaws. 

In more details:
I've been playing battlefield games for past 15 years. After a failure of previous game (BF2042) this game felt like a step in good direction. Well, I don't think it is. 

Starting with positives:
- semi-modern setup is cool,
- gun play feels really good.

And that's it, thought this positive list would be longer.

The negatives:
- Maps are mediocre at best - 90% of them follow "funnel" pattern, they are long, but narrow. It forces you to be in some kind of meat grinder. I have a list of maps when I see start to load I immediately want to quit. For example "New Sobek city", you will die because someone is sitting on roofs that are not accessible by anything, other then helicopters.
-  Game modes - there are too many useless gamepoints that seems like a copy from CoD, but done worse. Just keep it will full-scale warfare, that's what we want.
- Vehicles for most part are terrible against infantry - the splash damage doesn't make sense. You can shot a group  of people and get between 30 and 60 DMG dealt to each individual. I understand it's about the balance, but come on - it's easy to destroy a tank if 2 or  3 engineers starts to throw bodies at it.
- You will constantly die behind cover - you can be 5m to 10m behind wall, yet magically the game have smart guns from cyberpunk that can kill you around the corner.
- Skins - they told us they will be kept grounded - now it's starting to look like BF2042 again, it's not bad yet, however they start to feel grotesq.
- Don't get me start on campaign - it has it moments, and that's it.
- Season Pass that forces you to play very boring game modes  and Battle Royale.
- Battle Royale per se is not bad, however it's missing solo queues -  it's annoying to play with randoms that don't understand what's going on + you are still forced to play it because of the season pass (because you want to unlock new guns, don't you)
- netcode - we were told fixes were deployed, but still to this date I can hit a helicopter with rocket and not receive any hitmarkers -  I can hear the explosion, but the pilot is still alive.
- game crashes - it crashes - like a lot - I can play maybe up to 3 to 4 matches before it fails to load next game (have to restart) or just completly blue screen my PC (Game per se runs fine on 2K monitor for me, getting over 144FPS).

So to summarize - it could have been a great game based on the setup, but oh my god they failed to do so.

BLUF: It is a COD-adjacent shooter. If you want arcade play with frenetic gunplay, slide-canceling and bunny hopping, and long progression, this may appeal to you. If you were seeking a tactical shooter, where placement, deployable or entrenched cover, and coordination matters to take and hold objectives, look elsewhere. Looks and sounds nice, and can be a lot of fun with friends... as long as they keep playing. 

The critique - since that' what you came to read:
First and foremost, the excessive monetizing is truly EA, an a reminder to never buy an EA product again. Bought the game at 100$ CAD? Buy a better version! Want to enjoy some progression? Buy a season pass! No, that doesn't come with the base game, it's extra! Bought a season pass and want to host your own server (with limits)? Buy a better season pass for more money! Don't like the humdrum unlockable skins? We have new skins! For money! We have AI GENERATED CONTENT! For money! A free to play game needs some monetization to keep the servers running - people paid a hundred for this, and still it's not enough to enjoy the baseline experience. 

Second was the bait and switch, a perennial hazard in the 21st century gaming universe. They promised casual bot play on make-your-own servers, with XP, to allow you to enjoy the game, unlock components needed for gameplay, and not grind versus people who cheat or haven't blinked since 2010. Then they took it away. 

Movement is too fast. I find the COD-esque slide/hop/slide/hop/hop/kill cancerous and that's mostly what this is.This makes creating and holding hardpoints - defended positions - very difficult. Enemy players feel like they come from everywhere and can just slide-cancel through your team, removing tactical play and making it feel like Unreal 2004. You will die (and kill other players) by 10 rounds to the head before you hear the first bullet zip by, thanks to poor server syncing. Likewise just before you turn the corner (or well after cover). Some of this is expected in an online game - the speed of light sets hard limits on processing - but Battlefield 6 honestly makes my actions feel fairly meaningless and gives the impression everyone else is cheating. 

The gunplay is ok, and scratches that quasi-mil-sim itch. But things like sub-machine guns (short-ranged weapons) outfighting dedicated long-range weapons at any range, and acting like phasers, becomes quite frustrating. The grind to unlock weapon components is excessive. I've been playing 200 hours as of this review, and I've hardly gotten past 20% on 20% of the weapons available. Forced engagement is a poor design choice, and always bites the vendor in the end. 

The learning curve for aircraft is a little rough, but "good" players can effectively destroy a server with few viable counters aside from somehow wrangling half your team to laser-lock and spam AA missiles - while not doing anything else. Further, Battlefield still suffers from the "1 person grabs the vehicle and plays it the whole match" syndrome, making it hard to practice*. I'm not sure how to resolve without putting timers and reservations on vehicles. *And if you do get a vehicle, and you know, have rarely used it because you haven't had the chance to play one, expect a lot of toxic behavior from players...

The single player campaign is... servicable. If you get motion-sick, note that it locks you into FPV mode for cutscences that cannot be skipped. You also need to grind out achievements to unlock multiplayer components. The plot is mediocre and clearly a rush job, but they needed to justify why you can have a tank fight in Brooklyn, NY. 

All in all, it's a bit of a sunk cost for me, and I will enjoy playing with what few friends still play - or against bots for little gains - but if you were on the fence about this one, expecting to relive nostalgic memories of Battlefield 4 or Bad Company 2, this is Battlefield COD. I'd skip it.

Battlefield 6 launched with a lot of hype and seemed to resurrect the franchise, initially. It was fantastic to have a somewhat fun game launched reasonably optimized and relatively bug free. However, it seems to be losing its playerbase at a rapid pace due to lack of variety in maps and also things to do after a certain level (due to repetitive nature). As players eagerly await the release of Season 2, a few things EA can do to bring back players or at least help maintain the interest of the current ones. I would not mind a minor delay in Season 2, if we could get 1 (especially the first) or more of these included in the game.
1) Introduce more large maps. We currently have Siege of Cairo and Operation Firestorm, but the former does not support aerial combat. It does not have the feel of a true Battlefield game without these large maps (I know I will draw some flak here, but honestly some of the Battlefield 2042 maps were more fun than Blackwell Fields and Empire State and can be reworked in some form to introduce here). It almost feels like fighter/attack jets crross the length of maps in a matter of seconds (for most maps) and are already outside combat zone, making them pointless over choppers.
2) Stop catering to the PUBG and CoD playerbase, they will not last long in such games outside of a few CQB maps/modes. Sure, some fast-paced gameplay can be fun, but not with a whole bunch of morons jumping/sliding around corners with SMGs/shotguns. In fact, SMGs can use a small nerf on hip-fire accuracy  (especially while moving) to make them more balanced. The same goes for the new Redsec modes, Gauntlet can still be fun with good teamplay, but Battle royale seems absolutely unnecessary (I'd rather focus on Strikepoiint to see how it can be made more appealing) in a Battlefield game.
3) I agree with one of the YT reviewers when they suggested what they themselves felt may sound controversial (and honestly do not know why it should). It would be great to have a main weapon swap between Engineers and Support. Support classes need to be in the middle of battle reviving players and healing/dropping ammo and would do better with SMG proficiency. On the other hand, engineers would be better off at range with their rocket launchers and laying mines so it would serve them better to have LMG or DMR proficiency instead.
4) If they indeed prefer to go with this Battlepass mode (not much complaint as such), please consider adding more content in it to make it worth the money and have it last longer for each Season.
TLDR: Some tweaks in current game will strongly help revive the original Battlefield playerbase and make it more fun, espcially introduction of a few large maps for the true "Battlefield experience".
