The modern version of a classic bait and switch. The beta was legitimately the best part of this game because, at the time, I assumed the full release would be more fleshed out.

Boy was I wrong.

Battlefield 6 is a game that keeps showing you it could have been a real Battlefield, then immediately reminds you it chose to be something else. The gunplay is ok enough to hook you for a few matches, and there are moments where the action feels like classic Battlefield. Those moments are so rare they feel almost accidental.

A lot of it comes down to flow. Good Battlefield maps give you options. You can push the objective straight on, flank, take a side route, go up a neighboring building, or use vehicles to create pressure somewhere else. In BF6, you get funneled into the same two or three choke points, and once one team gets control, you might as well wait for the next objective. As a side note, I’m not sure who decided which maps get what vehicles and when, but that person should at least be given a stern talking to.

Maps are trash.

First off, they are tiny. The playable area alone limits options. Most maps only have a handful of lanes or are extremely flat and open. City maps are filled with locked doors and hallways that lead nowhere. Objective locations for game modes were not planned out well, and in combination with small maps and limited lanes, some rounds are not even worth playing.

For comparison:

BF6 launch maps average: 0.189 km² (9 maps)
BF4 launch maps average: 0.784 km² (8 maps I could find sizes for)
So BF4’s launch maps are about 4.15x larger.

TTK is trash too. It plays like COD so they could appeal to a larger player base.

For comparison:

In Battlefield 4, most assault rifles used the standard 24.5 max damage model, which means 5 point blank body shots to kill a 100 HP player.

So the math looks like this (stock, point blank, body shots):

AEK 971 (900 RPM, 5 shots to kill)
TTK = (shots to kill − 1) × (60 ÷ RPM)
TTK = (5 − 1) × (60 ÷ 900) = 4 × 0.0667 = 0.267s (267ms)

M416 (750 RPM, 5 shots to kill)
TTK = (5 − 1) × (60 ÷ 750) = 4 × 0.0800 = 0.320s (320ms)

ACE 23 (770 RPM, 5 shots to kill)
TTK = (5 − 1) × (60 ÷ 770) = 4 × 0.0779 = 0.312s (312ms)

Now compare that to Battlefield 6. DougS2K’s BF6 Weapon Stats Spreadsheet (posted on the Battlefield 6 subreddit and hosted on Google Sheets) has point blank body TTKs like:

TR 7: 0.167s (167ms)
M4A1: 0.200s (200ms)
B36A4: 0.250s (250ms)
M433: 0.217s (217ms)

So in BF4, typical AR gunfights are around the 312 to 320ms zone. In BF6, it can be as low as 167ms. It may not seem like much, but in game it is extremely noticeable, especially if you are a veteran Battlefield player.

Weapons…

Not even sure where to start here. I will just say that the weapons seem to contradict how the intended class playstyle is supposed to go down. The whole point of classes is tradeoffs. You pick a role, you bring certain strengths, you accept certain weaknesses, and your team makes up the difference. That is the Battlefield multiplayer identity. BF6 does not respect that. Everyone can build into everything, so class identity gets watered down into basically nothing.

Some more comparisons:

BF4: 80+ launch weapons
BF6: 45 unlockable weapons
BF6 (extra): +12 weapons via assignments after Career Rank 50

How long to unlock each weapon (worst case, last rank gated unlock):

BF4: Rank 60 total = 3,520,000 XP
25,000 XP/hr: 3,520,000 / 25,000 = 141 hrs
40,000 XP/hr: 3,520,000 / 40,000 = 88 hrs
60,000 XP/hr: 3,520,000 / 60,000 = 59 hrs

BF6: Career Rank 2 to 50 unlock track
About 72 hrs to hit Rank 50 and unlock all Career weapons (not counting the extra 12)

How long to unlock all attachments per weapon?

BF4 (kills based): 400 to 500 kills to “finish” a gun
40 KPH: 400 to 500 / 40 = 10.0 to 12.5 hrs
60 KPH: 400 to 500 / 60 = 6.7 to 8.3 hrs
90 KPH: 400 to 500 / 90 = 4.4 to 5.6 hrs

BF6 (mastery): Mastery 50, about 1,800 kills per gun
40 KPH: 1,800 / 40 = 45 hrs
60 KPH: 1,800 / 60 = 30 hrs
90 KPH: 1,800 / 90 = 20 hrs

Finally, Vehicles…

They can be fun for a bit, but nothing like previous installments. Map size and cover really limit options. Variety is also extremely limited.

For comparison:
BF4: ~50 vehicles at launch
BF6: 15 vehicles

Makes sense considering the size constraints the BF6 maps introduce. Vehicles seem like they may have been an afterthought, with no map specifically built around vehicle use.

Unfortunately, this is probably as close to classic Battlefield as EA is going to give us these days. Buy it if you want to scratch the BF itch. It will not be satisfying, but it is all you are going to get.

After 2042 I had some low expectations, and was surprised how good bf6 was at launch. It was mostly fun too. I don't get why people hate the maps so much, maybe my frame of reference is not as educated as others. 

However, my mostly positive feelings are starting to sour. The campaign returned, but this time with no characters you cared about or plot that was gripping... meh. The multiplayer is better, but I am frustrated by a few aspects.

1) Inconsistent damage and bizarre outcomes. I can land 8 hits on a guy close up, see the bullet impacts on their torso and head, and do 25% damage. They hit me 3 times and I'm dead. It doesn't make sense. Obviously hit registration is mixed, and my 2 cents is that it's worse across different platforms. Console players sometimes seem to have god-like aim and god-mode invincibility. Not the most engaging play experience. 
 
For example- today I blew up a guys tank. An engineer standing next to it took splash damage, and then I hit him 12 times in the face with an SMG close up. 2) Matchmaking - There is definitely something going on to build teams. But it's not a friendly AI that's looking to build competitive matches with evenly matched teams. There's a little back-and-forth early on, but after 5-10 minutes the momentum is all going one way. And for me the momentum is usually going against me. 

3) Console microphones - they seem to be turned on by default, and have no threshold whatsoever for what noise is passed into the game. No push to talk either.  If I hear one more asshat eating a bag of chips while listening to hip-hop and yelling at their little brother I'm going to lose my mind. OH and mute doesn't work sometimes. Yup.

Battlefield 6 is a complete waste of time and patience.
A game that is supposed to be a AAA military shooter instead feels like a broken early-access build that was never properly tested. The biggest issue? Constant crashes. Relentless, random, unavoidable crashes.

You load into a match, play well, complete objectives, earn XP… and then BAM — crash to desktop. No warning, no error message, no recovery. And the best part? All the progress from that match is gone. No XP, no unlocks, no rewards. Just hours of your life erased as if you never played at all.

This doesn’t happen once in a while. It happens all the time. Every longer match feels like a gamble: Will the game survive until the end, or will it crash and delete everything again? When a game can randomly wipe your progress at any moment, what’s the point of playing?

Battlefield 6 literally punishes you for playing it. Skill doesn’t matter. Effort doesn’t matter. The only certainty is that sooner or later the game will crash and make your time completely worthless. That’s not challenge. That’s not difficulty. That’s pure technical failure.

The optimization is awful, stability is nonexistent, and it feels like the developers either never tested the game properly or simply don’t care that players are losing hours of progress due to crashes. For a full-price release, this is absolutely unacceptable.

Summary:
Battlefield 6 isn’t frustrating because it’s hard — it’s frustrating because it doesn’t work. Constant crashes turn it into a game where progression is meaningless and playing feels like waiting for the next crash. A total waste of time, nerves, and money.

I paid €70 for Battlefield 6, and the game delivers nowhere near what that price suggests. It’s filled with bugs, lacks polish, and feels like it was released far too early. The developers are extremely slow to push out updates and rarely address the issues that matter most.

The crossplay is a complete disaster, mainly because the aim assist on controllers is absurdly overpowered, giving console players a massive advantage and heavily punishing keyboard-and-mouse players. It’s so exaggerated that it destroys any sense of fair competitiveness.

In the RedSec mode, the balance problems become even more obvious. Tanks and RPGs are completely disproportionate, with tanks being overwhelmingly strong. The amount of anti-tank equipment available is nowhere near enough to counter the number and power of tanks, turning matches into vehicle-dominated chaos.

On top of that, for a casual player who works eight hours a day, leveling up weapons is almost impossible. The progression is so slow and grindy that, by the time you finally manage to upgrade anything, another Battlefield game will probably already be on the horizon. It makes long-term investment feel pointless.

Overall, Battlefield 6 simply doesn’t justify the investment. It’s unstable, poorly optimized, unbalanced on multiple fronts, and leaves you with the clear feeling that you wasted your money.

Unfortunately, Battlefield 6 is an incomplete game with many technical issues and greed. 

It's already known that the development of this game was rush as a response of BF 2042 failure and you can see the result of that with technical issues (a lot of them), bad campaign with a bad story, small MP maps, low number of vehicles in MP, no naval warfare in any map of MP and much more.

Now the main reasons why I stopped playing and why I’m leaving a negative review it's because of two things:

- First the connection, is awful. I’ve never seen an AAA game with servers that are so bad, having constant packet loss and high latency.  As a South American player I have accepted that most online games will have some kind of connection issue or high ping, but BF 6 literally gave me the worst MP experience ever. Even compared to other BF games, BF 6 is for some reason the one with the worst connection. Unfortunately it gets worse, because in big game modes like Conquest you can suffer from some kind of slow motion caused by the servers that make all big game modes unplayable. That's why most of my playtime is in smaller game modes like Domination and TDM. According to what I searched, this problem only occurs on servers of low populated gaming areas (like south america), but it's funny how this problem was never present in the beta and with each new update it's making this issue even worse. DICE it's doing absolutely nothing to resolve it but somehow they are busy making BF 6 Memes with the ingame engine for social media.

- Second the greed, the game is filled with "microtransaction". It's sad how one of the only things in the game that kind of work without issues is the store, with $20 skins that are inflated in price because of being bundle with filler content like AI generated stickers and a battle pass that is too grindy mainly do to the progress of the tiers being granted through challenges. Let's don't forget the limited time paths that only show for one week making you play MP only to complete the event challenges in time because of FOMO, one of the latest limited path of season one for some reason launch with not enough challenge point to complete the path on time, you can't tell me that was a mistake it's seems more like EA it’s trying to see if players are willing to pay for tiers skips or not.

These are the main problems with the game, but as I said at the beginning, they are not the only ones and with the delay of season two things are just going to get worse. Overall I can't recommend the game, if you are a BF fan you'll be very disappointed, even if you don't experience the connection issues or don't mind the “microtransactions”. Compared to other Battlefield games it lacks a lot of content, so it's better to stick to with BF 4, BF 1 or even BF V.

[h2]Battlefield™ 6[/h2]

The king is dead, long live the king… oh wait, this one is a corpse too.

After Call of Duty turned into an outright content conveyor belt, it was only a matter of time before the quality inevitably degraded. At a certain point, even the fans themselves grew unhappy with what was happening. And then the legendary Vince Zampella, may he rest in peace, stepped onto the stage, promising to make the Battlefield series great again.

It is worth mentioning that Battlefield had also been stagnating. After the lackluster fifth installment, it released the even more controversial 2042, and it genuinely felt like the series had hit a dead end and perhaps even exhausted itself completely. The last part that, in my opinion, was truly successful and genuinely good, and probably my favorite, was the one set during World War I, Battlefield 1.

In modern times, it is no longer interesting or impressive that you can destroy a building. That amazed people back in 2011 or 2013, but not in 2025. Or so we thought until the release of the sixth installment.

The launch itself was grand. It set a record for concurrent players on Steam, introduced an innovative mechanic that allows you to drag a downed teammate to safety before reviving them instead of reviving them on the spot just so enemies can gun them down again for free points, and delivered solid optimization. Although, in the end, that optimization was likely achieved due to a lack of graphical innovation, which is almost nonsensical for DICE, since they were always known for breathtaking visuals. Still, if you want a mass audience, system requirements need to be reasonable, and this decision turned out to be more successful than not.

The problem is that the game did not die just because of a dark horse like the incredible Arc Raiders, which gradually pulled part of the player base away by offering a more unique setting, a deeper meta, and fresher experiences. The real issue is that Battlefield, as a live service game, simply does not work well by design.

You cannot flood it with skins because it relies heavily on realism. The main source of revenue was never really battle passes, as is common nowadays, but new maps, which are barely being added at all. Overall, post launch support was very slow, and I would even call it lazy.

I would say the story of Battlefield 6 ended just as sadly and bleakly as the story of its creator, Vince Zampella. A brand new Ferrari that had not even officially launched yet flew off the road at enormous speed and lost control. To be honest, I no longer believe in a revival of this installment through new content.

I may not be a "battlefield veteran" but I have put roughly 600 hours into the franchise over the last decade. So my opinion may not be one of absolute experience but it is one of passion and love for the franchise. 

Generative AI 
If I knew that Battlefield Studios was/is using gen AI for in-game cosmetics I wouldn't have bought this game in the first place. Sadly I somehow didn't hear about this until after I already bought the game and the season 1 battle pass.
AI is a blight on the creative industry. It takes away precious work from artists, writers, skilled coders, and basically anyone who would have put love and soul into their work. When AI is used in place of any one of those people it takes away from the soul and human aspect of the product. The decision to push and use AI emphasizes how little EA and the higher ups at Battlefield Studios truly care about the soul of this game. And more importantly it  also shows how little they respect their own employees. As the implementation of AI shows that these execs would rather get something of cheap low quality rather than pay someone that would have produced something of higher quality and have love, care, and passion put into it. The existence of AI in the studio's workflow also creates the side effect of putting the rest of the studio and its passionate teams in the crossfire of peoples debates about its implementation. As more (rightfully) speculative consumers can and [i] will [/i] speculate how much of the final product used AI in the process of its creation. Ultimately diminishing the hard passionate work that real humans put into the game.
[b] The use of generative AI in Bf6 shows that just like in previous installments, EA and the studio execs are willing to sabotage their studios dignity and public perception for a quick buck. [/b]

Where's the sandbox?
Bf6 had a glimmer of hope in the beta for being a return to form for battlefield having a fun and engaging sandbox, but just like bf2042, the "sandbox" we got at launch has been uninspired and bafflingly balanced. To put it short as sandboxes are temporary, and also steam has a 8000 character limit on reviews, Bf6s sandbox feels like it has dumbed down the class aspect massively to appeal towards a wider audience. Gadgets do little to change the flow of gameplay outside of Defibs and Repair tools which only slow down the flow of gameplay. Grenades feel more of an after thought as none of them really feel good to use and some don’t make sense in their classes kit (Mini-Nades, Incendiary, and Motion Sensor). And all of this seemingly is to be in favor of the most bland weapon sandbox I have seen. All automatic guns seemingly fit into one of three damage classes, which all share the very very very similar damage falloff that I thought for a second they all had the same damage fall off. So ultimately the only thing that makes a gun stand out is it’s rate of fire and if you can mod it to be a laser beam. Which like %50 of the guns can be laser beams. So in the end it isn’t a one weapon dominated sandbox, but it sure feels like it is as every gun feels the same to shoot and be shot with. But unlike Bf4 where this was pretty much the case, Bf6 having three damage classes makes it so a good portion of the sandbox just can’t compete because the only state that matters is rate of fire.

What happened to the closed weapon promise?
I remember seeing the response to them announcing we would be having closed weapons and open weapons as playlists in the months building up to the game. The community was super excited. It was a lot of good karma for the devs. Everyone I played the Beta with agreed that closed weapons playlist felt way better, even those not enfranchised with Battlefield. So why have they quietly stepped back from this?
I have played both types of playlists a decent amount in my 40 hours of playing and I feel like there isn't a point of even playing the [b]singular[/b] closed weapon playlist most of the time cause it's one half bot filled lobby after another. On top of that they have it on a rotating set of "attack and defend" and "all-out warfare". What if I just wanted to play conquest with closed weapons? I don't get to if it's "attack and defend" or I have to leave the escalation matches to requeue, god forbid I match into a map I dislike playing. I understand it’s not as simple as adding the option to custom search. But Battlefield studios not only needs to do more with closed weapons, but they need to give it the custom search treatment also to actually keep closed weapons on par with open weapons.

The Maps
Pardon my french but holy cr*p what happened to the maps team, are they okay? It feels like they took all the hard learned lessons from 2042 and drew straws on which maps would remember which lesson. Each map feels like they were designed with only infantry or vehicles in mind, and it feels like an accident if they do work in tandem. Every map feels more like playing a certain aspect of Battlefield as they seemingly were only designed with a wedge of the sandbox in mind. None of these maps feel like they support everything in the sandbox. And the only “lesson” they truly seem to keep across the board was designing all the infantry areas as CQB as possible if it isn’t a sniper lane. Every building feels claustrophobic and choke pointy. Medium range engagements are few and far between, as every lane that opens up seemingly stretches on into sniper distances without much line of sight blockers.

Cross-platform
I want to put forward that I am happy to see Battlefield get such a large influx of players. But jesus christ it feels like they turned up the aim-assist on controllers up to feel familiar to Call of Duty players. Idk if it’s just how weapon sway and aim-assist interact but it feels like a majority of my gunfights against controllers across any distance devolves down to their bullets hitting more consistently. I am not the best aimer in the world, but I know I end up performing above average in other more competitive shooters. Sometimes it feels like I can’t take certain gunfights without having to dip out into cover despite landing the first shots cause I’m fighting a controller player and their laser gun is seemingly lacking bloom compared to my laser gun. I am not saying controllers' aim-assist should see a nerf, but I do think they need to give a pass on how bloom works in this game if they wish to continue with the current sandbox philosophy.

Just like they did with Battlefield V and Battlefield 2042. Both of them failed horrifically at launch due to their additions and twists to the Battlefield formula and failed to keep a user base as they didn’t appeal to the average battlefield fan or a new audience. What makes this even worse is that EA is fully aware of this issue. It has been reported many times by the community, acknowledged, and discussed. Yet, more than four months after the official release, it is still not fixed. That’s honestly a slap in the face to their player base. When people invest their time and money into a game, they expect core problems like this to be treated as a priority.

I’ve done all I could on my side, and it’s clear the problem comes from the game itself, not from my setup. If I had the choice, I would ask for a refund. This feels like a joke on the players, especially considering how long we waited and how much hype there was around this title.

Once again, despite having a clear blueprint for making one of the best FPS franchises in gaming, the developers have delivered a half-baked, uninspired product. The game feels stagnant, underdeveloped, and eerily reminiscent of Battlefield 2042. In trying to appeal to everyone, it ends up appealing to no one.

The identity crisis is obvious. The game attempts to cater to Call of Duty–style players with faster movement and pacing, yet CoD players don’t want Battlefield—they already have CoD, and they quickly go back to it. Meanwhile, long-time Battlefield fans are alienated from the start. The slower, immersive experience of BF3, BF4, and BF1—defined by weighty gunplay, powerful sound design, large-scale immersion, and meaningful destruction—is largely gone.

Instead of doubling down on what made Battlefield unique, the developers once again chose microtransactions and flashy skins that feel completely out of place. These cosmetics add nothing to the experience and only further erode the franchise’s identity. What truly set Battlefield apart from its competitors—Levolution—has been stripped down to the bare minimum. Watching a crane fall is dull compared to entire buildings collapsing in BF4. Minor environmental damage doesn’t come close to the widespread, dynamic destruction seen throughout BF1, or the unforgettable cinematic moments like the zeppelin crashing mid-match.

Map design only amplifies the problem. Air vehicles are placed into maps so small and restrictive that a single dogfight can push you out of bounds nine times out of ten. The scale feels wrong, the flow feels broken, and the chaos that once defined Battlefield is missing.

From the moment the game reused the BF2042 engine, expectations were already low. While it may be an improvement over that disastrous release, it still falls far short of earning the Battlefield name. At best, it’s a slightly more polished version of a failed direction—proof that the franchise still hasn’t learned from its mistakes.

BF6 is easily the best Battlefield experience I've had to date, a close second is BFV. It's not meant to be realistic and it's not meant to be as arcade-y as Call of Duty either, It fills a niche somewhere between arcade gameplay and mil-sim (not that it even gets close to mil-sim territory mind you, and that's by design.) and it does a fantastic job of it. 

What this does is give players the freedom of pulling off batshit insane flanks where you kill 3 squads from behind or otherwise very fun and stupid things (jihad jeep) while still being surrounded by a very authentic large scale war atmosphere.
What it does for the developers is give them the freedom of creating sandboxes that don't have to be tied down by 100% realism and where they can prioritize "balls to the walls" action over running/driving 20km to an objective and getting sniped/RPGd and having to do it al over again.

No, it isn't. And BF6 offers a lot more than just a "Metro-like" experience, despite what Reddit would like you to believe.)

On top of the atmosphere of the game being on par if not better than that of BF3, the game also runs incredibly well. By no means do I have a beefy PC, I run a Ryzen 5 5500 and an RX 6650XT w/ 16gb DDR4 with Digital Foundry's PS5 Performance equivalent settings at 1080p with FSR at Quality (Because FSR at Quality looks better than the native 1080p TAA implementation), and it *never* drops below 60fps (it used to a little bit when the game first launched but that has seemingly been fixed since.)

First off, this game is genuinely insane. For me it’s straight out of a dream. The scale, the chaos, mad stuff.  Was it a “billion-dollar game”? No. A lot of that number is marketing. Was drawn to BF6 by the promise of the franchise returning to its grounded modern shooter roots. 
I played the open beta and aside from some lag, de-sync and hit-reg issues the beta was super fun and really brought me back to how I felt playing BF4 and BF1. 
I was high on hopium and ignored all the people saying not to prepurchace.

While at first BF6 was a breath of fresh air basic gameplay is solid (aside from some rather annoying player movement) I quickly lost interest.

Weapons:

Weapon progression and unlocks were a tedious grindfest, (like the PSR 200 headshots from over 200 meters away challenge) and while the devs did their best to address some of the outrageous challenges weapon progression is still currently an extremely grind ridden affair.
Several weapons (in my opinion) have not had their attachments properly balanced in terms cost and effectiveness. For instance, the M277 carbine completely decked out with expensive attachments will still, without fail have worse control, fire rate, accuracy, ads, mag capacity. and muzzle velocity than an unmodified M4. Now this would be fine if these weapons didn't share the same DPS value despite the M277 firing a much stronger cartridge. 
If the M277 had worse control and mag capacity in exchange for better muzzle velocity and superior DPS it wouldn’t be an issue in my book. Spicier round = worse control/higher damage. However, because the M277 only does the same 25 DPS as the M4 but has so many drawbacks there is no reason to use it. Now that’s a rant about only one gun but, the point is there are several weapons in the sandbox that have similar issues, I simply think the M277 it's one of the worst cases.

Challenges:

Several challenges for XP, Battlepass progression points, and cosmetics don’t consider factors which affect the players ability to complete the challenge. For instance, my weekly challenges were constantly filled with Red Sec tied objectives even though I never installed it and don’t intend to. 

Some challenges related to even base game modes are impossible to attempt because as the mode is either dead or broken. Game lobbies often never fully populate and in some modes (like in all my attempts to play KOTH) they fail to populate with bots so the match simply never starts, making it sometimes impossible to complete:  "play this mode X times" challenges.

A more pressing issue concerning challenges relates to the paid battlepass.
The total number of points needed to complete the battlepasses is unreachable depending on what challenges the game randomly generates for you. Some people despite having completed every challenge possible were unable to unlock the items they bought because of this. (I think DICE gave them the items they missed out on in the mail but an issue like that shouldn’t have existed in the first place.)

Tech issues:

The hit reg and lag has never been fully fixed since the Beta, (and to my experience persists even now) I still often run into desync, hit reg, lag, and other networking/ server issues. 
As mentioned above certain game modes seem literally unplayable because of several issues concerning the match making. 
the game has often disconected me for 'inactivity' while im in the middle of an active firefight in breakthrough or conquest.

cosmetics/store/maps:

Maps:
There aren’t enough.
Many of the maps in BF6 simply pale in comparison to their counterparts in BF4 and BF1. while they're not horrible (for the most part) they're nothing outstanding either. levelution and destruction is super cool and looks absolutely awesome, it certainly outshines BF1 and BFV but, so far I’ve seen nothing close to the extreme destruction possible in BF3 and BF4.

Cosmetics & store:

One of my largest annoyances with BF6 is the cosmetics.
The grounded modern aesthetic and setting we were promised by the devs was abandoned the instant the game released. Instead of the grounded modern military feel the beta had, BF6 became airsoft LARP. 
Otherwise fine Skins were ruined with massive amounts of neon and fluro colours which in no way resembled nor belonged on military uniforms and equipment.
In many cases the skins blend the aesthetics of Nato and PAX making it hard to identify your enemies and friendlies. This issue was extremely prominent with the California Resistance skins. The update introduced a new Nato squad and the several individual Pax skins which could be purchased from the store. These skins all shared the dad operator making them indistinguishable from each other.

Some of the skins look fine, most of them don’t. The issue in general It’s not a biggie for some. Some even like the skins we're getting. However, for me it was a major selling point for the game. I got fed up with COD multiplayer because of this same issue (characters and players looking ridiculously out of place) and the devs for BF6 saying that their skins and designs would be grounded and realistic was music to my ears. (I legit kinda feel scammed looking back on it)
The game sells AI generated slop in the form of patches, player emblems, weapon skins, and other cosmetics and it sells this slop for disproportionally large sums of money. In general the store prices are extremely high for the quality of goods it offers thus why I’ve only ever bought a single item.

I put off giving a negative review for a long time, hoping that BF6's networking and server issues would be fixed. 
They haven't.
I hoped they would improve, progression systems, gun balance, and match making.
They haven't.
I hoped they would return to their promise of a grounded modern military shooter with grounded cosmetics.
They haven’t.

[i] Summary for Battlefield 6’s bizarre cosmetics and content choices so far:

NATO soldiers now look like airsoft clowns dunked in day-glo paint. Bright gas masks, silly balaclavas, random face paint — as if they’ve entirely forgotten they’re meant to be in an army. DICE have simply slapped on whatever nonsense took their fancy this season. Yellow paint smeared all over mercs, or blinding white with neon green, topped off with some so-called “camouflage” that achieves precisely the opposite of its intended purpose. It’s the kind of visual assault that makes you wonder whether anyone in the studio has even glanced at a real soldier in the last ten years.

Ally or foe? Who can tell. Everyone’s a glowing muppet. The same clownish colour palette, the same idiotic smiley skulls, gas masks covered in graffiti, or, for a real stroke of genius, literal airsoft masks with holes cut out for the eyes. Visual clarity is completely abandoned, and with it, any sense of tactical gameplay. The result is chaos masquerading as cosmetic variety — bright, incoherent, and entirely unnecessary.

And this is what DICE are calling “grounded” and “back to the roots”? Whose roots, exactly — Battlefield 2042’s? Right. Brilliant. Absolute muppets, clearly. A masterclass in misunderstanding what made the franchise work in the first place.

This is what a visual identity crisis looks like in full swing. No coherent style, no consistent language, no bloody clue what Battlefield is supposed to be anymore. Every season veers off in a different direction; none of it seems considered, and nothing respects the game’s own internal logic. Compare that to Battlefield 1’s first two big updates: content was delivered regularly, the art direction was disciplined, and even cosmetic additions respected the tone, setting, and, crucially, visual readability. Players could immediately understand what belonged and what didn’t. Here? Confusion is the only consistent feature.

And yet, people are expected to pay £60 for this. Sixty pounds for a game that struggles to deliver grounded cosmetics, let alone content, which is drip-fed as slowly as possible.

Disappointing? That’s generous. Pathetic? Closer to the mark. Unmitigated, mindless muppetry from top to bottom. Gimmicks and chaotic design choices are all that keep it moving. And the most galling part? DICE appear entirely unconcerned. This is not bold. It is not modern. It is a farce. Absolute, unmitigated farce.

These are my biggest issues with this game, and I'm leaving stuff out to not sound overly whiney:

1. Hit Registration in a shooter should be priority 1, and the hitreg in this game is terrible. You will have some games where you feel like you are shooting a laser beam and hitting everything, and other games where you will empty a clip in someone, all hits register on your screen, and they kill you and run away.

2. There is almost no bloom penalty for Jumping/Sliding and shooting, so the "meta" is to build a gun to be extremely accurate hip fire, and then jump/slide around the map causing lag and making you bounce around other peoples screens and killing them with pinpoint accuracy. If you aren't doing this, you are putting yourself at a disadvantage.

3. The main grind is weapon attachments, however the problem is the "good" ones...that make the guns actually usable....don't start unlocking until level 20 usually. For instance, a suppressor is pretty much required in this game to not be auto-spotted when you shoot your gun. Most don't unlock until level 20+, so you run around spotting yourself for the enemy team every time you fire your weapon. Most of the accuracy attachments that don't also come with penalties aren't available until later either. Couple this with an extremely slow XP grind for the weapons and it gets old fast.
Side Note: The xp boosters expire in real time. IE if you aren't in the game. If you are sitting in a queue. In a loading screen, etc. The booster timer is ticking down while you aren't even able to use it.

Bottom line, I would buy this at like $30 if I could get my money back. It is fun in some ways, but it is NOT worth $70. Especially if you have a hard time saying "no" to extra paid content because they push Season Passes and then they push shorter Battle Pass events all that you need to pay for to get all the content. And yes, there ARE weapons in these passes such as the Mini-Scout which is considered one of the best sniper rifles in the game right now.

Battlefield 6 is an ambitious entry that unfortunately struggles to justify its place in the franchise. While it attempts to modernize the Battlefield formula, the execution feels uneven and, at times, disconnected from what has historically made the series stand out.

The core gunplay lacks consistency. Weapon feedback and hit registration feel unreliable, which undermines confidence in firefights and makes engagements feel more frustrating than rewarding. Movement is serviceable but lacks the fluidity and weight expected from a modern shooter at this scale.

Map design is one of the game’s weakest elements. Several maps suffer from poor flow, offering either overly open spaces that punish infantry or congested areas that devolve into chaotic, unstructured combat. As a result, matches often feel random rather than tactical, diminishing the importance of positioning and teamwork.

Although environmental destruction is present, it rarely meaningfully impacts gameplay. Destruction appears more cosmetic than strategic, missing the opportunity to dynamically reshape encounters in a way that feels purposeful.

Vehicle balance is inconsistent. Some vehicles feel ineffective, while others dominate matches without sufficient counterplay, contributing to a sense that balance tuning is incomplete.

Ultimately, Battlefield 6 feels more like a transitional project than a confident evolution of the franchise. It delivers moments of spectacle but lacks cohesion, polish, and a clear identity. Longtime fans may find it difficult to recognize the Battlefield experience they expect, while new players may struggle to see what sets it apart from competing shooters.

Pros:

- Most game modes are fun, especially Gauntlet, where 8 teams participate in minigames, and the 2 bottom scoring teams get eliminated. Lots of action and feels very high-stakes, and encourages teamwork. Escalation is also very action-packed, where objectives get removed over time, making the later stages very intense as both teams fight over the same few objectives. Strikepoint, Domination and King of the Hill are also great, small-map based gamemodes.

- Weapons feel mostly balanced. No particular guns feel overpowered, and ou will generally see a large variety of weapons, rather than a few weapons dominating the meta. The animations are also very high quality.

- Classes mostly feel balanced. In every team, there is a good variety of classes. Every class has a clear role. Unlike in previous Battlefields, there are no restrictions on weapons for classes, permitting a wider range of playstyles. For example, the Recon, which by default has a sniper rifle equipped, can also equip an SMG for stealthy close range gameplay. Supports by default equip a machine gun, but you can swap this out for a shotgun and aggressively push, while throwing down smokes to cover your team's advance and reviving people.

- Some maps are very well designed and balanced BUT this heavily depends on the gamemode. 

Cons:

- Breakthrough and Rush are very poorly balanced; attackers win the vast majority of the time, because some objectives are almost impossible to hold as defenders, but this depends on the map. Tanks specifically in these modes are extremely oppressive. You will often get sniped from across the map with them, and they are very difficult to flank / destroy, because of the location of the objectives. Oftentimes, attackers will end up with multiple tanks, making defending extremely painful, and attacking boring, because you will simply steamroll the enemy team. 

- While no weapon feels overpowered, there are some guns which clearly underperform compared to others. Most assault rifles feel underpowered, as they have very high recoil and poor accuracy. SMGs often beat them at long range.

- There are occasionally some game-breaking bugs. Sometimes you are unable to deploy and so cannot play the game at all, forcing you to quit to the menu. My friend will often crash while playing Gauntlet. Sometimes you will experience extremely harsh lighting that completely overpowers your vision, and you cannot see anything; it is like staring directly into a flashlight.

- Some attachments are underpowered compared to others. Suppressors are almost mandatory, because most other muzzle attachments will cause you to show up on the minimap and place a marker over your head, making you a very easy target. Certain attachments cost too many points to equip (e.g. larger magazines). The dot on many scopes are too large, blurry, and dim, making aiming more difficult.

- The Assault class in particular feels too weak. Their primary gadget, the adrenaline injector, is near-useless. It gives you a slight speed boost but only after a long animation, which can often get you killed. The deploy beacon is useful but only allows squadmates to spawn on it, and breaks when the deployer spawns on it. Their grenade launcher feels too overpowered, as it can easily one-shot you and has a large blast radius. 

- While the graphics are very good and realistic, player visibility is very poor. I have to use thermal scopes on all of my weapons simply to be able to see people properly. 

- Sometimes you will spawn and immediately get killed, because an enemy happens to be already looking in your direction. There seems to be no spawn protection. This can be quite frustrating. 

- Weapon levelling takes an extremely long time.

- Lack of maps and weapons, at least for now. Later seasons will hopefully remedy this. 

- Some maps are poorly designed and / or unbalanced, but of course this is subjective. Blackwell Fields in my opinion is a terrible map, as there is very little cover. 

Overall, despite these downsides, I am still having fun playing BF6. Would recommend.

After sinking 132 hours into the game, I find it incredibly difficult to recommend in its current state. While I’ve had a blast at times and experienced some "only in Battlefield" moments, you can truly feel how the game is being held back by deliberate, poor design choices.

The Content Gap - The map selection is frankly terrible. I find myself cycling between the same three maps using custom search because the rest simply miss the mark. There is no reason for the selection to be this limited, especially when there is a vault of the best Battlefield maps in franchise history sitting right there, unused.

Furthermore, Portal feels like a massive wasted opportunity. It has been so poorly implemented that it feels like it’s been pushed to the wayside yet again. As for the Battle Pass, the greed is on full display; they aren't even trying to hide it anymore.

Servers and Bots - The biggest issue for me, however, is the lack of a Server Browser and the over-reliance on bots. I don’t understand the resistance to providing a proper browser. In a region like Australia, a server browser is essential for the longevity of the game.

The current system is a total loss for the player experience. Being kicked from a full game and thrown into an empty lobby populated by bots is a huge turn-off. When I play multiplayer, I want PvP. If DICE provided consistent, flowing servers, I could honestly overlook many of the other flaws, but as it stands, I can’t.

As a long-time fan who has been around since the days of Vietnam and Bad Company 2, I’m mostly just disappointed. I’m glad we have a new Battlefield title to play, but this isn't the experience a veteran community deserves.

Battlefield 6 feels like a real step back in the right direction for the series. The gunplay is tight and satisfying, movement is smooth, and the large-scale battles finally capture that classic Battlefield chaos again. Vehicles feel powerful without completely dominating every match, and when everything clicks, those big cinematic moments happen naturally — the kind Battlefield is known for.

The maps are mostly strong, with good verticality and lots of flanking routes, but a few of them can feel a little too open, which sometimes turns matches into long-range peek-fests. Destruction is better than recent entries, though I still wish more structures were fully destructible instead of just partially reactive.

Performance has been solid for me, and it runs way better than Battlefield 2042 did at launch, which is a huge plus. There are still some bugs and balance issues that need tuning, especially with a few weapons and gadgets, but nothing that completely ruins the experience.

Overall, Battlefield 6 isn’t perfect, but it’s fun, fast, and actually feels like Battlefield again. With a few more updates and balance passes, this could easily climb higher — for now, it’s a strong 8/10 and definitely worth playing if you’ve been waiting for the series to find its footing again. 🎮🔥

How do I describe my feelings about BF6’s singleplayer… There are moments in life you wait for, moments you let build and mature. After drinking a good cup of coffee, you know when it’s ready — that pressing feeling that needs to be dealt with. After gently delivering this number two, you look at it with a sense of completion. You call your partner’s name and ask her to come observe; you feel a gentle tap on your shoulder and receive an acknowledgement of greatness. You give it a name, flush it away, but never forget the journey.

Time and energy wasted. You try to wipe it away, only to realise you’re spreading it further, to the point of no return, forced to live with this smear of disappointment. After sinking 132 hours into the game, I find it incredibly difficult to recommend in its current state. While I’ve had a blast at times and experienced some "only in Battlefield" moments, you can truly feel how the game is being held back by deliberate, poor design choices.

The Content Gap - The map selection is frankly terrible. I find myself cycling between the same three maps using custom search because the rest simply miss the mark. There is no reason for the selection to be this limited, especially when there is a vault of the best Battlefield maps in franchise history sitting right there, unused.

Furthermore, Portal feels like a massive wasted opportunity. It has been so poorly implemented that it feels like it’s been pushed to the wayside yet again. As for the Battle Pass, the greed is on full display; they aren't even trying to hide it anymore.

Servers and Bots - The biggest issue for me, however, is the lack of a Server Browser and the over-reliance on bots. I don’t understand the resistance to providing a proper browser. In a region like Australia, a server browser is essential for the longevity of the game.

The current system is a total loss for the player experience. Being kicked from a full game and thrown into an empty lobby populated by bots is a huge turn-off. When I play multiplayer, I want PvP. If DICE provided consistent, flowing servers, I could honestly overlook many of the other flaws, but as it stands, I can’t.

As a long-time fan who has been around since the days of Vietnam and Bad Company 2, I’m mostly just disappointed. I’m glad we have a new Battlefield title to play, but this isn't the experience a veteran community deserves.

The gunplay is tight and satisfying, movement is smooth, and the large-scale battles finally capture that classic Battlefield chaos again. Vehicles feel powerful without completely dominating every match, and when everything clicks, those big cinematic moments happen naturally — the kind Battlefield is known for.

The maps are mostly strong, with good verticality and lots of flanking routes, but a few of them can feel a little too open, which sometimes turns matches into long-range peek-fests. Destruction is better than recent entries, though I still wish more structures were fully destructible instead of just partially reactive.

Performance has been solid for me, and it runs way better than Battlefield 2042 did at launch, which is a huge plus. There are still some bugs and balance issues that need tuning, especially with a few weapons and gadgets, but nothing that completely ruins the experience.

Overall, Battlefield 6 isn’t perfect, but it’s fun, fast, and actually feels like Battlefield again. With a few more updates and balance passes, this could easily climb higher — for now, it’s a strong 8/10 and definitely worth playing if you’ve been waiting for the series to find its footing again. 🎮🔥

Singleplayer:  
How do I describe my feelings about BF6’s singleplayer… There are moments in life you wait for, moments you let build and mature. After drinking a good cup of coffee, you know when it’s ready — that pressing feeling that needs to be dealt with. After gently delivering this number two, you look at it with a sense of completion. The journey was good and satisfying, and the outcome is something you’re oddly proud of. You call your partner’s name and ask her to come observe; you feel a gentle tap on your shoulder and receive an acknowledgement of greatness. You give it a name, flush it away, but never forget the journey.

BF6’s singleplayer is the complete opposite. The pressing feeling comes out of nowhere. It’s rushed, it’s not smooth, and it backfires after every drop, pulling you far away from any moment of peace or sanity. You look down at what you’ve done and feel only guilt. Time and energy wasted. You try to wipe it away, only to realise you’re spreading it further, to the point of no return, forced to live with this smear of disappointment. Thankfully, this kind of experience is only a once‑in‑a‑decade event nowadays. I cannot recommend the singleplayer.

This game was designed by the MBAs and not by the artists/game devs. There are so many design elements that are clearly there just to artificially boost their "metrics" at the expense of the end user experience. They made the maps tiny so that you were constantly forced to fight and there is no downtime to recover/plan, and no space for big flanks or vehicle play. The end result is a meat-grinder where you run in, maybe get a few kills, and die over and over. 

Most guns have a ridiculously fast time to kill (several are sub 200 ms at close range, meaning it is physically impossible to react if you start getting shot. And the maps are tiny, so 60-80% of the engagements are within 30 meters. See the problem? This plus the really twitchy movement they copied over from 2042 is seriously so exhausting. I find myself burning out and getting frustrated after about 2-4 rounds at most. There weren't that many maps at launch in the first place, and at least half of them are borderline unplayable, so I end up queueing for just the same 4 or 5 maps every game, which contributes to the burnout.

I will keep playing this game (mostly because there is just not a great alternative for this "all about battle" genre that Battlefield used to be) and hope content drops in future seasons will ameliorate some of the problems. But I think there are core design philosophy issues that won't be solved by just throwing more stuff at the problem. Maybe could pull a 2042 where they went back and overhauled every single map and resolved a ton of the pain points. I doubt EA will see that as providing enough short-term gain though, so I'm not optimistic.

Conclusion: I wish I had waited a year on this for them to flesh out content, listen to player feedback, and iron out glaring technical issues (which I didn't even get into here as this is already getting long).

With crossplay disabled it does take a long time to find games sometimes, so for that reason I leave it enabled. I find console players really let you down generally in this game, with behaviour such as not reviving team mates, not playing the objective, not using transport vehicles correctly and abandoning team mates at spawn and so on. Looking forward to seeing how this game evolves over time, hopefully cosmetics stay true to the look and feel of a Battlefield title.

Battlefield 6 is a hollow shell of its former self, trading the franchise’s iconic scale for a frantic, identity-less experience that feels more like a Call of Duty clone than a true tactical shooter. The lack of content at launch is staggering; with a pathetic selection of weapons and gadgets, you'll feel like you’ve seen everything the game has to offer within the first few hours. This emptiness is exacerbated by a transparently greedy leveling system that turns basic progression into a soul-crushing grind, clearly designed to frustrate players into purchasing XP boosters rather than rewarding genuine skill or playtime.

The map design is arguably the biggest disappointment, as DICE has abandoned the "All-Out Warfare" philosophy for cramped, tiny arenas that offer zero room for strategic maneuvering. Half of the maps in the rotation are absolute garbage, lacking any coherent flow and resulting in a constant, mindless meat grinder. By shrinking the play space and cranking up the movement speed to mimic its competitors, Battlefield has sacrificed its soul. It has replaced the deliberate, squad-based tension of previous entries with a twitchy, individualistic gameplay loop that makes vehicles feel irrelevant and tactics feel obsolete.

[h1]Disappointing — especially for solo players[/h1]


[h3]Portal Without Real Freedom[/h3]

Disappointing experience overall. Despite promising Portal trailers Battlefield 6 [b]no longer allows true solo vs. bots or proper small-scale co-op[/b], which was the main reason I bought it. Had this been clear before release, I would not have purchased the game, even at a discount!

[h3]The PvP is more than okay[/h3]

As a player of the series since Battlefield 2, I find the PvP quite solid, even if it is unfortunately less classic than expected and instead adopts a Call of Duty–like pace. This is disappointing and does not fully meet the advertising promise. The sound design and graphics, by contrast, are outstanding.

[h3]For the US of A![/h3]

Turning to the campaign, the story appears engaging at first but becomes increasingly absurd as it unfolds. The PvP gameplay mechanics are nevertheless integrated very effectively. The AI companions, however, seem to have skipped basic training: they constantly rush ahead, engage enemies with long-range rifles from 20 cm distance, then retreat toward the player—often stepping directly into the line of sight and blocking the view of enemies firing at their backs from behind. The result is a complete lack of immersion and considerable frustration. Even the supposedly “cool” voice lines fail to compensate.

[h3]Search and destroy — but mainly search, search, search[/h3]

The game menu, incidentally, appears to have been designed and implemented by a UX/UI intern who, at least in my estimation, suffers from any serious orientation disorder. The menu is a maze with a steep learning curve. The sole redeeming feature is the menu soundtrack, which was likely not that intern’s responsibility. ;-)

I have spent over 100 hours with Battlefield 6 across three separate uninstall and reinstall cycles, including getting a refund at launch, which means one of two things. Either I love it, or I am trapped in a complicated situationship with it and refuse to admit it is unhealthy.

On paper, Battlefield 6 is everything I asked for. Big maps, shiny explosions, helicopters doing things helicopters probably should not be doing, and that classic Battlefield promise that teamwork matters. In practice, teamwork is more of a light suggestion, like the speed limit or a warning label.

The gunplay feels fantastic when the servers agree with you. When they do not, it feels like your bullets are being politely negotiated away by the netcode. Hit registration can be rock solid one match and purely conceptual the next. Time to kill swings wildly between “tactical shooter” and “blink and you are dead”, often within the same firefight. It keeps you alert, mostly because you never know which version you are getting.

The maps are huge, beautiful, and occasionally so empty that you start questioning your life choices while jogging towards the objective. When the action clicks, it is glorious chaos. When it does not, you are being farmed by a jet you never saw while your squad mate is 600 metres away trying to snipe someone who moved on emotionally five minutes ago.

Balance changes arrive regularly and with great confidence. Sometimes they fix things. Sometimes they introduce exciting new problems. Specialists remain a bold design choice that not everyone asked for but everyone now has very strong opinions about. Vehicle balance still feels like it was discussed briefly and then committed to out of spite.

Performance and bugs have improved since launch, to be fair. The game now mostly works as intended, which is a low bar but one Battlefield has historically enjoyed limbo dancing under. Cheaters exist, patches break things, and every update is an adventure you did not consent to but are somehow still excited for.

For context, my longest recon kill is 851 metres (check profile if you don't believe ;). This is not a humblebrag, it is a cry for help. Because despite this, my squad mates still cannot seem to spot enemies, revive teammates, or understand that the objective is not optional side content.

Do I recommend it? Yes. In the same way you recommend a rollercoaster that occasionally throws you into a wall. It is loud, messy, ridiculous, frustrating, and when it is good, it is very, very good. Battlefield 6 does not always respect your time, but it will absolutely take your heart, stomp on it, and then distract you with a really nice explosion.

You will complain about it. You will swear you are done. Then you will queue for one more match.

I have mixed feelings. 

First of all, this game is definitely better than Battlefield 2042. For me personally, it’s also better than Battlefield 1 and Battlefield 5, mainly because I don’t really enjoy games set in World War I or World War II. I’m just not a fan of that period of history, so modern settings work much better for me.

The game still has a lot of serious problems.

The first and biggest issue is weapon progression. Upgrading weapons takes way too much effort. To fully level up a single gun in regular game modes, you need around 40 hours, which is just insane. The developers try to “help” by selling XP boosters, but honestly — do we really want to buy them? This system feels frustrating and unnecessary.

The second problem is the maps. About 50% of them are simply bad. Many maps feel unbalanced and are clearly designed either only for infantry or only for vehicles (or even worse for f* SNIPERS). Because of that, a lot of matches are not enjoyable at all.

The third issue is performance. Personally, I haven’t experienced major problems, but a lot of players complain that performance gets worse with every update. I also have a friend who has serious performance issues, so this problem clearly exists.

Another big disappointment is the Battle Royale mode. It’s bad, and I don’t even want to talk much about it. The real problem is that some Battle Pass challenges force you to play Battle Royale or other unwanted modes. That’s ridiculous. I don’t want to play those modes — so why am I forced to do it just to progress my Battle Pass?

I’ve spent around $100 and 200h on this game, and despite all these issues, I still have to say that the game is fun. I genuinely enjoy playing it, having Battlefield moments XD and I recommend it to my friends who already own it. I want to keep playing it.

I’d also really like to see a commander mode added to some game modes. Right now, a lot of players simply don’t know what they’re supposed to do. They just run around trying to survive — or worse, they don’t even understand their role. For example, players pick support classes and try to push the frontline alone, which usually doesn’t work.

Recently, I played Breakthrough, and our team was attacking from multiple directions. One side of the frontline was completely empty, so we could have easily pushed there and won. Instead, everyone was scattered all over the map, doing their own thing, and no one coordinated the attack. I even tried pushing one side on my own, but that obviously wasn’t enough.

If I’m not mistaken, Battlefield 4 had a commander mode. I don’t remember exactly how it worked, but I’d really like to see something like that again. I’m not even talking about being the commander myself — just having someone who actually knows how to play and can give directions to the team would already make a huge difference.

However, the community is slowly leaving the game — either because of these problems or others. The player count has dropped massively since release. Right now, it feels like less than 10% of the original player base is still active.

Hopefully, the developers will make the right changes so this game can survive and actually become something truly great. I really want to keep playing and enjoying it.

I came into Battlefield 6 cautiously optimistic.

I dipped my toes into Battlefield 1 and Battlefield V, but I didn't enjoy either of them for different reasons. Battlefield 1’s theme of World War 1 wasn’t my cup of tea and Battlefield V arrived deep into what I consider the “streamer era” of multiplayer shooters — faster, flashier, and less deliberate. The last Battlefield I truly invested time in was Battlefield 4 back in 2014.

Like many players from my generation, Battlefield 6 felt like it might be the long-awaited return to form and so I boarded the hype train.

Yet, after nearly 170 hours played — most of that within the first month — my feelings are overwhelmingly negative.

I know many modern gamers won’t agree with me but I come from a different era of shooters, and these are the reasons Battlefield 6 simply doesn’t make the cut.

[h1]Pacing Problems[/h1]
[h2]Maps: Smaller, Busier, and Less Battlefield[/h2]
Battlefield 6 launched with nine maps. Operation Firestorm is one such map but also a returning Battlefield 3 classic. Of the remaining maps, four feel extremely similar and notably small in scale.

This stands in stark contrast to earlier entries:

[b]* Battlefield 4 launched with 10 maps (23 total after DLC)[/b]

[b]* Battlefield 3 launched with 9 maps (29 total after DLC)[/b]

Each of those maps felt distinct. They catered to different playstyles, embraced scale and each had a character that fit the overall atmosphere of the game — a defining trait of Battlefield.

In Battlefield 6, most maps feel too small for Conquest, with Firestorm being the lone exception — and that’s only because it was designed during a different era. The developers appear to have prioritized minute visual detail over overall scale, flooding smaller arenas with assets, debris, foliage, and environmental clutter.

Since Battlefield 3, these games have looked good enough. The obsessive push toward hyper-detailed terrain like craters, grass, rubble, basically adding anything to a point of interests micro-detail really doesn’t improve gameplay. In fact, it actively harms it:

[b]* Vehicle play suffers by oversaturating barricades and other hurdles[/b]

[b]* Maps feel cramped not because there's actually focus on intriguing design but because each point of interest is so over-developed.[/b]

The time budgets in making maps are wasted on unnecessary visual noise.

Battlefield 3, 4, and even Battlefield 1 looked great not because they overstuffed maps, but because they stuck to strong themes and coherent atmospheres — [b]something Battlefield 6 sorely lacks[/b]. Seriously, what happened to Marine Corps. versus the People's Liberation Army or Russia's Armed Forces? Why must everything be focused on PMC's and other generic, rushed factions?

Modern texture quality, RAM usage, vRAM budgets, and compute resources don’t need to be blown on flashy, generic visuals. Ironically, that excess is exactly what makes modern shooters feel so bland.

[h2]Gunplay: Fast, Confusing, and Fundamentally Broken[/h2]
Battlefield 6’s gunplay is awkward at best and outright broken at worst.

SMGs dominate the meta and it's not just because of map size. The new attachment point system encourages hyper-specialization. In theory, that sounds interesting. In practice, it’s a disaster.

With the right setup SMGs and high fire-rate ARs become recoilless laser beams. Controller aim assist further exaggerates the problem.

It’s baffling this system wasn’t scrapped in favor of something closer to Battlefield 3 or 4’s simpler, clearer attachment design.

Adding to the frustration is the overwhelming number of settings. While customization can be good, there’s a point where moderation matters. The game throws so many sliders and toggles at you that it becomes unclear what actually needs adjusting.

Aiming itself feels wrong. I've had this strange blend of latency and stiffness with it. I play on mouse and keyboard, on a current-generation system (Core Ultra 7 265K, RTX 5070 Ti, 32 GB DDR5-6400, 4K60 display), and even after attempting extensive tweaking, aiming never feels as fluid or responsive as Battlefield 4.

Battlefield 6 is built around fast-paced gunplay, and while that initially sounded appealing, I quickly realized my reflexes aren’t what they were (skill issue) but what I deeply miss is the slower, more deliberate pacing of older Battlefield titles.

Weapon variety doesn’t help either. Guns feel copy-paste, differentiated mostly by fire rate. There’s little excitement in unlocking or experimenting with new weapons because none of them feel truly distinct.

[h1]Netcode Issues[/h1]
Battlefield 6 also suffers from poor netcode.

Hit registration and hit detection are inconsistent and unreliable. Portal was one of the game’s biggest selling points yet was borderline unusable for the first month and a half after launch. Connecting to matches was frustrating to the point of feeling broken.

For a feature that was heavily marketed, Portal launched in an unacceptable state.

[h1]Seasons, Battle Passes, and the Loss of Identity[/h1]
DICE today is not the same DICE from 15+ years ago. Most of the original developers are gone, replaced by new talent with fundamentally different priorities and the gaming industry itself has changed.

Gone are the days of buying a complete game that’s later expanded through substantial paid DLC.

For comparison: Battlefield 3 had five DLC packs, each adding four new maps. Battlefield 6 has re-released one map with a winter skin and added two new maps so far — one of which the community largely dislikes

More maps are “planned” via Seasons, but this drip-feed model feels like an excuse to deliver less content over a longer period of time.

Battle passes are another sore point. Locking weapons behind them is frustrating in a Battlefield game. Where are the weapon assignments? Where are the medals and ribbons? These systems were not just a method of progression, it was atmosphere and identity in a game that took itself seriously as a military FPS shooter. Their absence contributes heavily to my feeling that Battlefield 6 feels soulless.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
I gave Battlefield 6 a fair shot because many players from my generation were hopeful. But just months after release, the player base has dropped by nearly 90% and I am among those.

The initial excitement has faded into disappointment.

After 15 years of hoping to recapture the feeling of games like World at War, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Battlefield 3, and Battlefield 4, I’ve accepted the truth that that era is long gone.

The players have changed. The developers have changed. The industry has changed. All of what it was before came together to create a golden era that simply cannot be recreated.

Battlefield 6 is not the Hail Mary we hoped for.

Forget the identity crisis of the prior Battlefield games. Battlefield 6 is a full-blown "Back to Basics" apology tour that manages to be both a tactical masterpiece and a glorious physics-defying circus. It’s the game where you can finally stop pretending you enjoyed playing as a "Specialist" with a grappling hook and go back to being a nameless Engineer who lives and dies for a single repair tool.

Here’s the current state of the frontlines as we head into 2026:
The "I’m Not a Hero" Class System: Classes like Assault, Engineer, Support, and Recon are back, meaning your teammates now have actual jobs they will probably still ignore in favor of trying to jet ram that enemy helicopter laying down suppressive fire.

The 64-Player Sweat-Fest: DICE ditched the 128-player "Where is everyone?" maps for focused 64-player carnage. Now, you don't have to run for 5 miles to find a fight; the fight will find you, usually in the form of a tank shell coming through a window you didn't know was destructible.

REDSEC Chaos: The new REDSEC mode is a high-stakes battle on the homefront that makes every match feel like a cinematic trailer, right up until a teammate spawns on you and immediately starts laying down light-machine gun fire behind enemy lines.

The "Frostfire" Grind: We are currently in the Season 1 extension, featuring the Frostfire Bonus Path. It’s a great way to earn cosmetics while questioning why you just spent four hours trying to get 150m headshots with a weapon that has the recoil of a startled mule.

Battlefield Labs: This is where DICE lets you play with "Experimental" ideas, like rebuilding the legendary Golmud Railway. It’s essentially a "Gray Box" experience where you help test the game so it (hopefully) doesn't explode when Season 2 launches on February 17, 2026.

Verdict: It’s the most expensive $400-million-dollar apology in history, and honestly? It’s working. You’ll come for the destruction and stay for the sheer absurdity of watching a building collapse onto a guy who was just trying to change his weapon class.

      It's like the game has degraded, and is still in the process of getting worse since launch. It's not even the horrific slow leveling of weapons. Or the small crappy maps. Or the bad net code where you get shot around corners constantly. Or the most awful positional foot step audio in FPS history (it's actually laughable DICE won "Best Audio" award for this game). 
      Or the terrible Season 1 content. Or the ridiculous weapon balancing (SMGs with damn near perfect accuracy from across any map?). Or the insufferable player base. Nope...what absolutely 100% kills this game for me, to the point of uninstalling and not playing anymore? The scummy match making. 
      DICE took every note they possibly could with Call of Duty's manipulative, dirty SBMM and team balancing, and said "You know what?....we're going to implement an even more deceptive and underhanded version for Battlefield 6!" 

       l've played Battlefield 3, BF4, BF1, etc. I have also played 1000's of hours of Call of Duty over the years and experienced every version of SBMM in all these modern titles from Activision....and Battlefield 6 takes the crown for worst, most disgusting implementation I've ever seen. It's more prevalent in the smaller 8v8 game modes. If you have anything close to a 400spm, and 3.0-4.0KD....this game will absolutely make sure you're never winning a match again. They'll throw you a bone every once in awhile, but you'll be breaking out the largest backpack in gaming history to even barely squeak out your next win. 
      Just to give you an idea of how bad it is, I played a TDM match over the weekend on Mirak Valley and dropped 46 kills (out of a team of 8 people) 46 KILLS....and still lost 98-100. How does this even make any sense at all?  I regularly have to drop 30-40 kills in TDM matches to even get close to winning. Domination? I've had matches where I had 10 flag caps and 40+ kills and still lost. 
       Now onto the large game modes: Its even worse with the team balancing. EVERY SINGLE Conquest match ends in 12-15min, and is an absolute blow out. EVERY. SINGLE. MATCH ends with a score of 0-950 or it'll be 950-0 (or close to it). 
     Gone are the days of 45min to 1 hour Conquest matches where it comes down to each team fighting for their lives with only a few tickets left between each other. You're not getting that here. What you're getting here is a watered down version of "Conquest", that gives the illusion you're playing a "Battlefield" game. What DICE has done here is implement a "Come Back" mechanic, where it punishes a winning team by making them bleed tickets faster in an attempt to let the enemy team make a come back. Again....more deceptive and scummy team balancing. Whatever they implemented here, it's terrible and needs complete revamp. 
   This isn't the same DICE we all loved over the years that released legendary maps and game play to match. Nope, this is a whole different developer that took clues and hints from Call of Duty (a game which has basically cannibalized it's player base) and implemented them even worse here. Maybe visit this game in a year when it's been patched further and is heavily on sale.

This game was designed by the MBAs and not by the artists/game devs. There are so many design elements that are clearly there just to artificially boost their "metrics" at the expense of the end user experience. They made the maps tiny so that you were constantly forced to fight and there is no downtime to recover/plan, and no space for big flanks or vehicle play. The end result is a meat-grinder where you run in, maybe get a few kills, and die over and over. 

Most guns have a ridiculously fast time to kill (several are sub 200 ms at close range, meaning it is physically impossible to react if you start getting shot. And the maps are tiny, so 60-80% of the engagements are within 30 meters. See the problem? This plus the really twitchy movement they copied over from 2042 is seriously so exhausting. I find myself burning out and getting frustrated after about 2-4 rounds at most. There weren't that many maps at launch in the first place, and at least half of them are borderline unplayable, so I end up queueing for just the same 4 or 5 maps every game, which contributes to the burnout.

I will keep playing this game (mostly because there is just not a great alternative for this "all about battle" genre that Battlefield used to be) and hope content drops in future seasons will ameliorate some of the problems. But I think there are core design philosophy issues that won't be solved by just throwing more stuff at the problem. Maybe could pull a 2042 where they went back and overhauled every single map and resolved a ton of the pain points. I doubt EA will see that as providing enough short-term gain though, so I'm not optimistic.

Conclusion: I wish I had waited a year on this for them to flesh out content, listen to player feedback, and iron out glaring technical issues (which I didn't even get into here as this is already getting long).

I found Season 1 very grindy and just when you think you’ve finished it all they release another tier of the battlepass.

My only other gripe with the game would be that crossplay is enabled by default with no way to turn it off in-game. You have to edit an .ini file to disable crossplay. With crossplay disabled it does take a long time to find games sometimes, so for that reason I leave it enabled. I find console players really let you down generally in this game, with behaviour such as not reviving team mates, not playing the objective, not using transport vehicles correctly and abandoning team mates at spawn and so on. They can really turn the tide of battle and can cause your team to loose more often than win.

With a large number of weapons and gadgets available to suit your play style the devs have done a good job with weapon feel, bullet drop etc. Some complained of hit registration issues, but this is not something I have had a problem with at all in 100+ hours.

Looking forward to seeing how this game evolves over time, hopefully cosmetics stay true to the look and feel of a Battlefield title.

With the number of vehicles and their impact, I find it rarely makes sense to play anything but engineer. SMGs also seem to be the most consistent and provide great short to mid range options. After getting bored of it, I switched to recon. The mini scout is the way to go and is significantly easier to make short to mid ranged hits with. Its easy to control an obj from a short distance with a little positioning and skill. The problem is, with limited maps, you end up doing the same thing each map. You know this is the best route, the best sniping spot, that the enemy will helicopter to F to take it so you need to protect it, etc. With all the chaos and variety, it becomes a game of simple, repeating options unless you voluntarily choose todo something unique, like waste your time on assault class.

Battlefield 6 is a hollow shell of its former self, trading the franchise’s iconic scale for a frantic, identity-less experience that feels more like a Call of Duty clone than a true tactical shooter. This emptiness is exacerbated by a transparently greedy leveling system that turns basic progression into a soul-crushing grind, clearly designed to frustrate players into purchasing XP boosters rather than rewarding genuine skill or playtime.

The map design is arguably the biggest disappointment, as DICE has abandoned the "All-Out Warfare" philosophy for cramped, tiny arenas that offer zero room for strategic maneuvering. Half of the maps in the rotation are absolute garbage, lacking any coherent flow and resulting in a constant, mindless meat grinder. By shrinking the play space and cranking up the movement speed to mimic its competitors, Battlefield has sacrificed its soul. It has replaced the deliberate, squad-based tension of previous entries with a twitchy, individualistic gameplay loop that makes vehicles feel irrelevant and tactics feel obsolete.

[h1]Disappointing — especially for solo players[/h1]


[h3]Portal Without Real Freedom[/h3]

Disappointing experience overall. Despite promising Portal trailers Battlefield 6 [b]no longer allows true solo vs. bots or proper small-scale co-op[/b], which was the main reason I bought it. Had this been clear before release, I would not have purchased the game, even at a discount!

[h3]The PvP is more than okay[/h3]

As a player of the series since Battlefield 2, I find the PvP quite solid, even if it is unfortunately less classic than expected and instead adopts a Call of Duty–like pace. This is disappointing and does not fully meet the advertising promise. The sound design and graphics, by contrast, are outstanding.
