I have spent over 100 hours with Battlefield 6 across three separate uninstall and reinstall cycles, including getting a refund at launch, which means one of two things. Either I love it, or I am trapped in a complicated situationship with it and refuse to admit it is unhealthy.

On paper, Battlefield 6 is everything I asked for. Big maps, shiny explosions, helicopters doing things helicopters probably should not be doing, and that classic Battlefield promise that teamwork matters. In practice, teamwork is more of a light suggestion, like the speed limit or a warning label.

The gunplay feels fantastic when the servers agree with you. When they do not, it feels like your bullets are being politely negotiated away by the netcode. Hit registration can be rock solid one match and purely conceptual the next. Time to kill swings wildly between “tactical shooter” and “blink and you are dead”, often within the same firefight. It keeps you alert, mostly because you never know which version you are getting.

The maps are huge, beautiful, and occasionally so empty that you start questioning your life choices while jogging towards the objective. When the action clicks, it is glorious chaos. When it does not, you are being farmed by a jet you never saw while your squad mate is 600 metres away trying to snipe someone who moved on emotionally five minutes ago.

Balance changes arrive regularly and with great confidence. Sometimes they fix things. Sometimes they introduce exciting new problems. Specialists remain a bold design choice that not everyone asked for but everyone now has very strong opinions about. Vehicle balance still feels like it was discussed briefly and then committed to out of spite.

Performance and bugs have improved since launch, to be fair. The game now mostly works as intended, which is a low bar but one Battlefield has historically enjoyed limbo dancing under. Cheaters exist, patches break things, and every update is an adventure you did not consent to but are somehow still excited for.

For context, my longest recon kill is 851 metres (check profile if you don't believe ;). This is not a humblebrag, it is a cry for help. Because despite this, my squad mates still cannot seem to spot enemies, revive teammates, or understand that the objective is not optional side content.

Do I recommend it? Yes. In the same way you recommend a rollercoaster that occasionally throws you into a wall. It is loud, messy, ridiculous, frustrating, and when it is good, it is very, very good. Battlefield 6 does not always respect your time, but it will absolutely take your heart, stomp on it, and then distract you with a really nice explosion.

You will complain about it. You will swear you are done. Then you will queue for one more match.

I have mixed feelings. 

First of all, this game is definitely better than Battlefield 2042. For me personally, it’s also better than Battlefield 1 and Battlefield 5, mainly because I don’t really enjoy games set in World War I or World War II. I’m just not a fan of that period of history, so modern settings work much better for me.

The game still has a lot of serious problems.

The first and biggest issue is weapon progression. Upgrading weapons takes way too much effort. To fully level up a single gun in regular game modes, you need around 40 hours, which is just insane. The developers try to “help” by selling XP boosters, but honestly — do we really want to buy them? This system feels frustrating and unnecessary.

The second problem is the maps. About 50% of them are simply bad. Many maps feel unbalanced and are clearly designed either only for infantry or only for vehicles (or even worse for f* SNIPERS). Because of that, a lot of matches are not enjoyable at all.

The third issue is performance. Personally, I haven’t experienced major problems, but a lot of players complain that performance gets worse with every update. I also have a friend who has serious performance issues, so this problem clearly exists.

Another big disappointment is the Battle Royale mode. It’s bad, and I don’t even want to talk much about it. The real problem is that some Battle Pass challenges force you to play Battle Royale or other unwanted modes. That’s ridiculous. I don’t want to play those modes — so why am I forced to do it just to progress my Battle Pass?

I’ve spent around $100 and 200h on this game, and despite all these issues, I still have to say that the game is fun. I genuinely enjoy playing it, having Battlefield moments XD and I recommend it to my friends who already own it. I want to keep playing it.

I’d also really like to see a commander mode added to some game modes. Right now, a lot of players simply don’t know what they’re supposed to do. They just run around trying to survive — or worse, they don’t even understand their role. For example, players pick support classes and try to push the frontline alone, which usually doesn’t work.

Recently, I played Breakthrough, and our team was attacking from multiple directions. One side of the frontline was completely empty, so we could have easily pushed there and won. Instead, everyone was scattered all over the map, doing their own thing, and no one coordinated the attack. I even tried pushing one side on my own, but that obviously wasn’t enough.

If I’m not mistaken, Battlefield 4 had a commander mode. I don’t remember exactly how it worked, but I’d really like to see something like that again. I’m not even talking about being the commander myself — just having someone who actually knows how to play and can give directions to the team would already make a huge difference.

However, the community is slowly leaving the game — either because of these problems or others. The player count has dropped massively since release. Right now, it feels like less than 10% of the original player base is still active.

Hopefully, the developers will make the right changes so this game can survive and actually become something truly great. I really want to keep playing and enjoying it.

I came into Battlefield 6 cautiously optimistic.

I dipped my toes into Battlefield 1 and Battlefield V, but I didn't enjoy either of them for different reasons. Battlefield 1’s theme of World War 1 wasn’t my cup of tea and Battlefield V arrived deep into what I consider the “streamer era” of multiplayer shooters — faster, flashier, and less deliberate. The last Battlefield I truly invested time in was Battlefield 4 back in 2014.

Like many players from my generation, Battlefield 6 felt like it might be the long-awaited return to form and so I boarded the hype train.

Yet, after nearly 170 hours played — most of that within the first month — my feelings are overwhelmingly negative.

I know many modern gamers won’t agree with me but I come from a different era of shooters, and these are the reasons Battlefield 6 simply doesn’t make the cut.

[h1]Pacing Problems[/h1]
[h2]Maps: Smaller, Busier, and Less Battlefield[/h2]
Battlefield 6 launched with nine maps. Operation Firestorm is one such map but also a returning Battlefield 3 classic. Of the remaining maps, four feel extremely similar and notably small in scale.

This stands in stark contrast to earlier entries:

[b]* Battlefield 4 launched with 10 maps (23 total after DLC)[/b]

[b]* Battlefield 3 launched with 9 maps (29 total after DLC)[/b]

Each of those maps felt distinct. They catered to different playstyles, embraced scale and each had a character that fit the overall atmosphere of the game — a defining trait of Battlefield.

In Battlefield 6, most maps feel too small for Conquest, with Firestorm being the lone exception — and that’s only because it was designed during a different era. The developers appear to have prioritized minute visual detail over overall scale, flooding smaller arenas with assets, debris, foliage, and environmental clutter.

Since Battlefield 3, these games have looked good enough. The obsessive push toward hyper-detailed terrain like craters, grass, rubble, basically adding anything to a point of interests micro-detail really doesn’t improve gameplay. In fact, it actively harms it:

[b]* Vehicle play suffers by oversaturating barricades and other hurdles[/b]

[b]* Maps feel cramped not because there's actually focus on intriguing design but because each point of interest is so over-developed.[/b]

The time budgets in making maps are wasted on unnecessary visual noise.

Battlefield 3, 4, and even Battlefield 1 looked great not because they overstuffed maps, but because they stuck to strong themes and coherent atmospheres — [b]something Battlefield 6 sorely lacks[/b]. Seriously, what happened to Marine Corps. versus the People's Liberation Army or Russia's Armed Forces? Why must everything be focused on PMC's and other generic, rushed factions?

Modern texture quality, RAM usage, vRAM budgets, and compute resources don’t need to be blown on flashy, generic visuals. Ironically, that excess is exactly what makes modern shooters feel so bland.

[h2]Gunplay: Fast, Confusing, and Fundamentally Broken[/h2]
Battlefield 6’s gunplay is awkward at best and outright broken at worst.

SMGs dominate the meta and it's not just because of map size. The new attachment point system encourages hyper-specialization. In theory, that sounds interesting. In practice, it’s a disaster.

With the right setup SMGs and high fire-rate ARs become recoilless laser beams. Controller aim assist further exaggerates the problem.

It’s baffling this system wasn’t scrapped in favor of something closer to Battlefield 3 or 4’s simpler, clearer attachment design.

Adding to the frustration is the overwhelming number of settings. While customization can be good, there’s a point where moderation matters. The game throws so many sliders and toggles at you that it becomes unclear what actually needs adjusting.

Aiming itself feels wrong. I've had this strange blend of latency and stiffness with it. I play on mouse and keyboard, on a current-generation system (Core Ultra 7 265K, RTX 5070 Ti, 32 GB DDR5-6400, 4K60 display), and even after attempting extensive tweaking, aiming never feels as fluid or responsive as Battlefield 4.

Battlefield 6 is built around fast-paced gunplay, and while that initially sounded appealing, I quickly realized my reflexes aren’t what they were (skill issue) but what I deeply miss is the slower, more deliberate pacing of older Battlefield titles.

Weapon variety doesn’t help either. Guns feel copy-paste, differentiated mostly by fire rate. There’s little excitement in unlocking or experimenting with new weapons because none of them feel truly distinct.

[h1]Netcode Issues[/h1]
Battlefield 6 also suffers from poor netcode.

Hit registration and hit detection are inconsistent and unreliable. Portal was one of the game’s biggest selling points yet was borderline unusable for the first month and a half after launch. Connecting to matches was frustrating to the point of feeling broken.

For a feature that was heavily marketed, Portal launched in an unacceptable state.

[h1]Seasons, Battle Passes, and the Loss of Identity[/h1]
DICE today is not the same DICE from 15+ years ago. Most of the original developers are gone, replaced by new talent with fundamentally different priorities and the gaming industry itself has changed.

Gone are the days of buying a complete game that’s later expanded through substantial paid DLC.

For comparison: Battlefield 3 had five DLC packs, each adding four new maps. Battlefield 6 has re-released one map with a winter skin and added two new maps so far — one of which the community largely dislikes

More maps are “planned” via Seasons, but this drip-feed model feels like an excuse to deliver less content over a longer period of time.

Battle passes are another sore point. Locking weapons behind them is frustrating in a Battlefield game. Where are the weapon assignments? Where are the medals and ribbons? These systems were not just a method of progression, it was atmosphere and identity in a game that took itself seriously as a military FPS shooter. Their absence contributes heavily to my feeling that Battlefield 6 feels soulless.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
I gave Battlefield 6 a fair shot because many players from my generation were hopeful. But just months after release, the player base has dropped by nearly 90% and I am among those.

The initial excitement has faded into disappointment.

After 15 years of hoping to recapture the feeling of games like World at War, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Battlefield 3, and Battlefield 4, I’ve accepted the truth that that era is long gone.

The players have changed. The developers have changed. The industry has changed. All of what it was before came together to create a golden era that simply cannot be recreated.

Battlefield 6 is not the Hail Mary we hoped for.

Forget the identity crisis of the prior Battlefield games. Battlefield 6 is a full-blown "Back to Basics" apology tour that manages to be both a tactical masterpiece and a glorious physics-defying circus. It’s the game where you can finally stop pretending you enjoyed playing as a "Specialist" with a grappling hook and go back to being a nameless Engineer who lives and dies for a single repair tool.

Here’s the current state of the frontlines as we head into 2026:
The "I’m Not a Hero" Class System: Classes like Assault, Engineer, Support, and Recon are back, meaning your teammates now have actual jobs they will probably still ignore in favor of trying to jet ram that enemy helicopter laying down suppressive fire.

The 64-Player Sweat-Fest: DICE ditched the 128-player "Where is everyone?" maps for focused 64-player carnage. Now, you don't have to run for 5 miles to find a fight; the fight will find you, usually in the form of a tank shell coming through a window you didn't know was destructible.

REDSEC Chaos: The new REDSEC mode is a high-stakes battle on the homefront that makes every match feel like a cinematic trailer, right up until a teammate spawns on you and immediately starts laying down light-machine gun fire behind enemy lines.

The "Frostfire" Grind: We are currently in the Season 1 extension, featuring the Frostfire Bonus Path. It’s a great way to earn cosmetics while questioning why you just spent four hours trying to get 150m headshots with a weapon that has the recoil of a startled mule.

Battlefield Labs: This is where DICE lets you play with "Experimental" ideas, like rebuilding the legendary Golmud Railway. It’s essentially a "Gray Box" experience where you help test the game so it (hopefully) doesn't explode when Season 2 launches on February 17, 2026.

Verdict: It’s the most expensive $400-million-dollar apology in history, and honestly? It’s working. You’ll come for the destruction and stay for the sheer absurdity of watching a building collapse onto a guy who was just trying to change his weapon class.

I cannot and will not recommend this game to anyone. I legit gave this game a chance and really wanted to love this one. Sunk almost 400 hours into this, and I'm done.  It's just frustrating and exhausting to play. I played every single multiplayer game mode, the whole campaign, leveled a ton of weapons, etc. 
      It's like the game has degraded, and is still in the process of getting worse since launch. It's not even the horrific slow leveling of weapons. Or the small crappy maps. Or the bad net code where you get shot around corners constantly. Or the most awful positional foot step audio in FPS history (it's actually laughable DICE won "Best Audio" award for this game). 
      Or the terrible Season 1 content. Or the ridiculous weapon balancing (SMGs with damn near perfect accuracy from across any map?). Or the insufferable player base. Nope...what absolutely 100% kills this game for me, to the point of uninstalling and not playing anymore? The scummy match making. 
      DICE took every note they possibly could with Call of Duty's manipulative, dirty SBMM and team balancing, and said "You know what?....we're going to implement an even more deceptive and underhanded version for Battlefield 6!" 

       l've played Battlefield 3, BF4, BF1, etc. I have also played 1000's of hours of Call of Duty over the years and experienced every version of SBMM in all these modern titles from Activision....and Battlefield 6 takes the crown for worst, most disgusting implementation I've ever seen. It's more prevalent in the smaller 8v8 game modes. If you have anything close to a 400spm, and 3.0-4.0KD....this game will absolutely make sure you're never winning a match again. They'll throw you a bone every once in awhile, but you'll be breaking out the largest backpack in gaming history to even barely squeak out your next win. 
      Just to give you an idea of how bad it is, I played a TDM match over the weekend on Mirak Valley and dropped 46 kills (out of a team of 8 people) 46 KILLS....and still lost 98-100. How does this even make any sense at all?  I regularly have to drop 30-40 kills in TDM matches to even get close to winning. Domination? I've had matches where I had 10 flag caps and 40+ kills and still lost. 
       Now onto the large game modes: Its even worse with the team balancing. EVERY SINGLE Conquest match ends in 12-15min, and is an absolute blow out. EVERY. SINGLE. MATCH ends with a score of 0-950 or it'll be 950-0 (or close to it). 
     Gone are the days of 45min to 1 hour Conquest matches where it comes down to each team fighting for their lives with only a few tickets left between each other. You're not getting that here. What you're getting here is a watered down version of "Conquest", that gives the illusion you're playing a "Battlefield" game. What DICE has done here is implement a "Come Back" mechanic, where it punishes a winning team by making them bleed tickets faster in an attempt to let the enemy team make a come back. Again....more deceptive and scummy team balancing. Whatever they implemented here, it's terrible and needs complete revamp. 
   This isn't the same DICE we all loved over the years that released legendary maps and game play to match. Nope, this is a whole different developer that took clues and hints from Call of Duty (a game which has basically cannibalized it's player base) and implemented them even worse here. Maybe visit this game in a year when it's been patched further and is heavily on sale.

I have 70hrs+ on PC (EA app), so here's my thoughts.

Positives : 
* Immersion is top-tier. The explosions and atmosphere make you feel like you are in a true battlefield.
* It's very polished. The graphics look amazing, even on lower settings. 
* In-game skins look fairly grounded. No COD Nicki Minaj BS.

Negatives :
* There's constant battlepass pop-ups that are intrusive and annoying.
* The battlepass system is designed with FOMO and manipulation in mind. There's certain events that are way too 
   short to grind them normally, promoting you to spend cash, to speed things up. You played 4 hrs per day, every 
   day for the event but didn't manage to unlock your favorite one-time skin? womp womp, poor you, next time 
   swipe your credit card to 'skip tiers'.
* The weapon grind is horrendous. Reaching mastery soft-cap per weapon requires 1k'ish kills. If you game 
   casually (battledad, non-unemployed, etc), expect MONTHS of grinding, just to master a single weapon.
* Unlocking skins for your favorite gun forces you to grind other guns you may not necessarily like, and as i said, 
   grinding your main gun is a pain in the ass, let alone grinding 2+.
* There's clear Netcode and Hit Registration issues with the game, where you'll die while hiding behind objects.
* Maps are poorly designed. They 're either too small (for BF standards), or the big ones are designed in such a 
   manner that heavily promotes camping with sniper rifles. In other words, lots of times you'll die from someone 
   hiding in the bushes 300m away, and there's not much you can do about it. 
* Last, and worst : the TTK. The freaking TTK! It's frustratingly low. In smaller maps, it feels like COD. If they see 
   you first, they'll hipfire you and bang! You 're dead. Which makes the game more of reflex-based, instead of 
   strategy-based.

Overall : 4.5/10. I would NOT recommend BF6, unless it's on discount AND you play for the immersion.

Seems this is gonna be a controversial take but RedSec can co-exist with the vanilla experience, there are enough studios under the EA and Battlefield Studios umbrella to support both experiences. We can have the classic BF and RedSec experiences as long as it is a stable and fully supported experience for each audience that it is intended for. The issue some seem to be mistaking for resource issues is proper leadership and management as this gets harder given there's practically a team in every timezone working on this game, I can only imagine the difficulty for managing that. 

I believe that the technical debt networking/game engineers have need to be addressed first and foremost as it is a basis across all experiences for the game. Server infrastructure needs to have audits and fixes applied to correct some of the issues that are prevalent. The sysadmin team needs more hands or bigger budget. The game clearly has gameplay bugs that signal underlying game engine issues that need more TLC to make a stable foundation for the systems that rely on it for the other teams to make passes without needing bandaids or spot fixes to unjank the gameplay until the next pass that rejanks the game.

I, quite frankly, don't want bigger for the sake of bigger maps but maps that truly serve the core focus each experience and variety. The community seems to just say bigger maps or better maps but the truth is that maps are not allowed to have identity if they have to fall into specific algorithmic requirements that fatigue the playerbase or then give way to more quickly fall into a gameplay loop that has no way to be broken out of that breaks player engagement over time. I want to be clear, bigger maps will not fix the issue as barren wastelands are just a repeat of past mistakes. Maps need to have a clear overall purpose and ways for each class and their playstyle to work while allowing there to be a clear Rock, Paper, Scissors flow for vehicle/infantry interactions with intermission areas for players to breathe. Does that make maps larger, in some cases it will but there can be a way for maps to have better variety if one map has a greater focus on ground combat and another a bit of combined arms or all-out-warfare. Clarity of who's the invading force and the defending force and the asymmetry that provides gives greater gameplay roles to each team. This would break up the impression of whether you are PAX or NATO, you remove the spawn menu reminder no one would be able to tell who they were.

I will agree with the rest of the community that the promises made for portal haven't been kept and a large reason of which is that I honestly don't care if bot farming exists. I don't get a worse experience if someone wastes hours of their life playing against bots. Let them play the way they want especially if you promised them the ability to do so with full XP and the same experience as if they played versus real players. In a few years time, this may be the only way players returning to the game will be able to experience the game. Streamlining the server browsing experience and discoverability of portal experiences would fix the impression of the overrunning of bot farms and xp servers.

Progression in this game has two main issues. Career progression is long but ultimately pointless and weapon/class progression is long but gatekeeps the full experience. This is why there are so many bot farms because instead of using every gun or gadget in the game to figure out your playstyle or needs your team needs over the course of a game or play session, you are grinding a weapon for hours or navigating challenges that may or may not track progress correctly, are confusing or require a specific playstyle for longer than a player should have to endure to figure out if they want to do it at all. I've thought about the way that challenges could be optional to leveling up a class linearly or branch out to subclasses so players can unlock what they want to use without making it required to use a gun or gadget on the mountain outskirts of Firestorm they don't like to get the one they want. Career rank should either stay pointless or truly give the player rewards for their time investment.

Leveling weapons for attachments should not be a grind but mastering them should. Leveling a gun up should allow the player to play the strategy game of working out what attachments to adapt it to the situation they up against or picking a better gun for the task without the time investment of months to have said options. 

Battle passes work fine but seasonally gatekeeping them has passed. Many players, myself included, do not have the time to invest for weeks to grind a pass that I should be able to earn the content I paid for at my own pace. Item bundles, shop items, LTMs and events are understandable to support a game but as long as they are not broken, mismanaged or grindfests for subpar or AI generated items. I will pay to support games that support real developers and artists that make content that is real or as promised for the genre and art style of the game I was sold on.

Call of Modern Battle Warfield 6 is my favorite shooter. Okay in all seriousness this game is not that bad, but exceptionally mediocre. It's a grilled chicken breast without seasoning, its hearty, filling, classic, and dependable but bland AF. It's like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2019 and Battlefield had a baby that's confused about its identity. I want to love it and there are many times when playing where I see a shred of something deeper and more unique but it is quickly replaced by the reality of the undetailed world the developers have created. I mean this game's whole marketing scheme is that its not Call of Duty while it replicates everything about the best of last generation's Call of Duty (Black Ops 7 has more personality). Can I have Ghost? BF6: We have Ghost at home (Hemlock I'm looking at you). That doesn't mean that there aren't some great things and moments, but in my opinion, its overshadowed by the games of the past. As a long-time Battlefield fan I'm just disappointed because it feels like the series has lost its identity. I mean what even is that progression system? Battlefield 2042 has a better progression system, why reinvent the wheel? The maps are also tremendously small and cramped like COD's arena styled maps (a completely different genre of FPS than Battlefield). Remember when we had genre-defining maps like Golmud Railway, Operation Locker, Iwo Jima, Siege of Shanghei, etc. I truthfully have and do enjoy Battlefield 2042's maps and map design over BF6's. Despite all of this I will continue to play it occasionally because of the awesome graphics and good times with buddies. I really wish this title had a few more years in the oven, because they could have had something really special here but instead settled for mediocre. But in terms of recommendations this is what I recommend within the genre of Modern or semi-Modern Warfare FPS. Best COD multiplayer: Modern Warfare 3 (2023), Best modern Battlefield multiplayer: Battlefield 2042, Best Battlefield multiplayer: Battlefield 4, Best campaign experience: Modern Warfare (2019) (Battlefield 4's campaign is also kickass). I feel as though all of these previous titles offer better experiences depending on what you are looking for. The best case I can make for this game is that if you do not already have these titles or want to get them, Battlefield 6 is a good way to get all of these previous experiences at a much cheaper rate with a live service in 2026. Ultimately, its not that its bad, its just that I want my Battlefield game to be a Battlefield game and my Call of Duty game to be a Call of Duty game. I don't want this confused, convoluted slop.

I have 70hrs+ on PC (EA app), so here's my thoughts.

Positives : 
* Immersion is top-tier. The explosions and atmosphere make you feel like you are in a true battlefield.
* It's very polished. The graphics look amazing, even on lower settings. 
* In-game skins look fairly grounded. No COD Nicki Minaj BS.

Negatives :
* There's constant battlepass pop-ups that are intrusive and annoying.
* The battlepass system is designed with FOMO and manipulation in mind. There's certain events that are way too 
   short to grind them normally, promoting you to spend cash, to speed things up. You played 4 hrs per day, every 
   day for the event but didn't manage to unlock your favorite one-time skin? womp womp, poor you, next time 
   swipe your credit card to 'skip tiers'.
* The weapon grind is horrendous. Reaching mastery soft-cap per weapon requires 1k'ish kills. If you game 
   casually (battledad, non-unemployed, etc), expect MONTHS of grinding, just to master a single weapon.
* Unlocking skins for your favorite gun forces you to grind other guns you may not necessarily like, and as i said, 
   grinding your main gun is a pain in the ass, let alone grinding 2+.
* There's clear Netcode and Hit Registration issues with the game, where you'll die while hiding behind objects.
* Maps are poorly designed. They 're either too small (for BF standards), or the big ones are designed in such a 
   manner that heavily promotes camping with sniper rifles. In other words, lots of times you'll die from someone 
   hiding in the bushes 300m away, and there's not much you can do about it. 
* Last, and worst : the TTK. The freaking TTK! It's frustratingly low. In smaller maps, it feels like COD. If they see 
   you first, they'll hipfire you and bang! You 're dead. Which makes the game more of reflex-based, instead of 
   strategy-based.

Overall : 4.5/10. I would NOT recommend BF6, unless it's on discount AND you play for the immersion.

Seems this is gonna be a controversial take but RedSec can co-exist with the vanilla experience, there are enough studios under the EA and Battlefield Studios umbrella to support both experiences. We can have the classic BF and RedSec experiences as long as it is a stable and fully supported experience for each audience that it is intended for. The issue some seem to be mistaking for resource issues is proper leadership and management as this gets harder given there's practically a team in every timezone working on this game, I can only imagine the difficulty for managing that. 

I believe that the technical debt networking/game engineers have need to be addressed first and foremost as it is a basis across all experiences for the game. Server infrastructure needs to have audits and fixes applied to correct some of the issues that are prevalent. The sysadmin team needs more hands or bigger budget. The game clearly has gameplay bugs that signal underlying game engine issues that need more TLC to make a stable foundation for the systems that rely on it for the other teams to make passes without needing bandaids or spot fixes to unjank the gameplay until the next pass that rejanks the game.

I, quite frankly, don't want bigger for the sake of bigger maps but maps that truly serve the core focus each experience and variety. The community seems to just say bigger maps or better maps but the truth is that maps are not allowed to have identity if they have to fall into specific algorithmic requirements that fatigue the playerbase or then give way to more quickly fall into a gameplay loop that has no way to be broken out of that breaks player engagement over time. I want to be clear, bigger maps will not fix the issue as barren wastelands are just a repeat of past mistakes. Maps need to have a clear overall purpose and ways for each class and their playstyle to work while allowing there to be a clear Rock, Paper, Scissors flow for vehicle/infantry interactions with intermission areas for players to breathe. Does that make maps larger, in some cases it will but there can be a way for maps to have better variety if one map has a greater focus on ground combat and another a bit of combined arms or all-out-warfare. Clarity of who's the invading force and the defending force and the asymmetry that provides gives greater gameplay roles to each team. This would break up the impression of whether you are PAX or NATO, you remove the spawn menu reminder no one would be able to tell who they were.

I will agree with the rest of the community that the promises made for portal haven't been kept and a large reason of which is that I honestly don't care if bot farming exists. I don't get a worse experience if someone wastes hours of their life playing against bots. Let them play the way they want especially if you promised them the ability to do so with full XP and the same experience as if they played versus real players. In a few years time, this may be the only way players returning to the game will be able to experience the game. Streamlining the server browsing experience and discoverability of portal experiences would fix the impression of the overrunning of bot farms and xp servers.

Progression in this game has two main issues. Career progression is long but ultimately pointless and weapon/class progression is long but gatekeeps the full experience. This is why there are so many bot farms because instead of using every gun or gadget in the game to figure out your playstyle or needs your team needs over the course of a game or play session, you are grinding a weapon for hours or navigating challenges that may or may not track progress correctly, are confusing or require a specific playstyle for longer than a player should have to endure to figure out if they want to do it at all. I've thought about the way that challenges could be optional to leveling up a class linearly or branch out to subclasses so players can unlock what they want to use without making it required to use a gun or gadget on the mountain outskirts of Firestorm they don't like to get the one they want. Career rank should either stay pointless or truly give the player rewards for their time investment.

Leveling weapons for attachments should not be a grind but mastering them should. Leveling a gun up should allow the player to play the strategy game of working out what attachments to adapt it to the situation they up against or picking a better gun for the task without the time investment of months to have said options. 

Battle passes work fine but seasonally gatekeeping them has passed. Many players, myself included, do not have the time to invest for weeks to grind a pass that I should be able to earn the content I paid for at my own pace. Item bundles, shop items, LTMs and events are understandable to support a game but as long as they are not broken, mismanaged or grindfests for subpar or AI generated items. I will pay to support games that support real developers and artists that make content that is real or as promised for the genre and art style of the game I was sold on.

Call of Modern Battle Warfield 6 is my favorite shooter. Okay in all seriousness this game is not that bad, but exceptionally mediocre. It's a grilled chicken breast without seasoning, its hearty, filling, classic, and dependable but bland AF. It's like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2019 and Battlefield had a baby that's confused about its identity. I want to love it and there are many times when playing where I see a shred of something deeper and more unique but it is quickly replaced by the reality of the undetailed world the developers have created. I mean this game's whole marketing scheme is that its not Call of Duty while it replicates everything about the best of last generation's Call of Duty (Black Ops 7 has more personality). Can I have Ghost? BF6: We have Ghost at home (Hemlock I'm looking at you). That doesn't mean that there aren't some great things and moments, but in my opinion, its overshadowed by the games of the past. As a long-time Battlefield fan I'm just disappointed because it feels like the series has lost its identity. I mean what even is that progression system? Battlefield 2042 has a better progression system, why reinvent the wheel? The maps are also tremendously small and cramped like COD's arena styled maps (a completely different genre of FPS than Battlefield). Remember when we had genre-defining maps like Golmud Railway, Operation Locker, Iwo Jima, Siege of Shanghei, etc. I truthfully have and do enjoy Battlefield 2042's maps and map design over BF6's. Despite all of this I will continue to play it occasionally because of the awesome graphics and good times with buddies. I really wish this title had a few more years in the oven, because they could have had something really special here but instead settled for mediocre. But in terms of recommendations this is what I recommend within the genre of Modern or semi-Modern Warfare FPS. Best COD multiplayer: Modern Warfare 3 (2023), Best modern Battlefield multiplayer: Battlefield 2042, Best Battlefield multiplayer: Battlefield 4, Best campaign experience: Modern Warfare (2019) (Battlefield 4's campaign is also kickass). I feel as though all of these previous titles offer better experiences depending on what you are looking for. The best case I can make for this game is that if you do not already have these titles or want to get them, Battlefield 6 is a good way to get all of these previous experiences at a much cheaper rate with a live service in 2026. Ultimately, its not that its bad, its just that I want my Battlefield game to be a Battlefield game and my Call of Duty game to be a Call of Duty game. I don't want this confused, convoluted slop.

This is my first Battlefield game, and I have never played Call of Duty either. For players like me, this is a solid entry point into the Battlefield franchise. If you are new to these types of games, you will most likely have a lot of fun.

The gameplay is fast paced and can feel sweaty at times. I expected it to be slower, but it is still very enjoyable. Teamwork plays an important role, although with random squads it can be inconsistent. For the best teamwork experience, I would recommend playing with people you know or with friends.

The visuals, audio, gunplay, atmosphere, and environments are all top notch. It is genuinely a beautiful game to play.

One thing I am not a fan of is how classes have assignments/missions and how weapons and gadgets are locked behind them. This system can turn the game into a grind, where you end up playing just to unlock gear instead of simply playing for fun.

The single player campaign isn't the reason to buy this game either. The campaign wasn't engaging at all in my opinion. This game is great because of the multiplayer.

Overall, as a new player, I think the game is worth trying. If you are interested like I was (as a new player into the franchise and into FPS games like this), I would recommend picking it up when it is discounted.

This is my first Battlefield game, and I have never played Call of Duty either. For players like me, this is a solid entry point into the Battlefield franchise. If you are new to these types of games, you will most likely have a lot of fun.

The gameplay is fast paced and can feel sweaty at times. I expected it to be slower, but it is still very enjoyable. Teamwork plays an important role, although with random squads it can be inconsistent. For the best teamwork experience, I would recommend playing with people you know or with friends.

The visuals, audio, gunplay, atmosphere, and environments are all top notch. It is genuinely a beautiful game to play.

One thing I am not a fan of is how classes have assignments/missions and how weapons and gadgets are locked behind them. This system can turn the game into a grind, where you end up playing just to unlock gear instead of simply playing for fun.

The single player campaign isn't the reason to buy this game either. The campaign wasn't engaging at all in my opinion. This game is great because of the multiplayer.

Overall, as a new player, I think the game is worth trying. If you are interested like I was (as a new player into the franchise and into FPS games like this), I would recommend picking it up when it is discounted.

First, for context, battlefield is my most played franchise, thousands of hours between 3,4,2042, and a few hundred in V and 1. I have 110 in this game. I could go on for quite a while regarding this game, but I will just highlight a couple of things here. 

1. 70 dollar price tag, and a somewhat recent update has introduced AI generated content, including a emblem with a double barrel, double dust cover, AR rifle. This was acknowledged by DICE, even in an update from today, with "changes" and all they did was update the brightness. Initial response was extremely negative on the release of this btw. I mentioned the 70 dollar price tag, you can use your brain and make the connections on how that is far worse than I will make it sound here. 

2. At some point they introduced an update that if I remember correctly had a fair amount of changes. Well the next update actually UN-DID, many of those changes, and came with even more bugs. Rumor has it, they released it on the wrong branch of the game. Since this update there has been something as small as a UI bug showing the SCAR rifle having a magazine as a foregrip, and nothing where the magazine goes. This update also undid changes to the ticket amounts in conquest. It reduced them, after raising them, I believe they then raised them back because it was of course an unintended consequence of what I mentioned before.  This update also reintroduced bot kills being included in player KD, even though they acknowledged this was unintended, and removed it before. 

3. LOD pop in issues, texture issues. At some point they released an update that made it so helicopter blades dont even spin if they are a "not-so-far" distance away from you. Looks ridiculous. 

4. Small things like mispelling, stats of attachments not reflecting properly and their descriptions actually contradicting the stat profile. Along with this, there are challenges of the same type, lets use headshots as an example. These challenges will have the same goal: "x amount of headshots" but they will be worded completely different. Its inconsistent. 

5. Gun balance is OK, but there are of course outliers that have been prevalent since launch, community has mentioned it since, but there has been almost no weapon balancing done in any patches. 

6. I could go on about bugs and inconsistencies, but I will mention portal being a flop with 0 support. I will lump more in here too. No server browser. No persistent matchmaking. Ping spikes constantly because of 60hz servers, widely reported on reddit and forums. Maps are terribly balanced and designed. 

7. I realized I can actually just keep going here. At some point they updated breakthrough, reduced player count to 48 from 64. This has been complained about constantly by players and it has not been reverted for 2 months. At some point they also released a patch that increased the vehicle count to ridiculous numbers on breakthrough, I think they fixed that after outlash on reddit and forums. 

8. Hit reg problems plague the game, probably due to connection problems that are consistent regardless of spec and networking. Again widely reported online. 

9. going back to point 1, to touch on the 70 dollar price point. I will just say: battlepass, microtransactions, exp boosts cost money, AI SLOP. The skins are honestly objectively bad outside of a few outliers as well. 

10. This one is a bit nitpicky but the grind for attachments is a slog, absolutely. People have done the math and it takes exponentially longer (like 6x) to unlock all attachments compared to previous games. 

This is what I can think of on the spot for current date, 2/3/26. And listen, I know some of the stuff is small, but its the sheer amount of problems and inconsistent garbage that is mind blowing. And its mind blowing because you have to realize the fact that this was a VERY large release for EA/DICE/Battlefield. They wanted to capture the COD player base, which they said, and they DID IT. But they dropped the support within like a month and now the game is legit dying, which is insane considering the circumstances. Like I am sure at some point it will get better, after like a year, just like every other past Battlefield, but WOW. Its just unbelievable the state of this game considering all this. Its like EA is TRYING to fumble. Its just pure negligence, ignorance, and lack of care. 

PS I realized I didnt mentioned Redsec. Well thats because I didnt play it because it looks like a mobile warzone rip off, I am also not a fan of battle royale. Its a shame it even released because it takes away from the primary game that actually costed money.

I booted up Battlefield 6 expecting chaos.
I got chaos.
But like… the cinematic, “my squad just accidentally leveled an entire shopping mall” kind of chaos.

First of all, this game understands that sometimes you don’t want to be a soldier. Sometimes you want to be a mildly trained tornado with a rifle. And BF6 says, “Absolutely. Here’s a tank, a helicopter, and a building that used to exist.”

The destruction is back and it’s personal. Walls? Optional. Cover? Temporary. That sniper who’s been camping for 12 minutes? Congratulations, he now lives outside because the building doesn’t.

Gunplay feels chunky in the best way. Every weapon sounds like it was recorded by someone aggressively slamming car doors in a thunderstorm. Recoil feels real enough that I look tactical, but forgiving enough that my panic spraying occasionally counts as “suppressing fire.”

Vehicles? Absolute menace. I spawned, blinked, and suddenly I was in a jet I absolutely did not know how to fly. Did I survive? No. Did I look cool for three seconds? Also no. But I tried, and that’s what matters.

The real magic though? Battlefield moments™.

Random medic revives you while bullets are flying everywhere.

Entire squad charges through smoke like we rehearsed it (we did not).

That one engineer who exists solely to ruin every vehicle’s day.

Pros:

Destruction that solves camping problems permanently

Huge maps that make every match feel like a war movie

Vehicles that let me roleplay as “professional accident”

Squad plays that make you feel like tactical geniuses

Cons:

I still cannot land helicopters

My K/D ratio is a suggestion

Overall: 10/10 would accidentally redeploy my entire squad into a burning crater again.

If you like big maps, loud explosions, and turning “strategic objective” into “historical landmark that used to be here,” Battlefield 6 delivers.

The game is good. I built a PC and bought it because I played BF4 when I was a teenager and I've missed every Battlefield since then. I really wanted to play each of them. And I finally got my hands on BF6, and it feels great to be back, personally as someone whose best weapon was the M98B, I like the sniping, I like getting to experience the sweet spot mechanic from BF1, the fluid crawling from BFV.
In BF4, we used to say: "PTFO". And unless I'm playing Rush, it seems like the playerbase has turned away from that motive. When I play engineer, no vehicles are getting painted. When I play recon, none of the painted vehicles are getting hit. It has become a giant game of Team Deathmatch, same goes for the Gauntlet. I think priorities have changed, people desire more intensity, more dopamine, less need for patience, and they're getting that with smaller maps, faster close range TTK. Holding the objective has become perceived as camping.
BUT, I have no idea what people talk about when talking about disastrous maps or bad hit registration or sniping AAs. The pilots and tankers in my games live for very long, to the point where I need to switch to engineer and die to them many times before I get one shot off at them and deal 650 damage when their flares are down, only for them to tuck behind a hill and restock. My bullets seem to hit just fine and I'd argue that my hit registration in Valorant is worse than in BF6. Maps are fine. I do not see myself wanting a 20x scope again, the bullet travel time starts getting troublesome already on maps like Blackwell fields or Mirak Valley. I've seen the record shots of 2km plus on Firestorm, and I don't desire those kills. There isn't a range point bonus, and aggressive recon has always seemed as a better way to play than sniping from a hill. Again, PTFO, my score per minute with M98B was abominable. Speaking of Blackwell Fields, I get that people don't like that map. I, for one, love it. The hills have good blind spots to hide in from the snipers and tanks. There are 5 man squad vehicles to provide transport to objectives as well as a mobile spawn point that's somewhat protected from tanks. Unless AA is LITERALLY sniping from its spawn, it is at risk of getting taken down by engineers and tanks as soon as it crests the first hill. If my memory serves me well, I've almost never seen AA far away from spawn in BF4 either.
My only complaint about this game is the progression. I saw that there is XP tweaking incoming, but right now, I only have one weapon at level 50, and with how thermal 6x scopes or suppressors or synthetic tips are unlocked at level 35+, and there being 3 camo unlocks per weapon, I don't want the 500 kill masteries back. And then yet again, the way I'd do those in BF4? I'd grind Rush or Domination or Metro or Operation Locker until I had the mastery, and only then I'd use the fully customized weapon in Conquest. Unlocking the suppressor and bipod for a gun often required me to get 100 kills with it first, excluding battlepacks. I had to run the SAR-21 with the same muzzle break and red dot combo for 80 kills. And I wasn't good with recoil, now i at least get progress for kill participation and getting kills at objectives.

I could likely write a book on my thoughts on BF6, but I'll likely keep this brief as most of the issues have been written about ad-nauseum at this point.

Like most other veteran battlefield players (I've been playing since BF2), I was extremely excited seeing gameplay trailers for 6 because it seemed like DICE (what was left of it anyway) was finally listening to it's players, and we were finally getting back to what makes Battlefield feel distinctly different from other shooters on the market. How wrong we all were. 

During the beta, there was a big sentiment in the community that the game perhaps was feeling more like a mix of BF and CoD than BF itself. Now, i will say that I didn't really mind this, if it was a way to pull some players away from CoD while still trying to keep BF players happy, so be it. I'm willing to compromise on certain things that other hardcore vets of the series very clearly were not. The beta showed off only small maps with 1 larger map being liberation peak. The problem was Liberation Peak is terribly designed and produces some of the most one-sided games you'll play. The other maps were small and just didn't feel properly balanced vehicle wise and were just way too fast paced with a the TTK of guns being so low it felt more like you were in a meat grinder of just spawning and dying constantly. Overall, it felt like the bones were there, but something was just off about the gameplay itself.

Come launch time, really not much had changed from the Beta. It was hard to understand that all the feedback basically was ignored. I personally did not really care. I played A LOT of this game in a pretty short amount of time. However, a lot of the common Battlefield issues showed their head. Netcode was horrendous (this has been marginally improved at least). The TTK is still far far too low, it just feels like you die so fast that for a battlefield game it makes your typical strategies/squad based play tough. SMG's for so long have been absolute laser beams, and honestly most guns feel like laser beams. Burst firing is not really needed after you unlock certain attachments for guns. Speaking of attachments, the unlock time/system for this game is absolutely horrendous. It takes SO LONG to unlock the attachments needed for guns it's unreal. They claim as of this review that's being looked at for season 2 and changed so we'll see.

We get to season 2 and there's just hardly any content in a 3 month timespan, which honestly, would not be as big of a deal if the current maps available were actually fun to play. Most of them are terrible, too fast paced, and just don't feel like Battlefield. DICE and EA have never understood that CoD players are not going to play their games long term. Your core audience wants Battlefield. If you don't deliver on that, they will simply not play it and then you have neither audience captured. 

I want to make clear that I actually enjoyed most of my time playing the game, it just got exhausting to play. There's simply too much going on all around you at all times, there's no time to breathe on almost any map. You're being shot at from so many angles with a TTK so low you barely have time to respond. The netcode is still an issue, the gun balance is still an issue, and in my opinion, it's simply too late to reverse course. 

My advice? Go find something else to play. The issue of course if you're like me, there really isn't many modern military shooters to play anymore. I thought this was going to be my game to play for years. I and most of us were so very wrong.

I'm torn whether I should make a + or - review, but I think it's gotta be negative.
BF6 is mostly very enjoyable, but has a few major issues that really ruin the game for me.

TLDR: Botched classes, bad pacing and maps, lack of persistent servers and browser, bad live service, tedious progression, but some great new features. Still might be fixable in the future.


Lets start with core gameplay issues.

- The Class system. BF3 and BF4 mediocre class balance, but DICE revised classes in BF1 and BF5 into a system where each class feels very useful and is well defined. Each class fits their role because of their gadgets AND weapons. But, all that refining of the classes in BF1/V was thrown out in BF6, and now they've basically gone back to mediocre BF3/4 class balancing. Class roles are now less defined because anyone can use any weapon at any time.
For example: They moved the spawn beacon from Recon to Assault. Honestly not a bad change if you think about it. Makes sure spawn beacons are used more aggressively on the frontlines instead of camping in the back of the map. Except, wait a minute. An assault class can equip a sniper rifle due to open weapons so now DICE has basically just made a more powerful Recon class by giving it grenade launchers too. This isn't the end of the world, but why a step back?

-My next issue is the pacing of the game. There is simply no downtime or time to breathe in this game due to  intentional design. All the maps feel optimized so that you run in to fights around every corner or two. Part of the issue is that you auto heal, and heal from medic bags and pouches insanely fast. In previous games when someone takes damage, they're stuck holding a building for a while slowing down the entire match. In BF6 you auto heal back to full health in 10 seconds, if you have a medic bag nearby it's 5 seconds. In previous games a medic bag heals you in 10 seconds and auto heal takes 20-30. Remember in previous games how you could poke someone for half health and push and finish them off while they regen behind cover? That doesn't happen in this game because while you push them they've already healed and then they peek and kill you in the open. There might be too much reviving lol.

- The small average map size also adds to the pacing issue. Every map in this game is way too small. The average BF6 map feels smaller than Argonne Forest, Suez, Devastation, Aerodrome, Flood Zone, Propaganda and feel like the following small maps from older games: Al Marj Encampment, Fort De Vaux, and Operation Locker.
Out of the 11 maps in the game right now, there are only 4 that have jets, and 2 of them barely feel big enough for jets. Season 2 brings 2 new maps and neither supports jets. Only 1 supports helicopters.
The lack of variety is what makes me burn out on this game so quickly. There are like 2 truly large scale "Battlefield" Maps. Mirak Valley and Operation Firestorm. Mirak Valley is by far the best map in the game, but compared to any BF4, 1, or V map its so average. Playing Mirak Valley Conquest or Escalation is actually very fun most of the time. But it's like one of 2 or 3 maps that play like traditional large scale BF, and so I almost exclusively play those and get burnt out quickly and quit playing.
I love BF for its variety in gameplay. I love playing large scale vehicle maps, I also love playing my meatgrinder maps like Operation Underground from time to time and everything in between. But this game just has way too many meat grinder Tank and infantry only maps. I play BF for its sandbox. This game doesn't allow a whole lot of that. Most maps are corridors and alleys instead of battlefields.

- The lack of a server browser, but more importantly persistent servers is a massive issue. Everyone keeps talking about the missing server browser but a server browser is near useless without persistent servers. I don't even know how to hammer this into DICEs brain more than it already has been.
Every single time I've played Battlefield 3, Battlefield 4, Battlefield 1, and Battlefield 5 I have used the server browser to join a persistent server. Do not remove these features. 
I do not want to matchmake every 20 minutes. I'm already in a server with 63 other people, why split us all up and matchmake us again? Just to make me sit on the waiting for players screen or to fill my match up with bots? I don't care if it costs more money for a more permanent server. Have servers spin down like they did in BFV if there are too little players in them. Save money that way. Save money, but not at the cost of the product.

- Progression is way too long and tedious. Weapons take way too many kills to progress. It takes about 2000 kills per gun to fully level a weapon up and unlock all attachments. Someone crunched the numbers and it would take like 3000+ hours to level up all weapons. Gadgets can be a hassle to unlock due to the quite specific challenges. 

Live Service Issues:
- I used to despise live service games, but a few great ones like Helldivers 2, The Finals, and Arc Raiders have proven that they can be done very well. Battlefield has done the opposite of those 3 games. DICE has fumbled 4 live service games. SWBF2, BFV, BF2042, and BF6. 
If you compare the content you used to get out of DLCs in BF3, BF4, and BF1, to the live service content of BFV, BF2042, BF6, and SWBF2, it's laughable. BF4 did 23 post launch maps, and BF1 and 3 did 20. On the other hand BF5 did 11 post launch maps, BF2042 did 8, and BF6 is on track to do 8 over the course of 4 seasons or 1 year. 
There are also only like 3-4 guns per season instead of 6-10 per DLC like in previous games. On top of that there are no map variations and no weather conditions for any of these maps to make each match feel a little more unique which brings me to my next point.

Dice has taken map variations and game modes from previous games and turned them into limited time modes. The only map variation "currently" in the game is a snowy version of Manhattan. Well, actually it's not currently in the game because it was a limited time mode for Christmas. You can't play it anymore.
In season 2 DICE plans to add night variations to certain maps as more Limited Time Modes. If that wasn't bad enough they're bringing back the Operations game mode from BF1/V except IT'S A LIMITED TIME MODE. 

Yes, I want to play these modes so I'll come try them while they're limited, but then stop playing because they're no longer available. WHY NOT JUST MAKE THESE MAP VARIATIONS ALWAYS AVAILABLE SO THAT IT ADDS PERMANANT, NOT LIMITED, VALUE TO YOUR GAME AND I KEEP COMING BACK TO PLAY INSTEAD OF A LIMITED NUMBER OF TIMES. I honestly do not understand how they keep shooting themselves in the foot like this. They try to mush previous games features into the live service mold instead of finding new ways to add to the live service.

- This is an obvious one but I have to mention it. $20 skin pack microtransactions in a full priced $70 game is ridiculous. You aren't getting a single dime out of me. Cosmetics and Battlepasses that cost real money is a monetization method for Free to Play games. This game costs $70 and has more predatory MTX than The Finals which is an entirely Free to Play game. You can't have your cake and eat it too, but somehow AAA studios have found a way.

Despite all that they still added some fantastic things that I can't help but miss when I play older BF games.
- Dragging is a fantastic feature that is pretty much perfectly implemented. Feels great to do and very rarely bugs out.
- The loop from when you die, to being revived is entirely seamless and very immersive. 
- Performance and graphics are overall very good, but not phenomenal.
- The new Escalation gamemode started off rough, but they've made the matches way longer and it's actually really fun and one of the best additions to the game.
- Weapons are very sexy and feel pretty good to use. Weapon customization is pretty solid.

Ok, the game genuinely seems fun, and I would probably have more to say on that topic if it ran properly on my computer. I'd like to play it more, and maybe I will in the future if I get a console / dedicated machine for it.

But after getting the game, I later found out it uses kernel level permissions for its anticheat (EA Javelin Anticheat), which is becoming an increasingly more popular practice. I love that Valve requires game that use such permissions to say so on the store page, as it really helps on the topic.

The reason I take issue with this is because its a direct violation of the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP). Its not core to the functionality of the game. And on principle, a video game isn't nearly important enough the have the same kind of permissions other software has thats core to functionality of the device. It sets bad industry standards, and as a result, user expectations on what kind of permissions other software generally needs.

Its a fun game, and has a lot of really cool mechanics, from what I can see. But this comment is mostly to apply whatever minuscule level of pressure I can vote for better dev practices in the industry.

Users can do what they want with their computer. I'm not one to get in the way of that. But do keep in mind they're also the biggest security risk.

And again, Steam does have this nice little section of the store page that requires sellers to say if their game requires kernel level permissions.

Review Title: 200+ Hours Verdict: Great Combat Ruined by Bugs, Cheaters, and Greed
Overall Verdict: Recommended (7.5/10)
After 217 hours, I can say this game is truly enjoyable in bursts, but there are some atrocious, frustrating issues that cannot be ignored. These flaws make the experience repulsive at times.

The "Ugly" Side (Issues & Bugs):

1-The Insane Weapon Grind: It is hard to understand the logic behind forcing a player to take on an "extra work shift" just to unlock attachments. Requiring over 3,000 kills to unlock all attachments for a single weapon is pure madness. Reaching the max weapon level can take 1,500+ kills, with later levels needing over 44,000+ XP.

2-Game-Breaking Glitches: On Operation Firestorm, snipers are prone and invisible to hits—even when their whole head is visible, shots don't register.

3-Map Exploits: On Iberian Offensive (Objective C), players reach rooftops that should be unreachable. This map is riddled with errors I reported at launch that still aren't fixed.

4-Cheaters & RedSec: The free-to-play RedSec mode has opened the floodgates for cheaters, making Battle Royale unplayable.

5-Broken Physics: Tank and vehicle explosions leave parts floating in the air until the match ends. It looks very poorly optimized and ruins the immersion.

The "Greed" Factor:

Pricing: Paying $60 for the game plus $10 for a Battle Pass is extreme. It’s the price of a full legendary game on sale.

Final Thought:
The core gameplay is fun, but the technical failures, the cheaters, and this ridiculous "work-shift" progression kill the enjoyment. Fix the game and respect our time!

Star Wars Outlaws is a RPG set in the Star Wars universe where you play as a Outlaw named Kay Vess who decides to risk it all for the one big score that will set her up for life, after fully completing the game i'll give some pro's, neutrals and cons.

PRO'S:
-Good protagonist who is well written and mostly well designed with one grievance see Neutrals
-Very good environments and level designs with good attention to details and some easter eggs from the movies
-Good story with plenty of twists and turns
-Good companions that are well designed and well written, Nix is the best of the bunch
-No radio towers to climb, that's a plus as far as i'm concerned...
-Tons of accessibility options to tweak the gameplay however you want, turn off Q.T.E.'s, auto climb etc.
-Lots of clothes to find and buy for customization, designs are ok could use more spice
-Good stealth which is important for this type of game
-Has a skill tree that is based on completing challenges instead of gaining XP that improve the characters abilities and gives passives
-Good combat that got improved with updates, can take enemy guns and fight if you get caught, no reset if you get discovered
-Good map movement with the Speeder that is well designed and improved with updates, can fire blaster while mounted etc.
-Good space exploration with a well designed ship that can be customized and space battle is well designed and fun, lots to find and being able to go to the planet and land without visible loading screens was pretty cool
-Mostly good performance, cutscenes were a tiny bit choppy on occasion and textures failed to load in once in one area but that was easily fixed with a quick reload, no other bugs or problems at all, so overall pretty good

NEUTRAL'S: "No Score Change From These"
-Protagonist doesn't properly match up visually with model she is based on, eyes too big, proportions from model wrong etc. but can be fixed via a mod on Nexusmods
-Game length for full 100% Completion about 60-70 hours
-Bounty Hunter antagonist is ok but wish they had a better design and flair like a cool helmet and jet pack or just something that made them stand out a bit more, more visual flair that Bounty Hunters are known for
-Keyboard inputs are a mess and will need to be remapped a bit
-Main protagonists fathers absence is never mentioned or explained, either the story didn't demand it be addressed or the writer has some daddy issues...
-Pazaak game replaced with Sabacc, while the new Sabacc game is fine it's not as fun as the Pazaak game from Kotor was
-Npcs are visually bland, boring, Kotor 1 and 2 Npcs looked better and that was over 20 years ago

CON'S:
-Too much backtracking that only served to pad out the game, not needed in modern games anymore, relic of the past
-Losing rep with gangs and always being forced to always choose a side just seems unfair sometimes as the other gangs always seem to know exactly what your doing at all times and get upset if you don't side with them, it happens too much and feels unrealistic
-Game feels way too toned down and sterile, can't rob or swindle innocents, no bad language, no blood, watered down PG dialogue etc.
-No dancers in Jabba's Palace, this breaks Star Wars lore, whatever their reasonings it's a lore break
-Forced Ubisoft Launcher and Denuvo, so many lost sales because of these, you'd think they learn by now

Overall Star Wars Outlaws a decent enough RPG, it definitely has some flaws and is a bit too watered down, but overall ok game i would say and if you like Star Wars games or just RPG's in general you will probably like this game just fine, but i recommend waiting for a sale, but as always, It's.. [h1] Star Wars Outlaws: a massive surprise [/h1]

[i]130 hours gone without ever checking the clock.[/i]

[hr][/hr]

[b]Calling it good is an understatement.[/b]
I was honestly very unsure about buying this game. I had seen and read several negative reviews and that really held me back. In the end, I decided to trust my instinct and buy it anyway, because I wanted to experience it firsthand and see if it was really as “bad” as people were saying.

The result?
Every single expectation I had was completely surpassed.

It had been months since a game managed to grab me like this. [b]130 hours[/b] flew by with not a single moment of boredom, something that rarely happens these days.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Story and pacing [/h2]

The story is [b]spectacular[/b], full of twists, intense moments and sequences of pure action that know exactly when to push and when to slow down.
That said, the beginning is fairly slow. Some mechanics feel a bit stiff at first, especially combat, and during the early hours stealth is heavily encouraged due to the lack of upgrades.

But then the game shifts gears.

What comes after is simply [b]WOW[/b]. The main missions and side storylines become more engaging, intense and carefully crafted. Some side activities can feel repetitive at times, but the narrative context and atmosphere keep them enjoyable.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Exploration, environments and cities [/h2]

Exploration is one of the strongest aspects of the game. The environments are highly detailed, with diverse planets, lively cities and that perfect mix of grit and charm that makes the Star Wars universe feel believable.
Walking through urban areas, listening to ambient dialogue and discovering optional activities makes the world feel alive and immersive.

The minigames are well integrated and help break up the pacing without ever feeling forced, adding variety and personality to the overall experience.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Companion, visuals and technical notes [/h2]

Visually, the game looks great, although it does come with fairly demanding system requirements. On a solid PC, however, the visuals truly shine, with strong lighting and some genuinely stunning scenery.

And then there is [b]Nix[/b].
My god, I loved that companion from the very first moment. He is not just useful, but a core part of the experience. Personally, I would easily place him among the best companions ever made, right alongside Dogmeat from Fallout.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Final thoughts [/h2]

I was [b]genuinely surprised[/b] and [b]extremely satisfied[/b].
Star Wars Outlaws is not perfect, but it is a game that grows on you, keeps you invested and delivers many hours of real enjoyment.

If you love the Star Wars universe and enjoy narrative driven games with exploration, memorable characters and a believable world, this game absolutely deserves a chance.

[h1]Wasted Potential in a Galaxy Far, Far Away[/h1]

There are some things to love about Star Wars Outlaws, but so, so much more to hate. It achieves greatness in isolated moments - like stunning vistas - only to fumble key gameplay elements into mediocrity or worse, all while hammering home a heavy-handed "message" straight out of the Ubisoft/Disney playbook, “Men are bad”.

This is unmistakably a product of both companies, where DEI takes centre stage, forgetting that gaming and Star Wars were forged by men, for men - women are welcome, but constant lectures on male villainy become so tiresome and boring. Here, the cast skews heavily female (ignoring Kay Vess, the vast majority of NPCs are female), with several implied or overt lesbians, sidelining the rugged scoundrel vibe fans crave.

Combat is lacklustre at best. Weapons lack punchy feedback, aiming floats aimlessly (obviously tuned for controller aim-assist), it's functional but never mediocre. A core loop that should entertain falls flat, meaning that at times you avoid a shoot out due to it being tiresome.

Ship Combat is an embarrassment. 90s gems like the X-Wing series (X-Wing, TIE Fighter, X-Wing vs. TIE Fighter, X-Wing Alliance), FreeSpace 1/2, Privateer, and Descent deliver superior Star Wars-style dogfights with depth and thrill. Outlaws' version looks cinematic but plays sluggishly - no reverse thrust, no strafing, this is painfully obvious, as I’m still playing X4 Foundations, and it is painful when I have to complete some of the ship combat tasks in Outlaws.

Stealth is a total joke. Remember launch clips of (female) Stormtroopers being blind to you, while they are tripping over you in the grass? It's barely improved. As this game is ostensibly from the makers of early Assassin's Creed, it's a joke - basic crouch-and-hide, with laughable AI. "Heavily stealth-focused" yet offering just Nix distractions feels insulting.

Now for the bugs and tech problems. Over a year and a half post-launch, issues linger. Nix routinely fails interactions, stalling story beats - having to equip/unequip gear or reload saves as a workaround. Crashes to desktop hit without warning, and recent Steam reviews (71% Mostly Positive overall, but 69% Mixed recent) confirm glitches like Nix clipping or getting stuck persist despite patches.

Breathtaking visuals at times - magical planetary vistas immerse you in the Star Wars universe. But clunky level design (cumbersome navigation on foot/speeder) and grating verticality turn exploration from fun to frustrating, pushing fast travel or YouTube guides.

The story has a solid heist narrative keeps you hooked, with authentic Star Wars flavour. Worlds feel lived-in, though immersion falters - perhaps fewer lectures, or shoehorning more women in, and adding more grit would of helped here.

Ubisoft needs to be taken-over by competent people. The Guillemots drove it into the ground: first for profit, then ignoring bullying/sexual harassment scandals (2020-2021), swinging to DEI overkill. Talented devs fleeing to form studios like Sandfall Interactive (Clair Obscure: Expedition 33 – brilliant game) and Motive (Dead Space Remake) prove it - ex-Ubisofters outshining the corpse.

[b]Verdict:[/b] Deep-sale filler for diehards (avoid full price). Wasted Star Wars license.

Another element, but a positive one, of Ubisoft games is the customisation of game options: You can disable the mini games like hacking and lockpicking (even without a mod, looking at you, Bethesda games). Okay, so I've completed the entire Outlaws with all the Steam achievements, found all the treasures, made all the possible upgrades, and completed all the side quests.

TLDR: Basically, for Star Wars fans, for them it would be really nice and tasty expantion of the universe. For everyone else, well, you can quickly run through mainquest to just soak up the vibes, because the vibes and twists are really fine, despite the underdeveloped characters and the Ubisoft-like side-stories.

The mainquest is short, you can finish it all in about 20 hours if you're going fast.
In total, it took me about 60 hours excluding metagaming.
The story itself has a lot of cool twists, but the characters, as is usually the case these days, are underdeveloped. I can't believe their bonding, but that's just a nitpick.
Gameplay-wise, if you play on Hardcore, it really hits you hard at first and really encourages stealth. You need to collect gear sets and unlock abilities from the so-called experts as you progress to get sturdy and feel comfortable, taking out everyone in open combat. There are tons of gear sets with boosts for different playstyles, so you can play around with them in any way you want.
The side quests here are more symbolic: the so-called Intel is plentiful and fairly simple, like finding a stash with contraband, cash, gear, and so on.
The main quest is important because you unlock various tools along the way that allow you to access various types of stashes, like breaking down a wall, or cutting down a gate with a cutter, and so on (the cutter is given very late, and it's just ridiculous).
Over time, these side quests start to feel boring, and the so-called contracts for boosting reputation with syndicates are completely generic, but at the beginning they're okay to do a little. 
There are two DLCs, both short but intense. The second DLC is post-game and introduces a number of new mechanics, a new blaster module, a new ship, new contract types with a ton of ship upgrades. But why the hell do we need them after the main game, I don't know. IMHO it's dumb, probably designed for those who rush the main quest and then clear all the sides, then it's okay. Personally, I always do the opposite, so the main game leaves a proper aftertaste at the very end, so for me it's meh.
There's also an awesome poker-like card game called Sabbac to spend hours into. The hacking is done with sound, hitting the right beat, which is refreshing after the standard stuff of finding the right angle for a lockpick in most RPGs. It's downright immersive in places, especially when you're stealthy and trying to get there before someone comes around the corner.

The main reason I'd give the game a solid 4/5, even though it's clearly not a masterpiece, is the atmosphere and tons of lore references for real nerds. The atmosphere is like you often find this intel, eavesdropping on people at the bazaar or getting bonus info by hacking the code at the imperial base. It feels very organic. Regarding the lore, the developers are great: it's between parts 5 and 6, you can see a still-living Boba Fett, Jabba, a frozen Han Solo, you can see Luke's stepfather's farm in ruins and listen to the locals discuss the horror of what happened, there is a connection with the ISB from Andor, the whole meta-plot about the syndicates is clearly an attempt to tie in the dropped line from the meta-lore that Darth Maul wanted to return through this, there is Qi'ra herself from the Han Solo movie, she is already in charge and the codex references how she came to power, there are Pykes and other stuff from the Clone Wars. In the second DLC, Hondo Ohnaka from the same Clone Wars is wildly amusing. As expected in the situation after part 5, everyone looks at the rebels as some deluded losers for the most part. There's a small cameo of Vader, the Empire's elite death troopers in that black armor that appeared in many films, which are probably objectively the most dangerous opponents in the entire game, and, like in Andor, a smooth introduction, as the main character, who doesn't give a damn about the Rebels or the Empire, gradually gets involved in all of this with a semi-forced tilt toward good, etc.
