Outlaws was never going to win any awards for its writing, characters, or gameplay. I went in knowing that the formula for Ubisoft games for the last 15 years boils down to an open world that a level designer vomited map markers ontop of. But after finishing E33, I needed to experience a 6-7 out of 10 game as a palate cleanser.

With a few mods found over on Nexus -- including a few that I tweaked myself -- I was able to make Kay's blaster be a one-shot kill in most cases. The accessibility settings allow you to strip out some of the tedium. 

Was it easy? Sure. But it ain't that kind of game, kid.

What results is a fun little RPG-lite that lets you fulfill that Han Solo fantasy for a while. A decent $25 or less game when it's on sale.

The Great: This game won an award for accessibility settings and it is well deserved. Outlaws has the most comprehensive accessibility configurations of any game I've ever played, so if that's something that matters to you, you will be blown away.

The Good: It's a gorgeous game with scenic set pieces-- photo mode lovers will be happy. My favorite planet was Toshara, and an hour in I was immersed in the story and the world. The cities are moody and very well crafted, and they nailed the Star Wars underworld vibe. Influences from The Mandalorian, Andor season 1, and the original trilogy definitely feel like they're in the DNA of this game. Zipping around in my speeder and playing Kessel Sabacc (a brilliant card game) were some of my favorite gameplay moments. The main story missions on Tatooine had an excellent narrative and ended up being my favorite part of the story.

The Meh: Combat and stealth in Outlaws reminds me a lot of the Sniper Elite games, but without the sniping focus. It's not bad, but it's not particularly satisfying either. You spend a good amount of time solving easy puzzles and climbing around areas like in an Uncharted or Tomb Raider game (you can turn off the obnoxious yellow painted ledges in the settings). The spaceship combat is solid but nothing to write home about. I found the planets Kijimi and Akiva to have generally meh missions, forgettable characters, and environments that were annoying to navigate. That said, none of these things made me want to stop playing. 

The Bottom Line: In my opinion, Outlaws isn't a bad game. It's an inconsistent game. Passionate developers who care a lot about Star Wars clearly put their heart and soul into this game, but that can't save it from being a Ubisoft title. Get it on sale and I think you'll be pleasantly surprised.

Star Wars Outlaws feels like the Star Wars game we never had in recent times. No space wizards, no giant battles... just an outlaw, her furry friend, a blaster and the wits needed to survive in the galactic underworld.

[h2] The pros: [/h2]
[list]
[*]The atmosphere is incredible, Star Wars in it's purest form. Trying food stalls with Nix, hearing the various galactic languages, gambling, buying and selling supplies... It's so immersive!
[*]The sound design is very cool! the blasters have such meaty impacts and the TIE fighters doing low altitude fly-bys are so brilliant. really sells the "planet under occupation" vibe.
[*]the OST is incredible. Classic instruments just like in SW.
[*]The voice acting is also great, ND-5 is definitely my favorite in that regard.
[*]No qualms about the character design either, it could be a little more varied, but it's not bad
[*]The story is outstanding! At times it felt a little "rushed" but it's a very captivating Star Wars experience nonetheless, with some very high stakes and breathtaking action.
[*]I love how the rebels are [spoiler] portrayed as much more morally ambiguous than they usually are [/spoiler]
[*]The DLCs are well worth it in sale.
[*]Nix is so incredibly cute.
[*]Kessel Sabacc isn't a bad game but the cheats trivialize it easily.
[*]Hearing Ank speak Huttese is so fun, lol.
[*]The game is insanely cinematic: almost every view is so breathtaking: from the humid forest of Akiva to the wind swept plains of Toshara.
[*]I loved the skill system, requiring you to perform some feats before unlocking certain abilities. It's so much more engaging than the standard "level up, buy skill, repeat".
[/list]

[h2] The cons: [/h2]
[list]
[*]space flight gets a little stale mid to end game: you can't exactly modify the Trailblazer (your ship) all that much. you only have a few options and IMO, most feel subpar to others.
[*]The sidequests are many, but they aren't engaging to do and they are often repetitive. Some even have very cool premises: (e.g. "space ship that has spent 50 cycles in hyperspace that suddenly reappeared) only to reveal themselves as being the same type of quest you've done time and time again (fly to a point in space and retrieve the yellow box) It got to the point that I didn't complete them all despite getting every achievement in the game.
[*]The rebels, despite being a big part of the story are characterized in such an odd way. Halfway between ruthless pragmatists and idealistic heroes.
[*]It sucks that the second DLC is only doable after the main story's ending and there is no NG+ to enjoy the rewards
[*]The Syndicate interactions are an interesting addition but they aren't all that "important". You can easily keep every syndicate at 100%.
[*]Stealth is too heavily encouraged. I've heard that originally, being spotted in certain missions failed them. now you have the option to go loud, but it's almost never worth it IMO, especially since enemies in bases respawn infinitely.
[*]Lockpicking can easily be frustrating. On one hand I'm glad it's not another skyrim "clone", on the other, the rhytm thing can be terrible
[*]Worst of all, Unlike the cover art, you can't take ND out for missions except a few story ones. It sucks since he's one of the most interesting characters in the game.
[*]Some places fall short of their mark. [spoiler]A clone wars era spaceship crashed on a planet without even one clone armor or almost no environmental storytelling, or a CIS droid factory, full of droids but we don't even get to fight any. again, barely any environmental storytelling.[/spoiler]
[*]It's a little sad how [spoiler] the crew just dissolves after the heist, they would be so great working together, especially since Gedeek and Kay already have a prior story[/spoiler]
[*]Despite we being able to see the empire being tyrannical, Kay is never really the target of such petty abuses of power.

I am honestly making this review for the person who is intrigued by the game but is holding off due to the mixed review rating. I do not understand the mixed reviews for this game, to me the game is amazing, I would rate it 8.5-9.0/10. To best describe this game, its like Uncharted and Hitman (suprising comparison, but accurate) in a semi-open world with lite RPG elements. One of the concerns going into the game was if it was going to be structured like the Far Cry series in terms of narrative/quest hubs; luckily it is not and feels more organic like the Witcher 3 (and that to me is high praise as Witcher 3 for me is as close to a perfect game as I could hope). Any ways these are my pros/cons:

+ Visuals and the world you explore are stunning
+ Exploration is heavily encouraged with easter eggs and rewards in unexpected places 
+ World building through interactions and quests feels organic and engaging
+ Quests/activites always felt rewarding and not like a chore
+ Set pieces (i.e. abandoned temples, clone war factories, star stations etc.) are absolutely stunning and feel like they are part of the SW universe; I wish there was an art book for this game
+ Pacing of the game is very well done; out of the 65+ hours of in-game time I've put in I was never bored
+  Character building is well done with choices in keeping with the scoundrel/smuggler/outlaw theme
+ Progress systems (character, ship, reputations, cosmetics, etc.) are very well done and feel rewarding and not like a grind (thank goodness)
+ Ship combat feels arcady, but for me it was enjoyable. 
+ Companion interactions feel great, I bonded more with ND-5 then the protagonist (although she was enjoyable)
+ There are quality of life features throughout the game, which helps the game not be bogged down
+ The timeframe they chose to ground the game in is excellent (dont want to expand on this as it may lead to spoilers)

- Movement mapping was occasionally off, infrequently for some of the climbing/platforming sections
- There are considerable "woke" undertones for the first half of the game, I would say approximately 80% of character interactions you have are with female characters (as either quest givers or plot driving devices) and 80% of those are homosexual. There are two main interactions that also define the main character as homosexual. For some this may be an issue. I found the "love interests" (if they can be even called that) disappointing, simply because they did not lead to character development or interesting situations. They could have explored themes such as betrayal or putting those you love in harms way (ie. being a scoundrel and outlaw, etc.) but it was a missed opportunity 
- In the last quarter of the game I did experience several crashes, however the save system is very forgiving so it was never too bothersome

Star Wars Outlaws is a very enjoyable game and I really do hope they expand on this in the future. Or perhaps the same team can work on a similar project exploring other aspects of the SW universe. If you do buy this I recommend getting the Ultimate edition as the DLC content is actually substantial and worth it.

It isn't the best game ever for sure, but it does feel like a team poured some heart and love into it. A sequel would have been awesome, but Ubisoft did Ubisoft things and cancelled it for some dumb reason. If it gets un-cancelled, it'd be a day one buy for me after this game. The upgrade mechanics feel well balanced and nice. It's fun to upgrade a blaster for once instead of working on your lightsaber. Spoiler warning: You don't even SEE a lightsaber for most of this game, it's mostly based around being a scoundrel. IMO serious kudos to the team at Massive that worked on this. I really wish I'd see more of it, and I can only hope Ubisoft does greenlight a sequel after reconsidering. I know it won't happen, but Massive did a lovely job. It's graphically beautiful with some wonderful vistas, great animations, and interesting looking. The mechanics aren't necessarily doing anything novel in gaming, but it's a well oiled system here. Systems that are known to work well are combined nicely here and it's very fluid. Would recommend, however, I do have some criticism. While railroading the player through the first section of the game isn't that bad, once you are off Canto, the game does continue to railroad you through certain objectives and force scenarios and pathing. I get that it is trying to tell a story at some points, but there are mechanics that force you into a linear playstyle even in side quests.

The grapple for instance; it has different mechanics depending on the location and objective, designed to force you to follow a specific path. They do this a lot.

Locations are amazing, cinematic moments feel like they are trying to pull off a Star Wars experience and failing, as often as not. It's especially jarring when they just grab you and throw you in, like with Jabba, give you 30-40 seconds of thematic experience, then drop you in a run and gun wher you get locked in a room with a homicidal and invulnerable Rancor, then get you to play puzzle games while it tries to kill you. 

That's what I consider a failure. 

Otherwise, they should make an actuall Open World game, give you optional first person, (I prefer it), and keep most of the game mechanics, while making things like the grapple actually have flexible usage, and the ability to buy new ships, and build your own character. 

That would be a pretty good game. This... this I like, but it feels like it could have been better.

Star Wars: Outlaws is a game that is exactly the sum of its parts, and most of its parts are pretty good. If you enjoy Star Wars, some stealth-action combat, and a jaunt through an engaging story, this game is worth a purchase.

In summary:

* The good - the core game is fun. It has a fun story and fun core gameplay.
* The mediocore - It has a lot of "good enough" systems that never quite land
* The bad - The performance is still not ideal, and the side characters are undeveloped

* The story is pretty good. The classic "found family" cliche works for ND, but the rest of the crew is undeveloped (they're fairly 1 dimensional side characters, see below). Nevertheless, the pacing is fairly good
* The factions system is fun to juggle - for a while. The idea is good, but the execution is a bit lackluster, since you rarely ever get to any of the extremes of either faction unless you *really* try. Also, the bug faction is extremely underdeveloped.
* The combat is passable, even fun at times. The later parts of the game end up just throwing waves of enemies at you, but small engagements can be pretty fun to "solve" as combat geometry. You're very squishy, which makes sense in-context, but that makes the lack of a true cover system unfortunate.
* The stealth is fun. I am a good stealth player (I completed both of the new Deus Ex games in "ghost" mode) and this system is not too challenging. It definitely is a "stealth until you can't" and it works.
* The speeder and starfighter sections are good enough, but they are not the primary draw. It's fun to get around Tatooine on a speeder.

If I were to diagnose the problem with this game, and why it disappointed many folks (beyond the technical/performance problems), it's that the game doesn't know what it wants to be:

* It wants to create a bond between you and the crew like Mass Effect, but (1) the crew comes in slowly as you complete each recruitment quest so they have little screentime and (2) outside of 1-2 missions the crew never actually comes with you. This means that you feel pretty detached from everyone except ND, but since they make him the only recurring/constant presence, it works (and only for him).
* It wants you to play on the ground, in space, on a speeder - but all of those systems end up being underdeveloped individually. It's a cohesive experience because none of them truly shines.
* It doesn't want to be a combat game. It wants to be a stealth game. But it doesn't commit to a full stealth experience especially post-patching (before there were missions you could insta-fail because of detection). This clashed with audience expectations quite heavily, since most players don't *want* to play "Assassin's Creed but in Star Wars".
* It wants you to play the factions against each other, but since the draw of the game are the main missions, you can basically ignore the faction shuffle completely.

If you've read this far and you're still on the fence - buy the game on sale. It's pretty fun!

I have had 0 crashes, noticed no bugs, don't care that Kay Vess isn't a known character, have no issues using the Ubi launcher, and think it has great graphics.

- Using your animal helper to fight and grab stuff is fun, easy, and useful

- Upgrading your blaster and loadout makes a difference that actually makes a difference you notice.
- The side card game called Sabbac is a little simple but still has enough to it that I find myself wanting to do it and gain the special cards for it
- The exploration parts of the game during missions have you in unique areas that aren't difficult but feel fun to explore in kind of a tomb raider sort of way.  

I feel like I should put a few things I didn't care for just to prove I'm not paid or fake or something so here's a few:
- Switching between blaster functions (after you get more than "light") feels difficult in that you have to choose before fighting areas what you want it set to.   
- Looting opportunities are everywhere and lead to liking getting rare stuff but common stuff is almost too common.  A lot of it is just vendor bait which you should hold on to until you NEED more money, which, for a cheapskate like me, haven't needed yet.  When I need money I will be able to see things for way more than enough, so it feels like I'm rich already..

- Faction happiness plays a role and has a lot of ways to influence them but never feels impossible to keep them where you need them
- Upgrading skills requires actual tasks that give you something else to try for and make a difference once you earn them.
- The maps work well and tracking quests is easy and fair.

[h1] Score: ◆◆◆⬖◇ (3.5/5) [/h1] 

[b]TLDR:[/b] A solid but familiar Ubisoft open world experience, carried largely by its IP and a surprisingly enjoyable main story. While the atmosphere and core narrative are great; it is held back by shallow side content, low difficulty, and underdeveloped characters. Grab on a sale if possible.

Outlaws reminds me of Hogwarts Legacy in a lot of ways. It is a serviceable game whose IP is doing a lot of heavy lifting. Both include an open world that is filled with junk to pad out the game's length, though I think Outlaws justifies its open world a little better. I also think it has slightly more memorable characters and a more compelling story to tell. It is not as good as the Jedi games, but Star Wars fans have not had many options over the last decade, and there are certainly plenty of worse games in the franchise.

Outlaws tells the story of Kay Vess, a young thief who, after receiving a death mark, assembles a team with the help of a mysterious outlaw and his droid bodyguard to pull off the heist of a lifetime. I actually enjoyed the main story, especially the ending, but it is not without its faults. For a plot centered around building a crew, they sure do not spend much time exploring these characters. ND-9, the previously mentioned droid, is the only supporting character given proper screen time besides Kay’s pet sidekick, Nix. There was one crew member I actually thought might be interesting whom you do not even end up recruiting in the end. On the other hand, the villains are great, and big name characters like Lando, Jabba, and even Qi’ra are used in fitting ways that do not feel overtly fan servicey.

Unfortunately, story content outside of the main quests and the DLC is mostly bland and forgettable. Remember, at its core, this is a Ubisoft game, and nine times out of ten that translates to an open world checklist simulator. Look, the atmosphere of the world is impeccable. The environments are breathtaking, and the game captures the feel of Star Wars quite well, especially in previously established locations like Tatooine. But when I look back on what I enjoyed during my time with the game, it certainly was not opening my 60th crate for yet another slight color variation for my speeder. The game also includes space combat which, while not bad, was always something I wanted to rush through just to get back on the ground. The game itself even seems aware of this, as space combat is used sparingly in the main story.

Kay Vess has a pretty solid toolkit that starts basic and gradually expands as you gain abilities from so called experts you meet along your journey. Slicing terminals and lockpicking both have their own mini games, which I never found tedious, and that is probably the biggest compliment I can give to systems like these. You have grenades, smoke bombs, your pet to create distractions, whistling, three different modes for your blaster, and a long range stun shot ability to quietly take out enemies with a cooldown. You even have a slow motion, dead eye style skill similar to Red Dead Redemption that lets you dispatch multiple enemies like a proper gunslinger. Unfortunately, the game is simply too easy, to the point where you rarely need all of these tools. I seldom used grenades and often forgot I even had smoke bombs. It becomes noticeable very quickly that enemies are usually placed with their backs turned in highly convenient locations, practically begging to be taken down silently.

Some miscellaneous notes. Sabacc is present as a card gambling mini game and is actually a welcome break from the rest of the game whenever it appears. While the environments are gorgeous, the lip syncing is distractingly rough for a 2024 game outside of major cutscenes. There is a moment early on where Nix steals a ring from a crime lord, and you can either sell it for cash or later return it to earn reputation with that faction. This is one of several moments where you are given a choice, but the outcome is rarely interesting. Most decisions simply result in gaining reputation with one faction and sometimes losing it with another. This is a nitpick, but many of the alien voices, in particular, just do not fit. It is genuinely grating to hear a Trandoshan without a reptilian inflection or a Rodian missing their iconic vocal echo. Details like this do not matter much in the grand scheme, but they help make each species feel distinct. It is nice to see Huttese used frequently, given that this is a game centered on the criminal underworld of Star Wars.

Outlaws, at the end of the day, is just another Ubisoft open world game. I cannot help but wonder what we might have gotten if the experience were more focused, with the bloat stripped away and more development time spent enhancing what is already the strongest part of the game: the main story. All of the most interesting locations and events take place there, yet it still feels like not enough time is spent fleshing out the cast. The saving grace is that the open world does not feel as bloated as something like Assassin’s Creed Valhalla, and the different planets go a long way in breaking up the tedium. Fans of the Ubisoft formula will feel right at home, and those looking for their next adventure in the Star Wars universe have already endured so much mediocrity from the franchise that something slightly above average will feel like an oasis in the desert.

- graphics 9/10
- level/world design 8/10
- UI & controls 7/10
- gameplay (movement/combat/puzzles) 6/10
- rpg systems (gear customization, abilities, reputations, looting, crafting, vendors) 3/10
- writing (story/characters/dialog) 4/10

[b] pros: [/b]

The game looks incredible and runs very smoothly. The ambience and sound design is also very good as are all the alien races, and attention to detail with respect to world/level design. I like that it is heavily inspired by the original star wars movie trilogy and it definitely feels like you are walking (or speeding) around in an immersive star wars universe.

One notable thing about the gameplay for me was the addition of Nix, who is not just a cute companion but also can assist you with puzzles, stealth and combat. I thought this was generally well designed and implemented, however I found that in a lot of cases it is easier and quicker to just stun, stealth attack or blast an enemy in the head, than to use nix to distract or set traps which requires more preparation and good timing.

Another stand out feature was the space battles which were pretty fun and well made. I also like that there is no hard loading screen when landing or taking off from a planet which adds to the immersion.

[b] cons: [/b]

My main problem is the game is a linear story action game dressed up as an open world rpg. I found all of the underlying systems (abilities, gear customization, reputations, looting, crafting, vendors) were very shallow and there was very little motivation to engage with any of them and to explore the world, participate in events, and do side quests. The few side missions and intel locations I completed usually rewarded me with a collectible or cosmetic item which I personally don't care about. I would have enjoyed the game much more if it had more traditional rpg systems eg. experience points, level up system with attributes, skills, perks, more in depth crafting and gear customization.

Also I think the base difficulty of the combat needs to be a little higher, then you have incentive to actually put time into exploring, gathering materials and making your character stronger. I found that a lot of the abilities and upgrades are just there for flavour and none are necessary to complete the game, although some of them do make it easier or provide fun alternatives in combat.

The reputation system was interesting, but ultimately the decisions you make don't have any impact on the way the story unfolds, and it becomes an awkward balancing act of trying to keep factions in good standing. occasionally one faction will drop to terrible status and you have to spend a while looking for a contract (which are sometimes unavailable) or a vendor to sell encryption keys to. Not a terrible system but a lot of room for improvement.

I wont say too much about the story, as its more subjective, but I found the main character and her backstory to be quite boring and didn't really engage me at all. With a few exceptions most of the characters were boring and predictable, and the dialog was flat, sterile and lacking genuine human (or alien) emotions and personalities. There are a few attempts at humor, but I cant remember laughing at any of them :( Probably not as bad as some of Ubisoft's other recent games (cough AC mirage cough) but it does feel like all the writing has to go through some kind of ethical filter where all the gritty or potentially offensive material gets removed. I did enjoy the plot twist at the end after you finally complete the big heist and the occasional references to the original movies.

[b] summary: [/b]

Overall its a fun game if you treat it as a linear story/action game and not as an open world rpg. Set in a beautiful and immersive 'old school' star wars universe. I would say its worth it (just about) if you are a star wars fan and can pick it up on sale, but I cant whole heartedly recommend it when there are hundreds of other games out there that offer a more in depth, addictive rpg experience and more engaging story and characters.

Given the many negative reviews I had seen about the game, I started it with a lot of reluctance .
Today, after around fifty hours of gameplay, I have to say it’s a real knockout . 
The gameplay, while not revolutionary, is still very enjoyable and fun . 
The stealth is simple but effective, and the Ubisoft style open world works perfectly with the sheer number of activities on offer . 
But in my opinion, the game’s real strength lies in its Star Wars atmosphere, recreated with remarkable fidelity to the universe .
Riding a speeder across Tatooine, managing your reputation with the cartels, or playing a game of Sabacc between two contracts all contribute greatly to immersion . 
On top of that, there are some subtle references, such as Han Solo frozen in carbonite at Jabba’s palace, or mentions of the Clone Wars, Grievous, or the CIS .
Having started with many preconceived notions, I now believe this game is a must-play for fans of the franchise. In conclusion, if you love the Star Wars universe, go for it you won’t regret it .
That said, the game constantly oscillates between moments of total immersion and others where the limitations of the video game become all too noticeable .

Among the negative points :
The “you are leaving the mission” screen, which is particularly frustrating during single-attempt missions
Stealth sections that are sometimes not very engaging .
Bugs or development oversights: after dying and respawning, all enemies reappear, which is problematic during scripts that are supposed to completely clear an Imperial base .
Speeder handling with mouse or keyboard, neither option being truly satisfying .
Collision bugs with Nix and objects: funny at first, but quickly harmful to immersion .

[i]Star Wars Outlaws[/i] does not deserve all the hate it’s getting. In fact, it’s one of the most engaging games I’ve ever played. It’s one of those games I simply can’t stop playing. So why all the hate? From what I’ve heard, the game wasn’t very polished at launch, and a lot of the things that bothered people have since been fixed. It was marketed as an open world Star Wars game, and I think many players expected something closer to GTA or Cyberpunk, where you can do absolutely everything. But that’s not what this game is. Its mechanics are more limited, and for me, that’s completely fine.

The controls are okay. If you’re used to [i]The Division[/i] games, you’ll feel right at home. They can be a bit fidgety at times, but as long as you don’t rush, it’s manageable. Movement feels closer to [i]Uncharted[/i], which isn’t perfect either, but it works.

The storytelling is really good. I honestly couldn’t stop playing. You manipulate factions, earn their trust, and build a reputation that unlocks new gear and buffs. I love this system. You plan quests based on which reputation you want to max out, but it can also drop quickly if you double cross someone. The main quest is engaging and fun, and just focusing on it can keep you playing for hours. Add all the side quests, and you could play this game forever. This is one of the very few games, [i]Cyberpunk[/i] being the other, where I’m genuinely excited for the DLCs.

What about the downsides? The voice recording quality is pretty bad, and the sound perception isn’t great. It’s often hard to tell where enemies are based on their voices alone, which could have been handled much better. I already mentioned the controls, they don’t bother me personally, but there’s definitely room for improvement. The game loop is repetitive, like most games, but I actually enjoy sneaking, shooting, and looting. The AI is also quite bad, almost stupid, but it feels intentionally designed that way for the stealth loop. Once you figure out a method, you can take down many enemies stealthily with Nix, your companion.

The graphics are outstanding overall, but Kay’s face could have been better. I’m sure the real life model is beautiful, so this feels like a limitation of the engine rather than a design choice. I would also have liked some extra features, such as hair customization, the ability to create a personal safe place, or even getting a different ship. But at this point, I’m just listing things from my wishlist.

I must say, this is a [b]10/10[/b] for me. The graphics are amazing, I’m playing on a 4090, the music is great, the quests are engaging, stealing is satisfying, and the game loop is a lot of fun.

This is the Star Wars game that truly makes you feel like you’re living in the Star Wars universe. I honestly can’t stop playing it. [b]Highly recommended.[/b]

Performance and graphics. I just came from playing through AC Mirage to this game, and I would say the graphic quality to my untrained eye were about the same (caveat, there were a ton of new models and lots of detail introduced in Outlaws, while I can't say the same for the recycled bits in Mirage). That is to say, the graphics were good but it didn't necessarily blow me away. One of the reasons for that is the compromises I had to make to achieve a solid 60fps in 2K resolution on a 4070 super. I had to use DLSS framegen to achieve this, which is unacceptable in my opinion. As a result, any time I'm zooming in my speeder you can tell the framegen is struggling to keep up and becomes visibly blurry, pixilated, or delayed. Or if I'm watching a cutscene, I can see the blurry pixilated mess of hair strands around Kay's head. For a game released the same year as my card, it essentially means that in order to play it without AI tricks, I would have had to spend four times as much money on my graphics card. It very much shows that the devs started by aiming for the top end of the specs and then attempted to bolt on options to scale down the graphics in order to meet performance benchmarks, and had to use AI tools as a crutch in addition to that. Again, having come straight from AC Mirage, released just months prior to the 4070 super being released, you can clearly tell that they developed that game with a more modest spec sheet in mind, and scaled UP to beautiful the game for higher spec machines. It's hailed as the "first open-world Star Wars game," and as far as first attempts go, it's not a bad one. It's an ambitious idea with an execution that works in some ways, and flops in others.
The core gameplay is where Outlaws excels. Running firefights against pirates, shootouts with gangsters, and sneaking around Imperial bases are peak Star Wars, and this game hits that mark each time. That said, riding around jungles, open fields or deserts to search for every little secret that offers rewards that amount to a cosmetic change or an upgrade that offers minimal changes is a drag.
The main story (no spoilers here) is good, to a point. The main character feels like they tried to make Rey with a heavy dose of classic Han Solo. It works, but again, only to a point. There are times where Kay Vess feels very two-dimensional and mediocre as a character. The narrative, however, suffers from the problem of having high stakes but no urgency or impact. In short: A heist goes wrong, and you're marked for death by a powerful syndicate. You'd expect agents of that syndicate to hound your every step, right? Aside from the story missions, where the encounters are very scripted, you almost never face off against the Zerek Besh syndicate. And this lack of impact and urgency is felt in the Reputation System too. There are four factions to work with and take contracts from. Work with them, your rep goes up. Work against them, your rep goes down. This primarily just gets you faction-specific cosmetics, and makes navigation of specific areas much easier. You can also use special dialogue options with high enough rep, but ultimately, this is a system that reflects the story: The player is presented with high stakes, but there's very little payoff or impact from the choices. You'll still be able to take contracts from those factions and get your rep back up to what it used to be.
The biggest criticism is the same one I had for Solo: A Star Wars Story: One person double-crossing you is a sucker punch. Making it a consistent happening is just lazy writing. Especially when it's established at the beginning that people will double-cross you at any given point.
All that aside, though, this game is fun. Is it worth replaying to try other routes through the narrative? Yeah, maybe on a really slow week. If you're willing to commit the hours to it, there's definitely enough to keep you entertained. Do I like this game? Yes. Could it be better? Definitely. If it's on sale, I'd recommend picking it up.

This game isn’t the disaster that the internet has made it out to be—but it absolutely is a game held back by some baffling design choices. 
Underneath the controversy and noise, there’s a genuinely fun open-world Star Wars experience here. The gunplay works. The planets feel alive. The outlaw fantasy has potential. But Ubisoft once again managed to kneecap its own product by ignoring what players actually want.
Let’s start with the elephant in the room: Kay Vess.
Ubisoft created a protagonist that is visually awkward in a way that feels intentional. Her face looks strangely constructed, flat in cutscenes, and oddly proportioned—especially noticeable when standing next to a much better-designed supporting character. What makes this more confusing is that the voice actress looks significantly better than the in-game model, which raises the obvious question: why didn’t Ubisoft use her likeness? 
Games like Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order and Survivor proved how effective that approach is with Cameron Monaghan. If you’re trying to build a new franchise with a new hero, you want that character to be instantly recognizable, appealing, and memorable—not distracting. 
Instead, Kay ends up looking like a potato, like she received less design attention than the NPCs around her, which is a strange choice when she’s supposed to carry the entire game and potentially a sequel. 
This ties into a broader issue in modern gaming: a visible trend toward deliberately unattractive character design, especially for female protagonists. It’s not that people are against strong women—far from it—but when every modern AAA game seems to follow the same aesthetic and ideological template, it becomes stale. Players don’t want every protagonist to feel like they came from the same design committee. I mean, hell, people who are overweight don’t design their characters in games that allow them to be fatties; they create their characters all in the image that pleases themselves, or even how they desire to look. It’s basic human psychological behavior. 
Customization would have solved this.
This game screams for a character creator. Even if Ubisoft wanted to keep Kay as a named protagonist (like Assassin’s Creed does), giving players male/female options, hairstyles, facial features, and customization would massively increase immersion and replayability. In 2025, it’s absurd that a massive Ubisoft open-world game doesn’t allow you to customize your character beyond outfits and weapon skins. 
Even better, Ubisoft missed an obvious slam-dunk: This should have been a bounty hunter game.
The outlaw theme is fun, but a full bounty-hunter system—procedural targets, tracking, reputation, and contracts—would have made this game infinitely more replayable. The Star Wars universe is tailor-made for that loop, and it would’ve fit perfectly with syndicates, reputation systems, and open-world exploration. 
If EA didn’t have the nemesis system locked behind a copyright, that would be a dope game to play.
Technically, the game is a mixed bag. 
I’m running it on a 4070 Super, and performance has been mostly smooth—but that doesn’t excuse some of Ubisoft’s typical mess. The syndicate reward bug is still present, which is unacceptable this long after launch. Ubisoft has a long history of releasing games in a half-finished state and patching them slowly (or not at all), and Outlaws sadly continues that tradition—just look at what happened with Skull & Bones. 
Graphically, forced ray tracing is another problem. The fact that you can’t fully disable RT means you’re stuck with reflective static floors and weird lighting artifacts no matter how much you tweak the settings. Players should be able to choose performance or visuals—not be locked into Ubisoft’s idea of what looks “cinematic.” 
And the fanbase has its own list of frustrations:
•	Stealth is inconsistent and often punishing.
•	Enemy AI is dumb one moment and psychic the next
•	Gunplay lacks punch compared to other modern shooters.
•	Missions feel repetitive.
•	Syndicate systems feel underdeveloped.
•	Choices don’t meaningfully affect the story. 
I mean, Christ, you couldn’t even shoot from your speeder when it first came out. That was one of the craziest things to experience, then seeing the developer in an interview make an excuse of how it wasn’t possible. We all have played RDR2; we know it’s possible to shoot from a horse. Don’t blatantly gaslight gamers because you’re incompetent. 
But none of these complaints are deal-breakers on their own—but together, they create a feeling that this game needed another six to twelve months in the oven. 
The frustrating part is that Star Wars Outlaws has real potential. 
The world design is strong. The Star Wars atmosphere is there. The core gameplay loop is fun. But Ubisoft’s refusal to listen to players—and their obsession with design trends instead of player freedom—keeps holding the game back. 
This isn’t a bad game. 
It’s a good game trapped inside a mediocre one. 
And that’s honestly the most Ubisoft thing imaginable.

I see a lot of negative reviews on Steam, but the bottom line is that this is a stealth game. If you enjoy sneaking and viewing combat as a last resort, you will likely enjoy this game. I played the game the first time around with all difficulty sliders maxed, so in my experience, stealth was mandatory because combat was fairly difficult early on. Your experience may vary. If you want to collect an arsenal of powerful weapons and become an unstoppable killing machine, there are games that will scratch that itch. Go play Doom or something. This is a stealth game. 90% of the tools you're given are to evade your opponents and sneak past them. This is a stealth game. If you don't enjoy stealth mechanics, this game is not for you because it is a stealth game. So now you know what you're getting into.

My biggest critique is that it's often unclear where to go when platforming/climbing to an area. Ledges that you can jump to or areas that you can climb are inconsistent and not always visible. I never got stuck anywhere, but it took me an annoying amount of time in certain areas jumping to my death a few times trying to figure out which ledges I could grab and which ones I couldn't.

Other than that, the game doesn't handhold you. Like, at all. You will probably find yourself looking up how to find stuff, how to do certain things, or how some mechanics work. That might be frustrating for some players, refreshing for others. I personally didn't mind because it didn't feel like I was being spoon-fed the game. Just like Kay, you're plopped into an unfamiliar world and have to just figure it out. I had to pause and think critically about certain things or look stuff up instead of blindly following the nav marker on the compass. A genuinely great game that doesn't deserve the negativity hurled at it. As a Star Wars game, Outlaws features a good mix of new and old: it's space western samurai meets the classic heist trope. Tattooine has the same score it's known for, with details like Luke's old homestead and a fully explorable Mos Eisley. Across the galaxy we have Akiva, where we explore a sprawling CIS droid factory sleeping under the towns and jungles. We've got an easy to hate bad guy who never blinks when he's on the screen. A cast of lovable misfits filling in our crew roster, recruited specifically for breaking into a guarded vault for the score of a lifetime. And of course, Kay Vess: a refreshingly honest portrayal of a girl in the middle who has to pull it all off -or else-. The acting does a great job of feeling real: get caught where you're not meant to and you'll briefly stammer an excuse, or when plans go awry you'll pick up on Kay's frustration.

The story has a good pace, and even if you think you can spot all the surprise twists, it'll still surprise you in places. And I have to stress - this is a true open world game. You can go from cruising around an open area, into the port where your ship rests, take off and watch in real time as you break the atmosphere, and have a good chuck of the surrounding space to explore, loot and dogfight in. A quick hyperdrive jump/loading transition takes you to the next orbit where you do it all over again. And if that get's old for you, you can fast travel from almost anywhere to any previously discovered fast travel node, regardless of which planet it's on. A quick black loading screen and you're just there. 

I have one single nitpick about this game, and it is this: it falls victim to the same bloat that so many other Ubisoft open world games have. It doesn't have malicious, pay-to-win "time saver" dlc like Black Flag, but there is so many discractions, collectables and syndicate jobs that fully completing it would demand a lot of time and energy. The sheer number of named areas concealing a treasure chest on your map will easily reach the hundreds by the time you've finished exploring the last planet.

Star Wars Outlaws – Missed Potential

I was really looking forward to playing a new Star Wars game. I love the franchise, and I was genuinely excited to finally play something other than a Jedi. The idea of being a bounty hunter, living in the criminal underworld, making shady deals, and surviving as an outlaw sounded incredible.

Unfortunately, that’s where the praise mostly ends, because the idea of Star Wars Outlaws is the best part of the game.

You don’t actually feel like a bandit. You don’t feel like an outlaw. Instead, you feel like a stock protagonist with a rough upbringing who is secretly a good person. I don’t want to feel like the hero. I don’t want to feel like the good guy. I want to steal things, betray factions, and feel like those choices actually matter. Nothing in this game feels worth stealing or betraying anyone over, and that completely kills the fantasy.

On top of that, progression can be frustrating. A lot of the time I wasn’t even sure where the game wanted me to go or which mission I needed to do next. I would get distracted running around the map doing side quests and sometimes forget what the main story even was. If the story is going to be this basic, why not let me create my own character? Let me immerse myself in my own outlaw fantasy. Instead, you are locked into Kay, with customization limited to changing her outfits.

To be fair, it is cool that most cosmetics are earned through gameplay rather than microtransactions. But honestly, every other character you meet is more interesting than Kay. Even her name feels uninspired. In a galaxy where literally anything is possible, we went with Kay.

The standout character for me was ND, the combat droid from the Clone Wars era. He is awesome and has so much personality and presence. I kept thinking, why isn’t this guy the main character? It really highlights how much missed potential there is here.

The DLC, though, is the best part of the entire experience. It is the only time I actually felt like I was gambling, scheming, and caught in a real bandit conflict. I won’t spoil anything, but if you buy this game at all, buy it with the DLC. It was the first time I felt genuinely intrigued and engaged.

Factions: One of the Strongest Systems

The gang faction system is actually really well done. I liked earning reputation with different factions and betraying others. Higher reputation unlocking vendors, gear, and safe access to faction areas is a great idea. Not getting shot on sight alone makes grinding reputation worth it.

I do think it could have gone a bit further. For example, if you reach excellent reputation with a faction, you should be able to access restricted areas without consequences. Maybe even call in faction reinforcements during missions. That would add more incentive and make reputation feel even more impactful. Still, overall, this system was executed very well.

Looting, Stealing, and the Outlaw Problem

Raids and treasure areas are extremely underwhelming. Most of them are copy paste rooms with the same looting animation every time. You don’t even see what you picked up unless you dig through your inventory, where you are greeted with a terrible UI hologram and a short description.

Most of the time, the treasure is worth only a few hundred credits, so the sense of accomplishment is basically nonexistent.

And for a game about being an outlaw, why is there no pickpocketing? Outside of Nix stealing grenades or keycards, that is it. Coming from games like Assassin’s Creed, this feels like a massive missed opportunity. Why can’t I steal speeders and sell them, or at least ride them around? Why can’t I feel like I am actually living a criminal lifestyle?

You can technically steal weapons, but only until the magazine runs out. After that, it is back to the same pistol for the entire game, just with upgrades. It gets old fast.

Clunky Gameplay and Weak Combat

The gameplay feels clunky, especially for a Ubisoft title. Mantling and climbing do not feel natural at all. You can only climb exactly what the game allows. For an open world game, the openness feels very restricted. I constantly found myself hunting for specific climbable paths just to reach my objective.

The grappling hook, which should be fun, is painfully slow. I often avoided using it entirely because it was faster to find another route. Traversal in general feels like a chore.

Combat is fine if I am being generous. You shoot brain dead AI with a blaster, and that is about it. It feels overly simplified and unchallenging. Stealth is barely supported, with only a handful of repetitive melee animations that get boring almost immediately. There is no depth and no challenge, and it makes the entire experience feel dull.

Space combat is pretty cool, especially once you upgrade your ship. And going into hyperspace never gets old. That part is genuinely awesome.

Presentation, Atmosphere, and Missed Immersion

Visually, the game looks great. I caught myself stopping just to admire environments and Easter eggs. The set design and world detail really sell the Star Wars universe.

That said, the world does not feel alive. Outside of city areas with scripted AI, most planets feel empty, especially familiar ones like Tatooine. I really wish they explored more original planets instead of recycling locations we have seen countless times already.

Mini games like Sabacc are a highlight and genuinely fun. I even think they would work great as multiplayer features in future games. But limiting gambling, like horse racing, to only a few attempts feels weird. Aren’t we supposed to be outlaws? Even basic immersion stuff is missing. You cannot order a drink at a cantina. I am a street rat criminal, but I can't buy a beer.

There are small moments I enjoyed, especially interactions with Nix. The food bars and quick time events are cute, even if they do not affect the story. That said, I was not a huge fan of Nix being such a central part of the game. Sometimes he breaks immersion, like when he bites a main villain and makes them look unintimidating. It can feel more like a merchandising decision than a storytelling one.

The Easter eggs, especially on Tatooine, were great. Han’s cantina, Luke’s farm, and nods to Anakin’s podracing all made me geek out a bit. Those moments, along with overhearing conversations in cantinas, are when the game comes closest to feeling immersive.

Final Verdict

I would give Star Wars Outlaws a 5 out of 10.

There are some genuinely great Star Wars moments, strong visuals, and a solid faction system, but the gameplay is boring, the combat lacks depth, and the outlaw fantasy never fully lands. The story is just o"kay".
If you want to explore a start wars setting game buy this but if you're in it for more, just wait. 
I would recommend buying this on sale, preferably with the DLC. It is not worth more than 30 dollars, and even then, you are mainly paying for the potential rather than the execution.

Star Wars Outlaws suffered from a fate of its own making: expectations. Creating the first major non lightsaber focused Star Wars game in years naturally drew a lot of attention. In my opinion, those expectations were not met.

-Steam Curator: store.steampowered.com/curator/36307721-Healthy-Criticism/

Before getting into the issues, a brief overview of what Star Wars Outlaws is. It is an open world third person shooter set in the Star Wars universe. You are required to manage your reputation with three main factions, plus a bonus faction, across their respective planets.

The gameplay loop largely revolves around picking up main quests and completing them until you reach progression walls. These walls strongly encourage completing side quests in order to move forward. While technically optional, the emphasis on completing them is clear.

Faction reputation is easy to lose and equally easy to restore, but doing so often requires engaging with repetitive and tedious side quests. There is very little variety here. While some repetition is expected, the sheer number of these quests makes the problem more noticeable.

On a technical level, the game has some baffling design decisions. Depth of field cannot be disabled and is frequently forced on the player. It activates when aiming down sights and during cinematics, often obscuring the image and becoming distracting.

The dialogue is one of the game’s weakest elements. Delivery is flat, the protagonist feels restrained and emotionally disconnected, and the writing plays things far too safe. It appears to aim for a Han Solo inspired character, but lacks the charisma and tension needed to make that work. Even in high stakes moments, the dialogue fails to convey urgency or danger.

Gunplay is serviceable but limited. You are restricted to a single blaster, with alternate firing modes that can only be changed aboard your ship. While enemy weapons can be picked up, they are discarded once their ammo runs out, further limiting combat variety.

The open world can look appealing at times, but often feels purposeless. Exploration mostly consists of moving from point A to point B, with occasional minor detours that offer little reward. Dialogue sequences frequently lock you out of fast travel or space travel until they finish, further disrupting pacing. Combined with the lack of role playing systems, this limits player expression. You cannot create a class, develop a build, or meaningfully shape dialogue outcomes.

Stealth missions are often mandatory and result in instant failure if you are detected. Enemy AI behavior is predictable, and immersion suffers when enemies can be silently knocked out with little resistance. This is especially true when you can simply bonk a stormtrooper's helmet with your bear hands and knock them out effortlessly. Progression is largely tied to repeating specific actions multiple times to unlock new abilities, which feels more like checklist completion than organic growth.

You are meant to play as an outlaw operating in the most dangerous parts of the Star Wars universe, yet the underworld presented here feels heavily sanitized. There is little sense of lawlessness, danger, or consequence, undermining the fantasy the game is built around.

I went into Star Wars Outlaws wanting to like it. Despite the mixed reviews, I gave it a chance because I genuinely love the Star Wars universe—and more importantly, I love good Star Wars games.

Unfortunately, my experience so far has been deeply disappointing.

From a technical standpoint, the game struggles constantly on PC. Textures frequently appear blurred or fail to load properly, breaking immersion almost immediately. On top of that, the game crashes from time to time, despite the fact that my hardware is more than capable of running modern titles like this one. This is not a low-end system issue—it’s a clear case of poor optimization, at least on the PC/Steam version.

What makes this even more frustrating is Ubisoft’s decision to cancel the sequel while shifting blame onto the audience, claiming that players no longer want Star Wars games. That argument feels disingenuous. Players don’t dislike Star Wars—they dislike poorly executed games. Proof of that is my recent experience with Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order. Even though it’s relatively simple and linear, it delivers a polished, engaging experience that respects both the player and the franchise. I had a blast with it, which is precisely why I decided to give Outlaws a chance.

Sadly, the criticism surrounding Outlaws turned out to be accurate.

For the brief moments when the game actually runs well, it’s genuinely impressive. The animations are excellent, the graphics can look stunning, the stealth gameplay is fun, and the lore feels authentic and well-crafted. In those short windows, the game shows real potential and reminds you of what it could have been.

But those moments don’t last.

After just a few minutes, the experience starts to fall apart—stuttering becomes noticeable, texture quality drops dramatically, and crashes pull you out of the game entirely. What’s especially concerning is that this is happening right at the beginning (early missions), which should be the most polished portion of the experience. It raises serious concerns about how the game performs later on. I’m hesitant to invest more hours only to discover that the technical issues worsen over time. I constantly spending more time re-opening the game, than actually playing it.

In the end, Star Wars Outlaws feels like a game with strong artistic vision and solid design ideas that are completely undermined by technical instability and poor PC performance. It’s not that players don’t want Star Wars games—we want games that are finished, optimized, and worthy of the universe they’re set in. Unfortunately, this one doesn’t meet that standard.

[h2]A Galaxy Worth Exploring, If Your PC Can Handle It and if You Can Handle...Intermittent Crashes[/h2]
Star Wars Outlaws nails what matters most: feeling like you're in the Star Wars universe. The atmospheric design is exceptional—every locale drips with that lived-in aesthetic the franchise does so well. From bustling cantinas to desolate frontier outposts, Massive Entertainment clearly understood the assignment. The RTX lighting deserves special mention; it's genuinely immersive, lending each environment a cinematic quality that makes you want to just... linger.

The voice acting and narrative are genuine strengths. The performances land, the writing keeps you engaged, and the story threads pull you through the campaign with purpose. Combat strikes a satisfying balance too—gunplay and stealth both feel appropriately scrappy for an outlaw who's not a Jedi or trained soldier. There's an endearing awkwardness to it that fits the character. Also note that this awkwardness apply to the movement, and gunplay.

Nyx, your merqaal companion, deserves his own spotlight. The little creature adds genuine charm, warmth, and moments of levity that elevate the experience beyond typical solo action fare. He's not just a gameplay gimmick—he gives the journey more heart. In a franchise known for memorable sidekicks, Nyx earns his place in a physical way, like a dog companion would.

Space sequences, while not groundbreaking, serve as a welcome change of pace from the on-foot action. They're a nice complement rather than a main attraction.

Note: I haven't spent significant time with the crew mechanics yet, so I can't speak to that aspect of the game.

[h2]The Technical Elephant in the Room[/h2]
Here's where frustration sets in. Coming from the team behind The Division, the technical state is baffling. The game crashes like clockwork every 90–120 minutes. VRAM usage leaks relentlessly—starting around 8–9GB on an RTX 5080, then climbing until the experience degrades into a slideshow or an outright crash. A year post-launch, on high-end hardware, this shouldn't be happening.
It's a shame, because every crash yanks you out of a world that's otherwise easy to get lost in.

[b]In a nutshell:[/b] A deeply atmospheric Star Wars experience worth it for people who appreciate the universe (I'm not a fan, but definitely a lover of [i]some[/i] of the movies/series ) undermined by persistent technical instability. Worth playing—just good thing autosave is  present...

To escape the squalor of Canto Bight and it's wealth built on the Galactic Military Industrial complex, she decides to pull a major heist to steal her freedom. Kay's part in the heist is completed perfectly, but the team she partnered with betrays her at the last moment and she is captured by a ruthless crime lord. Deus ex machina strikes and she miraculously escapes death's clutches. So dramatic! After escaping you steal the evil white man's starship and blast off to freedom. TLDR: When this was announced I got curious. A year ago I saw the hate and avoided. I remained curious and got it on sale. I do not regret this. Maybe I should have gave it a go earlier. This is a solid Star Wars game with decent gameplay, good visuals/environments and a fun story that does not focus on Jedi/Sith Good vs Evil cheese (So far at least...).

[b]Performance[/b]
It runs really well on my system even if its not all ultra settings. So it looks great and runs smooth in 2k res.

My PC is not superb but I have a decent 4 year old processor, a cheaper 4000 series gpu and 32GB RAM.

[b]Visuals and Sounds[/b]
The environment artists earned their money, it is so pretty and interesting to explore so far. I've seen only two planets and the prologue area but they're all beautiful. I've also noticed zero frame drops so far. 

I think the sound design is really good and authentic to Star Wars media in terms of blasters and speeders etc. It's mixed well and I never struggle to hear voice lines over other things. The voice acting is decent nothing ground breaking but fits the game and tone.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is fun and the AI is a bit easy but hey I'm here to have fun not torture myself in my free time. 

Combat is not hard but you can get caught out. Kay isn't invincible. If you miss your shots and don't take cover you can die. 9/10 times though you can run away if getting overwhelmed. 
Stealth is also easy but again I don't torture myself for perfect runs or hard difficulties.
So the gameplay is fine but it does seem like it might get repetitive eventually.

[b]Story, Tone and Star Wars[/b]
The story and writing so far is not amazing but solid standard for a singleplayer open world game. If you want focus and tight writing open worlds don't usually have that. This is solid not revolutionary.

Also  I'm familiar with Star Wars in general and I always liked the stories that were not about the Jedi and Sith. My favourite thing in the universe is Andor. This game isn't as gritty or realistic as Andor felt but its a fun representation of being a criminal in the Star Wars universe. Imo it so far hasn't hit that family friendly cheese so much star wars media does. So if you like the setting but prefer a more grounded story you will probably like this.

[b]Overall[/b]
Overall this is a solid game a 6 or 7 out of 10. I feel I got a great deal on the price. Knowing what I know now I probably would've bought it a while back for £30 I saw one time. I feel like decently good games get slammed these days for no reason. I don't see any of the negatives I had heard about so far. This is a solid game totally worth it on discount.

Star Wars Outlaws (Steam – PC) Review

When Star Wars Outlaws first launched, I had my doubts. Performance hitches, minor bugs, and uneven pacing dulled what could’ve been an incredible experience. But now that Ubisoft has patched and polished it, I can confidently say: this game absolutely delivers; especially for fans who’ve always wanted to live in the Star Wars underworld.

What sets Outlaws apart is its restraint. This isn’t another Jedi-centered storyline or Force-heavy epic; it’s something grittier, more grounded. You step into the shoes of Kay Vess, a thief and survivor navigating a galaxy ruled by Syndicates, Imperials, and opportunists. It’s refreshing to experience Star Wars from street level - to cut deals, steal ships, and explore new corners of a galaxy that finally feels alive again.

The open world is vibrant and layered, filled with races, rogue traders, and unexpected encounters that make wandering worthwhile. The visual detail is stellar on PC, especially after the latest patches, and the DualSense controller setup adds some satisfying tactile feedback during dogfights and blaster duels. Missions now run smoothly, with load times and framerate issues largely handled; leaving you free to lose yourself in the slice-of-life chaos of being a name in the galaxy’s criminal mix.

As someone who reveres the Original Trilogy and appreciates the creativity of the old Expanded Universe (while ignoring most modern Disney takes), this game struck a chord. It respects the feel of Star Wars - the texture, the humor, the worn edges; without leaning on nostalgia or lightsabers. It doesn’t try to rewrite the galaxy. It simply opens it up, invites you in, and says: “Go make your own story.”

In short, if you’ve ever wanted to live Star Wars from the ground up  - not as a hero, but as a hustler - Star Wars Outlaws finally makes that fantasy real. It’s not perfect, but it’s daring, immersive, and genuinely fun. A solid return to form for those of us who still believe the magic of Star Wars lives between the margins of its biggest legends.

[h1]First of all: [/h1]
If you like Star Wars and this game is on sale, give it a try! I love Star Wars but i would not consider myself a "fan" either, i have watched the movies, couple of TV shows and played both Jedi Survivor and Jedi Fallen Order, as well as some other games but thats about it.

It is the first open-world singleplayer Star Wars game, so that in and of itself is pretty cool and worth checking out in my opinion.

[h2]As for the review:[/h2]

[h2]Performance:[/h2]
The game runs wonderfully for me from start to finish, idk what people are yapping about, maybe the people reviewing don't have the specs to run a 2024 AAA game and just blame it on the devs.

I played on high settings on a 32:9 monitor and it ran very smoothly and looked stunning.

[h2]Story:[/h2]
I think the story is pretty mid, the characters are also mid (except for nix, he's the goat), but all in all i would say that its biggest weakness is that the games main storyline is too short to establish any meaningfull bond with any of the characters (appart from Kay and Nix).

The story isn't bad, don't get me wrong, it's just not the aspect i will remember this game for, at all.

[h2]Gameplay:[/h2]
It's an open-world in structure but a stealth game in design. The main missions are 90% stealth and side missions are a bit more diverse from what i can tell, but it is still very heavy on stealth.

But in my  opinion it's not the "annoying" type of stealth, if something goes wrong you can mostly shoot your way through the rest of the mission, which i enjoy.

Other than that, it is responsive, the stealth i straight forward and enjoyable, the shooting is decent, the driving and space ship stuff is easy but engaging enough to be very enjoyable.

[h2]The world:[/h2]
Obviously the world building is great, it's Star Wars, the planets are beatiful, so is space (especially on OLED), the overall textures are great and lighting is too. Nothing much to complain visually.

Gameplay wise the world is also engaging and feels alive and populated. its fun to traverse thanks to plenty of stuff to see, as well as little jumps and stuff to do on the speeder while you travel.

[h2]The accessibility:[/h2]

I love the way this game enable you to change difficulty for indiviual aspects of the game, there are also plenty of options for people with disabilities so thats always nice.

[h2]Other stuff:[/h2]
The lockpicking and hacking in this game is extremely fun, lockpicking is basically a little rythm mini game and hacking is basically Wordle wit little symbols instead of letters.

The Star Wars vibes are immaculate, from the music, to the UI and the nods to the movies etc, its a really good game immersion wise.

Overall i'd say this game isn't perfect, but it oozes with charm and it's biggest flaw is that it is too short. Oh, and that it doesn't really run on Steamdeck, understandable of course, but still a bummer.

[h2]I will give it a 7/10[/h2]
It's a game that is not trying to be anything more than it is, which a lot of games fall victim to. It's nothing ground breaking or revolutionary, but it is a good ol' videogame, and i kinda missed ubisoft these past years since i haven't kept up with their games since like 2020, i think people treat them too harshly compared to other companies that make legit dog doodoo games, but hey, thats a debate for another day.

The stealth isn't breaking any new ground and feels like the whole design package is from last decade - Binary stealth: on/off grass you can enter, cameras rotating with clear "found" zones, every enemy has amnesia, and area-wide alerts are immediate if you don't do a takedown and instead knock them out with a punch. 

There's also still bugs with reloads being needed a few times. And some odd design/writing problems with the players ability to tackle whatever they want. While some parts stand out as excellent, most of the gameplay and story feel like they're struggling to hold together and carry it across the finish line.

Typical Unisoft game. World is rendered well but player interactions shallow and unrewarding. Gameplay loop involves traveling across the map to pick up individual items or trigger dialogue in a way that feels like the world is merely a slow way of navigating one big menu. The player is asked to travel 10 minutes, pick up an object, travel 10 minutes back again, trigger a dialogue cut scene then be prompted to go do another variation of the same thing.

Honestly, I am surprised on how good this was.
The maps, especially Tattooine, are 1:1 modeled after the "original maps" that were released when Star Wars first premiered. Sure, the scale is wrong, but it's still true to the originals. 

That being said, it seems that 7 or so major patches have gotten rid of the major bugs.
I did not play the game when it came out, but when it was on sale for 20 bucks. 
Is it a Ubisoft Open World where you climb towers to reveal areas? No!

It was refreshing to see an interesting approach to exploration and skills. 
I do not want to spoil too much about the "leveling" process but in my opinion it's well executed. 

The additional options like "turn off yellow climbables" are super refreshing. 

For the bad part:
Kay Vess, as a protagonist, is often very unlikeable and her features are bordering on the uncanny valley. 
Her choices are inconsistent
The plot itself is okay. You can see story elements coming from a million miles away, but it's also not "OH HEY MARK!". 

While I know this game was riddled with horrendous bugs and bad enemies at launch, dare I say it became a playable and enjoyable Star Wars title? Yes. 

Would I play the story again? Probably not.

I'd give this game 82/100.

One thing Star Wars Outlaws genuinely does well is making me feel like I’m living in the Star Wars universe, not just playing through another high-stakes, galaxy-saving storyline. This is a nice deviation from the usual epic Jedi narratives the franchise often leans on. Instead of destiny, chosen ones, or world-ending threats, Outlaws lets me exist in the day-to-day underbelly of the galaxy

The world design, visuals, and overall atmosphere are easily the game’s strongest elements. Environments are detailed and believable, packed with small touches that sell the fantasy.

The gameplay itself feels surprisingly shallow for a modern AAA release. Combat lacks weight and variety, stealth feels basic, and many missions fall into familiar open-world patterns without doing much to evolve them.

Character animations are another weak point. Facial expressions and movement can be stiff, which is especially noticeable during dialogue and cutscenes. It’s frustrating because the environments look so good, yet the characters inhabiting them sometimes feel oddly lifeless

Customization exists, but it’s mostly cosmetic and shallow. Gear upgrades and abilities rarely change how I approach the game in meaningful ways, making progression feel flatter than it should.

In the end, Star Wars Outlaws feels like a game with an incredible sense of place but underwhelming execution. I enjoyed my time with it mostly because I love Star Wars and because the world itself is such a joy to explore.

Ok, so, here's my full review if you want to hear more:
[Disclaimer]: I went into this game blind; I read quite a lot of reviews, but I hadn't seen any gameplay except for the show-case and the trailer. I'm a huge Star Wars fan, so obviously my review is biased. I also bought the game on sale for 20 bucks. I also haven't finished the game yet, so my review is probably incomplete. I'll branch my thoughts into some seperate topics, but I'll start with the main-point first. There's some editorial remarks at the end after having completed the game.

First, what needs to be said: This game is a typical Ubisoft game. Meaning there's a LOT of side-quest with (somewhat) pointless collectibles as a reward, and an open-world game without a real sense of freedom. I don't mind linear games, and this game definitely didn't need to be open world for it to be fun. I'd rather have had a Fallen Order experience with linear gameplay and some slight room for deviation, and it seems this game wants to offer more freedom without letting go of your hand. My biggest critique would be the price. I can see how much love has been put into the details, and this game's been made by people who're clearly star wars-fans, but at the same time the gameplay is really not worth the $70. Let me go into detail a bit between the good and the bad.

[Story]: It's ok. It's there, and it's fun.... kind of? I don't care about it, but it's fun to see the characters do things. I'm not bored by it either. I agree with some that the story should feel more heavy and serious, and the main character is not taking herself seriously. She's naive for the sake of tutorial, and suddenly jumps to 'I'm the most experiences scoundrel' without it being earned. Yet, the robot and the little creature are fun-ish. You'll see 'plot-twists' coming miles ahead, don't expect mind-blowing plot, but it's fun to see characters react to your choices. Then again, I still can't really remember the characters names, which says a lot about their depth.

[Gameplay]: Very ambiguous in how much fun it is. I'm playing on 'scoundrel' difficulty (3/4) and it can be challenging at times. You can't go guns-blazing, so you do have to get creative at some points. Your pet is useful, your gun is not. It's just AC-stealth (think Odyssey) with a gun. Once you use your gun though, it becomes an incredibly generic shooter and it's definitely not the most fun part. 
Also, it surprised me there was ship-combat at all, but it feels like lego-star wars; incredibly easy. Kinda like a mini-game. And even Lego understood it's not fun being attacked every 5 seconds.

[Immersion/graphics]: This is really why you play the game. It's a set piece of Star Wars and it's beautiful. Almost every scene, you'll go 'woah that looks awesome'. Ubisoft does know how to put the details where they belong, and in terms of world-building, this is a love letter to the franchise. I've heard people complain about Tatooine, but I haven't been there yet and so far all the worlds feel alive, and real. I've also seen people complain about the main character's looks... pls get over yourself. However, I do think being able to customize her hair would've been a nice touch. But there's plenty of options for customization. Although I do think your speeder/ship customization is quite lacking. There's plenty of options, but essentially they're all 50 shades of grey (ba dum ts). But this game looks absolutely beautiful in every way.

[Sound]: Another slam-dunk by Ubisoft. The soundtrack, the lasers, the speeder, the ships, the background noises, the creatures... it's all top-notch. And it's all so well mastered. Nothing to complain here, only props for the sound-designers.

[Performance/Bugs]: There's some jank. I've read reports of crashed games, but haven't experienced that yet myself. However, the climbing mechanics are quite awful (which is hilarious to me, given this company's made ac and still can't do free-running properly xD) and really janky. Stealth-takedowns makes people teleport, there's framerate drops in big areas and who thought the 'use for everything' button should be r3 (for controller)? It's not 'cyberpunk that just got released bad', but it's too janky for a $70 game.

[Unique mechanics]: The game has, as far as I know, two unique mechanics: Reputation and Sabacc.
Reputation is essentially gta's 'respect+', but I do think they use it a bit more actively. Eventually you can max out your reputation with everyone, and I think it would've been more fun to see you having to constantly choose between factions, as I think it is a good idea to never allow players to max out all factions. Yet, it's fun to see the world react to your rep, and being able to double-cross factions. 
Sabacc is a card game (the one Han played against Lando and won his ship) and I think they implemented it in a very fun way. It's like texas hold' em, with some more opportunities to screw people over. 

Conclusion:
This is a fun game if you like Star Wars, and stealth-games. It's immersive, fun to play, but also janky with a 'meh' story. I'd pay 40 bucks for it max, buy in discount.

Editorial notes after completion:

Star Wars Outlaws Review: A Beautiful but Hollow Experience
After two days of playing Star Wars Outlaws, I can say without a doubt that this game has potential but it feels vastly incomplete. Beneath its gorgeous visuals lies a shallow experience that struggles to deliver on the promise of being an RPG.

Gameplay: Cooldowns and Limited Choice
You’re stuck with the same blaster throughout the game. Yes, it can be upgraded, but the cooldowns for useful abilities like stun are outrageously high, making combat feel dull and repetitive. Nix, your companion, is relegated to distractions that lock him into long animations, leaving you to rely on melee far too often.
RPGs are supposed to be about choice, yet Outlaws does everything it can to negate or block that freedom. Enemy weapons can be picked up, but they’re temporary and discarded once ammo runs out and the drop rate is horrendous. The result is a combat loop that feels restrictive and uninspired.

Lack of Depth in RPG Mechanics
The game desperately needs reworked cooldowns and permanent stealth options beyond melee takedowns. Imagine a toxic dart launcher or other secondary tools that expand stealth gameplay but instead, you’re left with barebones mechanics.
Character creation and class progression are nonexistent. The opportunity to roleplay as a bounty hunter or craft your own outlaw persona is completely missed. Instead, you’re forced to follow a protagonist who feels like a female version of Han Solo without the charisma, tech skills, or charm to carry the narrative.

Monetization Missteps
To make matters worse, customization options are locked behind DLC and paywalls. For a game already lacking in personalization, hiding skins and extras behind additional costs feels exploitative. It’s hard not to see this as rushed development aimed at pushing out a product quickly, then monetizing what should have been core features.

The One Bright Spot: Visuals
Credit where it’s due Star Wars Outlaws looks stunning. The environments are beautifully crafted, and the presentation captures the Star Wars aesthetic perfectly.
However, while the visuals are stunning, the landscape and space feel barren. Vehicles and ship combat are clunky and uninspired, NPCs are spread too thin across the world, and interactions with creatures or characters are minimal. You can’t kill or farm anything outside of what the game explicitly allows, meaning there are no material farming mechanics. Most NPCs can’t be shot or meaningfully engaged with, blocking free-will choices that should define an RPG. The same restrictions apply to space combat, which feels just as limited and lifeless. These shortcomings undermine immersion and remind you that despite appearances, this is not the expansive RPG experience it should be.

Verdict
Long story short: buy Star Wars Outlaws only if it’s on sale. Paying full price would be diabolical, and the DLC won’t fix the core gameplay issues. This is a game with potential, but right now it’s a hollow shell of what an RPG should be.
