Pros:
The worlds are big but not so big that every planet feels like a slog. There is also enough variety in the flora, fauna, and terrain that every one feels distinct and novel. 
Graphics are great even at medium settings and after playing a while I turned the settings up realizing that I wasn't pushing my system all that hard but I would still have to say the game engine optimization is good. 
Quite a few of the decisions feel like they have a real impact in your relationships with the syndicates.
Taking place between Empire and Jedi there are quite a few Easter Eggs tied to the original movie trilogy and some of the expanded universe stuff (comics, books, other games, Legends material) so that is always nice to see. Also it pays to listen to the conversations around you, especially by Imperials, for more Star Wars Easter Eggs.
Fighting Death Troopers is always an iffy proposition especially early on-not impossible but very challenging.
KD and Nix are great supporting characters and help flesh out Kay's emotional journey.
Combat, sneaking, and space combat are fun and well balanced for the most part.
The characters, settings, and music definitely feel like classic Star Wars.
Cons:
While a few of the decisions feel like they have a real impact by the time you reach the final phase of the original game it kind of feels like nothing you did mattered one way or the other. It's too easy to max out the relationship with all the syndicates and I think you have to really work at it to consistently stay on a syndicate's bad side.
While there is a decent replay factor after a while randomly generated events get repetitive and seem to trigger in the same spot (or three). 
The lack of true smuggling missions is a shame as it's too easy to dodge or zoom past Imperial patrols. Having to smuggle goods between planets and NOT get involved in firefights would have been an interesting element.
Overall I would recommend this game if you're looking a fun romp in the Star Wars universe and it's seedier side. A definite buy if you can grab it and the DLCs on sale and it's structured that in 30 minutes of play you can knock out an objective or two.

Since Disney took over the franchise this is the only game which comes close to one of my absolute favorite Star Wars games, Dark Forces.  I think the devs did a great job at creating a game which makes you feel like a small time petty thief who stumbles into a story a little larger than themselves.  Key Vess is an enjoyable protagonist and I like that she is presented as basically being a noob who is constantly in over her head backed up by some great voice acting.  The supporting cast are all entertaining as well and I especially enjoyed ND-5's story arc (though I think his jacket is kind of stupid looking).   The plot itself isn't anything revolutionary but it's functional and presented well enough.  Even though this game isn't an RPG there is still a system of skill progression you unlock by getting to know various experts and I absolutely LOVE this system and it reminds me a bit of the first Division game (which I also loved).  There's just...a lot to love here.

Graphics-wise this is a very pretty game and Massive's Snowdrop engine really shines here.  Everything looks grungy and lived in and really gives you the feel of being in your own Star Wars story.  On the flip side Imperial facilities are very clean and shiny looking.  Photomode is included so you can take great shots of this wonderful engine in action.

As for negatives it has me asking the question, "why is this an open world game?" often enough but I think they just scrape by in justifying it, as it has you searching the world for goodies and experts to learn new skills from.  The other big negative for me is that mechanics across the board have been done better in other games and are simply good enough here.  Controls can be a bit awkward leading you to commit actions you had no intention of doing from time to time.  The positive to that all of these 6/10 systems come together and gel into an 8/10 game for me.

I originally played this game on Uplay+ so I can also say mechanically this game has come a long way and the most obvious change happened with the speeder controls.  They were serviceable in their original incarnation but are quite elegant today by comparison.  A number of systems have been improved since release so now is really the time to dive in and enjoy all the wonderful refinements for the first time if you haven't already.

In short: it looks great, game mechanics have improved over time, and the sum of the game is greater than its individual parts.  If you're a fan of Star Wars, old or new, do yourself a favor and pick this game up.

My take on Star Wars Outlaws so far

I’m not very far into the game yet — but even so, the story and world-building have been very well done. The setting feels immersive, the factions add meaningful variety, and there’s a sense that you can tackle missions in multiple ways depending on your style. When you sneak around, use stealth takedowns, or try to bluff your way through — that’s where the game really shines.

That said… if you go in wanting to be a brawler or “guns-blazing” type, Outlaws doesn’t always deliver. My character often feels weak — like there’s no weight behind the blaster-shots or melee hits. Combat works okay in short bursts, but unlike stealthy, calculated infiltration, it rarely feels satisfying.

So far, I’m enjoying Outlaws most when I embrace the sneaky scoundrel vibe. If that’s not your thing, I can see how it might feel underwhelming. All in all: a strong, atmospheric Star Wars experience — but not always the “shoot-first, ask questions later” adventure some might expect.

I initially bought the game on sale because I'd heard that all the bugs had been more or less ironed out, and that it had gotten the atmosphere of Star Wars right. Thankfully, I did get what I paid for, but I think there's so much that can be improved. Here are some places where I feel it has performed above my expectations, some points where I felt it fell slightly short, and some areas where I feel it is just irredeemable short of a major content update.

Pleasant surprises: 

1. When you dial enemy health up to max, stormtroopers actually feel like a menace. You have to, as Thanos says, 'go for the head', and their armor finally feels like it makes a difference in terms of stopping blaster bolts. 

2. The Empire's recruitment campaigns and canvassing is actually quite believable (sign up and make a difference!), and not at all comic-book-villain-esque (wanna be evil? Get a cool black uniform? Join us and TAKE OVER THE UNIVERSE!!!)... unlike a certain other villain that will be mentioned later.

3. The speederbike conveys the feeling of effortless, hovering speed very well.

4. Truly breathtaking scenery and epic platforming areas. Potential horror spin-off? Who knows.

5. Kay Vess's skepticism of the Rebel Alliance. I haven't played the whole thing through yet, but I'm pleased to note that she doesn't just up and join them within the first 10 minutes of meeting them, which is absolutely consistent with her character thus far. Even in later encounters, she's wary and guarded, working with them only because she absolutely has to.

6. The planet approach and takeoff scenes. These actually feel like Star Wars! They should have led with the soundtrack for those in the start menu...


Weakpoints:

1. Myopic enemies make the stealth aspect of missions overly easy, or not sufficiently challenging.

2. There's not enough depth to the upgrade tree. I'm not asking for a Nioh-style upgrade system, though that could be nice. 

3. Kay can only really customize one weapon (her trusty blaster)

4. The first five or eight seconds of the start music is REALLY annoying. It's like they're trying to tell you 'omg, this is going to be such a frantic scrabble for survival in a fast-paced galaxy'... but it's the game's job to SHOW that. Show that in gameplay, don't TELL me that with an accomplishment in the top left corner of the screen that says 'we made it'. An example of a game franchise that does this REALLY well is the Uncharted series (especially 2 and 3). The music is grand, optimistic, and suggests a sense of awe in some places - in short, all the ingredients of an adventure. Then the game takes you and puts you through the wringer, forcing you through some genuinely frustrating and gut-wrenching moments that SHOW you Nathan Drake battling a small army. An example of a game franchise that did this REALLY badly was Mass Effect: Andromeda (Ryder didn't even wait till after his/her first battle to say 'we made it'). To fix this, stop trying to tell me 'we made it', cut out the first 5 seconds of the intro music (the rest of it is actually good), and... well, the rest is actually pretty decent.



Fatal/unfixable flaws (at least not without a massive content update):

1. One of my pet peeves is that Sliro refers to himself and his rivals as being part of 'the Underworld'. Oh, come on. 13-year-olds understand that comic-book villains who prance around in black capes and say 'eeeeevill' are focused on children who are 10 and under. There are so many ways Sliro could have SHOWN the audience that he was not an upright citizen instead of telling them. He could have said something like 'you won't be arrested as long as you don't get caught', or looked over at his aide after receiving a report and said 'all right, pull the trigger - and make sure Governor Pudark gets his cut in unmarked beskar this time.' or 'that man has crossed me for the last time, make sure he's never seen again', or when someone at the table looks at him and says with a nasty grin, 'last week, a village got wiped out in the crossfire between two rival tribes - do you know something about that', he could have smiled, shrugged his shoulders, and said in the most disgustingly mock-innocent voice 'why would I know anything about tribal wars? I just sell blasters to this guy, and blasters to that guy, and what they do with it is their business,' before everyone bursts out laughing, and then he could have said 'I propose a toast - to all the dear, departed villagers!' Even that exaggeratedly heinous and sociopathic dialogue would have been preferable to saying 'the Underworld' while a conveniently-placed source of light casts sinister shadows across his face.

2. Lack of a leveling system in lieu of a deep equipment customization tree. The reason I say 'in lieu of a deep equipment customization tree' is that I was ultimately persuaded by Monster Hunter: World that not having a leveling system was okay as long as you had a diverse and deep customization aspect for your weapons.

3. The use of Nyx for EVERYTHING instead of the Force for SOMET things. This is the BIGGEST issue for me. Without the Force, it isn't Star Wars. They could fix this by letting the ability to sense people be explained by Kay Vess always having this sort of a 'sixth sense' all on her own, and later in the story have someone explain that she had SOME sensitivity in the Force, but that it wasn't strong enough for her to move objects (which would be why she needed Nyx). Then maybe at some point in the story, she could be told that she didn't really need her macrobinoculars to mark people, because her power came from the Force - and then all of a sudden for maybe a final mission, she would be able to sense everyone and everything without marking them with her macrobinoculars, and maybe manages to Force pull something tiny (but mighty enough) to take down a big baddie right at the end. In the post-game, she'd still need Nyx to move objects, but at the same time, she'd still retain some advanced sensing abilities even without her macrobinoculars. The ability to sense what others are thinking (suspicious, giving up the search) can ABSOLUTELY be attributed to the Force, and I'm confident it'd work wonders too if the players were initially given a few game portions without that ability worked in, just to show how much of an edge that ability can give her.

⭐ Star Wars Outlaws – 6/10

Visually striking, thematically hollow, narratively wasted potential.

I’ve just finished Star Wars Outlaws, and I can honestly say this game is the definition of “so close, yet so far.” Beneath the glossy visuals and cinematic presentation lies a creative tragedy: a sandbox full of missed opportunities and shallow design choices that could have made this one of the greatest Star Wars games ever made.

Let’s start with the obvious: the world is stunning. On OLED in HDR, the art direction shines — the lighting, the environments, and the sense of scale are genuinely breathtaking. There are moments that feel alive, and Massive Entertainment clearly knows how to make a planet feel like a place. The Snowdrop engine can deliver magic. But that magic quickly fades once you realize how empty the experience is beneath the surface.

The writing is serviceable at best. It’s safe, sanitized, and devoid of the grit and complexity that defines the best Star Wars stories. Every character feels like a checkbox archetype. The protagonist — an entirely new and forgettable smuggler — lacks any of the depth or charm that made figures like Han Solo or Cassian Andor resonate. Ubisoft had decades of expanded universe lore to draw from, and they chose to invent the blandest possible scenario instead.

Gameplay? Classic Ubisoft. Outposts, fetch quests, repetitive stealth sections, and “open world” exploration that feels more like a checklist than an adventure. The bones of something good are here, but the studio never commits. The story pretends to be about survival and rebellion, yet never dares to touch the philosophical heart of Star Wars — the corruption of power, the moral ambiguity of empire and rebellion, or the human cost of resistance.

It’s a shame, because this could have been so much more. Imagine a story set during the Dark Times — the fall of the Republic, the rise of the Empire — showing the galaxy’s descent into tyranny through the eyes of ordinary people. Or a game set during the Mandalorian Wars, a morally grey era of warriors and Jedi torn by duty and pride. The material is right there. Instead, Ubisoft played it safe and made another open-world checklist game with Star Wars wallpaper.

Even the technology falters. HDR is inconsistent, with strange softness and shimmering in highlights; FSR upscaling introduces noticeable artefacts, and XeSS helps but at a performance cost. The irony? The game looks better in SDR with AMD’s Radeon Image Sharpening enabled — except you can’t use it in HDR. The visual clarity on OLED is unforgiving, exposing every flaw in the engine’s upscaling and post-processing.

And yet… I still finished it. Because buried under all that mediocrity are flashes of brilliance — the art direction, the score, the occasional moment where the world feels real. When the game stops holding your hand and just lets you exist in the galaxy, you can almost see the masterpiece it could have been.

Final Verdict:
A beautiful shell with a hollow core. Ubisoft had the license, the lore, and the technology to make something truly special. Instead, they delivered a focus-tested corporate product — safe, shallow, and forgettable.

6/10 – “The Force was there, but management said no.”

Star Wars Outlaws pleasantly surprised me. The gameplay is fluid, dynamic, and—unlike what usually happens in Ubisoft games—it doesn’t fall into the trap of repetitiveness. The missions have a good rhythm, and the variety of activities keeps the experience consistently engaging.

Immersion in the Star Wars universe is one of its strongest points. The environments are rich in detail, the cities and planets feel authentic, and the soundtrack helps you dive completely into this galaxy. The space combat, in particular, stands out — it’s smooth, fun, and gives a real sense of control and speed.

The game doesn’t quite earn a perfect score because, despite all the fun, there’s an excess of simplicity in the overall mechanics. It could use a bit more depth in certain systems and choices to make the journey even more captivating.

Even so, Star Wars Outlaws is an excellent surprise: a game that honors the franchise, delivers an exciting adventure, and proves that Ubisoft can, indeed, innovate within its formulas.

👉 Final Score: 8.5/10 — one of the best recent experiences in the Star Wars universe.

Journey to a galaxy far, far away and play as Kay Vess, a freelancer who is willing to do almost any job if the credits are right. She'll use her skills to try to survive the syndicate underworld in Star Wars: Outlaws. You'll be zooming around the galaxy trying to hire a crew for a huge heist job, perhaps the biggest score of anyone’s life. The problem is that to get the best crew you’re going to have to jump through some serious hoops to convince them to join you.

This game definitely has plenty to keep you busy with when it comes to the puzzle aspects. You will be splicing into computer systems to open doors, turn off security cameras, clear your wanted status with the Empire, and more. You’re also going to have to electric lockpick, by rhythm, your way through doors, systems, and locked chests. The game will have some required upgrades for those two systems so you’ll be forced to come back to certain areas/planets.

You’re also going to have to deal with 4 different syndicate factions. These factions, if you’re in their good graces, will give you access to certain perks such as discounts and faction specific equipment. If you’ve ever played against rival organizations you’ll know that you can’t make EVERYONE happy, your actions for one group is going to make another angry. If you do enough to a certain group they will try to kill you on sight ANYTIME you’re even close by. I personally learned that the hard way when it came to The Pykes (ironically one of the very first syndicates you’re introduced to in the game). 

Let’s talk about combat real quick. There’s really two forms of combat you’ll be partaking in, the 3rd person shooter variety and the space craft kind. When it comes to the 3PS version you’ll have to be fast on your feet aiming for the head, and praying that you don’t take too much damage. You do have health bars, and as long as there is still a bit in one bar it can, potentially, heal back to full, but if you’re getting clobbered you’re going to have to use your very limited Bacta Vials to try to bring you back from the edge of death. You’ll be armed with a blaster that you can upgrade as you go through the game, it comes with 3 different shooting modes, and it will be your task to make sure you’re proficient in all 3 and know when it is best to use them. There will also be chances to pick up certain dropped weapons that have a limited amount of ammo that you can use to defeat your enemies.

Now let’s talk about ship combat, something that until I had most of my ship parts upgraded to close to maximum, I was terrible at. For the most part this form of combat is not going to play that big of a role in the overall game, but there are definitely going to be some situations where you’re going to have to survive through waves of enemy ships, and if you’re not careful you’re going to have quite a few game over moments. You’ll have 3 attack options by the end of the game, and to be honest I think I really only used the lasers and on REALLY rare occasions I’d remember that I had rockets, which never really did enough (in my honest opinion).

This game has enough content that you can easily go over 28 hours. I know that because that’s exactly what I did. It pays to explore every area you come upon, you’ll find hidden areas that can give you rare parts, or just give you more credits. Speaking of credits, let me give you some sage advice: If you think you have stockpiled enough credits, you haven’t. Some of the upgrades that you have to make to your Speeder (think hoverbike) or your ship will clean you out. Not only do you need to collect all the parts, but it's going to cost you to complete the upgrade. Another bit of advice is that if there is something that is highlighted as something you can pick up, pick it up, you’re going to need that constant stream of junk that you can sell to vendors to keep your pockets somewhat filled.

One of my favorite mechanics in this game, and I’ve been saving for one of my final paragraphs, is Nix. Nix is a Merqaal and is your character’s most trusted companion (sidenote, trust is a concept that is going to be all over the place throughout the entire game… except when it comes to Nix). You can use Nix to distract enemies, push buttons, sabotage security systems, attack enemies, and in stressful times give you a little cuteness to calm you down. There are also food vendors on each planet that you visit that if you have the credits you can trigger a quick time event with Nix and both of you will be able to enjoy a new exotic meal together. Those meals will also unlock special abilities for Nix, so you should seriously make sure you get all the food vendors.

I really liked the game, I played it for 24 hours straight (it was for Extra Life), but even if I wasn’t playing for charity I’d still have put in the hours that I did so that I could play the game from start to finish. The only thing that bugged me about the game, and I’m hoping it was just me, was the random game crashes where the game would just freeze and I would have to restart the game. Thankfully the autosave feature is pretty solid so I never really had to backtrack too much in order to be right back to where I was in the game. Remember Division 1's snowy and foggy New York (especially in the Dark Zone) with all its ambience? 

The same guys made this game - yes, it uses the snowdrop engine, though now modified to use forced raytracing everywhere (in a way that works with or without nvidia cards). 

Everything from the world design, environmental design, sound (which I suspect is also raytraced) and graphics are S tier. 

Even the grass swaying in the wind looks extremely nice, like how it is in Ghost of Tsushima (if you watch its trailer it perfectly showcases how the grass moves and makes the 'shape' of the winds visible as it washes across the land). 

The world is vibrant, and genuinely feels lived in. It is generously populated with people too - these people are also very animated, they're not just sitting around looking like static props (though some are). Even exploring the world outside on your speeder you might run into another speeder going the opposite direction and kicking you off your bike. 

The quality of the alien worlds's exotic locales and NPCs therein reminds me of Eidos-Montreal's Guardians of the Galaxy game, which I think also uses its own in-house engine, though its game mechanics and controls are far more polished and fluid-feeling than this game. 

Where this game falls short is the writing (basically look at what Star Wars has become after Disney), and the janky gameplay and controls that wrap around everything, and also the fact that it is an Ubi game, with the traditional Ubi collectathon mechanics, though ironically this may be the only game where I will tolerate this as the world of Star Wars itself makes it worthwhile just to explore and walk around all the different locales and planets (you get 4 explorable cities/towns/spaceship orbit area, across 4 different planets, 3 of which are fully explorable planets). 

The other place where the game falls short, is the main character design (idk if it's her pet alien's influence or what, but she looks a little like an alien). You want your main character to be an anchor for your game - just like news anchors. They need to attract people's attention, especially since this is what people will be looking at 100% of the game. Sure your world design, your individual blades of grass, your cantinas, are all S-tier, but they aren't your anchors, and they're also not being looked at all the time unlike the main character which is ever-present on-screen. You can have an amazing game but if the face of your game is not appealing to people, you can basically consider your game to be non-existent and without any form of marketing - no matter how much we all disagree with this, this is what it comes down to in reality. 

It isn't that people are bored of Star Wars, it's that people don't want an annoying Disney-esque quippy teenager in their face 24/7 doing Disney-esque things with other Disney-esque princesses (im not kidding - these princesses saturate more than 50% of key characters in the game). 

The other place where the game supposedly falls short is stability - and this, I am unable to replicate. I also have a beefy rig, so this probably won't be the same experience for others, but the game's been pretty smooth and stable for me so far, even with mods (which exist!). 

I also really dig the function that dials the game down to sub-10 fps to save power when you're alt-tabbed out - the same function exists in the recent ARC Raiders game - you could have the game in the background and it literally dials itself down and your CPU/GPU would be at near zero loads while you do something else. 

Fun note: you can even do an air-to-assassinate here, which means the main character is probably an unofficial Assassin ;)

as of writing this, i have just finished the main storyline of the game, with two dlc's left to go. this will be presented as spoiler-free as i can manage.

this game presents an atmosphere unlike any that i've witnessed in a star wars game before. there's *so much* going on at any given time, no matter where you are, it's incredibly easy to immerse yourself in the world. from small side conversations that you can listen in on, to the native critters of your selected planet wandering around (yes, you CAN pet just about all of them), to just the ambient noise surrounding you when you're out in the wild or in someplace more civilized.

pretty much all of the characters you meet in your journey feel like they'd fit in the universe like a glove. kay feels like she's trying to fake it till she makes it in a criminal underworld that, a lot of the time, proves itself to be way beyond her league; all of her crew (as you meet them during story progression) have their own unique quirks as well. is some of the writing cheesy? yeah, most of it is, but that's part of the charm in my opinion.

the gameplay is pretty run of the mill as far as ubisoft stealth/action-adventure games are concerned. it's nothing groundbreaking, but it also doesn't try to be. it can be a little rough around the edges at times, but issues are few and far between from my experience. there's plenty of stuff you can do to spin the tide of battle in your favor, mostly involving using your companion to distract enemies or otherwise preoccupy them while you deal the heavy hits. i also appreciate that the game respects your right to choose whether you want to go in quiet and take your time clearing out enemies, or launch head-first and guns blazing into a huge firefight. entirely up to you.

as for graphics, the game's beautiful. there were a lot of times i found myself stopping on different planets to admire the scenery or the lighting, and the game gives you plenty of areas where you can have kay lean against something or sit down to get some really *really* pretty shots to share with others.

performance-wise, it's not too shabby either. my specs are just barely above recommended, and i was able to play on high graphics with minimal issue. some frame drops in spots, but usually only when there was a lot going on at once on the screen, and not very huge drops either. i had a handful of crashes (funnily enough, one was right after i finished the main story and went to upgrade my ship), but they were infrequent enough for me to not really mind all that much. stuff happens, y'know?

ymmv on that last point, of course, but i try not to let things like that bother me if i can help it. i think i experienced like, maybe 4 crashes over my (currently) 36 hours in-game.

yeah, overall i'd recommend this if you're a fan of star wars and/or ubisoft open-world games. personally, i'd maybe wait for a sale, but that's mostly just because i don't really enjoy paying full market price for games nowadays lmao.

In my opinion, isn’t a bad game at all — especially if you’re already familiar with the IP and the dev behind it, Massive Entertainment. I’ve played some of their previous works like The Division and The Division 2, and honestly, the gameplay scripting here feels quite similar to those titles.

In terms of gameplay, I’d say it’s decent enough. On patch 1.7, most of the major bugs have been fixed, so it’s definitely more stable now. But still, this game feels like it’s made for Star Wars fans. If you don’t follow the universe, you might get confused with all the syndicates and factions popping up.
What I really like, though, is the environmental design. Massive absolutely nailed the worldbuilding — it’s exactly what fans like me would expect from a Star Wars open-world game.

Now for the downsides… despite being called “Outlaws,” there’s honestly not much “outlaw” in it, lol. The stealth kills feel more like stealth stunts — like, how does a simple punch knock someone out cold instantly? And weirdly enough, the stun weapon feels way deadlier than an actual blaster. That part’s kinda hilarious and confusing at the same time.

Story-wise, it’s pretty simple. Nothing too deep, but it delivers. There are cameos, the plot’s light, and overall it’s fine if you’re a Star Wars fan.
But if you’re a random player who just bought it without knowing the franchise — or you’ve never played third-person shooters like The Division — honestly, you can skip this one. It’s not really worth the full price.

That said, if you meet all those criteria (Star Wars fan, familiar with similar games), then yeah, it’s worth buying — but only with at least a 70% discount, and just the base game. Don’t bother with the deluxe or expansions lol.

Star Wars Outlaws – A Casual Review

If you’ve ever dreamed of stepping into the gritty, chaotic underworld of a galaxy far, far away, Star Wars Outlaws delivers on that fantasy. It’s not perfect, and I wish there was more of it, but I had a blast.

I didn’t play the game at launch. It caught a lot of flack back then, and I was hesitant. Partly because of the criticism, partly because of the price, but honestly, I just wasn’t in the mood to be a Star Wars smuggler in August 2024. I’m glad I waited, though, because coming into it fresh, and with any early issues mostly patched up, I found myself really enjoying the ride.

Right from the get-go, the game oozes Star Wars atmosphere. The planets are exactly what you'd expect: classic Star Wars "mono-climate" zones, a snowy planet, a jungle world, a windy one, a flashy casino planet, and of course, Tatooine. Each is beautifully crafted, immersive, and full of life (or sand, in Tatooine’s case).

And it’s not just the visuals. The sights and sounds of Star Wars are absolutely spot on. From the chatter of aliens and beeping droids as you walk through a busy street, to the hum of engines, the pew-pew of blasters, and the ambient noise that fills the world, the sound design is brilliant. It doesn’t just look like Star Wars, it sounds like it too, and that really helps transport you to the galaxy far far away. You're not just observing the world, you're in it.

Space exploration? Also very cool. Most planets (except the casino world) have a space zone to explore. One looks like a space junkyard, another feels ripped straight from Solo’s Kessel Run nebula, all super atmospheric. Tatooine’s space is a bit of a letdown, but to be fair, that’s pretty accurate to how the films portray it: vast, empty, and on the edge of nowhere.

The characters are a strong point. Kay Vess is a great lead, very much her own person. She’s not trying to be Han Solo or Jyn Erso; she feels like a real character in the Star Wars universe with her own arc and personality. Her little companion Nix is adorable and genuinely useful (think Grogu meets your in-game toolkit), and I loved their dynamic. Kay’s co-pilot, a gruff separatist commando droid, plays the Chewie role with a unique twist, though I do wish he was around more during missions.

The criminal underworld vibe is a major theme, and it’s handled pretty well. Different syndicates have distinct aesthetics and personalities, though if you boil it down, they do play similarly. The reputation system is interesting but a bit too forgiving; I was expecting to make enemies along the way, but I ended up on everyone's good side. No bounty hunters chasing me after 100 hours? C’mon, I wanted that drama!

Space combat and smuggling missions are fairly simple, but the Pirate DLC spices things up. Adding cargo types makes smuggling feel more meaningful, something most Star Wars games haven’t really explored. SWTOR, for example, never gave the smuggler class this much flavor.

Outfits are surprisingly cool. Not only do they give you that “dress for the planet” vibe (snow gear on the icy world, leather jackets in the jungle, etc.), but they come with set bonuses and perks that actually affect gameplay. You can kit yourself out for stealth or go loud with grenade-boosting gear, it’s a nice, lightweight way to tweak your playstyle without needing to grind skill trees.

Speaking of skills, the “Expert” system is another neat touch. Instead of unlocking abilities through menus, you go find someone to teach you. It’s very in-universe. The skills themselves aren’t Force powers or anything flashy, but they work well for a scoundrel. I especially liked “Fast Talk,” where you can stall enemies with a quick lie before blasting them, felt super Han Solo.

Riding around on your speeder (or swoop bike, more accurately) also captures that Star Wars spirit. It’s fun, stylish, and helps keep exploration from feeling like a chore.

There are also a couple of mini-games sprinkled throughout the galaxy that I really enjoyed. Sabacc, for one, was surprisingly fun. I usually steer clear of card games in RPGs, but I ended up playing quite a few hands across the galaxy. The “cheats” system kept it interesting, and one of my highlights was facing off against Lando. Let’s just say I had a winning hand... and then, spoilers, something happened. It was great.

Even the in-game arcade machines were a fun surprise. They're styled like retro 80s games and feel like something you’d find in-universe and in real-world arcades during the original trilogy era. It’s a small thing, but it added a lot of charm and helped tie the world back to the roots of the Star Wars franchise.

And the story? Classic Star Wars. No spoilers, but it checks all the right boxes: reluctant hero on the run, a stolen ship, shootouts, quirky aliens, evil Empire entanglements, emotional beats, and a satisfying finale. It’s nothing revolutionary, but it feels like Star Wars, and that’s all I really wanted.

As someone who’s played other big open-world games like Assassin’s Creed Odyssey and Valhalla, I did find myself wishing Outlaws had more customization, more depth, and more DLC options like those games. But honestly, wanting more is probably a good sign. It means the foundation is solid. I’d rather come away from a game thinking “I wish there was more” than “that was too much.”

Final Thoughts:
Star Wars Outlaws nails the vibe. It feels like you're in the Star Wars galaxy, living a rogue's life among smugglers, scoundrels, and syndicates. Sure, I wish the world was bigger, the systems deeper, and the danger more present, but what’s here is a solid foundation and an enjoyable ride.

I play on Xbox but played on PC too. I want to give extra praise to Outlaws. Yes its ai can be hilariously broken and is essentially braindead when driving speeders and there is an almost persistent game breaking bug when you enter hyperspace but it is truly practically heartbreaking that this literally Massive game has been brushed off. It was released far too early but the craftmanship and worldbuilding is surreal. It doesn't even feel like this was made by anyone. The dynamic weather, day/night, random quests and events, choice-based systems, and the overall relaxing and immersive vibes like finishing a job then taking a breather alongside npc's to the suns set on tatooine. 

The lore from datapads even has so much care put into them, referencing obscure and known Star Wars stories and characters. Unlike games like No Man's Sky where there is a sole reliance on procedural generation that leads to empty and repetitive worlds and quests, hand crafted "limited" open worlds and universes like Outlaws will always have the most value because there is attention to every detail and making the world feel lived in. The main negative this game has is not fullfilling the experience of playing as an outlaw by not allowing you to hijack vehicles - even imperial and cartel vehicles, and attack non-enemy NPC's. 

I fully absorb every game I play especially because I know the insane amount of hard work that goes into making them. Every game should have every part of it experience because it's all crafted by people. Just as Rocksteady did with Arkham Knight, which is another game I constantly revisit and find new details in its gorgeous world, I hope Massive adds some surprise content to Outlaws. There is more than enough content but even allowing us to fully be a criminal/outlaw would be fantastic. 

This is a game that I can't believe exists especially as a star wars fan. The more focused exploration is what Starfield needs and Starfields character customization and class selection is what Outlaws needs but I understand why it's better for a Star Wars game to follow a canonical character.

Oh and the other incredible feature - CROSS PROGRESSION. I hate requiring third party login portals for offline games but being able to continue my save on any other device is amazing.

Overall Star Wars Outlaws is the most immersive Star Wars game, alongside Kotor, and one of the most immersive games. I criticized its release state but it feels like a new game now and the most insane part is that the world building just doesn't stop. If you've played red dead 2 then you know you can't go 5 minutes without random encounters, mysteries, and side quests stopping you. Outlaws is that but cranked up. Sure many of the quests involve smuggling and treasure hunting but it's star wars and the world is so incredibly alive, although still feeling very scripted as the NPC's don't even react to you, say for enemies. 

But most interestingly this game does something I've never seen any other game do which is use optimization to enhance the world building. If you reload a save  due to an issue or just wishing to change a decision, many NPC vendors and others will be different and contracts you acquire will also be entirely different so you truly need to manage your time and make your decisions wisely. Truly fantastic and if any game deserves to get more content, it's this.

Star Wars Outlaws gives you exactly the kind of scoundrel fantasy you hope for. You slip into the skin of Kay Vess, skirt alliances with crime syndicates, pull off heists, and try to make your mark in a galaxy that is more interested in control than redemption. It is loud in the best ways, full of atmosphere and swagger, with planets that actually feel alive.

But there is a tension always present: the idea of big cinematic ambition versus the reality of what you get to do.

The highs:

The worlds are lush, the visuals often gorgeous, and in the quiet moments, the game captures that Star Wars magic.

Kay’s story feels familiar but human, about survival and small victories against a massive system.

The syndicate system and player choices give weight to your actions, and some missions land with surprising moral punch.

The soft spots:

Stealth and combat are solid but predictable, and you see the same patterns repeat fast.

Enemy AI often behaves oddly, breaking tension during fights or stealth runs.

Side content feels thin once the main story cools off.

Some story beats miss their payoff, leaving emotional gaps where there should be closure.

What I wished for:
I always wanted the option to command a small wing of ships, not just the Trailblazer. It would have made the fantasy complete, turning a lone smuggler’s run into something closer to a crew-led saga.

In the end, Star Wars Outlaws is satisfying for what it tries to be. It lets you live the rogue dream, fly under the radar, and carve a name in the galaxy. But you can feel the edges of its world, like a heist that almost pulled it off.

[h1] My Honest Review of: Star Wars Outlaws [/h1]

Star Wars Outlaws had a rough launch, but [b] after consistent updates and hotfixes, [/b] it’s now in very good shape.

Kay Vess isn’t a Jedi or a soldier, she’s just a regular person, and that’s what makes this game feel so fresh. It gives off the same grounded energy as Andor: gritty, small-scale survival in a galaxy dominated by bigger powers. She has her blaster, her wits, and her companion Nix, and together they survive the only way they can: stealing.

[h3] Why it works so well [/h3]

The Kay & Nix duo: Their friendship is phenomenal. Ubisoft really nailed the charm here, whether it’s small “minigames” like Kay struggling with spicy alien food while Nix teases her, or gameplay moments where Nix helps out, they feel alive together.

Nix’s abilities: You can send Nix to snatch money from tables, open doors Kay can’t reach, jump on enemies while you clean up the rest, or even grab weapons and medkits for you. He’s not just cute, he’s useful.

Immersive world: The planets look incredible, the guns feel weighty, the Empire is ever-present, and the soundtrack when you boot up the game sets the tone perfectly.

Things to do: Side quests, exploration, encounters etc. The world feels active in the same way big open-world games (Red Dead 2, Horizon) feel alive. NPCs feel as believable as in any other top-tier open-world game.

[h3] The score [/h3]

I give this game a solid 10/6.9. That’s my way of saying it’s truly a good game. It surprised me, it entertained me, and I’m glad I bought it.

[h3] The negative reviews problem [/h3]

Yes, the launch was rough, and yes, Ubisoft has a bad reputation. But too many people are giving this game a thumbs-down just because of the publisher, even when they like the game. That’s unfair. Those negative reviews drag the overall score down to “Mixed,” which scares people away.

I’ve read the complaints, and honestly, I disagree with 60% of the negative reviews. The game now is not what it was at launch.

It’s the same story with other games. People hated Alan Wake 2 just because it was on Epic. But if not for Epic, the game wouldn’t even exist. Why punish the game itself for the platform or publisher?

[h3] Final word [/h3]

If you’re still reading this: stop. Buy the game while it’s 55% off. It’s an amazing experience, and I don’t regret my purchase at all.

People will always trash-talk things online. But when you actually play Outlaws, it speaks for itself.

Star Wars Outlaws – Review

I put just under 60 hours into Star Wars Outlaws, completing nearly all of the main story and side quests I could find, apart from the Radiant contracts. With that much time invested, I can say I had a really good experience overall.

Kay Vess turned out to be a surprisingly interesting protagonist, with distinct quirks and some genuinely engaging character beats. Her story was well put together, and her interactions with notable lore figures were a highlight.

The game is packed with fun easter eggs. Boba Fett and Han Solo showing up in the Jabba’s Palace sequence was a standout moment. I also really enjoyed the chance to duel Lando in Sabacc: not just once in the main story (to unlock ability upgrades), but again in the DLC. It was a clever way to weave character-driven moments into gameplay.

Speaking of upgrades, I liked how ability progression was handled. Instead of a bland menu system, you complete small challenges to improve your skills. It made the process feel like a natural part of the adventure rather than a checklist.

The Radiant contracts did get a bit repetitive, but they never felt boring. There was always something fun about doing them.

One of the biggest wins for this game, though, was ship gameplay. It is rare for an RPG like Outlaws to actually let you fly your own ship, upgrade it, and dive into dogfights, smuggling runs, and all those quintessential “Star Wars outlaw” experiences. That feature alone made the game stand out compared to other Star Wars titles.

I also want to highlight the DLCs. Both added stories were engaging, packed with genuine emotional beats that hit exactly where they were meant to. - Traversability. A big one imo for open-world games. MC is quick on foot, the speeder is a great time when exploring the open worlds, and flying the ship around from planet to planet made it feel like a true Star Wars experience.

Lowlights:
- Character Design. While there are some good characters in this (Kay, Nix, ND-5, Hondo), lots of them were boring and lacked depth.

Later on she opens up, but imo the story really could have used a section around the halfway mark where she confronts herself with all the people she's put in danger (including Nix).

What I liked about this game was combat. I didn't do any sneaking on purpose because I knew it was bad. I just killed everyone, even several times in the game when I was forced not to raise alarms i just shot everyone before they could. So that was nice I could do that. Shooting blasters feel satisfying. I love the blaster holes, the smoke, the effects, explosions, all that very Star Wars like. I ran around with the first fully upgraded Light Plasma mod most of the time. It scratched my gunslinger Red Dead SW itch but I also used all the pick up guns too (those were nice, too bad they end). I tried all the modules but most of them were bad. 

What I dislike about shooting is the fact that I can't turn off the hit markers. they are huge even when reduced to 75%. And I wanted to install a mod but found out that for some reason some genius tied the hit markers to the rest of UI and HUD so disabling them turns off most of it and requires heavy modding too. Why would they do such a thing beats me especially when they figured out it was annoying and gave us an option to reduce it to 75%. Should've given us an option to reduce it to 1% at least. Or hide it completely and not tie to the rest of HUD. It is immersion breaking. 

The other thing I liked is a plethora of options to choose from. From skipping annoying mini-games, to even highlighting the objects around you when you get lost in a special graphics high contrast mod that almost looks like a dev kit mod. That is nice. You can really customize how you play this game (EXCEPT FOR THE HIT MARKER! Yyy)

The world of the game is believable. Tatooine is by far the best of all, of course. It is the most iconic Star Wars place and the level designers really put their thought into making the world feel fun to look around at even though there is no really good or fun loot to collect in any Ubisoft game. It was still a lot of fun to explore. Beautifully crafted believable Star Wars world. 

The story starts of promising and fun. You meet cool characters, factions and what is hopefully a good storyline unfolds before you. Quickly becomes boring and mismatched on each planet that you forget you had a story to begin with. It is just 3 quests on each planet that have completely different sub stories and break the pacing of the game. The finale they also ruined. I couldn't wait for it to be over, it became a dull soap opera with boring predictable characters. And your mom. LOL. 

Tatooine storyline was the best, thankfully they pulled themselves together and worked with SW material and made it believable and iconic. Also it was fun sneaking onto an imperial station off Tashara. But later on it just loses the momentum. Other planets where writers had their creative freedom run wild were rather dull compared to Tatooine. They aren't good at making their own new material without basis. 

ND-5. I thought this was going to be as cool a droid companion like in SW: Jedi series KX droid. It had all the potential to be as cool being from clone wars, being bad ass, roger roger type droid. Looking menacing they somehow made him ANNOYING as hell. So annoying I had to turn off dialogue while free-roaming in space and every time I heard his voice lecture me it was just boring. Even the voice actor was cast wrong for this role. The robot is an annoying grumpy dad that does not feel like a cool bad-ass murder bot but rather... a boring dad. Voice, emotion, voice lines. Everything makes it a boring dad. I wish it just shut up. It is worse than Kay Vess btw. It is the worst thing. The best thing is probably that fish tank guy Bosnok. He is annoying but in a funny way. In all seriousness, Lady Q'ira, Jabba, Lando, Hutts, Jawas. You know the real Star Wars characters are the best here. Not the protagonists and main characters. Side characters are the best. 

DLCs not worth getting each of them I reviewed separately in their own review.

Ubisoft Connect gave me lots of pain. I had to repair the game for it to work. It gave me Doplhin 028 error of not being online. I had problems logging in and several times I wanted to played it would not let me in for hours until I found a fix. It just wouldn't let me start the game... I had previously started and they say it can be played in offline mod. 

The game crashes a few times too. Mainly in space. I run it on an old system on Medium, it looks nice. 2080 RTX 3900 ryzen series on m.2 SSD. 16 gb ram. I had no problems with the frame rate. DLSS on. Overall, stable no lag. But had some annoying crashes. 

Good thing about Ubisoft Connect is that you can manually upload a single save file for cloud sync. No more than that but you get to control it. Unlike on Steam it backs up everything but if there is a discrepancy in saving it will ask which ones you'd like to keep local saves or the cloud ones and you can accidentally erase the most recent saves on Steam so I have it off. 

Parkour is annoying at times. Thankfully there is this high contrast mod if you get really lost and don't feel like figuring it out sometimes, wish more games had it. 

Nix in many ways annoying, plays dead when shouldn't. 

There is not much loot diversity and you kinda just explore for the feel of the world and Star Wars. Side missions are nice but it lacks a cinematic dialogue camera making it more boring than it should be. Sabacc and Food vendor mini-games are fun. I purposely left the button QTE mini-games in and on hard because it made it more fun. Sabacc is also very easy, but some people say they spend 50 hours trying to figure it out lol. To each their own I guess but it is hardly poker. 

This is a standard Ubisoft game. Smaller and more fine crafted than their Assassin's Creed slop. Connect is a pain. Lack of loot variety. Combat is not the worst. Speeder piloting is okay. Ship combat is okay. The reputation idea and choices can be fun to play with. The story becomes awful, characters are awful that you want to mute them. 

Should you get it? Absolutely not. Only die hard Star Wars fans should get it. At a huge discount like 55% off or better yet 90% off. Do not get the DLCs they are cash grabs. 

Will I come back to play this again? Maybe one day when I need a Star Wars game and there is nothing SW to play I might tackle side quests that I left out but I never again want to play this story. I just want to explore the world and shoot cartels like in Red Dead. The story you can only tolerate once and it will cringe you out anyway.

This is probably the most underrated game on Steam.... *if* you're a Star Wars fan.

If you ever wanted a Han Solo simulator, this is it. I'd still argue Jedi Survivor remains the best single player Star Wars game I've ever played, but this title *nails* the atmosphere of being in the Star Wars universe better then any other game I've touched. When you're wandering the streets of Mos Eisley, turning a corner to see the very bar Luke and Obi-Wan wandered into a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away... you really do feel like you're there. Add on some reasonably enjoyable combat, sky-high production values, great voice acting and music and some weirdly well-tuned speeder bike and arcade space-sim gameplay, and you have yourself a really awesome package that every Star Wars fan owes themselves a playthrough or two. The characters grown on you, some familiar faces pop up when you least expect them (and not just as cameos too), and I challenge anyone not to find Nix - your MVP space-lizard-cat sideckick - as absolutely adorable. In terms of tone, if you mashed up Solo, Empire Strikes Back and Book of Boba Fett then you're about there.

It's not all plain sailing, though. Strip away the Star Wars veneer and you have a technically dazzling but somewhat unstable open world adventure game that is weighed down with some weird design decisions and stuff that gets annoying quickly. The stealth mechanics don't really work very well - being a bit primitive for a stealth game but too front and centre to ignore entirely - and loot/rewards have a distinct cap of usefulness that you'll reach long before the end of the game. Even basic stuff like manual savegames are handled in a bizarre way, where the game can never really make up its mind on what it wants you to rely on. You can only save in 'roaming' areas, but what defines roaming vs being in a mission or in a dangerous area can be very inconsistent. From a technical standpoint its riven with stuff that doesn't really work - if you're an Nvidia gamer, you need to switch off RTXDI if you want frame rates better then 20fps, for example.

None of this should block you from getting it if you're a fan, though. It's just a massive shame we won't get a sequel.

In terms of edition - honestly, during a sale, get the Gold or Ultimate editions. Both DLCs are really good and worth a playthrough.

Star Wars Outlaws : A Perfectly Serviceable Game

Rating 7.8/10

At its core, Star Wars Outlaws does a well enough job in alot of its gameplay aspects, it doesn't try too hard to something so outrageously innovative, instead it follows its objective of delivering a nice enough game to play, with the big budget Star Wars presentation.

Speaking of presentation, the game is absolutely beautiful, its implementation of lighting is at times one of the best I have ever seen in a videogame, lighting every biome, every cavern and every location to bring its finest details. It has this stylized filmic cinematic look that you come to expect of the old Star Wars film or SciFi film of olden days. The animations and motion capture are well executed. The environments are richly detailed and truthful to the franchise. Ubisoft and Massive has definitely put alot of money, time and effort to bring out the best presentation of a franchise this gigantic. From the space food to the cities, it is recreated in excellent fashion.

The available content is good as well, without the season pass you will still be able to enjoy roughly 20-40 hours of gameplay. Which for me is more than enough for an open world action-stealth game like this. The stuff that really holds this game back from achieving a higher rating is a decent but painfully predictable story, lacking gunplay (you can have a blaster with different configurations, but your arsenal is limited to guns you can only pick up from elimited NPCs. One things I cannot stand and one I deduct a full point from the game is its decision to have respawning enemies in missions or quests involving raiding outposts, making missions involving these activities extremely annoying to deal with (unless you disable the alarms, which sometimes are very hard to locate, be ready to face and endless wave of enemy stormtroopers, officers, droids and even deathtroopers). And people who expect this to be more a  Red Dead Redemption but in space, its not, it plays more like a stealth action game rather than a hardcore shoot em up western.

Overall, I enjoyed most of my near 30 hours of game time with Star Wars Outlaws, I am truly impressed with its presentation and even sound design. The story is just decent at its best. But I wished i had a better experience with its lacking combat mechanics and at times questionable game design.  I recommend getting this on sale, the game's presentation alone is worth its price of admission.

From the perspective of someone who really doesn't engage with Star Wars much at all, I can find a lot of things to like about Star Wars Outlaws. The primary reason is that it has the advantage of being the first single player open world game in the Star Wars universe, and that's generally my favourite genre in which to explore settings like this one. Ubisoft did a great job of fleshing out Star Wars Outlaws with tonnes of cool looking characters and interesting environments that are worth exploring. My one issue is that one of the areas is a lot less well realised than the other three worlds because it's just a hub town, and I really wanted to explore a bigger snow environment.

The story is well written. I really like Kay Vess as a character, and think she has a lot of funny mannerisms. She's a terrible liar, has severe mommy issues, and a lovely dog - all of which are traits that I can relate to. Nix is a really awesome companion, and I liked how he can be easily commanded to carry out useful interventions in combat, stealth and exploration. My primary complaint about the story is that the whole narrative arc focuses on finding and building a team of companions. None of these companions had the same attention to detail found in some RPGs where each of them has their own narrative hook that allows the player to feel more connected to them and their background. I had very little attachment to them by the end of the game, and that was a real disappointment.

Mechanically, I found that the controls on PC were well implemented. Stealth mechanics are suitably challenging, while combat is satisfying, but best avoided. I like the fast talking mechanic a lot, and I really enjoy stunning NPCs who spot you with Kay's blaster. Her speeder is fun to pilot and upgrade, but I just don't like the aesthetic design of it, and would have liked to be able to change to one of the long nosed speeders from the films. The space combat is a lot of fun too, because it's not too challenging or frustrating, while also allowing for the player to feel quite powerful by upgrading it and becoming a flying death machine very early on in the game. The roll mechanics and dodge maneuvers are so cool to pull off that you'll feel like a fighter ace without really needing to be particularly skilled. 

So all in all, Star Wars Outlaws is worth the price of admission. I'm looking forward to finishing the DLCs, and I'm maybe in the market to replay it one day.

I enjoyed pretty much the entire time I spent on the game. I loved the planets, the way they looked and felt and how you could explore them, how each gives you multiple types of environments to explore (grasslands to hills to canyons and ruins or dense jungles divided up by traversable rivers and big lakes, etc.) and all the different things you can find and the side activities you can do and the structures you can explore in and outside of the story missions.

BUT, as much as I enjoyed it, I think at least a bit of that amount comes down to how I am able to approach games these days. I can't spend multiple hours every day on games anymore just because of how life goes, so I usually get about an hour or two every couple of days and maybe on or two days on less busy weekends where I can devote about 5-6 hours at a time to gaming. All that is to say, most the time I spent with the game was in relatively "short" bursts over a fairly long stretch of time and I was genuinely excited every time I could jump back on my speeder, my ship or just continue exploring on foot. (OTHERWISE THOUGH, I can see how you could get bored or burnt out on it pretty quickly because it does get very repetitive.)
Because that is really what this game comes down to for me. It's the exploring. Ubisoft, known for their cluttered maps full of objective markers, have actually managed to strike a fairly decent middle ground between letting you fully off the leash and leaving uncovering new things entirely to the player and guiding you towards various points of interest and mission objectives. You can customize the experience to your liking and choose how much you want those guides to intrude on your experience. I played with everything turned off as much as possible and I had a blast. I encourage everyone to do the same.
Outside of purely exploring for the sake of it, the gameplay is fun most of the time. The speeder is nice to ride around on once fully upgraded, otherwise it felt quite slow at the start of the game. Sneaking around enemy bases is quite nicely implemented and the enemy AI isn't the dumbest I've seen over the years, but certainly far from the smartest. Same for the combat. The enemies aren't stupid, they even try to rush you, flush you out of cover with grenades and try to pummel you with high powered and explosive weapons towards the latter half of the game, but even on the harder difficulties, you can survive every battle with ease with the right clothing and charms equipped.
Here comes a big BUT again though. This, the sneaking around and fighting, it essentially stays the same from start to finish. Yes, you do unlock more firemodes for your blaster  and some new gadgets. Yes, you encounter enemies with more varied weapons and some that are a lot tougher to take down. But the as long as you keep up with your own upgrades and equipment, it all feels the same. The only substantial change comes when you unlock something that let's you perform stealth takedowns on enemies you previously had to avoid or fully engage in combat otherwise. (Here the repetitiveness rears its ugly head again...)
ALSO ANOTHER VERY INTERESTING ASPECT FALLING JUST SHORT IN ITS EXECTUION
The faction system is a great idea, but I don't think they went far enough with it and they give you a very easy way to manipulate it without any consequence. It works very well at the beginning of the game on Toshara and then in Kijimi, but as soon as you can buy the (very cheap) items to just boost your rep with every faction at any affiliated trader, it's no challenge at all and you never have to worry about managing the different syndicates again. And after reaching max rep with a syndicate ONCE for just a second, you don't have any incentive of keeping it that high ever again since you still have to fuck them over and sneak around behind their backs for any side missions and collectables in their hideouts. It only gives you a couple of items and that's it. Anything above good isn't really worth it. The system is a really great idea, but it is very shallow in the way it's implemented and has far too little consequence.

The story is...fine. It's not bad, but it's nothing life changing. The best thing about it are the two main characters and their interactions. The star wars flavor is captured pretty well, but the story they are trying to tell still feels a little too tame for my liking. Many of the little twists and turns can feel quite predictable and it feels rushed in it's finale while also leaving me a bit underwhelmed. The first DLC (Wild Card), is a fun little side quest in which you get to meet and briefly work together with Lando Calrissian on a space casino heist. I would recommend getting it as part of the gold edition on a discount, otherwise it's not something I'd pay an additional 15 bucks for. The second DLC (A Pirates Fortune) can only be started after finishing the main campaign. It gives you an entire new space based location to explore with about a similar scope as the spare areas around the existing planets and a new on foot location that is only available in the story missions as far as I could tell. It is a bit longer than Wild Card, but not by much. The new location looks really nice, but doesn't offer much new in terms of gameplay besides a new type of contract and after finishing the story you can fly around in the new type of ship you get during the story missions. The real star here though are the interactions with another familiar character if you've watched the clone wars show. Hondo Ohnaka. He is very fun, has some great dialog with the main character and doesn't outstay his welcome. Everything else about the story was just sort of meh though. It feels very meandering with the way it drags to back and forth between the new location and the old planets. The old base on tatooine was nice, but otherwise I feel like it should have stayed in the new location entirely. The story also starts in an interesting way. A tale of pirate treasure, a new mysterious thing in space, legends and ruins of a lost civilization. But all you end up with is sneaking around and fighting new random pirate goons the same way you've been doing the entire game, but in a cool looking asteroid base, until the finale where the game basically says "You didn't want to see any of the cool ancient and possibly dangerous treasure that was the whole point of coming here anyway, right?" and then it ends.

After hundreds of hours I conclude this is a quite underrated piece of SW gem. Flawed? Sure. What isn't? But definitely didn't deserve that bandwagon-hate that has befell it.
But let's get to the TLDR:

You'll enjoy this game, if:
- You want SW world immersion.
- Can view characters and their path as core importance of a story.

You probably won't enjoy, if:
- You're after elaborately designed combat experience/leveling up.
- You don't like open world.

Without any superlatives I think this is one of the most beautiful games so far I ever witnessed. There might be much better SW combat games but I sure never felt like I'm right there in the world as I did here. Some don't like that this is an open world piece, but I do think exploring all the settlements and cantinas and whatnot wouldn't be the same in a more confined style. Filling the world up with content is another matter, and while the game makes sure to lead you to every major, worthwile locations to see in the form of treasure hunt (which I enjoyed thoroughly, loving the gear designs) I somehow missed a little bit more dynamic approach of exploration, like finding the actual creatures in some of the lairs and having a conflict out of it or some other unexpected throw-in from time to time. Also it's really bothering when you find an interesting ruin and can't go in to explore, it's true for parts of the city (especially on Akiva) too which are built but not walkable at all, I can only hope that further DLC's will lead us there. But then again, the maps are already huge and there definitely are some hidden encounters and curiosities to discover. I'm pointing at space too!

Some felt the world to be rather static, not being able to interact with many NPCs etc. I beg to differ. While it's true that you can't speak to any and everyone, it's not needed at all. There are so many conversations and comments going on, sometimes even reflecting on your actions. Syndicates and types of gangs have different batches of convos, I barely heard the same reactions twice for spotting Nix, the stormtroopers I found after 200 hrs in the most remote corner of a map had lines that I never heard before, and while I wish there were other replies that the common "uh-huh" from many of them, still the variations were plenty and interesting enough all over the world. There are also NPC-s that are appearing and giving a little quest only when you return to a scene a second time, in an absolutely organic way. I never felt for a minute that I'm not in a living world. 

The story is nothing convoluted but it's enjoyable, where it really shines is its very real characters and in fact it's all what it was supposed to be about in the first place. Kay and ND's chemistry and journey, both physical and mental, carry the whole thing on its back and honestly I'd pay over and over again just to be able to go on more adventures with them. The voice acting is STELLAR (starry-eyed shoutout to Jay) and there are quite a few memorable lines up their sleeves. 
Heads-up, a LOT of conversations happen while taking off and jumping to hyperspace with your ship. I advise doing this a lot without skips if you're really interested in what everyone has to say. It really adds to the depth of characters.
Mocap, scene direction and pacing is mostly good especially where it really matters, but there were some instances where it was so low effort and rushed it threw me out of immersion entirely. Other times even the smallest gestures and expressions were in place. Odd alternations of quality among scenes.

While it's mainly designed to be a stealth game (entertaining but a bit too easy on that side even on challenging settings, imho), armed combat is not without its fun factor and although you can't permanently keep an extra gun on your back, the type range of weapons to grab at any spot and try make it really fun, being able to go from a pesky sniper holed up in a conquered imp tower to a bold heavy, slowly but steadily marching forward in the relative safety of the shield of your repeater. Space fight is even more solid, and once you properly upgrade your speeder/ship it becomes real partyhard. Here I have to honorable mention the speeder physics which are excellent fun at this point, zooming around on the terrain jumping over anything you can and tricking pursuers head-on into rocks is a separate game in itself. 

Loved working for syndicates and trying to keep the balance in my reputation and thus gathering rewards and making my journey a lot smoother, but I wish the jobs would have been less repetitive, if nothing else by leading us to more  locations instead of the usual four or five. 

All in all, this game is loveable. If you really like the world of SW and always wished to experience something other than the jedi/rebel aspect and also love good characters, you'll have a lot of well spent hours in this. Warning: Kessel Sabacc is addictive. Have fun!

The gun-play actually does a very good job of capturing the feeling of the movies, with inaccurate blaster shots ricocheting off of surfaces and causing sparks all around, and feeling wise I would kind of compare it to the gun-play in Red Dead Redemption 2... but with blasters.

Stealth is familiar but still very enjoyable, as long you enjoy the slower pace of stealth game-play. Infiltrating bases is kept engaging by offering plenty of different ways to approach them, and a few options to take out the guards, whether it's one by one, or by setting off an explosive object to take out multiple at a time. One oversight by the developers was not giving protagonist Kay some sort of melee weapon, as you will just have to accept that she has a mean right hook, and will punch, chop and slap her way through many a Stormtrooper through out your adventure. You do get used to it though, and the satisfying sound of each hit makes it more enjoyable.

The sound design and music are on another level in Outlaws. I highly recommend playing with headphones. Cities have so much going on within small areas, and it stands out as a game that has so many overlapping conversations and environmental noises happening simultaneously, but nothing is clashing, there is just a huge amount of depth to the soundscape. Comparing it to Assassins Creed Shadows, which has some very nice sound design, but it's environments don't sound nearly as alive as Outlaws, and it doesn't feel like there's as much distance between noises. Massive deserve a lot of praise for the work they do in environmental and sound design.

My one recommendation for playing Outlaws, is to turn the difficulty up. The whole game is built around stealth, and although shooting your way through everything is an option, the game just doesn't really stand up as an all out action shooter. At least with the difficulty up, getting caught in a shootout feels dangerous, so it pushes you to use stealth more, and then the challenge of getting through undetected is very rewarding.

I went into Star Wars Outlaws hoping for a gritty, immersive experience in the Star Wars underworld — something different from the usual Jedi/saber fare. What I got, at least early on, felt more like a checklist open-world game wrapped in a Star Wars skin.

Let’s start with the good: the game looks great. The environments are detailed, the world feels alive, and there’s clearly a deep love for the source material in the art direction. For Star Wars fans, that aesthetic alone might be enough to carry you through. The premise — a scoundrel navigating the criminal underworld — is also a refreshing change of pace, at least conceptually.

But once you start actually playing, the cracks show quickly.

Gameplay feels rough. Movement is clunky, combat lacks weight and responsiveness, and the stealth mechanics feel like they were tacked on without much depth. It’s hard to feel immersed when your character controls like they’re stuck in molasses during shootouts. There’s a sense that the game is trying to do too many things at once — stealth, cover shooting, open-world traversal, choice-based dialogue — but none of them feel particularly polished or engaging out of the gate.

The story and voice acting are another letdown. The protagonist, Kay Vess, just doesn’t have much charisma early on, and the performances feel flat and overly restrained. I wasn’t drawn into her journey or the stakes of the narrative. It plays safe and lacks the grit or emotional depth you’d want from a story set in the morally gray parts of the Star Wars universe.

There’s also a hint of modern corporate “wokeness” — nothing extreme, but it’s there in the way the cast and world are presented. It feels less like a natural part of the story and more like Ubisoft trying to check boxes. Diversity itself isn’t the issue — Star Wars has always had a wide galaxy of characters — but when it feels performative or pushed without nuance, it just rings hollow. It’s less about what is shown and more about how it's implemented, and here, it comes off as surface-level.

To be clear: I didn’t spend a massive amount of time with the game, so maybe it gets better. But from what I saw, Star Wars Outlaws struggles with identity. It wants to be an open-world action-adventure, a story-driven character piece, and a love letter to fans — but doesn’t fully succeed at any of them.

If you’re a die-hard Star Wars fan, there is some enjoyment to be found here. But for more critical players looking for tight gameplay and a gripping narrative, you might walk away underwhelmed — as I did.

I held off on buying Outlaws until a decent sale after reading a good chunk of negative reviews and feedback after its release, and I'm glad I did because I'm positive my view of the game would be very different had I picked it up earlier. Up until about a month after I purchased Outlaws there were significant bugs and crashes being encountered by players that made the game frustrating for some, unplayable for others. I write this to acknowledge that the game (like many others) had a very problematic launch, and that for me most of the issues are now resolved.

Outlaws has been described as Assassin's Creed with a Star Wars skin, and from a high-level that's a fair assessment. It doesn't break Ubisoft's mould, it's not revolutionary, but it's fun and captures the feel of Star Wars without throwing you into (too many) of the same old backdrops.

The stealth game play is fun, but not overly challenging. Having a partner (Nix) to distract or attack goes a long way to making things easy. The gun play is pretty basic, and I'd probably describe it as point-and-click Jedi Survivor/Outcast: some enemies have mechanics you need to account for, but beyond that you can customise your blaster to a style that fits you and stick with it. Ship combat is about the same. The AI isn't very bright in space, so I do think folks will be disappointed there.

The story isn't overly complex, but I think if you made an honest comparison to either A New Hope or even Solo you'd say it's on-par. The characters are likeable, and there's lots of side-missions to keep you entertained when you feel like pausing the main story. My one gripe is that, for people living in a seedy underworld, Kay and her companions are a bit too wholesome. Kay is also a bit too naive to actually survive some times.

All-in-all it's a fun Star Wars game that follows Ubisoft's regular formula. If you've enjoyed an Assassin's Creed game and you're a Star Wars fan you should enjoy this. Not that I've not completed the story as yet, nor have I purchased any of the DLC. My assessment is based on buying the game for half-price; I might feel different paying the full amount.
