I think this is a genuinely good game, and I enjoyed it a lot more than I'd thought I would, just based on the seemingly overwhelmingly negative reception at launch and the mostly negative reviews I saw in the online community. That being said, for me at least, this game came with a whole bunch of caveats that significantly impacted the initial enjoyment and overall, this was absolutely not a plug and play experience for me.

Starting with the initial technical hurdles, just getting this game optimized and working to a reasonable balance of visual fidelity, smooth FPS and low latency was extremely difficult, perhaps the most painful optimization I've ever done. This lasted almost 7 hours, done in three separate sessions, just trying to tweak the various settings, testing stable FPS and latency values and trying to get the best performance-visual ratio out of the game. The NVIDIA App optimization preset was terrible (for me at least), so heavy manual tuning was required. 

Initially, I got very good results from an FSR-based setup and that would have been the end of it, but then Patch 1.6 just seemed to completely break AMD FSR upscaling (and frame generation), locking the camera while FSR is active. This made FSR completely unusable and I went with DLSS in the final version, trading lower latency and some FPS for slightly better looking Ray Tracing. Nonetheless, the final results were not terrible (Ultra graphics preset, High Ray Tracing, stable 90 FPS, 40-50 ms latency with external Low Latency set to Ultra), it just took long to get there. Unfortunately, whatever hardware I have that the game does not like meant that I still experienced frequent crashing throughout my playthrough and despite extensive efforts to identify the reason (anything from G-Sync interfering to Low Latency problems), nothing worked, so eventually, I just accepted crashing as a cost of playing this game. Fortunately, most of the crashes either occurred right after launch or on reloading or fast traveling between planets, so I just tried to avoid those as much as possible. However, I very rarely experienced random crashes during missions, almost all of them were linked to a specific action (fast travel or entering a cutscene). Again, this may just be related to my hardware setup and you might be completely fine but I did have this issue. 

As for story and gameplay elements, I honestly enjoyed the vibes and atmosphere more than the main story, which I found to be kind of bland and it can be summed up as the smuggler with a heart of gold realizes that the friends made along the way are the real treasure. It's kind of generic and predictable but it does have Han Solo and Lando vibes from the films, so I guess it's authentic in that regard. Also, many of the side stories force you to lose reputation with one of the crime syndicates, so if you are trying to manage reputation with all four syndicates, it can mean a lot of repeatable contract missions just to preserve what you already have. I found this to be slightly annoying throughout the game.

You can recover mission intel from basically anywhere and these can often send you on interesting and rewarding side missions. Some of them are a bit repetitive but engaging with side content can still be very enjoyable. There is a ton that you can explore in this game, though a lot of the rewards are cosmetic-only. Exploration enjoyment factor is one thing that I value very highly in any open-world game and in that regard, Outlaws did not disappoint. There is a lot to find in this game if you bother to look, and many times you can come across genuinely beautiful vistas and locations. Almost all the locations feel authentic and braving the sandstorms of Tatooine or the rainy jungles of Akiva at night are completely different and unique experiences. Just walking (and flying) around and experiencing what each planet had to offer was ultimately much more fun than doing the main story.

Stealth had a terrible reputation upon launch but I think the patches have dramatically improved stealth mechanics and it was probably the most interesting and enjoyable gameplay aspect. Honestly, the stealth tools and environmental options at your disposal are quite good and while the enemy AI isn't the smartest, I did enjoy sneaking around patrols, quietly disabling defenses and walking away with all the loot unnoticed. Kay is a thief, first and foremost, so this was very on brand for me.

Ranged combat, on the other hand, is pretty simple and you are limited to one blaster (with three configurations) and a pick-up weapon. It's passable, I guess, but I never had as much fun shooting as I had sneaking around.

The two main types of side activities (flying and upgrading the Trailblazer and playing Kessel sabacc) are both genuinely fun. Playing sabacc is probably the best minigame I've seen in any game, on par with Machine Strike in Horizon Forbidden West. It is easy to learn but you can develop many different strategies with cheats and shift tokens that always keep rounds interesting, and I've had a few laughs turning the game around from obviously losing hands. You don't have to be good at playing cards to enjoy sabacc, it is just a genuinely fun minigame. 

As for the DLCs, while both are good, I liked 'A Pirate's Fortune' a lot more than 'Wild Card'. It is longer, has more interesting missions and expands the ship upgrade system and allows you to take proper smuggling contracts and do difficult smuggling runs. It's a bit weird because I am not sure if it's advertised anywhere but I think this post-DLC content is some of the best in the entire game. I don't understand why this was shoved to the very end, when you don't have any need for credits anymore, perhaps this was originally a core content idea that was cut during development. 

As for the 'Exclusive Jabba's Gambit' mission that you can do in the Ultimate Edition.....it's a joke. The idea that you would sell one 5-minute mission for 20 EUR that is literally just two shootouts and one conversation with Jabba is a total ripoff. I picked up the Ultimate Edition mainly for the cosmetic items (which I liked and used a lot) but had I done that for the 'exclusive mission' instead, I might have been very angry and disappointed.

Which brings me to the main point, I enjoyed the vistas and the vibes of this game far more than the stories and missions. If you are the type of person who just wants to experience the main story of the game, it is really not that good. However, if you want to explore unique locales and want to see the Star Wars galaxy come to life in interesting ways, there is a lot for you here. I just hope the crashing will be patched by then. 

To be wallet friendly as much as possible, I would probably buy the Gold Edition (for the Season Pass) when it is on 50% discount. I think the 50-60 EUR paid that way is a fair price for this game if it includes both DLCs. However, do not buy the Ultimate Edition only for the exclusive mission, it really isn't worth it.

This game has its issues, despite the budget, and the huge studio behind it, it has its issues. But I'm a Star Wars mega fan and I like to give everything a try and form my own opinions. 

The GOOD

- The worldbuilding is insane, next level and genuinely incomparable to any other modern Star Wars game. Absolutely stunning, even down to the finest detail it's worth it alone for a megafan to just be able to listen in on conversations across multiple planets of all the different species. Graphically/visually this game is so beautiful, the planets, the space combat, the characters big and small. Notable locations include: Jabba's Palace, Mos Eisley and pretty much the entirety of Tatooine. Akiva is a beautiful planet despite the near constant rainfall and Toshara also has some beautiful scenery and locations.

- The story is fun and unique to Star Wars, the concept might not be super unique but its not something I've seen before, there's four syndicates that all require attention and all do not like each other so you have to do jobs which often pin two syndicates together, making it difficult to be in the good graces of multiple syndicates at one time. But it's a fun concept. After completing the game and the DLC, the story is definitely the best thing about the game. I could see some not enjoying it but I did think it was a nice addition to the Star Wars universe. I could nitpick it, but it was good. Don't expect Jedi Fallen Order or Survivor level though.

- Sabaac, A unique, space poker (not really, I don't know if there is a real life game similar to it), I think this game does it better than any other in game card games, like Fallout New Vegas didn't create a card game nearly as fun as this. It's a simple concept but this to me doesn't get stale, the rewards are good and it's just the right amount of virtual gambling to satisfy my needs.

THE NOT SO GOOD

- Some stuff just throws me off a bit but not enough to stop playing, such as the takedown system, I feel like I just ignore it after so long but as others have pointed out, it's a little hard to believe that you can just knock out stormtroopers in full armor with one punch, and you have to do it consistently if you don't want to be Rambo the entire game. Not unbearable, but it isn't great. 

- On each planet you can sit down at a street vendor, pay a [i]measly[/i] 200 credits and eat a meal that can become a permanent buff to your companion Nix (only one at a time though, it doesn't stack). Which is cool, except it utilizes Quick Time Events. It feels kinda out of place and I feel as if I understand the concept, like they're trying to be cute but I found them to be annoying and out of place. Again not unbearable but everytime I just questioned why this was greenlit. They take way too long imo.

THE BAD

- Glitches, none too game breaking but with a budget this size and again made by a not so indie developer, and now it's been what, a year since the game released? It still has glitches/bugs. I haven't seen any incredibly major ones but I have had my character get stuck in a wall or get stuck while dismounting the speeder, or when walking by objects I've kicked one and it spazzes out and multiple items go flying everywhere. Again this isn't major but it does take away from the overall aesthetic as it doesn't happen in most games I've played.

- Ubisoft repetitiveness. I can't see any casual gamer wanting to get anywhere near 100% completion. Like the last few Ubisoft titles I've tried, I get to a point, maybe 15-20 hours in where it just becomes incredibly monotonous and boring. Rinse and repeat and it makes you want to just streamline the main story or quit entirely. I again am a Star Wars megafan so I will go for most if not all achievements and find everything this game has to offer, I do wanna say I am enjoying it still at 40 hours, but I have spent 10+ hours at this point avoiding the main storyline (I think it's the final mission) so that I can do nonstop side missions and exploring/ achievement hunting etc.

- The price.... how in the world they could justify a $70 base and a $130 max is beyond criminal. Compare this to games like Star Wars Jedi Survivor and it doesn't hold a candle to it, there are major differences and this game comes out on top when it comes to free roaming and just enjoying the worlds, but that shouldn't justify the price difference. Like previously stated I got this on a deal, I didn't even remember buying the top version and I'm sure it's mostly cosmetics and such as there's no DLC (extra missions, unless I'm mistaken), so it doesn't really seem worth it to spend more then the base price.

THE DLC

- Hondo Ohnaka was a great character in the Clone Wars and his character was portrayed very well in this DLC. However that's probably the only good thing I'd have to say about the DLC. The new world was enjoyable but arguably my least favorite and shortest compared to the planets in the base game. This added a few extra hours but wasn't very long. Overall the DLC doesn't seem like it would be worth the additional purchase, unless like previously mentioned there is a huge discount and you're a big Star Wars fan. I wish I could write more but it was generally lackluster. 

IN SUMMARY

- I went into this with little to no expectations, I had heard mostly negative reviews, but I enjoyed it. The story isn't bad, the worldbuilding is beautifully insane and worth buying this on sale alone. If you've played other Ubisoft titles and have gotten burnt out from their repetitiveness, you might feel the same on this one, but if you're a huge Star Wars fan, maybe put up with some of the crap in this game and enjoy exploring some new and old planets and an interesting storyline , or don't who am I but a random reviewer.

Star Wars Outlaws had a lot of potential but ultimately ended up being another typical subpar AAA Ubisoft experience. I can only recommend the game when it's on sale and if you are a big fan of Star Wars. Outlaws was probably the wrong title for this game and I feel like the game was held back not focusing on more adult aspects and ideas of being an outlaw. If this wasn't set in the Star Wars universe, I probably wouldn't have played it as much as I did, if at all. The game is definitely in a lot better state than when it launched, but still feels like a half baked experience.

Fidelity/Performance:
Be ready to crash and experience quirky bugs. Over my 52.7 hours of playing I crashed 33 different times. I crashed 7 times in a row at the beginning of the game when you first acquire the EML850 and you escape Sliro's mansion. I have a beefy system; RTX4090, i913900k, 64gb ram and game was installed on a M.2, there is definitely something wrong with the game that is conflicting with RTX users. I have seen many others complain about constant crashes and looks like most of them were on an RTX card of some sort. Other than the crashes, performance seemed okay with everything maxed out in 4k with DLSS on. DLAA seemed to not look as good or perform as well as DLSS on quality for some reason. Frames were usually good and would sometimes dip here and there but nothing too jarring. What was jarring were some of the cutscenes and especially in engine cutscenes. There is an option to limit frames in cutscenes and even with that off, there was a noticeable difference in frame rate quality between in engine and pre rendered cutscenes versus when you are actually playing. There were also some pre rendered cutscenes where 3d models are mixed with what I will describe as a hand drawn or paper like background and it just seems very off. I didn't encounter any gamebreaking bugs, but minor things like glitching on textures, falling through the level, NPC AI bugging out etc. The biggest annoyance is with the contextual prompts, sometimes they don't appear and you have to reload the game or you have to be in some arbitrary spot to activate the prompt. Graphics overall were definitely above average for a modern title but nothing ground breaking. One thing I will commend them on was the lighting, with RTX lighting settings on high it provided for some really stunning scenes and I found myself taking a lot of screenshots. It was awesome as a SW fan to see some of great things from this universe in 4k. 

Gameplay:
Outlaws offers some fun gameplay moments and you do get to experience classic Star Wars blasting opportunities (in their own Ubijank way) but this starts to become stale after awhile. Blasting is focused around your sidearm blaster, with many iconic SW weapons appearing in game as pickup weapons that have limited ammo. I feel like this was a big mistake, with so many weapons in the SW universe, why are we stuck with one blaster and everything else is a throwaway? The blaster is also your tool to solving puzzles while exploring throughout the game world, utilizing the ion charge and explosive blast. The upgrades seem superficial at best, with the only tangible upgrade being the damage increase and changing the shape of the projectile. This is why I feel the shooting gets stale after awhile, the blaster gets boring and any other weapon that you find has a very short time of use. It's the same issue with vehicles too. You get a cool ship, the EML850 and a speeder which I forget the model. You can upgrade them somewhat, changing armaments on the ship and your stereotypical gamey upgrades for damage, durability, speed etc. These are the only vehicles you can interact with, period. I would be okay with only having one ship and speeder if you could commandeer other speeders, or mount Banthas and other wildlife like you see the NPCs do. You can't and it's disappointing. Seeing the dreadful amount of pointless paintjobs and trinkets that I never used constantly reminded me time could've been better spent elsewhere. This leads into another dislike about the idea of this game in general, being an "outlaw". It seems the only crimes you can commit are against the Empire and other crime syndicates and oh, being able to pickpocket select npcs. You can't attack/rob random people, you can't steal vehicles, you can't really do much of anything. If the game was rated M or at least focused on the more adult aspects that would've been involved with being an outlaw in the gritty SW universe, I feel like it could've been better. The one thing in relation to crime that was a good idea, but needs better implementation is their Crime Syndicate Reputation system. Kinda self explanatory, you do work for a faction to boost your rep but depending on what it is, it can affect your reputation with other factions too. It made it interesting in the beginning, balancing your rep with the factions but quickly you learn that you just want to be friendly with everyone. There are reward tiers for increasing rep, and you can gain access to different Syndicate areas without being shot and hassled. An interesting idea that ultimately made redundant by menial rewards. There should have been more balance and thought put into it other than just make everyone happy. For example, maybe you get higher tier rewards with the Hutt's because you have a negative rep with another faction?

Quick note on Nix too. He's adorable, but I feel like all the devotion to the game mechanics and extra exploration spots around the world just to find more trinkets for Nix could have been better spent focusing on adding more depth and polish to the game. For example, the galactic food street vendors. I did think this was a cool way to earn buffs and show off the weird side of SW food, but the whole 5-10 minute animations and minigame to eat the food were overdone and dragged out. The random jumping/climbing puzzles to get Nix more pointless trinkets was tiring too.  

Story:
The story is kinda what you would expect, it wasn't terrible but had your typical ups and downs, some hits and misses. The one memorable thing about the story was Kay's relationship development with ND5, I thought that was done well and they had some good moments together cringy humor aside. The voice acting overall ranged from mediocre to well done but the story was overall forgettable. One thing that I didn't like which is gameplay and story related was their reliance on a certain formula for 3 "boss" fights. For the three fights, they are essentially the same. The enemy is impervious to your blaster and you have to use something in the environment to hurt them. I don't mind that once, but using it for three biggest fights in the game just seems lazy and unimaginative. 

I could definitely go into more detail about more of the game systems, story, areas etc and probably some bigger points that I missed but this is already long enough. 
TLDR; Even for a Star Wars fan like myself, I don't think I would ever come back to experience this game again. For a Star Wars game, there's too many missed opportunities and it doesn't make you feel like an outlaw. Being rated teen and not focusing on more adult/mature themes I feel held the games premise back. For an open world game, its lifeless world and typical Ubisoft repetitive structure leave a lot to be desired and feel like a game you already played. I would only recommend this when its on sale and if you're really into Star Wars like myself, seeing a modern SW universe game in 4k with RT is the most positive thing.

To describe this game, Ubisoft tried its best to put together Assassins Creed, Tomb Raider, and No Man's Sky into one game.  I wouldn't say it particularly does any individual one of those games phenomenally but together it definitely creates a wholesome experience.  If you are looking for more of the hardcore sneaking around/puzzle game this might not be for you.  But, Outlaws fully makes you feel like you were immersed in the Star Wars world while you play through the story of a young Freelance Smuggler named Kay Vess.  In my opinion, the story had a great mix of comedy, cuteness (from Nix of course), anger, making friends, and plenty of twists and turns in the story throughout the game.  

There is plenty to do in this game; from enjoying the experience of riding a speeder bike through the desserts of Tattoine and the jungles of Akiva or trying to snag a tooth from the 2nd mouth of a Sarlacc pit.  Or fly your starship through the electricity storm in Kijimi's orbit.  Or better yet, sneak past tons of Storm Troopers and AT-ST's and loot an imperial base.  

This game has so much to offer in experiencing the Star Wars Universe, its crazy that anyone could think different.  

Highly recommend! Side note: I have 41 hours in the game and that was just beating the main story line while simultaneously taking on some of the side quests but I still have tons more to do!

It's a really, really beautiful game.  Absolutely gorgeous.  It drips with detail and it very, very, very "Star Wars".  The animal sidekick is cute, the robot sidekick and their developing relationship with the main character is well-handled, and the game largely (but not entirely) stays away from the more mythical elements to concentrate on the story of a kind of scummy loser trying and constantly failing to make a big score and forever insisting the next one will be better, all while largely not caring or being actively irritated by the big factions running roughshod over everything: including the Rebellion who constantly come across as overly dramatic blowhards.

The main story though really doesn't make a lot of sense, some of the twists are so incredibly telegraphed as to defy all reason - when the big "twist" came I was waiting for the ACTUAL twist because surely it wasn't going to be that predictable (and worse, lame!) but... it was! There are attempts at redemption for key characters that make no sense and are entirely undeserved, and the main bad guy is absent for 95% of the game and underwhelming and unimpressive when he does show up even though the game tries its best to make him seem formidable.

It's packed with a huge amount to do, often to its detriment as it suffers from the typical Ubisoft collectathon issues that their other games often struggle with.  But there's enough there to make you keep playing if only because you can see that they've ALMOST nailed it, they've ALMOST gotten it right, and those moments when everything does align and you get wrapped up at being inside a Star Wars you can see how good it could have been with some further tweaking.

In the end, I enjoyed it enough and was impressed enough with the parts I did like to give it a recommendation in spite of all the problems I had with it.  It's hardly a ringing endorsement, but if you really like Star Wars, if you like Ubisoft style open-world games, and if you like tootling around the galaxy doing crimes, getting into fights, playing cards and riding around on your space-bike there is a lot to enjoy here.

I've been very cautious about picking up a Ubisoft game since AC: Odyssey. A game so grindy and repetitive they have an in game store where you can pay real money to avoid playing the game you already bought. 

Outlaws by contrast is actually fun, and gives meaningful(ish) progression without grindy gameplay. In fact the core gameplay loop of infiltrate -> steal things -> trip an alarm -> panic -> blast your way out, is fun and rewarding. I did get to a point about 40 hours in where I decided to play another game for a bit as I was getting a bit tired of this, but I felt strongly enough to come back and finish it. It could use a couple of other options to break things up, e.g. more violent approaches, and more incentive to spend time in space, but generally I enjoyed playing it.

I particularly like the reputation system with the various crime syndicates, it drives home that you're navigating an underworld where betrayal is expected and favour and disfavour rise and fall. I'd have liked it to be a bit harder to get in the good books of everyone however. If you're even slightly attentive to what jobs you pick and rarely betray your employer, you can (and I did) end the game with Excellent reputation with every faction.

I also found the save system annoying at the start - in the open world you can save freely, but when you're somewhere you shouldn't be, or in an extended mission, you cannot save and saving is done through checkpoints. I usually despise checkpoint save systems but this grew on me: the checkpoints were generally well placed, so I felt tension (not wanting to lose progress) without being punished (e.g. sent back too far).

Story-wise it's a fun Star Wars romp but I found the plot became messier as the game went on. It felt like the game designers wanted to do gritty and lean more towards Andor, while they were pressured to instead go a bit more classic Star Wars positivism. This leads to the plot becoming a bit incoherent at the end unfortunately. Particularly, and this is major spoilers: [spoiler] Kay's insistence on saving ND-5 who has repeatedly made clear that he doesn't care and this is a job to him is particularly questionable. I didn't really see her having much of a motivation beyond "I like freedom and ND-5 is a slave", but ND-5 repeatedly insists that this is the way it is and he's got a job to do, and Kay shows herself repeatedly to be a cynic, hostile to any sort of 'cause' until she does a 180 and decides that one particular instance of robot slavery in a universe full of robot slavery is worth risking her life for. It's possible I missed something or didn't pay enough attention to their banter between missions which could have foreshadowed this more.[/spoiler]

To be honest, this game isn’t very good. From the start, we’re hit with constant crashes, making the gaming experience incredibly frustrating. It’s impossible to play for more than 30 minutes without the game crashing. This is a major issue, especially for a title of this scale, and it completely ruins the immersion.

The biggest problem, though, is the protagonist. She’s completely lacking in charisma, and it’s hard to get invested in her story. She spends the entire time insisting that she doesn’t need help and can’t trust anyone, which gets really annoying after a while. This “woke” attitude, as some might call it, only weighs down the narrative, making it almost unbearable. There’s no real emotional connection to the main character, and the story lacks any real impact.

The game also suffers from the classic Ubisoft syndrome: a ton of "FedEx" content (repetitive, meaningless tasks). As with all the Assassin’s Creed or Far Cry games, there’s a ton of items to collect, but most of them serve no purpose and only pad out the game’s length. It’s becoming a tired and repetitive formula. The game seems to force you to spend extra hours collecting pointless things instead of offering a more rich and engaging experience.

And then there’s the Star Wars license. Ubisoft somehow managed to ruin a legendary franchise. How did they manage to turn such a rich and captivating universe into such a disappointing experience? Honestly, I’m starting to question what they have planned for the future. At this point, I’m doubtful of their ability to deliver anything but empty shells filled with soulless content.

To wrap it up, it’s clear that I’ve come to realize that Ubisoft’s direction isn’t changing anytime soon. All their recent games, like this one, have been a letdown, and it’s unlikely I’ll return for any future titles. If this is the future of Ubisoft games, I think I’ll pass.

Figured I'd jump in a give my two cents on this game. 

The TL;DR is that its kind of underrated and a hidden gem. Its not going to bring home Game of the Year, its not anywhere near the same league as recent Larian or CDPR games, but I would definitely put it above average for RPG games in the past few years, and prolly the best of Ubi’s recent releases. And one I would recommend getting, tho wait till its on sale. 

Okay, so to be a little more in depth. For the Pros, in my opinion, the strongest aspect of this game is its story and characters. I feel like Ves’ character development, while subtle, is nice. Her interactions with the delightfully sarcastic ND are interesting, and the way the antagonists were written was actually good. This game’s take on the generic “gather the specialists and do a heist” I found interesting as well. The hacking and lockpicking are unique and were refreshing on a first playthrough. The maps are immersive and frankly beautiful. The stealth is very Ubi, tho I enjoy that kind of stealth gameplay so I personally liked it. I will grant I have not played on a higher difficulty than normal so I don’t know if the stealth action becomes more Splintercell on higher difficulties, but at normal its very Far Cry/Ghost Recon. The game also has a deluge of side quests, and many of them include encounters that require some level of problem solving to get to the objective. The reputation system was a balancing act that had me weighing which side quests I do in what order to achieve what I thought would be the best outcomes with various factions.

The cons. The game is a generic take on Oceans 11 with less characters. Just straight up, thats what it is. I know I said the maps were beautiful and immersive but they also would not be out of place in Far Cry or Ghost Recon and for a map like Kijimi, more could have been done to flesh out the local. The flight model of your ship isnt bad per say, but given one of my most played games is Elite Dangerous and I am a big fan of Ace Combat and DCS, I found it uninspired (aka I really wanted to map a HOTAS). The gunplay is IMO terrible compared to other Ubi games, further shoehorning stealth gameplay, but thankfully the game forces the player into situations where stealth is necessary without your tools on only one occasion. Speaking of that one occasion, its a very specific part of a very specific mission involving a Star Destroyer, and I ended up having to turn off the mini-games just to make it winable. And I was on normal difficulty. I cant tell if that was a failure of game design or the devs going full Soulslike. Speaking to sidequests one more time, honestly the rest of the sidequests I didn’t talk about, which is most of them, could be cut and pasted from Far Cry. Another criticism I have is the save system that limits where in the map that you can manually save and an autosave system that didn’t feel as reliable as I’d like for a game like this. I have also heard of game breaking bugs, but for my current run, I only had 2 so far and they full CTDs that also crashed my graphics software. 

But, ultimately, I would recommend this game in spite of the cons I listed. And prolly give it a good 7.5/10. Like, this game isnt Balder’s Gate 3 or Cyberpunk 2077 in its story. It isnt CoD or Battlefield in its gunplay. It isnt Splintercell or Sniper Elite in its stealth. This game isnt going to bring home many awards and might not hit the expectations of those of us that use Larian or CDPR as our metrics of “what makes a good game.” But in my opinion, this game is better than average and worth your time (but don’t buy it unless its on sale!), and for Ubi’ and its recent titles, thats actually good.

If this game didn't have open world, it would be pretty good adventure game. But here it is.

--
As a guy who loves Star Wars it is heartbreaking for me how this game came out, and I think that there are only two options for what went wrong: either the team behind the game totally doesn't understand how Star Wars work, or they fought the publisher for the whole time during development over every detail they wanted to do (and knowing Ubi I think it's the latter).
--
I bought this game only because it was on decent sale AND I read in the reviews that "Star Wars fan will enjoy it", and I can't say I did. There are couple moments when you can feel the soul the team wanted to pour into this game, but over the whole game it is catastrophically bland. 

GAME ENGINE
This is important - the game just isn't stable. I don't even know if it's better than Cyberpunk 2077 on the release day. I didn't have single day of playing without game crashing, freezing, Mission NPCs not moving, or even soft breaks, when after I died in a fight, the enemies didn't spawn after reloading and I had to load older save game to fix that. This isn't how the game should work after release, even more almost a year after release.

VISUALS
The Star Wars always stood with the great visuals - massive deserts, huge forests, breathtaking cities. In the game you can catch a glimpse here and there, but overall the game doesn't really shine. 
Also for the whole game I had a feeling that it just LOOKS BAD. For the GPU it requires to run smoothly, it should look a lot better (compared to Horizon Zero: Dawn, Witcher 3 or CP2077, they look a lot better and doesn't require such a GPU).

The movement animations are really mediocre. Kay Vess isn't introduced to us as ninja-skilled freerunner, yet when she climbs on walls, she leaps up high like well-trained assassin. The faces (even main characters!) are just bad. The animations rarely fit to the voiceover.

Even so simple things like making the barriers in the world feel real - no, if you come out of map, you're teleported back on it facing the other way. And there are possibilities - for example on Tatooine the even mention that the area is surrounded by sand ocean infested with krayt dragons, yet they didn't use them to kill the player when he leaves the map.

Jumping into water also causes a reload instead of explaining why she can't swim or why she cannot enter the water in this place.

And even that I disabled most of the UI before playing (knowing how Ubisoft loves to overflow screen with it), it still bothered me every 5 minutes with some unlocks.

SOUND DESIGN
Am I nitpicking? Maybe. For the price they're asking I expect nothing but excellent game. Also Star Wars was always relied on sounds - the lightsabers, blasters, THE SEISMIC CHARGE. And the music. The sound design in the game lacks, it's just flat, doesn't have extra oomph. The engines don't roar with the bass, the blasters doesn't sound like deadly weapons. Nix sounds are cool. The good boy is fine. The main theme is very nice but loops after a minute or so and halfway through the game it becomes boring for the player.

MECHANICS
Shooting is incredibly bad. Aiming is done very bad, and recoil seems inadequate to weapons used (basic pistol is uncontrollable, yet player is forced to use it whole game).
Game heavily relies on stealth yet it doesn't have option to move corpses.
Speeder is worse than Witcher's Roach. I can't say how many times I had to chase the speeder which I called and it drove god knows where. Sometimes it can drive over 1.5-metre boulder, and other time it shoots you in the air because it got caught on the curb.

WORLD&STORY
The main bad guy is so badly introduced, that until last mission I really didn't give a F about him. 
The world, even its size is impressive, delivering 3 big biomes (planets consisting of 1 biome) + 1 city and fragments of space around the planets, feels empty, because it's filled with repetitve tasks "go to my garden and get me the carrots", chests that don't really give you useful things and skins you won't use. Typical Ubisoft open world - big and useless.
At least closing act is done decently, so I will remember this game a little warmer.

OVERALL
Buying this game I knew it won't be excellent, but I didn't expect it to be straight mediocre. Most of the time playing I felt like I was playing Assassin's Creed with poor Star Wars texture pack. If you really want to play it, wait for big sale.

My number one surprise with SW:Outlaws is that it's a really good game.  Got it on sale, can't remember what interested me, beyond that I really needed something new to play and.... wow, no regrets.

It reminds me a little of an assassin's creed game - lots of sneaking around and bonking people from bushes - but unlike assassin's creed, it's fun.  Stealth isn't objective, it's a means to an end - you sneak to avoid getting caught, not because some arbitrary game mechanic or rule tells you to.  When you get seen, or start a fight, you deal with the natural consequences and move on.

There are 4 factions that you can be buds or enemies with - as long as you do a few missions here and there for each faction, it's easy to stay on their good sides.  The major faction missions tend to get you in good with one faction while pissing another off, but once you're past that it's pretty easy to stay off their hit lists.

This game makes you think on your feet.  I love games that do that.  They give you a few key skills right off the bat, and getting new skills often requires using the ones you already have.  This is genius - I probably would never have bothered, for example, quick-talking guards when caught, except it unlocked another skill if I did it 5 times and... actually use it on the regular now, it's usefulness having been properly demonstrated.

The game is big.  Lots to do.  Every planet is practically a whole game's worth of content.  I'm at 36 hours, and I still have tons to do.  I think I could tackle the end game any time, but I'm having fun just being an outlaw in the star wars universe.

Only gripe about the game itself is crashes - I'm at 36 hours, and I've had 5 or 6 crashes.  Two were in the first hour - that had me worried.  Strangely, it's always when I'm just having a conversation with an NPC in town.  Only sets me back a minute or two.

outlaws is a fun game, but it has a big problem. it's got fun adventure and stealth and stealing, and your trenchcoat robot friend is neat and should have been more of an active character, and it is SO nice to have a star wars game completely devoid of jedi and light side/dark side nonsense. the problem with this game is one that pervades the entirety of it, and it's how the main character, Kay Starwars-Outlaws, is written as an absolute dope.

to be clear up front: this is NOT about kay's voice actor or appearance or performance, i absolutely hate the creepy chuds online who are mad about "having to" play as a woman - this is about how she is written, the bad material that her actor had to try and make work. i was in fact extremely excited at the idea of being a cool lady smuggler in star wars world, and was very impressed when she meets the rebel alliance early on and simply does not give a heck about them. the problem is everything else - through the mechanics you learn that she's a good marksman and climber, but is otherwise written as a complete idiot with no drive or ambition or charm. for a movie criminal she's a horrible liar and it is Always clear when she's lying, and she constantly swerves on a dime between naive good-hearted helpful main character and weird bumbling greedy idiot. she doesn't even seem to know how the communication of criminal culture works despite growing up on crime world with crime mom, and she would be absolutely incapable of doing the work she's supposed to do without her cute sentient alien dog with the convenient ability to do most of her stealing and button-pressing for her. nyx is great, but it's so clear through the writing and gameplay that he is effectively the only one of the pair who can get things done.

i understand the impulse to make outlaws a story about the origin of an eventually successful smuggler, but Massive swung way too hard in the "inexperienced" direction and made her an oaf who never stops being an oaf. instead of being a cool down-on-her-luck small time criminal with dreams of glory, she's an arrogant screw-up who only survives through luck and wild coincidence. we meet her and are immediately told by every other character that she's a screw-up, despite being taught by her very experienced crime mom, and then she screws up the first two heists you do by either not paying attention or suddenly pointing her gun at her squad and yelling about money. you learn very quickly that kay is a strangely unlikeable protagonist.

the story then just dumps a bunch of convenient resources on her with very little justification - she just Happens to stumble on a big cool spaceship that is equipped with a speeder and a dude's jacket that somehow fits her perfectly, as if it was designed for her, and then just Happens to crash land on top of a guy who wants to help her fix her ship, and she's barely even suspicious when he says he'll do it for the love of the game. even with this huge stroke of luck, she still constantly complains, even to crime bosses and people who will give her jobs, that she actually has to do small stealing to be trusted for big stealing. she's not a loveable awkward person that needs to learn to trust her instincts and her dog buddy, she's portrayed as a constantly confused person who always seems baffled that she managed to make it through these harrowing situations, then thinks "oh yeah, i'm the best, that's why" like she's in denial, like she somehow knows that the player was the one who actually did it.

on and on this goes through the entire game - she's always either weirdly standoffish, completely incapable of reading situations, or confused that criminals don't want to be buddies with her. every time she tries to "play it cool," she stammers and gets herself into trouble. she doesn't even grow into the cool han solo-archetype charming rogue they seem to want her to become, people just seem to purposefully ignore her empty-brain awkward stumbling and assume she's more capable than her communication style implies. Kay is written like, if this was a movie and the player didn't get to guide her through heists and missions, she'd immediately get shot because she'd get spotted in enemy territory immediately and fail to stammer her way out of it. the *entire* game hinges on a huge coincidence that saved her from being killed by a criminal syndicate, and then she continually proves that she as a character perhaps wasn't worth saving. and yet the ending is treated as if she's grown into herself, somehow, which never actually happened.

in terms of representation, this game sucks and only serves to play into the false narrative that women can't be cool. i was *so* excited to play a game as a cool smuggler lady, but instead i had to play as a three stooges smuggler lady - me as moe, the idiot who thinks he's a genius, and nyx as a hyper-competent curly (ND-5 is larry in that he is just kinda there a lot of the time and doesnt really do all that much). if they continue this game as a series, they need to write in enough time between games to where kay is *actually* badass. i want to play a character who thinks her way out of trouble, not one who's about to die when a huge deus ex machina gets her out of it.

now that i think about it, though, if they had truly, *purposefully* leaned into the slapstick nature of kay being an idiot, and effectively made outlaws a a mr. magoo/mr bean/wallace&gromit-type doofus comedy in which she literally stumbles into success with the help of her actually-smart companions, this may have been the best video game story ever written

edit: i just learned that outlaws' writer was the same guy who wrote far cry 4 through 6. it now makes a lot of sense that outlaws is full of *ideas* of interesting characters, without any actual effective character writing. that's a problem that's plagued the far cry series for a decade.

Quick thing with how I review stuff. I don’t hark on the story too much as I’m a general proponent of “skip the story, play the game”. I’m an open world sandbox veteran so I can deal with bad writing, acting, or script as long as the gameplay can hold itself up. This is why the bad lip syncing doesn’t bother me as much as it may others, because I only have to deal with it for short cutscenes before the game just gives control back to me and we move on. As such, you’re an up and comer smuggler that messes up a couple of times in short order, angering a well connected syndicate that puts a half-million bounty on you after stealing his one of a kind ship. Not a prototype this time, just a sort of “last surviving” type ship as it was too expensive to mass produce. So we’re let off into the world to make some friends and allies, while Kay Vess learns a very common lesson in the media; You can’t do everything alone. Something she probably should have learned nearly immediately when she almost torpedoes an entire mission when she points a gun at her client in the middle of an imperial base. Girl, can you at least wait until we’re outside?

The story here is serviceable, though it clearly wishes our protagonist Kay Vess was just Han Solo. Not every in-universe smuggler needs to be a Solo analog, but here we are. I will say it gets dangerously close to being as annoying as the protagonist from Forspoken, in that she won't shut the farrik up about nothing... But she hasn't quite crossed that line. There's moments very early on when she calls her contact a couple times to say almost nothing, something like "I've made it to the wall of the compound", I forget the exact words. It was a few days and 30 hours of gameplay ago. Absolutely worthless as an exchange, but it evens out later where a lot of her quips are to her helper pet Nix which tend to be more acceptable in context. In similar games like Horizon it makes more sense when Aloy is self-narrating as she grew up very lonely but I'm sure we all grew tired of hearing "Looks like a cave..." as we're driving by to some other objective. Vess does not do this. I’ve also been informed that this has some practical use; the game relies heavily on autosaves. So when you save, exit, or crash to desktop… Loading back in mid-mission may treat you with one of these nothingburgers of dialog to help remind you of what your task is.

The gameplay is familiar. It’s a Ubisoft game, so that means it’s one of two things. Creed or Cry? This is on the Creed scale as you sneak around in bushes or ventilation smoke, knock out helmeted stormtroopers, and find vent shafts as alternative routes into large bases and complexes. With us we have Nix, a little furry critter that just functions as our cellphone or drone from Watch Dogs as it helps pickpocket guards, pushes buttons, distracts and even attacks enemies in what is basically a stun/crowd control move. I love him a lot. At a certain point he gets kidnapped for a mission and I had to resist just going John Wick on everyone because I was dealing with tougher guards that couldn’t just be tapped down.

This game doesn't so much throw you map icons ad nauseum, though I am finding myself a little overwhelmed with quest entries. I find it difficult to discern which are the most important and relevant. My whole quest log is absolutely filled to the brim with this kind of stuff, none of them really tell you what the reward is (only the contracts do that) so it's difficult to discern which to focus on and what's just flavor. At some point on a day off work I kind of want to just clear my entire log that isn't my main quest... at least as my tools allow. I keep running into objectives that require tools I don’t have yet, like being able to drive over bodies of water. I wish the game made this a bit more obvious before I spent twenty minutes circling a mountain before googling the objective name and learning I needed some kind of cutter tool I won’t get until later in the story.

The game is absolutely gorgeous. It reminds me of Cyberpunk, with how lighting fixtures will pierce through the fog and weather. Every now and then I’ll be driving or walking and just be struck by a stunning vista where I need to stop and enter photo mode. Alas I can’t put images in Steam reviews so if you’re seeing this on my other socials, some of my favorites will be littered throughout this review. (On Steam you can likely just jump to my profile). I was particularly impressed with how realistic the walkways in Kijimi were. Seeing the snow clumped around the walkways is very much how it behaves in real life as people walk through or kick some off to the side. I’ve almost taken a screenshot of the literal ground once because I was so impressed with the melted snow clumping.

The upgrades to your speederbike are too few and far between. Since my first impressions post I’ve upgraded it a couple more times and it doesn’t stop the vehicle from being heavily unresponsive. Turning barely actually turns but if I hold the turning key down a second longer than the game wants me to, I just make a hard left into a rock and that will send Vess flying and losing a health bar. There’s a mission where you have to keep pace with a teammate as you escape some imperials and I had to restart it about seven times because she’d fly off into the distance while I struggled with running into rocks, walls, and even enemy speederbikes and I couldn’t nitro boost back to her quick enough because she just -leaves-. Maddening. I hate it.

The stealth gameplay is variable. At certain times the stealth will fail through somewhat inconsistent rules. When infiltrating a large imperial base the game is nice enough to just let me shoot up one room and then I can proceed as normal. However, other times… There’s a phrase that Yahtzee coined that lives rent free in my brain called the “cockup cascade”. This happens more often in the open world syndicate bases, where if you mess up the stealth it will alert the whole area, an alarm will sound, and enemies will constantly come pouring out of noninteractable doorways to the point where it’s not worth the time. I once reloaded a save and saw that I lost about ten minutes, including having made purchases from a nearby vendor and some progress to a new Nix ability. There’s aspects to the game that incentivize heavy use of save scumming, which I don’t like. It reminds me of attempting old racing games where if you get spun out you may as well restart the entire match. 

I’m almost afraid to admit how much of my current hour count is from the card game. I don’t fully comprehend how it all works but the rush of winning after two or three failed attempts is incredibly exciting, but I’m not looking forward to one of the DLC’s where it’s highly Sabaac focused. It’s become a sort of night capper for me before bed where I go find a table to play a couple games.

[h1]STAR WARS OUTLAWS[/h1]

The most recent, much maligned, and not hugely popular Star Wars game. 
Was it worth the hate? TLDR: [spoiler]Ehh... somewhat, yeah? Buy it at a big discount if you like Star Wars as a setting, and/or Tomb Raider-style games.[/spoiler]
Let's start with - 

[h3]THE GOOD:[/h3] The core gameplay loop is very satisfying when it's performing well. Sneaking through areas, stealing everything you can put your hands (or pet's teeth) on, killing guards that you can't avoid, or going loud when you feel like it or mess up. It feels like you're always improvising when you're in serious combat, which is absolutely a good thing, and intended. The main gimmick of your pet 'Nix' is actually pretty well implemented and is fun to use (most of the time - more on that in a minute). He can bite enemies, pickpocket them, break stuff, open things - it's a pretty decent system. There's a vast array of areas and biomes, zones and vaults to do this across, and the level design tends (again, more in a minute) to be pretty good. This core gameplay is broken up by a wide array of side activities which tend to be alright, though certain things like Sabaac will not be to everyone's taste. Space combat feels fine, not exceptional, but fine. Progression to me felt fine, but really if you have no taste for side activities it may treat you worse than me. [b]Just racing through the main story is really not the way to go.[/b] The story and side stories have their moments of genuine tension or other decent parts, but unfortunately, that's about all I have to say about that in the "good" category. 
All in all, this is a pretty decent list of things to have going for a game. So why am I on the fence about recommending it? Because of - 

[h3]THE BAD:[/h3] We will start right out of the gate with what is by far the biggest negative this game has going for it - the STANK of JANK. This game is absolutely LACED with jank, and it is immensely frustrating, because it is always lurking to disrupt your plans or ruin your immersion at the worst times. Trying to find the exact right pixel to stand on to initiate conversations with some of the NPCs in some scenarios. Trying to pick up the right item on a crowded floor in a hurry during combat when seconds count. Parkour feeling clunky ALL the time, and your character missing ledges or sliding off of stuff that it really feels like you should have grabbed or landed on. Carefully aiming a critical shot from behind cover, and having your reticle light up red, only to pull the trigger and hit some random piece of bullshit terrain, thereby alerting every guard in the vicinity to your presence and ruining your quiet approach. Guards randomly seeing or spotting stuff that it feels like they shouldn't have. Guards NOT seeing or hearing stuff that it feels like they should have. Finding a perfect hiding spot and preparing to send Nix to go cause some mischief - only to realize that the angle makes it impossible to control him. Perhaps worst of all, being in the middle of a big, cinematic mission only to realize the door button or other thing you need to move forward hasn't loaded properly, forcing you to reload a save, lose progress, and totally break your flow to progress. The game, in short, just does not feel polished at all, and keep in mind that this review (and playthrough it is based on) is way after release. This is absolutely brutal because it often totally ruins what would otherwise be really, genuinely good gameplay. This is the core sin of Star Wars Outlaws, and it is a tough one to swallow. 
There are some other complaints to go with it, though - 
Level design and parkour: while the level design is pretty good, it tends to be a bit 'railroad-ey.' What do I mean? Almost every mini-area in the open world that is a restricted zone or other place a thief would be trying to get has about two entrances: the front door, and the totally-not-obviously-badly-secured-back-or-side-or-vent entrance screaming PLEASE GO IN HERE. While you tend to have a decent amount of agency on how you do business once you're IN a level, how you GET IN a level has essentially no nuance to it at all. It might be a minor gripe to some people, but I couldn't help but think back to titles like AC Unity with nearly infinite ways to get through a place, and how poorly this compared. And on the topic of parkour, for a game that seems like it should really have climbing as a major element, it's pretty shocking how much stuff you simply... can't climb. Most buildings - no. Most rocks - no. Kay slides right off them like hot butter. Climbing is allowed in designated yellow paint areas only, and nowhere else (on the topic of yellow paint; there's more of it than I'd like. There's literally arrows pointing to where you need to go in many cases.). 
We will spoiler the story (and general narrative tone) complaints just in case anyone cares: 
[spoiler]The story, unfortunately, is usually pretty predictable. Every character that you think will betray you or have a change of heart and work with you will do so. Every job that you think will go sideways will. Most of the side characters are just forgettable tropes - we have droid guy, who fucking loves droids and has no other characteristics. Bomb girl, who fucking loves bombs and doesn't really have much else going on. Rebellion guy(s), who will not shut up about their moral high ground over everyone else, and also (you guessed it) do not have any other real traits. Your player character is not too much better, and spends the entire game bitter at almost everyone (yet somehow too friendly), and cocky (yet needs constant reassurance and handholding). Kay Vess is totally selfish, but then acts on other people's behalf randomly, without warning, and while I'm sure it was intended to feel like character development, it doesn't read that way to me. It just feels inconsistent. 
The narrative tone, as well, is a bit frustrating, and while this part is definitely my personal opinion, I wish that the franchise would take the kid gloves off just a little bit with the writing, especially characters like Kay Vess. The reality is that Kay Vess is a thief. She is out for herself, she's been surrounded by petty crime her entire life, and she grew up on a rough planet with almost no one to look out for her. Why is she so appalled by killing or double crossing/a general lack of loyalty among criminals (especially when the player character has the opportunity to kill hundreds and betray every single employer that they get)? Why is she punching stormtroopers in the head with her bare hands (and why is it working)? She should be carrying a vibroknife or other lethal melee weapon (a baton? something?), and she should be killing people in cold blood. She should know that business is business - obviously, everyone is trying to pull one over on the next guy.[/spoiler]
Lastly, while I don't love to harp on 'woke' in games, if you hate 'woke' you should absolutely skip this title. You'd think the galaxy was suffering some sort of horrible, multi-species genetic crisis the way that every single character that you interact with is female (literally about 85%), and the male characters are reserved for the absolute worst villains in the story, or random cannon fodder. It is girlboss simulator, and I don't mean that in a positive sense. 

[h1]So what's the verdict?[/h1]
There's a game that could have been genuinely really good hiding under A LOT of problems - if you like games of this type, or Star Wars (especially if you want to get away from force users), this game might be worth playing anyway. It's good for about 50 hours of mixed gameplay, longer if you want to do more side content. If you wait for a discount, I'd say it's probably worth $10-$20, depending on how much it interests you. I got it for about $20, and I don't really regret it, and so at the end of the day, I guess it's a recommend from me.

Star Wars Outlaws is not a power fantasy — and that’s exactly why it works.

If you slow down, read the journal, listen to conversations, and play like a cautious scoundrel instead of a checklist-chasing hero, this game really opens up.

What surprised me most is how thoughtfully designed it is at a human scale. Quests are clear without being hand-holdy. Intel often comes from listening instead of icons. NPCs will sometimes call out to you rather than waiting to be clicked. You’re encouraged to weigh risk, reputation, and timing — not just rush in swinging a blaster.

The reputation system matters, stealth is situational (not puzzle-box perfect), and the world rewards restraint. You don’t have to do everything, and in fact, you shouldn’t. Ignoring opportunities that feel risky or inconvenient is often the smart, in-character choice — and the game supports that.

Exploration is clever too: speeder races and traversal help you learn the planet naturally, landmarks matter, and some jobs give directions instead of map pins, which keeps immersion intact if you resist the urge to waypoint everything.

It’s not flawless. NPC interaction depth is limited, and time-of-day transitions can feel abrupt if you linger and observe. But these are small seams in what is otherwise a surprisingly grounded and atmospheric Star Wars experience.

If you’ve ever wanted a Star Wars game that lets you exist in the galaxy rather than dominate it — one that respects patience, discretion, and moral restraint — this is absolutely worth your time. I strongly recommend it to players who enjoy slow-burn RPGs, immersive worlds, and thoughtful design. Give it a chance, play it deliberately, and it may surprise you as much as it did me.

The most frustrating thing about this game is that it could have been great. But it's such a miserable slog that it's just not worth it. Buggy quests, locations, and terrain. Obtuse interface with no mini-map, requiring you to constantly pause and bring up the full map, even when blasting along at full speed on the bike. 
The bike controls are awful, too; good luck avoiding terrain or hitting anything during the many speeder-focused missions. Don't worry; the starship controls also suck, with tiny or no indicators for cooldowns, target locations, or orientation (and again, no mini-map, so you're still constantly pausing).
Most major missions are on rails, and simply walking a few feet to the wrong direction brings up a full-screen "RETURN TO GAME" warning with an absurd 10-second countdown; so much for immersion. 
The gameplay loop is infuriating. The game can't decide if it wants to be a stealth game, assassin game, or action game, so it just does all three poorly. There's little to no indication of whether stunning someone (which actually kills them, by the way) will immediately summon every enemy in the area. The enemy detection is worthless. There's no way to survey an area before entering, so for stealth, you're stuck with blind luck or reloading a save once you have a full count of enemies. You can't move or hide bodies, so the first time you assassinate (oh, sorry "permanently knock out") someone, it starts a timer as to when someone will see the body and trigger an alarm. Unlike pretty much every other stealth/assassin game out there, whistling doesn't bring one guard over; it brings literally everyone in earshot, and the moment any of them see you, again, the WHOLE PLACE goes active. That would be fine if this was a functional action game, but your weapon choices are boring, and every useful weapon is gated by the game's idiotic pick-up system that disallows reloading or storing weapons you've found, making every firefight just the same repetitive pew-pew with your little peashooter. Given that these stealth quests make up most of the game's "action," the frustrating and drawn-out gameplay loop is a constant source of misery. 
I played all the way through, in the hope that the decent story and characters would lead to a fun payoff, but no, the endgame is a complete letdown, too. The end "boss" is just a bunch of running and whistling combined with instant death and constant reloads. The best DLC isn't playable until after the main story, so you don't get the most useful upgrades and gear until there's nothing left to do in the game except rep missions (which you don't need because the game's over) and shipping quests (which are pointless because, again, the game is over). 
If you're a huge Star Wars fan, I recommend just reading the storyline on Wookieepedia or watching some videos, Don't slog through this mess like I did, hoping for something good at the end.

Outside of that trademark Ubisoft performance issues, some repetitive gameplay design, outdated exploration and a large quantity of fetch quests, Star Wars Outlaws is one of my favourite action-adventure experiences in recent memory. I really fell in love with the story, the characters, several systems, world design, and a very true to promise recreation of the Scoundrel fantasy. When it gets running, Outlaws is at the top of its game, seamlessly weaving an engaging Star Wars underworld tale, with a high-stakes heist adventure. Set pieces and main story missions are fantastic, even if enemy encounters are disappointingly one-dimensional, and the endless typical Ubisoft platforming gets in the way. Combat feels thrilling, and tactical to a certain degree thanks to Nix, and smart permanent blaster pistol that offers quite a bit of versatility in playstyle. Unfortunately, for a game built around stealth, the systems are disappointingly barebones, relying on simple button takedowns, and few environmental elements. Massive's expertise with guns makes for great weapon design, that really allows for you to land on some choice weaponry throughout the game, which is why its confusing as to why they made a stealth-driven game. The game's four open worlds are a major highlight though. Impeccably designed, rich with detail, and full of things to do, even if they are largely fetch quests. It also helps that the game's (disappointingly) simple space flight sequences in the Trailblazer are made all the more engaging in space dogfights with overwhelming odds. 

Overall, a lot of Outlaws feels like wasted potential, a sad reoccuring tale within Ubisoft's many talented and skilled studios. But when it really puts its best foot forward, and commits to the Scoundrel fantasy, Outlaws remains one of my favourite Star Wars gaming experiences ever.

Star Wars represents a galaxy of endless possibility with thousands of planets, countless stories, limitless character potential. Outlaws takes this premise and funnels you through a linear, planet-locked narrative that wastes the IP's open-world potential. You're not exploring a living galaxy; you're moving through set pieces on rails.

The Protagonist Problem
Kay Vess embodies everything wrong with modern AAA character design: she's simultaneously unremarkable and inexplicably successful. She lacks the roguish charm of Han Solo, the earned competence of a seasoned scoundrel, or any real personality that justifies her meteoric rise in the underworld. She doesn't earn her reputation—she stumbles into it through plot convenience. Compare this to games like Cyberpunk 2077, where V feels like your character navigating Night City. Kay is just someone you're forced to watch make questionable decisions.
Shallow Systems Disguised as Depth
The game mechanics feel like checkbox features rather than engaging systems:

Minigames lack substance
The speeder feels like a theme park ride, not a vehicle
The economy is meaningless—credits have no weight
Customization is surface-level at best

It's the Ubisoft formula dressed in Star Wars clothing: pretty, but hollow.

What Actually Works (And Why It's Not Enough)
The presentation is genuinely solid—visually authentic Star Wars, excellent music, decent shooting mechanics and a cool slicing mechanic. The problem? These are the baseline features for a AAA Star Wars title, not selling points. A beautiful facade doesn't compensate for weak foundations.

The Rockstar Standard
This game needed the depth of a Rockstar production: meaningful choices, a living world with economic systems that matter, characters with actual depth, emergent gameplay that creates stories rather than following them. Instead, we got a nice looking game that plays it safe and delivers nothing memorable.

The Bottom Line
Star Wars Outlaws is visual spectacle without substance, a game that understands Star Wars aesthetically but fundamentally misunderstands what makes great games in this universe compelling. It's not broken, it's just aggressively mediocre in the worst way possible.

End of the line, its maybe worth it on sale if you're DESPERATE for Star Wars content. Otherwise, spend your money on another game.

Star Wars represents a galaxy of endless possibility with thousands of planets, countless stories, limitless character potential. Outlaws takes this premise and funnels you through a linear, planet-locked narrative that wastes the IP's open-world potential. You're not exploring a living galaxy; you're moving through set pieces on rails.

The Protagonist Problem
Kay Vess embodies everything wrong with modern AAA character design: she's simultaneously unremarkable and inexplicably successful. She lacks the roguish charm of Han Solo, the earned competence of a seasoned scoundrel, or any real personality that justifies her meteoric rise in the underworld. She doesn't earn her reputation—she stumbles into it through plot convenience. Compare this to games like Cyberpunk 2077, where V feels like your character navigating Night City. Kay is just someone you're forced to watch make questionable decisions.
Shallow Systems Disguised as Depth
The game mechanics feel like checkbox features rather than engaging systems:

Minigames lack substance
The speeder feels like a theme park ride, not a vehicle
The economy is meaningless—credits have no weight
Customization is surface-level at best

It's the Ubisoft formula dressed in Star Wars clothing: pretty, but hollow.

What Actually Works (And Why It's Not Enough)
The presentation is genuinely solid—visually authentic Star Wars, excellent music, decent shooting mechanics and a cool slicing mechanic. The problem? These are the baseline features for a AAA Star Wars title, not selling points. A beautiful facade doesn't compensate for weak foundations.

The Rockstar Standard
This game needed the depth of a Rockstar production: meaningful choices, a living world with economic systems that matter, characters with actual depth, emergent gameplay that creates stories rather than following them. Instead, we got a nice looking game that plays it safe and delivers nothing memorable.

The Bottom Line
Star Wars Outlaws is visual spectacle without substance, a game that understands Star Wars aesthetically but fundamentally misunderstands what makes great games in this universe compelling. It's not broken, it's just aggressively mediocre in the worst way possible.

End of the line, its maybe worth it on sale if you're DESPERATE for Star Wars content. Otherwise, spend your money on another game.

Despite the common complaints concerning performance issues, my game only crashed twice during my entire playtime. I played on GeForce Now, so I believe if played with a sufficiently powerful computer such issues are not relevant. Just thought I should put that out there in case its useful. 

Now, the actual game itself. 10/10. This is what a Star Wars game should be. Having played and loved Jedi Fallen Order/Survivor, I was initially hesitant to approach this game, since I wasn't too excited about the idea of playing as an average "outlaw" as opposed to a Jedi. BUT, I was 100% WRONG! The experience of playing this game, is as "Star Wars" as it gets. The amount of love put in by all of the development team is absurd. The detail to attention, the cameos/references, the world building. Everything is true to the soul of Star Wars and builds on it masterfully. The music is memorable and fitting, at times with clear motifs from John Williams' scores. The sounds, graphics, combat. Everything feels really immersive and natural. The story feels simple, yet there is depth to the character(s). The main character (Kay Vess) has a sidekick pet (Nix) and it's amazing how they've managed to build so much functionality into him. For the first time playing a game, I felt like the "pet" was not just decorative but actually part of the experience. That brings me to level design. The level design is also brilliant. It is obvious, clear, there is a good bit of challenging combat, and ease of navigation (especially with climbing which is actually fast and not frustratingly slow). The amount of diverse aliens, languages, enemies, worlds, environments, lighting is really immersive in the vast universe of Star Wars. Playing is satisfying, stealth is actually rewarding and not frustrating or boring. The side quests are nuanced. There is also a lot of dynamic interactions in the game: dialogues adapt based on the actions/decisions/quests you do. The story and relationships are also nuanced and doesn't just feel like a boring or repetitive story. 

This is a really fun, impressive, and original game--all the while being a STAR WARS game. It is sad this game hasn't been optimized to be playable for the more general consumer. If I had played this on my own gaming computer, I am sure I would have had a very different view. As I said, I was running it on GeForce Now with MAXXED out settings on a 5080RTX card, and it was running at around 10-12 GB of VRAM. If you have a very capable machine, or are able to play through cloud gaming, I would very much recommend this game. Oh I also got it for $20 bucks discounted so that's pretty sweet. Anyways, I hope this was helpful.

For anyone who is worried about Ubisoft open worlds, I actually found this one to be good. There are no radio towers to climb - you discover locations either by getting really close to them, through quests, or by looking through your binoculars. And while many don't contain loot, they do contain upgrade materials (don't worry, there isn't a crafting system, and if you want, you can buy most materials from merchants anyway), and usually some fun lore. And because of this, I didn't feel the need to 100% the game, and it was better for it. If I visited a location, it was because I wanted to be there for story/quest reasons, or to find some item I learned naturally, or just because the location looked interesting, not because I climbed a tower that revealed a busywork icons on the map.

If it sounds like this isn't the most overwhelming praise, it is because it isn't. Taken individually, all the elements (except for the story, which I actually found pretty dang good) are good, but not great. Despite that, I think the game is more than the sum of its parts. I can't quite describe it, except to say that I had way more fun with this game than I expected, and than it had any right to be, just looking back over my own comments.

TL;DR, this is a good game that is better than the sum of its parts, and I had a lot of fun with it. Definitely worth getting on sale, and maybe full-price if you like open-world games, now that the devs fixed the gameplay and added some free DLC.
